4.1  Introduction
Artificial intelligence is not just a form of technology; it is also, in many ways, about us. AI 
has profound implications for us as humans, for our own self-­image, and for how we think 
about and experience “the self.” Many seek to use AI to understand the human mind, to 
replicate or even to exceed human minds. There are intimate overlaps between AI, cognitive 
science, and philosophy of mind, wherein issues such as the nature of consciousness and of 
intelligence is scrutinized. AI feasts on data and this includes data about human beings. New 
technologies using AI gather information, analyze it, and feed it back to us, within a ­fast-­
changing world where ideas about, and images of, AI are impacting how we think of ourselves. 
What data is used, when it is used, how, and by whom can impact on how we see ourselves. 
These issues also concern knowledge: the quest to gain knowledge about our minds and our 
intelligence through AI research, and the ways in which AI technologies now mediate so 
much of our knowledge. The manner in which we conceptualize and imagine AI has a two-­
way relationship with how we think of the self: it both arises from, and potentially impacts, 
how the self is conceptualized and experienced.
Many philosophers of technology have noted how our technology both bears our stamp 
and influences us in response, and naturally others working specifically on AI have likewise 
recognized that a central issue in understanding AI is understanding how it is shaped by us 
and in turn shapes us. Some of my past work raises such issues, including the need for AI 
ethics to explore and understand human nature (Boddington 2017), and multiple ways in 
which AI brushes up against the self (Boddington 2023). In her book The AI Mirror (2024), 
published after this chapter was first completed, Shannon Vallor investigates the ways in 
which certain forms of AI which receive and reflect “data gathered from human lives and 
persons” (p.  35) are both powerful and dangerous, exploring the precise nature of this 
metaphorical “mirror” in order to illuminate the questions. Such contemporary work 
indicates the ongoing importance and interest of such topics.
Will we conclude that, in its advanced forms, AI is another being to whom we must 
somehow relate? Will I find that AI “knows my own mind” better than I do? Will AI predict my 
AI and Knowledge of the Self
PAULA BODDINGTON
4

--- Page 54 ---

Paula Boddington
44
wants and provide them before I am even aware of them, and if so, what of my own agency? 
Might the boundaries of our own selves be blurred as we “merge” with such technologies in 
various ways? Ethical issues regarding AI, such as questions of our agency, control, and 
autonomy; the spectre, or promise, of transhumanism; even deceptively simple questions 
such the benefits and harms of AI, all rest upon assumptions about the self. They require us 
to consider how AI might impact our very perception of personal agency and the nature and 
boundaries of our selves.
The term “artificial intelligence” covers a wide array of possibilities, from grand projects to 
create intelligent and even conscious machines and extravagant imaginings about distant 
possibilities, to precise technical specification of discrete tasks for a multiplicity of concrete 
applications. Indeed, much of the complexity, interest, and difficulty of discussing the impli-
cations of AI is precisely related to the wide applications and context of the field. There are 
similar complexities in discussing “the self.”
Within the discourse around AI, there exist not simply different views on the relationship 
between AI and the self, but different ways of conceptualizing the self. This mirrors the 
complexity of discussions of the self in other discourse. Perhaps different notions of the self 
are in play here, parallel discussions that should be treated separately; or perhaps there are 
interesting relationships between seemingly different ways of looking at the issues, upon 
which our fast-­changing technological world is having an impact. This chapter examines the 
impact of AI upon how we conceptualize, experience, and gain knowledge of the self.
Consider one example. Philosophers, along with sci-­fi fans, have for many years pondered 
what it might be like to be a “brain in a vat,” whether it makes sense to conceive of finding 
oneself in a totally different body, and so on, to address ethical theories, questions of mind and 
body, and personal identity. But these thought experiments are becoming increasingly reified 
as we experience life in a virtual world of screens and action-­at-­a-­distance; erstwhile armchair 
contemplations acquire an aura of technological feasibility as we contemplate the possibilities 
of “mind uploads.” What might be the effects of moving these thought experiments from the 
comfort of the philosopher’s armchair or the sci-­fi fan’s bookshelf into the experiences and 
imaginings of the everyday?
AI exists within an explicit or assumed arena of technological progress, sometimes with 
the presumption of progress towards “fully” understanding the mind and, with it, the self.1 In 
contrast are claims that ideas of “the self” are conditioned by culture and by technology itself, 
so that technology does not so much help us to reveal the self but influences our very 
understanding of it. Hence, we must take seriously the complicating factor that we increasingly 
experience the world, including ourselves, through the lens of the very AI that we are 
examining. The need to consider these issues from a historical perspective should be evident 
when we reflect that ideas about the nature of the mind have tended to reflect contemporary 
technology. In an age dominated by progress in computing, the mind is so often seen as a kind 
of computer and in terms of information: an idea of the mind as, roughly, essentially about 
information gathering and processing, goal-­directed behavior, about patterns of responding 
(outputs) based on inputs, with the possibility of recursive self-­improvement.
AI is present to us not simply as hardware and software but as a social imaginary, in what 
its presumed possibilities mean for how we think of ourselves both individually and collectively. 
As well as discourse around AI and its progress and everyday use, this includes the visual 
imagery of AI which can convey ideas in a very impactful manner (Cave et al. 2018). What 
might be the links between everyday experience and imagination around AI technologies on 
the one hand, and scientific, technological, and philosophical explorations of the mind on 
the other?

--- Page 55 ---

AI and Knowledge of the Self
45
Consider a contrasting example. Ask someone who was a child in, say, the 1960s how they 
envisaged life in the future, and one likely common answer is that we expected to be travelling 
around on our own personal jetpacks. Disappointingly, this invigorating futuristic possibility 
never happened. There may be interesting questions about our naïve hopes, and interesting 
engineering questions too, but there seems no essential link between these two domains of 
inquiry. We were just wrong.
In contrast, if our experience, use, and imagination regarding AI have an impact upon 
how individuals or societies experience and understand the self, this is, at least prima facie, 
centrally relevant to discussions about the nature of the self. Suppose we fear that linking our 
minds directly to the internet might destroy our individuality, or we find that life in the virtual 
world or our everyday experience of remote technology leads us to experience our bodies as 
irrelevant to who we “really” are. Perhaps we find that everyday experience of outsourcing 
tasks, or using AI which is opaque to our understanding, leads us to adjust our sense of our 
own agency. To insist that it is not pertinent to consider the responses of “ordinary” human 
beings here because cognitive scientists, computer scientists, and philosophers are able to 
supply the answers for us simply does not work in the same way as in the jetpack example. For 
to tell me that I am wrong about how I experience the nature and boundaries of my own self, 
that I am wrong to feel my agency is constrained is to beg certain questions about the nature 
of the individual self. At the very least, we would need an account of why views of ordinary 
people about their own selves differ from those of “experts.”
Charles Taylor’s Sources of the Self (1989) explores the historical and cultural development 
of notions of the self. Topics of relevance for us include an individual’s control of the self, the 
ability to remake themselves and how such re-­makings might be understood, and the manner 
in which boundaries are drawn around the self. Taylor describes what he calls the “punctual 
self”: a conception of the self whereby a person is able to look at aspects of their mind as if 
these were somehow external to a core self, and open to manipulation and change. He charts 
how this notion developed through changing accounts of the mind and the body, and the 
abandonment of a teleological view of the world in favor of a world which humans are able 
to understand and control, finding its full form through Locke and those Enlightenment 
thinkers Locke influenced (Taylor  1989, p.  160). Taylor distinguishes the “buffered self,” 
characteristic of modernity, where definite boundaries are drawn around the self and what is 
external to it, from the “porous self” which is much more permeable to outside forces such as 
from those of the spirit world (Taylor 2007, 2008). Such distinctions will be useful for fram-
ing questions about the impact of AI upon our knowledge of the self. A complex picture with 
elements of both buffered and porous selves arises from aspects of the social imaginary 
around AI juxtaposed with the actual and proposed uses of AI.
We will now further unpack some contrasting ideas of the self in relation to different areas 
of AI. Certain questions about the self will come to the fore: prominently, the role of cognition, 
agency, embodiment, and the boundaries of the self. In the second section of this chapter, we 
examine some bold aspirations for AI and for humanity and how these relate to and depend 
upon certain conceptions of the individual mind and its potentials. This section will note 
some profound differences between the first and third person case and the use of thought 
experiments both past and present, the question of agency of the self, and how the notion of 
embodiment might be eclipsed or conversely brought to the fore. The third section examines 
concrete applications of AI and some of the considerable body of work produced by social 
scientists who have closely examined the impact of uses of AI upon how we understand and 
experience the self and ideas such as the “digital self.” The role of data is crucial, as well as 
issues of the boundary of the individual and how we perceive our own agency and control 

--- Page 56 ---

Paula Boddington
46
over the self. The considerable complexity of these issues, and much conflict and potential 
confusion, becomes apparent, especially when comparing ideas and attitudes toward the self 
which arise from very different ways of imagining or applying AI. Lastly, we discuss how very 
different aspects of AI impinge upon notions of self-­control and self-­mastery, ending by briefly 
illustrating such questions via examining dementia, chosen for the profound questions it 
raises for the concept of the self, and how well-­meaning uses of new AI technologies may 
disrupt and unsettle our ideas of the self.
4.2  Aspirations for AI
We start by exploring some bold aspirations for AI which help to highlight a certain cluster of 
views regarding the self: the notion that in essence, the human mind is basically a compli-
cated computer which contingently happens to have a rather messy, warm, wet manifestation 
in our biological being. Such a picture fits well with a common modern idea of the isolated 
individual, where the individual person is identified with the mind conceived of in certain 
ways, and closely identified with the brain seen not so much as one part of a whole biological 
organism but as the crux of the matter, and as a computational device. There are those who 
work towards a future for humans which depends upon some such position holding true. 
Even if their futuristic ambitions are not universally shared by communities working with AI, 
they hold considerable sway in sections of the popular imagination and among the tech 
world, and represent a regular theme in sci-­fi and thus feed into the social imaginary around 
AI. There are objections to such a view within cognitive science and psychology, with debates 
about the necessity of some kind of embodiment for intelligence and cognition, but such 
objections appear to be less visible in the popular imagination.
Martine Rothblatt and Ray Kurzweil are among the enthusiasts for the ambition to build 
“virtual humans”: beings “like us” which exist in digital or robotic form. “After all, what 
difference does it make if our mental circuits are biological or electronic if the result is the 
same?” writes Kurzweil in the foreword to Rothblatt’s Digitally Human (2014). Kurzweil has 
himself written extensively on the promises of AI technology in books such as The Age of 
Spiritual Machines (2000) and How to Create a Mind (2013). Such views are patently built 
upon certain beliefs about both technology and the mind.
The quest to produce “virtual humans” is heralded by some as feasible and full of promise 
for the aim of “uploading” one’s own mind to a machine (details generally remain 
sketchy –­ some suggesting a gradual route of replacing individual neurons one by one). There 
are also hopes to fully replicate individual human beings, living or dead, in machine form: a 
project to recreate Rothblatt’s wife in the robot BINA-­48 appeared in various videos in an 
early, but nonetheless spooky, stage (Rothblatt  2014). Such aspirations often extend to 
improvements in one’s mental capacities by transcending the limits of our “wetware” such as 
being driven by emotions and impulses left over from our evolutionary past, as well as for 
“digital immortality.” Given that the life cycle of the current computer is far less than that of 
the average human, this presumably involves a continuing self somehow existing in an ever-­
changing network of machines. Other relatively prosaic hopes include linking minds to 
render possible direct communication, and the idea that one’s own mind might “merge” with 
AI, although depending on what this might mean, some would argue this has already 
happened via our use of the technology.
The general aspiration to build a virtual mind in and of itself does not necessarily imply the 
view that mind has a first-­person sense of itself, unless such is necessary to a certain level of 

--- Page 57 ---

AI and Knowledge of the Self
47
cognition. But the hopes to digitize one’s own mind, or to recreate the minds of others, do 
generally seem to presuppose that a self survives or is recreated; that there is some continuing 
“inner self” along the lines of Locke’s “thinking intelligent being, that has reason and 
reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and 
places” (Locke 1975, p. 335). An interesting first person/third person asymmetry arises with 
regard to knowledge of a continuing self, and focusing on one or the other might give rise to 
rather different notions of the self. In the third person case, the hopes to recreate the mind of 
a particular individual have typically rested upon the idea that by building a complete picture 
of a person’s personality traits and a complete bank of their memories, we can to all intents 
and purposes know that this is the same person continuing over time. In this third person 
case, we might test this by interacting with the purportedly continuing individual, determining 
if, firstly, this seems like a person (hence, with a sense of self), and if the personality and 
memories seem to fit. An issue arising from this which will be addressed further below 
concerns the parameters and consistency of personality.
But in the first person case of survival by digital upload, we seem simply to have the sense 
of a self: the idea of the self with no essential qualities, a sense which might survive consider-
able or even total memory loss and personality change. The element of self-­agency is tacitly 
injected into such imagined cases via the agency involved in striving to survive or to be 
“upgraded” to digital form. The first personal “what it is like to be a self” is accessible in a 
manner absent in the third personal case.
Testing the feasibility of future possibilities for intervention in the human mind often 
involves thought experiments where one is invited to consider whether, following some tech-
nological intervention, one would still be the same person. For example, Susan Schneider pro-
vides extensive critique of future purported possible uses of AI, applying findings from cognitive 
science, philosophy of mind, and AI to using such scenarios, running through imagined “mind 
uploads” and imagining the (often disappointing and worrying) results (Schneider 2019).
Locke himself, of course, conducted such thought experiments when, having arrived at a 
view of the mind whereby even the properties of the world around us become “secondary 
qualities” belonging to us rather than to an outer world, it became possible and indeed 
necessary to wonder what, if anything, connected this mind, this string of inner sensations, 
into a continuing self across time. His answer required memory (giving rise to concerns about 
how purported memories could be verified, among other questions) and is thus only a 
relatively short step from a computer-­influenced view of the mind that sees it in terms of 
information, and from a view of the mind/the self as having a somewhat precarious –­ to use 
a rough-­and-­ready shorthand –­ relationship with the body.
For many of us, including those familiar with Derek Parfit’s Reasons and Persons (1987), as 
well as for aficionados of much science fiction, such thought experiments may by now seem 
like second nature. But if Taylor’s account of the development of the self has any merit, these 
thought experiments are indeed “second” nature insofar as it is only following the development 
of certain conceptions of the self that attempting such thought experiments appears possible. 
The very proliferation of such thought experiments, coupled with the tantalizing allure of 
their putative reality, in turn may only reinforce a social imaginary which helps to ground 
such a conception of the self. This self is perhaps a thin and ethereal entity compared to the 
more robust creature one must build when attempting to replace the vibrant personality and 
mannerisms of one’s deceased loved ones, to bring back to life an individual self as viewed by 
a third party.
The nuts and bolts of a recognizable personality guide us into a material world, as do 
questions of continuity of memory viewed from the third person perspective. An attempt to 

--- Page 58 ---

Paula Boddington
48
replicate Elvis in digital form might immediately spark the questions “What is his singing 
voice like?”, “Does he still eat peanut butter, bacon, and banana sandwiches?” and “Does he 
wiggle his hips in the same way?”: in other words, the question of embodiment and its 
relationship to the self. Let us differentiate some possible positions in this complex area.
On one view, we are simply our bodies: the notion of a “disembodied self” is incoherent 
not just in practice but conceptually. On another view, we need some form of body that 
enables us to express and manifest our personality, our thoughts, desires, and so on. But 
there may be a certain contingency creeping in. Perhaps the self just needs a body of some 
appropriate sort, just as the tea needs the cup, but the self could be (somehow) transferred, 
at least in theory, to another vessel. A first personal experience is of a self as if disembod-
ied; hence the body itself is, in some vaguely specified way, contingent. Once the body is 
viewed as somehow contingent, the way is open to thinking of the self as nothing but an 
inner, purely mental core.
There is generally an agency implied in such a conception of the self, which has mastery 
over aspects of itself, controlling and improving aspects of its mind, hence the close alignment 
with the futuristic hopes of virtual minds with fusion with AI and various forms of 
transhumanism which see individuals as surviving, but radically transcending and improving 
their current relatively puny and cognitively constrained selves –­ something closely akin to 
Taylor’s buffered, punctual self. These radical aspirations for technology could be reinforcing 
an idea of such a self and its self-­mastery which could include both increasing our mental 
capacities and altering and improving our own material instantiation, and could impact our 
understanding and experience of the boundaries of the self through experience of those 
things over which we appear to have unmediated agency and/or through the experience of 
unmediated access to the minds of others in scenarios involving forms of “hive mind.”
4.3  Implications of AI Use
We now examine the implications of some more concrete uses of AI, surveying some work 
examining the impact of new technologies upon the self: how we regard the self in general, 
how we gain self-­knowledge mediated via such technologies. Here we will find a rather differ-
ent story with interesting comparisons and contrasts with our discussion so far.
AI utilizes vast amounts of data. The collection and analysis of data about ourselves and 
its feedback to us may play a major role in how we experience and conceptualize the self. 
Issues concerning embodiment, the boundaries of the self, and the limits of self-­agency will 
again arise. Here follows a necessarily brief overview of the significant body of work, much by 
social scientists as well as technologists, which explores such issues. It is useful to consider 
different aspects of data collection and analysis.
Data can now be collected from many sources, and can include an extremely wide range of 
types of data about individuals who are thus seen from multiple viewpoints. This can include 
data from activity online, encompassing not just obvious data such as social media comments 
or responses to adverts, but “data exhaust” from any element of online activities. Data 
collected may include much that is below our level of awareness, such as typing speeds and 
patterns. It can include both audio and visual data, as well as physiological data.
Vastly increased possibilities of data analysis driven by growth in processing powers, the 
sheer amount of data, and the capacity to draw conclusions from combining data of different 
types together mean that we may give away a considerable amount of personal information, 
including things of which we are unaware: our “data shadow.”

--- Page 59 ---

AI and Knowledge of the Self
49
This can mean that data which was previously innocuous or meaningless may now take 
on new or increased significance. For illustration, a BBC reporter has claimed that Netflix 
knew she was bisexual before she did (Tarrant 2023). Supermarkets discovered years ago that 
it was possible to predict the onset of dementia by changes in shopping habits detected from 
loyalty card data (Deetjen et al. 2015). What is public may now reveal things thought to be 
private; small details of seemingly irrelevant behavior may reveal information of medical 
significance, hence taking on new import.
Data may be collected about us without our explicit agency and with or without our 
consent. We may actively seek to collect data about ourselves, for instance via self-­tracking 
devices. However, a person may participate in self-­tracking unaware of all the potential 
information to be mined. New possibilities arise from developments in technology itself, and 
from advances in knowledge gained using such data. A critical question is what “ecological 
validity” the findings from such data analysis might have; in other words, how accurate a 
picture is produced, including what aspects of humanity might be omitted or misrepresented.
What happens to this data? Data is fed back to us in various ways, which may be explicit, 
such as receiving requested results from self-­tracking. But data also impacts us via the 
pervasive manipulation of behavior entrenched within much new technology. To consider 
what impact this might have on our sense of self and our self-­knowledge, we must consider 
not just technological capabilities but the manner in which the technology is actually applied 
and the ubiquitous ways in which it is now embedded in infrastructure and daily use. The 
persuasive technology which underlies so much social media and other technology not only 
manipulates obvious behavior such as buying choices, but shapes and even creates desires 
and opinions. Moreover, it does so by design, with persuasive technology a subject of study for 
many in the tech world (Fogg 2003).
One rampant method of manipulation is through the hacking of attention. Attention to 
certain issues and images and away from others is readily achieved by a variety of means. 
This generally involves exploiting aspects of human psychology. Certain emotions are more 
likely to keep us engaged online, notably anger, generally not our best feature (Munn 2020). 
Social media engagement frequently involves striving for “likes,” and the dopamine hit that 
this produces, together with devices such as continuous scroll, maintains attention. This 
engagement is driven by the advertising model of revenue: you are the product 
(Lanchester 2017).
Hence, AI-­driven technologies may be powerful forces regarding (putative) self-­knowledge 
and the knowledge that others have about us. But note that at the same time, these technol-
ogies provide powerful ways of molding the individual self. How we understand ourselves 
may be shaped via such means, but also may in turn shape fundamental attitudes towards the 
very nature of the self. Questions such as these have fed into discussions of digital identity, the 
“quantified self” and the “data self.” The sociologist Deborah Lupton, who has made extensive 
study of data use and self-­tracking, considers that to understand experiences of personal 
data, we have to see how the use of digital technologies in everyday life “enacts” concepts of 
selfhood, identity, and embodiment (Lupton 2020, p. 12).
How does feedback from data about ourselves and our bodies shape how we view 
ourselves –­ not just our own specific characteristics but the very assumptions we make about 
what it is to be a particular self? The answer is likely to be complex with individual variations 
and potentially with inconsistencies, but those who have studied the question often conclude 
that we are in a state of flux and that boundaries around the self are porous. “The line between 
ourselves and our data is where we choose to draw it,” say Neff and Nafus (2016, p. 189); 
knowledge about our selves is a “social product” (ibid., p. 10). The picture of individual agency 

--- Page 60 ---

Paula Boddington
50
here is perhaps blurred; Lupton argues that people and their data are now entangled in 
human–­data assemblages, with implications for the ontological boundaries between self and 
other, human and nonhuman, and even living and dead (Lupton 2020, p. 13). This is not of 
merely intellectual interest. Lupton claims, drawing on and interpreting substantive evidence, 
that details about our bodies and lives are subject to depersonalization and dehumanization 
and in the light of this, we need to develop different meanings about the self and about data 
(Lupton 2020, p. 20). The picture of individual agency Neff and Nafus give is somewhat 
ambiguous. If “we” choose to draw the line around ourselves in particular ways, this “we” 
might refer to societal changes over which an individual has reduced control, might refer to 
the agency of an individual to make such a choice, or a mixture of the two.
Vastly different meanings may be attached to data that is used by individuals in attempts at 
control or self-­mastery, for example using data to try to improve fitness, change habits, or con-
trol unhelpful emotions, in contrast to the use of data by others to control and manipulate. 
These may appear to be diametrically opposed forces operating on our sense of self-­agency 
and autonomy, yet each kind of example is complex, and multiple aspects are operating simul-
taneously. A sense of agency, self-­mastery, and self-­knowledge may indeed arise as a result of 
interacting with new technologies which are, viewed from another vantage point, manipu-
lating and altering core elements of individual selfhood and agency, such as fundamental 
preferences and ways of interacting with others. This potentially malignant agency may be 
attributed to “the machine” but, although aspects of the operation of AI may be unintended 
by its creators, it is important to realize that attribution of agency to AI frequently masks the 
human agency of those who design and implement these technologies. We are increasingly 
obliged to be subject to such technologies as they are built into the warp and weft of 
everyday life.
This is worthy of much more detailed discussion than is possible here. One’s sense of 
agency, and the scope and nature of boundaries over the self are at issue. How we think about 
these will be nested within general ideas about the self which may be impacted by how we 
experience the world mediated via AI, and the powerful hold that new technologies have over 
our attention is a significant factor here. Consider the idea that personality is a fundamental 
aspect of one’s self. But how do we construct the notion of a personality? Features of 
technology design may nudge us in certain directions, corralling our attention onto certain 
features as especially relevant to personality and to selfhood.
Some working within AI are critical of basic features of design which include chasing 
specific objectives which may skew interactions and the perception of self and other (Stanley 
and Lehman,  2015). The chasing of social media “likes” and the now perpetual task of 
ranking preferences paints a particular view of what the core of an individual personality 
is –­ roughly, personality comprising in the main a bundle of preferences formed under the 
watchful gaze of others whose favorable opinion one is constantly soliciting (or whose 
unfavorable opinion one is eliciting by trolling). Note that the point here is not simply that our 
likes and dislikes may be changed, that our social relationships may be altered, but that our 
sense of what it is to be a person, what makes up the individual self, may be skewed to give 
undue prominence to fleeting preferences often oriented towards consumerism and to hastily 
formed yet vehement opinions on current topics chosen by some algorithm. Alternative views 
of structures of the self might be encouraged by providing different incentives and 
configurations in online engagement.
Compare and contrast these selves striving for existence within a world brought to them 
via screens and a digitally curated view of themselves, the others, and the world, with the 
general picture of the digital mind outlined earlier. The latter is a conception of the ideal self 

--- Page 61 ---

AI and Knowledge of the Self
51
which is based upon rational cognition, collating relevant information, and eschewing 
irrelevant emotion efficiently to achieve its chosen goals. The former is a rather more mixed 
picture, insofar as new AI-­driven technologies themselves ironically demonstrate how 
susceptible we mere fleshy beings are to having our emotions and motivations hacked, and to 
acting on dubiously accurate data, while also offering us the chance to track and monitor our 
emotions. It is almost as if AI is laughing at us: on the one hand, luring us into a view of an 
aspirational mind as an ideal intelligence in rational pursuit of its own goals while taunting 
us with our own irrational weaknesses, thinking we are maximizing our pursuit of goals 
which we pursue only within a limited arena, and which are only dubiously “ours.” There is 
a certain pathos in the comparison with the social imaginary of control that leads some to 
hope for mind uploads to achieve digital immortality. The source and manner of operation of 
any control over the self are critical.
Since as humans we grow and develop, it is necessary to consider the range and type of 
personality changes possible within the same self; an answer should include consideration of 
how quickly and under what influences any changes happened. Consider a thought 
experiment where you accept an offer to be “uploaded” only to discover your temperament, 
likes and dislikes, and values had nothing in common with what you remember of your past 
self. How would you construct what had happened? From the point of view of a buffered, 
punctual self, extreme changes could be conceptually possible, but it may matter whether any 
such changes were self-­directed. Contrast noticeable changes of personality and values after 
years of striving to overcome weaknesses, bad habits, biases, and addictions, compared to a 
similar level of personality change following years of kidnap, isolation, brainwashing, and 
torture. It is critical to an idealized notion of the rational autonomous self that it is the major 
driver of any self-­transformation, taking into account realities but according to its own plans 
and values.
Yet frequently, the manipulations of new technologies take advantage of human emotions 
in ways that seemingly decrease rationality, and hence agency. Consider the transhumanist 
objectives of surpassing and improving the self via technology. Transhumanism does not 
typically include the aim to have one’s sense of identity, one’s beliefs, preferences, and daily 
activities molded by foreign tech giants in a bid to boost advertising revenue and share prices. 
Note, too, that any sketch of ambitions to change oneself for the better, or fears of being 
manipulated for the worse, will rest upon some ideal of the self towards which one is striving, 
and a sense of where the boundaries of a core self are traced. Yet our ideals can also be shaped 
and manipulated by new technologies.
Our sense of self-­agency also hangs on how we understand causal possibilities. AI-­driven 
data collection and analysis may provide explanations which present different accounts of 
causation and agency whereby phenomena are constructed as self or not self, or of liminal 
status within a self with permeable or loosely determined boundaries. There is no straightfor-
ward answer as to whether interactions with technologies will expand or contract a sense of 
the embodied self. The capacity for biomedical explanations based upon the analysis of a wide 
range of data has been argued to produce a cultural change whereby “(b)iomedicalization 
carves a groove in our collective imagination that makes close measurement of the body both 
conceivable and desirable” (Neff and Nafus, 2016, p. 20). This data may create a “prosthetic 
of feeling” through which we can sense our bodies and the world around us (ibid., p. 77). But 
will our bodies feel part of our self, or something we somehow inhabit in a manner foreign 
even to the dualist Descartes who considered that “I am not merely present in my body as a 
sailor is present in a ship, but that I am very closely joined and, as it were, intermingled with 
it”? (Descartes, 6th Meditation).

--- Page 62 ---

Paula Boddington
52
Perceptions of control will be one crucial factor. Self-­trackers often use data for “habit 
hacking,” creating new habits and eliminating old ones. Since habits are routines of behavior 
we may have limited direct control over, using new technologies to mold habits may expand 
our sense of self-­agency, although those subject to surveillance beyond their control may beg 
to differ. A sense of control is strongly linked to perceptions of embodiment: the self may 
possibly experience being extended beyond the body via technological control, may experience 
increased control using the body, or may experience the body as something external to the 
self as control over it increases with technological assistance. Social science research 
examining experiences of disembodiment when interacting online so far suggests that no 
easy answer to questions of technology and the sense of embodiment is forthcoming. There 
are mixed indications of the impact of interacting online free of the constraints and possibilities 
of physicality present during real-­world interactions for experiences of disembodiment and 
the various implications for personal identity and selfhood (Kang 2007; Rodogno 2012).
Let us briefly illustrate some of these complex dynamics with an example. Dementia is 
frequently linked with discussions of selfhood. The debates around dementia and the self 
closely mirror those outlined above. Dementia impacts upon cognitive functioning and this 
factor often links it to the notion that dementia undermines or destroys the self. The condition 
is often spoken of explicitly in these terms, as the death of the self, as a “funeral without end,” 
as rendering individuals “zombies,” and so on (Mitchell et  al.  2020; Schweda and 
Jongsma 2022). A recent controversial advertisement from Alzheimer’s UK presents dementia 
as a series of “deaths” starting from first symptoms (Alzheimer’s Society, n.d.). Such attitudes 
are closely linked to conceptions of the self, which foreground cognitive rationality and 
autonomy and focus on brain functioning.
There are many critics of such an approach who support a person-­centered model of 
dementia as counter to the dominant medical model of dementia focused on the brain. Such 
critics stress the impact of dementia upon the whole person and the need to recognize 
relational and embodied aspects of personhood (Boddington et al. 2024). Hence, debates 
about the person and the mind within dementia care closely mirror debates in AI. Pia Kontos, 
among others, has conducted ethnographic work demonstrating that a person living with 
dementia may retain a sense of self, of how one appears to others, one’s place in a social 
world, and the presence of others, despite serious cognitive impairment (although dementia 
is a progressive condition and this is not per se to claim that a sense of self will always persist) 
(Kontos 2004, 2005).
There are many proposed or existing uses of new technologies in relation to dementia 
research and dementia care (Astell et al. 2019) which potentially have profound significance 
for our sense of our self, not just for those with a dementia diagnosis but for anyone, since 
proposals include mass population screening from readily available data. Since dementia may 
impact so many areas of functioning, many different kinds of data may be used in pursuit of 
the goal of increased capacity for diagnosis of the condition, including data from administered 
tests; wearable trackers; routine medical records; gait analysis; analysis of voice patterns from 
telephone conversations; analysis of keyboard strokes; analysis of sleep patterns; use of smart 
technologies around the domestic living space, and many more (Li et al. 2022). There are 
proposals to develop diagnosis apps for personal smartphones. Research projects aim to 
diagnose dementia years, and maybe even decades, before first symptoms, since indications of 
the condition may lie well below levels of awareness by the individual or by others, with 
suggestions of routinizing such monitoring into medical systems. Everyday life becomes 
medicalized, routine actions become potentially signs of an illness which is portrayed 
culturally by some as the death of the self, and all this powered by technology which rides 

--- Page 63 ---

AI and Knowledge of the Self
53
upon prioritizing, even eulogizing, the cognitive. Note the diversity of data, some concerning 
cognitive functioning, some behavioral, some physiological. Out of this many different 
meanings for “the self” may arise. We may come to see ourselves through this data as a third 
party may see us, as if viewing ourselves from the outside.
It may be possible to construct out of this a robust sense of self wherein the mind is closely 
integrated with the body, with awareness that routine and minute bodily movements and 
actions might betray something about the state of one’s cognition and mental functioning, 
without necessarily undermining a sense of self, indeed perhaps boosting it. The impetus for 
mass and early diagnosis is generally framed in terms of starting early treatment, which might 
encourage a sense of autonomous self-­control over health. Yet the impetus for diagnosis using 
AI is given as the necessity of research, given that there are few if any effective treatments; a 
sense of surveillance may lead precisely to a sense of loss of self-­agency. A punctual, buffered 
self might view technologically mediated knowledge of cognitive decline not simply with 
concern for health, but as heralding a death of the self even while the body lives.
The buffered self becomes porous to the technology which is increasingly pervasive, 
routinized, and even mandated, which is finding new ways to know our deepest recesses. The 
porous self of the past of which Taylor writes was porous to a range of outside influences, 
material and spiritual, for good and for ill. “Consider melancholy: black bile was not the cause 
of melancholy, it embodied, it was melancholy” (Taylor 2008). One present possibility is that 
we hang on, perhaps more firmly than ever, to the punctual self and its powers of self-­control, 
arming ourselves with technology to defend it, all the while being faced with realizing its 
vulnerability on multiple fronts –­ our desires, our beliefs, our very sense of our cognitive 
rationality all porous, for good and for ill, not just to the technology itself but also to the 
ideologies, corporations, and individuals behind this technology.
