5.1  Introduction
Modern societies are characterized by an enormous degree of specialization and epistemic 
division of labor. The ongoing differentiation of science has now produced more than 10,000 
specialties (Stichweh 2014). Each of these can be understood as a separate epistemic domain 
for which there are individuals who, by virtue of their education or special intellectual 
abilities, have privileged access to and a special epistemic authority over the knowledge rele-
vant to that domain  –­  knowledge which they can make available to others who are less 
familiar or unfamiliar with the domain. Such persons are usually referred to as “experts.”
One of the reasons for the prominent role of experts in contemporary epistemic practice is 
that, as the total amount of available knowledge increases, the proportion that any one 
individual can master becomes smaller. The “universal geniuses” of the past may have always 
been a phantasm. This is not to deny that Leonardo da Vinci, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz or 
Benjamin Franklin, who have often been described in this way, had impressive intellectual 
abilities. But they certainly did not have comprehensive access to all the knowledge available 
in their time. In the present day, however, it has become completely illusory for even the 
brightest individuals to possess substantial portions of all human knowledge. On the other 
hand, there are many situations in which both individuals and institutions –­ such as politi-
cians or courts that want to make evidence-­based decisions –­ need knowledge that they do 
not possess first-­hand, and therefore have to rely on experts in the relevant fields. This applies 
both to communication within science1 and to knowledge transfer between science and other 
parts of society.2
Intense debates over the last three or four decades have seen social epistemology acknowl-
edge the central role of experts, epistemic authority, epistemic dependence, and epistemic 
trust.3 Now it faces another new development. More and more powerful AI systems are emerg-
ing and becoming essential elements in our epistemic division of labor (Hauswald 2021a). It 
is no longer uncommon for human experts to be outperformed by AI systems in certain tasks, 
and AI is increasingly being used to assist experts in their work or even to replace them alto-
gether. For example, medical AI systems can analyze medical images such as X-­rays, MRIs, 
AI and the Philosophy of Expertise and Epistemic 
Authority
RICO HAUSWALD
5

--- Page 66 ---

RICO HAUSWALD
56
and CT scans and detect certain diseases like cancer better than many radiologists. DeepMind’s 
AlphaGo has beaten the world’s best Go players, a game long thought to be too complex for 
computers. And large language models such as ChatGPT are often more readily available and 
can answer questions on a much wider range of topics than human experts, whose expertise 
is typically limited to narrow domains (although in many cases, the AI’s answers are still less 
accurate than those of human experts) (Špecián and Brown 2024).
These developments pose new challenges for both our epistemic practice and socio-­
epistemological theorizing. In this chapter, I outline some of these challenges. The chapter is 
divided into four main sections, each of which discusses a key issue in the philosophy of 
expertise and epistemic authority: the definition problem (section  5.2), the identification 
problem (section  5.3), the deference problem (section  5.4), and the transfer problem 
­(section 5.5).4 In each section, I will first briefly discuss these problems in general and outline 
some of the solutions that have been proposed in the epistemological literature, followed by 
an application of these considerations to AI systems.
Note that my discussion will be limited to what I will call “epistemic AI systems,” i.e. AI 
systems that are used for purposes and tasks previously reserved for human experts and epi-
stemic authorities. In contrast to AI that is used to solve practical problems (e.g., AI systems 
that control self-­driving cars), epistemic AI systems are primarily used as sources of 
information or epistemic instruments, where an “epistemic instrument” can be characterized 
as “any instrument that is designed so that its outputs convey worldly information so as to be 
accessible to parties who learn to comprehend these outputs” (Goldberg 2020, p. 2785). 
Examples include medical AI systems used to diagnose diseases, large language models such 
as ChatGPT, AI systems that predict weather patterns, and AI-­based trading systems that 
analyze market data and help make trading decisions.5
Epistemic AI systems can be designed either to be used directly by laypeople or to assist 
human experts. Systems designed to be used directly by nonexperts can perhaps be expected 
to eventually replace experts. The layperson–­expert relationship could then shift (at least in 
part or in some situations) to an epistemic AI–­user relationship. Alternatively, AI systems 
may not replace experts but support them in their work and thus indirectly benefit laypeople.6 
In both cases, similar issues arise to those discussed in the literature on epistemic authority 
and expertise. Users of AI systems –­ whether lay or expert –­ face problems of identification 
and deference, and there are problems of definition and transfer.
5.2  The Definition Problem
5.2.1  Defining Experts and Epistemic Authorities
Although there is no consensus among philosophers on how to define terms such as “expert,” 
“expertise,” and “epistemic authority,” there are at least some aspects that are relatively 
uncontroversial. When the term “expert” is used as a noun, it usually refers to people who 
have some epistemic advantage relative to nonexperts, laypeople or novices. “Expertise” refers 
to the property that these people have. In contrast, the term “epistemic authority” is ambig-
uous and can refer both to people and to the property that these people have (one can say that 
someone is an epistemic authority or has epistemic authority).
Another relatively uncontroversial feature is that the notions of expert, expertise, and epi-
stemic authority need to be relativized with respect to particular domains. For example, 
someone may be an expert or epistemic authority in arithmetic, the history of the Habsburg 

--- Page 67 ---

AI and the Philosophy of Expertise and Epistemic Authority
57
monarchy or a particular programming language. However, there is disagreement about how 
exactly to individuate these domains.
While it is relatively uncontroversial that paradigmatic scientific (sub)disciplines and spe-
cialties can be domains of expertise or epistemic authority, some authors have proposed a 
more liberal definition of the term that includes nonscientific domains of knowledge, such as 
what someone had for breakfast (Coady 2012, p. 31). However, other authors have objected 
that “to call beliefs about what one had for breakfast ‘expertise’ seems to stretch the notion in 
an unhelpful way” (Watson 2022, p. 116).
There is also no uncontroversial way of distinguishing between the concepts of expert and 
epistemic authority. Elsewhere, I suggest defining epistemic authority in purely relational 
terms (Hauswald 2024a): If EA is an epistemic authority for a layperson L with respect to 
domain D, this implies that EA is epistemically significantly superior to L with respect to D, 
where epistemic superiority can in principle be analyzed in terms of true beliefs, accurate cre-
dences, knowledge, understanding or other epistemic goods. Experts, on the other hand, must 
cross an absolute epistemic threshold. They must be superior to most other people in the 
community with respect to D. For example, according to Goldman (2018, p. 5), “S is an expert 
about domain D if and only if (1) S has more true beliefs (or high credences) in propositions 
concerning D than most people do, and fewer false beliefs; and (2) the absolute number of true 
beliefs S has about propositions in D is very substantial.”
It follows that someone can be an epistemic authority without being an expert, and an 
expert without being an authority. Croce (2019) uses the example of a grandmother who 
does not have the status of an expert in zoology but who nevertheless knows enough to teach 
her grandson about fish respiration, and in this respect acts as an epistemic authority for him. 
An example of how a person can be an expert without also being an epistemic authority 
would be an interaction between two experts: both meet the absolute threshold, i.e., they are 
superior to most people in the community, but to each other they are on a par; neither is an 
epistemic authority for the other.
5.2.2  The Epistemic-­AI Definition Problem
Can epistemic AI systems in principle be understood as experts or epistemic authorities? This 
is what we might call the “epistemic-­AI definition problem.” The answer to this question 
depends on which definition of expert and epistemic authority one prefers. It is beyond the 
scope of this chapter to discuss every possible or existing definition but as an important step 
towards solving the problem, we can at least review some potentially relevant similarities and 
differences between epistemic AI systems and human experts and epistemic authorities.
Let’s start with the similarities. It’s no coincidence that a subclass of AI systems came to be 
known as “expert systems” (although this term primarily referred to “GOFAI” systems that 
were not yet based on machine learning and artificial neural networks).7 The most striking 
similarity is that users of AI systems can acquire knowledge and other epistemic goods from 
them, just as laypeople can acquire epistemic goods from human experts. Functionally, they 
can play similar roles in our epistemic division of labor. A second similarity is the large epi-
stemic asymmetry between users and AI systems, which resembles the epistemic gap between 
laypeople and experts. AI systems are often better at finding the truth than humans. As a 
result, both the expert–­layperson and the epistemic AI–­user relationships can be character-
ized as “epistemically imbalanced relationships” (Seger 2022). Third, experts and epistemic 
authorities often have knowledge that is esoteric to laypeople. While laypeople can ask them 
about the truth-­values of propositions, they often do not understand the experts’ reasoning; 

--- Page 68 ---

RICO HAUSWALD
58
they cannot understand how the experts arrived at their beliefs. Similarly, AI systems are 
often opaque black boxes, especially systems based on machine learning in artificial neural 
networks, and it can be difficult or impossible to explain how an AI has transformed its inputs 
into its outputs. As Kleinberg and Mullainathan (2015) put it: “As generations of algorithms 
get smarter, they’re also becoming more incomprehensible … We have, perhaps for the first 
time ever, built machines we don’t understand.” Fourth, due to the aforementioned similar-
ities, users of epistemic AI systems face similar challenges to laypeople interacting with 
experts or epistemic authorities (which I will discuss in more detail in the subsequent 
sections).
On the other hand, there are also obvious differences between epistemic AI systems and 
human experts and epistemic authorities. Most importantly, current AI systems do not have 
beliefs, nor are they capable of engaging in genuine testimonial exchange –­ at least according 
to most conceptions of what beliefs and testimony are.8 If one assumes that the ability to 
function as a genuine testimonial source or the possession of beliefs are among the defini-
tional requirements of an expert and an epistemic authority (and many definitions, such as 
Goldman’s mentioned in section 5.2.1, do indeed include one of these requirements), then it 
would seem to follow that epistemic AI systems cannot fall under these concepts.
But there are two alternatives. One is to try to show that AI systems can have genuine 
beliefs or be testimonial sources and thus satisfy the definitional requirements after all. The 
other is to modify the definitions of an expert and an epistemic authority so that AI systems 
can satisfy them by abandoning the testimony and belief requirements. Elsewhere I argue 
that the latter is the most attractive option (Hauswald forthcoming): It best captures the 
functional similarities between epistemic AI and human experts/authorities, it is supported 
by the fact that laypeople can sometimes learn from experts or epistemic authorities without 
interacting with them in a testimonial way (a point I return to in section 5.3.1), and it is sup-
ported by independent reasons for extending the notions of expert and epistemic authority so 
that they can apply to entities without genuine beliefs, such as scientific communities or epi-
stemic institutions.9
5.3  The Identification Problem
5.3.1  The Identification of Experts and Epistemic Authorities
How can genuine experts and epistemic authorities be reliably identified, especially by lay-
people who have little or no familiarity with the domain of expertise in question? This problem 
is particularly pressing given the possibility of “fake experts” or “false authorities” –­ people 
who claim to be experts or epistemic authorities without actually being one (Jäger 2023, 2024).
A particular variant of this problem is the “novice/2-­expert” problem (Goldman 2001), in 
which a layperson is faced with conflicting testimony from two (apparent) experts. Since lay-
persons have no or very limited knowledge of the domain in question (which is typically why 
they need the advice of an expert or authority in the first place), they are usually unable to 
directly compare the truth-­value of the experts’ claims with the corresponding facts. The 
question is whether the laypersons can nevertheless make a (more or less) justified decision 
about which expert to rely on.
Goldman has argued for an affirmative answer to this question, suggesting a number of 
indirect methods by which laypeople can decide which expert is a better epistemic source. They 
can (1) look at the rhetorical and argumentative skills of the purported experts, (2) consider 

--- Page 69 ---

AI and the Philosophy of Expertise and Epistemic Authority
59
which of the competing positions is held by the majority of other experts or supported by 
scientific consensus, (3) look at the formal qualifications and credentials of the purported 
experts, (4) use evidence of the experts’ interests and biases in relation to the issue at hand, and 
(5) use evidence of the experts’ past “track record” (e.g., have the purported experts’ predic-
tions come true in the past?)
Goldman’s proposal has triggered a broad discussion about the quality of these methods, 
which I cannot follow in detail (see for example Anderson 2011; Brennan 2020; Coady 2006; 
Matheson 2005; Scholz 2009). But at least it seems clear that the layperson’s situation is not 
entirely hopeless. In many cases they are able to identify genuine experts or epistemic author-
ities with some degree of reliability, even if they have little or no expertise of their own.
There is a second dimension to the identification problem. Not only do laypeople need to 
identify a genuine expert or authority as such, but they also need to identify their relevant 
beliefs. If I, as a layperson, know that E is an expert in domain D and knows the truth-­value 
of proposition p falling within D, then this is of no use to me unless the content of E’s belief is 
transparent to me. Of course, in many cases I will ask E, and E will convey her belief to me by 
testimony. But in some circumstances this is not so easy. E may be inaccessible or otherwise 
unavailable as a testimonial source. But even if E is available, it is possible that E will withhold 
her knowledge of p (e.g., because p is a secret). Or E might mislead or lie to me for strategic 
reasons.
However, testimonial transmission is not the only method of determining E’s beliefs. 
Sometimes there are indirect methods, such as inferring the beliefs of an expert or authority 
from their behavior, and sometimes such methods are even superior to testimonial transmis-
sion. Here is an example inspired by John (2011, p. 508). When parents are considering 
whether to have their children vaccinated, they may fear that doctors will give them subop-
timal advice about the efficacy and safety of the vaccine in question because of financial con-
flicts of interest or other strategic considerations. Instead of relying (exclusively) on what the 
doctors say, some of them prefer to rely on observing whether the doctors vaccinate their own 
(i.e., the doctors’) children. These parents think that there is a risk that doctors will say 
something that is not in line with their beliefs. But if they vaccinate their own children, that 
is strong evidence that they really believe it is safe and effective. They would not do it if they 
did not really believe it.
5.3.2  The Epistemic-­AI Identification Problem
Just as laypeople face the challenge of identifying reliable experts or epistemic authorities, 
users face the challenge of identifying reliable epistemic AI systems. In addition to the 
novice/2-­expert problem formulated by Goldman, a user/2-­AI problem arises when two 
alternative, prima facie reliable AI systems produce conflicting results. A user/AI-­expert 
problem can also arise when a user is confronted with the output of an AI system that sug-
gests a particular doxastic attitude, while a human expert promotes an incompatible view. An 
example would be a patient who is given a particular diagnosis X by her doctor. Suppose the 
patient wants a second opinion and consults a medical app that does not support the doctor’s 
diagnosis (Kempt and Nagel 2022). Who should the patient trust? Should she believe that 
diagnosis X applies to her or not?10
I cannot discuss these questions at length here, let alone answer them definitively. But I 
would like to suggest that one possibility might be to take up Goldman’s methods and consider 
the extent to which they are applicable to epistemic AI systems, or how they might need to be 
modified. Goldman suggests that laypeople orient themselves according to the rhetorical and 

--- Page 70 ---

RICO HAUSWALD
60
argumentative skills of supposed experts. Similarly, orientation could be based on the way an 
AI system interacts with the user, how easy it is to use. Of course, this is at best a weak crite-
rion, just as an expert’s rhetorical skills are at best a weak indicator of how accurate their 
testimony is.
Goldman’s second method of considering which of the competing positions is supported 
by the majority (whether of other experts or of epistemic AI systems) or by scientific con-
sensus also seems applicable. The criterion of formal qualifications is not so easy to apply to 
AI systems. AI systems do not (at least for the time being) acquire academic degrees, honors, 
or the like. However, a certain parallel is that while experts are trained by universities or other 
institutions –­ whose credentials can then be used to assess the experts’ degrees –­ AI systems 
are trained by human developers or companies. Thus, the trustworthiness of its human devel-
opers may be an important proxy for assessing the trustworthiness of an AI system. 
Furthermore, it is conceivable that in the future, an infrastructure will be created to certify 
reliable AI systems, similar to an academic certification system. For example, independent 
certification bodies could be envisaged to test AI systems and issue a certificate if the results 
are positive. The extent to which users can rely on such certificates will, of course, depend 
again on the reliability of the certification bodies. It would be necessary to ensure that these 
institutions are truly independent and do a good job, which implies that they themselves are 
subject to public scrutiny.11
Goldman’s bias criterion also has an equivalent in epistemic AI systems, as evidenced by 
the extensive debate on algorithmic bias (for a discussion, see Fazelpour and Danks 2021). An 
AI system may be subject to bias without anyone being aware of it, or it may also persist 
despite deliberate countermeasures. A bias may even be deliberately programmed into the 
system. In this case, it may be advisable to check the potential interests of the programmers.12 
Goldman’s track record criterion is also applicable to epistemic AI systems. Just as one can 
assess the reliability of a human expert, for example by the extent to which their previous pre-
dictions have come true, one can in principle judge the reliability of an AI system by the extent 
to which its predictions have come true.
I am not suggesting that the application of these five methods is always unproblematic. On 
the contrary, in individual cases it may be unclear whether or how a method should be applied, 
it may be unclear to what extent it can actually be used to determine the epistemic reliability 
of an AI system, and it may be unclear how to proceed when different methods produce diver-
gent results. However, all these problems can also arise when applied to human experts and 
epistemic authorities. My point is merely to suggest that there are, in principle, methods for 
solving the epistemic-­AI identification problem that are similar in some respects to those pro-
posed for solving the identification problem with human experts and epistemic authorities.
Let us turn briefly to the second dimension of the identification problem. In the case of 
human experts and epistemic authorities, the second identification problem was that even if 
a layperson has identified a genuine expert or authority, she still faces the further challenge of 
identifying their actual beliefs. Although we may be reluctant to attribute genuine beliefs to 
AI, a similar challenge may arise with epistemic AI systems. This is because an AI system may 
achieve a certain result but may not communicate this appropriately to the user, for example 
because a block has been installed for some reason that does not allow the result to be output, 
or that only allows outputs that meet certain requirements.13 An example of this is censor-
ship in generative AI chatbots. If Ernie Bot, a chatbot developed by the Chinese company 
Baidu, is asked about what happened in China in 1989, it won’t give any information about 
the Tiananmen Square massacre due to government censorship (see Funk et al. 2023) but the 
phenomenon is by no means limited to authoritarian regimes (see Calvet-­Bademunt and 

--- Page 71 ---

AI and the Philosophy of Expertise and Epistemic Authority
61
Mchangama 2024). A user may therefore be uncertain as to whether the output she receives 
from an AI system actually corresponds to the result obtained by applying its algorithms. 
Again, an examination of the possible nonepistemic interests of the programmers, but also of 
the possible governmental or official requirements, may be relevant.
5.4  The Deference Problem
5.4.1  How to Defer to Experts and Epistemic Authorities
The deference problem is this. Suppose a layperson has correctly identified an expert or epi-
stemic authority and their relevant beliefs. How should the layperson behave epistemically 
towards them, what attitudes should she adopt towards them, and how should she update her 
own beliefs?
The philosophical debate on this issue has mainly focused on the discussion of two opposing 
positions: the Total Evidence View and the Preemption View.14 In simplified terms, the 
difference between the two positions can be illustrated as follows. Suppose a layperson is 
interested in the truth-­value of a proposition p and already has a set of reasons SR for or 
against p (for example, the layperson may have followed the principle of “do your own 
research,” gathered her own first-­order evidence, and drawn her own conclusions).15 Perhaps 
the layperson has already formed a belief that p or non-­p on the basis of SR. Then the lay-
person learns the fact F that an epistemic authority E has a certain doxastic attitude towards 
p, e.g., believes p. For the layperson, F is another reason relevant to p to be added to SR.
Up to this point, the Total Evidence View and the Preemption View are likely to agree with 
the description of the case. However, they now diverge with respect to the epistemic behavior 
they recommend to the layperson. According to the Total Evidence View, the layperson should 
add F as an additional reason to SR and weigh it against the other elements already present in 
the set. Since F is usually a very strong reason, this weighing will often lead the layperson to 
endorse the doxastic attitude of E (i.e., to believe p in this case). However, other situations are 
also possible, in particular the case in which the layperson comes to a different conclusion 
than E, especially if SR contains other very strong reasons that point in a different direction.16
The Preemption View, on the other hand, recommends treating F as the only reason rele-
vant to p. The layperson should not weigh F against the other reasons contained in SR, but 
instead ignore them and base her doxastic attitude towards p solely on F, and adopt E’s belief.17 
Preemptionists argue that following their advice maximizes the likelihood that laypeople will 
hold accurate beliefs in the long run. On the other hand, they are open to the charge that they 
are promoting a form of epistemic trust that is far too strong and that leaves laypeople too 
vulnerable to potential exploitation and predatory behavior by experts or authorities 
(Lackey 2018, 2021). Moreover, as I have argued elsewhere, they fail to account for cases of 
rational disagreement between laypeople and experts/authorities, i.e., cases in which it seems 
reasonable for a layperson to remain steadfast in her position even when an expert or authority 
disagrees (Hauswald 2021b, 2024a).
5.4.2  The Epistemic-­AI Deference Problem
When a user interacts with an epistemic AI system that is assumed to be reliable, and the system 
provides a certain output –­ e.g., an output that suggests that a proposition p is true –­ the 
question arises as to how the user should epistemically deal with this output. In particular, 

--- Page 72 ---

RICO HAUSWALD
62
the question is whether the fact that the output suggests that p –­ O(p) for short –­ is a preemptive 
reason for the user to believe p, i.e., a reason that should replace the other reasons the user has 
for or against p and not simply one that should be added to those other reasons. In other words, 
should the user treat O(p) according to the Preemption View or the Total Evidence View?
As just argued, there are strong reasons for rejecting the Preemption View, and I think 
these reasons carry over to epistemic AI (see also Wolkenstein 2024). As I also argued, reject-
ing the Preemption View does not mean that the layperson cannot have epistemic trust in the 
expert or authority, or give much weight to their testimony. Trust in an expert or authority 
does not require blind deference, but is compatible with a weighing of reasons. In my view, 
trust in epistemic AI systems should be modeled in a similar way. In particular, our attitude to 
epistemic AI should follow the principle of caveat usor, which states that trust in AI systems 
should always be accompanied by epistemic vigilance.18
It might be objected that talking of “trust in AI systems” is misguided from the outset. 
Although the phrase “trust in AI” is very common in public discourse (Reinhardt 2023), 
many philosophers have criticized this phrase, arguing that trust is incompatible with the 
black box nature of AI systems (e.g., von Eschenbach 2021; Koskinen 2023) or amounts to 
something like a category mistake (e.g., Hatherley 2020; Kerasidou et al. 2022; Ryan 2020).
As I argue in more detail elsewhere (Hauswald 2024b), neither argument is convincing. It 
does not follow from the black box nature of AI that AI is in principle unsuitable as a possible 
object of trust.19 Human experts and epistemic authorities also exhibit a form of opacity in 
that they possess knowledge that is justificatorially or semantically esoteric to laypersons (see 
section 5.5.1). Nevertheless, most authors would not see this as a decisive reason for denying 
that epistemic trust in them is possible. One might even ask whether epistemic trust is needed 
at all in fully transparent contexts. Trust functions precisely where there is uncertainty and 
complexity; it serves to reduce this uncertainty and complexity and make it manageable 
(Luhmann 1979; see also Ross 2022).
The claim that talking about possible “trust in AI” amounts to some kind of category mis-
take or “conceptual nonsense” (Freiman 2023) also seems untenable. While I acknowledge 
that the paradigmatic forms of trust are interpersonal in nature, that is, they can only be 
directed towards humans,20 there are varieties of trust for which this is not true. In particular, 
I have in mind Nguyen’s (2023) concept of trust as an unquestioning attitude. Nguyen gives 
the following definition for this form of trust: “To trust X to P is to have an attitude of not 
questioning that X will P” (Nguyen 2023, p. 225). In addition, Nguyen also provides a formu-
lation for the special epistemic case, i.e., the case where X serves as an epistemic instrument 
or source of information, which reads: “To trust X as an informational source in domain Z is 
to have an attitude of not questioning X’s deliverances concerning Z” (ibid.). Nguyen explic-
itly emphasizes that this form of trust is more than mere reliance and that it can also be 
applied to the relationship with technical artefacts, including AI systems.21
5.5  The Transfer Problem
5.5.1  The Transfer of Epistemic Goods to Laypeople
To state the transfer problem: What epistemic goods can be transferred from experts and epi-
stemic authorities to laypersons, and what are the conditions for such transfer? So far I have 
focused on the transfer of beliefs and knowledge but there are other epistemic goods, such as 
understanding or wisdom. Can they be transferred in a similar way? Can they be transferred 

--- Page 73 ---

AI and the Philosophy of Expertise and Epistemic Authority
63
at all? Recently, growing interest has been shown in such questions, albeit with varying 
degrees of attention being paid to different epistemic goods.22
A fundamental problem with acquiring understanding from experts or epistemic author-
ities is that understanding appears to be an epistemic state that requires a significant amount 
of cognitive activity on the part of the person acquiring the understanding. In order to under-
stand an issue, a person has to make up their own mind and think it through to some extent. 
They cannot be purely passive; understanding is not something that can simply be received. 
This seems to be a crucial difference from the acquisition of knowledge or beliefs, which can 
be transmitted much more easily by testimony.
However, some qualifying remarks are in order here. First, although understanding requires 
a significant amount of cognitive activity on the part of the person acquiring the understanding, 
experts and epistemic authorities can certainly help a subject in this process. Jäger (2016) calls 
epistemic authorities who act in this role “Socratic authorities” because Socratic dialogue, asking 
critical questions and encouraging people to think about certain aspects of an issue, is one of the 
most important ways to promote understanding processes in people.
A second aspect suggesting that there is less difference between the acquisition of 
knowledge and the acquisition of understanding than might appear at first glance is that the 
transfer of knowledge can sometimes also be challenging, for example when the knowledge is 
semantically or justificatorially esoteric for the recipient. A proposition is semantically esoteric 
for a person if she does not understand the proposition linguistically. Not only does the person 
not know its truth-­value (in this case we could speak of an “epistemically” or “weakly eso-
teric” proposition), but also she does not know its truth-­conditions. One possible reason for this 
is that the proposition is formulated in a technical vocabulary that the person does not know 
(Goldman 2001, p. 94). A proposition is justificatorially esoteric for a person if she cannot (or 
cannot without considerable effort) understand the reason why the proposition is true or 
false, even if she understands it linguistically and can also easily inquire about its truth-­value 
from an epistemic authority (Hauswald 2024a, p. 30f.).23
The possibility of semantically and justificatorially esoteric knowledge poses a particular 
challenge for interactions with experts and epistemic authorities. Often what we need from experts 
and authorities is not just a simple “yes” or “no”, or “true” or “false”; we also need the reasons why 
this is the correct answer. As Ward (2017) points out, this applies, for example, to the field of law, 
where the judge should not be seen as a passive recipient of various external expert opinions, but 
rather as an actor who must also actively engage with the background, reasoning, and evidence 
provided by the experts in order to formulate and justify a coherent judgment of her own.24
However, in order for laypeople to understand the reasons, experts and authorities have to com-
municate them in a way they can comprehend, which is often not a trivial matter but requires 
special skills such as intellectual empathy (Jäger and Malfatti 2021) or the ability to explain difficult 
contexts in simple language. Croce (2018) calls such skills “novice-­oriented abilities.” The problem 
is that experts and epistemic authorities do not necessarily have such abilities, and even if they do, 
it often takes more time to provide laypeople with sufficient justification than is available.25
5.5.2  The Epistemic-­AI Transfer Problem
What epistemic goods can be acquired from epistemic AI systems? Elsewhere (Hauswald forth-
coming) I argue that users of epistemic AI systems can gain from them not only knowledge 
but also understanding, and even wise advice (see also Tsai 2020). However, for reasons other 
than those just discussed, the term “transfer” may seem misleading, or at least unfortunate, 
in this context. “Transfer” suggests that there is knowledge, understanding, or wisdom on the 

--- Page 74 ---

RICO HAUSWALD
64
part of the epistemic source, and that these goods are being transferred to a recipient. While 
this may typically be the case with human experts and epistemic authorities, many authors 
are reluctant to attribute knowledge, understanding, or wisdom to epistemic AI systems. If 
the systems themselves do not possess these epistemic goods, how can they be “transferred” 
to the users of these systems?
While I acknowledge that this is a legitimate question, it should be noted that, again, the 
difference between epistemic AI systems and human epistemic sources may be smaller than it 
might appear at first glance. For, as Lackey (2008) famously argued, there appear to be cases in 
which the recipient of a testimonial interaction acquires knowledge that the source itself does not 
possess. Lackey’s most famous example is her “Stella the creationist teacher case” in which stu-
dents learn about evolution from a teacher who does not believe in evolution herself.26 Analogous 
cases regarding the acquisition of understanding have been discussed by Malfatti (2019).
Perhaps in these cases we should speak of knowledge or understanding being generated in 
the recipient rather than transmitted or transferred. More precisely, we observe something in 
between the transfer and generation of epistemic goods, or a combination of the two. The 
source –­ human or AI –­ does possess something of epistemic value, but it is not yet genuine 
knowledge or understanding. However, when it is transferred to the recipient, genuine 
knowledge or understanding is created in the latter.
5.6  Conclusion
I have argued that AI systems will be increasingly integrated into our epistemic division of labor. 
This will fundamentally change the traditional relationship between experts and laypeople in a 
number of ways. AI systems will increasingly support experts in their interactions with lay-
people, or even replace them altogether. This raises questions about the interaction between AI 
systems and their users that parallel questions that have been discussed for decades in the episte-
mology of expertise and epistemic authority. In particular, I have focused on the definition 
problem, the identification problem, the deference problem, and the transfer problem.
Some authors expect that epistemic AI systems will eventually surpass humans in all 
respects, and that the epistemic distance will continue to increase until the capabilities of AI 
far exceed human cognitive abilities. Perhaps future AI systems will confront human users as 
super-­intelligent “oracle AIs” (Armstrong et al. 2012; Hauswald 2021a), their inner work-
ings being, even in principle, completely incomprehensible to users. The emergence of such 
systems could raise entirely new challenges, such as how to ensure that these systems do not 
themselves become an existential risk to humanity (see also Bostrom 2014).
Whether or not this development comes to pass, reference to the philosophy of expertise and 
epistemic authority can provide valuable insights that can significantly enhance our under-
standing of the relationship with epistemic AI systems and should be pursued in the future.

6.1  Background: Opacity and Data Protection
6.1.1  Opacity and Justification
It seems that the literature on opacity or explainable AI has not sufficiently “framed” the 
issue, i.e., it has not sufficiently explained why “opacity” or the “black box problem” in AI is 
an issue, when, and for whom. It is not clear that we can assume there is one overarching 
question that can be dealt with through one theory. As in any conceptual issue, it is good to 
state where the interest in the problem originates from. Here we start from an explicitly stated 
societal problem, data protection, and then show how this leads to a taxonomy of opacity at 
three levels: shallow, standard, and deep.1
I will suggest that at bottom, the phenomenon of epistemic “opacity” in computational 
modeling (Humphreys 2009), machine learning (Burrell 2016), and data science (Symons 
and Alvarado 2016) stems from our human practice of explaining and justifying our actions, 
especially our decisions. This is why we are worried when a computational system just decides 
something (“Your application for a credit card is rejected”), and does not provide any further 
justification. This is why we are concerned that such decisions may be based on the wrong 
criteria, i.e., they may be unfair because they rely on a bias that discriminates against certain 
groups (e.g., foreigners). When we ask “why?”, in such a context, we are not just looking for 
an explanation in causal terms, we are looking for a justification in terms of reasons. In the clas-
sic paper, Humphreys had defined “[A] process is epistemically opaque relative to a cognitive 
agent X at time t just in case X does not know at t all of the epistemically relevant elements of 
the process” (Humphreys 2009, 618). This was usefully focused on the issue of justification 
by Durán and Formanek (2018): “[A] process is epistemically opaque relative to a cognitive 
agent X at time t just in case X at t doesn’t have access to and can’t survey all of the steps of 
the justification.” So this discussion falls mainly within the realm of normative discourse. It is

(Bath: AISB), 18–­21.

72
part of the explanation why we worry about the allocation of “responsibility” in the context 
of AI, and about the criteria for “moral agency.” Opacity is a central issue in what is now often 
called “data ethics” (Floridi and Taddeo 2016; Mittelstadt and Floridi 2016).
One may wonder whether a demand for transparency is not asking a bit too much of 
humans and machines –­ but what we ask for is not full transparency but justification to an 
extent. Human practices and demands on the ability to justify actions vary strongly with 
context –­ when the stakes are high, they are extremely high and codified, e.g., in legal 
decisions and in safety-­critical contexts, whereas in many other contexts they are more 
relaxed. It is an open question how far “explicability” should go, given that the abilities of 
humans in that regard are not too impressive. Zerilli et al. (2019) argue that there is a 
double standard.
Of course, humans hardly ever know the full implications of their actions, or have full 
knowledge of all relevant facts. In fact, the “epistemological frame problem” seems to indicate 
that such knowledge is impossible because it is never clear in advance which knowledge 
might turn out “relevant” and what needs to be updated after an action (Dennett 1984).
There are several technical activities that aim at “explainable AI,” starting with Lomas 
et al. (2012) and Van Lent et al. (2004) and, more recently, a 2017–­21 DARPA research 
programme (Gunning  2017) and the AI4EU.eu project on “human-­centered AI.” More 
broadly, the demand for “a mechanism for elucidating and articulating the power structures, 
biases, and influences that computational artefacts exercise in society” (Diakopoulos 2015) is 
sometimes called “algorithmic accountability reporting.” This does not mean that we expect 
an AI to “explain its reasoning” –­ doing so would require far more serious moral autonomy 
than we currently attribute to AI systems. What we are currently looking for is to enable 
humans who use the AI system to explain their decisions which were based on the AI system.
6.1.2  Big Data
It turns out that the opacity issue is not limited to AI; it appears in data analytics, also, par-
ticularly in big data analytics. In a first approximation, “big data” analytics really is charac-
terized by just being “big,” i.e., it is not a radically new technique but it does what has been 
done elsewhere on a big scale. Having said that, we often think that a significant increase 
on a gradual scale can make the difference that is worthy of a new name and separate 
scientific treatment (so we distinguish babies from adults); also, such a significant increase 
can pass a threshold and lead to entirely different system state (add more weight and the 
bridge collapses). In the case of big data, the measurement of size can be done in various 
dimensions, but the classical ones are data at high volume, with high velocity, and variety –­ 
big data is often characterized through these “3Vs.” And indeed, the 3Vs are changing 
things in an impressive way.
The volume of data is enormous: 90% of the total digital data extant today was only cre-
ated in the last 2 years. We add 200 million emails and 200,000 Instagram posts per minute, 
but far more data is added automatically by digital processes –­ for example, each of the 20 
sensors on a single GE wind turbine generates 520GB of data per day (Saran 2013). The 
velocity of this addition is such that many systems stream data continuously in real time, e.g., 
video cameras and other sensing devices.
Note the importance of technologies like “smart cities,” “smart homes” (including “smart 
light bulbs,” “smart floors,” “smart doors,” etc.), “smart phones,” “wearables,” the “quanti-
fied self” (e.g., 23andMe.com), electronic toys and the “Internet of Things” –­ these are signs 
of the general digitalization of the human environment, mainly through more sensors, that 

--- Page 83 ---

DEEP OPACITY IN AI: A THREAT TO XAI AND STANDARD PRIVACY PROTECTION MECHANISMS
73
automatically generates a massive volume of data, with high velocity and variation (3Vs). So, 
there is now about nine times more digital data than 2 years ago, not just because almost all 
the classical data (medical records, business data, governmental data, etc.) is now digital, but 
because our lives are conducted to a large extent digitally, and there are many more sensors 
that generate a stream of digital data from the nondigital aspects of the world. This last trend, 
particularly, is the driving force of the “big” data increase.
6.1.3  Big Data and Surveillance
This big data contains valuable information that analysis can reveal; in particular, it can 
reveal patterns of how certain parts of the data relate to other parts, whether or not the data 
was generated for this purpose. One example from medical research is that the continuous 
flow of monitoring data of prematurely born babies in neonatal intensive care (EEG, ECG, 
blood oxygen, blood pressure, temperature, drug infusion pump data, growth data, etc.) is 
normally recorded at regular intervals, or used for alarms –­ i.e., almost all data is discarded. 
When such data was fed into a big data system under the supervision of medical experts 
(McGregor 2013), researchers were able to find early signs for the onset of potentially fatal 
conditions –­ patterns that indicated something was coming before any pathological symp-
toms occurred. Following this discovery, real-­time analysis is now used to detect these pat-
terns and save lives (Miotto et al. 2016).
Of  course, the patterns might also say other interesting things, e.g., whether 
someone is likely to buy a particular product, what political views they might hold, or 
what sexual preferences they may have. The detection and analysis of  these patterns 
in ever more data are now part a business model that is used on a large scale in IT ser-
vices that are provided “free of  charge.” “Surveillance is the business model of  the 
Internet” (Schneier  2015). Why are they provided without an obvious payment? 
Because the payment is in the form of  data, or, as the saying goes: “If  you are not pay-
ing for the product then you are the product.” So, companies like Google provide their 
services and connect their use to my ID (email, phone number, name, address), so they 
know my various devices, email traffic, account use, log-­on patterns, search patterns, 
YouTube use, gaming use, cloud documents, friends and collaborators, photos and 
videos (geo-­tagged), calendar, address book, location, etc., etc. As a PBS documentary 
sums it up, “In this vast ocean of  data, there is a frighteningly complete picture of  us” 
(Smolan 2016, 1).
In some ways, Google knows more about me than any person does; it even knows many 
things about me that I don’t know myself. Perhaps I am more right wing or more homosexual 
than I would like to admit. And of course, I forget lots of details but Google doesn’t. And if I 
turn off my mobile phone or don’t use a service . . . well, that’s a pattern, too. And that is just 
one company. Add government sources that may be able to access more than just one 
company or add classical surveillance from sensing in homes and on the streets (micro-
phones, cameras, motion sensing, temperature, etc.), add private peer-­to-­peer surveillance 
and we are already pretty close to a total surveillance situation –­ without noticing much of it. 
My personal data has become a commodity that is accessed out of my control.
The ethical evaluation of this situation may just turn on the consequences and in this 
situation there is a (small) probability that the overall outcome may be more beneficial than a 
scenario in which it is transparent who has access to my personal data and where I can 
­control that access. However, the current situation is problematic from a rights perspective 
since it involves deception and, crucially, it does not respect a right to privacy, in particular 

--- Page 84 ---

Vincent C. Müller
74
informational privacy, which is usually considered to be fundamental for a person’s autonomy 
(Roessler 2017). The question is what can be done to protect and continue positive use of AI 
and data analytics, while protecting privacy. We thus need a brief look at the requirements for 
policy in the area.
6.1.4  Standard Regulations
In the EU, many of these issues have been taken into account with the General Data Protection 
Regulation (GDPR 2016). The GDPR was agreed in the European Parliament and the EU 
Council in April 2016 and became law from May 2018 in the member states. Member states 
have the right to specify further rules that do not contradict this regulation (Section 10, cf. 
Section 13). It is a very powerful regulation that embeds a number of new features, while 
being the result of extended negotiations. I expect it to be a setting the political debate for a 
number of years and would be surprised if substantial changes in the political and regulatory 
situation were to occur in the next 10 years. Note that the major prior EU document, 95/46/
EC, was approved 21 years earlier, only at the level of a “directive” for national law (EU 
Parliament 1995), whereas the GDPR automatically became law itself. The GDPR foresees a 
“right to explanation” –­ although the extent to which this goes and to which it can be enforced 
is disputed (Goodman and Flaxman  2017; Wachter et  al.  2017,  2018). In any case, an 
inability to explain decisions appears to violate due process, especially when such decisions 
are challenged.
I will thus take this regulation as a general indicator of what kind of criteria are needed to 
act lawfully and, to some extent, ethically in privacy matters. It is not my aim to evaluate this 
regulation, but rather to take it as “what we’ve got” and see what kinds of problems we can 
expect in our special case: big data.
The GDPR can be summarized in the following points.
(1)	 It concerns “personal data”: name, address, localization, online identifier, health 
information, income, cultural profile.
(2)	 Communication: who gets the data, why, for how long? (No use for other “­incompatible” 
purposes. Use as long as necessary.)
(3)	 Consent: get clear informed consent.
(4)	 Access: provide access to my data.
(5)	 Right to be forgotten (not for research).
(6)	 Right to explanation for contracts (and right to have a person decide).
(7)	 Marketing: right to opt out.
(8)	 Legal: maintain EU legislation when transferring data out.
(9)	 Need for a “data protection officer” in your organization.
(10)	 Impact assessment prior to high-­risk processing (new technology, personal information, 
surveillance, sensitive).
The crucial points for our discussion of opacity are no. 3 (informed consent) and 6 (right to 
explanation), to a lesser extent 4 (access to my data) and 5 (right to be forgotten). To stress this 
again, these demands of an exemplary data protection regulation like the GDPR just reflect 
the demands that we make on human agents: to be able to justify their decisions and actions 
to some extent.

6.2  Types of Opacity
Here, we will try to explain opacity as a property of the relation between a person and a system.
6.2.1  Shallow Opacity: AI as an Instrument of Power
AI is used in automated decisions systems and decision support systems, especially 
through “predictive analytics.” The output of  such a system may be relatively trivial, 
such as “this restaurant matches your preferences,” “the patient in this X-­ray has com-
pleted bone growth,” or have greater significance for a person, e.g., if  it says “applica-
tion for credit card declined,” “donor organ will be given to another patient” or “target 
identified and engaged.” At the same time, it will often be impossible for the affected 
person to know how the system reached this output, i.e., the system is “opaque” to that 
person, who is typically also the/a data subject. The institution using the system (e.g., 
the bank) may just tell me that “the system has decided” but not how and why –­ even if 
the institution can find out what the reasons were.
In such cases, opacity is just a matter of decision from some party that is in power and 
which could find a justification, if it wanted. The opacity in these cases I shall call “shallow 
opacity.” This kind of asymmetric opacity to users only exemplifies the classic (and important) 
slogan “knowledge is power.” The users have no control over output and thus are not respon-
sible for the output. This kind of opacity is not specific to AI –­ it can happen in any use of data 
science for a decision or decision support system.
This has been used to classify the notion of opacity in general: “They are opaque in the 
sense that if one is a recipient of the output of the algorithm (the classification decision), 
rarely does one have any concrete sense of how or why a particular classification has been 
arrived at from inputs” (Burrell 2016, 1), but as we shall see, it is really a special case. It 
appears that shallow opacity is the notion Surden and Williams (2016) had in mind when 
they talk about “technological opacity”: “‘technological opacity’ applies any time a techno-
logical system engages in behaviors that, while appropriate, may be hard to understand or 
predict, from the perspective of human users.”
It is often said that such matters raise “significant concerns about lack of due process, 
accountability, community engagement, and auditing” (Campolo et al. 2017, 18ff). These 
algorithmic systems are part of a power structure, which is why Danaher talks about an 
“algocracy” and concludes that “we are creating decision-­making processes that constrain 
and limit opportunities for human participation” (Danaher 2016, 245). Again, however, the 
issue of power structure also applies when the opacity does not concern only the user or data 
subject –­ this kind of opacity is the subject of our next section.
6.2.2  Standard or “Black Box” Opacity
Many AI systems rely on machine learning techniques in (simulated) neural networks 
that will extract patterns from a given dataset through “learning.” These networks are 
organized in “layers,” one of which is the “input layer” and one the “output layer,” with 
one or many “hidden” layers in between. If there is more than one such hidden layer, the 
network is often called a “deep” neural network (DNN) and the learning is “deep learning” 
(Goodfellow et al. 2016). Data either flows from one layer to the next in one direction, in 
“feed-­forward” systems, or in any direction, in “recurrent” systems. The network can be 

--- Page 86 ---

Vincent C. Müller
76
recalibrated through a feedback system, which changes the outcome on a given income, 
i.e., the system “learns.”
These networks broadly learn in three different ways: supervised, semi-­supervised (e.g., rein-
forcement) or unsupervised –­ though these ways are not mutually exclusive. In the “supervised” 
case, the system is advised whether an output is correct or incorrect, or is shown “good” outputs 
(AlphaGo was of this sort, which beat a top-­ranked Go player in 2016, using a supercomputer 
with 1920 processors and 280 GPUs) (Economist 2016). In the “reinforcement” case, it is told 
about a broader target (e.g., win the game of Go) but not whether an output (e.g., a move) was 
correct or incorrect (AlphaGo Zero is of this sort) (Silver et al. 2018). Finally, in the unsupervised 
case the system tries to find patterns by itself, without feedback on which patterns are useful or 
correct (these systems are of central importance in statistics) (Hinton and Sejnowski 1999). We 
may find patterns we were not looking for, that nobody knew, and that we cannot explain.
With these techniques, the “learning” captures patterns in the data and these are labeled in a 
way that appears useful to the programmer while the programmer does not really know how 
these patterns came about: “We can build these models, but we don’t know how they work” 
(Knight 2017). In fact, the programs are typically evolving so when new data comes in or new 
feedback is given, the patterns in the learning system change. There is a significant recent litera-
ture about the limitations of machine learning systems (Castelvecchi 2016; Marcus 2018), that 
are essentially sophisticated data filters –­ and quite possibly at the peak of the “hype cycle” at the 
moment. Furthermore, the quality of the program depends heavily on the quality of the data 
provided, following the old slogan “garbage in, garbage out.” So, if the data already involved a 
bias (e.g., police data about the skin color of suspects or job data including gender), then the 
program will reproduce that bias. There are proposals for a standard description of datasets in a 
“datasheet” that would make the identification of such bias more feasible (Gebru et al. 2018).
What this means for our purposes is that the outcome cannot really be explained, it is opaque 
to the user or programmers, especially but not uniquely in the less supervised learning ways. It 
is thus more opaque than the cases of “shallow opacity” above, in that the opacity does not just 
apply to the users or data subjects; it also applies to the experts –­ the agent relativity was stressed 
by (Zednik 2019). Opacity for experts is not only about what the experts know at a particular 
point in time, but also about what they can know, even after research. For that reason, the 
resulting AI is often called “black box AI” –­ it features a black box between input and output 
rather like the human mind is a black box in the eyes of a (methodological) behaviorist.
This kind of opacity is what is often mentioned in general discussions of opacity, so I call it 
“standard opacity.” It is, however, specific to AI, in fact to a particular method of AI, namely 
machine learning. It features the problems of distribution of power mentioned under shallow 
opacity, and it shows the inability to provide justification for its output. It is probably what 
authors have in mind when they say that the systems “. . . are opaque: it is difficult to know 
why they do what they do or how they work,” how to explain their “explanatory success” 
(Zednik  2019). The systems know things but we do not, i.e., in the terminology of the 
“Rumsfeld cases” there are “unknown knowns” (Nickel 2019).
Perhaps the issue of democratic legitimacy is more urgent in the case of standard opacity, 
since it cannot be easily relieved. Kissinger pointed out that there is a fundamental problem 
for democratic decision making if we rely on a system that is supposedly superior to mere 
humans, but cannot explain its decisions. He says we may have “generated a potentially dom-
inating technology in search of a guiding philosophy” (Kissinger 2018). In a similar vein, 
Cave (2019) stresses that we need a broader societal move toward more “democratic” decision 
making to avoid AI being a force that leads to a Kafka-­style impenetrable suppression system 
in public administration and elsewhere.

--- Page 87 ---

DEEP OPACITY IN AI: A THREAT TO XAI AND STANDARD PRIVACY PROTECTION MECHANISMS
77
6.2.3  Deep Opacity
What has not been sufficiently taken into account in the discussions of opacity and the “black 
box” is to whom the system is opaque, and to what extent. It can be opaque to a user but not to the 
programmer. It may be opaque to both, but in a way that the expert analyst can overcome. I 
suggest there is a third case, where opacity cannot possibly be removed, even for the human 
expert, even if best efforts are made in the generation of the algorithms; this I call “deep opacity.”
In order to introduce deep opacity, it will be useful to remind ourselves of the kinds of ques-
tions we are supposed to answer, where opacity gets in the way –­ this follows from the section 
“Standard regulations” above. We said “The crucial points for our discussion of opacity are 
no. 3 (informed consent) and 6 (right to explanation), to a lesser extent 4 (access to my data) 
and 5 (right to be forgotten).” Some questions that follow from these demands are listed below.
•	 Does this data include information about me?
•	 Can you give me access to all the data about me?
•	 Does this data include personal information?
•	 Does this data include a particular piece of information “that p”?
•	 Is the data in this dataset anonymous? Can it be deanonymized?
•	 What information can be derived from this data?
Data analytics and AI for data are ways to find information that is in the data. Prior to carrying 
out the analysis, and prior to combining this data with other data, we cannot even know what 
kind of result the analysis will reveal. It might even reveal patterns that are unknown to the 
subject of the data itself, if the data is about a person or a company. It will reveal statistical 
patterns that only allow predictions with a certain degree of certainty –­ and correlation is not 
causation. It can be shown formally that certain sets of queries to a database will reveal the 
entire database (Abowd  2017) or that the data can be reidentified. No matter how well 
blended the data soup is, there are ways to de-­blend some of it and find some information.
Anonymization is a case in point. A dataset that provably cannot reveal any information about 
a particular item in it would have to be devoid of information. If there is information, who knows 
how useful it can be? For example, the nationality of individuals may reveal very little but if a 
particular piece of data is a rare property, perhaps even unique, it can unravel the whole information 
about that person. There is a host of examples of databases that were deemed safe to be released into 
the public domain –­ and then a smart way to deanonymize them was found (Rocher et al. 2019).
The data contains information, but how much? We cannot know. We can only know what 
a particular method can reveal on a particular dataset, not what future methods might reveal 
or what a dataset might reveal when combined with another dataset. So even under ideal 
conditions and with perfect expert knowledge, we cannot justify answers to the questions 
above. That is deep opacity.
6.3  Ethical Judgment under Opacity
If an agent operates under opacity (on a set of data), they cannot judge certain things, e.g., 
whether that data constitutes a threat to privacy. They can also not “give informed consent” 
to the use of data since being “informed” would require knowing at least the main implica-
tions of giving that consent. I cannot be responsible for what I cannot know (which is more 
than what I can know, which is more than what I do know).

--- Page 88 ---

Vincent C. Müller
78
There is a long tradition in ethics that recognizes what one knows as an important factor 
in how one’s actions are evaluated. This tradition is especially important and developed in 
criminal law, so I will use this standard to explain –­ note that the terminologies used differ in 
different jurisdictions.
Say you perform an action that results in the death of another human. Let us assume you 
acted without legal justification, so not as a solider or hangman, for example; not in self-­
defence and not on demand of the victim. Whether you are guilty of a crime, and which one, 
depends on what your intentions were, what you believed at the time, and what you should 
have known at the time. So, for example, in 2013 the well-­known runner Oscar Pistorius shot 
his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp. Pistorius admitted shooting her. He also admitted intention-
ally shooting his gun. However, he shot her at night, through a closed toilet cubicle door and 
claimed he had believed a burglar to be in that room –­ so he claimed not to have intentionally 
shot her, in particular. The sentencing depended on what he believed at the time and what he 
should have known but perhaps was negligent of, For these reasons, his defence argued for 
dismissal due to “self-­defence” but Pistorius was sentenced for “culpable homicide” due to 
negligence in 2014 (Lyall 2014), and then in a retrial for “murder” (due to intent to kill who-
ever was in the bathroom) in 2016; appeals by both the prosecution and the defense were 
rejected (Onishi  2016). These discussions on the role of ignorance in ethics go back to 
Thompson (1976); for more recent developments, see Peels (2017).
Opacity in big data analytics is thus truly a dilemma. Big data analytics always has deeper 
opacity (it is definitional for this field), and if we have deeper opacity, then we do not have 
standard data protection. So, with big data we get the worst of both worlds: increasing poten-
tial to do harm, with less ability to find out what is ethically right and to enforce what we think 
is right.
6.4  Outlook: Data Science under Opacity
Given that we value data protection and data analytics, we must try to strike a balance bet-
ween these two –­ or determine some absolute rules that must be respected, even if violating 
these rules would increase overall utility. For a data scientist, the situation presents itself as 
follows: “It is easy to say that anonymization is impossible and that re-­identification can 
always take place. It is just as easy to be complacent about the privacy risk posed by the avail-
ability of anonymized data. It is more difficult to evaluate risk realistically and in the round 
and to strike a publicly acceptable balance between access to information and personal pri-
vacy” (Elliot et al. 2016, vi).
There are some promising ways to avoid these problems, following the slogan “as much 
data as necessary.” Most uses of data science aim for general statistical insight, not for insight 
about particular individuals. So, for example, an epidemiologist who works on the causal 
factors of a particular disease does not need data about individuals but only about popula-
tions –­ she can work with “aggregated data.” In order to prevent deanonymization, this data 
can be “stuffed” with additional synthetic data points, while preserving the informational 
content that is relevant for the particular research. Such data can also be used for training 
machine learning systems. The conclusions from such data can be used to explain individual 
cases, though this is known to raise significant problems (Garrett 2003).
This idea is often called “differential privacy” where there is a guarantee that no method 
can lead from publicly available output back to individual private data; in other words, any 
combination of queries to a database should not reveal private data. This is achieved by ­adding 

--- Page 89 ---

DEEP OPACITY IN AI: A THREAT TO XAI AND STANDARD PRIVACY PROTECTION MECHANISMS
79
calibrated “noise” to the output to queries (Dwork et al. 2006). It is also possible to add this 
noise at the source of data collection, so that identifiable data is never even generated, or 
transmitted. One way to achieve this is as follows –­ a randomly selected (e.g., via the toss of a 
coin) half of the respondents answer randomly, the other half answer truthfully. This version 
is called “local differential privacy” because it produces the desired data (if the sample is large 
enough) but no “local” dataset with personal data is ever generated (Abowd 2017). Local 
differential privacy is apparently used by Apple to generate user data on iOS while guaran-
teeing that the company does not know what an individual user has done (Apple Differential 
Privacy Team 2017; Greenberg 2016).
6.5  Conclusion
We have proposed an analysis of opacity in AI and data science that is shaped by the societal 
context in which the issue arises, namely data protection and justification in automated 
decision systems. It appeared that there are three main types of opacity: “shallow” opacity, 
which is a matter of power structures; “standard” opacity, which is a matter of processing 
method; and “deep” opacity, which is a matter of informational content and robustness in the 
face of new methods or additional data. It would appear that avoiding the standard and deep 
varieties of opacity would require massive changes in the practices of data science, in 
particular the avoidance of identifiable data altogether, as well as openness about data 
sources, processes, and stakeholders –­ this is not impossible, but it may prove a large demand 
for this very fruitful new science.
