7.1  Introduction
Much has been made about the opacity of certain AI-­based decision systems. Many have 
argued that in high-­stakes decision contexts, a failure to be able to interpret, explain, or justify 
the outputs of such systems results in a failure of our obligations to those over whom we 
deploy these decision systems. These obligations are typically understood as obligations to 
provide information to decision subjects (or their proxies) so they may assess whether they 
have been treated appropriately. Concerns about black box systems have motivated work on 
so-­called “explainable AI” (“XAI”) tools and techniques to render black boxes transparent. At 
the same time, these concerns have been met with skepticism about both the meaning and 
value of explainability, especially given the opaque nature of much human decision making.
In this chapter, we summarize the current state of the debate between explainability pro-
ponents and skeptics. We then go on to articulate an alternative basis for grounding explain-
ability requirements that appeals to duties of consideration – duties decision makers have to 
ensure that they are reasoning about decision subjects appropriately. We explain how this 
alternative approach helps address explainability skepticism and orient our thinking about 
how decision makers ought to integrate AI-­based tools into their decision-­making processes.
The plan is as follows. Section 7.2 surveys recent philosophical accounts of what explain-
ability is and why it matters. Section 7.3 summarizes recent arguments for explainability 
skepticism. Section 7.4 shows how these arguments can be addressed by appeal to duties of 
consideration. Section 7.5 concludes.
7.2  The Black Box Problem
Our interest here is in cases where an institution uses a predictive algorithm to decide which 
individuals receive some important benefit (such as a job or loan) or burden (such as being 
detained pretrial or investigated for fraud). In this context, an “algorithm” is a set of unambig-
uous instructions for performing some task, and a “predictive algorithm” is an algorithm used 
Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
JOHN BASL AND DAVID G. GRANT 
7

--- Page 93 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
83
to make predictions. These algorithms typically take as input data representing various prop-
erties or “features” of the individual, and return a prediction about whether they possess 
some property that is taken to be relevant to how they should be treated. In lending, for in-
stance, an algorithm might be used to estimate the probability that the person will repay a 
loan, based on data taken from their credit report.
It is tempting to think that there is something morally problematic about distributing 
important benefits and burdens on the basis of predictions made by an algorithm no one 
understands. Call this the “black box problem” for AI-­based decision making. Concerns about 
the black box problem have led to widespread calls for algorithmic explainability (Burrell 2016; 
Mittelstadt et al. 2016), although just what sort of explainability is required is seldom spelled 
out. Expert responses to these calls vary widely. Some argue that the black box problem is real 
and important – call them explainability proponents – though they disagree about how difficult 
it is to solve. Others – explainability skeptics – deny that the problem is a problem at all. In this 
section, we discuss what explainability is supposed to be and why it is supposed to matter. We 
will discuss explainability skepticism in the next section.
Broadly speaking, there are three senses in which an algorithm might be said to be a black 
box (Burrell 2016):
(1)	 Secrecy: explanations of the algorithm’s behavior are known but not disclosed to some 
stakeholders.
(2)	 Insufficient expertise: explanations of the algorithm’s behavior are known and disclosed, 
but some stakeholders lack the expertise to understand them.
(3)	 Lack of explainability: even the designers and users of the algorithm are unable to explain 
its behavior.
Our focus here will be on algorithms that are black boxes in this third sense, as this type of 
opacity is supposed to be characteristic of black box artificial intelligence. When computer 
scientists talk about “black box AI”, they typically have in mind predictive algorithms based 
on machine learning, and especially those based on advanced machine learning techniques 
such as deep learning. Whereas traditional predictive algorithms are coded “by hand,” these 
algorithms are generated by a second “training algorithm” through a largely automated pro-
cess. While machine learning techniques vary, in many cases designers feed historical data 
(“training data”) into the training algorithm, which then attempts to produce a predictive 
algorithm that both performs well in predicting the training data and will generalize well to 
future cases. For example, in the case of an algorithm that estimates the probability that 
mortgage applicants will default, the training data might consist of information about past 
applicants’ credit reports at the time of application as well as their subsequent repayment his-
tory. This process is known as “supervised learning.”
The behavior of the resulting algorithms is often difficult to explain for three reasons. First, 
machine learning algorithms are capable of exploiting patterns in training data that are not 
only unfamiliar to human experts but so complex that they are difficult to reason about effec-
tively. Deep neural networks, for example, are capable of modeling complex, nonlinear rela-
tionships between the variable being predicted (“target variable”) and an arbitrarily large 
number of input variables (Burrell 2016; Selbst and Barocas 2018). Second, since these pat-
terns are identified automatically, the algorithm’s designers need not have any idea why they 
allow the algorithm to make predictions as successfully as it does, or why the algorithm pro-
duces particular outputs given particular inputs.1 Third, these algorithms are capable of 
combining the properties or “­features” that are explicitly represented in the input data into 

--- Page 94 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
84
arbitrarily complex “higher level features” representing highly abstract properties of decision 
subjects. While these properties may be recognizable to human experts, they may also be 
“alien features” that are not recognizable to human experts and may be difficult or impossible 
for them to understand (Selbst and Barocas 2018; Creel 2020; Buckner 2020). The net result 
is that even the experts who design these algorithms may be unable to adequately explain 
their input/output behavior.
This much is uncontroversial. Researchers disagree, however, on two key points. First, 
why does it matter whether decision-­making algorithms are explainable in the relevant 
sense? While basing high-­stakes decisions on black box predictions strikes many of us as 
problematic, how to spell out the worry is not immediately obvious. Second, what kind of 
explanations would be “adequate” given those concerns? After all, it is not true that we are 
entirely unable to explain the behavior of black box algorithms. We can, for example, freely 
inspect the calculations that black box algorithms perform when they process inputs, and 
so can explain their outputs by appeal to these calculations.2 The problem is supposed to be 
that we cannot provide explanations of  the right kind of black box predictions. But what 
kind is that?
7.2.1  Why Does Explainability Matter?
Explainability is a kind of transparency, and transparency is an instrumental value – it is not 
valuable for its own sake but rather because it promotes other values. Arguments for explain-
ability requirements thus appeal to values other than transparency itself. We will discuss 
arguments that appeal to safety, autonomy, legitimacy, fairness, and respect. We take these to 
be the values that are most relevant to the context of institutional decision making, but other 
values may be central in other contexts.3
7.2.1.1  Safety
Explainability can promote safety, in the sense of helping to ensure that AI systems behave as 
desired in the context in which they are used, with the risk of harmful or otherwise undesir-
able behavior kept to an acceptable minimum (Tutt 2017). Richard Caruana, for example, 
has argued against using black box AI in clinical contexts on the grounds that it creates an 
unacceptable risk to patient health. In a widely discussed study, Caruana’s team found that an 
AI model trained to estimate pneumonia mortality risk was classifying patients with asthma 
as at low risk of death. This assumption is quite reliable when applied to historical data from 
hospitals, but only because doctors know that patients with asthma are at an elevated risk of 
death and treat them aggressively. Using a system that exploited this fact to assign risk scores 
to patients could lead to disaster.4 Caruana takes such examples to show that ensuring patient 
safety requires being able to predict how an AI system will behave in the context of deploy-
ment, which in turn requires explainability.5
7.2.1.2  Autonomy
Second, explainability can promote autonomy. AI systems are increasingly used to automate 
decisions about how to distribute important benefits and burdens, such as jobs, loans, med-
ical care, fraud investigations, and pretrial detention. Moreover, these systems are increas-
ingly integrated into our day-­to-­day lives, influencing what we read, how we work, what we 
buy, and even who we date. As a result, our ability to promote our own interests – and more 
generally to exert control over our lives – increasingly depends on our ability to understand 
how these systems function.6

--- Page 95 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
85
In light of this, some authors argue that explainability matters because it promotes our 
individual interests in autonomy. Vredenburgh (2022b), for example, argues that we have a 
“right to explanation” from institutions that exercise power over us because providing these 
explanations is necessary to promote our interest in informed self-­advocacy, a “cluster of 
abilities to represent one’s interests and values to decision-­makers and to further those inter-
ests and values within an institution” (p.  212). Respecting this right requires disclosing 
information about the rules used in decision making, which in turn requires a form of explain-
ability. Here the notion of “explainability” is outward-­facing; a system is “explainable” in the 
relevant sense if important details about the system are disclosed to third parties in a form 
that they are able to understand.
7.2.1.3  Legitimacy
Third, explainability can promote political legitimacy. Many believe that exercising certain 
forms of power, such as the coercive power of the state, requires being transparent in various 
ways with those subject to it. When an AI system is used to exercise power, legitimacy may 
thus demand that decision makers be able to explain the decision-­making behavior of the 
system itself to decision subjects and other members of the political community. Seth Lazar, 
for example, has recently argued that the legitimate exercise of power requires satisfying a 
variety of transparency requirements, such as publicizing in advance the rules that will 
govern decision making and explaining the basis for particular decisions (to enable those 
affected to challenge them). Since black box AI systems often “bury the rules that they pur-
port to apply,” basing decisions on their outputs increases the risk that these requirements 
will be flouted.7
7.2.1.4  Fairness
Fourth, explainability can promote fairness. Defenders of a “right to explanation” argue that 
the use of explainable decision systems enables decision subjects and their advocates to iden-
tify and challenge algorithms that wrongfully discriminate against particular social groups, 
apply legitimate decision-­making rules incorrectly, or use otherwise unfair criteria (Goodman 
and Flaxman  2017; Grimmelmann and Westreich  2017; Selbst and Barocas 2018; 
Vredenburgh 2022b). Further – and just as crucially – using explainable decision systems 
helps decision makers to ensure that they are making fair decisions in the first place (Grant 
et al. 2023).
7.2.1.5  Respect
Finally, explainability can be a necessary precondition for showing proper respect to decision 
subjects. Grant et al. (2023) argue, for instance, that respecting decision subjects sometimes 
requires making decisions by exercising our own moral faculties, rather than outsourcing the 
decision to an automated system. In a different vein, Dishaw (n.d.) argues that we owe it to 
decision subjects not just to treat them with respect but also to make it possible for them to 
recognize that they are being treated with respect. In his view, this sometimes requires 
providing justifications in terms of the “particular reasons” that apply to the individual’s 
case – justifications that are only available when our decision systems are explainable.
7.2.2  What is Explainability?
As we have seen, researchers appeal to a wide variety of more fundamental values to ground 
the value of explainability. But what exactly is explainability? At a first pass, a decision system 

--- Page 96 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
86
(AI-­based or otherwise) is explainable in the sense that is relevant to the black box problem 
when we are in a position to grasp explanations of its behavior (Fleisher 2022). While this is 
a promising start, it leaves some important questions unanswered:
(1)	 Which aspects of a decision system’s behavior must be explained?
(2)	 What form must the explanations take?
(3)	 Who must be able to grasp the explanations?
7.2.2.1  What Must be Explained?
Explainability proponents differ on what aspects of decision-­making algorithms’ behavior 
require explanation. We can distinguish at least three relevant explananda. First, explainabil-
ity might require that we be in a position to grasp explanations of particular outputs of the 
algorithm. In the case of a credit default risk algorithm, for example, it might require that we 
be in a position to understand why the algorithm rated a particular applicant as high risk. 
Computer scientists call this local explainability. Second, it might require that we be in a posi-
tion to explain the algorithm’s decision-­making behavior in general. In the case of our lending 
algorithm, explainability might require understanding why a lending algorithm tends to 
assign the risk scores it does in general, across a broad range of cases. Computer scientists call 
this global explainability. Finally, it might require that we be able to explain particular sets or 
patterns of outputs. In our example, this might require that we be able to explain why men 
receive more favorable scores on average than women, or why a husband and wife who share 
all their assets and accounts in common receive different risk scores.8 We can call this pattern 
explainability.9
7.2.2.2  Explainable to Whom?
To whom must decision algorithms be explainable, according to explainability proponents? 
Different explanations will be useful to different stakeholders, both because they have differ-
ent epistemic capacities and because they have different explanatory goals. In the context of 
decision-­making algorithms, we can distinguish a few key stakeholder groups that are impor-
tant to keep in mind:10
(1)	 Designers: the experts designing the algorithm in question.
(2)	 Decision makers: the institutional decision makers who use the algorithm.
(3)	 Decision subjects: the individuals who are or may be subject to the algorithm’s decisions.
(4)	 Regulators: third parties who play some role in regulating the system from the outside, 
including journalists, advocates, ethicists, and government regulators.
Which group of stakeholders is emphasized by explainability proponents depends on the 
values their arguments focus on. Authors who focus on safety tend to emphasize the need for 
designers and regulators to understand an algorithm’s behavior, as this can help them antic-
ipate and mitigate undesirable behavior (Caruana et al. 2015; Tutt 2017). Authors who focus 
on autonomy emphasize the need for decision algorithms to be explainable to decision sub-
jects, so that they can exploit that understanding as they seek to promote their interests 
(Vredenburgh 2022b). Authors who focus on fairness may focus on any of the four groups. 
For instance, Grant et al. (2023) and others argue that decision makers need to be able to 
understand the decision algorithms they use in order to ensure that they are satisfying var-
ious duties of procedural fairness. Other authors emphasize the need for algorithms to be 

--- Page 97 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
87
explainable to regulators so that they can determine whether algorithms comply with 
­applicable laws prohibiting wrongful discrimination.11
7.2.2.3  What Form Must the Explanations Take?
Philosophers of science often emphasize that a single fact can be explained at different levels 
of abstraction and using different theoretical resources. For example, we could explain why a 
round peg does not fit into a square hole by drawing on resources from either geometry or 
physics (Putnam 1973), or why a rabbit was eaten by a fox by appeal to physics or population 
dynamics (Garfinkel 1981). Whether a given explanation is successful will depend on whether 
the agent seeking it has the capacity to understand it, as well as whether it is useful relative to 
the agent’s explanatory goals (Garfinkel 1981; Haslanger 2016). This raises the question of 
what form explanations of decision system behavior must take, for those systems to count as 
“explainable.”
Here the literature on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has presented us with a 
bewildering array of options. Broadly speaking, we can distinguish approaches that attempt 
to explicate the concept of explainability from those that attempt to operationalize it. Explications 
of explainability shed light on the concept by providing a philosophical account of one or 
more properties and arguing that they can play the theoretical and practical roles that the 
concept of explainability (and its cognates) were supposed to play.12 Operationalizations of 
explainability do not try to tell us what explainability is, but rather identify properties that are 
sufficient for it in at least some circumstances.
Examples of the operationalization approach include views on which systems are explain-
able when they are simulatable or decomposable. A computational system is simulatable 
when a human agent can “take the input data together with the parameters of the model and 
in reasonable time step through every calculation required to produce a prediction” 
(Lipton 2018, p. 13). A system is decomposable when “each part of the [system] . . . admits of 
an intuitive explanation” (Lipton 2018, p. 14). Such properties are not kinds of explainability; 
that a system is simulatable or decomposable does not entail that anyone is able to explain the 
system’s behavior. Nonetheless, it is at least plausible that systems that are simulatable or 
decomposable are more likely to be explainable in the sense we care about.13
The operationalization approach dominated the literature on explainability until fairly 
recently, which helps to explain widespread skepticism about whether the concept is well 
defined.14 However, philosophers have made considerable progress pursuing the explication 
approach over the past several years. Since a thorough survey of their proposals is outside 
the  scope of this chapter, we will discuss the examples that are most relevant for our 
purposes here.
Intentional Stance Explanation
Zerilli et al. (2019), Zerilli (2022) argue that decision-­making systems – whether human-­ or 
AI-­driven – are explainable in the senses that matter to us when we are capable of providing 
Dennettian intentional stance explanations of their behavior (Dennett 1998). These explana-
tions are folk-­psychological in nature, and cite the system’s reasons for acting as it did by 
appeal to its beliefs and desires (or suitable analogues).
Functional, Structural, and Run Transparency
Creel 2020 distinguishes three species of explainability for computational systems. A system 
is functionally transparent when we are in a position to know what algorithm it imple-
ments – “the high-­level, logical rules according to which the system will transform a given 

--- Page 98 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
88
input into an output” (p. 573). A system is structurally transparent when we are able to know 
how the computer code the system runs implements that algorithm. Finally, a system is run 
transparent on a particular occasion when we are able to know the details about how the 
system operated on that occasion, including details about how the system’s hardware, soft-
ware, and input data interacted on that occasion. According to Creel, these three types of 
transparency are “dissociable” (p. 581) and are useful for identifying different kinds of prob-
lems with how a system functions. For example, whereas functional transparency can reveal 
explicit racial bias, run transparency can identify racial bias that occurs due to biases in the 
input data used (p. 580).
Rule-­based Explanation
Both Vredenburgh (2022b) and Grant et al. (2023) emphasize the importance of rule-­based 
explanations – explanations that appeal to the high-­level rules that a decision system uses to 
make decisions. Vredenburgh argues that providing decision-­subjects with information about 
the high-­level rules used by a system promotes autonomy and fairness by helping decision 
subjects to (1) provide input on how the rules used will affect their interest, (2) modify their 
behavior in pursuit of better outcomes, and (3) challenge outcomes that are erroneous or 
unfair. For Grant et al., a system is rule transparent for an agent when that agent is in a position 
to know what inference and decision rules the system implements. Decision and inference 
rules are distinguished by the role they play in the system’s decision-­making behavior: 
Inference rules are used to form descriptive beliefs about decision subjects, and decision rules 
are used to decide how to treat decision subjects, given those beliefs. As discussed below, Grant 
et al. argue that rule transparency promotes fairness and respect by enabling decision makers 
to ensure that they meet important duties to decision subjects.
Normative Explanation
One final kind of explainability bears mentioning. So far, we have focused on kinds of explain-
ability that are characterized in terms of causal explanation. These kinds of explainability 
require that we be in a position to explain the outputs of a system by characterizing the causal 
process that generated them. Some explainability proponents emphasize a different kind of 
“explanation” of a system’s outputs, however. While one way to “explain” an outcome is to 
cite its causes, another is to provide an account of why it was morally justified. Similarly, one 
can “explain” the overall behavior of a decision system by either characterizing its underlying 
causal structure or providing a moral justification for using the system to make decisions. 
Vredenburgh (2022b) argues that such “normative explanations” are crucial for promoting 
autonomy and fairness, as they enable decision-­making subjects to advocate for themselves in 
cases where the rules being used are unfair. Dishaw (n.d.) instead argues that normative 
explanations are necessary for promoting respect, as enabling others to see that we are treat-
ing them with respect often requires providing a moral justification for our actions. Both 
argue that the need to provide such explanations grounds an objection to the use of black box 
decision algorithms, at least in some contexts.15
7.3  Explainability Skepticism
Now that we have surveyed recent accounts of what explainability is and why it matters, we 
turn to explainability skepticism. Explainability skepticism has at least three sources. First, 
some explainability skeptics argue that the relevant notion of explainability remains so 

--- Page 99 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
89
obscure that it is impossible to determine whether it picks out a coherent property – much less 
a morally important one. Second, some argue that human decision makers are not explain-
able in the relevant senses either, with the upshot that explainability proponents are imposing 
an unjustifiable double standard on decision algorithms. Third, some argue that the goals 
that explainability promotes can be achieved in the absence of explainability, rendering 
explainability requirements unnecessary or even harmful. Call these the definition problem, 
the double standard problem, and the otiosity problem.
7.3.1  The Definition Problem
Some argue that the concept of explainability is so vague that it is not clear that it picks out a 
normatively important property, if it picks out anything at all. While there is broad agreement 
that many machine learning algorithms are black boxes, there is little consensus about what 
exactly distinguishes them from more “explainable” methods for making decisions. Part of the 
problem is sheer terminological confusion. Researchers use many different terms to describe the 
property that makes some algorithms “explainable” and others “black boxes”: “Interpretability,” 
“explainability,” “explicability,” “intelligibility,” “scrutability,” and others. These terms lack pre-
cise, agreed-­upon definitions, and how they are related to other system properties is controversial 
(Lipton 2018; Krishnan 2020; Clinciu and Hastie 2019). The fact that the concepts in this family 
have proven difficult to pin down has engendered skepticism about whether they can really 
matter that much, or even whether they are even coherent. Lipton, for example, argues that
the term interpretability is ill-­defined, and, thus, claims regarding interpretability of various 
models exhibit a quasi-­scientific character (p. 4).
Similarly, Krishnan (2020) notes that
The absence of a clear articulation of what makes an interpretation different from a list of facts 
also leaves space for more extreme skepticism about interpretability-­talk. The skeptic can charge 
that the reason an adequate definition has not yet been proposed is because there is not, in fact, 
anything that it is to be an interpretation or an explanation of an algorithm (p. 491).
Part of the problem, Krishnan argues, is that we lack an account of the concept of interpret-
ability (which we are calling explainability16) that is sufficiently precise to allow us to deter-
mine what more concrete properties a system would have to count as interpretable 
(explainable). Calls for regulation prohibiting black box decision making are therefore prema-
ture, since it is not even clear which systems they would rule out.
As we have seen, explainability proponents have gone a long way toward addressing the 
definition problem in recent years. In our view, their arguments identify a variety of explana-
tory goals that explanations of algorithmic behavior are needed to serve, and give solid rea-
sons for thinking that suitable explanations are often unavailable. Explainability skeptics may 
protest that these explanations are often characterized at a high level of abstraction, leaving 
it unclear just which decision algorithms count as “explainable” in the relevant senses. We 
agree. However, existing arguments for explainable decision algorithms make a powerful case 
that explainability of various kinds promotes important values. They also give at least a high 
level of characterization of the kinds of explanations that are fit for purpose, together with 
helpful concrete examples. In our view, this suffices to show that concerns about black box 
decision algorithms are well founded.

--- Page 100 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
90
That said, we should make one concession to explainability skeptics. Showing that 
­explainability matters is one thing; formulating suitable regulations that require it is another. 
Operationalizing the relevant accounts of explainability for regulatory purposes will likely 
require substantial additional work.17 All in all, though, the definition problem no longer pro-
vides a compelling reason for skepticism about calls for explainability.
We are more sympathetic to the double standard and otiosity problems, at least as they 
apply to some explainability proponents. For the sake of space, the remainder of this section 
will focus on these problems as they apply to arguments that decision algorithms must be 
explainable to external stakeholders, including decision subjects and regulators. In the next 
section, we will explain why our approach to defending explainability requirements has an 
easier time addressing these problems.
7.3.2  The Double Standard Problem
Some argue that arguments against the use of black box AI to make decisions impose an 
objectionable “double standard” on AI-­based systems. Zerilli et al. 2019, for instance, argue 
that the standard of explainability that is appropriately applied to human agents requires the 
provision of intentional stance explanations that cite folk-­psychological states such as beliefs 
and desires (or suitable analogues). Calls for algorithmic explainability, in their view, err by 
requiring what Dennett (1998) calls “design stance” explanations – mechanistic explana-
tions that cite details of the relevant system’s “inner workings.” Since decision-­making sys-
tems play very similar roles as the human decision makers they replace, there is a defeasible 
presumption in favor of requiring them to satisfy similar standards of explainability. In their 
view, there is no asymmetry between the two kinds of systems that would justify requiring 
design stance explanations in the case of algorithms but not humans. Since providing inten-
tional stance explanations of a system’s behavior does not require knowledge of its under-
lying computational architecture, the requirement to use explainable decision systems does 
not rule out the use of black box AI systems such as those based on deep neural networks.
In our view, the double standard problem is particularly potent as it applies to arguments 
that black box decision systems are problematic because they interfere with requirements to 
disclose information about the decision-­making process to external stakeholders, such as 
decision subjects and their proxies. We seldom expect institutions to provide much in the way 
of an explanation to decision subjects, even in high-­stakes cases. Anyone who has ever been 
on the job market, for instance, knows that employers almost never provide meaningful 
explanations when they reject candidates, aside from stressing the number and quality of 
applicants. The same goes for college and graduate school admissions, many competitions for 
honors and awards, and some momentous legal decisions (such as when the US Supreme 
Court decides to deny certiorari). True enough, decision makers are sometimes required to 
provide explanations to external stakeholders, such as when lenders deny loan applications. 
However, these contexts are the exception, not the rule (Grant et al. 2023) . Moreover, it’s not 
clear to us that decision makers should be required to provide highly detailed explanations of 
their decision-­making processes, outside these exceptional cases. For one thing, providing 
explanations that are detailed and accessible enough to be useful can be extremely expensive, 
diverting valuable resources that might be better spent elsewhere. For another, providing 
such explanations can have a variety of negative side-­effects: Facilitating gaming (Bambauer 
and Zarsky 2018), distorting expert judgment (Nguyen 2021), undermining privacy (Shokri 
et al. 2021), and undermining intellectual property rights (Brauneis and Goodman 2018). 
Taken together, these doubts significantly limit the reach of the relevant arguments.18

--- Page 101 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
91
7.3.3  The Otiosity Problem
Some explainability skeptics argue that we can achieve the goals that explainability is sup-
posed to help us achieve in the absence of explainability, rendering transparency require-
ments unhelpful if not counterproductive. Krishnan (2020), for example, argues that the 
goal of algorithmic explainability is to justify algorithmic outputs, and that mechanistic 
explanations are unlikely to be useful for providing such justifications (at least in many cases). 
Similarly, Walmsley (2021) suggests that explainability is useful for promoting goals such as 
“justice, fairness or impartiality” largely because it helps third parties to challenge algorithm-­
based decisions, and that there are a variety of mechanisms by which we can facilitate these 
challenges that do not require transparency. Finally, London (2019) argues that calls for 
explainability in medical contexts are misguided, as medicine “is a domain in which the ability 
to intervene effectively in the world by exploiting particular causal relationships often derives 
from experience and precedes our ability to understand why interventions work” (p. 17). In 
such domains, he argues, we should follow standard practice by prioritizing “predictive and 
diagnostic accuracy” over transparency (p. 20).
7.3.4  Defending Explainability?
What lessons should we draw from these arguments for explainability skepticism? One pos-
sible lesson is that concerns about basing decisions on black box AI have been wildly over-
stated. Since any justification that we have for demanding (a particular kind of) explainability 
from AI systems will carry over to other methods for making decisions – including relying on 
human decision makers – there is little to the idea that we have a special complaint against 
black box AI systems.
In our view, this isn’t the right lesson to draw. As we saw in the previous section, researchers 
have identified a variety of reasonable grounds for concern about basing decisions on black 
box AI. Nonetheless, the problems that underlie explainability skepticism highlight the bur-
dens that explainability proponents must meet. To meet these burdens, explainability propo-
nents must both identify a set of duties that decision makers owe to stakeholders and show 
that basing decisions on black box AI interferes with their ability to satisfy those duties. In the 
next section, we articulate our approach to the black box problem, and show how it meets this 
burden.
7.4  The Due Consideration Approach
In “What we owe to decision-­subjects: beyond transparency and explanation in automated 
decision-­making,” Grant et al. (2023) defend the explainability thesis:
In many contexts, decision-­makers are morally obligated to avoid basing their decisions about 
how to treat decision-­subjects on the outputs of black box AI systems (p. 2).
Central to their argument is the claim that decision makers have duties of consideration to 
decision subjects. Duties of consideration constrain how decision makers make decisions 
about how to treat decision subjects, rather than requiring them to explain how they make 
those decisions to others. There are many decision-­making contexts in which there is seem-
ingly no obligation to disclose how decisions are made, or in which failures to make such 
­disclosures are readily excused. Consider, for example, deciding not to hire someone after an 

--- Page 102 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
92
academic hiring interview, deciding to surveil someone for legitimate national security rea-
sons, deciding to award someone a valuable prize, and deciding to find someone guilty of a 
crime. In these contexts, it is doubtful that decision makers have even a pro tanto duty to dis-
close either the grounds for particular decisions or the general process by which such decisions 
are made. However, this does not absolve decision makers from the responsibility to make 
decisions carefully and with – as we would put it – due consideration for decision subjects. 
Duties of consideration, then, need not ground duties to explain decisions to decision subjects 
(or their advocates). Nonetheless, relying on black box AI systems can make it difficult, if not 
impossible, for decision makers to satisfy their duties of consideration.
In this section, we summarize the due consideration approach to the black box problem, 
highlighting how it answers the questions about explainability raised in section 7.2 and the 
arguments for explainability skepticism raised in section 7.3.
7.4.1  What is Explainability and Why Does it Matter?
As we saw in section 7.2, we can distinguish approaches to the black box problem by consid-
ering how they answer a few key questions about what explainability is and why it matters. 
We will begin by explaining how the due consideration approach answers these questions. 
Here’s the short version: On the due consideration approach, basing decisions on black box AI 
is morally problematic because it interferes with decision makers’ ability to provide due 
consideration to decision subjects. To provide due consideration, decision makers must satisfy 
a variety of duties of consideration that place constraints on how decision makers go about 
deciding how to treat decision subjects. The values that ground these duties are respect and 
fairness. The target of explainability – the individuals to whom black box AI systems must be 
made explainable – is the decision makers that use the system to make decisions, as opposed 
to decision subjects, advocates, or regulators.
Both what must be explained and the form that the explanations must take will depend on 
the context, as they will depend on what duties of consideration apply and what kinds of 
explanations will facilitate their satisfaction. In general, the explanations must render the 
system rule transparent (see section 7.2). This may – depending on the context – require iden-
tifying the inference and decision rules that explain particular decisions (local rule transpar-
ency), sets of decisions (pattern rule transparency), or the decision-­making behavior of the 
system in general (global rule transparency).19
The duties that the due consideration approach focuses on are primarily grounded in the 
values of fairness and respect. This isn’t to say that showing due consideration never involves 
working to ensure that decisions are safe, accurate, or autonomy promoting. Nor are these 
values unrelated. Plausibly, treating decision subjects fairly will often require evaluating them 
using accurate methods; similarly, respecting decision subjects will often require ensuring 
their safety or promoting their autonomy in particular ways. However, if showing due 
consideration were solely a matter of promoting safety, accuracy, and autonomy, then it 
would be unlikely to ground a broad case against using black box AI systems to make decisions. 
For one thing, black box AI systems will often be both safer and more accurate.20 For another, 
while the value of autonomy may give decision makers strong pro tanto reasons to use sys-
tems that they can explain to decision subjects, the foregoing examples suggest that these 
reasons are often defeated.
One of the strengths of the due consideration approach is that it changes the target of 
explainability  –  the subject to whom an AI system must be made explainable  –  from the 
decision subject to the decision maker. Why is this a strength? Defenses of the double standard 

--- Page 103 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
93
problem typically rely on the fact that decision-­making procedures that do not rely on black 
box AI are often incredibly opaque to decision subjects; for instance, unsuccessful job appli-
cants are rarely told much about why they were unsuccessful. If it is permissible to use these 
more traditional decision-­making procedures, then using AI-­based procedures that are simi-
larly opaque to decision subjects should be similarly unproblematic. However, this objection 
loses its force when we shift our attention from whether decision makers can explain their 
decisions to decision subjects to whether they can make them appropriately in the first place.
Suppose that a hiring manager is advised by a colleague not to hire a particular candidate, 
but refuses to explain why the candidate should not be hired. Suppose also that, were the 
manager to rely on their colleague’s testimony, there would be no obligation to disclose its 
basis to the candidate. Nonetheless, the manager should be hesitant to take their colleague’s 
testimony into account; it might be unfairly biased in some way, based on incomplete 
information, or otherwise problematic. On the other hand, suppose the manager knows that 
their colleague never maligns a candidate unless there is compelling evidence that the candi-
date has committed fraud. Now relying on the colleague’s advice does not seem problematic 
in the same way. This simple pair of cases illustrates how basing decisions on the outputs of a 
black box system can interfere with a decision maker’s ability to make decisions appropriately, 
regardless of whether they are obligated to explain those decisions to decision subjects.
What about concerns that humans are subject to bias, poor at introspection, and prone to 
confabulation?21 On the one hand, we want to be appropriately concessive to this kind of con-
cern. We recognize that human decision makers can be biased, dishonest, and mistaken about 
their true motivations. On the other hand, we don’t want to concede too much; objecting to 
the use of black box AI in decision making does not commit us to an objectionable double 
standard, the failings of human decision makers notwithstanding.
First, the concession: When we cannot ensure that a human decision maker will show due 
consideration to decision subjects, we have at least a pro tanto reason to reject that decision 
maker. If we are forced to choose between a human decision maker that we do not fully trust 
and a black box model that we do not fully understand, then our view does not entail that we 
should prefer the former over the latter. Indeed, considerations of accuracy, robustness, and 
the like may weigh in favor of the AI system, or a hybrid of the two.22 Note, however, that there 
are often other options available; for example, instead of relying on black box AI or human 
clinical judgment, decision makers can often rely on statistical models that are inherently more 
explainable, such as those based on simple linear models or decision trees (Grant et al. 2023).
Second, we want to resist the view that human decision makers are incapable of making 
decisions in a way that shows due consideration, or of assessing whether they have succeeded. 
While we might struggle to overcome our biases and introspective limitations, and while dif-
ferent people might succeed to varying degrees, we see little reason to think that human 
decision makers are wholly incapable of showing due consideration (or knowing that they 
have). So long as we have these abilities to at least some degree, the worries we raise about 
black box systems AI apply. In particular, a decision maker will have at least a pro tanto reason 
not rely on a black box AI system whenever they reasonably believe that making decisions 
themselves would better satisfy their duties of consideration.
7.4.2  Duties of Consideration
According to the due consideration approach, decisions about how to treat others are often 
governed by duties of consideration grounded in the values of respect and fairness. These 
duties shape how we may permissibly form beliefs about decision subjects and decide how to 

--- Page 104 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
94
treat them on the basis of those beliefs. Decision making of the sort we are interested 
in – where there is some possibility that we might integrate or deploy AI systems – can be 
decomposed into two tasks: forming beliefs about relevant descriptive properties of decision 
subjects (“fact-­finding”), and making decisions on the basis of those beliefs. For example, a 
hiring manager deciding between two applicants will first read their application materials in 
order to form beliefs about their qualifications and other distinguishing characteristics. Then, 
on the basis of those beliefs, the manager will employ some decision procedure (formal or 
informal) to decide whom to hire. According to the due consideration approach, distinct 
duties apply to each of these tasks or phases. Duties of evidential consideration govern the fact-­
finding phase, whereas duties of practical consideration govern the decision-­making phase.23
7.4.2.1  Duties of Evidential Consideration
Fact-­finding is constrained by a variety of duties. Straightforwardly, we have duties to form 
accurate beliefs about decision subjects. For instance, forming beliefs about the qualifications 
of job or loan applicants randomly and on the basis of no evidence would wrong them. What 
exactly does this duty of accuracy require?
One thing it might require is that, when choosing between different methods, tools, or 
rules for forming beliefs about decision subjects, we choose the method that performs best on 
average in generating true beliefs (or best satisfies some other aggregate standard of 
performance). Another thing it might require is that we avoid ignoring readily available evi-
dence that would benefit a particular decision subject, were we to take it into account. These 
two requirements can pull in different directions (Grant et  al.  2023, sections 5.1–5.2). 
Suppose a hiring manager knows that asking applicants about their hobbies tends to produce 
distorted beliefs about their qualifications, biasing them in ways that are both unfair and 
counterproductive. Suppose also that, during a particular interview, an otherwise unremark-
able applicant reveals that they have an unusual hobby: They are a talented graffiti artist, 
albeit not professionally. In the right context, this evidence could be highly relevant. Suppose, 
for instance, that the manager’s company is secretly developing a piece of software called 
“graffiti simulator” but has not disclosed this to applicants. Plausibly, it would be unfair for 
the manager to ignore the fact that the applicant’s hobby makes them uniquely qualified for 
the job, even if there are competing reasons to set it aside.
Importantly, our duties of evidential consideration are not solely duties to ensure that our 
beliefs are likely to be true (or at least well informed). Sometimes we have duties to ignore evi-
dence when forming beliefs, even when ignoring that evidence comes at a cost to predictive 
performance. This is because some evidence is morally inadmissible, in the sense that we have 
moral reasons to set it aside when we make a particular decision (Grant et  al.  2023, 
­section 7.3). For example, suppose a company has evidence that women applicants for a 
particular type of position are more likely to take parental leave than men applying for the 
same position, and that taking parental leave negatively correlates with job-­relevant 
performance measures. Even if gender provides useful evidence of future job performance, 
taking gender into account in a way that would disadvantage women applicants seems clearly 
unfair.24
7.4.2.2  Duties of Practical Consideration
Whereas duties of evidential consideration govern how we form descriptive beliefs about 
decision subjects, duties of practical consideration govern how we make decisions on the basis 
of those beliefs. Clearly, decision makers can form beliefs about a decision subject in an unim-
peachable way, and yet base decisions on those beliefs in ways that fail to treat decision 

--- Page 105 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
95
­subjects fairly or with due respect. Examples abound; suppose, for instance, that a racist judge 
comes to rationally believe that a Black defendant is not a flight risk, but orders them to be 
detained out of spite.
Broadly speaking, there are two kinds of duties of practical consideration. The first requires 
decision makers to implement morally appropriate decision rules – rules that specify how to 
treat particular decision subjects given the results of fact-­finding (Grant et  al.  2023, 
­section 8.1). If fairness requires that we treat like cases alike, for instance, then a decision 
maker can fail to show due consideration by drawing invidious distinctions among decision 
subjects, issuing decisions that are influenced by morally irrelevant factors. We take it that 
this is relatively uncontroversial; nonetheless, it has important implications for when and 
how decision makers should rely on black box AI.
Other duties of practical consideration do not directly constrain the decision rules that 
decision makers use, but instead require them to exercise their deliberative capacities in 
particular ways. These duties of agential consideration (Grant et al. 2023, section 8.2) require 
that we exercise our deliberative capacities with appropriate care and in ways that are suit-
ably responsive to the rights, interests, and moral status of decision subjects. For instance, 
showing due consideration in some contexts might require empathizing with the decision 
subject by seeing a given choice from their perspective before making a decision.25
Grant et al. 2023 do not provide a full theory of agential consideration, leaving it as a 
research program. However, they do motivate the existence of duties of agential consideration 
by giving examples like the following:
Computer scientists announce that they have discovered a method to create customized models 
for any individual eligible to serve on a jury. The models are trained on personalized data sets and 
can predict with perfect accuracy how a given juror would find in any given criminal case by 
implementing the inference and decision rules of the modeled individual. After years of testing, 
the court system adopts the Juror Substitution Policy. The policy requires that individuals be 
called for jury duty using the usual method: They come to court, lawyers are given a chance to 
evaluate and dismiss them, and so on. However, once jurors are selected, they may leave and their 
juror model will be used to adjudicate the case. Imagine that these models take as inputs whatever 
written, visual, or auditory information a human juror would process during a criminal trial, and 
perfectly replicate the judgments their human counterparts would make in light of such 
information (including instructions from the judge to disregard certain information). Further, 
imagine that these models reach their judgments by implementing the same inference and 
decision rules that their human counterparts would have used (Grant et al. 2023, p. 23).
Grant et al. (2023) make two claims about this case. First, it would be at least problematic 
(if not all-­things-­considered wrong) to replace jurors with juror models. Second, we cannot 
explain why it would be problematic in terms of failures to implement appropriate inference 
or decision rules. However, we can explain why it would be problematic by appeal to duties of 
agential consideration, since such duties require decision makers to exercise their deliberative 
capacities in particular ways. While juror models and jurors might implement similar infer-
ence and decision rules, juror models lack the deliberative capacities that human jurors have, 
and so cannot exercise those capacities in the ways that duties of agential consideration 
require. For instance, perhaps showing a defendant due respect requires having fellow mem-
bers of their political community decide  –  through careful exercise of their deliberative 
­capacities – whether conviction is warranted. If so, then showing defendants due consideration 
is incompatible with outsourcing jury deliberations to mere machines (Grant et al. 2023, 
pp. 23–24).

--- Page 106 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
96
While much more could be said about duties of agential consideration, we must set the 
matter aside. What matters for our purposes is that recognizing the existence of duties of 
agential consideration opens up a novel class of arguments against the use of black box AI in 
decision making.
7.4.3  Defending Interference
With a variety of duties of consideration at hand, we are in a position to show how relying on 
black box models can interfere with decision makers’ ability to show due consideration. 
Consider duties of evidential consideration first. If duties of evidential consideration required 
only that we form beliefs about decision subjects using truth-­conducive methods, then it 
might seem unclear how such duties could ground objections to using black box models. 
After all, the primary selling point of these models is their superior predictive performance.26 
Once we recognize a duty not to ignore available evidence, however, we can easily see how 
relying on black box models could lead to failures of due consideration. Most straightfor-
wardly, if a model is not rule transparent, then the decision maker may not be in a position to 
determine which pieces of evidence influenced the model’s outputs, and so may be unable to 
ensure that all available evidence that might benefit decision subjects has been taken into 
account.
Turning to duties to set aside morally inadmissible evidence, suppose that a hiring man-
ager has a choice of two predictive models that they can use to augment their decision about 
which candidates to hire. One model is rule transparent in our sense, the other is not. Let’s 
also assume our decision maker is opaque to themselves in the sense that, try as they might, 
they will be unable to tell whether their fact-­finding is influenced by an applicant’s gender. If 
the decision maker were evaluating applications unaided – without assistance from a predic-
tive model – then they could safeguard against gender bias by scrubbing information about 
gender and problematic proxies for it from the applications. Similarly, if they were to augment 
their judgment by consulting the rule transparent model, they would be able to inspect the 
model to determine whether its outputs are based on gender or its proxies in a problematic 
way. By contrast, consulting the black box model would make the task of avoiding gender bias 
far more difficult. Black box models such as deep neural networks are remarkably capable of 
inferring features that are not explicitly represented in their input data,27 and their opaque 
nature makes it difficult to determine what features they are relying on and how.28 Even if 
relying on the black box model would enable better performance according to some relevant 
measure, it would also carry a greater risk of relying on morally inadmissible evidence.
What about duties of practical consideration? We have seen that relying on black box 
models in fact-­finding can make it difficult to ensure that one is implementing inference rules 
that show due consideration. A similar problem arises when decision makers use black box 
models during the second phase of the decision-­making process, where they decide how to 
treat decision subjects given the results of fact-­finding. Pretty obviously, it is hard to ensure 
that one is implementing appropriate decision rules without knowing what rules are being 
implemented. Moreover, reflecting on duties of agential consideration  –  which require 
decision makers to exercise their deliberative capacities in certain ways, rather than to imple-
ment decision rules that satisfy certain constraints – reveals a second way in which black box 
models can interfere with duties of practical consideration.
Where we have duties of agential consideration, we have a pro tanto duty not to turn over 
full decision-­making authority to any alogrithmic system, on the assumption that such sys-
tems simply can’t exercise the relevant capacities at all.29 The contexts in which we have 

--- Page 107 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
97
duties of agential consideration are those contexts in which it is important that a 
human – ­perhaps a human occupying a particular role, like a juror – ultimately decides.30 
However, in most high-­stakes decision contexts, AI is integrated as part of a broader decision-­
making system rather than deployed as a decision maker. In such cases, black box models can 
interfere with duties of agential consideration in ways that rule transparent models need not.
Whenever decision makers rely on AI models, they risk compromising their ability to 
exercise agential consideration. This is why it is important to reflect carefully on the form that 
information generated by models and provided to decision makers takes. For example, model 
outputs can be provided in isolation or supplemented with details about how the model works 
and when its outputs are likely to be reliable. For example, a judge that might be inclined to 
make pretrial detention decisions too hastily on the basis of algorithmically generated risk 
scores might well pause were they told those scores are based partly on zip codes. When black 
box models are used, this potential backstop against failures of agential consideration in 
hybrid human–AI decision making is compromised.
This is not to say that a black box model will always interfere with duties of agential 
consideration in hybrid decision systems; some human decision makers might be very 
conscientious, always exercising the relevant capacities with appropriate care. Nor do we 
think that rule transparent models will be sufficient to ensure that human decision makers 
show due agential consideration. However, hybrid decision systems that incorporate black 
box models have a different risk profile from hybrid systems that do not; their integration 
raises the risk that decision makers will fail to satisfy duties of agential consideration. 
Evaluating and mitigating that risk in particular cases will require context-­sensitive, socio-
technically oriented ethical analysis.
7.4.4  Due Consideration and Explainability Skepticism
To wrap up our discussion of the due consideration approach, we will briefly expand on how 
it addresses the sources of explainability skepticism identified above.
7.4.4.1  The Definition Problem
As discussed in section 7.3, our view is that concerns about vagueness of the concept of 
explainability are overwrought, given the current state of the field. This is not to say that it 
will always be easy to determine whether a particular system is explainable. There are many 
kinds of explainability that matter in the context of institutional decision making, and deter-
mining whether they are instantiated by particular systems may require considerable norma-
tive and empirical investigation. However, we do not see this as a problem with the concept of 
explainability itself; we can know perfectly well what it means to be kind, for instance, while 
finding it difficult to determine which particular actions were kind.
7.4.4.2  The Otiosity Problem
We concede that there will be cases in which showing due consideration is consistent with 
relying on a black box system. Indeed, in some cases it may be the best way to show due 
consideration on balance. For example, we agree that – in some contexts – the value of accu-
racy may be so important that decision makers should simply use the most accurate fact-­
finding methods available (even if they are not explainable). However, rule transparency will 
never be entirely otiose with respect to due consideration, as satisfying some duties of 
consideration requires knowledge of the inference and decision rules one is using. (Consider 
the duty to avoid relying on morally inadmissible evidence, for instance.) Moreover, using rule 

--- Page 108 ---

JOHN BASL and DAVID G. GRANT 
98
transparent decision aids will at least normally make it easier for decision makers to satisfy 
their duties of consideration (as Grant et al. 2023 argue).
7.4.4.3  The Double Standard Problem
As we have seen, focusing on duties that decision makers have to make decisions in a 
particular way – as opposed to duties to disclose how decisions are made – goes a long way 
toward addressing the double standard problem. To summarize what has already been said, 
it’s true that we often don’t expect human decision makers to disclose the basis of their 
decisions to decision subjects. It’s also true that human decision makers often fail to show 
due consideration, whether or not they rely on black box systems. Neither observation 
undermines our argument, however. Regarding the first point, disclosure requirements play 
no role in our argument. Regarding the second point, we are happy to concede that some of 
the concerns that we have raised apply to human decision makers as well. All our argument 
needs is the claim that – as we have argued – relying on a black box model will often make 
showing due consideration more difficult. For instance, while human decision makers are 
prone to relying on morally inadmissible evidence when they make decisions for themselves, 
relying on a black box model can make avoiding such failures even more difficult (see 
section 7.4.3).
One last response bears mentioning. According to the double standard problem, we do 
not require human decision makers to be explainable, so we should not require AI-­based 
decision systems to be explainable, either. However, this argument tacitly assumes that we 
should not expect more from such systems than we have traditionally expected from human 
decision makers. Zerilli et al. (2019) consider and reject a narrow set of reasons why we 
might hold algorithms to higher standards, such as that doing so will increase their 
performance. When we consider the broader set of reasons why we sometimes allow human 
decision makers to be opaque, we see that calls for algorithmic explainability need not involve 
a double standard but merely an (appropriately) different standard. For example, consider-
ations of efficiency, practicality, safety, or confidentiality plausibly justify opacity in many 
cases where humans make the decisions. A parallel justification will not always be available 
when human decision makers are replaced by algorithmic systems. For example, algorithmic 
systems cannot be compromised by the threat of retribution, so one widely applicable 
argument for allowing human decision makers to operate in secret does not apply. The same 
will sometimes be true with respect to duties of consideration. The standard of due 
consideration that we should demand is not the one we have historically demanded, but 
rather the one that it is reasonable to demand given the tools that are now available. If 
explainable AI can help us show due consideration to a greater extent than was previously 
possible, then perhaps it is time to raise the bar.31
7.5  Conclusion
In this chapter, we have shown that focusing on the obligations of decision makers to show 
due consideration provides new normative foundations for calls for algorithmic transpar-
ency while addressing some of the most common criticisms. More broadly, we hope to have 
highlighted how much normative philosophical work is needed to properly analyze “the 
black box problem” and related notions such as transparency, interpretability, and explain-
ability. As our survey of the literature shows, whether an AI system counts as a “black 
box” – and, if so, whether using it would be objectionable – does not just depend on its 

--- Page 109 ---

Explainability in Algorithmic Decision Systems
99
technical features. Instead, it depends on what kinds of explanations we care about, what 
obligations we have to decision subjects, and how using the system might affect our ability to 
meet those obligations.
