8.1  Introduction
Machine learning is a technology that performs many tasks more quickly and reliably than 
humans. From a pragmatic point of view, it therefore seems beneficial to delegate such tasks 
to machine learning because their completion would be less time-­consuming and costly while 
the outcomes would be of a higher quality. This conclusion, however, is premature on ­different 
grounds –­ not least for politically relevant fields.
Much of politics is about making decisions: whether taxes should be increased or decreased, 
whether public transportation should be expanded or downsized, or whether climate-­friendly 
subsidies should be introduced. In many cases, such decisions directly affect sensitive fields of 
high practical relevance. For instance, political decisions as to who is allowed to reside in a 
particular country have a direct impact on the operations of border control.
Much of machine learning, by contrast, is about making predictions: whether there is a 
dog or a cat in an image, whether a patient will develop a certain disease, or whether a 
financial transaction is fraudulent.1 Despite this focus that diverges from the one of politics on 
making decisions, machine learning is increasingly deployed in politically relevant and 
sensitive fields.2
This chapter focuses on the tension that arises from such a deployment. Besides empha-
sizing the general relevance of this still underexplored topic, we specifically address the question 
of whether deployment of machine learning can be justified and how this question of justifica-
tion interrelates with considerations about epistemological aspects of machine learning.
To come up with an answer, we start with the latter part and investigate epistemological 
aspects of machine learning. Building on that, we evaluate the epistemic state that individual 
decision makers can reach when relying on predictive machine learning systems. Most 
importantly, it needs to be clarified whether beliefs that are gained or decisions that are made 
based on machine learning can be considered justified.
We then broaden this first-­person perspective and turn to political justification. It is a 
central claim of liberal democracies that political action is only legitimate if it is justified. 
A common strategy of justifying political action is by means of the public justification principle 
Epistemology and Politics of AI
OLIVER BUCHHOLZ AND KAROLINE REINHARDT
8

--- Page 115 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
105
(Vallier 2022). We will lay out this principle of justification that is used to provide standards 
to distinguish legitimate uses of political power from illegitimate ones.
The legitimacy of the use of political power becomes particularly relevant in areas where 
state power is most imminently exercised, such as border control, policing, criminal law, and 
the protection of vulnerable populations. At the same time, machine learning systems are 
increasingly deployed to these areas. Consequently, the interplay between the justification 
required for the legitimacy of political action and epistemological considerations raised by the 
characteristics of machine learning is particularly strong here, with insight into this intricate 
relationship being much needed. We will therefore focus on these areas.
In sum, then, by examining the deployment of machine learning systems in politically 
sensitive fields, we will have to deal with two different but connected types of justification, an 
epistemic and a practical one. While there is extensive literature on both of them, our goal is 
to advance their characterization in the context of machine learning and, in partiular, to shed 
light on their relation, an issue that is rarely addressed.3
8.2  Epistemological Aspects of Machine Learning
As pointed out above, the field of politics is special: it is about making consequential and par-
ticularly sensitive decisions that are often opposed to routine tasks for which machine learning 
has the ability to outperform humans. When trying to justify the use of machine learning in 
such a field, the question is thus whether the technology can actually help with decisions of 
this sort. To make good decisions individually, what is needed first and foremost is for the 
decision maker to be in the right epistemic state, that is, to possess sufficient information or 
relevant knowledge for the decision at hand –­ or to put it in the words of Grant and Basl 
(Chapter 7 in this volume):
“[d]ecision-­making of the sort we are interested in, where there is some possibility that we might 
integrate or deploy AI models, can be decomposed into two tasks: forming beliefs and deciding on 
the basis of those beliefs.” (p. 94)
However, it is unclear how machine learning can fit into this picture. More precisely, the 
­following issues need to be clarified:
(a)	 What is the epistemic status of (the outputs of) machine learning systems?
and
(b)	 What is the epistemic state arising in agents relying on machine learning?
For (a), the question is whether the outputs of machine learning systems should be interpreted 
as beliefs held by some artificial agent or whether they constitute mere evidence. For (b), the 
subsequent question is what kind of epistemic state arises in agents that base their reasoning 
and decision making on the outputs of machine learning systems.
Clearly, any answer to (b) will depend on the answer given to (a) because the epistemic 
status of machine learning outputs will affect the epistemic state of the agent relying on it. 
For instance, granting machine learning systems the status of artificial agents that hold and 
utter certain beliefs would give rise to situations in which individuals attain beliefs or even 
knowledge based on the artificial agent’s testimony. Such peculiar cases of testimony would 
raise many difficult epistemological questions. However, since we are here concerned with the 

--- Page 116 ---

Oliver Buchholz and Karoline Reinhardt
106
overarching question concerning the justified use of machine learning in politically sensitive 
fields, we will restrict our attention to (b), for this is the more relevant question in the present 
context. After all, political decisions are made by people, and it is crucial to examine the 
epistemic state they are in when they rely on machine learning. We will therefore not deal 
with (a) and instead simply assume that the outputs of machine learning can be seen as mere 
evidence.4 Question (b) is then about the epistemic state arising in agents that are relying on 
machine learning-­based evidence.5 A seemingly straightforward way to proceed would be to 
investigate what kind of knowledge agents attain from machine learning-­based evidence. 
This, however, would place knowledge center stage and require us to defend some particular 
definition of this debated concept to be adopted here. Additionally, in that case, our results 
would be confined to this particular definition.
To avoid both issues, we proceed by focusing on the concept of justification that is usually 
regarded as a necessary condition for knowledge regardless of its exact definition 
(Lammenranta 2004, p. 468). The question then is whether agents basing their decisions 
on machine learning are justified in believing the outcomes of such systems or, put 
differently, whether there are sufficient reasons for believing them. Although we here treat 
the outcomes of machine learning systems as mere evidence, mostly to sidestep the 
question of whether they qualify as an artificial agent’s beliefs, a closer look at them is in 
order because the particular way in which they arise distinguishes them from other types 
of evidence.
That particular way starts with data. Data is needed because machine learning systems 
attain their functionality through a process in which they learn patterns from data that are 
relevant for the task that the system is meant to perform. For instance, when the task is to 
predict whether an image belongs to a certain category, a machine learning system is provided 
with a large set containing images and the corresponding categories to which each of them 
belongs. The system then adjusts its functionality in an iterative, so-­called learning or training 
process: for each of the images, the machine learning system predicts a category, and it is 
assessed whether it matches the right category or whether it makes a mistake. Then, the 
system’s functionality is adjusted in a way that leads to fewer mistakes in the next iteration of 
predicting the categories for the given images. This process continues until the number 
of mistakes cannot be reduced further. The functionality leading to the lowest number of 
mistakes then is the final functionality of the machine learning system. It is in this set-­up that 
the system is deployed and will perform its actual task, namely predicting the categories of 
new images that it did not process before.
Machine learning systems are therefore in contrast to other technological artifacts, for the 
latter are usually equipped with their desired functionality right from the outset 
(Schubbach 2021). Before exploring the implications of this observation, let us briefly focus 
on the nature of the outcomes of machine learning systems –­ after all, the outcomes are what 
we are most interested in, since their characteristics are crucial for the decision makers 
relying on them.
As it turns out, the fact that machine learning systems attain their final functionality 
through a training process implies that there are two different things that might be described 
as outcomes: the final set-­up of the system, which is the outcome of the training process and 
constitutes a general rule for making predictions, a so-­called prediction rule, and individual 
predictions made by the system after deployment, for instance a category for a given image. It 
is important to note that the latter depend on the former. Individual predictions are entirely 
predetermined by the overall set-­up of the system in the sense that, for a fixed set-­up, the same 
inputs will always lead to the same prediction.

--- Page 117 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
107
Within a fixed machine learning system that already completed the learning process, the 
computation of individual predictions is therefore a straightforward procedure governed by 
the relevant prediction rule. However, as pointed out above, the process leading to this 
prediction rule depends on data and the patterns it includes. This makes the learning process 
in machine learning an inherently statistical endeavor, since it is about inductively inferring 
a general rule for making predictions from given data.6 The final set-­up of a machine learning 
system is thus not exactly a general prediction, rule but instead crucially based on statistical 
properties of the given data such as, for instance, co-­occurrences between certain inputs and 
corresponding image categories. The generality of the final set-­up thus hinges on the extent 
to which statistical properties of the given data are also present in new data for which the 
machine learning system is used to make predictions. Since individual predictions depend on 
a system’s overall set-­up, they also inherit this statistical grounding. Unsurprisingly, this 
raises several methodological problems.
One such problem is that machine learning systems often lack robustness. Despite 
producing accurate predictions under training conditions and in settings closely resembling 
them, their performance deteriorates when they are applied in new environments. A 
prominent example for the occurrence of this problem is the healthcare sector in which, for 
instance, hospitals or patient populations might differ considerably from the training data 
(Freiesleben and Grote 2023). However, politically sensitive fields such as border control or 
the judicial system are likely to give rise to the same problem, since they usually possess 
characteristics that are highly specific to certain countries, cases, or legislations.
Another methodological problem arises from the task of machine learning to exploit 
patterns in given data. The samples on which machine learning systems are trained are vast, 
since this is where their ability to identify relevant patterns for making predictions exceeds 
human abilities the most. Ever increasing possibilities of data collection and processing tend 
to enlarge datasets even further. Identifying patterns in such datasets that are commonly 
described as “big data” (Wheeler  2016) requires a high capacity of doing so, namely to 
process, analyze, and adapt to a vast amount of information. Consequently, the structure and 
functionality of most machine learning systems are highly complex. Especially in the case of 
deep neural networks, the final set-­up arising from the training process often comprises 
millions of parameters that jointly contribute to the computation of predictions. Paired with 
the fact that this set-­up is not fixed in the first place but the result of the data-­based and hence 
not foreseeable learning process described above, the complexity of modern machine learning 
systems essentially makes them black boxes, with their functionality being opaque (Boge 2022; 
Søgaard  2024). In many cases, both the mechanisms and reasons leading to individual 
predictions thus remain unclear such that it is intransparent how and why machine learning 
systems reach their predictions –­ sometimes even to the experts developing or using these 
systems (Creel 2020).
In sum, then, this brief outline reveals that the outcomes of machine learning systems –­ 
both general prediction rules and individual predictions  –­ are ultimately outcomes of a 
learning process that relies on data. Their nature is therefore statistical and (at least on a 
frequentist interpretation) probabilistic. This is part of the reason why machine learning 
systems often lack robustness when applied across different settings. Furthermore, their 
functionality is often opaque, both because it is established in a learning process and due to 
the overall complexity of machine learning systems. Accordingly, as mentioned above, the 
outcomes of these systems are a special type of evidence. The crucial question is whether 
beliefs and, ultimately, decisions that are based on such outcomes can be considered justified 
given their particular nature.

--- Page 118 ---

Oliver Buchholz and Karoline Reinhardt
108
Intuitively, the answer should be negative. After all, the characteristics of machine 
learning systems seem to conflict with any requirements for epistemic justification. How 
could decisions be considered justified, if they are based on statistical information that, in 
addition, arises from black-box systems whose functionality is opaque? As it turns out, 
however, not all is lost: there are attempts to provide applications of machine learning 
with a more solid epistemological basis by arguing that, indeed, the outcomes of these 
systems might be a source of justification for beliefs and decisions that are based on them. 
The guiding idea is to focus on the concept of reliability and show how machine learning 
systems can, despite the methodological problems discussed above, at least lend a reliabilist 
version of justification.7
One such attempt originated in the context of computer simulations where Durán and 
Formanek (2018) proposed the framework of computational reliabilism. Recently, Durán and 
Jongsma (2021) adapted it to the case of machine learning. The framework takes inspiration 
from Goldman’s (1979) process reliabilism in the sense that it assumes that considerations of 
epistemic justification are exhausted by the question as to whether beliefs are brought about 
by reliable processes. With that assumption in place, the strategy of the framework consists in 
showing how machine learning systems and, in particular, the way in which their outcomes 
arise, can be seen as reliable processes. Or to put it in the words of the authors:
“[i]n a nutshell, [computational reliabilism] states that researchers are justified in believing the 
results of [machine learning] systems because there is a reliable process (i.e. the algorithm) that 
yields, most of the time, trustworthy results.” (Durán and Jongsma 2021, p. 332)
There are a number of objections one might want to raise against these accounts.8 Perhaps 
the most pressing one concerns the central concept of computational reliabilism: apart from 
some hints on so-­called reliability indicators, it is unclear how reliability is supposed to be 
evaluated let alone interpreted within the framework.
Fortunately, there is another framework that can step in. The field of statistical learning 
theory is concerned with rigorously assessing the reliability of machine learning systems.9 Its 
approach consists in employing tools of mathematics to derive and prove statistical guarantees 
for their predictive performance. In their most common form, these guarantees provide an 
upper bound on the predictive error that a machine learning system is likely to incur such 
that, with a high probability, the predictive performance of the system will be at least as good 
or better than this bound. In other words, the guarantees provided by statistical learning 
theory allow for a worst-­case assessment of the predictive performance of machine learning 
systems. These guarantees are statistical because they consider that all of machine learning 
relies on data and a particular performance can, thus, at best be highly probable but never 
certain. Nevertheless, they are guarantees because they can be mathematically proven if 
certain assumptions obtain. Due to their statistical aspect, the performance guarantees 
provided by statistical learning theory could therefore be interpreted as a reliabilist justification 
for the predictive performance of machine learning systems (Grote et al. 2024, Section 2). 
Consequently, one might argue that agents relying and basing their decisions on the outcomes 
of these kinds of systems have reasons to believe these outcomes if appropriate performance 
guarantees can be provided.10
Clearly, such an argument rests on the assumption that reliabilist considerations are a valid 
source of justification in the first place. Furthermore, the question remains whether and how 
this version of epistemic and, hence, first-­person centered justification contributes to a more 
general justification of the use of machine learning systems in politically sensitive fields, or not.

--- Page 119 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
109
8.3  Political Justification
The normative concept of political legitimacy is frequently linked to the idea of justification: 
political action is only legitimate if it is justified. Political justification, however, differs signif-
icantly from epistemic justification. While epistemic justification pertains to the validation of 
beliefs based on evidence and reason, political justification concerns the legitimacy of actions 
and decisions in a social and political context, where the emphasis is on the acceptability of 
these actions to the public or the people affected by them. There are many ways to justify 
politics normatively speaking, yet there is a common principle of political justification that 
unifies and allows categorization of these different ways: the public justification principle. 
Vallier (2022) defines the principle as follows:
The Public Justification Principle (PJP): A coercive law L is justified in a public P if and only if each 
member i of P has sufficient reason(s) Ri to endorse L.
Though there are multiple definitions of political justification, this definition provides a 
sufficient starting point for our discussion since it captures key elements necessary for framing 
the distinction between political and epistemic justification. At the same time, the definition 
permits the discussion to take various directions, as it allows for multiple clarifications of its 
components, such as the relevant scope of the public (P), the nature of justificatory reasons, 
and the criteria for determining when those reasons are sufficient.11
One first aspect to note is that a central concern of public justification is coercion: how and 
when can the coercive use of political power be justified and what are the kinds of reasons 
that can justify coercion?12 Apart from the PJP, this theme is also reflected in the writings of 
many authors, including Larmore (2008, p.  86) and Rawls (2005, p.  68). Importantly, 
however, public justification is not merely a process of exchanging reasons but rather a means 
of uncovering or generating a public justification. This can be achieved through deliberative 
or nondeliberative means, such as bargaining or adjudication.
Furthermore, the fact that political justification is about generating a public justification is 
crucial; political justification centers around the idea that political decisions must be justifi-
able to all reasonable members of society. Starting from the assumption that these members 
are normatively speaking equals, public justification refers to a rationale for exercising power 
that every member of the public can accept because the reasons that are provided can be rec-
ognized as valid by them.13 Proponents of this standard are often referred to as public reason 
liberals. Liberal institutions, such as freedom of speech, the rule of law, and democracy, are 
seen as publicly justified, while illiberal institutions are typically rejected by these theorists.14 
In line with this reasoning, our task below will thus consist in evaluating whether the use of 
machine learning systems in political decision making can be justified in a similar way, that 
is, whether one can bring reasons to bear that can be recognized as valid by each member of 
the public, or not –­ and under what circumstances.
Before proceeding to this task, however, a remark concerning the nature of the reasons Ri 
mentioned in the PJP is in order, since this is a crucial aspect in the debate about how to inter-
pret public justification. Some theorists, known as consensus theorists, argue that public justi-
fications must be based on shared or accessible reasons, while convergence theorists allow for 
the inclusion of diverse, unshared reasons (Vallier 2022, Section 2.3). When examining the 
justification of machine learning-­based political decision making, we will therefore have to pay 
close attention to the potential justificatory reasons that we encounter and assess whether 
they might be considered as shared or rather as only accessible to some members of the public.

--- Page 120 ---

Oliver Buchholz and Karoline Reinhardt
110
8.4  Epistemic and Political Justification in the Age of Machine Learning
The discussion above reveals a close interplay between coercion, justification, and legitimacy: 
state coercion is only legitimate, if it is justified, where the latter could be analyzed in terms of 
the PJP. What implications does this have for specific policies or actions taken by state institu-
tions that rely on the outcomes of machine learning algorithms? A first issue in this context 
concerns the epistemic justification to which machine learning systems can give rise, since 
we have seen above that it is inherently statistical and, hence, reliabilist in nature. Furthermore, 
it is an open question whether and to what extent this reliabilist justification transmits to 
public justification in cases where political decision making is based on the outcomes of 
machine learning systems.
Some characteristics of the relation between epistemic and public justification can be 
spelled out independently of machine learning-­specific considerations: epistemic justification 
concerns the reasons that validate beliefs or knowledge claims, where the focus is on the truth 
or epistemic accuracy of those claims. In contrast, political justification pertains to the legiti-
macy of exercising power, where the emphasis lies on whether the reasons provided can be 
accepted by all members of the public. Despite these differences, both forms of justification 
operate under a standard of public reason that demands inclusivity and accessibility of the 
reasons presented. In political justification, particularly within the framework of public 
reason liberalism, liberal institutions are deemed publicly justified because they are supported 
by reasons that everyone can recognize as valid. In some ways, this parallels epistemic justifi-
cation, where a belief is justified if it is supported by reasons that are widely acknowledged as 
truth-­conducive. However, political justification faces unique challenges, especially 
concerning coercion: it must address not only the validity of reasons but also their ability to 
justify the use of coercive power. While epistemic justification typically aims at consensus 
through shared truth, political justification may tolerate a diversity of reasons, as long as they 
can be publicly recognized, even if not universally shared. This dual focus on inclusivity and 
the legitimacy of power in political justification sets it apart from epistemic justification, 
though both are deeply concerned with the validity of reasons in their respective domains.
Political decisions that are based on machine learning systems challenge both epistemic 
and public justification in different ways. As highlighted by Amoore (2013), machine learning 
systems operate on the surface with a veneer of objectivity. However, beneath this surface lies 
a complex structure characterized by “incompleteness, multiple moments of intuition and 
proxy judgement” (Amoore 2013, p. 54), raising profound questions about the legitimacy 
and justification of decisions informed by such systems. More precisely, machine learning 
systems often operate in ways that are opaque to the public, lack transparency, and embed 
biases stemming from the datasets employed in the learning process that may not align with 
the shared values or norms of justice required for public justification. Moreover, the use of 
algorithms in political decision making can obscure the human responsibility for those 
decisions, making it difficult to hold decision makers accountable and to ensure that the 
rationale behind political actions is accessible and acceptable to all members of society. To 
shed further light on these challenges, we will investigate how the epistemology of machine 
learning interrelates with justificatory questions regarding the implementation of machine 
learning systems and attempt to derive some normative implications of these interrelations.
Surprisingly, these questions have not yet received much attention, even though the 
interplay of epistemology and politics has gained increasing attention in contemporary 
political philosophy. Vogelmann (2022), for instance, suggests that knowledge is inherently 
political, and the decisions based on this knowledge carry significant epistemic weight. This is 

--- Page 121 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
111
­particularly relevant in the context of machine learning, as it is a technology that increasingly 
influences political decisions, thereby embedding its own biases and uncertainties into the 
process. The ethical implications of how this technology shapes and informs political choices 
are profound, necessitating a deeper exploration of the ways in which machine learning 
interacts with and impacts political legitimacy and justice. To mention only a few examples, it 
is unclear, considering these developments, what changes in policy decisions are based on 
systems that rely on “incompleteness, multiple moments of intuition and proxy judgement” 
as Amoore argued; when such systems may nevertheless justifiably be used; and what form 
of justification would be needed for this. There are also practical questions arising from these 
considerations, for instance concerning the areas in which machine learning systems may or 
may not inform state actions.
8.4.1  Epistemic Issues as a Challenge for Political Justification
Many issues in deploying machine learning systems in political decision making arise from 
the epistemological problems outlined above, that is, from intransparency and a lack of 
robustness. Additionally, the pronounced statistical nature of these systems indicates their 
reliance on data –­ and their susceptibility to issues that might be caused by this reliance. For 
instance, while machine learning systems can process vast amounts of data and offer 
predictive insights, the accuracy of these predictions is always contingent on the quality and 
scope of the input data. Moreover, the systems often infer conclusions from incomplete data, 
introducing a significant degree of uncertainty and risk of misinterpretation.
The implications of this uncertainty are profound: the ability to predict and quantify risks 
in political decision making could enhance the rationality of state actions, allowing 
governments to base decisions on data-­driven insights and to potentially preempt future 
challenges. This predictive power could lead to more efficient resource allocation, better 
targeted policies, and improved public services by addressing potential issues before they fully 
materialize. Provided that the outcomes are based on accurate, representative, and unbiased 
data, and the models are transparent and well calibrated, this predictive power could 
significantly improve decision making.
Moreover, reliance on the outcomes of machine learning systems that are inherently 
probabilistic challenges traditional notions of responsibility and accountability. As decisions 
become increasingly informed by algorithmic outputs, it becomes harder to pinpoint who is 
ultimately responsible for the consequences of those decisions. Political leaders may shift 
blame onto the technology, distancing themselves from the moral and ethical implications of 
their choices.
This is problematic not least because political justification involves the exchange of 
reasons. However, when decisions are based on algorithmic outputs, the focus might shift 
away from the reasoning behind decisions to the mere presentation of data-­driven outcomes. 
Political justification, which hinges on deliberation on, for instance, competing values, ethical 
considerations, and social implications, risks being reduced to a technocratic exercise in risk 
management or optimization. This shift would undermine the ideal of political justification 
presented here that political processes should be about decisions being justifiable to those 
affected by them. Machine learning systems, by their nature, do not engage in reasoning in 
the sense necessary. This lack of reasoning behind machine learning processes challenges the 
expectation that we should engage in moral and ethical reflection when making decisions. 
Instead of debating values, the focus may narrow to technical questions about the validity or 
accuracy of predictions.

--- Page 122 ---

Oliver Buchholz and Karoline Reinhardt
112
Additionally, decision making might become less about responding to concrete events and 
more about managing calculated risks, which may lead to a focus on prevention at the 
expense of responding to immediate problems. This could alter the nature of political action: 
when political attention is predominantly focused on managing uncertainties, there is a risk 
that present, concrete problems may be neglected or deprioritized. It also raises the question 
of when and in which areas risk prevention should take precedence over addressing present 
cases and it is indeed an open question which probabilities of what events –­ assuming they 
can be accurately calculated –­ are sufficient to justify preventive state action.
Furthermore, it is unclear what ethical obligations arise from the reliance on such systems, 
particularly when the results they generate challenge human judgment because they are 
difficult to interpret and the way in which they arise is opaque, as described above. Moreover, 
machine learning systems reflect the data they are trained on and if that data contains biases, 
the resulting predictions and policy recommendations may perpetuate or even amplify them. 
In this way, the use of such systems could inadvertently reinforce systemic disadvantages, 
posing further challenges to the legitimacy and fairness of political actions.
Considerations of this kind boil down to the question of whether the state can justify 
actions based on predictions that are not only inherently uncertain, but in many cases also 
not traceable to the factors that brought them about.15 Our previous discussion revealed that, 
ultimately, this is a question about the (epistemic) reasons justifying the beliefs of individuals 
that rely on machine learning systems in their decision making and about whether these rea-
sons can be recognized as valid by all members of the public in line with the PJP.
As for the first part, we have seen that despite the epistemological shortcomings of machine 
learning systems, the performance guarantees provided by statistical learning theory might 
be interpreted as a reliabilist justification for the predictive accuracy of these systems. They 
guarantee that, with a high probability, a given machine learning system will make predictions 
that are at least as accurate as some predefined threshold. Consequently, agents relying and 
basing their decisions on the outcomes of these systems arguably have reasons to believe 
these outcomes if such performance guarantees can be provided.
However, there are two caveats: on the one hand, as indicated by the latter conditional 
statement, statistical learning theory is not able to provide appropriate performance 
guarantees in all applications of machine learning. In particular, deep neural networks, one 
of the most popular and successful methods in the field, still escape the analysis of statistical 
learning theory (Bartlett et al. 2021). On the other hand, even if said performance guarantees 
can be provided, their statistical nature needs to be considered: even though their assessment 
of the performance of these systems is as good as it gets, it only holds with some probability. 
This entails that there is also a margin of error that includes the possibility for a machine 
learning system to perform considerably worse than reported by the corresponding 
performance guarantee, thereby introducing a further type of uncertainty to applications of 
machine learning.
These epistemological aspects carry over to the question whether the reasons for believing 
the outcomes of machine learning systems can be recognized as valid by all members of the 
public as required for public justification. In principle, the performance guarantees provided by 
statistical learning theory can be mathematically proven and are, thus, objectively valid. This 
seems to suggest that, indeed, they might not only lend epistemic but also public justification 
in line with the PJP. However, we have just seen that these guarantees include a margin of error 
that adds further uncertainty to applications of machine learning that are already 
methodologically brittle, for the reasons outlined above. This intricate cluster of uncertainties 
crucially undermines the justifiability of machine learning-­based decisions to all members of 

--- Page 123 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
113
the public as required by the PJP. Especially, reliabilist arguments in favor of machine learning 
rely on statistical reasoning and, hence, on considerations that hold in the limit of a very large 
sample. By contrast, they are almost meaningless for small samples, that is, for small groups of 
people or even individual cases. Although unlikely, machine learning systems could in principle 
lead to arbitrarily poor results in these cases, thereby putting minorities and other vulnerable 
groups at a particular risk. Clearly, at least for people belonging to the latter groups, reliabilist 
epistemic reasons for the use of machine learning systems will therefore not be acceptable as a 
justification for the use of these systems in politically sensitive fields.
It is straightforward to illustrate this insight by referring to the deployment of machine 
learning in critical areas of state power, such as border control, policing, and the judicial 
system, for any of them necessitates a rigorous examination of the justifications for using 
these systems.
For example, in border control, machine learning applications are being used for biometric 
identification, emotion detection, and risk assessment. These technologies, while promising 
efficiency and accuracy, also raise serious ethical concerns. In particular, it is unclear what 
standards and procedures must be in place to ensure that their use is legitimate within a liberal 
democratic framework that relies on a concept of public justification as explicated by the PJP. 
Similarly, in policing, machine learning-­driven data analytics tools are being developed to combat 
cybercrime and terrorism. These tools generate knowledge that directly influences political 
decisions, but they also introduce new challenges for justification and legitimization: there is no 
straightforward answer to the question of when and at what cost individuals may be restricted in 
their freedom of movement if they are, for instance, suspected of planning a terrorist attack. 
What margin of error are we willing to accept in these cases? Which margin of error is justifiable?
In light of the methodological issues discussed above, it is particularly salient to assess how 
the state can justify surveillance or exclusion based on predictions of low-­probability events, 
such as terrorist attacks. Moreover, in the context of the judiciary, predictive systems are 
being used to inform sentencing decisions and risk assessments. This raises questions about 
the role of probability in legal reasoning and the potential shift from case-­based evidence to 
probabilistic assessments. In the protection of vulnerable populations, particularly children, 
machine learning systems are being developed to predict and prevent crimes such as sexual 
abuse. However, the use of these systems introduces a tension between the need to protect 
vulnerable individuals and the risk of generating false suspicions: what margin of error is 
acceptable in such cases? As Zimmerman and Lee-­Stronach (2022) argue, “procedural jus-
tice [. . .] requires that we base our human response to algorithmic outputs on a deliberate 
acknowledgement of how much uncertainty remains in a given decision scenario” (p. 23). 
These real-­world examples highlight the difficulties associated with the deployment of 
machine learning systems that, in addition to being data-driven and thus inherently probabi-
listic, are highly complex and therefore opaque in politically sensitive fields, which in turn 
raises the issue of how and on what basis individuals can contest the inferences made about 
them by such systems.
Most importantly, while such a deployment might in certain cases be justifiable on 
epistemic grounds, it becomes evident that it is nevertheless in conflict with the requirements 
of public justification. The reasons that lend epistemic justification to the outcomes of 
machine learning systems in the sense that individuals are justified in believing them are in 
most cases not suitable to also achieve the public justification to base political decision on 
these outcomes. This is because the main reasons giving rise to epistemic justification are the 
performance guarantees provided by statistical learning theory that are not generally 
acceptable as a justification for the use of machine learning in politically sensitive fields, not 

--- Page 124 ---

Oliver Buchholz and Karoline Reinhardt
114
least because they leave room for uncertainties regarding the outcomes for minorities and 
marginalized groups. In fields like the ones just outlined, however, the stakes are too high to 
allow for these kinds of uncertainties, which is why the use of machine learning systems 
cannot be justified off-­hand as legitimate.
8.4.2  The Politics of Designing Probability
Another important aspect of the interplay between politics and epistemology is that machine 
learning systems are not merely tools deployed to improve or worsen specific political 
frameworks. As technological artifacts, they do not emerge in a vacuum but are intricately 
woven into social systems and human interactions in various ways. Consequently, they 
embody the norms and values, the beliefs and viewpoints, the inequalities and injustices of 
existing societies (Johnson 2023). This means that the political convictions of those who 
design and optimize these algorithms are also inscribed in them, thereby affecting their 
outputs. In that sense, machine learning systems do not only rely on probabilistic reasoning, 
but on a whole set of predetermined factors that affect them in various ways. Accordingly, 
said probabilistic reasoning is to some extent actively designed.
One way in which this occurs is through the definition of goals and problems. Machine 
learning systems amplify existing biases and injustices through the value judgments embedded 
in the determination of their objectives or the definition of the problem they are intended to 
solve (Fazelpour and Danks 2021): the development of any problem-­solving system begins 
with decisions about which problems are to be addressed and which goals are to be pursued. 
These decisions reflect the values, priorities, and perspectives of those who design and imple-
ment these systems. If these value judgments include implicit biases or a particular, perhaps 
very narrow understanding of social justice, they will inevitably be embedded in the algorithm.
Furthermore, machine learning systems based on probabilistic models can exacerbate 
existing biases and injustices because they often rely on data that reflect the historical and 
systemic inequalities of our society. When models are trained on such data, they adopt and 
reinforce these biases rather than correcting them. The opacity of many machine learning 
systems might even prevent such biases from being detected, because the exact way in which 
certain outcomes arise remains unclear in many cases. Furthermore, even assuming the lat-
ter would not be an issue, certain biases might still remain hidden because they are driven by 
so-­called proxy variables and, thus, occur even in the absence of crucial factors like gender or 
ethnicity in the data.16 In this way, machine learning applications can cement existing power 
structures and transform inequalities into new, seemingly objective forms.
At the same time, however, they also hold the potential to reveal biases and injustices that 
often remain hidden in human decision-­making processes. By systematically analyzing large 
datasets, algorithms can uncover patterns and biases that would otherwise go undetected. For 
example, they can demonstrate how certain demographic groups are consistently disadvan-
taged by employing machine learning to expose statistical inequalities and correlations. 
These insights can be used to identify and overcome discriminatory practices.
8.5  Conclusion
This chapter has focused on ethical issues that arise from deploying machine learning in 
politically sensitive areas. Specifically, we analyzed whether such a deployment can be justified 
and how this question of justification interrelates with considerations about epistemological 

--- Page 125 ---

Epistemology and Politics of AI
115
aspects of machine learning. Our analysis reveals that, seen from the epistemological 
perspective, basing decisions on the outputs of machine learning systems can be considered 
justified in situations in which statistical learning theory provides reliabilist guarantees for 
the accuracy of such systems.
However, this form of justification does not necessarily extend to the political realm: 
political decisions that lead to coercive use of state power must be legitimate. According to 
the PJP, they thus must be justifiable to all members of the public. Given the uncertainties 
surrounding machine learning, particularly regarding its treatment of marginalized 
groups and the opacity of its decision-­making processes, these systems often fail to meet 
the requirements for public justification. Consequently, while machine learning systems 
might allow for downstream decisions being epistemically justified in some contexts, their 
deployment in politically sensitive areas requires cautious and context-­sensitive 
consideration.
While the latter poses a very pressing but rather practical challenge, this chapter was also 
meant to put emphasis on the philosophical relevance of a still underexplored topic. Most 
importantly, the exact relation of epistemic and political justification is still largely unclear, 
especially beyond the realm of machine learning. The same holds for the relation of the PJP 
to single instances of coercion and the question as to how political justification is transmitted 
from a general to a specific level of abstraction. We consider this chapter to be a first step, but 
much more work is needed to further illuminate both relations that are central in connecting 
epistemology and political philosophy.

not have access to before making the prediction. In particular, unlike forecasts, predictions need not

9.1  Introduction
In the context of artificial intelligence (AI), epistemic considerations refer to the way AI-­based 
systems acquire and process knowledge. The underlying epistemic reflections concern the 
nature, scope, and limits of knowledge as well as the conditions under which knowledge is 
generated, validated, and justified. AI is primarily regarded as an epistemic tool due to its 
ability to analyze vast amounts of data, identify patterns, and generate insights which 
contribute to knowledge acquisition and decision-­making processes in various social settings. 
As Alvarado (2023) puts it, AI-­based systems, such as machine learning (ML), “are first and 
foremost epistemic technologies,” because they are used in epistemic contexts, work with 
epistemic content and do so through epistemic operations.
As AI-­based systems become more and more integrated into our epistemic (social) 
practices, a large and growing body of literature has investigated ethical issues in the context 
of AI, such as transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, and discriminatory outcomes. 
For instance, if algorithms are trained on biased datasets, they may inadvertently reinforce 
societal prejudices, leading to unjust outcomes. Moreover, the opacity of AI-­based processes 
can hinder individuals’ ability to challenge or contest decisions, and thereby undermine their 
epistemic agency. There is therefore an urgent need to address the ethical implications of 
AI-­based systems in the context of our epistemic practices. It is particularly pertinent to 
analyze these issues with theories of epistemic injustice since they offer tools to understand 
harms at the intersection of ethics and epistemology, with special attention given to societal 
power relations.
This chapter provides an overview of epistemic injustice and its variations that are of 
particular importance in the context of AI. The first section describes nuanced forms of 
epistemic injustice, such as testimonial injustice, hermeneutical injustice, and contributory 
injustice. The second section highlights the relevant characteristics of AI regarding 
epistemic injustice with a focus on ML as a currently prominent approach. Aspects 
regarding training data, the use of categories and systems of classification, opacity, and 
epistemic fragmentation are discussed. Various examples, such as AI-­based health apps, 
AI and Epistemic Injustice
