algorithmic profiling, and automatic gender recognition, are then used to illustrate how 
the forms of epistemic injustice described are manifested in and through algorithmic 
systems.
As it has been shown that AI-­based systems contribute to different forms of epistemic 
injustice, the conclusion of this chapter emphasizes the importance of further research in 
understanding the interrelation of AI-­based epistemic injustice with structural forms of 
injustice in specific contexts of application.
9.2  Mapping Variations of Epistemic Injustice
Being a knower includes activities such as making sense of one’s social experiences, shaping 
concepts to capture and evaluate them adequately, or sharing one’s beliefs. It is considered 
an essential and valued aspect of social agency (Fricker  2007). Theories of epistemic 
injustice draw on ethics, epistemology, and political philosophy to examine how a person 
can be harmed specifically in their capacity as a knower. They consider two interrelated 
aspects in relation to how epistemic practices can go awry. They take into account ethical 
aspects –­ how particular knowers or groups of knowers can be morally wronged specifically 
in their epistemic agency. Additionally, they consider epistemic aspects –­ how the set-­up of 
epistemic practices and institutions can be epistemically disadvantageous (Pohlhaus 2017). 
Various scholars, especially from feminist epistemology, critical race and post-­ and 
decolonial theory, have emphasized the gendered and racialized dimension of power 
structures that shape epistemic practices and institutions, among them Spivak (1988), 
Crenshaw (1989), Lugones (2003), Harding (2004), Alcoff (2005), Mills (2008), Hill 
Collins (2009), Dotson (2012), and Toole (2022). The publication of Miranda Fricker’s 
(2007) Epistemic Injustice. Power and the Ethics of  Knowing was influential in providing 
concrete conceptual tools with which to describe and understand two forms of epistemic 
injustice: testimonial and hermeneutical injustice.
The research literature evolving around epistemic injustice can be broadly divided into 
literature which refines the concepts proposed by Fricker (e.g., Bratu and Haenel  2021; 
Fricker  2017; Wanderer  2017); literature which introduces further forms of epistemic 
injustice such as wilful hermeneutical ignorance (Pohlhaus 2012), contributory injustice 
(Dotson 2012), epistemic exploitation (Berenstain 2016), conceptual competence injustice 
(Anderson 2017), epistemic appropriation (Davis 2018), epistemic coercion (Dandelet 2021), 
anticipatory epistemic injustice (Lee 2021) or intragroup epistemic injustice (Tobi 2023); 
and literature that applies the concepts within various fields, including healthcare (Carel and 
Kidd 2014; Jongsma et al. 2017; Peña-­Guzmán and Reynolds 2019), education (Kotzee 2017), 
the criminal system (Jenkins 2017), and digitalization (Hull 2023; Pozzi 2023a, b; Milano 
and Prunkl 2024).
In the following discussion, we will map different forms of epistemic injustice on the 
individual, the structural, and both levels. Rather than aiming to provide a complete list, we 
understand them as examples of conceptual tools that have proven helpful in understanding 
different aspects of epistemic injustice (Pohlhaus 2017). To do so, we first need to give some 
definitions. Based on Dotson’s account, we understand epistemic agency as “the ability to 
utilize persuasively shared epistemic resources within a given community of knowers in order 
to participate in knowledge production and, if required, the revision of those same resources” 
(Dotson  2014, p.  115), where epistemic resources refer to concepts, theories, standards of 
judgments or metaphors (Pohlhaus 2012).

--- Page 130 ---

Mirjam Faissner, Janne Lenk, and Regina Müller
120
One form of epistemic injustice, as defined by Fricker (2007), is testimonial injustice. 
Testimonial injustice refers to the unjustified downgrading of a person’s credibility based on 
prejudice. As Fricker notes, when we listen to a person’s testimonies, we automatically and 
mostly unconsciously check the person’s trustworthiness, i.e., their sincerity and competence 
regarding the subject matter. Such judgments are relevant, amongst other things, in order to 
check whether we need to adapt our belief system based on the content of the testimony. 
However, the credibility assessment can be distorted by prejudices that involve epistemically 
culpable overgeneralizations. Some types of prejudice are structural insofar as they are based 
on stereotypes, i.e., associations between members of a group and traits that track members 
of that social group across different social settings. These prejudicial stereotypes related to a 
person’s social identity are often the basis for testimonial injustice. For instance, the 
structurally available stereotype that “many women are intuitive” (Fricker 2007, p. 31) may 
lead to the unjustified downgrading of a woman’s trustworthiness when she proposes a 
complex philosophical argument. While the prejudice is structural, the harm happens on the 
individual level, where the communicative exchange between epistemic agents is disturbed 
based on the undue downgrading of the person’s credibility. Wanderer (2017) calls this 
transactional testimonial injustice. Testimonial injustice may also occur on the structural level 
in the form of structural testimonial injustice, if members of a social group are institutionally 
excluded from testifying on a certain matter (Anderson 2012), e.g., when a government has 
no process of including the voices of people principally affected by a certain law.
Another form of epistemic injustice introduced by Fricker (2007) is hermeneutical injustice. 
As knowers, we need epistemic resources that are adequate to capture our social experiences. 
Hermeneutical injustice describes a person’s unfair disadvantage in understanding or 
communicating relevant social experiences because of gaps in collectively shared epistemic 
resources, used to understand and communicate social experiences. Fricker (2007) gives the 
example of the concept of sexual harassment. It allows many women to call out inappropriate 
behavior by colleagues at the workplace that was difficult to capture, communicate, and 
contest before the concept was developed in groups that raised women’s consciousness. 
Hermeneutical injustice describes a structural form of injustice insofar as it stems from a 
structural prejudice in collectively shared epistemic resources (Fricker 2007). Such structural 
prejudice may result from hermeneutical marginalization, a precondition for hermeneutical 
injustice.
Hermeneutical marginalization describes the systematic unequal hermeneutical 
participation of members of a disadvantaged group in relevant areas of social experience 
(Fricker 2007). Marginalized social groups, based on intersectional systems of dominance 
and oppression, may experience the social world differently from members of socially 
dominant groups. For instance, women or gender minorities are more likely to experience 
gender-­based violence. To describe different forms of violence and their impact, they may 
need fitting concepts. Yet, if a group is socially, politically, and economically marginalized, its 
ability to access relevant social positions (in the media, politics, education, and law) in order 
to shape collectively shared epistemic resources may be impacted. As a consequence, the 
collectively shared epistemic resources are structurally prejudiced and are inadequate to 
reflect the social group’s experiences (Medina 2013).
Epistemic injustice may also arise at the intersection of the individual and structural levels. 
Many authors have stressed that marginalized groups develop and use fitting epistemic 
resources to understand, communicate, and evaluate their social experiences (Pohlhaus 2012; 
Medina 2013; Dotson 2014). Rather than assuming one set of collectively shared epistemic 
resources, we should think of epistemic resources in terms of multiple coexisting and differing 

--- Page 131 ---

AI and Epistemic Injustice
121
sets of epistemic resources available in different epistemic communities. Pohlhaus (2012) 
introduces wilful hermeneutical ignorance as failures that occur when dominantly situated 
knowers actively refuse to acknowledge the epistemic resources developed within marginalized 
epistemic communities.
Wilful hermeneutical ignorance can lead to further forms of epistemic injustice when the 
dominant knower A, who shows active wilful ignorance, interacts with knower B. Contributory 
injustice, a concept introduced by Dotson (2012), occurs when A cannot understand B’s 
testimony based on A’s wilful hermeneutical ignorance, and B’s testimony fails to have the 
intended uptake. In this case, B is constrained in their epistemic agency, since B relies on A to 
acknowledge the epistemic resources B uses. For instance, psychiatric service users organized in 
self-­help and activism groups have very nuanced epistemic resources to understand psychiatric 
symptoms, such as hearing voices, that differ from dominant biomedical approaches. Yet these 
concepts are not considered by most psychiatric professionals (Miller Tate 2019). If a service 
user’s (B) report is misunderstood by a psychiatric professional (A) as a consequence of them 
using different sets of epistemic resources, this is an example of contributory injustice. Finally, 
another form of epistemic injustice introduced by Dotson (2011) that may follow from wilful 
hermeneutical ignorance is smothering. In the case of smothering, B self-­censors their own 
testimony, especially content considered risky or unsafe, to ensure that it only contains contents 
for which A demonstrates sufficient conceptual competence.1 For instance, if the psychiatric 
service user (B) refrains from explaining their understanding of voice-­hearing because they 
assume the psychiatric professional (A) lacks the conceptual competence regarding alternative 
approaches to voice-­hearing, this is an example of smothering.
9.3  AI Features Relevant for Epistemic Injustice
In a seminal 1955 research proposal, AI was defined as the undertaking of designing 
machines that can simulate complex capabilities generally associated with human intelligence, 
like the use of language, solving problems, or forming abstractions and concepts (McCarthy 
et  al.  1955). In other words, AI research aims to break down real-­world problems into 
mathematical problems and then offer mathematical solutions to those problems through 
algorithms. In this sense, an algorithm can be understood as an automated procedure for 
mathematical problem solving (Lenzen 2018).
Since its onset, the term AI has been applied to a variety of research aims related to those 
proposed by McCarthy et al. (1955). These projects have been pursued with varying success 
and have alternately been met with euphoria and pessimism. AI is also a proliferating inter-
disciplinary research field, drawing from informatics, mathematics, psychology, philosophy, 
linguistics, neuroscience, and further disciplines (Lenzen  2018). Currently, ML and deep 
learning-­based technologies are at the forefront of AI applications and public discussions. 
Such systems are used for predictions, categorization, natural language processing, image 
generation, recommendations, data analytics, and more (Google 2024).
We will focus on ML as a prime example of AI. In ML, an algorithm is developed through 
an iterative process of receiving feedback and making adjustments to generate a desired 
output from input data. The algorithm initially goes through a training phase, where it is 
presented with training data, generates output, receives feedback, adjusts itself to better 
match the desired outcome next time, generates output again, and so on. This training 
phase can be of a finite duration or ongoing while the algorithm is in use, and the way the 
algorithm receives feedback and adapts depends on the methods chosen. Because the way the 

--- Page 132 ---

Mirjam Faissner, Janne Lenk, and Regina Müller
122
algorithm arrives at the output is not hard-­coded but adaptive and acquired through feedback 
and repetition, it is called machine “learning” (El Naqa and Murphy  2022). The desired 
output could, for example, be a prioritized list, the assignment of a category to an object, 
filtered data or the mapping of associations between objects (Diakopoulos 2014).
As Alvarado (2023) argues, AI systems can be viewed as epistemic technologies in that 
they are primarily used in epistemic contexts to manipulate epistemic content, and do so 
through epistemic operations. In what follows, we aim to highlight multiple areas where 
forms of epistemic injustice may ensue from the design, development, and application of 
ML-­based systems that have been discussed in research literature. To do this, we will consider 
four features of AI relevant to epistemic injustice: the reliance on training data, the use of 
categories and systems of classification, AI’s opacity, and epistemic fragmentation. In the 
following discussion, we will explain how these features may lead to specific forms of epistemic 
injustice, based on concrete case examples.
9.3.1  The Reliance on Training Data
As ML methods depend on feedback loops to achieve accurate results, they require suitable 
training data and often large datasets. Datafication describes the process of rendering the 
world into digital data that computational systems can interpret (Cukier and Mayer-­
Schönberger  2014). Datafication is taking place on a large scale and in many domains, 
ranging from the economy, the environment and education to public and private 
communication and individual bodies. This rendering of the world into data can be seen as a 
way of representing knowledge that necessarily results in losses of information and complexity. 
At the same time, datafication allows new knowledge to emerge from data analysis and 
interpretation (Lenzen 2018, 2020). We can therefore understand datafication as a shift in 
epistemic practices that may lead to forms of epistemic injustice (Haarman 2021).
Societal power dynamics shape practices of generating, collecting, accessing or harvesting 
data, and interests of different societal agents may influence these practices. For example, 
datafication is largely driven by corporations that generate surplus value from rendering 
human experience into behavioral data. The knowledge they generate from this data and their 
computational systems may thus mainly serve commercial interests (Zuboff  2019). Other 
interests, such as those of groups affected by the algorithm, may be secondary, and data 
generated within these communities is often neglected. For instance, in the case of algorithms 
used at courts for pretrial decision making, training data is sourced exclusively from criminal 
legal institutions such as the police, pretrial services agencies, and the court system, while data 
developed within communities particularly affected by such algorithms is not considered. If 
certain sources of knowledge are systematically excluded from training data, the training data 
may be incomplete and thus epistemically insufficient. Moreover, various kinds of unwanted 
societal bias can be reflected in datasets by the over-­ or underrepresentation of certain groups 
or inaccurate and missing data (Hull  2023; Okidegbe  2022; Sardelli  2022; Symons and 
Alvarado  2022). Data quality is further impacted by a demand for increasingly large and 
complex datasets to avoid overfitting, that is, ending up with an algorithmic model that relies 
on peculiarities of the training data and therefore produces inaccurate results for new input. 
For example, to train image classification algorithms, training images are labeled to indicate 
the correct category that the algorithm should learn to identify. As labeling and maintaining 
such datasets can be costly, attempts to cut costs include hiring low-­paid crowd workers to label 
images under heavy time constraints, or employing further algorithms to label training data. 
This may result in further errors and distortions in the datasets (Hull 2023).

--- Page 133 ---

AI and Epistemic Injustice
123
9.3.2  The Use of Categories and Systems of Classification
Another relevant feature of ML algorithms is their use of machine-­interpretable categories 
and systems of classification to analyze data, for example to classify, predict, cluster, or filter 
it. When such categories and associated systems of classification are applied to complex and 
contextual social identities, they can become harmful beyond the issues raised in the previous 
section. Highlighting the importance of classifications, Hull (2023, p. 38) refers to them as 
the “grammar of the dataset,” influencing what the data can express, what algorithms based 
on this data can do and how people interact with the resulting algorithmic systems. As Hull 
(2023) notes, how the world is represented in data can ossify and enforce socially constructed 
categories, such as race and gender categories, while presenting those categories as apolitical 
and natural. For instance, representations of racial identity or gender in image datasets often 
use a very limited number of categories, which are applied inconsistently across datasets. In 
the UTKFace dataset, the images are annotated with gender as either male or female, and race 
as White2, Black, Asian, Indian and Others. Systems trained on such a dataset depend on 
these labels to predict properties of further facial images, thus propagating the predefined cat-
egories. In this way, other possible classifications and the contextual nature of social cate-
gories remain illegible (Hull 2023). Moreover, the classification decisions of algorithms based 
on those classificatory systems are not necessarily more objective than human judgments, as 
many human choices become built-­in during the algorithm design process, including 
“defining features, pre-­classifying training data, and adjusting thresholds and parameters” 
(Burrell 2016, p. 3).
Additionally, simplified systems of classification built into training data and design choices 
can reinforce stereotypes and prejudice. AI that generates images is an illustrative example 
here. For one, AI-­generated images can reinforce prejudices by replicating stereotypical 
thinking embedded in the labels of the training images, thus reflecting the views of the 
annotators. Another reason for stereotypical output is that generative AI systems 
fundamentally rely on pattern recognition, so they amplify what is more frequent in a dataset 
and tend to discard outliers, to the point that attempts at mitigation by entering counter-­
stereotypical prompts remain ineffective (Bianchi et  al.  2023; Turk  2023). In this way, 
preexisting distortions can persist and find new outlets in digital epistemic infrastructures 
(Sardelli 2022).
9.3.3  Opacity
As illustrated above, ML methods suggest that the outcome defines a good result, while the 
patterns that the algorithm uses to arrive at the outcome may remain unknown. For recipi-
ents of a classificatory algorithmic output, such opacity means that “rarely does one have any 
concrete sense of how or why a particular classification has been arrived at from inputs” 
(Burrell 2016). However, to analyze epistemic injustice it is helpful to distinguish between 
different causes and kinds of opacity.
Humphreys (2009) introduces “essential epistemic opacity” as one distinctive and 
philosophically new feature of computational processes such as those employed in ML. 
According to Humphreys, there is epistemic opacity if an agent does not know all of the 
epistemically relevant elements involved in a process, but there is essential epistemic opacity 
if it is impossible for any human agent to know all of the epistemically relevant elements of 
the process due to the nature of the process itself. To illustrate, the first of three kinds of 
opacity identified by Burrell (2016) is opacity that follows from intentional secrecy on the 

--- Page 134 ---

Mirjam Faissner, Janne Lenk, and Regina Müller
124
part of companies and institutions, e.g., via proprietary access limitations to training or 
coding data. Opacity may also result from technical illiteracy, as the specialized skills of 
coding and designing algorithms are accessible only to a small subset of the population. 
The third kind of opacity stems from the scale and complexity of the data and the 
computational processes involved in computational systems, and the divergence of 
computational decision processes from human modes of interpretation and comprehension. 
Therefore, many current AI applications are structured in such a way that they remain, to 
some degree, incomprehensible and uninterpretable even for computer scientists 
(Burrell 2016). According to Humphreys, only the third kind would qualify as the essential 
epistemic opacity intrinsic to certain computational methods. Even so, the different kinds 
of epistemic opacity have in common that they limit the capacity of agents to evaluate AI 
applications, making it difficult to identify and track potential harm.
9.3.4  Epistemic Fragmentation
Milano et al. (2021) have argued that algorithmic systems, such as targeted advertising 
online, systematically induce epistemic fragmentation. Epistemic fragmentation describes a 
structural characteristic of digital epistemic infrastructures in which individuals are iso-
lated by reduced access to context information. Context information involves other users’ 
personal information or which content other users see, e.g., on their social media. This 
isolation hinders people from comparing their experiences to the experiences of other 
users (Milano and Prunkl 2024). Using the example of algorithms on social media plat-
forms like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, Stewart et al. (2022) show that such epi-
stemic fragmentation occurs through two algorithmic processes: targeting and sorting. 
Algorithmic targeting presents users with content aligned with their preferences. This can 
also be described as algorithmic profiling or online personalization, which determines which 
posts, products or news a certain user sees, for example on their social media account 
(Milano et al. 2021). Algorithmic sorting leads to the segregation of users into distinct 
epistemic spheres, often referred to as “filter bubbles” (Stewart et al. 2022). Such algo-
rithmic influences are relevant because they shape users’ epistemic agency when using 
social media.
9.4  Epistemic Injustice In and Through Algorithmic Systems
9.4.1  Testimonial Injustice
As a reminder, testimonial injustice refers to the unjustified downgrading of a person’s 
credibility due to prejudice. It may thus occur, for example, when a person prejudicially 
attributes less credibility to a human decision than an AI-based system’s decision. Recently, 
several authors have shown the link between AI-­based systems and testimonial injustice 
(El Kassar 2022; Faissner et al. 2024; Hull 2023; Origgi and Ciranna 2017; Pozzi 2023b; 
Sardelli 2022; Stewart et al. 2022). For Walmsley (2023), three developments in recent years 
are crucial: ML, big data, and algorithmic appreciation. Algorithmic appreciation means the 
growing trust in AI-­based systems, for example to make predictions, recommendations, and 
decisions. According to Walmsley (2023), the combination of these three factors leads to 
epistemic injustice, in particular to testimonial injustice: 

--- Page 135 ---

AI and Epistemic Injustice
125
Given our epistemic limitations with respect to contemporary AI systems –­ and the problems to 
which these limitations can give rise –­ coupled with our tendency to defer to their advice and to 
trust them over and above other humans, I want to suggest that we run the risk of perpetuating 
novel instances of epistemic injustice. (Walmsley 2023, p. 255)
Walmsley (2023) illustrates the risk of testimonial injustice in the context of AI using the 
example of a digital symptom checker app. Symptom checker apps are AI-­based systems that 
assist patients by checking symptoms, creating differential diagnoses, and triaging for further 
care. For Walmsley (2023), the ethical problem is not that we trust such apps because of their 
“expertise” but that we trust them simply because they are computers: 
[...] we would assign a deflated level of credibility to a human GP’s judgment because they are 
human, and an inflated level of credibility [. . .] to the app, and these assignments occur because 
of the groups to which their targets belong, and not because of any justifiable appraisal of their 
relative expertise. (Walmsley 2023, p. 258)
The assessment of the credibility of both the GP and the app may be distorted by biases that 
involve prejudicial overgeneralization, such as “GPs are more partial compared to neutral 
technology.” Such prejudices are commonly based on stereotypes, i.e., associations between 
members of a group (being human) and characteristics that members of this social group 
exhibit in different social environments (being partial). According to Fricker (2007), 
stereotypes related to a person’s social identity that deflate credibility judgments may lead to 
testimonial injustice. While the prejudice is structural, the harm occurs at the individual 
level, where the communication between the app user and the GP is disrupted due to the 
inappropriate downgrading of the GP’s credibility. This may also relate to people from 
marginalized groups who are affected by prejudice in medical practice as patients. Pozzi 
(2023a), for example, argues that algorithmic risk scores for opioid misuse may be treated as 
markers of trustworthiness, so patients’ testimonies may be unduly downgraded if it conflicts 
with the calculated score. Similarly, Faissner et al. (2024) argue that self-­tracking apps for 
depression may result in testimonial injustice against people with mental health symptoms if 
such technology is broadly implemented.
9.4.2  Hermeneutical Marginalization
Hermeneutical marginalization, which is the background condition for hermeneutical 
injustice, describes the systematic unequal participation of members of disadvantaged groups 
in relevant areas of social experience and knowledge production. Several authors have 
suggested different links between algorithmic processes and hermeneutical marginalization. 
Milano and Prunkl (2024), for example, see a crucial aspect in the statistical nature of ML, 
because “[. . .] the statistical nature of ML de facto prevents groups underrepresented in the 
data from contributing to this epistemic resource on an equal ground to dominant groups.” If 
we understand training data as contributing to shared epistemic resources, the insufficient or 
inadequate representation of marginalized groups in these datasets (e.g., due to low data 
quality, biased data collection, or data reuse practices) may constitute unjust hermeneutical 
marginalization. Hermeneutical marginalization may also follow from the interplay of a 
dataset and the task it is applied to, for example when choosing a proxy variable that leads to 
wrong inferences that disproportionately affect marginalized groups (Milano and 
Prunkl 2024). To give an example, Rafanelli (2022) examines algorithms used to classify 

--- Page 136 ---

Mirjam Faissner, Janne Lenk, and Regina Müller
126
résumés in the context of job applications. In this example, an AI-­based résumé screener 
systematically favored the résumés of men over those of women, because it was trained on 
data from résumés previously submitted to a tech company, most of which were from men. 
The system was therefore trained on a dataset that represented one group (men) to the 
exclusion of another group (women). Based on the disproportionately male training data, the 
AI-­based system “learned” that a good résumé equates to a résumé of a man. A company 
adopting this system would therefore equate “being qualified” with “being a successful man.” 
Rafanelli (2022) summarizes this as follows: “[I]f dominant ideas about what it means to be 
‘good’ or ‘qualified’ are constructed based on men’s data, to the exclusion of women’s, this is 
arguably an instance of hermeneutical marginalization” (Rafanelli 2022, p. 4).
Additionally, algorithms on social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram 
may contribute to the hermeneutical marginalization of social groups (Stewart et al. 2022). 
As explained above, algorithmic targeting and sorting processes may lead to epistemic 
fragmentation, which undermines the epistemic agency of users by only allowing a partial 
and distorted vision of the content available on the platforms. This may create conditions con-
ducive to hermeneutical marginalization. Epistemic fragmentation isolates individuals within 
digital infrastructures, meaning that these individuals have no or only limited access to 
information about other individuals’ personal contexts, making it difficult to compare their 
experiences to the experiences of others and their interpretation thereof (Milano and 
Prunkl 2024). Epistemic fragmentation may make it more difficult for marginalized knowers 
to develop new epistemic resources, if the algorithm constrains exchange with members of 
other social groups who share similar or related experiences. Additionally, if people have 
already developed fitting epistemic resources, epistemic fragmentation may sustain herme-
neutical marginalization by “prevent[ing] the uptake of epistemic resources in the sense that, 
even if conceptual resources are readily available, their collective uptake might be hindered” 
(Milano and Prunkl 2024).
Stewart et al. (2022) argue that algorithms on social media increase epistemic and moral 
distances between different social groups and deepen ignorance about the experiences of 
other social groups. They speak of a “perfect storm for epistemic injustice because the very 
same conditions that make marginalized voices less likely to be heard and given proper uptake 
in general are compounded by the algorithmic processes of sorting and targeting, thereby 
creating a vicious cycle in which interpersonal epistemic injustices are worsened both on and 
offline” (Stewart et al. 2022, p. 12).
Stewart et al. (2022) show widening gaps between social groups, the social phenomenon 
of Othering, and systematic underrepresentation and exclusion of certain groups or 
individuals from the process of knowledge production and sharing on social media platforms 
with the example of so-­called “mommy blogs.” Mommy blogs are online platforms where 
mothers share their experiences, advice, and insights about parenting, usually covering 
topics like child-­rearing, homemaking, and family life, often surrounded by advertisements 
for sponsored products. However, the lives of the bloggers –­ at least of those who become 
famous –­ are not representative of most mothers’ lives. The type of experiences that are 
successful or increasingly shared on social media is very narrow: white, straight, thin, and 
wealthy. This narrow and stereotypical presentation of motherhood is reinforced through 
the algorithms on social media, while different perspectives and experiences, such as those 
of queer, low-­income or racialized mothers, are filtered out. As a consequence, socially 
nondominant perspectives disappear, whereas the dominant perspectives remain 
unquestioned. As Stewart et  al. (2022) emphasize, such algorithmic processes lead to a 
growing distance between different groups of “mommies” and thus to gaps in seeing, 

--- Page 137 ---

AI and Epistemic Injustice
127
understanding, and trusting each other’s experiences. Both Stewart et al. (2022) and Milano 
and Prunkl (2024) argue that these processes particularly affect already marginalized 
groups more than other groups.
9.4.3  Hermeneutical Injustice
Several authors have examined predictive algorithms that are supposed to support decisions 
based on calculating a specific risk score. Such algorithmic risk scores are used in healthcare 
to estimate the likelihood of opioid addiction and misuse (Pozzi 2023a), in the criminal justice 
system for pretrial detentions, bail calculations, parole hearings or sentencing based on a 
recidivism risk score (Hull 2023; Symons and Alvarado 2022), and by the police to determine 
operation areas based on the likelihood of future crimes (El Kassar 2022). These examples 
share some important features: members of marginalized groups are affected by the systems 
in the sense that the decisions have a real-­life impact, the social group is marginalized in the 
development of the algorithm, and the algorithm’s functionality is opaque.
The concept of hermeneutical injustice is beneficial to understanding such instances of 
injustice. As we have established, hermeneutical injustice describes a person’s unfair 
disadvantage in understanding or communicating relevant social experiences because of gaps 
in collectively shared epistemic resources. The person is disadvantaged in their epistemic agency 
because the collectively available epistemic resources are inadequate for their epistemic 
enquiries. This constitutes injustice if the inadequacy in collectively available hermeneutical 
resources stems from the epistemic marginalization of the social group to which the person 
belongs.
Consider, for example, the COMPAS pretrial detention system. Its input data consists of the 
defendant’s criminal record and answers to a 137-­question survey, asking, amongst other 
things, for prior arrests and convictions of the defendant. The output is a risk score that pre-
dicts the likelihood of the defendant committing another crime in the future (Fraenkel 2020). 
According to Hull (2023), arrests and convictions are an inadequate proxy for criminality, in 
part because they systematically overestimate the criminality of Black defendants compared 
to white defendants. Importantly, even if the risk prediction proves accurate in that it estimates 
future convictions equally well for Black and white populations, it does not help to illuminate 
the underlying racialized practices of the criminal system but may even serve to obscure them.
It is especially the opacity of systems like COMPAS that can lead to hermeneutical injustice 
(Symons and Alvarado 2022). For a person detained based on a COMPAS algorithmic risk 
score, it is impossible to transparently assess how the system calculated the risk score; the 
different questions are weighted differently and included in a predictive model protected by 
proprietary trade secrets. Due to the system’s opacity, no one is able to judge whether the 
system made a mistake because neither the convicted person nor any lawyer or judge involved 
in the decision can understand the calculated risk score. It is thus nearly impossible to 
challenge a COMPAS risk score. This is a situation in which the epistemic agency of people is 
constrained based on an inadequate epistemic resource. This can be analyzed as a form of 
hermeneutical injustice, because not only were detainees and prisoners not involved in the 
development of COMPAS, but communal sources of information were also ignored 
(Hull 2023).
El Kassar (2022) explains a further aspect of the hermeneutical injustice associated with 
algorithmic risk scores. PredPol, an algorithm the police use to determine the likelihood of 
criminal offences in a particular neighborhood to plan future police operations and patrols, 
relies on past police operations as a proxy for criminal offences. Given that police operations 

--- Page 138 ---

Mirjam Faissner, Janne Lenk, and Regina Müller
128
are more likely in primarily Black neighborhoods in the US, PredPol also directs more police 
officers into Black neighborhoods. According to El Kassar (2022), this might influence our 
collectively shared epistemic resources by strengthening racist stereotypes about racially 
marginalized groups as dangerous and criminal. The injustice therefore also lies in the 
reproduction of prejudice in the collectively shared epistemic resources.
9.4.4  Wilful Hermeneutical Ignorance
As mentioned above, ML classification algorithms depend on preexisting categories and 
classification systems. Using simplified social categories may lead to a distorted “grammar of 
the dataset” which is insufficient in representing the social categories of the designated people 
(Hull  2023). The failure that occurs when dominantly situated knowers (such as the 
developers) refuse to acknowledge the epistemic resources developed within marginalized 
epistemic communities is what we previously defined as wilful hermeneutical ignorance. 
Using the example of automatic gender recognition, El Kassar (2022) argues that forms of 
wilful hermeneutical ignorance may influence the development and design of algorithm-­
based technologies.
Automatic gender recognition refers to the process of using algorithms to identify and 
classify a person’s gender based on various inputs (Scheuerman et al. 2019). These algorithms 
analyze visual or auditory features, such as facial characteristics, body shape or voice pitch, 
to determine a person’s gender. Automatic gender recognition is often used in the context of 
surveillance, security, and marketing (Scheuerman et al. 2019). El Kassar (2022) uses airport 
security scanners to illustrate how wilful hermeneutical ignorance manifests itself in these 
algorithm-­based systems. The injustice arises because the programs operate exclusively with 
a binary understanding of gender: The systems can only identify “men” or “women”; 
nonbinary genders are not an option, and trans people must conform to stereotypical ideas 
about “female” or “male” traits. The system does not represent the existence of nonbinary or 
trans people. Even more, the systems cannot acknowledge the existence of nonbinary and 
trans people because the corresponding terms and concepts have not been programmed into 
these systems. The epistemic injustice experienced by nonbinary and trans people can be 
traced back to deliberate decisions in the development and design of the systems. As El Kassar 
(2022) emphasizes, when today people design and develop systems based on a binary 
understanding of gender, they ignore terms and conceptions that nonbinary and trans people 
use and that are publicly available. This amounts to wilful hermeneutical ignorance.
9.5  Implications for Epistemic Justice and Digitalization
Sharing knowledge, testifying, making sense of social experiences or contributing to the 
understanding of concepts are central to what it means to be a socially interdependent 
human. Fricker therefore stresses that cases of epistemic injustice inflict primary (intrinsic) 
harm, which needs to be distinguished from secondary (instrumental) harm: “To be wronged 
in one’s capacity as a knower is to be wronged in a capacity essential to human value” 
(Fricker 2007, p. 44). In both testimonial and hermeneutical injustice, people are excluded 
from participating in knowledge production, in the first case based on prejudice related to a 
person’s social identity, in the second based on prejudice in collectively shared epistemic 
resources. Dotson (2014, p. 115) suggests that “persistent epistemic exclusions that hinder 
one’s contribution to knowledge production” constitute epistemic oppression. The examples 

--- Page 139 ---

AI and Epistemic Injustice
129
of epistemic injustice in algorithmic design involve persistent forms of epistemic exclusions 
and therefore cause intrinsic harm in and of themselves.
Additionally, the examples indicate the instrumental harm of the cases of epistemic 
injustice analyzed above. In the case of testimonial injustice, the instrumental harm is often 
epistemic: information that ought to be transmitted gets lost. As Pozzi (2023b) suggests in 
the context of healthcare, undermining patients’ capacity to contribute knowledge is 
particularly relevant because this supports a more paternalistic form of medical practice in 
which patients are considered (passive) recipients of treatment rather than active agents of 
their health. Additionally, people may experience psychological harm associated with 
epistemic injustice. El Kassar (2022) quotes Costanza-­Chock (2020) describing the burden 
of being confronted with security systems that work with a cis-­binary understanding of 
gender as a gender-­diverse person: “[M]y heartbeat speeds up slightly as I near the end of 
the line, because I know that I’m almost certainly about to experience an embarrassing, 
uncomfortable, and perhaps humiliating search by a Transportation Security Administration 
(TSA) officer, after my body is flagged as anomalous by the millimeter wave scanner” (El 
Kassar 2022, p. 290). Being identified as “anomalous” by algorithmic systems based on 
socially dominant assumptions of normality may thus contribute to minority stress that, in 
the long term, increases the risk of mental illness among marginalized social groups 
(Hoy-­Ellis 2023).
In cases of hermeneutical injustice, the instrumental harm may also be social, legal, and 
material. With regard to the example of COMPAS, for instance, individuals who are detained 
for too long or on unjustified grounds are denied the chance to challenge their conviction, 
possibly leading to major infractions of their personal rights, as well as social exclusion and 
difficulties in keeping their job or apartment.
Considering these different forms of instrumental harm allows us to see that epistemic 
injustice associated with ML tools never occurs in a vacuum but is intertwined with other 
social processes. The context of applying algorithmic systems is crucial because it influences 
the severity of the harm in question. To evaluate possible risks of using an algorithm, one 
can distinguish between high-­ and low-­stake application contexts, where high-­stake 
contexts involve decisions directly impacting human life trajectories, like the aforementioned 
pretrial algorithms (El Kassar  2022). While the forms of epistemic harm caused by 
algorithm-­based decision making can affect individuals across different social statuses, 
they often disproportionately affect social groups affected by structural injustice (Symons 
and Alvarado  2022). For instance, the US criminal justice system, where COMPAS is 
employed, is heavily imbued with structural racism, which particularly affects members of 
racially marginalized communities (Lee 2024). Applied in a context of structural racism, 
which intersects with further systems of oppression, such as classism, the algorithmic 
systems can exacerbate prior disadvantages and thereby support structural systems of 
oppression. Thus, algorithmic knowledge production should not be regarded as an apolitical 
or purely technological process but as a process of societal, moral, and epistemic impact 
that requires critical evaluation.
Finally, it is noteworthy that despite the rich and diverse literature on the intersection 
of knowledge production and social systems of oppression and injustice, most current 
analyses of epistemic injustice take Fricker’s (2007) framework as a point of reference. 
Given the fine-­grained conceptual repertoire and the complexity of the current develop-
ments in ML, for instance in the context of generative AI, further analyses taking into 
account the entire range of tools to name and analyze different forms of epistemic injus-
tice would be welcome.
