10.1  Introduction
Normative reflection on questions of artificial intelligence (AI) is currently in full swing. We 
are encountering a variety of approaches to AI, some contradictory yet others complementary, 
all of which merit detailed analysis.
The aim in this chapter is to systematize the ethical theories surrounding AI.1 This 
systematization is necessary in order to make it clear that there can be no one-­size-­fits-­all 
theory for solving ethical questions in the context of AI. To this end, we will distinguish 
between first-­order theories and second-­order ethical approaches. By first-­order theories, we mean 
highly nuanced moral theories whose transfer to practical application contexts is anything 
but trivial and requires special effort. Examples of this are consequentialism, deontology, and 
virtue ethics. With second-­order approaches, we refer to ethical approaches that are restricted 
by the normative requirements of the application context and that incorporate some elements 
of first-­order theories but cannot be reduced to these again.2 As examples, we discuss 
regulations and guidelines (hard law, soft law, and self-­regulation) as well as different design 
approaches (value-­sensitive design, embedded ethics, ethics by design, and community-­led 
ethics). Finally, we discuss a combination of these models and their relevance and effectiveness.
Our systematization project faces a few primary challenges: the traditional ethical theories 
of consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics often lack the specificity required to 
address practical issues in AI effectively. Additionally, AI ethics is frequently regarded as a 
transformative venture, overshadowing the classical ethical theories. The application of these 
existing moral theories to AI’s unique subject matter and its various implementation contexts 
remains ambiguous. An applied philosophy of AI sees its task as reorganizing the current 
fragmented discourse. To this end, it seems important to categorize the existing ethical 
theories and examine their effectiveness in terms of solving practical problems. If our analysis 
proves the importance of all ethical theory perspectives and there is no uniform ethical theory 
due to the context dependency of AI applications, then the question arises as to whether 
effectiveness is the decisive criterion for choosing the right ethical theory or the right set of 
Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing 
the Discourse
MARTIN HÄHNEL AND REGINA MÜLLER
10

--- Page 145 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
136
ethical theories in relation to AI. One would then even have to ask whether a form of ethics 
for AI is possible at all.
Our reflections start with exploring, organizing, and comparing ethical theories for 
evaluating AI. In this context, ethical theories can be categorized into sophisticated types (see 
next section). The ethical theories of consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics are 
considered the most developed (sometimes referred to as high-­level theories). There are also 
synthetic approaches that merge elements from these high-­level theories, with the principled 
ethical approach of Beauchamp and Childress being the most notable (Beauchamp and 
Childress 2019). These less analytical and conceptual accounts, while sometimes labeled as 
mid-­level theories, are not necessarily less complex than the high-­level theories. They can be 
even more intricate, though in terms of their practicality rather than their theoretical 
complexity. Mid-­level theories, which are derivative and eclectic, serve to connect to ethical 
concepts or presuppositions that do not inherently require theoretical development, such as 
Beauchamp and Childress’ idea of a “common morality.” Atypical ethical theories, such as 
casuistry, feminist (see Chapter 14), narrative, and intercultural approaches, do not always 
stem from high-­level theories. However, it is possible to trace these theories back to the high-­
level theories, thereby making them conceptually stronger, which is an endeavor occasionally 
undertaken. With less fine-­grained approaches, we refer to the collective knowledge about 
ethical behavior, ethical compliance aspects, and common-­sense morality that exists beyond 
the inner circles of academic theory building. These aspects are especially significant, for 
example in medicine and nursing where ethics is a perpetual concern, but there is often 
insufficient time or resources available to delve into these approaches, their underlying 
rationale, and the ethical practices that emerge from adopting one approach over another.
In the following sections, we will not distinguish between high-­level and mid-­level theories, 
but will instead categorize theories according to their specific tasks.
However, before we try to systematize the discourse on AI’s ethical theories, it is crucial to 
acknowledge a significant issue: for years, there has been competition for the title of the most 
persuasive theory among the high-­level ethical theories (Borchers et  al.  2020). With no 
definitive winner, some continue to support the theory that aligns with their intuition while 
others, like Derek Parfit, suggest that all high-­level theories ultimately aim for the same goal, 
albeit through different methods (Parfit 2011). The emergence of AI presents new challenges 
to established ethical theories at both the high and mid-­levels (see more on this relationship in 
Flynn  2020). Ethical theories for AI also compete, but identifying the superior theory or 
harmonizing them at a meta-­level is challenging due to the necessity of contextual relevance.3
10.2  Ethical Theories for AI
Ethical theories for AI are currently developing under volatile conditions.4 They have been 
criticized as mere ethics-­washing (Hao 2019) and not effectively put into practice, leading 
some to consider them meaningless and toothless (Munn 2023). Instead, there is a call for 
established practices and validated methodologies in ethical AI design. Therefore, the 
reconciliation of ethical theory with different value-­laden forms of technological applications 
becomes pivotal in both scientific and public discourse on AI ethics. As Morley et al. (2020) 
emphasize, the crucial aspect is bridging the gap between the theoretical “what” and the 
practical “how” of AI ethics. It therefore depends to a large extent on how we relate our 
ethical theories to AI issues and tailor them accordingly for their design and practical 
implementation.

--- Page 146 ---

Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing the Discourse
137
To properly address the relatively new phenomenon of AI, we must reconsider how to 
accurately systematize the existing ethical theories. Before delving into the distinction between 
first-­order and second-­order ethical theories, we should begin by identifying the essential tasks 
and questions that a comprehensive moral theory should tackle. These theories need to:
•	 define and identify moral issues
•	 give answers to fundamental questions of right and wrong, the right balance between 
partial and impartial reasons, etc.
•	 provide the theoretical basis for solving moral dilemmas.
Ethical theories are thus specified in terms of the explanatory, normative, and practical 
tasks they are supposed to fulfill. Of course, it can happen that an ethical theory may be able to 
explain one aspect (of AI) well, but does not fulfill the practical and normative requirements of 
the same aspect. In the following, we limit ourselves primarily to narrow ethical concepts and 
are aware that ethical concepts can be broadened, for example when it comes to how AI can 
contribute to living a good and meaningful human life (Nyholm and Rüther 2023).
10.2.1  First-­order Moral Theories
In the following, we categorize theories based on their specific explanatory, normative, and 
practical tasks. First-­order moral theories, often mistaken for high-­level theories, are designed 
to define and identify ethical issues within the discourse of AI. In practical ethics, it is common 
to develop first-­order theories that help resolve moral dilemmas. Currently, three paradigms 
of first-­order moral theory have surfaced, known collectively as the “trinity of ethics”: conse-
quentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics. These theories are crucial as they lay a solid 
foundation for continuous ethical research and assessment, with ongoing enhancements 
within each paradigm. They are also considered first-­order theories because they address 
fundamental ethical questions of right/wrong, permissible/impermissible, and good/bad. 
Nevertheless, the accuracy of thin ethical terms is always challenged by a
lack of specificity needed to tackle the issues raised by new technologies. Instead of applying 
highly abstract traditional ethical theories such as Aristotle’s account of Virtue, Mill’s principle of 
utility, or Kant’s Categorical Imperative, straightforwardly to particular AI issues it is often more 
helpful to utilize mid-­level normative ethical theories, which are less abstract, more testable and 
which focus on technology, interactions between people, organizations, and institutions. 
Examples of mid-­level ethical theories are Rawls’ theory of justice, Pettit’s account of freedom in 
terms of non-­domination, or Klenk’s account of manipulation, which could be construed as 
broadly Kantian, Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum’s capability approach, which can be con-
strued as broadly Aristotelian, and Posner’s economic theory of law, which is broadly utilitarian. 
(Buijsman et al. 2025, p. 60)
It is not our task here to assess how relevant the three most prominent first-­order moral 
theories of consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics are to addressing AI issues (see 
Chapters 11, 12 and 13 in this companion). However, it is undisputed that the theories 
mentioned here can make a positive contribution to AI ethics. For example, we cannot avoid 
speaking of virtues in the training of computer scientists and engineers (Harris  2008). 
Deontology “can help to look at our obligations as well as at the rights of those who are 
impacted by AI systems” (Buijsman et al. 2025, p. 60). It is also important “to consider the 
consequences of developing an AI system, just as it is important for those involved in the 

--- Page 147 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
138
operation of the system to consider the consequences of the individual decisions made once 
the AI is up and running” (ibid.).
Nevertheless, Buijsman et al. (2025) argue that “we need to supplement the main ethical 
theories with more detailed accounts that apply to more specific concerns raised by emerging 
technologies” (ibid.). The parameters of second-­order ethical approaches, which we will dis-
cuss in detail in the next section, are often derived from the normative requirements of the 
context in question or by comparing various but commensurable contexts. First-­order moral 
theories may be self-­sufficient to some degree, but seemingly unsolvable problems arise when 
trying to apply them to a certain context. This is due to the introduction of parameters not 
accounted for in those theories, such as:
•	 a specific subject of investigation (e.g., AI)
•	 the analysis of competing theories necessitating the selection of a specific moral theory or 
family of theories5
•	 the form of practical application in accordance or discordance with the chosen moral 
theory or family of theories.
First-­order moral theories are indeed pivotal for a deeper comprehension of practical issues 
and theoretical insights. Consequentialism is advantageous for decision making on a large 
scale, where results are measurable and can be maximized, such as in allocating resources 
and public health endeavors. Deontology fits well within legal and regulatory frameworks 
that require steadfast rule adherence, as seen in autonomous vehicles and financial opera-
tions. Virtue ethics is particularly apt for AI systems that engage intimately with humans, 
emphasizing the importance of fostering trust and moral behavior, which are evident in 
healthcare support and among customer service agents.
10.2.2  Second-­order Ethical Approaches
Second-­order ethical approaches for AI focus on ensuring consistent ethical behavior, 
fostering accountability and considering AI’s wider societal effects. These are primarily top-­
down ethical strategies that encompass the establishment of comprehensive ethical guidelines 
and legal regulations, for example by companies, governments or international bodies. 
However, as we will see later, there are also bottom-­up approaches.
10.2.2.1  Top-­down Regulatory and Ethical Approaches
Regulations, which have a considerable influence on the scope and validity of moral theories, 
are formal laws and guidelines established by governments and international bodies to enforce 
ethical practices in AI. For instance, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation 
(GDPR) includes provisions that affect AI, particularly regarding data privacy and security. 
Additionally, the European Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) aims to create a comprehen-
sive regulatory framework for high-­risk AI applications,6 thus mandating rigorous testing 
and certification. Organizations like the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers 
(IEEE) and the Partnership on AI, on the other hand, contribute to setting ethical guidelines 
and best practices for AI development. These frameworks encourage collaboration between 
stakeholders, including policymakers, technologists, and the public, to create AI systems that 
align with societal values and human rights. Overall, the integration of ethical standards and 
regulatory measures is essential to foster trust in AI technologies, thus ensuring they are 
developed and used in ways that are beneficial and equitable for all.

--- Page 148 ---

Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing the Discourse
139
Hard Law and AI Regulation
The EU AI Act, a pioneering regulatory framework, has significant ethical implications for the 
development and deployment of AI. One of its primary goals is to ensure transparency in AI 
systems, requiring that users are informed when they interact with AI. This transparency is seen 
as crucial for building trust and enabling informed decision making. Accountability is another 
key aspect of the AI Act. It mandates that companies deploying high-­risk AI systems conduct 
thorough risk assessments and maintain documentation demonstrating compliance. This 
requirement helps to prevent harm and ensures that entities can be held responsible for any 
negative impacts caused by their AI systems. The AI Act also addresses fairness by aiming to 
eliminate biases in AI. Discriminatory practices in AI can have severe consequences, particularly 
in areas like hiring, law enforcement, medicine and credit scoring, especially for already 
vulnerable groups (e.g., Buolamwini and Gebru 2018; Hurley and Adebayo 2016; Obermeyer 
et al. 2019; West et al. 2019). By enforcing strict standards for data quality and algorithmic 
fairness, the AI Act seeks to protect individuals from biased outcomes.
Privacy protection is another significant ethical consideration embedded in the AI Act. 
The regulation stipulates robust data protection measures to ensure that AI systems do not 
infringe individuals’ privacy rights. This is particularly important given the vast amounts of 
personal data processed by AI technologies. Ultimately, the AI Act aspires to align AI 
development with societal values and human rights. By setting comprehensive standards for 
transparency, accountability, fairness, and privacy, the Act aims to foster ethical AI prac-
tices. This regulatory approach seeks to balance innovation with the protection of 
fundamental rights, thus promoting the development of trustworthy and socially beneficial 
AI systems.
However, from an ethical perspective, it is questionable to what extent these new regulations 
are effective and support ethical behavior. Regulatory frameworks are to be seen as second-­
order approaches because they do not justify ethical behavior, but only demand ethical 
compliance. There might be too little dialogue between representatives of AI ethics and legal 
scholars, who mostly focus on data protection issues. There are also several reasons to dispute 
the assertion that the AI Act regulation is ethically well founded. For example, there is no real 
guidance to help make AI trustworthy by ensuring that actions are consistent with the ethical 
principles enshrined in legislation (Ho and Caals 2024). It is to be expected that the regulations 
in the AI Act will not be able to fulfill the normative requirements of the contexts in which AI 
systems are to be used. It is also reasonable to assume that the AI Act is a kind of trademark 
with which AI products can be labeled so that they can be sold more easily –­ AI “made in 
Europe.”
Finally, it is debatable whether the AI Act, as a legal document, should be discussed under 
ethical approaches at all. Even if legal regulations are to be distinguished from ethical 
regulations (in many respects), many ethical considerations have been incorporated into the 
AI Act which impose ethical standards on AI. Ethical considerations and principles, such as 
privacy, have been shaped for a specific context and into a fixed legal framework, which is why 
we consider the AI Act to be relevant for discussion under second-­order ethical approaches.
Soft Law and Ethical Guidelines
Ethical guidelines for AI constitute frameworks of principles intended to steer the development, 
deployment, and utilization of AI systems in a manner that is responsible. These guidelines 
strive to align AI technologies with human values and societal standards, enhancing AI’s 
benefits and reducing its risks. The ethical ramifications of AI guidelines are significant, 
prompting critical questions about their practical application.

--- Page 149 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
140
With numerous ethical guidelines for AI proposed (see the overview in Brey et al. 2019), it 
has become evident that they often mirror political, economic or social agendas rather than 
addressing genuine ethical dilemmas. Consequently, there is considerable skepticism 
regarding the true efficacy of these ethical guidelines for AI (Munn 2023). This skepticism 
has spurred the development of bottom-­up ethical approaches, which do not seek to impose 
ethical norms on AI but to collaboratively shape ethical frameworks with AI and all parties 
involved. Nevertheless, this paradigm shift has not rendered ethical guidelines redundant 
(Lundgren  2023); rather, it has underscored their relevance. Indeed, guidelines are now 
being tailored more precisely to address the challenges of their implementation.
Finally, the implementation of AI guidelines must consider the balance between innova-
tion and regulation. While guidelines are necessary to prevent harm, they should not stifle 
technological progress. Striking this balance requires ongoing dialogue between policy 
makers, developers, and society to adapt guidelines as AI technology evolves.
Self-­regulation and Self-­certification
Self-­regulation and self-­certification in AI have significant ethical implications. These methods 
depend on developers and organizations setting and following ethical standards without 
external oversight. Self-­regulation and self-­certification measures are certainly important to 
increase trust in AI systems. There are promising approaches in the healthcare sector (Kim 
et al. 2024) but there appear to be insurmountable obstacles here, as it is difficult to place 
complete trust in self-­regulation processes, partly due to a lack of clear delineation of 
responsibilities. The absence of external validation can lead to poor disclosure or the 
misrepresentation of ethical adherence. This opacity can erode public trust and impede 
accountability. Additionally, the success of self-­regulation hinges on each organization’s 
dedication and ability to uphold high ethical standards, leading to variable forms of user 
protection and inconsistent application of ethical principles across the sector. Another major 
concern is the possibility of conflicts of interest, with companies potentially valuing profit 
over ethical considerations, thus leading to inadequate measures against biases, privacy 
breaches, and other damage.
Although self-­regulation and self-­certification may promote innovation and adaptability, 
they need strong external oversight and definitive, enforceable guidelines to ensure the 
responsible development and application of AI technologies, thus protecting the public 
interest and human rights.
10.2.2.2  Bottom-­up Design Approaches
Ethics-­by-­design
The concept of ethics-­by-­design originates from European research in computer science, 
ethics, and responsible innovation during the mid to late 2010s (Dignum et al. 2018).7 It may 
be seen as an extension of the “privacy-­by-­design” concept (Cavoukian 2009). The core idea 
is that ethical considerations can be integrated into technology through the design process 
(Tonkinwise 2004; Van Der Hoven and Manders-­Huits 2020).
AI ethics design approaches emphasize identifying values, translating these values into 
design requirements and evaluating technologies based on these values. This proactive stance 
in ethics engages system designers in ethical reflection, guiding the critical decisions that 
shape the systems. It seeks to bridge the frequently noted gap between ethical principles and 
practical application.
Ethics-­by-­design is a topic of discussion and application across various fields of techno-
logical innovation used for developing ethical and responsible designs. This includes 

--- Page 150 ---

Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing the Discourse
141
information system design (Brey 2010; Friedman et al. 2013), human–­computer interac-
tion (Borning and Muller 2012), energy projects (Dignum et al. 2018), medical technology 
(Kellmeyer et  al.  2019; Ienca et  al.  2018), sensor technology (Dechesne et  al.  2013), 
augmented reality (Friedman and Kahn 2000), nanotechnology (Timmermans et al. 2011), 
robotics (van Wynsberghe  2016) and, currently, AI technologies (Simon et  al.  2020; 
Umbrello 2019).
Ethics-­by-­design goes beyond mere compliance with ethical guidelines or regulations. It 
involves proactively identifying and addressing potential ethical issues during the design 
process. This approach ensures that the resulting technology functions effectively and aligns 
with societal values and norms. In medical technology, for example, ethics-­by-­design could 
involve considerations about patient privacy when designing electronic health records or 
fairness and transparency when developing AI diagnostic tools (Price and Cohen 2019). For 
instance, a team developing a new AI system for diagnosing skin cancer might incorporate 
ethics-­by-­design by ensuring the algorithm is trained on a diverse dataset, thus minimizing 
potential bias and improving the system’s fairness. Design approaches are poietic and 
proactive,8 insofar as they integrate ethics into system design from the outset, providing clear 
guidelines and frameworks for developers and promoting standardization with uniform 
standards and best practices in the industry. However, they require thorough initial planning, 
may lack flexibility in relation to new issues, and risk overlooking details if not continually 
reviewed and adjusted.
Value-­sensitive Design
Value-­sensitive design (VSD) adopts a bottom-­up approach, embedding ethical values into the 
technology design process from the beginning (Borning and Muller  2012; Friedman and 
Hendry 2019). In contrast to top-­down methods that enforce ethical standards via regulations, 
VSD engages stakeholders like users, developers, and impacted communities in the design and 
development phases. This inclusive approach is supposed to guarantee that the technology 
reflects the values and requirements of its users. VSD prioritizes the early identification and 
resolution of potential ethical issues, nurturing technologies that honor values such as 
privacy, fairness, and autonomy. VSD strives for more inclusive and fairer AI systems by 
embracing a variety of viewpoints. This bottom-­up method enhances the understanding of 
the social and cultural contexts in which technology functions, making ethical considerations 
a core element of design. In essence, VSD aspires to construct AI systems that are technically 
adept as well as ethically robust and socially considerate.
The VSD methodology has also been subject to criticism (Jacobs and Huldtgren 2018). 
Problems highlighted by critics are the identification of stakeholders (Manders-­Huits 2011) 
and the lack of embeddedness in political and social contexts.
Embedded Ethics
Embedded ethics involves integrating ethical considerations into professional practices and 
processes. Broadly speaking, an embedded ethics approach is characterized by a bottom-­up 
and inductive perspective, focusing on the engineering process of technologies and the moral 
intuitions and knowledge of stakeholders. The interdisciplinary team led by McLennan et al. 
(2022) suggests an applied ethics framework designed to thoroughly incorporate social, 
ethical, and legal considerations into the technological development process of AI. Ethicists, 
serving as integral members of the AI development team, contribute an ethical viewpoint, 
tackle pressing ethical concerns, elucidate dilemmas, and offer continuous ethical advice to 
technology professionals.

--- Page 151 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
142
This approach recognizes that ethical issues are not just design problems to be solved but 
are deeply intertwined with the contexts in which technology is used. The advantage of this 
approach is its consideration of the implementation context, which is often overlooked by 
other methods. However, embedded approaches represent a situational ethics model that does 
not base moral behavior on overarching norms and values but rather relies exclusively on an 
individual’s situations and circumstances.
In the field of  AI, embedded ethics primarily occurs within an education-­oriented 
engineering context (Grosz et  al.  2019; Zuber et  al.  2022). This involves integrating 
ethics modules into engineering courses or incorporating interdisciplinary reflection 
and deliberation into engineering processes. The goal is to infuse ethics into AI 
engineering by providing ethical training for engineers. While this virtue ethics approach 
primarily focuses on engineers, it also extends to ethics experts who become part of  AI 
engineering teams, such as when large tech companies hire and integrate ethics experts. 
Despite these common practices, this form of  ethics has not yet been explicitly labeled as 
“embedded ethics.”
Criticism arises on two fronts. First, the bottom-­up orientation prompts questions 
about the ethical criteria and principles that guide decision making. Second, integrating 
theory  –­ comprising professional ethical judgments  –­ into practice raises concerns about 
­preventing biases, subjectivity, and power abuse. Notably, the lack of clear guiding 
­principles and justification theories leaves ethical judgments without robust support, 
challenging the foundation of the embedded ethics theory–­practice concept (cf. Bleher and 
Braun 2023).
Both the ethics-­by-­design and embedded ethics approaches can be informed by first-­order 
ethical theories, but they apply these theories differently: ethics-­by-­design is more structured 
and rule based, aligning closely with deontological ethics while incorporating elements of 
consequentialism and virtue ethics; embedded ethics is more dynamic and process oriented, 
aligning with virtue ethics and consequentialism through continuous ethical engagement, 
reflection, and adaptation, while still respecting deontological principles by upholding 
ongoing ethical standards. Thus, the balanced integration of these approaches, informed by 
a combination of classical moral theories, can provide a comprehensive ethical framework for 
the development and deployment of AI.
Community-­led Approaches
Community-­led participatory research focuses on the alignment of AI systems with human 
values during the development of these systems. Unlike ethics-­by-­design and embedded 
ethics, this approach starts by analyzing the conceptual elements of participation (research 
methods in the social sciences, particularly social work, educational science, and peda-
gogy), current AI development paradigms, and the challenges posed by AI technologies. It 
critiques the prevailing ethics-­by-­design and embedded ethics paradigms in aligning the 
values of technologies, highlighting their shortcomings. The community-­led approach 
“emphasizes the importance of involving communities in all stages of the research process, 
from defining the research question to interpreting the results. It also highlights the 
need  to  balance context-­specific research and scalability to ensure representativeness” 
(Kellmeyer 2024, p. 19).
Especially due to the discriminatory effects of AI, many authors advocate alternative 
approaches to be used in the research, development, and design of AI-­based technologies that 
include marginalized communities. These approaches focus on marginalized communities in 
the AI development process, considering their perspectives, for example more ­human-­centered 

--- Page 152 ---

Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing the Discourse
143
approaches (Auernhammer  2020), participatory approaches (Birhane et  al.  2022), 
community-­based design (Murphy and Largacha-­Martínez,  2022), and AI that addresses 
local community needs and interests (e.g. Birhane 2020).
10.2.2.3  Hybrid Approaches: The Best of Both Worlds?
To make hybrid approaches attractive, the problem of the dependence of mid-­level theories on 
high-­level theories, which become dysfunctional through top-­down applications, must be 
solved. We try to figure out this derivation problem, which leads to an implementation 
problem, by talking about first-­order and second-­order approaches and trying to combine 
them in a new way. In analogy to Harry G. Frankfurt’s theory of secondary volitions 
(Frankfurt 1971),9 the second-­order approaches –­ in terms of their determinative power and 
not their general valence –­ are higher than the first-­order approaches. In this sense, second-­
order approaches are also higher than the first-­order theories in AI ethics. Second-­order 
approaches determine practice in the same way that secondary desires determine people’s 
behavior. However, second-­order approaches are not worth as much without first-­order 
theories. Second-­order approaches and first-­order theories are also not in conflict with each 
other. Second-­order approaches are not neutral but remain conviction bound due to their 
dependence on first-­order theories (but the conviction must be well founded). However, these 
convictions must take a back seat at the level of second-­order approaches.
We are therefore determined by a type of theory that we choose voluntarily or to which we 
tend if we cannot choose it voluntarily (e.g., for reasons of lack of expertise, lack of time to 
reflect when under great pressure to decide, because we are not asked about it, etc.). This 
determination is usually restricted –­ especially when we leave the realm of reason –­ by the 
normative requirements of a specific context of application and action (i.e., a specific AI 
application), which is also the basis for the development of second-­order approaches. The 
development of a hybrid theory is therefore recommendable but, in our view, it can only be 
successful if the choice or determination of a first-­order moral theory flows into the second-­
order ethical approach, not in the sense of a derivation or a supplement but in the sense of a 
transformation that also allows feedback to the first-­order moral theory, which can be 
modified using the feedback. The relationship between first-­order moral theories and second-­
order approaches should not describe a tiered or layered model with deviating normative 
force,10 but rather a relationship of transformative specification and contextualization. 
Although content is specified and restricted or modified by context, the qualitative 
requirements for a moral theory to be simple, accurate, and coherent (Driver 2022) remain 
the same for first-­order moral theories and second-­order approaches. The success of the 
feedback and the transformation of existing ethical theories with regard to AI depends on the 
willingness to meet these requirements, to enter into dialogue with colleagues who have 
made a different choice and to work together to solve an application problem.
Ethical approaches specific to AI seem to remain useless, not because they are too elabo-
rate but for other reasons. The effectiveness of an ethical theory for AI depends on the specific 
context and goals of the AI application. In practice, a hybrid approach that combines ele-
ments from multiple theories (first-­ and second-­order theories) is often recommended to 
ensure a comprehensive and adaptable ethical framework for AI. This allows for flexibility and 
responsiveness to the diverse and dynamic nature of AI applications and their impact 
on society.11
In order to evaluate the effectiveness of an ethical theory or approach to AI, we would like 
to categorize hybrid ethical approaches to AI according to their type of theory construction 
(Table 10.1). To assess the effectiveness of an ethical theory or approach for AI, it is necessary 

--- Page 153 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
144
to determine if the approach is grounded in one or more ethical theories (= foundational the-
ories). In derivative approaches, foundational theories are the starting points for the formation 
of more specific normative judgments, and nonfoundational theories are the endpoints of the 
successful testing of foundational theories in concrete practice. The reference value to which 
the derivation refers is different for the foundational and nonfoundational theories. Whereas 
foundational theories refer to various sources of normativity (divine legislator, principle of 
utility, moral role models, etc.), nonfoundational theories do not refer to the sources of nor-
mativity but to the respective moral theories, such as utilitarianism, deontological ethics, and 
virtue ethics, which emerge from them. The classical ethical theories are deemed derivative as 
they stem from core moral considerations like basic intuitions, certain worldviews, metaphys-
ical assumptions, traditional customs, and impressive testimonies, which then form the basis 
of generalizable ethical judgments (think of Kant’s “starry heavens” and moral law).
In nonderivative approaches, recourse to ethical theories plays little or no role. Norms are 
not derived from practical reasons, a common morality or sophisticated ethical frameworks, 
but have other sources that are often difficult to explain in philosophical terms (e.g., positive 
norms in law, professional norms, etc.). Nonderivative approaches are either normative 
frameworks based on themselves (as understood in legal positivism) or developed in the pro-
cess of undertaking certain actions with specific goals in mind (these are often theories that 
aim to bring about moral progress).
Furthermore, it must be clarified whether an ethical approach to AI is seen as founda-
tional. If no single approach is foundational, this implies that multiple ethical approaches 
may coexist and potentially be integrated. It is important to note that foundational and non-
derivative are distinct concepts; the latter relies on specific assumptions or design choices, 
whereas the former relies on condensing moral arguments into a few justificatory paradigms 
of normative ethics.12
Table 10.1 shows various ways of reorganizing heterogeneous ethical theories to prepare 
them to be put into practice. There are certainly overlaps between the various approaches in 
some respects, and it is not always possible to clearly distinguish between them. Foundational 
approaches have the advantage that they can provide a precise conceptual source for their 
considerations (e.g., categorical imperative, account of virtue, principle of utility) and can 
develop standards for practice on this basis. However, this recourse does not necessarily have 
to go back to ethical theories but can also take place in terms of positive law or with recourse 
to a “common morality” as a pretheoretical set of principles, intuitions, and judgments. 
Foundational approaches, regardless of whether they are derivative or nonderivative, tend to 
be imposed on practice from above (top-­down), whereas nonfoundational approaches tend to 
be inductive (bottom-­up). In the course of their implementation, nonfoundational approaches

Ethical Theories for AI: Systematizing the Discourse
145
are not subject to the constraint of having to fall back on the conceptual resources of a 
particular theory or family of theories. Without making any ontological commitment, they 
can be better adapted to the complex circumstances of a particular practice (e.g., the 
development and use of AI) and are more tolerant of unforeseen contextual changes.
With regard to ethical approaches to AI, the following picture has emerged in recent years, 
not without tension. Derivative approaches, whether foundational or not, cannot be purely 
top-­down approaches, as they are blind to contexts and trade-­offs and therefore cannot guide 
action. In contrast, nonderivative approaches are often regarded as genuinely instrumental 
or solutionist without giving normative reasons. The truth here –­ as is often the case –­ lies in 
the middle. Why?
In the field of AI in particular, hybrid ethical approaches must be developed that mediate 
between reflecting on ethical questions and “answering” them with action, between 
adherence to normative beliefs and openness to weighing these convictions against competing 
convictions in individual cases, between responsible individual action and ethical compliance, 
between soft and hard law, and so forth. Good ethical conduct will not occur if, for example, 
no ethical guidelines are issued and enforced in research on new high-­risk AI systems and all 
stakeholders do not work simultaneously to develop character traits or virtues that are in line 
with these guidelines or do not falsify them. For this congruence to be possible, it must be 
universally understood that guidelines do not tell the researcher, designer or user how to 
achieve an ethical goal, but primarily make it clear when the researcher, designer or user has 
fulfilled an ethical requirement.
10.3  Summary
Ethical theory reflections on questions of AI are currently in an intensive phase. There are 
numerous, partly contradictory but also complementary theories that not only require detailed 
analysis but also need to be systematized and related to each other. The systematization of the 
discourse is constantly at risk of sudden fragmentation, but nevertheless our explanations offer 
reliable guidance to help stakeholders find their way through the jungle of theories and are 
always open to revision and specification. It is advisable to consider all theories and approaches 
of an ethics of AI, which we have distinguished in our matrix according to the character of their 
derivability and strength of foundation, for a comprehensive analysis. It is likely, however, that 
in the end the respective context of application and the demand for practical concreteness will 
decide which theory has the overriding explanatory and justifying power.
The frequent issues with translating terminology, which arise from various disciplines 
addressing AI without a shared understanding of it, impede the development of a unified eth-
ical theory. However, medical ethics, which consistently addresses AI concerns, has a distinct 
advantage. It develops its models through interdisciplinary collaboration with practitioners and 
nonphilosophical stakeholders, as exemplified by Beauchamp and Childress. Consequently, 
there are ongoing efforts to adapt the theoretical frameworks of medical ethics to the ethical 
challenges of AI (Floridi and Cowls 2022). This adaptation strategy is often additive rather than 
transformative. For instance, the four principles of biomedical ethics mentioned by Beauchamp 
and Childress are supplemented by other principles, such as explainability (cf. Ursin et al. 2022), 
which raises questions about how these additional principles relate to the established ones.
If no single theory can adequately address the ethical concerns surrounding AI, and there 
is no guarantee that a combination of approaches will succeed, why should we continue to 
rely on these theories? Ethical debates, especially regarding the practical effectiveness of 

--- Page 155 ---

Martin Hähnel and Regina Müller
146
ethical theories, have persisted since the beginning of ethics. First, we must consider whether 
ethics needs to be effective. Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that ethics, as elaborate theories, 
cannot be effective because he believed no ethical theory could be universally applied to any 
worldly object (Wittgenstein 2014). Bernard Williams echoed this sentiment, stating that 
morality is inherently antitheoretical (Williams 1985). Contrary to Wittgenstein, some do 
not dispute the importance of ethical theories but question their specific applicability and the 
overall effectiveness of ethical inquiry. This issue becomes particularly critical with new 
technologies like AI, where the proper application or enactment of ethical principles is crucial. 
Given the nature of disruptive technologies (Perleth et al. 2022; Sounderajah et al. 2021), 
ethical analyses are indispensable. However, for ethical theories for AI to be justifiable, they 
must be effective or robust enough to promote good and prevent harm; otherwise, we might 
have to accept Wittgenstein’s sobering perspective.

abstractness of a theory in favor of some of the concreteness of an approach. Second-­order ethical

controlling technological innovation and predicting its consequences (Collingridge 1980). In the 
early stages of technology development, it is easy to make changes to the technology because it is 
not yet widely used. However, the impacts and risks of the technology are often unclear and difficult 
to predict at this stage. At a later stage, when the technology is established and widespread, its 
impact is clearer but then it is very difficult (and costly) to make changes or limit its spread because 
society has already come to depend on it. The dilemma is that ethical design becomes more difficult 
the more entrenched the technology becomes.

8	 In the history of philosophy and ethics, several points of reference for design thinking can be

morality, reminiscent of Descartes’ sixteenth-­century discussions, which assumes a state of 
uncertainty regarding absolute ethical norms (Marshall 1998). Concurrently, they challenge 
the Aristotelian distinction between poiesis and praxis (EN VI 4, 1140a 1–­6), igniting a debate 
over whether ethics that is designed can still be considered an end in itself, thereby conflicting 
with the traditional concept of praxis (a modern defence of this distinction can be found in 
Charles  1986). This change has to do with the idea of conceptual design or conceptual 
engineering, which follows an ontology of relations rather than an ontology of substance and 
thus no longer understands concepts essentially, but always uses them in relation to a purpose 
that is set.
9	 Frankfurt assumes that there are second-­order volitions (e.g., “I wish that I no longer wanted to

the determining power in relation to its practical application. The two often diverge from each 
other. MacIntyre (1984) holds that it cannot be the case that we first and independently 
comprehend the rules of morality and then secondly enquire as to their application under 
particular circumstances. The aim is therefore to ensure that a sound hybrid theory is enforced in 
a way that best corresponds to its characteristics.

appear to be flexible enough in their use of terms (Müller and Hähnel  2024). The 
“nonderivatists,” who often see themselves as conceptual engineers, assume that, for instance, 
the concept of virtue can be applied to machines in a nonmetaphorical sense. The 
“foundationalists” see this use as a violation of the classical rules of conceptual analysis and 
the softening of their basic moral theory assumptions.

11.1  Introduction
Deontology, in its most general conception, is an ethics of duty. Those duties –­ to act in certain 
ways and to refrain from certain actions –­ can be expressed by rules and principles and may 
also take the form of positive laws, e.g., against force, fraud, and theft. In the mid-­twentieth 
century, questions about the suitability of deontology for AI arose even before AI itself, in the 
form of Asimov’s fictional intelligent robots that must follow his Three Laws of Robotics: not 
to injure or disobey human beings, and to protect their own existence under defeasible condi-
tions (Asimov 1950). Decades have passed since Asimov’s fictional deontology, and while 
much progress has been made in AI, it remains to be seen how a deontological approach to AI 
ethics can contribute to the proper behavior and control of intelligent machines of the pre-
sent and near future.
This chapter will provide a survey of forms of deontology in AI, with a focus on some 
philosophical influences and also on future applications in fields such as robotics. Two main 
distinctions will play a large role in the structure of our survey. One distinction concerns the 
history of AI, the other a difference in how ethicists employ the concepts of deontology. 
Historically, AI can be thought of as an “ecumenical” research program to simulate or repro-
duce human intelligence by employing either logical formalisms, or (more recently) 
mathematical and statistical techniques, to converge on intelligent computer outputs. The 
first approach, symbolic AI, has sometimes been considered as “classical AI” –­ work in this 
vein dates to the 1950s  –­ and its main feature is its reliance on symbolic logics 
(Thomason 2024). Contemporary mathematical and statistical approaches operate differ-
ently; they learn from data (often training on “Big Data” such as the entirety of the internet) 
to classify, recommend, predict, and even intelligently answer human questions or “prompts.” 
This is subsymbolic AI (Norvig and Russell 2021). In thinking about how deontological ethics 
could be applied to either of these forms of AI, we will look at intrinsic approaches –­ prospects 
for programming ethical rules into an AI system –­ as well as extrinsic approaches which could 
supply a post hoc ethical evaluation of AI system performance based on how it fares against 
duties, rules, and principles. We will look in greater detail at these two distinctions below.
Deontology in AI
THOMAS M. POWERS
11

--- Page 161 ---

Thomas M. Powers
152
Another feature of the survey to follow is that it will cast a broad net, to consider forms of 
deontology in AI from various philosophical, scientific, and engineering perspectives, and will 
include many different activities that enter into the creation of AI: model building, selection 
of data, training, fine-­tuning, and testing. In principle, all activities that go into the creation 
of an AI should be considered as AI proper, and thus subject to ethical evaluation. For our 
present purposes, we will not investigate related philosophical issues that are often connected 
to AI ethics. To do them justice would take us beyond our scope, and in any event these issues 
are treated in other chapters in this volume. We will adopt common practice in computer sci-
ence by referring to computational agents, without questioning the exact nature of that 
agency, whether it is genuine, how it differs from human moral agency, and similar issues. 
Further interesting and related philosophical questions must also be left to the side, including 
whether ethical AIs could be considered morally or legally responsible for their actions; the 
extent to which AIs are autonomous in a sense that goes beyond their automation of tasks; and 
whether the realization of ethical deliberation in a machine would support computational 
functionalism in the philosophy of mind. These are fascinating questions, and while there are 
many enticing comparisons between humans and these artificial beings that could be capable, 
someday, of ethical intelligence, we must first understand the sense in which applying ethics 
to them is even plausible.
In the following account we will refer to logical and computational formalisms that can be 
used in deontological AI ethics, but we will exclude technical details of the formalisms. For the 
reader with interests in logics and programming, references are supplied for further reading.
11.2  Loci of AI Ethics: Two Distinctions
In this chapter we will look at the history, challenges, and future prospects for deontology as 
found in both symbolic and subsymbolic approaches to AI. The first approach to AI encom-
passes a variety of logic-­based and symbolic methods, developed over decades, to represent 
reasoning and intelligence in several domains. While these methods were developed to better 
understand the foundations of mathematics and logic, and to formally represent natural lan-
guages, by the latter part of the twentieth century they were being used in research on formal 
semantics, knowledge representation, theorem proving, expert systems, planning, and other 
domains.
One obvious pathway for deontological ethics is to align itself with the symbolic approach 
in order to introduce ethical rules to AI, and in this way to treat ethical reasoning as just 
another form of logic-­based intelligence. This alignment strategy owes its inspiration to sev-
eral formalistic conceptions of ethics, a leading example of which can be found in the universal 
law formulation of Kant’s Categorical Imperative. Under one interpretation of the Categorical 
Imperative, ethical judgment is a consistency check on our moral “maxims” or plans of action 
and on their logical consequents –­ suggesting a procedure which, according to Kant, should 
be almost automatic, requiring no worldly knowledge or acuity to determine how to act.1 
Indeed, checking for consistency and determining whether a theorem follows from a set of 
axioms is the main function of a theorem prover, a form of symbolic AI. It is not a stretch to 
think that Kant was the first machine ethicist, since as early as 1785 he had introduced the 
idea of such a formalism for ethics, and with it gave us a hint that duty could be computable 
from an effective logical procedure.
Other rule-­, duty-­, or principle-­based normative systems may suggest somewhat different 
strictures for an AI –­ think of Rawls’ Principles of Justice as Fairness or Hobbes’ Laws of 

--- Page 162 ---

Deontology in AI
153
Nature –­ but deontology need not come exclusively from grand philosophical treatises. For 
example, the Laws of War that emerge from Just War theory impose duties of just-­cause, 
­proportionality, and noncombatant immunity on those engaged in armed conflicts. Doctrines 
of research misconduct forbid plagiarism and fabrication and falsification of data. The duty to 
“do no harm” of the Hippocratic Oath is clearly deontological, as are the ethical principles of 
Respect for Persons, Beneficence, and Justice in the Belmont Report (National Commission for 
the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research 1979). If we look 
closely at all of our ethical guidance, we will find a healthy dose of deontology in it. The basic 
intuition behind deontology, which clearly separates it from utilitarian and other consequen-
tialist views, is that there are some right ways to act, and these ways can be known independent 
of evaluating consequences and thus prior to acting.
While rule-­based approaches to AI ethics may seem particularly apt for symbolic AI, in 
the last decade significant progress has been made in AI through subsymbolic approaches, 
via techniques based in statistical machine learning, artificial neural networks, and other 
mathematical systems which derive results from massive amounts of data. Prime examples 
of subsymbolic AI are the generative pretrained foundation models in the OpenAI GPT 
family, which were trained on data from the internet as a whole. Chat applications such as 
large language models in general have created much excitement and hype, and indeed one 
can even prompt ChatGPT with questions about ethics and get quite impressive answers.2 
Are these answers indications of ethical intelligence or are they mere reports from 
­“stochastic parrots” (Bender et al. 2021), mimicking results through statistical inferences 
from the internet?
So far, there is little reason to see results from language models as anything but highly 
accurate predictions of strings of terms that would satisfy a user’s prompt. And the problem 
of grievous errors or obviously wrong answers  –­ what have been euphemistically called 
­“hallucinations” (Thaler 1995) in some AI systems –­ still hangs over the technology. But as 
we shall see, model builders in subsymbolic AI have responded to perceived shortcomings of 
their models by employing techniques of training, reinforcement learning, and fine-­tuning. 
The same corrective techniques that produce better answers to prompts may one day address 
ethical concerns about offensive or dangerous AI responses. On this view, improving subsym-
bolic models in general could also improve the ethics of these models that classify, recommend, 
inform, etc. These techniques may signal the beginnings of a genuine mathematical/statistical 
model for ethics. It is also important to bear in mind that, while the subsymbolic approaches 
are no doubt ascendant in the last several decades, a combination of symbolic and subsym-
bolic approaches to AI ethics may yet prove to be the best recipe.
As mentioned in the introduction, we can also classify approaches to ethics as another way 
to “locate” deontology in AI, whether the ethical work is being done “inside” or “outside” the 
technology proper. First, we will look at deontology that is intrinsic to the AI itself –­ where one 
or several deontological rules or principles are implemented in the functioning or direct out-
come of the AI (i.e., as a constraint on a recommendation, classification, chatbot response, 
robotic movement, etc.) (Tolmeijer et al. 2021; Gerdes and Thornton 2015). In this first sense, 
a deontological ethics in AI would be considered, most literally, to be in or part of the AI system. 
In a Kantian version, an intrinsic AI ethics might be a formal representation of the Categorial 
Imperative that is computable. Intrinsic AI ethics is also what has come to be known as 
machine ethics, and is mostly of interest to philosophers and AI experts who research how a 
machine could implement an ethics in addition to, or as one component of, it exhibiting 
intelligence in a broader sense. Intrinsic AI ethics would be products of what Moor called 
explicit ethical agents (Moor 2006).

--- Page 163 ---

Thomas M. Powers
154
Second, we will consider cases in which we locate AI ethics external to the AI itself, and 
thus give an extrinsic analysis of the ethics of the AI. This refers to deontological ethics that 
are held up as requirements for the output of an AI, or a post hoc critique of an AI in its 
current implementation. Extrinsic ethics might be thought of as deontology about or for AI 
implementations. It can serve to improve but in some cases also to “cancel” an AI, to block its 
implementation as too dangerous, biased, or otherwise morally inappropriate, as in the offen-
sive chats produced by Tay, the Microsoft chatbot (Wolf et al. 2017). Considered as campaigns 
to improve technology, extrinsic approaches can set expectations or high-­level aspirations for 
AI in society by proposing values that can be given a deontological gloss; fairness, privacy, 
beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, and justice are some of the ethical value-­expectations 
that have been offered so far (Floridi et al. 2018).
Given the general inertia of AI in business, entertainment, national defense, policing, 
transport, and social media, and the risks that come with this large-­scale, global trend, it is 
important to consider whether intrinsic or extrinsic approaches are likely to be more effective 
in practice. Both have drawbacks. The hope of intrinsic AI ethics relies on considerable 
progress in AI ethics research, and there is no guarantee that pursuing such progress will be 
compatible with other goals for AI like consumer uptake, efficiency, scalability, cost, and accu-
racy. By the same token, extrinsic AI ethics may simply be underpowered as a social force in a 
world without effective global institutions to insist on these norms (Hagendorff 2020); this 
kind of ethics may be “too little, too late.”
11.3  The Ethical Moment for Rule-­based AI Ethics
Two convergent trends in computer science and in philosophy hold the key to AI ethics’ 
saliency in current thinking about technology. First, in computer science –­ especially since 
the onset of the era of Big Data –­ it has been acknowledged that impressive and powerful 
forms of AI have brought with them an urgent need for a better understanding of ethical con-
straints or “guardrails.” What began as a call for computer scientists to adopt ethical stan-
dards as specialized professionals (McFarland 1990) has evolved into a realization that AI and 
robotics products ought themselves to be subject to ethical evaluation –­ that “robots and AIs 
should do no harm, while being free of bias and deception; respect human rights and free-
doms, including dignity and privacy, while promoting well-­being; and be transparent and 
dependable while ensuring that the locus of responsibility and accountability remains with 
their human designers or operators” (Winfield 2019). All these goals can be stated as rules for 
AI. The daunting task at hand is how to apply ethical rules to professions and their products. 
If this is to happen, computer scientists would have to accept limitations, and give up on the 
dictum that everything that can be discovered scientifically must lead inevitably to an engi-
neering application for that new knowledge. Indeed, many of them have become self-­critical, 
due to outcomes of AI that are ethically dubious.
Second, in philosophy there is a growing acceptance of the view that technologies can 
“embed” or functionally manifest values and operate according to them. Thus, while there 
are many technologies “for good,” there are also technologies that are ethically problematic. 
While many examples from the past are “dumb” technologies such as landmines, there are 
now “smart” technologies such as driverless cars and facial recognition systems, and philos-
ophers are (perhaps belatedly) coming to contribute to the hard work that needs to be done to 
engineer a technological world that is less indiscriminately violent and, in general, better 
aligned with human values. In AI this is now called the “alignment problem.”

--- Page 164 ---

Deontology in AI
155
These two trends –­ critique and alignment –­ combine to make AI ethics both intellectually 
interesting and of great social concern. Fortunately, the deontological approach to ethics 
is often more straightforward than other ethical approaches. Many rules can be stated 
briefly and without much controversy; “Do not kill the innocent” and “Do not violate the 
privacy of individuals” are two such examples. By contrast, virtue ethics approaches often 
take entire books to articulate, and rely on experience, habit, and “practical wisdom” 
which are difficult to imagine machines ever acquiring. Similarly, consequentialist 
approaches to ethics require extensive information about costs, benefits, and probabilities 
of future outcomes. They require determining the spatial and temporal frames for counting 
“interested parties” –­ similar to the frame problem which has bedeviled AI for decades. A 
consequentialist prescription is typically nothing but a prognostication over expected util-
ities, and when the “best guess” turns out to be wrong, the next prescription may be the 
opposite of the one that preceded it.
But even though it seems that AI ethics is having its “moment,” one might still question 
when and how we intervene, ethically, in AI. The difficulty of these questions can be seen in 
the emergence of intelligence in automobiles since the early 1900s. Long before automo-
biles gained computer control, some had automatic transmissions that relieved the driver 
of the burden of selecting a proper drive gear over varying speed and acceleration condi-
tions. Initially this automation was a matter of mechanical engineering alone, though the 
control soon became electronic. Then very simple analogue computers, operating on 
impedance signals from sensors, were added to regulate fuel delivery across elevation and 
temperature changes. A further innovation was computer control of anti-­lock braking sys-
tems which made automobiles safer by automating the “pumping” of the brakes when 
driving on slippery surfaces. Again, more computation was added, and more control was 
taken from drivers. Now, twenty-­first-­century drivers are offered features that are basically 
AI for automobiles: lane control, automatic braking, speed modulation, and other crash 
avoidance technologies. Massive amounts of code and multiple computers are needed in 
automobiles. Presently, drivers find themselves subject to AI control of almost all functions 
in an automobile involving speed, braking, maneuvering, and route selection. The latest 
automobiles are intelligent robots.
When considering the increasing automation in machines, one might wonder whether the 
declaration of “intelligence” in the last stage also announces that ethical considerations are 
finally appropriate. This seems dubious and far too late. Over decades, many human actions 
which once fell under “driving” had been given over (almost) entirely by the time we reached 
the last stage. But it seems mistaken to conclude that only at this stage has the agency of the 
technology (the automobile) become “decisional.” Indeed, at every stage in this evolution, the 
automobile made decisions, and the detail of how automobiles would behave was a complex 
of design decisions, actions undertaken by the automobile, and those reserved to the human 
driver (Johnson and Powers 2008). Ethical issues decided by automobiles are primarily about 
safety, but extend to occupant comfort, automobile performance, fuel economy, and the like.
The lesson here is that, for almost any technology that has “become intelligent,” there will 
be some degree of arbitrariness as to when ethical scrutiny is applied, and what control and 
mitigation measures can improve the technology in the face of manufacturer intransigence 
and embeddedness in society. The phenomenon of path dependence, which comes from the 
social sciences, applies equally well to the ethics of intervening in AI technologies 
(Behnke 2007). Not all ethical options are still available to us, given how AI technologies have 
developed and are proliferating. No matter which ethics approach one adopts, the road ahead 
seems uncertain.
