11.4  Ethics for Symbolic AI
Let us return to a more optimistic outlook. It would be helpful to constrain all actions of AI 
systems in the design stage –­ effectively constraining AI systems a priori, by building into 
them the ability to make ethical decisions about their own possible behaviors. This would be 
the equivalent of ethical forethought in a machine. For many this will seem like a topic better 
suited to science fiction, but there are now several decades of research into such intrinsic 
machine ethics approaches.
We could start with the best-­known deontological theory, Kantian ethics, and the 
Categorical Imperative in its several versions that were claimed by Kant to be equivalent (“im 
Grunde einerlei”) (Kant  1785). In Kant’s rendering, the formulations of the Categorical 
Imperative represent one unified ethical system. Kant identified the first formulation of the 
Categorical Imperative as a formal requirement for ethical judgments; it obliges agents to act 
only on maxims that are universalizable.3 For our purposes, one can consider a maxim to be 
an intentional action plan (for humans) or an executable operation (for machines) in a 
particular state. What would the first formulation of the Categorical Imperative require?
Following O’Neill (1989), we can derive three requirements on maxims from this formula-
tion of the Categorical Imperative.
(1)	 Each maxim must be logically consistent with itself.
(2)	 Each maxim must be logically consistent with every ancillary maxim (those required to 
enact the maxim in question).
(3)	 Each maxim must be logically consistent with all other maxims that other agents hold.
Adapting these requirements to an AI would be tricky, to say the least. The last requirement, 
in particular, invokes multiagent systems and may lead to a “least common denominator” 
restriction on permissible maxims.
Subsequent formulations of the Categorical Imperative go beyond universalization, and for 
our purposes the most important one is the “formula of humanity” which forbids actions that 
treat people merely as means and not at the same time as ends in themselves. Here Kant’s 
theory may be most useful in substantiating our extrinsic judgments about AI –­ that their 
results not violate privacy or endanger lives, help to fulfill expectations of justice, and the like. 
The section below on extrinsic AI will explore these ethical ideas further.
We can represent (informally) the Kantian ethical rules in the following manner. Assuming 
a domain containing actions (A), circumstances (C), and purposes (P), we could say that 
obligatory actions are defined by rules of the form “If C and P, then A”; forbidden actions are 
of the form “If C and P, then not-­A”; and actions that are neither forbidden nor obligatory are 
permissible (Powers 2006). Thus we arrive at the basic structure of the deontic categories.
In the twentieth century logicians improved upon this account by replacing deontic cate-
gories with deontic operators in a symbolic system that worked much like the operators of 
necessity and possibility in modal logic (McNamara and Van De Putte 2022). Advantages 
with this approach, which became known as standard deontic logic, include the integration 
of deontic with propositional logic and an extension of the original deontic operators to 
include concepts such as permission, supererogation, omission, and responsibility. Deontic 
logic shares the possible-­world semantics of modal logic. Just as “necessarily X” is taken to 
mean that X is true in all possible worlds, “obligatory A” means that any agent must A when 
the circumstances proper to A-­ing arise. But there is an obvious problem with this scheme: 
many obligations that might normally hold no longer do so when the assumptions of 

--- Page 166 ---

Deontology in AI
157
circumstantial context change. A soldier may be obligated to tell the truth, but not when 
being interrogated by the enemy. We need to account for defeasible obligations to handle these 
kinds of cases.
11.5  Defeasible Duties
In a well-­known example from Kant (1777), we are asked to reconsider a duty to always tell 
the truth. Imagine that a murderous individual asks about the location of an innocent fleeing 
friend, and truthful communication of his whereabouts could get that friend killed. We might 
be tempted in such cases to think that the undesirable consequences of truth telling defeat duty. 
But the duty to tell the truth could be blocked by another, stronger or higher-­priority duty –­ 
such as preventing murders. Further, the duty of truth telling in this case could yield to a 
higher value than truth, e.g., the life of an innocent person. There is some evidence that Kant 
was open to the idea of defeasible duties, but the case is not decisive.4
One aspect of deontological ethical reasoning is the defeasible nature of obligations or 
duties, similar to the defeasibility of beliefs of fact. For instance, an agent may be obligated to 
help a stranger in need, but not when it is discovered that the stranger needs help in commit-
ting a crime. Deontic obligation should thus be defeasible; inferences from duty to a particular 
action are nonmonotonic in the sense that new information can block or defeat the inference. 
The key difference with monotonic rules is that any contrary information can defeat the 
rule –­ it can serve as a counterexample to the rule. If obligations are nonmonotonic, though 
defeated they can “live to fight another day.” As AI research advanced in the latter part of the 
twentieth century, it was seen that the defeasibility of ethical reasoning could not be handled 
straightforwardly through standard deontic logic alone. Aspects of more sophisticated ethical 
reasoning were subsumed under AI research programs in commonsense reasoning. Through 
these insights, defeasible deontic logic was soon developed and it has had some success in 
applications of AI and law (van der Torre and Tan 1997).
Another logic-­based approach in AI to handle defeasibility, answer set programming, pres-
ents a contemporary AI paradigm for representing knowledge, search, and nonmonotonic 
inference and has also been used for deontological ethics. Answer set programming is a form 
of declarative logic programming that differs from standard algorithmic conceptions of 
­computation in that its program consists of rules and facts for a specified domain, while the 
“solution” to the program is the set of atoms that satisfy the rules. Informally, answer set 
programming allows the program to query whether there are one or more “worlds” (or stable 
models) that satisfy its declared facts and rules (Gelfond 2008). The search for these worlds is 
performed by an inference engine or “answer set solver.” Importantly, the rules can include 
defeasible ethical rules and conditions in the facts and rules. Applications in ethics include 
duties that can withstand defeating conditions, as in the Kantian lying example discussed 
above (Ganascia 2007).
The tall order of AI ethics would suggest that nonmonotonic reasoning and the ability to 
adjust to new information will be critical. There is a strong presumption that ethical AIs will 
need to reason in dynamic situations in which much new information is on offer. So, for 
instance, an AI unmanned aerial vehicle might typically have the clearance to fire a missile 
toward any group of “high-­value targets” (Cummings 2021) but in a particular circumstance, 
new information might indicate the presence of noncombatants or even allies in the group, 
so the directive to send the missile would be blocked. In this vein, the roboticist Ronald Arkin 
has developed a framework of context-­sensitive rules for AI lethal autonomous weapons 

--- Page 167 ---

Thomas M. Powers
158
systems (LAWS), and in particular has developed a control architecture designed to have 
such systems obey military ethical obligations under the Geneva Convention rules and Just 
War theory.
11.6  Lessons from Robotics
What do we learn when other (seemingly stronger) ethical commitments defeat duties? 
Are duties so easily defeated, or might we be working with the wrong theory? This puzzle 
can be illuminated by revisiting the trolley problem introduced by Philippa Foot (1967) 
which as modified has become a central hypothetical case study in the ethics of intelligent 
autonomous vehicles (Lin 2015). By considering embodied AI, the limits of what an AI 
agent ought to do can come into clearer focus. We shall refer to the “new” dilemma as the 
AI trolley problem.
Imagine a contemporary version of Foot’s example: a driverless car with n passengers is 
proceeding down a road when an obstacle is introduced into its path. If the car hits the 
obstacle, it will kill all the passengers. It can swerve left or right (take evasive maneuvers), 
which will kill other (m : m > n) bystanders. Since one design goal of any car is to protect its 
inhabitants, it seems that the driverless car should follow its duty and swerve, thus killing the 
innocent bystanders. But more people will be killed by the autonomous vehicle, in following 
its duty, than if it does not take evasive maneuvers. Should duty be abandoned in favor of 
saving lives?
The problems generated by the AI trolley problem are not limited to this initial case, which 
closely resembles Foot’s original dilemma. Other plausible scenarios for an autonomous 
vehicle may include ones where passengers outnumber bystanders. If we give up so easily on 
duty in the first case, is the vehicle here obligated (by consequentialist considerations) to “stay 
the course” and kill the passengers? A third scenario might allow the vehicle to do additional 
computations before selecting an action. If it estimates that n passengers will die with proba-
bility p1 without “evasion” whereas m bystanders will die with probability p2 with evasion, 
must it alter course to obey the math? Further cases could be generated using calculations of 
property damage, pain and injury to passengers and bystanders, loss of income, distress over 
the incident, etc., assuming that damages could be quantified.
The proliferation of possible cases leads us to take stock of what kinds of variables are 
under consideration when we take the AI trolley problem seriously as a paradigm case for 
doing AI ethics. As in Foot’s original example, consequentialism directs the agent to consider 
direct, ethically relevant considerations such as the number of deaths, and similar measur-
able factors (money, pain, quality-­adjusted life-­years, etc.) that impinge on what the agent 
ought to do. A consequentialist agent must also take into account nonethical factors that 
come into play; the autonomous vehicle would have to compute highway speeds, number and 
mass of colliding objects, braking coefficients of friction, road surface moisture, and materials 
properties such as tensile strength. What started out here as an ethical thought experiment is 
now a science and engineering problem. Under consequentialist approaches, crashing will 
become an optimization problem –­ just like automated driving itself –­ and ethical values could 
become fungible.
Does this fungibility cross ethical lines that the deontologist will insist on upholding? There 
is a sense in which some solutions to the AI trolley problem would appear to settle ethical 
questions about autonomous vehicles in ways that are descriptive rather than prescriptive. 
What we mean by this is that, for any given crash, there is no “right” thing to do, prior to the 

--- Page 168 ---

Deontology in AI
159
calculations. If so, the deontological position on autonomous vehicles is in trouble as no rules 
about crashing actions could be programmed in advance. Instead, a descriptive ethics of 
autonomous vehicles might follow what “conventional wisdom” or sociological evidence tells 
us about human opinions on the ethics of crashing, as in the well-­known “moral machine 
experiment” (Awad et al. 2018). A prescriptive, deontological framework, on the other hand, 
involves the analysis of what machines ought to do and refrain from doing in varying con-
texts, based on ethical commitments that humans already have. Prescriptive frameworks are 
also tied to the ethics that humans have developed, over millennia, since what we now believe 
we ought to do is shaped by what other humans have believed about ethics over generations. 
True, deontologists still reject some past ethical positions that our ancestors held, but we do 
so after having considered the reasons (hopefully) on all sides of an issue.
The trolley problem seems to reveal a basic weakness in consequentialist approaches to AI 
ethics, and thus to strengthen the case for deontology. Crash and its complicated variations 
show that consequentialism (and description-­based ethics more generally) will not provide 
predictable ethical rules for AI. The consequentialist-­programmed AI suffers from a problem 
that is at the core of Mill’s rule utilitarianism. Because the basis of each of Mill’s rules is its 
usefulness in maximizing total social utility, the status of any rule is always up for reconsider-
ation in each of its applications. This is the lesson of the observation that rule utilitarianism 
collapses into act utilitarianism (Smart 1956).
Fortunately, there is evidence that autonomous vehicles and other AI robots can operate 
on a stable ethics. A promising line of research in ethical robotics has been demonstrated by 
the Human Robotic Interaction (HRI) Lab at Tufts. Researchers have developed several 
approaches to normative human–­robotic interaction using deontic logic, natural language 
modeling, speech act theory, and an interaction testbed called DIARC (Distributed Integrated 
Affect Reflection and Cognition) architecture (Kasenberg et al. 2019). They have programmed 
robots that interact with humans and provide normative explanations for their own actions 
by citing deontological rules regarding safety, legality, and the like. The robot has a represen-
tation of its own capabilities, information about the humans interacting with it, common-
sense knowledge about the implications of actions it can undertake, and the ability to interpret 
ethical principles to determine whether a human request is obeyed. When the robot refuses a 
request, it can respond with explanations of authorization, obligation and permission, and 
conformity with norms. For example, the robot can reject an action of leaving a store with 
property not purchased, giving the response “I do not leave the store while holding anything 
which I have not bought” (Scheutz et al. 2022). With these and similar examples, researchers 
have demonstrated that, in a controlled domain, robots can perform as though they under-
stand deontological rules.
11.7  Ethics for Subsymbolic AI
Now we turn to deontological approaches that can be applied to contemporary, mathematical/
statistical AIs such as large language models. Though these approaches are quite new and 
somewhat speculative, they had been anticipated by researchers in machine ethics prior to 
the advent of such models. In their groundbreaking book Moral Machines, Wallach and Allen 
(2008) introduced a triad of top-­down, bottom-­up, and hybrid approaches to machine ethics, 
and located deontological approaches in the top-­down category. Bottom-­up approaches to 
ethics are in their view data driven, but how exactly data can be used in ethics was only hinted 
at –­ and importantly, they did not consider ways in which data-­driven ethics could be combined 

--- Page 169 ---

Thomas M. Powers
160
with deontology. At the same time, Wallach and Allen seemed skeptical of the viability of 
deontological approaches –­ assuming that they must all hail from some grand theory which 
will be too abstract and probably difficult to apply to computing machines. As they were 
writing prior to the boom in Big Data models, Wallach and Allen may not have foreseen the 
possibility that deontological ethics could arise from statistical methods and from specific use 
cases of AI.
One example that combines data and ethical rules is a healthcare ethics “advisor” built 
from machine learning techniques and data from practitioners by Susan Leigh Anderson and 
Michael Anderson. They developed MedEthEx (Anderson et al. 2006) to adapt the deontolog-
ical theory of prima facie duties of W.D. Ross (1930) to analyze dilemmas that arise in health-
care settings. The dilemmas arise when a healthcare provider must deal with difficult decisions 
about patient care, which are often created by the tension between what a patient wants 
(autonomy), what is best for them (beneficence), and what will avoid harming them (nonma-
leficence), from a medical point of view. A situation such as a patient steadfastly refusing a 
medication that has been prescribed is a prime example of this kind of dilemma. The data here 
come from patients, the drug indications, and also medical diagnoses, and the duties approach 
used by MedEthEx supports the healthcare provider in making a decision that will be optimal 
for the patient, all things considered. While this tool is quite specific to its clinical context, 
MedEthEx has been used in an online version for medical students, with some success 
(Fleetwood et al. 2000).
Other examples recently have focused on large language models which are generically use-
ful but can give unsafe results when adapted for medical use, e.g., in clinical decision support, 
or issue inappropriate/offensive responses when giving patient feedback. How can we improve 
models to reduce and (perhaps someday) prevent such bad outcomes? Consider a medical AI 
that works much like ChatGPT, except on a restricted (medical) domain of possible responses. 
After a human prompt, the model gives a response –­ some action or advice that the clinician 
might undertake to improve the condition of a patient. A group at Harvard (Han et al. 2024) 
measured the degree of unsafe responses from several medical AIs and then fine-­tuned their 
models by developing a set of safety demonstrations –­ pairs of requests and responses that 
yield safe(r) responses to harmful requests. The fine-­tuning process involved human scoring 
of all results on the basis of implicit rules for safety, which gave improved query response pairs 
over the pretuned responses. In this way they created a benchmark for improving the model, 
which was post-­trained through reinforcement learning on the benchmark results. There 
was marked improvement on safety. Such research suggests that fine-­tuning of language 
models can make AI safer in at least some domains.
While training with human feedback has been shown to be effective, it is also costly and 
time-­consuming because large groups of human trainers must score the results. An 
automated version of safety tuning as reinforcement learning is explored in recent work by 
the AI company Anthropic. Reinforcement Learning from Constitutional AI Feedback 
(RLCAIF) is a “method for aligning general purpose language models to abide by high-­level 
normative principles written into a constitution.”5 The “constitution” in question could be 
one selected by the Anthropic scientists –­ such as the UN Declaration of Human Rights –­ or it 
could be “crowdsourced” by asking the public to contribute a set of rules for their language 
model. What is interesting is that explicitly ethical rules and principles are used; the interpre-
tation of the rules is likewise automated through natural language processing techniques. So 
far, there has only been proof-­of-­concept work in “constitutional” AI, but applications might 
follow simply because it is a cheaper way for companies to improve the acceptability of their 
models.

--- Page 170 ---

Deontology in AI

11.8  Extrinsic AI Ethics
For human reasoners, ethical deliberation sometimes comes antecedent to our choices or actions, 
but in addition may be used to analyze a past choice or action in order to avoid repeated mistakes. 
With the intrinsic approach to AI ethics we considered above, we hope to endow AI with the ability 
to deliberate antecedent to its acting (answering, classifying, recommending, and the like). If this 
approach works flawlessly, we would not have to worry about ethical “mistakes” by AIs. 
Realistically, however, we cannot expect to prevent all unwanted or even dangerous behavior by 
AIs through intrinsic ethics. So we should not neglect the importance of doing AI ethics “after the 
fact” –­ as an ethical analysis (by humans) of AI behavior through considering deontological rules.
As AI develops, we increasingly see the values behind deontological principles and rules 
employed as critiques of the technology, and this is a form of extrinsic AI ethics. A major 
thrust of ethical deliberation at the policy-­making level has been to create ethical guidelines 
and standards, and in some cases to introduce legislation, all of which involves ethical risk 
assessment (Winfield 2019). Indeed, the “Ethical Guidelines for Trustworthy AI” (European 
Commission 2019) produced by the EU High-­Level Group on AI is a prime example of values-­
based policy that is largely, though not exclusively, deontologically inspired. The following 
examples of extrinsic AI ethics can be seen as value-­oriented responses that focus on privacy 
and fairness, but other values may also be implicated as AI expands.
Since AI is an information technology, a consistent worry has been that it threatens to 
make public the private information about individuals that we guard most closely. While 
Personally Identifying Information (PII) and Personal Health Information (PHI) is protected 
by law in many jurisdictions, including through the Health Insurance Portability and 
Accountability Act (HIPAA) in the US and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in 
the EU, the privacy threat from AI goes beyond what information is already “out there” on the 
internet. The reason is that de-­identified data can become re-­identified data through merging 
of datasets. This requires vast comparisons of data, which most people would not take the 
time to do but can be accomplished in minutes or seconds by AI systems. To make matters 
worse, large social media platforms and streaming services operate with powerful AI systems 
that have access to much of the user data generated by using the platform or service. They 
store these data because they are valuable to them; they are a means of profiling us in order 
to recommend products and services, and to sell advertisements. In short, AI companies have 
unprecedented ability to assimilate data, access to huge amounts of data about individuals, 
and a profit incentive to continue to gather data about individuals. Deontologists are right to 
worry about these risks to privacy.
A second area where there has been much interest in AI ethics is around fairness or bias of AI 
models. For example, in supervised machine learning the available data for the model are divided 
into training and testing sets. When the data are about humans in some way –­ everything from 
medical or financial data to criminal records –­ the trained model should be based on data that are 
representative of the population in which the model will be deployed. When the data fail to be 
representative, the results of the model for the population that was mostly missing from the 
training data are said to be biased. When the bias works systematically against certain demo-
graphic groups, the model is thought to be unfair to those groups; they will be disproportionately 
misidentified, denied a mortgage, surveilled by police, and so on, because of defects in the model. 
Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru have shown that facial recognition AIs have significant gender 
and race biases in being unable to accurately classify faces of women and people with dark 
­complexion (Buolamwini 2018). Other research has shown remarkable examples of racial bias 
in AI systems to predict recidivism risk (Rudin et al. 2020).

--- Page 171 ---

Thomas M. Powers
162
These faults in AI systems, discovered by examining their outputs, are important contribu-
tions to extrinsic deontology in AI. They apply basic deontological rules against unfairness or 
bias to results that the AI is bound to reproduce unless it is retrained or corrected. In some 
cases, we may think that it would be better to discontinue use of the system altogether.
11.9  Conclusion
From our historical and conceptual survey, it would appear that deontological AI ethics has 
the intellectual resources to expand into AI in both its symbolic and subsymbolic forms. So 
far, deontological AI ethics has developed rather organically, by making incremental advances 
where the logic and science allowed, and by contributing to promising results in (mostly 
academic) robotics research. The ethics efforts of philosophers, computer scientists, and 
others can be understood as intrinsic ethics, working to infiltrate AI in effect, and by cri-
tiquing AI when deployed as extrinsic critique. Ethical improvements in AI need not explicitly 
rely on top-­down theories, as with the Kantian approach, but might align the performance of 
particular AIs with values expressed or inspired, albeit imperfectly, as a deontology.
At the same time, commercial AI is advancing at breakneck speed. Large corporate AI 
appears to be taking a very limited kind of consequentialist approach to AI ethics –­ sometimes 
touting safe and responsible AI, but quickly making choices in favor of profitable and unsafe 
AI. It should come as no surprise that the consequences that matter to these corporations 
most are profits. In the year since the public release of ChatGPT, the debates between advo-
cates of safe and beneficial AI and those focused on return-­on-­investment and market domi-
nation have made little headway toward consensus.
No matter which approach to the ethics of AI one favors, it is safe to say that time is of the 
essence.6

12.1  Introduction
Consequentialism, alongside deontology and virtue ethics, is one of the dominant ethical 
­theories in applied ethics. One reason for its prominence is the significant influence of Peter 
Singer, who, as the most renowned philosopher in applied ethics, has become the most famous 
living representative of consequentialism. At the same time, his application of consequentialism 
to various ethical issues has made him one of the most controversial and fiercely criticized 
philosophers. Singer’s case illustrates that no other ethical theory is as polarizing as conse-
quentialism. While deontology and virtue ethics are also contested ethical theories, neither 
provokes as intense opposition as consequentialism. For some critics, consequentialism is not 
just one of many ethical theories, each with its strengths and weaknesses, and each with a 
legitimate place in ethical thought. Rather, they see consequentialism as a dangerous theory 
that must be actively opposed.1
This hostility is directed primarily at Singer’s views on abortion, the treatment of severely 
disabled newborns, embryonic research, and euthanasia. In contrast, his equally influential 
views on animal ethics and global poverty, while still controversial, tend to be met with less 
hostility (with the possible exception of his advocacy of effective altruism).These differing 
reactions highlight two dimensions of consequentialism –­ a positive and a negative dimension 
(cf. Kahane et al. 2018) –­ that are crucial in assessing the suitability of consequentialism as 
an ethical framework for artificial intelligence. But before we can assess the role of conse-
quentialism in AI, it is essential to first develop an accurate understanding of the theory.
12.2  Consequentialism and Utilitarianism
The historically first, best known and still paradigmatic form of consequentialism is 
­utilitarianism. The term “consequentialism” was introduced by G. E. M. Anscombe (1958) to 
describe a central feature of utilitarianism (a feature she found appalling). Today, the term is 
used both to refer to this specific feature or component of utilitarianism, and as a general term 
Consequentialism and AI
JÖRG SCHROTH
12

--- Page 175 ---

Jörg Schroth
166
for ­ethical theories that share this feature. Over time, and in response to various objections, 
many ethical theories have been developed and labeled as consequentialist (e.g., rule-­
consequentialism, scalar consequentialism), which has led to a debate about whether there is 
a single defining feature that consequentialist theories share, or whether they merely bear a 
family resemblance to one another (cf. Horta et al. 2022). The feature that originally defined 
consequentialism is what might be called “consequence determinacy”:
Consequence determinacy: The moral rightness of an act depends solely on (the value of) its 
­consequences (compared to the consequences of the acts the agent could perform instead).
Given the uncontroversial assumption that ethics is not concerned with endorsing harmful out-
comes, and that it would be a perverse stance –­ utterly at odds with our moral intuitions and our 
conception of morality –­ to consistently prefer worse outcomes over better ones, consequence 
determinacy is equivalent to the maximization permission (see Schroth 2022, 39–­42):
Maximization permission: It is always morally permissible to perform the act with the best 
consequences.
These features are the defining features, if not of consequentialism in general, then at least of 
act-­consequentialism.
Maximization permission is a double-­edged sword. On the one hand, it is often referred 
to as the “compelling idea” of act-­consequentialism (Portmore 2001, 377), encapsulated 
in the seemingly rhetorical question: “How could it ever be morally wrong to perform the 
act with better consequences rather than an act with worse consequences?” On the other 
hand, it is precisely this feature of consequentialism that provokes the greatest hostility 
and the most vehement objections, which also explains the opposition to some of Singer’s 
views mentioned above. Conventional morality (along with all deontological theories) 
recognizes agent-­relative constraints (e.g., “Act in such a way that you do not yourself tor-
ture anyone”) that forbid an agent from performing certain terrible kinds of acts as a 
means of achieving better ­consequences. Such acts are forbidden even if they would lead 
to the best overall consequences, and even if they would minimize the total number of 
violations of the same constraint. Maximization permission rules out agent-­relative con-
straints and allows only agent-­neutral rules (e.g., “Act in such a way that as few acts of 
torture occur as possible”) which permit or rather require all kinds of instrumental harms 
(such as ­violations of dignity and individual rights, torture, lying, betrayal, etc.). Due to 
conventional morality’s strongly negative stance toward instrumental harms (and the 
associated principle that the end justifies the means), Kahane et al. (2018) refer to this 
aspect of consequentialism, which dominates the dispute over the theory, as the “nega-
tive dimension” of consequentialism.
Maximization permission does not entail, but strongly suggests, that we should always aim 
for the best possible consequences. The only objection to this maximization requirement is 
that it imposes an excessive burden on moral agents. Satisficing consequentialism, which holds 
that we are not required to produce the best consequences but only those that are “good 
enough” in some specified sense, attempts to address this objection. But since it faces its own 
difficulties, most consequentialists adhere to the maximization obligation:
Maximization obligation: It is always morally obligatory to perform the act with the best 
consequences.

--- Page 176 ---

Consequentialism and AI
167
Maximization obligation, maximization permission, and consequence determinacy are the 
defining features of maximizing act-­consequentialism and establish its criterion of rightness: 
An act is morally right if and only if no alternative act would have better consequences.
Maximizing act-­consequentialism is defined as a theory of the right only and does not yet 
specify the criteria by which consequences or states of affairs are evaluated as good or bad, 
better or worse. It does not specify which beings should be considered when calculating the 
best consequences or the best state of affairs and is thus compatible with ethical egoism, 
according to which each agent should act only to bring about the best consequences for them-
selves. However, egoistic consequentialism is incompatible with a fundamental idea of conse-
quentialism that historically precedes the other ideas discussed so far and served as the 
primary motivation and justification for the classical utilitarians. This is the idea of an all-­
encompassing, impartial, sympathetic, altruistic concern for the welfare of all people (and all 
sentient beings), which unites all individuals in the common goal of promoting the welfare of 
all sentient beings and making the world the best possible place: “The core precept of utilitar-
ianism is that we should make the world the best place we can. That means that, as far as it is 
within our power, we should bring about a world in which every individual has the highest 
possible level of well-­being” (de Lazari-­Radek and Singer 2017, 1).
According to Kahane et al. (2018, 133), this “all-­encompassing altruistic goal is at the 
very heart of a utilitarian approach.” It represents the positive dimension of consequentialism, 
and consequentialists regard this goal as the only meaningful purpose of morality: “The idea 
that the unifying –­ and justifying –­ function of all of our ethical categories is ultimately to 
make our lives go better, or to make the world a better place, is one that I find utterly compel-
ling. If that is not the point of the whole business of moral thinking, then I find it difficult to 
imagine what the point might be. What else could morality be for? And if it is not for anything –­ 
if it has no point –­ what claim can it have on our allegiance?” (Sumner 1992, 1).
Underlying this idea is the view, characteristic of utilitarianism, that the right consists in 
maximizing the nonmoral good. Utilitarians thus assume that the good to be maximized can 
be defined independently of the right, which means:
•	 the good consists only of the nonmoral good; it contains only nonmoral intrinsic goods
•	 the selection of nonmoral goods is independent of the right, and the theory of the right 
therefore does not render any goods morally impermissible: If pleasure is good, then any 
pleasure, including that of a sadist or rapist, is considered a good and must be included in 
the calculation of the best consequences.
To work out what the nonmoral good to be maximized is, we need a theory of the good that identifies 
what is intrinsically valuable and desirable for its own sake (rather than merely as a means to 
other ends). It is a theory of “what makes someone’s life go best” (Parfit 1984, 493). Utilitarians 
regard welfare as this intrinsic good and distinguish three theories of the nature of welfare.
•	
Hedonism, which holds that welfare consists of pleasure and the absence of pain or suffering.
•	 Desire-­fulfillment theory, according to which welfare consists in the satisfaction of our 
desires or preferences.
•	 Objective list theory, which suggests that welfare consists in realizing certain goods. 
According to Griffin’s list (Griffin 1996, 29 f.), these include enjoyment, achievement in 
life, deep personal relationships, understanding of ourselves and our place in the world, as 
well as elements of a distinctively human existence, such as autonomy, the capabilities 
necessary for action, and freedom.

--- Page 177 ---

Jörg Schroth
168
These theories of the good are not themselves utilitarian or consequentialist theories of the 
good. They are argued for independently of moral considerations and are not tied to any 
particular ethical theory. Thus, they are nonmoral theories of the nonmoral good. What dis-
tinguishes utilitarianism is its commitment to welfarism, the view that welfare is the only 
intrinsic good relevant to morality.
Utilitarians assume that, within certain limits, it is rational for a person to adopt the prin-
ciple “the more of a good, the better!” The more pleasure one experiences in life, the more 
preferences are satisfied, or the more goods on the objective list are realized –­ and the higher 
the degree of realization of each good –­ the better. This principle enables an agent to rank the 
potential consequences of acts from best to worst and to determine which act has the best 
consequences for the agent. However, consequentialists must determine which act produces 
the best overall consequences, taking into account all those affected. Yet, theories of the good 
do not address how to aggregate individual goods into a comprehensive evaluation. From an 
impartial, but nonmoral point of view –­ such as that of an impartial observer –­ it seems plau-
sible to extend the principle “the more of a good, the better” to multiple individuals as well. 
This leads to the idea of sum-­ranking, where the best outcome is the one that maximizes the 
total amount of good. Taken together, sum-­ranking, welfarism, and consequentialism consti-
tute maximizing act-­utilitarianism.
A distinctive feature of utilitarianism is that it is only the (total or average) amount of wel-
fare that matters, and not its distribution. In contrast, nonutilitarian consequentialist the-
ories are distribution sensitive and may hold that the best outcome is one in which the good is 
distributed equally or fairly. Moreover, nonutilitarian consequentialist theories are not bound 
to define the good independently of the right; they may also incorporate moral values and 
goods into their theory of the good, thereby rejecting the utilitarian premise that the right 
consists in maximizing the nonmoral good.
12.3  Direct and Indirect Act-­Consequentialism versus 
Rule-­Consequentialism
The positive dimension of consequentialism is associated with universal impartial benefi-
cence and the overarching goal of making the world the best place possible. Most consequen-
tialists interpret this as a maximization obligation and base act-­consequentialism on this idea 
(rather than on maximization permission). Arguably, making the world the best possible 
place is the strongest justification for the maximization obligation, and universal impartial 
beneficence and the goal of making the best possible world are undeniably attractive ideas. 
Who could object to that? But when interpreted as an unconstrained maximization obliga-
tion, these ideas entail the other features of act-­consequentialism, including the maximiza-
tion permission and its associated negative dimension. Moreover, the maximization obligation 
imposes enormous sacrifices on moral agents because, unlike in conventional morality, these 
sacrifices are not supererogatory acts –­ whose omission would not be blameworthy –­ but are 
instead morally required. Thus, when interpreted as the unconstrained maximization obliga-
tion, the seemingly positive dimension of utilitarianism, that makes it so appealing, cannot be 
separated from its negative dimension.
These are well-­known objections to consequentialism, which its opponents consider so 
serious that they reject consequentialism altogether. Consequentialists have long tried to 
counter these objections and convince their critics that the theory is not as counterintuitive 
as it is often made out to be. The main strategy for defending consequentialism is to ­distinguish 

--- Page 178 ---

Consequentialism and AI
169
between a criterion of rightness and a decision procedure, and hence between direct and 
indirect act-­consequentialism.
In direct act-­consequentialism the criterion of rightness formulated above also serves as the 
decision procedure, leading to the following imperative: “On every occasion, an agent should 
decide which act to do by ascertaining which act has the greatest expected value” (Hooker 2000, 
142). Thus, every moral agent would have to go through the following steps on every occasion.
(1)	 List your alternatives.
(2)	 List all the possible outcomes of the first alternative.
(3)	 For each outcome of the first alternative, write down its value.
(4)	 For each outcome of the first alternative, write down its probability given the alternative 
on your evidence.
(5)	 For each possible outcome of the first alternative, multiply the value of the outcome by 
its probability on the first alternative.
(6)	 Sum these products. This sum is the expected utility of the first alternative.
(7)	 Repeat steps 2–­6 for each of the other alternatives.
(8)	 Identify the acts that maximize expected utility.
(9)	 Perform one of those acts. (Quoted from Feldman 2006, 54.)
It is hard to imagine that we could go through this laborious process for every moral decision 
(and in direct act-­consequentialism this means every decision between different courses of 
action), because it would be cognitively and emotionally overwhelming. Trying to do this all 
the time would not make the world a better place for the following reasons.2
•	 Lack of knowledge
––
We are often not fully aware of the range of options available to us.
––
We often do not know what the consequences of each alternative might be.
––
We often do not know the probabilities of the consequences of different courses of 
action.
––
We often do not have a clear idea of the value of different outcomes.
––
We often lack the time to gather more detailed information about the possible alterna-
tives, their likely consequences, and their value.
•	 Bias and lack of impartiality
––
In many cases, we are biased and unable to judge the consequences of acts impartially. 
We tend to overestimate the good consequences of acts that will benefit us or those 
close to us, while underestimating the negative consequences (and their likelihood) for 
others.
•	 Incompatibility with friendships and other personal relationships
––
Personal relationships are an essential part of the good life. Without personal rela-
tionships, the world would not be the best place that consequentialism seeks to make 
it. However, personal relationships necessarily involve (i) moderate partiality, which 
allows us (within certain limits) to favor those close to us, and (ii) motives that relate 
directly to those close to us and not to maximizing the good. For example, someone 
who gives a gift should do so not because it offers an opportunity to maximize the 
good, but because he wants to bring joy to the recipient. The constant application of 
the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism and the impartiality it requires are 
incompatible with the motives and forms of partiality that are constitutive of personal 
relationships.

--- Page 179 ---

Jörg Schroth
170
•	 Lack of motivation
––
Compared to the moral rules of conventional morality, which refer to specific behaviors 
(do not lie, do not steal, etc.), the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism is 
too abstract to motivate us to act accordingly. The impartiality required would be emo-
tionally overwhelming and would not motivate us to act according to the decision 
procedure.
•	 High internalization costs
––
Because of the motivational difficulty of acting according to a very abstract decision 
procedure that requires complete impartiality, it is very difficult and costly to get people 
and educate children to internalize and consistently act according to this decision 
procedure.
•	 Lack of predictability, loss of trust, and barriers to cooperation
––
If everyone on every occasion considered which act would have the best consequences 
according to the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism, and then acted 
accordingly, we could not predict each other’s behavior, trust each other, or rely on 
others to keep their agreements and promises. This would make anticipatory action 
and cooperation almost impossible. This is true not only because of human failings but 
even if we were always fully rational and informed.3
These considerations show that the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism is 
counterproductive and does not make the world the best place it can be. It is therefore obvious 
that it is incompatible with the consequentialist idea of making the world the best it can be 
and cannot be accepted as a consequentialist decision procedure. Direct act-­consequentialism 
is therefore not a theory that is supported by consequentialists.4
The objections to the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism are empirical in 
nature, ultimately arguing that it is not an effective way to make the world the best it can be. 
Consequently, determining which decision procedure can be justified on consequentialist 
grounds is also an empirical matter. Consequentialists agree that it must be a rule-­based 
decision procedure that does not require finding and performing the act with the best conse-
quences on every occasion. Instead, in almost all situations, except for exceptional cases, one 
should simply apply the moral rule relevant to the situation. The question of whether the 
application of that rule in a particular case leads to the best consequences should generally 
not be asked. An act-­consequentialist theory with such a rule-­based decision procedure is 
called indirect act-­consequentialism.5 A plausible decision procedure of this kind might be: In all 
but exceptional situations, act in every situation according to the rules of the moral code 
whose general acceptance produces the best consequences. Since it is difficult, if not impos-
sible, to determine which rules meet this criterion, most act-­consequentialists settle on the 
following decision procedure: Apart from exceptional situations, act in every situation 
according to the time-­tested rules of our conventional morality.6
In practice, indirect act-­consequentialism is little different from conventional morality and 
deontological theories. This closeness to conventional morality has an important and welcome 
side-­effect for act-­consequentialists: Since, even as act-­consequentialists, we are supposed to 
follow moral rules in our everyday lives, the objection that consequentialists often engage in 
actions that are considered wrong because they conflict with conventional morality can no 
longer be sustained. As a result, consequentialists can, in one fell swoop, refute the objection 
that their theory is counterintuitive. (Similarly, it can be argued that indirect 
­act-­consequentialism demands no more of us than conventional morality does, thereby 
avoiding the criticism that it is overly demanding.)

--- Page 180 ---

Consequentialism and AI
171
Indirect act-­consequentialism must be distinguished from rule-­consequentialism (cf. 
Hooker 2000). In rule-­consequentialism, the moral rightness of an act depends on whether it 
is permitted, required, or prohibited by a code of moral rules selected according to consequen-
tialist criteria: An act is morally right if and only if it is permitted or required by the rules of 
the rule-­consequentialist moral code. An act prohibited by a rule is morally wrong, even if it 
would produce better consequences in a given situation. Conversely, an act permitted or 
required by a rule is morally right, even if it would produce worse consequences in that 
situation. By contrast, under indirect act-­consequentialism, an act may be morally wrong 
even though it follows the prescribed moral rule, if breaking that rule would have led to better 
consequences. This possibility of morally wrong behavior despite correct rule-­following is 
excluded in rule-­consequentialism.
In practice, however, there is not much difference between rule-­consequentialism and 
indirect act-­consequentialism, since although they have different criteria of rightness, both 
share a similar decision procedure: The decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism 
serves as both the decision procedure and the criterion of rightness in rule-­consequentialism. 
The rules in rule-­consequentialism are not absolute and can be overridden in cases of rule 
conflicts and to prevent catastrophic consequences (the “prevent disaster rule”). However, the 
prevent disaster rule itself does not specify how severe the negative consequences must be for 
a situation to qualify as a disaster. As a general guideline, the more important the moral rule 
to be violated, the more severe the negative consequences must be to justify the violation 
(Hooker 2000, 135).
Since consequence determinacy and maximization permission do not hold in rule-­
consequentialism, it is controversial whether it should be classified as a consequentialist or a 
deontological theory. For most consequentialists, rule-­consequentialism is out of the question 
as an alternative to indirect act-­consequentialism.
12.4  Consequentialism and AI
With this brief overview of the main features and variants of consequentialism, we can now 
turn to its application in the ethics of AI. Is consequentialism particularly well suited to 
addressing moral questions about AI and to be implemented as machine ethics in AI systems? 
Since the consequences of AI for humans (and animals7) are of paramount importance, eval-
uating these consequences is one of the most pressing issues. Given that consequentialism 
evaluates all actions solely on the basis of their outcomes, it seems an obvious candidate as 
the ethical theory best suited to morally assess the use and regulation of AI.
But the impact of AI on our lives is not just an issue for consequentialism; it is an issue that 
no ethical theory can ignore. No ethical theory can ignore general questions such as: Will the 
use and development of AI have a net positive or negative impact on humanity? Does AI pose 
an existential threat to humanity? What is the likelihood of specific benefits or harms arising 
from different applications of AI? Do the benefits outweigh the drawbacks and potential dan-
gers? As we do not yet have reliable answers to these questions, we need to consider how to 
proceed in the face of this uncertainty. However, questions about balancing potential risks, 
costs and benefits are not unique to consequentialism, and consequentialism is in no better or 
worse position than other ethical theories at providing answers to these questions.
But what is unique to consequentialism is that these questions about the consequences of 
AI are considered as the only morally relevant questions. Can consequentialism therefore 
adequately address the range of values and principles central to AI ethics, which, according 

--- Page 181 ---

Jörg Schroth
172
to recent surveys, converge on “transparency, justice and fairness, non-­maleficence, 
responsibility, privacy, beneficence, freedom and autonomy, trust, dignity, sustainability, and 
solidarity” (Jobin et al. 2019, 391; cf. Barton and Pöppelbuß 2022; Floridi et al. 2018, 2023, 
ch. 4). Further, can it address questions such as whether certain applications of AI violate 
human dignity, limit autonomy and freedom of action, increase injustice, unfairness, and 
discrimination, invade people’s privacy, or violate basic human rights? Consequentialists can 
address such concerns by framing them as questions about the consequences of AI. For 
example, if some applications of AI restrict human autonomy, this restriction could be seen as 
a negative consequence that consequentialists would include in their overall assessment of 
AI’s outcomes.
The question, however, is on what basis consequentialism can judge these consequences as 
good or bad. For utilitarianism, dignity, autonomy, freedom, justice, etc. are not intrinsic 
values. Since it sees only welfare as intrinsically valuable, these values could only be taken 
into account insofar as they affect human welfare (or serve as a means of promoting welfare). 
If some applications of AI were to violate the dignity of certain individuals, this would not in 
itself be an objection according to utilitarianism. An objection would only arise if these viola-
tions of dignity reduced the total sum of welfare. Similarly, transparency, one of the core 
values in all ethical guidelines for AI, is not an intrinsic value for utilitarianism.8
If ignoring these values or interpreting them merely as a means of promoting welfare 
seems implausible, or makes the theory less acceptable to the public, consequentialists might 
abandon utilitarianism in favor of a nonutilitarian form of consequentialism, extending their 
theory of the good to include these values (and any other value that people care about). 
Consequentialists would thus have to abandon welfarism and regard dignity, autonomy, jus-
tice, etc. as intrinsically valuable alongside welfare. But since dignity, justice, and fairness are 
moral values, this would mean abandoning the appealing utilitarian idea that the good is 
defined independently of the right, and that the right consists in maximizing the nonmoral 
good. The theory would also lose the simplicity praised by its proponents, since it would 
require weighing different values against each other to determine which acts lead to the best 
consequences, which would be difficult to implement in a machine ethics. Finally, consequen-
tialists would open themselves up to the objection that their theory of the good is merely an 
unconnected heap of values, mirroring the objection they often raise against deontology –­ 
that it is merely an unconnected heap of duties.9
Note that nonutilitarian consequentialism would still differ from deontological theories 
because, according to consequentialism, “whatever values an individual or institutional 
agent adopts, the proper response to those values is to promote them. The agent should honor 
the values only so far as honoring them is part of promoting them, or is necessary in order to 
promote them” (Pettit 1991, 231). Consequently, consequentialists would mandate acts that 
violate certain values if such violations were necessary to promote those values or to achieve 
the best overall outcome.
There is another reason for the apparent affinity between AI and consequentialism. 
Consequentialism appears to align well with the aspirations of AI because both pursue closely 
related objectives: It is widely agreed that AI should aim to benefit all people and enhance 
their lives. Similarly, consequentialism seeks to make the world the best place it can be. If AI 
can serve as a means to achieve this consequentialist aim, then from a consequentialist point 
of view, its development should be pursued. It does not follow, though, that if AI serves the 
good of humanity, consequentialism is necessarily the appropriate ethical framework for AI.
The consequentialist goal of making the world the best it can be is understood as express-
ing the positive dimension of consequentialism. While this positive dimension was 

--- Page 182 ---

Consequentialism and AI
173
fundamental to classical utilitarians, it is not unique to utilitarianism and consequentialism. 
Similar ideas are present in many ethical theories: Universalism, impartiality, and the duty 
of beneficence can also be found in the deontological theories of  Immanuel Kant and 
W.D. Ross,10 as well as in conventional morality. The differences lie, on the one hand, in how 
far this duty extends and what sacrifices morality can rightly demand of us. Yet even here, 
Kant and Ross agree with consequentialism in demanding a great deal of the individual –­ 
more than is typically required by conventional morality, where helping others and promoting 
their welfare is often seen as supererogatory. This is also evident in the fact that Singer’s 
famous argument for an extremely demanding duty to help people in need is explicitly not a 
utilitarian argument. Thus, the positive dimension of consequentialism that many find 
appealing or even compelling is not a feature unique to consequentialism, but one shared by 
other ethical theories.
However, there is a fundamental difference between consequentialism and other ethical 
theories that tends to work against public acceptance of applying consequentialism to AI. In 
deontological theories and conventional morality, the promotion of the good and the duty of 
beneficence are limited by constraints that prohibit certain acts, even if they would improve 
human welfare. In contrast, consequentialism turns this positive dimension into a require-
ment for maximization which implies the maximization permission and is therefore not 
bound by any constraints. Thus, within consequentialism, the positive dimension implies the 
negative, which is a significant obstacle to the widespread acceptance of consequentialism as 
an ethics for AI. The goal of making the world a better place is thus not a sufficient reason to 
accept a consequentialist ethics for AI and might as well be pursued by nonconsequentialist 
moral theories. Much depends on how one envisions the best possible world. Opponents to 
consequentialism would not regard a world in which the total amount of pleasure is maxi-
mized, but where this is achieved through acts traditionally considered horrific, as a better 
world than one with a lower amount of pleasure that is achieved without horrific acts.
At this point the question arises as to how pronounced the negative dimension of conse-
quentialism would be if used as a framework for machine ethics in AI systems. This negative 
dimension is particularly evident in direct act-­consequentialism. However, as explained 
above, direct act-­consequentialism is not endorsed by consequentialists because its decision 
procedure does not lead to the best possible world. Consequentialists advocate either indirect 
act-­consequentialism or rule-­consequentialism. When applied to human agents, both of 
these theories largely avoid the negative dimension of consequentialism and are more com-
patible with conventional morality.
This raises the question of whether the usual argument for indirect act-­consequentialism –­ 
that humans find direct act-­consequentialism overwhelming due to their cognitive and emo-
tional limitations –­ also applies to AI systems. AI systems could potentially lack many human 
shortcomings or reduce them to negligible levels. They would be free from situational biases, 
prejudices, and partiality (of the kind mentioned above [p. 169]), and as artificial moral 
agents, they would not face motivational deficits or high internalization costs. With their 
computational power and access to vast data resources, AI systems could systematically apply 
the decision procedure of direct act-­consequentialism, outperforming humans in identifying 
relevant act alternatives, assessing their potential consequences and probabilities, and calcu-
lating expected utilities. Even if AI systems were rule based, it would be possible to implement 
far more complex rules, as well as rules based on a greater amount of empirical data than 
human agents could access or process.
For example, if autonomous vehicles were able to use their sensors and communication 
with other autonomous vehicles to determine how many people in the vicinity would be 

--- Page 183 ---

Jörg Schroth
174
affected by different possible actions in the event of an imminent unavoidable accident, and to 
what extent (death, serious injury or less serious injury), they could be programmed to follow 
rules aimed at causing the least harm. In cases of conflicting rules, the vehicles could directly 
calculate which course of action would result in the least damage. Such rules could include 
minimizing the number of fatalities, reducing the severity of injuries, taking age into account, 
and, where possible, prioritizing harm to adults over children, and so on. Where multiple cri-
teria are in conflict, complex weighting rules would need to be implemented. However, there 
will also be clear cases where a decision must be made, for example whether the car should hit 
an adult or a child. Consequentialist decision making, whose sole aim is to minimize harm, 
would accept instrumental harm in order to reduce suffering and would differ from noncon-
sequentialist decision making, which prohibits the sacrifice of innocents or the instrumental-
ization of individuals.
In 2017, the Ethics Commission on Automated and Connected Driving (“Ethik-­Kommission 
Automatisiertes und Vernetztes Fahren”), established by the German government, published 
a report outlining ethical guidelines for automated and connected vehicle traffic. Some of the 
rules formulated in the report decisively reject act-­consequentialist decisions; for instance:
The protection of people takes precedence over all other utilitarian considerations. (10)
The introduction of higher automated driving systems, in particular with the possibility of 
automated collision avoidance, may be socially and ethically necessary if existing potential for 
harm reduction can be utilized. Conversely, a legally imposed obligation to use fully automated 
traffic systems or the creation of practical inescapability is ethically questionable if it is associated 
with submission to technical imperatives (prohibition of the “degradation” of the subject to a 
mere network element). (11)
Any trade-­off of victims is prohibited. A general programming aimed at reducing the number 
of personal injuries may be justifiable. Those involved in creating mobility risks must not sacrifice 
innocent bystanders. (11)
From a consequentialist perspective, none of these rules can be justified. For example, if a 
duty to use fully automated traffic systems or to sacrifice bystanders would lead to the best 
consequences, there would be no consequentialist reason not to implement such a duty or to 
sacrifice bystanders. (If consequentialists were to respond that a traffic system that operates 
according to deontological rules is preferable from a consequentialist point of view because 
people would feel more comfortable in such a world, and this gain in well-­being outweighs the 
harm to victims that deontological rules fail to prevent, then consequentialists would have to 
accept deontological rules in all cases where consequentialist principles face opposition. This 
would amount to accepting a deontological morality, rendering the debate between deonto-
logically or consequentially programmed autonomous vehicles pointless.)
Many people reject direct act-­consequentialism because it departs too far from conven-
tional morality and prescribes actions that according to conventional morality are morally 
wrong. For human agents, a plausible case can be made for an indirect act-­consequentialism 
that is reasonably close to conventional morality, at least in everyday situations. For artificial 
moral agents, however, a rule-­based system that closely resembles conventional morality 
cannot always be justified on consequentialist grounds, which means that the contrast bet-
ween consequentialism and deontology or conventional morality may be more pronounced 
in AI systems than in ethics for human agents. As a result, ethical decision making for AI 
systems shifts from a choice between indirect act-­consequentialism and a nonconsequential-
ist theory to a choice between direct act-­consequentialism and nonconsequentialist theories. 

--- Page 184 ---

Consequentialism and AI
175
(The extent to which consequentialist rules deviate from conventional moral rules depends in 
part on the complexity of the domain in question and on how complex and data-­intensive the 
rules that an AI system can process can be.)
Is consequentialism particularly well suited for implementation as a machine ethics in AI 
systems? This is essentially a technical question for computer science rather than an ethical 
one, once philosophers have provided a precise formulation of the theory. Consequentialists 
often emphasize that an act-­consequentialist theory precludes moral dilemmas and resolves 
rule conflicts that arise in indirect act-­consequentialism, thus providing clear guidance in 
every possible case. It is also claimed that consequentialist theories may be easier to imple-
ment because consequentialist moral decisions rely heavily on empirical facts and require less 
human judgment than deontological theories. However, as the example of autonomous vehi-
cles suggests, it is doubtful whether these theoretical advantages really apply in the real world. 
But even if consequentialist theories are easier to implement, this is of course not a sufficient 
reason to implement them if one finds consequentialism and its method of avoiding dilemmas 
and resolving rule conflicts morally questionable or counterintuitive. Ease of implementation 
alone does not justify actual implementation.
Irrespective of whether one is a proponent or a critic of consequentialism, the general 
question of whether consequentialism is an appropriate ethical theory for dealing with AI, 
and whether it should be applied as machine ethics to AI, must probably be answered in the 
negative by referring to a fundamental point that applies to all ethical theories. No ethical 
theory is without controversy, so no single theory, including consequentialism, is likely to be 
accepted by the public as the definitive ethical framework for AI. Given that consequentialism, 
because of its negative dimension, is much more polarizing than other ethical theories and 
often encounters fierce opposition, whether rightly or wrongly, it is less suitable than other 
theories as an ethical framework for AI.
Finally, the question can be raised as to what moral status consequentialism attributes to 
AI systems. Do we have duties toward them? Do they have rights against us? While conse-
quentialism does not fundamentally differ from other ethical theories on this issue, most con-
sequentialists endorse welfarism. Since welfare is only attributed to sentient beings, AI 
systems could only have moral status if they possessed consciousness and the capacity to 
experience pleasure and pain.
