13.1  Introduction
Evidently there is no such thing as AI as such. Rather, there is a family of diverse technolog-
ical systems that display different levels of artificial intelligence, produced for very different 
purposes and deployed in very different areas of human life. The family resemblance basically 
rests on the fact that the systems adhere to algorithms that have been trained in a specific way, 
i.e., by using methods of machine learning that enable the systems to process data (input) 
self-­determinately in order to accomplish a given purpose (output). This does not preclude, 
however, that an app like Spotify, for instance, differs significantly from a “killer robot.” The 
difference is obvious regarding not only the specific technology involved but also the specific 
purposes the two systems are supposed to serve. An ethical evaluation must take these and 
other (varying) aspects into consideration.
If there is no such thing as AI as such, there is, consequently, no such thing as the ethics of 
AI. On the one hand, this means that, if we are to evaluate any AI system in terms of ethics, 
then we must do this on the basis of its own peculiar technical functionality, and this entails 
taking into account both the fundamental risks and the conceivable merits of its production, 
maintenance, and use. On the other hand, it means that there is never a one-­to-­one relation 
between a specific AI system and a particular moral theory that we may apply to evaluate that 
system. Almost all familiar ethical approaches –­ virtue ethics included –­ have been used, for 
instance, to assess the moral status of “killer robots” (Vallor 2016, ch. 9).
And just as there is no such thing as the ethics of AI, there is also no such thing as the ethics 
of virtue. Rather, virtue ethics designates a family of quite diverse ethical views –­ some in the 
field of normative ethics, others with a more descriptive meta-­ethical approach. The family 
resemblance basically rests on the fact that virtue-­ethical accounts focus on the ethical 
quality of the agent, i.e., her character dispositions and attitudes, and not primarily on the 
ethical quality of her actions.
Virtue ethics focuses neither on the universality of the moral principle that a single action 
may accord with (like Kantianism) nor exclusively on the consequences of what is done and 
the overall benefit that might arise from it (like consequentialism). Rather, it focuses on ­virtues 
Virtue Ethics and AI
KATHI BEIER
13

--- Page 188 ---

Virtue Ethics and AI
179
such as justice, courage, temperance, humility, charity, and practical wisdom –­ on character 
qualities that a person can and should cultivate in the first place to be able to act morally in a 
firm and consistent manner. For virtue ethicists, virtues are per se morally good and they 
enable us to act in a morally good way, for example, courageously, temperately, mildly, grate-
fully, or amiably. By contrast, vices are taken to be per se morally bad and they are the reason 
we act in a morally bad way, for example, cowardly, intemperately, hot-­temperedly, ungrate-
fully, or harshly. So in virtue ethics, the virtues are the basic concepts: they are (i) prior to 
duties or rules of action because the virtues are not derived from them but vice versa; (ii) prior 
to single actions because the virtues essentially determine the moral quality of the actions 
that flow from them; and (iii) prior to the vices because vices are deformations of, and hence 
conceptually dependent on, the virtues.
Beyond this basic common ground, however, virtue-­ethical accounts diverge radically 
both in the history of moral philosophy and in contemporary ethics. We can find neither a 
standardized definition of what a virtue is nor a consensus on answering the question of 
which particular virtues are disjunctively necessary or jointly sufficient for a human being to 
flourish, and for what reason. Thus, the concept of “virtue ethics” turns out to be as general 
and as loose as the concept of AI.
It should come as no surprise, then, that when we look at “virtue-­ethical approaches to AI” 
we see that the virtues are addressed in very different forms, fields, and functions. At a conceptual 
level, with regard to human beings, virtues are conceived of as (i) dispositions that determine 
their excellence and help them live a good life, (ii) principles of motivation, or (iii) qualities that 
help humans realize the internal goods of human practices. Yet virtues have also been applied 
to machines. There have been numerous attempts to create artificial virtuous agents, e.g., a 
friendly chatbot or an autonomous weapon system that displays justice and discernment. At a 
practical level, virtues are regarded as essential across various fields of application such as in 
warfare, in medicine and healthcare, in education, public administration, and in commercial 
domains like gaming. At a professional level, virtues are considered necessary for all sorts of “AI 
practitioners,” i.e., for machine-­learning researchers, data scientists, industry engineers and 
developers, and AI regulators. Finally, at the consumer level, virtues and vices seem to play a 
crucial role too, i.e., for all those who use AI technologies for all sorts of private activities.
My overall aim in this chapter is to shed light on this diversity of virtue. I will first give a 
very short introduction to virtue ethics as a moral theory (section 13.2). Then I will examine 
the manifold conceptions of virtue that current virtue-­ethical approaches to AI refer to 
­(section 13.3). Subsequently, I will try to elucidate how the virtues are applied to our life with 
AI, focusing primarily on one particular virtue, honesty or truthfulness, and I will do this 
from both sides of the human–­machine interaction (section 13.4). I will conclude with some 
tentative remarks on the prospects of an applied virtue ethics of AI (section 13.5).
13.2  Virtue Ethics: A Very Short Introduction
Among the numerous ethical theories prevalent in contemporary moral philosophy, virtue 
ethics is by far the oldest. This holds true for both Eastern and Western traditions in ethics. For 
the Eastern world, we can see that Confucianism and Buddhism are concerned with practices 
of moral self-­cultivation, i.e., ways of acquiring attitudes and dispositions that help humans 
live a good life, that are comparable to Western virtue ethics (Ivanhoe 2014; Flanagan 2015; 
Sim 2015; MacKenzie 2018). For the Western world, it is Socrates, the protagonist in Plato’s 
dialogues, who in Greek antiquity was the first to introduce the terms virtue (aretē) and vice 

--- Page 189 ---

Kathi Beier
180
(kakia) into the philosophical discussion on how to live well as a human being. In his Republic 
(Plato  1997, 352e–­353c), Plato introduces a functionalist model of virtue according to 
which something’s virtue is nothing other than its fitness to serve its species-­related purpose 
(ergon). In this sense, Socrates says that to be virtuous means to be fit or to be apt to serve the 
ergon that defines the species that the virtuous thing belongs to: just as the pruning knife 
needs to be of good quality in order to be fit to do what it is supposed to do as a pruning knife, 
i.e., to cut vines, so the human being needs to be primarily wise and just in order to be fit to 
live a good life (a life of eudaimonia) as a human being, i.e., an animate being with rational 
capacities. In other words, the virtues make us excellent in doing what we as humans are 
characteristically supposed to do.
Aristotle builds on this thought that he adopted from his teacher Plato. In the Nicomachean 
Ethics, he claims that the virtue of a human being “will be the disposition (hexis) whereby he 
becomes a good human being and from which he will perform his own function (ergon) well” 
(Aristotle  2002, 1106a24).1 However, Aristotle strongly rejects Plato’s idealism, i.e., the 
assumption that goodness is an idea that infuses all things that are good, and instead defends a 
more down-­to-­earth account. The concept “good,” he claims, has many meanings, depending 
on what kind of thing we refer to as good. Accordingly, Aristotle is more specific about both the 
nature of human beings and the nature of human virtue. Based on his understanding of 
the human soul, he differentiates between two different kinds of virtues: on the one hand, the 
moral virtues or virtues of character like justice, temperance, and courage, i.e., the excellences 
of the desiring part of soul that make us capable of listening to and obeying reason in the way 
“one is reasonable when one takes account of advice from one’s father or loved ones” 
(Aristotle 2002, I.13: 1102b33); and, on the other hand, the intellectual virtues like wisdom 
(sophia) and phronēsis, often translated as prudence or practical wisdom, i.e., the excellences of 
the rational part of the soul that enable us to understand the true and the good. While Aristotle, 
unlike Plato, is far from claiming that the moral virtues are merely forms of wisdom, he does 
emphasize the interplay between moral virtues and practical wisdom (Aristotle 2002, VI.13; 
Kamtekar 2013). Aristotle lists more moral virtues than Plato does, deriving them primarily 
from the affections or emotions of the human soul: courage or fortitude or bravery, for example, 
has to do with the affections of fear and boldness; temperance or moderation has to do with 
bodily pleasure. Moreover, he offers a substantive account of what a moral virtue is 
(Aristotle 2002, II.5–­6), defining moral virtue as a disposition (hexis) that:
(i)	
is a good quality of a person, i.e., something that once acquired does not change or fade 
easily (Aristotle 1963, ch. 8)
(ii)	 must be acquired as early as childhood through a process of habituation, i.e., contin-
uous exercise, by which one learns to bring reason and affections into agreement so that 
what desire pursues is the same as what reason asserts
(iii)	 results in an intermediate state, the mean, between two bad, vicious states, one involving 
excessive affection (e.g., too much boldness equals rashness), the other deficiency (e.g., a 
lack of boldness equals cowardice).
Moreover, Aristotle claims that:
(iv)	 since the mean is relative to the agent as well as to the context and the circumstances, 
determined by rational prescription and in the way the practically wise person would 
determine it, the phronimoi, i.e., the experts in virtue, are the ones we should take as role 
models in the process of virtue acquisition.

--- Page 190 ---

Virtue Ethics and AI
181
To be virtuous, for Aristotle, is not easy but rather exceptional, since it means to be affected 
and to act “when one should, at the things one should, in relation to the people one should, for 
the reasons one should, and in the way one should” (Aristotle 2002, II.6: 1106b22). The moral 
or ethical virtues presuppose the intellectual virtue of practical wisdom; without ­practical 
wisdom, they are not genuine virtues but what Aristotle calls mere “natural virtues” 
(Aristotle 2002, VI.13: 1144b4), i.e., inborn tendencies to feel, decide, and act in a morally good 
way (Müller 2004). Yet without the virtues proper, it is not possible to live a good human life; 
hence, according to Aristotle, the virtues are necessary, albeit not sufficient, for eudaimonia.
Parts of this virtue conception have inspired a good deal of Western ethics, from the Stoics 
via the medieval thinkers to David Hume and Adam Smith. The conception even left traces in 
Immanuel Kant’s moral theory, most notably in his doctrine of virtue as part of his Metaphysics 
of Morals. For Kant, however, virtue amounts to fortitudo moralis, i.e., “strength of a human 
being’s maxims in fulfilling his duty” (Kant 1907, p. 394), so for him duty and obligation are 
primary. For a little while, then, virtue ethics somehow seemed to disappear behind Kantianism 
and consequentialism (Frede 2013). It was not until after the second half of the twentieth 
century that the virtue-­ethical tradition prominently reentered the stage of moral thinking, 
initiated most of all by the works of G.E.M. Anscombe and Philippa Foot –­ referred to as the 
two “main protagonists of the ‘ethical revolution’of 1958” (Chappell 2013, p. 158), the year 
that Anscombe’s influential essay Modern moral philosophy was published. While Anscombe, 
Foot and others of the first generation of modern virtue ethics tried to revive primarily the 
Aristotelian tradition, the family of virtue-­ethical accounts today is far more diverse and plu-
ralistic (Russell 2013; Van Hoft 2014; Besser-­Jones and Slote 2015; Snow 2018).
This also holds true for the ways in which virtue ethics is applied to the philosophical 
discussion of AI. Here, Aristotle is still a main reference but definitely not the only one. This 
seems to be both an advantage and a disadvantage. To include other thinkers and traditions is 
clearly an advantage, given that AI technologies are spread all over the world, presenting us 
with challenges that call for global solutions. It would be foolish, Shannon Vallor notes, to 
neglect potentially important sources “for the journey we need to make from our contempo-
rary condition toward the good life for us, where ‘us’ refers to the increasingly interdependent 
technomoral community now being constituted on a global scale” (Vallor 2016, p. 63). At the 
same time, it is not helpful to build on as many virtue traditions as possible if the traditions 
disagree with each other. Next, I will show in what sense this might be the case.
13.3  Conceptions of Virtue in Virtue-­ethical Approaches to AI
In this section, I will give a critical overview of the main virtue conceptions invoked in today’s 
virtue-­ethical discussion of AI. First, I highlight the diversity of these approaches. My second 
aim is to suggest that this diversity itself may pose a problem: the approaches may be too the-
oretically inconsistent to add up to a single and powerful virtue-­ethical theory that can guide 
us toward a good life with AI. I will proceed chronologically, beginning with the ancient 
accounts of virtue.
The functionalist model of virtue proposed by Plato has been taken up by some philoso-
phers trying to implement virtues into machines (Howard and Muntean  2017; 
Stenseke 2023, 2024). The model is appealing since AI systems differ significantly in the pur-
poses they are supposed to serve. A self-­driving car, for example, needs to display other virtues 
than does a companion robot used in elderly care. As Stenseke emphasizes, they serve differ-
ent roles, are equipped with different functionalities, and meet their own domain-­specific 

--- Page 191 ---

Kathi Beier
182
challenges (Stenseke 2024, p. 858). One should not forget, however, that the metaphysics 
behind Plato’s conception of virtue, i.e., his idealism, is radically different from other theories 
of virtue both old and new, especially from (neo)-­Aristotelian virtue ethics.
Of all the ancient Greek accounts of virtue, the Aristotelian one still dominates the field. 
Many philosophers use it as a cornerstone in thinking about a virtue-­ethical perspective on 
AI. So, for example, it is one of the main sources in Shannon Vallor’s pioneering work on how 
to live well with emerging technologies (Vallor 2016, 2018, 2021). While some philosophers 
focus on specific parts of Aristotle’s ethics, e.g., on how the dianoetic virtues can help develop 
responsible AI (Constantinescu et al. 2021), or on why some of the Aristotelian virtues ought 
to be part of the professional education of engineers (Harris 2008; Schmidt 2021; Griffin 
et al. 2024), Vallor is concerned with Aristotle’s ethics in its entirety. First, she emphasizes the 
general link between the virtues and human flourishing, i.e., the necessity of acquiring 
character traits to cope with the challenging conditions of new technologies that are shaping 
our life. Second, she highlights the fundamental need of moral habituation through the 
repeated practice of moral agency, i.e., the process of cultivating in oneself the moral virtues. 
And third, she underscores the crucial role of practical wisdom, i.e., the intellectual virtue 
that enables us to respond appropriately to the morally salient features of a particular 
situation and that, according to Vallor, makes Aristotle’s ethics better suited than any other 
moral theory to meet the technosocial conditions of the twenty-­first century. Now by 
including Aristotelian virtue ethics, Vallor seems to subscribe to Aristotle’s essentialism or 
speciesism concerning human nature. As she rightly notes, for Aristotle there are “certain 
biological, psychological, and social facts about human persons that constrain what it can 
mean for us to flourish” (Vallor 2016, p. 19); in the same manner, the character traits she 
proposes in her book will not be radically new, “for they must remain consistent with the basic 
moral psychology of our species” (Vallor 2016, p. 10). We should keep this in mind because 
this essentialism is not endorsed by other sources in virtue ethics that she likewise relies on, 
especially some neo-­Aristotelian approaches I will turn to in a moment.
Confucianism and Buddhism are the two other foundational sources Vallor uses for her 
virtue-­ethical framework. She acknowledges that, on metaphysical grounds, Buddhism 
seems to be fundamentally different from both Aristotelianism and Confucianism, yet espe-
cially from the former, for “Buddhists generally deny the substantial reality of the personal 
self (ātman)” (Vallor 2016, p. 88). This, without doubt, poses a difficulty because if Buddhism 
claims there is no real self, if individuality ought to be overcome and left behind in favor of a 
loving concern for others, indeed for all creatures, humans, and nonhumans alike, then 
Buddhism is incompatible with essential elements of Aristotle’s ethics, most notably with the 
doctrine of the mean as being relative to the agent and to the circumstances, and, more gener-
ally, with the idea of cultivating one’s character in order to be a good person and a good citizen. 
Critics have pointed to this kind of incommensurability, claiming “that it is not at all clear that 
Buddhist thinkers have anything like a concept of character” (McRae 2018, p. 278).
Kant’s moral philosophy is different in that it is not a kind of virtue ethics in the strict sense 
of the term; rather, it includes an “ethics of virtue.”2 Even though the concept of virtue 
occupies a prominent place, the virtues exhibit but a supportive function: to be virtuous, for 
Kant, means to have the strength needed to carry out one’s duty, i.e., to be able to obey the 
moral law. So, on theoretical grounds, virtue here means something completely different 
from what it does in Aristotle’s ethics. Kant’s account of virtue can also be found in AI ethics 
and is sometimes taken to be, albeit mistakenly, a virtue-­ethical approach. At any rate, being 
concerned with the question of “how to put AI ethics into practice,” some authors seem to 
take Kantian-­inspired principlism as given and to assign the virtues a supportive role. 

--- Page 192 ---

Virtue Ethics and AI
183
Hagendorff, for example, proposes four basic AI virtues –­ justice, honesty, responsibility, and 
care –­ which he selects by asking: “Does virtue A translate into behavior that is likely to result 
in an outcome that corresponds to the requirements of principle X?” (Hagendorff 2022, p. 8). 
Each of the four virtues, he claims, “motivates a kind of professional decision making that 
builds the bedrock for fulfilling all the AI specific ethics principles discussed in literature” 
(Hagendorff 2022, p. 19). Being motivated to act in accordance with moral principles is not 
the same, however, as being virtuous in the Aristotelian sense of the term. Furthermore, 
Kant’s conception of virtue is not embedded in an eudaimonist view of human life; on the 
contrary, he strictly rejects eudaimonism in moral philosophy.
Another prominent point of reference in virtue-­ethical approaches to AI is neo-­
Aristotelianism in its varying forms. The neo-­Aristotelian ethical naturalist Rosalind 
Hursthouse has proposed an account with which she attempts to appease the frequently 
raised concern that virtue ethics cannot offer action guidance. She claims that, quite the con-
trary, it can indeed offer action guidance, because it can provide what she calls “v-­rules,” i.e., 
rules derived from virtues and vices such as “Do what is honest, do not do what is unchari-
table” (Hursthouse  1999, p.  37). This view is attractive to AI developers trying to build 
­so-­called AVAs, artificial virtuous agents (Stenseke 2023, 2024). (I will come back to this in 
the next section.)
Other neo-­Aristotelian virtue ethicists take up a more skeptical stance on Aristotle’s natu-
ralism. Alasdair MacIntyre, for example, strongly rejects what he calls “Aristotle’s metaphysi-
cal biology,” i.e., the claim that living beings have an essence and that this essence determines 
their telos (MacIntyre 2007, p. 162). The essence of human beings, according to Aristotle, is 
having reason, so what human beings ought to do in order to live well is to develop their 
rational capacities. MacIntyre wishes to save the teleological thought in Aristotle’s ethics, 
hence his eudaimonism, while getting rid of his metaphysically and biologically based essen-
tialism. What he develops, then, is a “socially teleological account” of the virtues 
(MacIntyre 2007, p. 197) that assigns a central place to the concept of “practice.” For him, 
human beings are essentially participants in the practices of the community they belong to. 
He defines “practice” as “any coherent and complex form of socially established cooperative 
human activity through which goods internal to that form of activity are realized in the 
course of trying to achieve those standards of excellence which are appropriate to, and 
partially definitive of, that form of activity” (MacIntyre 2007, p. 187). Examples of practices 
in this sense are playing chess, farming, engaging in enquiries of physics, and painting.
The turn to the concept of practice is what Shannon Vallor finds appealing. For it is evi-
dent, she believes, that, with the emergence of new technologies, “we are now relying on 
cooperative technosocial activity as a means of seeking the good life, individually and collec-
tively” (Vallor 2016, p. 46). Just like MacIntyre, she defines “technomoral virtues” in terms of 
practice, i.e., as character traits that enable us to cooperatively achieve, through excellent 
activity, shared goods that are internal to our practices –­ goods such as global community, 
intercultural understanding, and collective wisdom. It is hard to see, however, how Vallor can 
combine Aristotle’s essentialism with MacIntyre’s anti-­essentialism. Again, the question is 
whether it is possible to have both.3
Julia Annas is another prominent voice in neo-­Aristotelian virtue ethics who is cited by 
some virtue ethicists of AI, especially those working in the field of machine ethics 
(Stenseke 2023). Annas proposes what she calls the “skill analogy” to virtue, i.e., the claim 
that virtues are analogous to practical skills with respect to both their nature and the way 
they are acquired (Annas 2011, ch. 3). “The ‘skill analogy’ comes in,” she says, “because the 
habituation in virtue takes the form of the kind of education in acting that you get in making 

--- Page 193 ---

Kathi Beier
184
and acting when you learn a practical skill” (Annas 2021, p. 95). Unlike Aristotle, who sometimes 
compares the acquisition of moral virtues to the acquisition of productive skills such as 
building a house, Annas focuses on performance skills such as playing the piano. In the 
­process of learning a practical skill such as how to play the piano, two things are essential: the 
need to learn and the drive to aspire. More specifically, it includes the following three compo-
nents. First, in learning from a teacher or role model, the learner wants to understand what 
she has to do and why she has to do it, i.e., she wants to understand the reasons behind every 
single step. Second, she aspires to do it for herself, not as a clone-­like impersonator and not as 
a matter of routine, but in her own peculiar and intelligent way. And third, she strives to 
improve, knowing that the first attempts at exercising the skill will certainly fail and that she 
has to keep practicing throughout life. This is a powerful analogy that can help us understand 
how human beings learn to be virtuous, and can, perhaps, be applied to the creation of arti-
ficially virtuous agents.
Before I examine this field of research in the next section, here it seems important to point 
to the fact that Annas overtaxes the analogy, so to speak, formulating a conception of virtue 
that is incompatible with Aristotle’s. Recall that, for Aristotle, virtues are praiseworthy and 
morally good dispositions (hexeis) and as such are to be distinguished from skills, competences 
or capacities (dynameis) in that the latter are morally ambivalent or neutral, i.e., can serve 
morally good as well as bad purposes. In some passages, Annas notes the difference, con-
ceding that “virtue involves more than skill (especially its orientation to the good)” (2015, 
p. 97), but generally tends to use the two concepts synonymously.
Finally, there is still another branch of modern virtue ethics that is applied to the ethics of 
AI, namely, Linda Zagzebski’s exemplarism (Zagzebski 2010, 2017). It is similar to Annas’s 
virtue conception insofar as it focuses on the development of the virtues. Again, what makes 
it especially appealing to AI machine ethicists is that it provides a source for moral education 
(Berberich and Diepold  2018; Mabaso  2020; Stenseke  2024; see also Chapter  20 in this 
volume). For Zagzebski, a virtue is “a deep and enduring acquired trait that we admire upon 
reflection, consisting of a disposition to have a certain emotion that initiates and directs 
action toward an end, and reliable success in reaching that end” (Zagzebski 2017, p. 113). So 
the admiration of exemplars, i.e., of paradigmatically good persons, forms one of the key 
components of the virtue concept. Exemplars exemplify what it means to be virtuous. 
Moreover, the admiration of exemplars stands at the beginning of the process of acquiring 
the virtues. Admiration, according to Zagzebski, has both a cognitive side by which we iden-
tify the things we admire –­ a person, a character trait, a motive or a whole life –­ and a motiva-
tional side since it moves us to emulate what we admire. Emulation, however, is something 
other than mere imitation in that it is directed at the admired person’s motivations of action. 
Emulation means seeing oneself as the admired exemplar and trying to realize this idealized 
version of oneself. As Zagzebski explains, “in projecting oneself into the image one then 
enacts, one gradually becomes the person one wants to be” (Zagzebski 2017, p. 136).
While there are striking similarities between Zagzebski’s theory and the virtue-­ethical 
accounts of both Aristotle and Annas, we should not overlook the differences. First, exem-
plarism for Zagzebski is a particular moral theory, distinct from Kantian deontology and 
classical utilitarianism as well as from Platonistic and Aristotelian virtue theory. This is 
because the construction of the theory begins with direct reference to exemplars of moral 
goodness, whereas all other moral concepts such as virtue, right act, duty, and so on are 
defined via indexical reference to these exemplars. Second, by defining virtue as “a disposition 
to have a certain emotion,” Zagzebski makes clear that Hume is more important to her than 
is Aristotle, since for Hume, like for Zagzebski, virtues result in good motivations, and a motive 

--- Page 194 ---

Virtue Ethics and AI
185
is nothing other than an emotion that initiates and guides actions. Third, unlike Aristotle and 
the neo-­Aristotelians, Zagzebski does not subscribe to any form of eudaimonism but to an 
agent-­based account of virtue; virtues are valuable not because they contribute to a good life 
but because they ensure that we have good motives.
13.4  Applied Virtue Ethics of AI
The comparatively young history of AI virtue ethics is characterized by three waves, each 
focused on a different set of questions concerning the application of virtues. A first wave was 
primarily interested in how we as human beings can become virtuous and act virtuously in 
our dealings with AI; hence, the focus was on the impact of artificially intelligent technol-
ogies on our conceptions of the good life and the challenges we face in integrating them into 
our daily practices. As Shannon Vallor has put it, the job is to figure out “how to live well 
with emerging technologies” (Vallor  2016, p.  1), a task that points in two directions by 
enquiring into “what we will do with these technologies once we have them, and what they 
will do with us’”(Vallor 2016, p. 5). A second wave emerged along with the progress made by 
methods of machine learning that made it possible to integrate ethics into machines. The 
focus then switched to the question of how AI systems can be constructed in such a way that 
they act virtuously, i.e., how to build so-­called artificial virtuous agents (AVAs). As a 
consequence of both developments, a third wave begins to enter the discussion: virtue ethi-
cists are now concerned with the question of how we as human beings are to act virtuously 
toward AVAs. Whereas the first and second waves regarded AI technologies primarily as 
tools, albeit clever ones that are able to act self-­determinately, now the view begins to emerge 
that they should be conceived of as autonomous moral agents, comparable to the kind of 
autonomy human beings possess. This, of course, radically changes our understanding of 
the human–­AI relation. In what follows, I will pick out one virtue in particular, namely hon-
esty or truthfulness, and briefly reflect on how it applies to both humans and AI across the 
three waves of AI virtue ethics.
Concerning the first wave, the virtue of honesty stands at the top of Shannon Vallor’s list 
of 12 technomoral virtues –­ 12 virtues that, as she writes, are “plausibly most crucial” to our 
flourishing and “especially under pressure from our contemporary technosocial practices” 
(Vallor 2016, p. 120). Honesty includes the more specific virtues of trust, reliability, and 
integrity, all of which play a central role in the communication of information. Vallor defines 
honesty as “an exemplary respect for truth, along with the practical expertise to express that 
respect appropriately in technosocial contexts” (Vallor 2016, p. 122).
Honesty encompasses two distinct virtuous character traits –­ one that makes us excellent 
as conveyers of information, i.e., in telling the truth, and one that makes us excellent as 
receivers of information, i.e., in being able to choose whom we receive information from and 
what to believe or take as true. We can elaborate this idea with the help of Bernard Williams’s 
distinction between sincerity and accuracy (Williams 2002). Sincerity, he says, is the virtue 
of trustworthiness in speech. It includes both the disposition not to lie, i.e., not to assert what 
one believes not to be true, and the disposition not to mislead others by implication, i.e., by 
telling the truth but suggesting a falsity. According to Williams, the former disposition is more 
important than the latter, but both are necessary for being fully sincere: “It is better when we 
can more or less rely on what people imply as well as on what they assert; it is worse when we 
cannot even rely on what they assert” (Williams 2002, p. 109). Accuracy, by contrast, is the 
virtue of acquiring true beliefs. It implies attentiveness, reliability, and rigor in discovering 

--- Page 195 ---

Kathi Beier
186
and coming to believe the truth. Accuracy consists in “the desire for truth ‘for its own sake,’” 
or, as he also puts it, “the passion for getting it right” (Williams 2002, p. 126). To be accurate 
means to be persistent and to make serious efforts even if there are external obstacles to find-
ing out the truth; at the same time, it means resisting one’s inner, psychological obstacles 
such as fantasy, wishful thinking and self-­deception.
The problem, according to Vallor, is that truth and honesty are under serious threat by so-­
called ICTs, information and communication technologies, especially those based on digital 
computing (Vallor 2016, p. 121). With the help of Williams’s distinction, we can say that ICTs 
pose a challenge to the two virtues of sincerity and accuracy. Regarding sincerity, do we 
always stick to the facts when we post something on Facebook? Or do we sometimes post what 
we believe to be entertaining and to bring clicks, though it is fibbed, hypocritical or an out-
right lie? Regarding accuracy, do we really make the effort needed to check information before 
we believe it ourselves and forward it to our friends and followers? Are we always aware of the 
fact that algorithmic-­driven internet sources and AI technologies can be biased or based on 
fantasy and can foster filter bubbles? As Vallor reminds us, to be untruthful in the digital age, 
i.e., to be either insincere or inaccurate, can have serious consequences: “For example, a habit 
of using digital tools to spread rumors and conspiracy theories is not only individually vicious 
in its deceptiveness and recklessness, but it also weakens the social conditions for honest 
politics and thus is broadly incompatible with eudaimonia as shared human flourishing” 
(Vallor 2022, p. 23).
The spread of AI-­driven chatbots is another example of how truth and honesty are under-
mined by new technologies. This is especially problematic when these new technologies are 
used for services in which we share sensitive information, e.g., in financial or medical con-
texts. Can we really trust them? In short, honesty is critical for everyone using AI. It is critical 
not only for AI users but also for AI practitioners, i.e., those who design, develop, and deploy 
AI systems. According to Hagendorff, honesty helps fulfill three ethical issues: it fosters orga-
nizational transparency, promotes the willingness to provide explainability or technical trans-
parency regarding AI applications, and enables the acknowledgement of errors and mistakes 
made in AI research and development (Hagendorff 2022, p. 6). For these reasons, it is one of 
the basic AI virtues.
Concerning the second wave, it is helpful to stress that in modern virtue ethics, virtues are 
human centered; hence they apply to AI users as well as to AI practitioners. Only human 
beings have affections and rational capacities. So only humans can learn to adopt their affec-
tions to the judgment of reason, i.e., to be morally virtuous. Machines have neither feelings 
nor human-­like intellect. AI technologies, both robotic and nonrobotic systems, are basically 
machines. In wanting them to be virtuous, we do not want them to “have” the virtues like a 
human being has them; rather, we want them to act, on the output level, like a virtuous 
person would act. If the AI system can learn to act like a virtuous person would act, then we 
have an AVA, i.e., a variant of an artificial moral agent (AMA). AI engineers and machine 
ethicists work on the assumption that it is possible to create AMAs (see Chapter 23 in this 
volume). As Wallach and Allen (2009) have put it, it seems that we can teach robots right and 
wrong. However, it is only recently that virtue ethics has been adapted, on a practical level, to 
methods of implementing moral decision procedures into AI (Howard and Muntean 2017; 
Berberich and Diepold 2018; Govindarajulu et al. 2019; Stenseke 2023, 2024). The goal is to 
create excellent moral machines that learn to be excellent by imitating exemplars and from 
real-­world experience.
According to some AI researchers, the way Aristotle describes how we humans learn to be 
virtuous seems “highly analogous” to the process of training an evolutionary learning 

--- Page 196 ---

Virtue Ethics and AI
187
algorithm on data, hence suggests “a sort of ‘fit’ between these forms of AI and virtue ethics” 
(Gamez et al. 2020, p. 799). In this respect, Jakob Stenseke has proposed a model of an AVA –­ 
one displaying courage, generosity, and honesty (Stenseke 2023) –­ that he believes is the “first 
computational implementation of AMAs that solely focus on virtue ethics” (Stenseke 2024, 
p. 870).
The third wave of AI virtue ethics is concerned with the following question. If one day 
there are AVAs around, how should we treat them? Amazon Echo’s Alexa and Apple’s Siri 
give us an inkling, according to Shannon Vallor, of what it is like to have artificial agents 
actively participating in our social milieu in ways that, in any other era, would have con-
stituted an interpersonal connection with reciprocal expectations and duties of care 
(Vallor 2022, p. 35). Are such agents autonomous systems that are equal to humans? Or 
are they just assistive companions, tools, “mindless, non-­sentient assemblages of silicon 
and plastic” (Vallor 2022, p. 36)? Should we understand them as technological slaves, as 
“assistive, yet intelligent and interactive, tools for human use and benefit” (Constantinescu 
et al. 2021, p. 812)? Or would this mean “not to be behaving virtuously toward the vir-
tuous machines that we created” (Tonkens 2012, p. 146)? In other words, could AVAs make 
a claim to membership in the moral community? As Gamez et al. (2020) have shown on the 
basis of experiments, including those testing honesty, humans “are indeed willing to see 
AMAs as possessing character,” which for the authors is reason enough to see AVAs as 
inhabiting our moral community (Gamez et al. 2020, p. 806). These are issues to be dis-
cussed in the near future. According to Vallor, virtue ethics is a powerful frame for this kind 
of discussion, since contributors will need to bring to the table many virtues, among them 
courage, compassion, and honesty.
13.5  Concluding Remarks
Virtue ethics is increasingly the focus of attention in AI ethics. It seems appropriate, then, to 
ask what we can expect from this growing field of applied ethics. What are the prospects for 
the future of virtue-­ethical approaches to AI?
For one, we can certainly expect more discussions –­ regarding more specialized and more 
general issues –­ on how to apply virtue-­ethical accounts to the ethics of AI. No clairvoyance 
is needed to predict that, first of all, we will see the same differentiation in virtue-­ethical 
approaches to AI as we have seen in modern virtue ethics in general. So the conceptions of 
virtue we can find there will most likely be taken up and transferred to the ethics of AI. This 
includes, for example, neo-­Platonic virtue ethics (Adams  2006; Pettigrove  2018), stoic 
­virtues (Gill 2021), and value-­based theories of virtue. Second, as in modern virtue ethics, we 
will probably see a shift of focus from the moral virtues to the dianoetic, intellectual or epi-
stemic ones, a shift now already in full swing (Sullins 2021). Third, and along with the second 
shift, more attention will be paid to the vices, both moral and epistemic. If it is too hard for us 
humans to become virtuous, then we should, as the second-­best option, at least try to avoid 
the vices. This, in turn, points to a fourth possible development in AI virtue ethics: a trend 
toward focusing on methods of virtue acquisition. In modern virtue ethics, a lot of research 
has recently been done to address the question of how humans become virtuous agents –­ 
research at the intersection of philosophy and psychology and often classified under the label 
“virtue development studies” (Snow 2015; Annas et al. 2016). We should expect the findings 
of this line of research to be taken up by AI virtue ethicists and applied not only to humans 
but to AI itself, i.e., to attempts at creating AVAs.

--- Page 197 ---

Kathi Beier
188
None of these potential developments will come as a huge surprise. They have the inevitable 
drawback, however, of increasing the heterogeneity of virtue talk. As in virtue ethics in gen-
eral, eudaimonistic accounts will coexist with noneudaimonistic, i.e., agent-­based, ones, 
functionalist models of virtue with human-­centered, i.e., psychology-­based, ones, and dispo-
sitional conceptions of virtue with nondispositional ones, etc. More basically, these develop-
ments will probably not settle the dispute about whether virtues ascribed to machines are 
virtues in the proper sense of the term. As discussed above, this diversity might even call into 
question the usefulness of virtue ethics as a moral guide in our dealings with AI. If AI virtue 
ethics is to compete with principlism, deontology, consequentialism, and other moral ­theories, 
then it has to be at least as coherent and comprehensive as these other theories; otherwise the 
useful answers it can offer to the many challenges with which AI technologies confront us 
will not be heard.
On the other hand, we can also ask what impact AI technologies will have on virtue ethics 
as a moral theory. This is harder to predict. It seems to me, however, that some effects can at 
least be foreseen. Generally speaking, we can envisage that some AI technologies will prompt 
us to reconsider some of the individual virtues. Virtues that were considered either outdated 
or difficult to grasp, or that never really had been conceived of as virtues within virtue ethics, 
may take center stage, and rightly so. Here are three examples. The deployment of “killer 
robots” and “drones” in warfare  –­ AI technologies that make it possible to kill or injure 
without the risk of being killed or injured oneself –­ suggest the redundancy of a virtue such 
as courage, i.e., fortitude or bravery. Yet it would be premature to think so. First of all, soldiers 
on the battlefield now also have to fight against these killing machines. Second, robotic medi-
ation, as Shannon Vallor states, “does not always prevent moral or psychological injury” 
(Vallor 2016, p. 215). And third, bravery reappears as a disposition to be manifested in cir-
cumstances we were not aware of prior to the rise of AI technologies, e.g., as a virtue charac-
teristically needed by industry AI ethicists (Gambelin 2021).
Artificial companions, my second example, be it “sex robots” or “AI friends,” encourage us 
to think about the virtues of love and friendship. Is friendship “a kind of excellence,” as 
Aristotle holds (Aristotle  2002, VIII.1: 1155a5)? And if so, does it presuppose that the 
friends are aware of their mutual feelings, that “the parties must have good will toward each 
other, i.e., wish good things for each other, and be aware of the other’s doing so” (VIII.2: 
1156a3–­5)? If so, can there ever be such a thing as a friendship between a human being and 
an AI chatbot?
Finally, AI technologies challenge our concept of trust. AI must be trustworthy, otherwise 
we would not use it. But can we trust AI? And how are we to conceive of trust at all –­ as an 
emotion, as a virtue or as both?
These are just three examples of how AI might serve as a boost for virtue ethics.4
