14.1  Feminist Ethics
There is a growing body of literature that recognizes the importance of feminist thinking on 
developments in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) (Browne et al. 2023). The connection 
between feminist ethics and AI lies at the intersection of social justice and AI-­based systems. 
Feminist scholars examine the social, cultural, and political conditions and effects of such 
systems. They focus on social categories, such as gender, race, and class, and analyze the 
extent to which AI-­based systems can reinforce (or reduce) existing injustices or create novel 
forms of injustice. Their topics include diversity in AI research and development (Collett and 
Dillon  2019; Daugtherty et  al.  2018), racialized and gendered robots (Atanasoski  2023; 
Locatelli 2022; Coeckelbergh 2019; Moran 2019), data (gaps) and data ethics (D’Ignazio and 
Klein  2020), online violence (Estrada  2023), structural and epistemic injustices through 
algorithms (Hull 2023; El Kassar 2022; Origgi and Ciranna 201), marginalization and injus-
tice on social media (Stewart et al. 2022), decolonization of AI (Birhane and Guest 2021; 
Murphy and Largacha-­Martínez  2022) and indigenous data governance and sovereignty 
(GIDA  2024; Rana  2024; Carroll et  al.  2020). Although there are feminist approaches 
that explicitly deal with aspects of AI, these are very heterogeneous and interdisciplinary 
approaches.
Feminist scholars have a long tradition of feminist thinking regarding science and technology 
(e.g., Loh  2019; Layne et  al.  2010; Haraway  1998; Longino  1987). They bring feminist 
knowledge, methodologies, theories, and epistemology to the field of AI. In recent decades, 
feminist approaches have emerged as a leading subfield in the scholarly examination of 
e­thical issues regarding AI. Emerging feminist approaches, such as data feminism (D’Ignazio 
and Klein 2020), emphasize the political, ethical, and social dimensions particularly of data-­
driven and AI-­based systems. It is a relatively young field, informed by a wide range of theo-
retical and methodological approaches, and enriched by scholars from different disciplines. 
Despite this diversity, it is characterized by the area it addresses, AI-­based systems, and its 
feminist lens.
Feminist Ethics and AI
REGINA MÜLLER
14

--- Page 202 ---

Feminist Ethics and AI
193
AI-­based systems are often defined as systems designed to replicate or automate complex 
capabilities generally associated with human intelligence, such as problem solving or decision 
making (McCarthy et al. 1955). The term “AI” is also used to describe the corresponding 
interdisciplinary field of research that draws on computer science, mathematics, philosophy, 
psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, and more (Lenzen  2018). Roughly speaking, AI 
research aims to translate real-­world problems into mathematical ones and then use algo-
rithms to solve them. Current AI-­based systems are often based on machine learning (ML). It 
is called machine “learning” because the way the algorithm progresses from the input to the 
output data is not pre-­programmed, but adaptive and developed through an iterative process 
of feedback, repetitions, and adjustments (El Naqa and Murphy 2022).
AI-­based systems, in particular ML, play a key role in debates on justice and digitalization, as 
they depend on the training and input of data, reproduce patterns contained in these data and 
thus entail the risk of perpetuating and even reinforcing inequalities, marginalization, and 
discrimination. Furthermore, because the operation of many AI-­based systems is not trans-
parent (“black box”), the injustice mirrored by AI systems is very difficult to verify and correct. 
This disproportionately affects already marginalized groups (such as women and BIPoC), who 
remain systematically disadvantaged, for example, due to biased data and higher error rates in 
facial or gender recognition technologies (El Kassar 2022). As the social groups affected are often 
already marginalized and as the systems can have far-­reaching consequences in their applica-
tion, such as job selection or police risk assessment, approaches like feminism that are responsive 
to such injustice are crucial in shaping digital developments in a just way.
Feminist approaches offer helpful knowledge, theories, and tools for identifying and ana-
lyzing different forms of injustice in and through AI-­based systems. But what is meant by a 
feminist lens is extremely polyphonic and far from clear. Feminist ethics is not a single theory. 
Rather, there are a variety of feminist approaches, ranging from liberal to radical positions, and 
adopting a wide range of perspectives. However, there is one recurring theme: an interest in 
(gender) justice. Behind this interest lies the basic feminist assumption that our societies are fun-
damentally characterized by socio-­structural power relations and structural mechanisms of 
oppression (e.g., Young 2011). Feminist approaches aim to create a different kind of perspective 
by integrating questions about (structural) injustice and how to overcome it into its academic 
approach. Besides this ethical and political interest in (gender) justice, feminist approaches often 
share some foundational perspectives, for example concerning ontology and epistemology, and 
some characteristic features, for example intersectionality and context sensitivity.
This chapter shows the relevance of feminist approaches in the context of AI, their con-
nections to AI-­based systems and their specific contributions to the surrounding ethical 
debates. Initially, the question of the relationship between feminist ethics and classical moral 
theories will be addressed. Then, basic feminist ideas about moral agency and epistemology 
and some characteristic features that are shared by feminist theories, such as intersectional-
ity and context sensitivity, will be introduced and contextualized within AI-­based technol-
ogies. At the end of the chapter, some limitations of feminist approaches and a short outlook 
on the future of feminist AI will be drafted.
14.2  Feminist Ethics and Classical Moral Theories
Feminist scholars work within every branch of ethics, such as normative ethics, meta-­ethics, 
and applied ethics. Feminist ethics has a normative ethical dimension as or when it deals with, 
among other things, questions of (in)justice and their moral evaluation. Normative ethical 

--- Page 203 ---

Regina Müller
194
theories reflect on which actions are morally right or wrong and provide normative standards, 
principles or guidelines for determining what actions are right or wrong in moral terms. 
Normative ethical theories are, for example, consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics. 
These normative ethical theories differ in the focus they offer; whereas consequentialism eval-
uates actions based on their outcomes, deontology emphasizes duties and rules, and virtue 
ethics focuses on character traits. The focus offered by feminist ethics is (gender) justice.
Feminist ethics also has meta-­ethical dimensions. Meta-­ethical theories delve into the 
nature and status of moral claims themselves. They seek to understand the meaning, justifi-
cation, and truth of moral claims. Meta-­ethical theories explore questions such as whether 
moral statements are objective or subjective, whether moral truths exist independently of 
human beliefs, and how moral language functions. As feminist ethics seeks to understand 
how social categories, such as gender, are linked with moral knowledge, theories, and terms, 
it also addresses meta-­ethical questions. One underlying idea is to examine, criticize, and 
change ethics for the better by reconsidering ethical theories and approaches (Norlock 2019). 
Feminist scholars therefore debate moral theories such as consequentialism, deontology, and 
virtue ethics. Some reject the classical moral theories because they are rooted in concepts and 
ideas they do not share, such as notions of moral agency. Others criticize the classical moral 
theories but advocate their expansion (Norlock 2019).
As far as consequentialism is concerned, many feminist scholars dispute utilitarianism, in 
particular John Stuart Mill and Harriet Taylor Mill (Morales 2005; Mendus 1994; Ball 1994; 
Annas 1977). Utilitarianism could meet the requirements of feminist thinking, as this moral 
theory is based on the principle that everyone counts equally and that no one’s preferences 
count more than another’s (Norlock 2019). Furthermore, empirical information, relation-
ships, and vulnerabilities could be considered within the utilitarian framework (Norlock 2019). 
Therefore, some authors defend feminist versions of utilitarianism or apply consequentialist 
thinking to feminist issues (Olsson 2018; Gardner 2012; Driver 2005; Tulloch 2005).
At the same time, the idea of impartiality within utilitarian ethical theories is much 
debated among feminist scholars because the idea of impartiality might ignore many aspects 
such as the individual situation, material contexts, emotions, commitments, and caring obli-
gations (Lindemann 2019; Norlock 2019; Driver 2005). Rather than being neutral, impar-
tiality has often meant a privileged position within unequal power structures (Norlock 2019). 
Another reproach is that the seemingly impartial perspective is a Western European perspec-
tive. Other arguments against a utilitarian line of thinking are that consequentialist ethics 
cannot capture forms of oppression or discrimination that have “more benefits than harm” 
and that oppression might be morally bad, irrespective of its consequences (Young 2009). 
Many feminist scholars also argue that the rights and freedoms of women and marginalized 
groups should not be instrumentalized, regardless of the consequences (Norlock 2019).
Feminist scholars critique deontology, for example, for being based on universal principles, 
which are prioritized over material contexts like embodied experiences and relationships 
(Lindemann  2019; Norlock  2019). Additionally, they dispute deontology’s distinction 
­between rationality and emotions, with the latter being considered morally inferior 
(Lindemann  2019, Norlock  2019). In particular, reference is made to Immanuel Kant 
(Sun 2024; Hay 2013; Denis 2002; Schott 1997). Some feminist scholars, however, support 
deontological theories (Varden 2018). Drawing on (political) liberalism, rights theory, and 
deontology, some argue for the same rights for women and other marginalized groups that 
they have been denied historically and seek to extend human rights to women and other 
­marginalized groups, viewing rights as a means to combat gendered and other forms of 
oppression (Norlock 2019). Nonetheless, proponents of human rights or universal moral 

--- Page 204 ---

Feminist Ethics and AI
195
duties are, at the same time, criticized for imposing their cultural perspectives on others, espe-
cially from transnational feminists, scholars of intersectionality, and postcolonial feminists 
(e.g., Khader 2018a, 2018b).
Feminist approaches to virtue ethics have critiqued and revised many aspects of traditional 
virtue ethics. They have highlighted character issues related to unjust social hierarchies, 
uncovered dimensions of women’s lives that have been ignored in classical virtue ethics, iden-
tified virtues necessary to resist oppression and discrimination, and drawn attention to the 
vices of privilege and the exercise of power (Norlock 2019; Berges 2015; Dillon 2012, 2018; 
Friedman 2009). Feminist scholars are interested in the conceptions of character, virtues, and 
vices, and the good life in the context of unjust social structures, such as oppression, domina-
tion, and discrimination (Dillon  2012,  2018; Friedman  2009). Feminist authors ask, for 
example, what virtues can lead to a good life, what hinders or promotes virtues in oppressive 
and discriminatory contexts, and aim to understand character in the context of  unjust 
­hierarchies of power (Norlock 2019; Dillon 2018). Many feminist scholars sympathize with 
virtue ethics and use feminist perspectives, methods, and concepts to revise virtue ethics 
(Norlock 2019). Some theorists argue that character studies are important for feminist work 
and thus use virtue ethics to advance feminist ethics (Dillon 2018). At the same time, feminist 
scholars criticize the idea of a good life within virtue ethics as being too abstract, rational, and 
idealized (Norlock 2019). Furthermore, the list and characterizations of virtues (and vices) are 
androcentric and elitist, ignoring, for example, virtues involved in caring (Okin 1998).
Another criticism is that the focus on the individual character ignores social structures 
and the sociopolitical context in which a character develops or a good life takes place. Some 
examine virtue ethics to understand how dominant conceptions of character, virtue, and the 
good life act in the service of power. Although feminist approaches extend and enrich tradi-
tional virtue ethics, the question “How does virtue ethics look from a feminist point of view[?]” 
(Okin 1998) remains relevant.
As the explanations show, feminist thinking is not tied to any particular branch of ethics or 
specific moral theory. Rather, the relationship between feminist ethics and classical moral the-
ories is complex: feminist scholars examine ethical theories, use them, develop them further 
and sometimes reject them while developing their own ideas. Depending on the interpretation 
of classical moral theories, feminist reasoning is either compatible with different theories, such 
as deontological, utilitarian, and virtue ethics, or not. Like the relationship between feminist 
and classical ethical theories, the relationship between feminist perspectives and ethical 
debates about AI is as complex. Despite this diverse landscape, however, feminist scholars share 
some basic ideas. In what follows, the focus is on some basic feminist ideas, how these feminist 
ideas are connected to AI, and how they can broaden the ethical discourse on AI.
14.3  Basic Feminist Ideas and their Entanglement with AI
14.3.1  Moral Agency: Embeddedness, Embodiment, Emotions
The conditions for moral agency and moral behavior play a central role in debates about AI. 
Technological developments and advances in research have led to situations that require artificial 
systems with moral decision-­making capabilities, such as the moral dilemmas that arise in auton-
omous driving. It is debated whether there can be artificial moral agents and whether moral 
decisions can and should be delegated to machines (see Chapter 29 in this companion).

--- Page 205 ---

Regina Müller
196
In very general terms, moral agency describes the capacity of a being to recognize ethical 
principles or values, make decisions based on them, and take responsibility for their actions. 
Intentionality, rationality, and free will play crucial roles in debating moral agency. Feminist 
conceptions of moral agency have brought different emphases to these debates, as feminist 
scholars often emphasize not only the individual agent, but their embeddedness in social rela-
tions and contexts, such as families, communities or identity groups. Moral agents thus 
operate in social structures, occupy social positions therein and are related to each other, for 
example through responsibilities (e.g., Haslanger 2023; Young 2011). This embeddedness 
enables and, at the same time, limits the actions and decisions of moral agents, for example 
through dependencies. One example is being a parent: the social role of being a mother or 
father and the relationships associated with being a parent create opportunities for action, 
but also parental obligations (Haslanger 2023).
Besides the social embeddedness, feminist approaches underline that moral agents have 
bodies, affects, and emotions (Scully 2023). And because embodiment and emotions influence 
our perspectives, they have to be considered when thinking about moral agency. Feminist 
scholars therefore highlight that the biological fact of embodiment and the social fact of 
embeddedness must be considered within ethical analysis (Scully 2023). The same applies to 
the ethical analysis of AI. Feminist scholars address, for example, how bodies, expressions of 
affects and emotions, and intimate experiences are linked to digital, algorithm-­ and AI-­based 
technologies (e.g., De Vuyst et al. 2022; Adam 1995a). Data feminism, as an example, explic-
itly focuses on emotions and embodiment as one of the ethical principles in the context of 
data sciences (D’Ignazio and Klein 2020). At the same time, feminist research that focuses on 
embodiment is going beyond the question of sex and gender and has expanded into fields such 
as queer studies, disability studies, and critical race theory.
Initially, the digital realm was associated with much hope for connecting with others 
through social media, experimenting with various forms of digital self-­expression and self-­
transformation, and transcending the materiality of the body, for example in cyborg (e.g., 
Haraway 1998), cyber (e.g., Plant 2020) or glitch feminism (e.g., Russel 2020). The potential 
of digital worlds to overcome differences and inequalities and to create online identities that 
are no longer constrained or predetermined by the material environment seemed enormous 
(e.g., Russel 2020; Haraway 1998). Cyborg feminism, for example, a movement from the 
1990s, stands for a nonclosed way of thinking. The image of the cyborg, a hybrid life form, 
neither machine nor organism, neither nature nor artifact, constantly expandable and recon-
figurable, serves as a prime example of this thinking (e.g., Haraway  1998). By merging 
human and machine, cyborg feminism hoped to overcome gender roles and relations. Because 
of new information and communication technologies and new media spaces, the movement 
intended a gender identity that was expanded and constantly changeable through tech-
nology, as well as a diverse, nonfixed subject identity (e.g., Haraway 1998). The movement 
thus drew attention to the significance of technology for the construction of identity and 
gender, criticized patriarchal and heteronormative structures in the development and use of 
technology, and emphasized the need to use technology as a tool for emancipation and social 
change (e.g., Hawthorne and Klein 1999).
These optimistic debates are often underpinned by transhumanist viewpoints celebrating 
digital progress and various forms of human technological enhancement (De Vuyst et al. 2022). 
The dream of the digital world as a place where new identities are created, gender boundaries 
are overcome, and power relations are renegotiated has unfortunately not been fulfilled. In 
contrast, algorithm-­ and AI-­based technologies have the potential to perpetuate power 
­relations and the discrimination which accompanies them. Several studies have documented 

--- Page 206 ---

Feminist Ethics and AI
197
biased algorithms, for example, in the context of online search engines (Noble 2018). Szita 
(2022) has shown, for example, how options for customizing avatars in virtual social spheres 
are limited and linked to rigid notions of body shape, gender, and age.
The question of the meaning or nonmeaning of bodies in the context of digital tech-
nologies such as AI remains one that many feminist scholars address, in particular new 
materialists and posthumanists (e.g., Reichert and Richterich  2015; Braidotti  2013; 
Ferrando 2013; Van Doorn 2011). They address the configuration of the human in these 
debates, the relationship between what is human and nonhuman (e.g., Braidotti 2013), 
and the ways in which embodiment, affects and emotions, relationships, and embedded-
ness are connected to digital, algorithmic, and AI-­based technologies (e.g., De Vuyst 
et al. 2022; D’Ignazio and Klein 2020; Adam 1995a). For example, embodied AI, such as 
robots, raises ethical issues of autonomy, safety, and responsibility. And although AI does 
not (yet) have emotions, ethical concerns arise about its ability to simulate or respond to 
human emotions. This in turn raises ethical questions about trust, manipulation, and the 
authenticity of interactions and relationships between humans and AI. Current feminist 
discourses examine the complex interconnections between AI-­based technologies, bodies, 
and emotions and emphasize the need to consider the social, cultural, and material 
dimensions of body and identity both in the development and application of AI technol-
ogies and within ethical analyses of AI.
14.3.2  Feminist Epistemology
Because AI-­based systems can primarily be understood as epistemic technologies that are 
used in epistemic contexts and manipulate epistemic content through epistemic operations 
(Alvarado 2023), epistemic issues are often discussed in the context of AI. In very general 
terms, epistemology seeks to understand cognitive success that parallels questions about 
knowledge and (its) justification (Steup and Neta 2024). Epistemological questions in the 
context of AI address, for example, how artificial systems acquire, represent, and justify 
knowledge, which in turn is central for their own epistemic status, the epistemic status of 
their output, their explainability and transparency, and related ethical aspects such as trust-
worthiness. Epistemological discussions around AI debate, for example, machine learning-­
based decisions in political fields (see Chapter 8 in this companion), the relationship between 
AI, experts, and laypeople (see Chapter 5 in this companion), or epistemic harm caused by 
AI-­based systems (see Chapter 9 in this companion). Feminist authors bring a certain focus to 
these debates, because they look at the social and political structures within which knowledge 
is created, maintained, and shared.
Feminist epistemology contains a fundamental critique, which is primarily directed 
against established ideas of knowledge and cognition (e.g., Haraway 1998; Harding 1987; 
Longino 1987). It examines the influence of gender and other social factors as well as 
power relations on our knowledge, our insights, and our status as knowers (Dotson 2012; 
Fricker 2007; Code 1981). Feminist epistemology criticizes established understandings 
of epistemic agency, practices, and institutions and often emphasizes epistemic injustices 
in these contexts (e.g., Fricker 2007). Feminist scholars criticize that researchers have 
often developed or continued hierarchical and discriminatory ways of thinking in their 
works and neglected the perspectives and experiences of women and other marginalized 
groups. The aim is therefore to expand knowledge as well as more inclusive knowledge 
practices, for example by including marginalized perspectives or participatory research 
designs.

--- Page 207 ---

Regina Müller
198
Feminist approaches often share a social understanding of knowledge, meaning that 
knowledge emerges in and through social contexts. Knowledge is seen as situated 
(Haraway 1998): it is always embedded in social, historical, and cultural contexts. It is col-
lectively developed, practiced, and shared, and epistemic resources, practices, and institu-
tions are shaped by power relations. Thus, for example, access to epistemic resources, 
opportunities to shape them, and epistemic authority differ for social groups. Feminist 
scholars therefore look to the social, cultural, and political setting of AI and ask how AI sys-
tems represent knowledge, what kind of knowledge, and, in particular, whose knowledge 
(Adam 1995b). They raise awareness that access to AI, ways to shape AI, and representation 
through AI vary for different social groups. 
Feminist standpoint theories even postulate that marginalized or oppressed social groups 
have epistemic unique insights into power structures (Harding 2009; Hartsock 1983). 
Because feminist standpoint theories emphasize that knowledge is contextual and that mar-
ginalized groups often have unique insights that dominant groups cannot access due to their 
privileged position, these theories can help to develop AI-­based systems that incorporate the 
marginalized or oppressed perspectives. For example, feminist standpoint theory could 
encourage the active involvement of BIPoC and their knowledge resources in the development 
of AI-­based systems, to include their perspectives and thus prevent the AI-­based system from 
exhibiting exclusion and bias.
As one feminist epistemological idea is that social identities and social positions determine 
how our epistemic authority, our experiences, and our knowledge are acknowledged by our-
selves and others, feminist scholars often focus on the knowing subject and its identity 
(Adam 2000). And if individuals (or groups) are harmed in their capacity as knowers, this is 
referred to as epistemic injustice (Fricker 2007). Epistemic injustice can manifest in different 
forms but according to Fricker (2007), testimonial and hermeneutical injustices are often 
discussed.1 Several authors have analyzed and developed further forms of epistemic injustice 
(e.g., Bratu and Haenel 2021; Pohlhaus 2012, 2017; Dotson 2012; Anderson 2012) and 
applied them to different settings.
In the context of AI, epistemic injustice is often discussed since AI-­based technologies 
can augment epistemic injustice. Therefore, recent attention has focused very intensely on 
epistemic injustices in the context of AI (Edenberg and Wood 2023; Hull 2023; Symons 
and Alvarado 2022; El Kassar 2022; Stewart et al. 2022; Origgi and Ciranna 2017). The 
authors analyze how certain individuals (or groups) can be harmed by AI-­based systems 
specifically in their capacity as knowers, show that AI-­based systems influence our epi-
stemic practices, structures, and institutions, and demonstrate that algorithms and AI-­
based systems can perpetuate, reinforce or even create new forms of epistemic injustice. 
The studies highlight several areas in which epistemic harm can arise from the data, 
development, design, and application of AI-­based systems, for example automated gender 
recognition (El Kassar  2022), facial recognition (Hull  2023; Kostan  2023), predictive 
policing (Hull 2023; El Kassar 2022), opioid risk scores (Pozzi 2023), language transla-
tion software and search engines (Edenberg and Wood 2023; El Kassar 2022), algorithms 
for placing advertisements (Edenberg and Wood  2023), algorithm profiling and algo-
rithms on social media (Milano and Prunkl  2024; Origgi and Ciranna  2017; Stewart 
et al. 2022), hiring systems, and even so-­called explainable artificial intelligence (Huang 
et al. 2022). Based on the rich and meanwhile very diverse literature on epistemic injus-
tice, the analyses of these authors help us to see and understand different forms of epi-
stemic injustice in the context of AI (for a more detailed analysis, see Chapter 9 in this 
companion).

--- Page 208 ---

Feminist Ethics and AI
199
14.3.3  Intersectionality
Different forms of discrimination or systems of oppression, such as gender or racial 
discrimination, are entangled. The idea of intersectionality draws our attention to these inter-
sections; it reveals that various social categories, such as gender, age, and discrimination, 
based on these categories overlap and thus lead to specific multidimensional experiences of 
discrimination. Although the term had long been used in Black feminist thought, Kimberlé 
Crenshaw popularized the term in 1989 using the metaphor of a crossroads where different 
paths of discrimination intersect to illustrate their interconnectedness (Crenshaw 1989). For 
example, a Black woman can experience the specific and unique form of discrimination at the 
intersection of gender and race that cannot be captured from the perspective of either gender 
or race discrimination alone. By illustrating these intersections, the idea of intersectionality 
describes how different forms of discrimination have mutually reinforcing, interdependent 
effects. Feminist scholars, such as bell hooks (2015) or Patricia Hill Collins (2019), have 
pointed out that these multidimensional forms of discrimination should be considered more, 
for example, in political and ethical analysis.
Intersectional thinking plays an important role in the analyses of AI, as algorithm-­ and 
AI-­based technologies have the potential to perpetuate multidimensional forms of 
discrimination. Several studies have reported intersectional bias within algorithms in the 
context of internet search engines (Noble  2018), AI bots and voice assistants (Chin and 
Robison  2020), recidivism prediction algorithms (Angwin et  al.  2016), automated facial 
analysis algorithms and datasets (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018; Perkowitz 2021), and AI-­
based hiring systems (Huang et al. 2022). For example, Buolamwini and Gebru (2018) have 
shown that Black women are highly misclassified by facial recognition systems because they 
are underrepresented in the database for the system. Huang et  al. (2022) have also 
­demonstrated that intersectional bias within AI-­based recruiting systems can lead to the 
discrimination of groups that fall into a combination of social categories, such as Black 
women. By choosing Black men and white women as candidates, a hiring system would 
­discriminate against Black women. Furthermore, Huang et al. (2022) show that intersec-
tional discrimination is hard to detect, even in so-­called explainable AI.
Against this background, there is growing concern about intersectional bias in AI and its 
impact, especially as the studies and examples indicate that society’s most vulnerable groups 
are disproportionately negatively impacted by such biased AI-­based systems. Accordingly, 
there is a huge debate about the potential benefits of intersectional approaches to AI (e.g., 
Gengler et  al.  2023). Some authors argue, for example, that incorporating intersectional 
approaches can protect vulnerable groups from the risks of biases in the context of AI-­based 
applications (López Belloso  2022). Current approaches, such as data feminism, are now 
informed by intersectional thinking (D’Ignazio and Klein 2020), and several studies in com-
puter science already use intersectionality as a conceptual tool for measuring AI-­fairness in 
machine learning systems (e.g., Foulds et al. 2020; Kearns et al. 2018).
At the same time, the ideas of intersectional fairness are questioned (e.g., Kong 2022). 
Some authors have even called for a step back to be taken in the analyses and discussions, as it 
seems questionable to them whether fair and just AI-­based systems can be created in an unfair 
and unjust society (Birhane 2021). Since AI-­based systems are integrated into social systems 
that are historically shaped by injustices and mirror these injustices, the focus of the discussions 
should move away from technical solutions and the optimization of datasets. Instead, increased 
attention should be paid to the social spheres in which the systems are used, and more focus on 
vulnerable and disproportionately affected communities (Birhane 2021).

--- Page 209 ---

Regina Müller
200
As the idea of intersectionality is rooted in Black feminist thought, many approaches 
(working with intersectionality) to AI-­based technology are informed by Afro-­feminism, Black 
feminism, de-­ or postcolonial feminism, critical race theory, and Whiteness studies. These per-
spectives focus on how race, racialization, racial identities, and colonialism are embedded in 
AI-­based technologies (e.g., Schelenz  2022; Birhane  2020,  2021; Cave and Dihal  2020; 
Benjamin 2019). By emphasizing these aspects, the authors make clear that technologies, 
such as algorithm-­ and AI-­based systems, do not exist in a neutral or value-­free sphere but are 
embedded in social and historical contexts shaped by racism and colonialism. Scholars like 
Birhane and Benjamin highlight that the prevailing structures in the development and imple-
mentation of AI-­based technologies often reproduce racist and colonialist dynamics. The 
authors therefore call for the decolonization of AI (e.g., Birhane and Guest 2021; Murphy and 
Largacha-­Martínez 2022) and the philosophy of technology in general (e.g., Cruz 2021) to 
challenge the deeply embedded power structures and develop alternative approaches for the 
research, development, and design of AI-­based technologies. This includes, for example, 
involving marginalized communities in the AI development process and considering their per-
spectives, more human-­centered approaches (Auernhammer 2020), participatory approaches 
(Birhane et al. 2022), community-­based design (Murphy and Largacha-­Martínez 2022), AI 
that addresses local community needs and interests (e.g., Birhane 2020), and conceptions of 
indigenous data governance and sovereignty (GIDA 2024; Rana 2024; Carroll et al. 2020).
What connects all these approaches is their aspect of intersectional thinking in the context 
of data-­driven and AI-­based technologies. Intersectional thinking can broaden the range of 
perspectives in debates about AI and show how complex the interconnectedness of social cat-
egories, such as gender and race, AI-­based technology, and discrimination, can be.
14.3.4  Thinking about Context and Diversity
As already mentioned, feminist scholars often emphasize the context of technologies and 
their application. Some authors advocate, for example, rethinking AI ethics toward relational 
ethics approaches (e.g., Birhane 2021). Since AI-­based systems never emerge in a social, his-
torical or political vacuum, relational ethics can provide a framework within which to rethink 
the nature of data science and AI-­based systems through a relational understanding of being 
and knowing (Birhane 2021). This perspective shifts the focus to the societal contexts in 
which AI-­based systems are applied, for instance to the economic structures. Feminist 
scholars often examine the current economic structures in which AI-­based systems are devel-
oped and used, as they sustain patterns of social and political domination. For example, access 
to technology and digital education remains limited for many women globally, affecting their 
chances of professional success and social participation (OECD Report 2018).
There is also a significant gender disparity in the AI workforce: “[T]hose designing, coding, 
engineering, and programming AI technologies do not exhibit a diverse demographic” (Collett 
and Dillon 2019). Women and minority racial groups are still significantly underrepresented in 
the tech sector (Nier 2018), impacting both their presence in leadership roles and their involve-
ment in technological research and development (Hupfer et al. 2022; Schneegans et al. 2021).
Against this background and as feminist efforts aim for transformation, feminist approaches 
to AI often call for greater diversity, such as the promotion of women and marginalized racial 
groups to key positions in the research, development, and production of these new technologies. 
Diversification of the AI workforce is seen as a crucial step in developing and implementing 
­technology that is equitable (Collett and Dillon 2019). At the same time, however, it is crucial to 
recognize that not all women and marginalized individuals have equal opportunities.

--- Page 210 ---

Feminist Ethics and AI
201
It should not be overlooked that those most visible in feminist debates on AI are often 
women in privileged positions, for example those with a good education. The discussions are 
predominantly led by white scholars from the Global North. At the same time, low wage 
earners –­ often women from the Global South –­ enable digital developments through their 
mainly invisible work. The workforce is typically poorly paid, works under unfair conditions 
and performs unpleasant tasks such as labelling toxic content (Fairwork 2023; Perrigo 2023). 
In light of such economic exploitation, feminist approaches, such as data feminism, advocate 
taking greater account of the economic context of AI-­based technologies and making invis-
ible work visible (D’Ignazio and Klein 2020). They highlight the need to consider the impacts 
of digital technologies on women in various global contexts and acknowledge the diverse 
experiences of women across different cultural and socioeconomic settings (Gajjala and 
Mamidipudi 2004; Markham 1998). More research and efforts are required to create a sus-
tainable culture of diversity that can be embedded in educational institutions, the work-
place, and the AI workforce in research settings and scientific and public debates (Collett and 
Dillon 2019).
After focusing on the problems that can be amplified and created by AI, some authors turn 
their attention to the possible positive aspects of AI-­based systems, for example the potential 
of AI to promote diversity.
What if, for instance, intelligent machines could help organizations recognize all worthy job 
­candidates by avoiding the usual hidden prejudices that derail applicants who don’t look or sound 
like those in power or who don’t have the “right” institutions listed on their résumés? What if 
software programs were able to account for the inequities that have limited the access of minor-
ities to mortgages and other loans? In other words, what if our systems were taught to ignore data 
about race, gender, sexual orientation, and other characteristics that aren’t relevant to the 
decisions at hand? (Daugtherty et al. 2018)
According to these authors, AI could perform these tasks guided by human specialists who 
create, train, and refine the systems, for example building diversity into AI design by using the 
right data to train AI systems to be inclusive (Daugtherty et al. 2018). However, more research 
is essential to understand and implement diversity in AI contexts. This involves not only using 
diverse datasets but also developing methodologies to ensure that AI systems are fair and 
unbiased. Such research could help address the current limitations and challenges in AI, cre-
ating more inclusive and fair AI systems. At the same time, feminist approaches emphasize 
that technical solutions alone are insufficient; instead, it is necessary to also address the 
social, historical, and political contexts.
14.4  Limitations and Outlook
Feminist ethics can offer transformative insights into debates about AI, emphasizing values 
such as relationality, intersectionality, and sensitivity to social contexts. However, there are 
also limitations to consider when applying feminist theories to AI. Feminist theories are 
diverse, encompassing various frameworks like liberal feminism, radical feminism, and inter-
sectional and postcolonial feminism. These sometimes differing perspectives may lead to 
conflicting values that cannot be uniformly applied to AI. For instance, one feminist approach 
may prioritize individual autonomy, while another emphasizes empathy and care, creating 
tensions in how AI-­based systems are developed and evaluated.

--- Page 211 ---

Regina Müller
202
Feminist ethics often highlights values that are inherently qualitative, relational, and 
­context dependent. These relational and context-­sensitive values may be challenging or 
impossible to quantify and incorporate into AI-­based systems. For instance, encoding “care” 
in an algorithm might be limited by the functionality of machine learning models. The results 
of machine learning systems are the results of processes based on quantified data. Their 
nature is statistical.2 This is one of the reasons why the integration of qualitative values into 
machine learning systems is very difficult. Furthermore, feminist perspectives often reject 
universal, one-­size-­fits-­all approaches, but context-­specific and localized solutions may not 
easily match international and global AI applications. Feminist ethics often demands that AI-­
based systems consider the unique social dynamics of different local communities. However, 
although creating distinct, culturally nuanced algorithms for every region and culture is not 
impossible, it is challenging in a practical sense.
Each of these limitations presents an opportunity to refine and adapt feminist ethics to the 
context of AI, addressing practical and philosophical challenges. Balancing feminist perspec-
tives with AI’s technological demands requires continuous dialogue between ethicists 
(regardless of their moral mindset), developers, users, and policymakers to meaningfully 
incorporate feminist insights into AI contexts.
The richness of feminist thinking on AI highlights the diverse ethical and political dimensions 
of justice in the context of digital technologies. Integrating feminist ethics into AI research and 
development and the identification of barriers to incorporating feminist thinking into AI remain 
central, as recognizing these obstacles is the first step toward overcoming them. This integration 
is not only crucial for addressing current ethical challenges posed by AI but also for ensuring that 
technological advancements contribute to social justice in the future. Reflecting on the broader 
implications of integrating feminist ethics into technological innovations extends beyond AI-­
based systems, promoting a more inclusive and just technological landscape. Moreover, digital 
developments also offer new opportunities for feminist research by facilitating access to digital 
education, information, and the networking of researchers worldwide.
New digital tools and social networks provide avenues through which to raise awareness 
about discrimination, work together and bring about new insights and social and political 
change. Transnational digital solidarity, for example, has been embraced by feminist scholars, 
who leverage technological advancements to support diverse individuals, groups, and com-
munities (e.g., Rahbari 2019). Utilizing online platforms and other digital tools, these scholars 
discuss solidarity, address (gender) inequality and social justice globally, bridge national and 
cultural divides, and foster a sense of global support and unity. Although more research is 
needed to understand what digital solidarity means, in what form and with whom, “[f]uture 
research should aim to be highly collaborative with other work in the field, and should strive 
to be intersectional, pluralistic, interdisciplinary and trans-­sectoral and as international as 
possible” (Collett and Dillon 2019).

15.1  Introduction
As social robots1 play an increasingly significant role in human daily life, there is a growing 
discussion about how to design them in such a way that humans will respond to them posi-
tively and accept them socially (Frennert and Östlund 2014). To gain insights about this facet 
of human–­robot interaction, researchers often turn to human–­human interaction. The hope 
is that such observations can help us understand what the most important aspects of 
human sociality are, which can then contribute to the advancement and improvement of 
human–­robot interaction. For instance, some have recognized how important mimicry is in 
human–­human interaction, and argued on the basis of this that if robots are going to be 
socially accepted by humans, they need to be capable of mimicry (Kahn et al. 2006).
One of the more controversial capacities currently under consideration in this discussion 
is reciprocity. Reciprocity has long been understood as a cornerstone of human social inter-
action (Gouldner 1960; Lorenz et al. 2016), and due to its importance in human–­human 
interaction, it has been brought up as a key design feature for social robots (Fischinger 
et al. 2016; Kahn et al. 2006; Lammer et al. 2014; Lorenz et al. 2016; Sandoval et al. 2015; 
van Wynsberghe  2022). Many have been in favor of implementing reciprocity in social 
robots, as it will likely (so they argue) improve human–­robot interaction (Lorenz et al. 2016; 
Sandoval et al. 2015), but some have warned that such implementation can lead to a decep-
tive relationship (van Wynsberghe 2022).
Throughout this discussion, however, very little has been said of the original function of 
reciprocity. Indeed, as many evolutionary biologists know, reciprocity evolved to foster coop-
eration among human groups, yet this fact has for the most part remained unexplored in the 
robotics literature. In this chapter, I aim to change that. Specifically, I examine what we know 
about the evolution of reciprocity in humans and consider to what extent this knowledge can 
weigh in on discussions about social robots. I argue that the evolutionary account of reci-
procity not only helps deflect van Wynsberghe’s (2022) arguments against using reciprocity 
as a design feature in social robots; it also reveals that reciprocity is a more complex 
phenomenon than is currently represented in the robotics literature. Indeed, there is direct 
Robots, Wrasse, and the Evolution of Reciprocity

Michael T. Dale
212
reciprocity and indirect reciprocity, and robot designers should take both into account if they 
want to most effectively enhance human–­robot relations.
15.2  Social Robots and Reciprocity
In the robotics literature, reciprocity is usually understood along the lines of the following 
doctrine: “We should try to repay, in kind, what another person provided us” (Cialdini 2009). 
Or, perhaps more straightforwardly: “If you do something for me I will do something for 
you” (Sandoval et al. 2015). Importantly, this applies to both positive and negative inter-
actions, so if I do something to harm you, you will treat me negatively in return. (As we 
will see, evolutionary game theory is going to fill this out more, but this is a good starting 
point.)
Many robotics researchers have claimed that because reciprocity is a foundational compo-
nent of human sociality (Gouldner 1960), it will help foster and encourage human–­robot 
interaction. Specifically, Kahn et al. (2006) offer reciprocity as one of six core aspects of 
human life that should be taken into consideration when building human-­like robots. 
Similarly, Lorenz et al. (2016) argue that because reciprocity is a “key mechanism of human 
interaction,” robots that can respond reciprocally will advance human–­robot interaction, 
especially when it comes to robot interaction with adults with neurocognitive impairments, 
such as dementia.
Importantly, the idea that reciprocity will help foster and encourage human–­robot interac-
tion has been supported by empirical data. For instance, Fogg and Nass (1997) found that 
participants were more willing to behave in helpful ways towards a computer when it had 
previously helped them. Participants also “worked longer, performed higher quality work, 
and felt happier” when their relationship with the computer was reciprocal (Fogg and 
Nass 1997, p. 331). Furthermore, Lammer et al. (2014) found that when a care robot behaved 
reciprocally with older participants, the participants perceived the robot more positively and 
accepted it more. There was also an increase in perceived usability and ease of learning. 
Finally, Kahn et al. (2004) found that children have an active interest in engaging reciprocally 
with a robot, and that they preferred interacting with an AIBO robot capable of reciprocity 
over interacting with a toy dog.
Sandoval et al. (2015) extend this discussion by using game theory to help shed light on 
human–­robot interaction.2 Game theory uses models to study strategic interactions between 
individuals. Perhaps the most well-­known game theoretic model is the prisoner’s dilemma, 
which has been used to help figure out how cooperation originally evolved in human popula-
tions. In this dilemma, two thieves are captured by the police, and they must decide what to 
do according to the following rules: “Each player has two choices, namely cooperate or defect. 
Each must make the choice without knowing what the other will do. No matter what the 
other does, defection yields a higher payoff than cooperation. The dilemma is that if both 
defect, both do worse than if both had cooperated” (Axelrod 1984).
By running an iterated computer simulation of this dilemma, it was discovered that the 
best strategy in this kind of dilemma is “tit for tat” (Axelrod 1984). Tit for tat cooperates at 
first, and then continues to copy whatever action the other player does. If the other player 
cooperates, then the two continue to have a cooperative relationship, but if the other player 
defects, tit for tat defects until cooperation starts up again. One of Axelrod’s overarching con-
clusions is that cooperation can evolve through the use of a strategy like tit for tat, as it both 
encourages cooperative relationships and guards against defectors and free riders.

--- Page 220 ---

Robots, Wrasse, and the Evolution of Reciprocity
213
Sandoval et al. (2015) ran a study in which participants engaged in the prisoner’s dilemma 
with robot agents. In line with their predictions, it turned out that tit for tat was the most prof-
itable strategy in interactions between humans and robots, and that human participants 
were equally reciprocal with humans and robots. The authors use this evidence to argue that 
the reciprocal tit for tat strategy is a generally profitable strategy between human and robot 
agents, and robot designers should consider developing robots that adhere to it (Sandoval 
et al. 2015, p. 314).
With all this said, however, some have pointed out the potential dangers of reciprocal rela-
tionships between humans and robots. In particular, van Wynsberghe (2022) argues that 
there are two reasons why reciprocal relationships, and specifically reciprocal care relation-
ships, between humans and robots are deceptive. First, robots that act “reciprocally” are 
designed to deceive humans into believing that they are capable and deserving of reciprocity.3 
However, because they only have basic needs –­ like a charged battery and updated software –­ 
they are not actually capable of reciprocity in the way humans engage in it, which requires 
actively recognizing and responding to another’s needs and interests in a way that fosters a 
bidirectional (as opposed to unidirectional) relationship. As a result, “the robot is able to draw 
the human in to a situation in which the human is deceived into thinking he/she ought to 
reciprocate to the robot the good that the robot has provided them rather than understanding 
that the robot is merely responding to the command it has been given and/or the role it has 
been assigned” (van Wynsberghe 2022, p. 483).
Van Wynsberghe’s second argument comes from the perspective of care ethics, according 
to which reciprocity is an inherently valuable end. In particular, for care theorists, good care 
is fundamentally relational insofar as it is built on individuals responding to each other’s 
needs and interests. And due to its ability to establish and sustain such relationships, reci-
procity should be understood as a value in and of itself that when expressed properly “restores 
power to  …  otherwise vulnerable cohorts” (van Wynsberghe  2022, pp. 481–­482). If 
­reciprocity is inherently valuable, however, then something is going wrong when a robot acts 
reciprocally with a human. As the robot is only using reciprocity as a way to increase its social 
acceptability, reciprocity is being used merely as an instrumental value (van 
Wynsberghe 2022, p. 482).4
The result is an especially deceptive relationship. Indeed, van Wynsberghe draws our 
attention to the “particular kind of deception” when “social robots designed for reciprocity 
use reciprocity as an instrumental value to enhance acceptability of the robot” (van 
Wynsberghe 2022, p. 482). She does not go into much detail here but the issue, I take it, is 
that when robots are using reciprocity instrumentally, they are deceiving humans in a partic-
ularly problematic way because they are using something that is inherently valuable for 
humans to trick the humans into accepting them. It is similar to knowing that someone cares 
deeply about something and lying to them that you also care deeply about it in order to be 
accepted by them socially. Most of us would think that such a deceptive strategy is morally 
wrong, and van Wynsberghe wants to argue that something similar is occurring in reciprocal 
human–­robot interaction.
15.3  The Evolution of Reciprocity
Now that some of the main facets of the discussion surrounding reciprocity in human–­robot 
interaction have been laid out, let’s consider how evolutionary biology might weigh in. To get 
there, we must begin with the evolution of human cooperation. Researchers have long 

--- Page 221 ---

Michael T. Dale
214
­wondered how it is that our species evolved to cooperate, especially when acting altruistically 
towards others can be costly for reproductive fitness. Theories of kin selection revealed to us 
why individuals cooperate with family members; because you share genes with your family 
members, it is advantageous for your genetic fitness for you to further the interests of close kin 
(Hamilton 1964). However, it is apparent that in human (and nonhuman) populations, indi-
viduals often cooperate with others who are not genetically related to them. Thus, additional 
theory was needed.
15.3.1  Direct Reciprocity
One such theory is Trivers’ theory of direct reciprocity.5 Trivers (1971) observed that certain 
species of wrasse are known to clean the parasites off reef fish. As this is obviously dangerous 
for the wrasse –­ they are getting close to, and sometimes inside the mouth of, a potential 
­predator –­ there is a question about why the wrasse would take such a risk. According to 
Trivers, it basically comes down to: I’ll scratch your back if you scratch mine. The wrasse is 
providing a helpful service for the reef fish in exchange for protection and the bits of food they 
find on the reef fish. Observations such as these were the foundation of the theory of direct 
reciprocity: If individuals repeatedly interact with each other, it’s advantageous for A to help 
B if B then helps A later on.
Recall the prisoner’s dilemma. In iterated trials, the most beneficial strategy was to copy 
your partner’s action (“tit for tat”), as it punished defection and often led to many rounds of 
mutual cooperation. This is one of the keys as to why humans behave reciprocally. It is always 
costly to help another individual (who does not share any of your genes), but if they help you 
in the future (when you are in need), then it is worth the cost. And individuals who establish 
and sustain cooperative relationships like this are going to survive and reproduce more than 
individuals who act selfishly.
With all this said, though, there were still many phenomena in nature that the theories 
of kin selection and direct reciprocity could not explain. For example, further observations 
of wrasse and reef fish revealed a more complex situation. Sometimes, instead of taking the 
time to find and eat the parasites and unhealthy tissue on the reef fish, the wrasse would 
simply bite the reef fish and receive a whole mouthful of healthy tissue (Bshary and 
D’Souza 2005). This “cheating” behavior was not very common but when it did occur, 
there were some interesting results. First, the reef fish chased the wrasse, which drew 
attention to their interaction. Second, other reef fish that observed this interaction were 
significantly less likely to offer themselves up for cleaning to the “cheating” wrasse. Which 
is to say, as a result of its actions, the “cheating” wrasse lost out on future cooperative 
relationships.
In addition to these observations in the animal kingdom, further study of different game 
theoretical models revealed that even though tit for tat was a very profitable strategy, and 
allowed cooperative interactions to spread in a population, it was not actually an evolution-
arily stable strategy; that is, it was invadable by other strategies (Boyd and Lorderbaum 1987). 
In particular, a mixture of tit for two tats (which defects only after an opposing player defects 
twice) and suspicious tit for tat (which is similar to tit for tat except that it begins with a defec-
tion) outcompeted tit for tat even when tit for tat was set in a population. Thus, both game 
theory and empirical observation revealed that theories of kin selection and direct reciprocity 
could not fully account for the widespread occurrence of cooperation in human (and non-
human) populations.

215
15.3.2  Indirect Reciprocity
Nowak and Sigmund (1998a, 1998b) showed that the answer to this puzzle was the ability to 
track reputation. Specifically, they introduced the concept of an image score. The image score of 
an individual is reflective of their tendency to engage in cooperative behavior. If they are seen 
doing a cooperative action, their image score increases; if they are seen doing an uncoopera-
tive action, their image score decreases. Through computer simulation, Nowak and Sigmund 
(1998a, 1998b) discovered that a discriminating strategy that cooperated with individuals 
with high image scores, and did not cooperate with those with low image scores, significantly 
outperformed the original tit for tat strategy, and many offshoots thereof.
Furthermore, this concept seems to capture what is happening in the animal kingdom, 
when, for example, the reef fish refuse to cooperate with a wrasse that has been observed 
“cheating.” The image score of the wrasse has decreased, and this results in it having fewer 
opportunities for cooperative exchange. Of course, reef fish are not able to communicate with 
each other about which wrasse to avoid, so this limits the ability of image scores to stabilize 
within populations. However, in human populations, such stabilization is possible through 
gossip. According to Dunbar (2004), gossip evolved in order for members of a social group to 
communicate with each other about potentially noncooperative individuals. This allows indi-
viduals’ image scores to become common knowledge within a population, such that everyone 
knows who would be good to cooperative with and who to avoid. In line with this, when 
Enquist and Leimar (1993) allowed players to communicate with each other about the 
behavior of noncooperative individuals during computer simulations, free riders were much 
less successful and cooperative reciprocation became the dominant form of interaction in the 
population.6
This is the theory of indirect reciprocity. Individuals track the image scores of potential 
cooperative partners, and cooperate only with those who have high image scores. This allows 
cooperative reciprocation to become fixed in populations, and it is one of the key components 
of the evolution of human cooperation.
15.4  Implications for Social Robotics
15.4.1  Robots as Capable and Deserving Reciprocal Agents
Recall van Wynsberghe’s two arguments. She claims, first, that “reciprocal” care relation-
ships7 between humans and robots are deceptive because robots are deceiving humans into 
believing that they are capable and deserving of reciprocity, when in fact they are not. Second, 
she maintains that these relationships are deceptive because robots are instrumentally using 
something inherently valuable to humans –­ namely reciprocity –­ in order to trick humans 
into socially accepting them. The evolutionary model just put forward will prove useful in the 
discussion of van Wynsberghe’s second argument. But before we get there, I want to engage 
with her first argument, as doing so will help fill out the overall narrative in such a way that 
will prove important for addressing her second argument.
Accordingly, I first want to argue that robots, in fact, are capable and deserving of reci-
procity, even by van Wynsberghe’s own standards. To understand why, let’s look more closely 
at how van Wynsberghe (via care theory) defines a reciprocal care relationship. In such a 
relationship, the element of responsiveness is important. Responsiveness “re-­calibrates care 
from a unidirectional action to a bidirectional practice in which care-­givers are both attentive 

--- Page 223 ---

Michael T. Dale
216
to the particular needs of care-­recipients as well as being attentive to if, when, and how such 
needs are met” (van Wynsberghe 2022, p. 481). Thus, in a reciprocal care relationship, there 
must be an understanding that care is not one-­sided, and that both individuals have a role to 
play in the care process. This enables each to recognize and respond to the other’s needs and 
interests.
Importantly, it is through this responsive process that reciprocal relationships can “[restore] 
power to … otherwise vulnerable cohorts” (van Wynsberghe 2022, p. 482). Indeed, if the care 
recipient is seen as having an active role in the care process, it is much less likely that a power 
imbalance will develop that could lead to the exploitation or harm of the care recipient, 
and  much more likely that the care recipient has their needs adequately recognized and 
responded to.
I believe that this type of relationship is also possible in human–­robot care relationships, 
and it is possible because both the human and the robot have interests and needs.8 Of course, 
by an “interest,” I do not necessarily mean a conscious interest or a morally salient interest, 
such as the interest in avoiding suffering (which is something that humans have but robots do 
not). I mean something much more basic, that does not need to rise to the level of awareness. 
A raccoon can be said to have an interest in survival, eating berries, and keeping its fur clean. 
Similarly, a robot can be said to have an interest in keeping its battery charged and its software 
up to date, and it can even be said to have an interest in carrying out its goals,9 for example 
caring for the (human) care recipient successfully in such a way that the care recipient is sat-
isfied with the robot’s care and continues to thrive under the robot’s care.10
In his recent Uehiro lectures, Railton (2022) agrees that robots can have interests in this 
way. He points out that when a robot pursues a certain goal, it can be said to have an interest 
in achieving that goal.11 Like I am, he is careful to state that such interests are not (neces-
sarily) enough to give the robot status as a moral agent, but they are enough to give the robot 
the ability to engage in social relations with humans. Railton mentions a few different social 
relations but I am only interested in one: Reciprocity. If the robot has an interest in respond-
ing to the needs and interests of the human care recipient, and the human has an interest in 
responding to the robot’s needs and interests –­ as thwarting such needs and interests would 
negatively affect the ability for the robot to carry out its duties, which, in turn, would nega-
tively affect the human’s own care –­ then it can be said that the robot and human engage in a 
reciprocal care relationship.12
It is also apparent that such human–­robot reciprocal care relationships can “[restore] 
power to … otherwise vulnerable cohorts” (van Wynsberghe 2022, p. 482). Most clearly, the 
robot as care giver can empower the human as care recipient insofar as it adequately recog-
nizes and responds to the needs and interests of the human, and acts in such a way that 
encourages a bidirectional care relationship. Perhaps more interestingly, though, the robot 
can be seen as a vulnerable party in such situations, even if it is the care giver, as robots are 
traditionally understood as lacking respect and moral standing.13 Thus, through engaging in 
a reciprocal relationship with the robot, the human care recipient can empower the robot in 
a way that robots have historically been deprived of.
At this point, van Wynsberghe might be willing to grant that a robot is capable of a care 
relationship in this way, but still claim that it is “not an entity deserving of reciprocity” (van 
Wynsberghe 2022, p. 483). However, if it is true that the robot has needs and interests in the 
way I described, and it is capable of engaging in a bidirectional, reciprocal relationship with a 
human, I do not see any reason to think that the robot is not deserving of reciprocity. We 
believe that our pets are deserving of reciprocity, and yet they are even less capable of bidirec-
tional care relationships. So why should we exclude robots?

--- Page 224 ---

Robots, Wrasse, and the Evolution of Reciprocity
217
Perhaps, one might say, because they lack emotions. Indeed, humans feel genuine care for 
those that they are engaged in reciprocal relationships with. That is, when a care giver acts 
kindly towards a care recipient, that care recipient experiences a feeling of gratitude towards 
the care giver and a desire to respond in kind. However, as a social robot is not able to experi-
ence emotion, such feelings simply are not there. Thus, a care relationship between a robot 
care giver and a human care recipient is a different kind of relationship.
I agree that this changes the dynamics of the relationship in some ways, but it does not 
change the robot’s deservingness.14 If we were to engage in a reciprocal relationship with 
some other socially intelligent being incapable of emotion, I think very few of us would claim 
that such a being is not deserving of reciprocity. Think, for example, of Spock or Data from 
Star Trek. Or consider autistic and psychopathic individuals, who are commonly understood 
as lacking emotional capacities. All of these beings are capable of engaging in reciprocal rela-
tionships that recognize and respond to the interests and needs of another, and as a result, 
most of us would accept that they are deserving of reciprocity.15 Social robots are no 
different.16
15.4.2  Reciprocity as an Instrumental Value
With this argument laid out, we can now return to van Wynsberghe’s second point. In 
particular, human–­robot reciprocal relationships are deceptive in an especially egregious way 
because robots are instrumentally using something inherently valuable to humans –­ namely 
reciprocity –­ in order to trick humans into socially accepting them.
This is where evolutionary game theoretical models become important. Because of these 
models, we now have a plausible understanding of the evolutionary foundations of reci-
procity. Specifically, reciprocity was a behavioral tool used to increase one’s image score 
within a population. This understanding of reciprocity is important because it reveals another 
way of conceptualizing the value of reciprocity. In particular, under this evolutionary 
account, reciprocity is instrumentally valuable. Indeed, the reason why we evolved to treat peo-
ple well in return for them treating us well is to improve our standing with that particular 
person (resulting in a more robust cooperative relationship) and to build our reputation 
within the community as a cooperative, reciprocating person. This results in a stronger net-
work of friendships and political alliances –­ which increases survival –­ and higher reproduc-
tive success.17
Of course, this does not give us a reason to doubt the care theorist’s account. It is certainly 
plausible that reciprocity has inherent value due to its importance in relational care, and, in 
fact, I want to grant that it does. However, this does not mean that reciprocity does not also 
have instrumental value, in the way suggested by the evolutionary account.18 Indeed, the two 
accounts can (and should) exist alongside each other. That is, reciprocity originally evolved as 
an instrument to increase reproductive fitness.19 Since then, however, philosophical reflection 
has enabled us to understand that reciprocity also has inherent value, especially as it pertains 
to relational care.20
It might help here to introduce a well-­known distinction in evolutionary theory: The dis-
tinction between a proximate cause and a distal cause (Tinbergen 1963). A proximate cause 
is an event that is immediately responsible for some observed result. A distal cause, on the 
other hand, is the deeper (and often evolutionary) cause for the observed result. So, adopting 
this causal language for the reasons why humans act reciprocally, the proximate reason we act 
reciprocally is our desire to respond to the needs and interests of others when they are 
responding positively to our own needs and interests.21 The distal reason, however, is that we 

--- Page 225 ---

Michael T. Dale
218
want to increase our reputational image score within a population. Of course, we may not be 
aware of the distal reason for our actions when we act reciprocally, but that does not take 
away from the fact that it is the underlying, evolutionary cause of our actions.22
With this distinction in mind, consider again reciprocity in human–­robot relationships. 
Van Wynsberghe is correct that if social robots are to behave reciprocally, the distal reason 
they will be doing so is to make themselves more socially acceptable to humans. In this way, 
they will be using reciprocity as an instrument to increase social acceptance. However, we 
now know that a similar story can be told for why humans evolved to engage in reciprocal 
relationships. They did so to increase their image scores and, in turn, their reproductive fit-
ness. Of course, van Wynsberghe will claim here that even though this might be the reason 
reciprocity originally evolved (i.e., the distal reason), it now has further, inherent value. But 
what I am claiming is that the same thing can be said of human–­robot reciprocity. The distal 
reason robots became reciprocal was to (instrumentally) increase their social acceptability, 
but once they engaged in certain reciprocal relationships (for example, care relationships), 
such relationships became inherently valuable in the same way that reciprocal care relation-
ships between humans are.
Of course, this argument would not go through if it were not, in fact, the case that robots 
were capable of reciprocal relationships. But as we saw in section 15.4.1, they are. Indeed, 
they are just as capable of developing and sustaining a bidirectional relationship in which 
they recognize and respond to the needs and interests of others as humans are. Thus, in the 
context of value, we should think about their reciprocal relationships in the same way we 
think about human reciprocal relationships.23 In both, the distal reasons they engage in 
reciprocal relationships are instrumental, and in both, the proximate reasons they engage in 
reciprocal relationships contribute to their inherent value.24 Which is all to say, if van 
Wynsberghe wants to claim that human–­robot reciprocal relationships are deceptive, she will 
have to maintain that human–­human reciprocal relationships are similarly deceptive.
15.4.3  The Importance of Indirect Reciprocity for Social Robots
As discussed in the introduction, many have argued that direct reciprocity is crucial for 
human–­robot interaction because of how important it is for human sociality (Kahn 
et al. 2006; Lorenz et al. 2016; Sandoval et al. 2015). Indeed, humans regularly engage in 
directly reciprocal relations with each other, and thus it seems clear that if a robot is capable 
of direct reciprocity, it will increase the chances of that robot being socially accepted by 
humans. Preliminary empirical data support this idea (Fogg and Nass 1997; Kahn et al. 2004; 
Lammer et al. 2014).
However, as we just learned, the full picture of human reciprocity is more complex than 
this. Humans not only engage in directly reciprocal relations; they also track the behaviors of 
potential cooperative partners, and discriminately decide to cooperate with those with a his-
tory of cooperative behavior. Because this is an important aspect of human sociality, and 
human sociality is crucial to finding out how best to advance human–­robot relations, I want 
to suggest that both direct and indirect reciprocity need to be taken into account by robotics 
researchers and designers when they are developing social robots.
To begin to see why, consider the following example. Sam is a (human) friend of yours who 
will help you in return for helping him. However, you also observe that Sam is easily exploited 
by those who want to take advantage of him. Some help him a little bit in exchange for a lot 
of help from him. Others exploit him and then later on, once they return, Sam does not seem 
to remember being exploited by them and attempts to help them –­ only to be exploited once 

--- Page 226 ---

Robots, Wrasse, and the Evolution of Reciprocity
219
again. Moreover, he does not observe or respond to the cooperative relationships of those 
around him. He does not see that he should probably refuse to cooperate with someone who 
regularly cheats others, or someone else who cooperates with humans with particular char-
acteristics (e.g., a certain skin color) but treats those without such characteristics poorly. He 
also does not want to help those who are regularly cooperative more than those who are reg-
ularly uncooperative, which ends up lessening the incentive for anyone to be cooperate within 
the social group. Finally, he does not refuse to cooperate with those who are uncooperative, 
which might otherwise encourage them to become more cooperative.
Clearly, something is off with Sam. He does not seem to understand how most humans 
interact socially, and his actions lead to him and others in the group being exploited more 
often (and perhaps even a breakdown in the group’s social dynamics). Of course, social robot 
capacities are currently nowhere near the level of an adult human, so some of Sam’s deficits 
won’t necessarily be important to understanding current advancements in human–­robot 
interaction. However, I want to argue that this example is still suggestive as to why it is impor-
tant to consider indirect reciprocity for this generation of social robots (and those of the 
immediate future).
Specifically, Heerink et al. (2010) assert that some of the most important factors in the 
acceptance of (current and near future) social robots are perceived social presence, perceived 
sociability, attitude, and trust. Perceived social presence is the amount to which a human feels 
that they are dealing with a social entity when they are interacting with a robot. Perceived 
sociability is the degree to which a human perceives that a robot is capable of social behavior.25 
Attitude consists of the positive and/or negative feelings a human holds towards a robot, and 
trust is the degree to which a human intends to listen and adhere to a robot’s advice.
I want to argue that a robot’s ability to engage in indirectly reciprocal relations can improve 
social acceptance in all these ways. To see how, let’s consider an in-­depth example of a care 
robot in a hospital. This care robot’s patient has a friend in the hospital (say another patient) 
who often comes to visit her. When the friend is around, the patient’s mood improves, she 
laughs more, and she seems more optimistic. If the robot is capable of indirect reciprocity, it 
will be able to recognize this, act positively towards the friend, and encourage a relationship 
between the patient and the friend. As a result, it seems very likely that the patient’s trust and 
attitude towards the robot would improve, as the patient will appreciate that the robot under-
stands (and encourages) some of her important social relationships. Moreover, because the 
patient will see that the robot has a fairly nuanced understanding of the social dynamics 
within the hospital (indeed, much more nuanced than a robot only capable of direct reci-
procity), the patient will perceive the robot as more socially present and sociable.
Let’s also say that there are two nurses who treat the patient differently. One nurse is espe-
cially caring and understanding, while the other nurse is curt and neglectful. If the care robot 
is capable of indirect reciprocity, it will be able to recognize the different nurse responses, 
support the caring nurse, and perhaps alert the curt nurse to the way he is acting. In response 
to the robot’s behavior, the patient will likely appreciate that the robot is understanding the 
complexities of social situation and advocating on her behalf within the hospital. This will 
increase trust, attitude, social presence, and sociability.
Finally, during one especially painful week, the patient is rude and abusive towards the care 
robot. Now, if it were the case that the robot were not capable of indirect reciprocity, then the 
robot would simply resume normal (reciprocal) operations with the patient afterwards. While 
the patient may appreciate this in some ways (e.g., in not having to apologize or explain her 
previous behavior), it is not likely that she will have much respect for the robot as a social 
entity. As a result, perceived social presence and sociability will be low. On the other hand, if the 

--- Page 227 ---

Michael T. Dale
220
robot is able to track such actions and respond to them (perhaps resulting in some acknowl-
edgment, discussion, or apology from the patient), it is much more likely that the patient will 
see the robot as a social agent.
Once again, I want to acknowledge that indirect reciprocity is complex, and it may be some 
time before social robots are capable of it in a similar way that an adult human is. But this 
does not change the fact that any step towards being more indirectly reciprocal will likely 
improve levels of social acceptance in the ways suggested. Indeed, small steps matter, and 
they do so insofar as they increase levels of trust, attitude, social presence, and sociability.
15.5  Conclusion
In this chapter, I argued that the evolutionary account of reciprocity has two important 
upshots for current discussions in social robotics. First, it helps deflect arguments against 
using reciprocity as a design feature in social robots. Second, it reveals that social robots 
should be capable of both direct and indirect reciprocity if we want them to be socially 
accepted by humans. Indeed, due to its importance in human sociality, it is difficult to believe 
that models of indirect reciprocity won’t play an increasingly significant role in the research 
literature.
As AI continues to become more complex and sophisticated, and we get closer to devel-
oping robots that have social capacities at or near the levels of adult humans, researchers will 
need an increasingly nuanced understanding of all social capacities proposed as design fea-
tures. This chapter can be used as a model for one currently underappreciated perspective. 
Specifically, in considering the evolutionary origins of human social capacities, we are 
provided with a valuable perspective that can advance discussions about which capacities 
should be implemented in social robots and why it is important to implement them.
