16.1  Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a topic of great current interest but what the public interest 
mostly focuses on is AI’s results. For example, ChatGPT produces text and even poems as well 
as code. This seems impressive –­ it even seems intelligent. However, breaking it down, AI is a 
“branch of computer science that attempts to replicate human problem-­solving procedures 
on computers in order to achieve new or more efficient task solutions” (Lämmel and 
Cleve 2008, p. 14).1 The unsupervised algorithms used in this branch of computer science 
can recognize patterns in large datasets. These patterns are not as easily identified by humans, 
which is why the algorithmic results are perceived as helpful.
Algorithms are used to extract knowledge, perceived as valuable, from large datasets 
(Mitchell 1997, p. 1). Thus, algorithmic results are only interpreted data. “Data by itself has 
no value. However, the extraordinary value-­adding potential of data lies in the ability to 
extract meaningful and actionable information from it” (Shah et al. 2020, p. 110). Data is 
valuable because of its potential to create new knowledge through its interpretation. And any 
AI result can only be produced because of training on large amounts of data. That is why 
everything is being recorded and made into data –­ what we call datafication.
Datafication turns individuals into data sources and prevents them from controlling their 
own data. This involuntary loss of control seems ethically questionable. That is why I argue 
that ethical considerations should be integrated in the design of datafication. In this chapter, 
I analyze whether Beauchamp and Childress’ Principles of Biomedical Ethics (PBE) can be 
helpful in ethically designing datafication. I discuss the objection by Mittelstadt (2019) that 
the principles were originally developed for the biomedical field and are not transferrable to 
the digital sector. I also debate the difficulty of application for the PBE. I find that the PBE is 
still an important approach in digital ethics, because Beauchamp and Childress’ principles 
support all three predominantly used moral theories. In addition, there is a lack of alternative 
ethical methods that are suitable for evaluating datafication.
As a solution, I discuss additions to the principles but it turns out they are not necessary. In 
spite of the difficulties of application, I use the biomedical principles to identify ethical issues 
Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles 
of Biomedical Ethics

Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles of Biomedical Ethics

in datafication. The PBE dictate that in order to facilitate the ethical design of datafication, the 
principles of respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice should be real-
ized. I highlight that this realization depends on informing and empowering data sources. In 
this way, I show that despite their problems, the PBE can be helpful in ethically evaluating 
datafication.
16.2  Datafication
Datafication is the process of making something into data (Mejias and Couldry 2019, p. 1). 
Data is created by abstracting the world into representational forms, such as numbers, 
­characters, and symbols (Kitchin  2014, p.  1). Thus, datafication is the “... conversion of 
qualitative aspects of life into quantified data ...” (Ruckenstein and Schüll 2017, p. 262). 
Historically, datafication was first applied in analogue population management and 
­bureaucratic organization (Flensburg and Lomborg  2021, pp.  1–­2). People and their 
­properties were listed on paper, in order to maintain an overview. So, quantitative aspects of 
life have been converted into data for many years. Since digitization made the conversion 
of analogue values into digital formats possible, datafication also denotes the conversion of 
qualitative aspects of life into digital data.
Through datafication in the context of digitization, many aspects of human life –­ from 
­diseases to emotional responses –­ can be turned into data. For example, the use of digital 
­communication platforms enables the conversion of personal information into data about 
friendships, interests, and emotional responses. In this way, individuals become data sources.
Essentially, the term datafication denotes the making of data by abstracting quantitative 
and qualitative aspects of life. But in the context of digitization, the collection of all that data 
also enables the derivation of knowledge through data analysis and therefore supposedly2 
allows for the generation of new value (Kitchin  2014, p.  1; Mejias and Couldry  2019, 
pp. 1–­3). Data is analyzed by searching for patterns. Therefore, if for example the same drug 
is given to several patients and it shows different results, a pattern in the data could explain 
the difference. Maybe the patients had different symptoms and the drug only responded to 
certain symptoms or maybe the drug worked better for patients of a certain age. Digitization 
makes the analysis of vast amounts of data easier (Altintac 2022, p. 5; Harwardt 2022, pp. 3, 
15; Klenk et al. 2020, p. 5; Donges 2022, pp. 212–­213), since this pattern recognition can be 
supported by algorithms that are designed to find patterns.
Thus, data analysis enables a data processor to find explanations for irregularities in the 
data and in quantitative as well as in qualitative aspects of life. The data itself does not have 
much worth without the ability to make sense of it. That is why I argue that data analysis is 
part of the definition of datafication in the context of digitization. Datafication is the 
conversion of quantitative and qualitative aspects of life into data, which is done by abstract-
ing the world into representational forms, enabling the derivation of knowledge and creation 
of new value through data analysis (Figure 16.1).
The natural persons, whose quantitative and qualitative aspects of life are abstracted 
into representational forms and turned into data, become data sources. For the data 
sources, it is mostly opaque what data is created about them and for what purposes they 
are analyzed (Vallor 2016, p. 10). “Even for willing subjects, the amount of time and effort 
required to attain the background knowledge and skills to understand the totality of data 
held about oneself may easily be overwhelming” (Mittelstadt and Floridi 2016, p. 330). 
However, the persons or institutions that create the data and carry out the analyses –­ the 

--- Page 233 ---

Antonia Kempkens
226
data processors –­ have full knowledge and control about what happens with the sources’ 
data. That is why there is an imbalance of control between the data sources and the data 
processors.
16.3  Ethical Evaluation
In order to analyze whether this imbalance of control in a datafication process is ethically 
problematic, we need to choose an ethical method. I argue that Beauchamp and Childress’ 
PBE offer four moral principles that can serve as conditions for ethical datafication 
(Beauchamp and Childress 1979):
•	 respect for autonomy
•	 beneficence
•	 nonmaleficence
•	 justice.
These moral principles are not ranked and they provide an important common basis for moral 
judgments. The principles were developed as “a common set of ethical principles” (Beauchamp 
and Childress 2019, p. 9) for a consequentialist as well as a deontological approach. “These 
principles aim to articulate general values on which everyone can agree, and to function as 
practical guidelines” (Whittlestone et  al.  2019, p.  196). The principles were originally 
established for and derived from bioethical discourse and practice. Nowadays, they are also 
used in the context of digital ethics (Floridi and Cowls 2021; Jobin et al. 2019; Ryan and 
Stahl 2021).
According to Mittelstadt, however, the PBE cannot simply be transferred to digital ethics 
because, unlike in the field of medicine, there are no common goals in the development of 
digital services, such as promoting the health and well-­being of patients. This transforms 
ethical decision making from a cooperative to a competitive process (Mittelstadt 2019, p. 3). 
Implicit solidarity in medicine is formally recognized in legally established fiduciary duties. 
Such duties are still lacking in the development of digital services, which is why users of 
digital services cannot trust developers to act in their best interests when implementing 
ethical principles in practice (Mittelstadt 2019, p. 3). In addition, the field of digitalization 
lacks a professional history and norms developed from it. In medicine, moral duties and

virtues have developed over centuries, so that negligent practices can be identified –­ the four 
bioethical principles of Beauchaump and Childress are helpful here (Mittelstadt 2019, p. 4). 
The use of digital services in all kinds of contexts and the inability to reliably predict the 
impact of development decisions undermine the creation of standards for being a “good” AI 
developer or requirements for “good” digital services (Mittelstadt 2019, p. 5).
In addition, the development of digital services lacks proven methods for putting principles 
into practice. While mechanisms such as professional associations and bodies, ethics review 
boards, accreditation and licensing systems, peer self-­governance and codes of conduct have 
been developed in medicine, there are no comparable empirically tested methods for putting 
principles into practice in real contexts in the development of digital services. This is a com-
plex methodological challenge that is usually discarded for reasons of efficiency 
(Mittelstadt 2019, pp. 6–­7).
Furthermore, there is a lack of robust legal and professional accountability mechanisms in 
the area of digitalization. In the medical field, “bad” behavior leads to professional sanctions, 
such as the loss of a license to practice, so that medical staff have a strong incentive to fulfill 
their fiduciary duties and patients can assert their claims against negligent professionals 
(Mittelstadt 2019, p. 7). In the area of digital service development, there are fines for data 
processors who violate the GDPR but in most countries, there is no license required to process 
data –­ so you cannot lose your license (Mittelstadt 2019, pp. 7–­8).
I agree with the differences between the medical field and the digital sector that Mittelstadt 
makes, but I disagree with his conclusion. Just because common goals, duties, standards, and 
accountability mechanisms are lacking in datafication, the bioethical principles are not use-
less. On the contrary, it is because the digital sector is not well regulated yet that we are in 
desperate need of ethical principles for guidance. With Mittelstadt, one could argue, that the 
principles alone are not enough, since we need common goals, duties, standards, and account-
ability mechanisms in the digital sector too. But that does not mean that the bioethical prin-
ciples are not helpful in trying to design datafication ethically.
The philosopher Rafael Capurro would disagree with Mittelstadt as well, since he argues 
that digital ethics is closely related to biomedical ethics, because in both “... ethical issues of 
information and communication ...” (Capurro 2017, p. 278) are raised. The digital ethicists 
Floridi and Cowls would agree with Capurro, since they are of the opinion that bioethics is 
similar to digital ethics in terms of the ecological handling of new forms of agents, patients, 
and environments (Floridi and Cowls 2021, p. 9). In an earlier work, Floridi argues that 
information ethics shares with biomedical ethics “... the same patient-­oriented approach” 
(Floridi  2013, p.  71). This means, in the terms of this chapter, that biomedical ethics is 
concerned with how patients should be treated and information ethics is concerned with how 
data sources are treated. In both cases, the concern is with a vulnerable group of people 
which is in danger of losing control over the processes that are to be ethically evaluated. In a 
medical context, patients are dependent on information from medical staff while in a context 
of information processing, which could be a digital context, data sources are dependent on 
information from data processors.
If the ethics of the digital sector is similar to the ethics of the medical field, does that mean 
that the biomedical principles are transferrable to datafication? These four principles have 
been developed to enable quick decisions to be made under pressure in everyday clinical 
practice (Beauchamp and Childress 2019, p. 9). It is questionable whether quick decisions are 
necessary for ethical design of datafication. When deciding on a design for datafication, there 
is enough time to consider where to get the data from and how to inform and involve the data 
sources –­ there are no lives dependent on a quick decision. But the possibility to come to a 

--- Page 235 ---

Antonia Kempkens
228
decision quickly is not the only criterion of application for the principles: “We appeal to them 
primarily in deliberation and justification in novel situations (e.g. involving a new technology), 
in uncertain or ambiguous circumstances, and in outright moral conflicts” (Beauchamp and 
Childress 2019, p. 10).
I argue that datafication in the context of digitization is still a novel situation, especially 
since new technological approaches are developed continuously, causing uncertain 
circumstances. For example, the storage of data has to be improved frequently in order to 
protect it from misuse by unauthorized persons. This is where moral conflicts arise regularly 
between the (in)adequate protection of data and the benefits of its processing. This is just one 
example of where the principles could be helpful for the ethical design of datafication.
16.4  Difficulties of Applicability
According to Mittelstadt, there is another problem with using the bioethical principles in a 
digital context, since there is a lack of proven methods for putting principles into practice in 
the development of digital services (Mittelstadt 2019, p. 9). The applicability in practice is a 
concern with the PBE approach in general (Attfield  2020, p. e427; Beauchamp and 
Childress 2019, pp. 10–­11).
The first issue with the applicability of the PBE is interpretation of the principles (Jobin 
et al. 2019, p. 391). In addition, there can be different meanings of one principle. For example, 
nonmaleficence can mean “... security, safety, harm, protection, precaution, prevention, 
integrity (bodily or mental), non-­subversion” (Jobin et al. 2019, p. 395). Even though the 
same principle is being used, it can be interpreted differently, there can be different reasons for 
why this principle is important, it can be applied to different issues or pertain to different 
actors, and there can be a diverse understanding of how it should be implemented (Jobin 
et al. 2019, p. 396).
Principles alone are not sufficient for protection against the harm caused by datafication: 
“In order to be useful in practice, principles need to be able to guide action –­ to help people 
navigate the competing demands and considerations of concrete situations” (Whittlestone 
et al. 2019, p. 196). Principles that are too general cannot guide concrete action, but specific 
principles are limited to one sector.
One solution for this dilemma is defining principles precisely, including instructions for 
their application (Whittlestone et al. 2019, pp. 196–­197). The philosophers Ryan and Stahl 
would agree: “On their way to being truly practicable, guidelines also need to go even further 
into detail than we have and at least provide pointers to ways of realizing and implementing 
normative statements” (Ryan and Stahl 2021, p. 77). Guidelines that consist of principles 
should be more detailed and provide instructions for how the principles ought to be imple-
mented. This way, the first issue with the applicability of the PBE could be solved.3
The second issue with the applicability of the PBE is the conflict between the principles. 
Jobin et al. found in their study that in practice, there is uncertainty concerning the choice of 
principles, especially when there are conflicting principles (Jobin et  al.  2019, p.  396). 
Principles can be in conflict if one has to be sacrificed in order to fulfill another. For example, 
if we want to find the best medical treatments and achieve better public health, we need a lot 
of sensitive health data from patients. Thus, patient autonomy is in conflict with the principle 
of beneficence for humankind.
Balancing conflicting principles against each other requires quantifying their moral 
weight which can lead to questionable suggested actions  –­ such as conducting medical 

--- Page 236 ---

Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles of Biomedical Ethics
229
research on a patient without their consent because of benefits to society (Veatch 1995, 
pp. 209–­210). Another possible solution would be ranking the principles “... so that one 
­principle must be completely satisfied before another is allowed to come into play” 
(Veatch  1995, p.  210). While balancing the principles allows for too many questionable 
decisions, ranking the principles would be too strict. That is why Veatch combines these two 
approaches. He suggests that we should “... rank the aggregate effect of the nonconsequentialist 
principles over the consequence-­maximizing ones” (Veatch  1995, p.  211), while the 
nonconsequentialist principles (respect for autonomy and justice) as well as the consequence-­
maximizing principles (beneficence and nonmaleficence) are balanced amongst each other 
with equal weight.
Prioritizing the principle of respect for autonomy over beneficence and nonmaleficence 
opens the PBE up to criticism concerning “the over-­emphasis of individualism” (Häyry 2003, 
p.  202). For example, the philosopher Daniel Callahan suggests that the principles of 
autonomy are already in a favored position, even without the ranking: “The individualism 
underlying principlism4 is best seen in the central place given to autonomy” (Callahan 2003, 
p. 288). This supposed emphasis of autonomy is criticized because in reality “... we are not 
isolated, autonomous individuals ...” (Callahan 2003, p. 288), because “in resource-­poor 
­settings, which have to do with social justice” (Azétsop and Rennie  2010, p.  1) the 
­individualistic approach is not helpful and because this picture of an individualistic society is 
not transferable to other cultures (Azétsop and Rennie 2010, p. 1; Callahan 2003, p. 288).
But Beauchamp and Childress explicitly decided not to rank the PBE: “Every moral ­principle 
can, in our account, be overridden in some situations by a competing moral consideration” 
(Beauchamp and Childress 2019, p. 11). For example, the PBE would have agreed to the 
restriction of autonomy through the COVID-­19 quarantine, because the beneficence of that 
measure for the vulnerable people in society has overridden the individual autonomy in that 
case. “... respect for autonomy is always relevant as a prima facie principle, along with other 
prima facie principles, but it has no more and no less weight than the others in the abstract” 
(Beauchamp and Childress 2019, p. 11).
Still, it can sometimes be less clear which principle should be overridden. According to 
Whittlestone et al., the tension between conflicting principles in the digital context can be 
resolved by making a distinction between contexts in which a technology may be used and 
contexts in which it should not be used (Whittlestone et al. 2019, p. 199). This approach is 
being pursued by the EU AI Act passed in April 2024. Here, AI applications are regulated 
differently depending on the area of application. In very sensitive contexts, the use of AI 
algorithms is prohibited; in less sensitive contexts, well-­tested AI algorithms may be used 
(European Parliament 2024). Applied to the healthcare sector, for instance, this would mean 
that, for example, the patient notes of a psychologist should not be made into data for 
processing. This is because the notes are very personal and therefore hard to anonymize and 
they could also be used against the patients because of the stigma of psychological illness.5 By 
prohibiting, or at least restricting, datafication in very sensitive contexts, like psychotherapy, 
the second issue with the applicability of the PBE could be solved.
16.4.1  Lack of Alternatives
The philosophers Clouser and Gert localize the issue of the missing guidance by the PBE in the 
lack of a moral theory: “Since there is no moral theory that ties the ‘principles’ together, there 
is no unified guide to action which generated clear, coherent, comprehensive, and specific 
rules for action nor any justification of those rules” (Clouser and Gert 1990, p. 227). The 

--- Page 237 ---

Antonia Kempkens
230
authors suggest that the different principles are not part of  one theory, but they are 
“... ­disparate concerns derived from several competing theories” (Clouser and Gert 1990, 
p. 233). According to Clouser and Gert, the PBE are appealing because they use features from 
well-­supported ethical theories. The authors attribute the principle of beneficence to Mill, the 
principles of justice to Rawls, the principle of autonomy to Kant, and the principle of 
nonmaleficence to Gert (Clouser and Gert 1990, p. 232).
However, I think that several of the principles can be found in all three predominantly used 
Western moral theories: Kant’s deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics. I agree with 
Clouser and Gert that respect for autonomy is what Kant calls for with his principle of 
humanity: “For all rational beings come under the law that each of them must treat itself and 
all others never merely as means, but in every case at the same time as ends in themselves” 
(Kant 1785, p. 429). But beneficence and nonmaleficence can both be consequences that are 
sought by an utilitarian and at the same time they can be principles that dominate decisions 
when Kant’s categorical imperative is used: “Act only according to that maxim whereby you 
can at the same time will that it should become a universal law” (Kant 1785, p. 420). I would 
argue that beneficence and nonmaleficence are suitable templates for a maxim that is 
­generalizable. In addition, beneficence and justice are values according to virtue ethics.
Even though the PBE find those four principles that all three moral theories can agree on, 
Clouser and Gert are missing a common theory that blends the principles together (Clouser and 
Gert 1990, p. 233). In their fourth edition, Beauchamp and Childress (1994) added the theory 
of the common morality. They claim “that these principles can and should be regarded as 
deriving historically and philosophically from the common morality, that is, the universal 
morality to which all morally committed persons subscribe” (Beauchamp and Childress 2019, 
p. 11). In this way, the authors manage to blend together the principles. According to Clouser, 
by that point, he and Gert had developed that account of the common morality for the last 
30 years (Clouser 1995, p. 235). Still, he saw the common morality as an alternative to the PBE 
and said about the principles: “They are, rather, checklists of concerns” (Clouser 1995, p. 235).
The reason for choosing the PBE as an ethical method in the digital context, despite them 
only being a checklist of concerns, is an argument from Shannon Vallor. She argues that moral 
theories, such as deontology and consequentialism, require information about who will gain 
access to the data and how it might be analyzed or shared, in order to assess possible courses of 
action. She concludes that these moral theories therefore are insufficient for deciding whether 
any future technological development should be implemented (Vallor 2016, p. 7).
Vallor argues that virtue ethics holds the solution to the problem, because in her opinion, 
virtue ethics can be used as an ethical strategy where the moral character helps to cope with 
an uncertain situation (Vallor 2016, p. 10). However, I argue that a virtuous character is not 
enough, because it does not provide protection to the data sources. The virtue ethics approach 
reaches its limits, because of the imbalance of control in datafication. Since the data collection 
and use are mostly opaque to data sources, they are forced to rely on data processors to be 
virtuous. A virtuous character in the data sources might help to cope with technological 
uncertainties, but it does not protect them from harm caused by nonvirtuous persons. Even if 
data sources and data processors have virtuous characters, an unauthorized, nonvirtuous 
person could gain access to the data.
Without the necessary information about the process and consequences of datafication 
and with an imbalance of control between data sources and data processors, these three 
established moral theories cannot sufficiently illuminate the ethically right design of datafica-
tion on their own. Thus, we have to depend on different conditions for the determination of 
ethical datafication. Beauchamp and Childress’ four principles can serve as such conditions. 

--- Page 238 ---

Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles of Biomedical Ethics
231
Most importantly, the PBE do not need information about the exact design or consequences of 
datafication, because the principles are simply applied to the present. We can judge whether 
right now, with all the information that we have about datafication and its opaque structure, 
there is respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice.
16.4.2  Feminist Critique
The US-­American philosopher Hilde Lindemann criticizes the fact that the PBE approach 
“... is centered in one way or another on rights-­based or consequence-­oriented moral ­theories” 
(Lindemann  2019, p.  127). She criticizes the application of the classical moral theories 
because in her view, they paint a false picture of people as individual decision makers without 
social relationships, of society as an exclusively public space in which the division of labor in 
private spaces is missing and of rationality that neglects emotions (Lindemann  2019, 
pp.  88–­96). Therefore, from Lindemann’s point of view, moral theories are not able to 
­illuminate the moral experience of all people (Lindemann 2019, p. 97).
Lindemann disapproves of these abstract biomedical principles, which do not take into 
account the people who are affected by the decision based on those principles –­ in particular, 
their social situation and their intimate relationships are neglected according to Lindemann. 
She claims that the PBE pretend that individuals are unattached, while they are not: 
“Obviously, a very sick and helpless patient looks nothing like this independent, unconnected, 
self-­interested individual, but bioethicists have expended a great deal of ingenuity on molding 
patients to fit the liberal ideal” (Lindemann  2019, p.  134). A feminist approach would 
give  consideration to the patient’s relationships and integrate them in the decision 
(Lindemann 2019, p. 135).
Lindemann criticizes that bioethicists serve “Government officials, hospital administra-
tors, policymakers, physicians, astronauts, scientists, technicians, and big business” 
(Lindemann 2019, p. 135). In her opinion, this elite and socially powerful clientele influences 
the ethicists’ outlook. However, she is not criticizing the bioethical principles themselves, but 
rather the ethicists who apply the principles in individual cases. The criticism is that the prin-
ciples can be interpreted in such a way that the decisions please the socially powerful clientele. 
Unfortunately, this is true for any ethical guidance, not just the PBE approach. It is implied 
that ethicists cannot be trusted, which is why this allegation rather questions the purpose of 
ethical consulting in general. It might be true that feminists are “... better equipped to mark 
the moral dangers arising from too prolonged an exposure to the corrosive effect of power” 
(Lindemann 2019, p. 136) –­ but this is an entirely different issue.
Lindemann finds that the PBE approach is inattentive to forms of oppression that are 
related to “... the power dynamics of race, class, gender, sexual orientation, and ethnicity” 
(Lindemann 2019, pp. 136–­137). In contrast, a feminist approach would explore how those 
power dynamics occur in the health context. From a feminist point of view, a practical ethical 
approach to medicine should take into account the personal perspective of the people affected 
by the decision in question (Lindemann 2019, p. 143). It should also analyze their social 
situation which could be influenced by certain characteristics that might lead to social 
oppression (Lindemann 2019, pp. 136–­137).
In individual, medical decisions “... collaboration with the patient” (Lindemann 2019, 
p.  139) might be possible, but in a digital context there is rarely just one specific person 
affected by the decision. Still, social power dynamics should be taken into account. But that is 
exactly what the PBE approach enables. The principles of justice and beneficence call for a 
treatment of persons independent of their social context or characteristics. That does not 

--- Page 239 ---

Antonia Kempkens
232
mean the social context should be neglected, but that it should not influence the decision 
made with the help of the principles. In addition, the principle of nonmaleficence can be 
understood as a call for prevention of social oppression –­ people should not come to harm 
because of their characteristics or social context.
16.4.3  Addition to the Principles
I have shown that the four PBE are necessary for ethical datafication, but they might not be 
sufficient. Beauchamp and Childress call their principles “... major moral considerations that 
are essential starting points” (Beauchamp and Childress 2019, p. 10). They do not claim that 
their principles are exhaustive and neither do I. Following the biomedical principles of 
Beauchamp and Childress (1979), digital ethics principles have recently been developed in 
the literature by reducing or supplementing the original four principles.6 For example, Floridi 
and Cowls identified a total of 47 principles in the literature and summarized these into five 
principles: the four biomedical principles  –­ respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmalefi-
cence, and justice –­ plus explicability (Floridi and Cowls 2021, pp. 8–­9).
In the course of this addition, Floridi and Cowls (2021) suggest an interpretation of the 
PBE for the digital sector. According to them, in digital ethics, the principle of beneficence 
refers to the use of digital technologies for the benefit of all people, for the preservation of 
human dignity and also the idea of sustainability. The principle of nonmaleficence warns 
against the misuse of digital technologies so that neither the privacy nor the autonomy of 
technology users is jeopardized. The principle of autonomy is about decision-­making 
power, because people should continue to be able to decide which decisions should be made 
with technical support. The principle of justice emphasizes that access to and control over 
digital technologies should be equal for all. This principle also warns of the risk of bias in 
datasets and, accordingly, in analyzed results. The added principle of explicability encom-
passes both the comprehensibility of technological processes for nonexperts and experts, 
as well as the question of who bears responsibility for them (Floridi and Cowls  2021, 
pp. 10–­12).
The five principles appear to be helpful in identifying digital ethical risks, but their only basis is 
that other authors also consider these principles to be important. Floridi and Cowls analyzed six 
publications on AI and its social impact from organizations with multiple stakeholders and at 
least national reach. They were able to summarize the principles mentioned in these publications 
into the five principles explained above (Floridi and Cowls 2021, pp. 8–­9). While this reveals an 
astonishing consensus among primarily political and academic authors from Western liberal 
democracies, no ethical justification is given for the selection of principles.
Floridi and Cowls (2021) would suggest incorporating their fifth principle, explicability. 
But I argue that explicability is not a principle like respect for autonomy, beneficence, 
nonmaleficence, and justice are. Explicability is a necessary condition for the realization of all 
the biomedical principles in the context of black box AI. If the algorithmic results are not 
explainable, meaning their genesis is not comprehensible for nonexperts as well as experts, 
then the results cannot show respect for autonomy. This is because opaque results would have 
to be simply accepted and it would not be possible to autonomously check the context and 
form one’s own opinion. In addition, without explicability, it is not possible to verify whether 
the algorithmic results are beneficent, nonmaleficent or just.
Another issue with the explicability principle is that it could only be a helpful pointer for 
algorithmic results –­ not for the development process of AI which relies on datafication. For 
the ethical evaluation of datafication, as the basis for AI training, one might think that other 

--- Page 240 ---

Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles of Biomedical Ethics
233
principles should be added to the PBE, principles like privacy and transparency, for example. 
In 2019, Jobin et  al. reviewed 84 existing AI guidelines and 73 contained the principle 
“­transparency” and 47 the principle “privacy” (Jobin et al. 2019, p. 395).
The principle of transparency is similar to the principle of explicability. A lack of 
transparency is something that can be identified with the help of the PBE. If the datafication 
process is not transparent, meaning that what happens with their data is opaque to data 
sources, then datafication cannot be respectful of the data sources’ autonomy. In particular, 
if the datafication process is transparent to data processors but not to data sources, it is not 
just. Furthermore, without transparency, data sources are not able to identify whether the 
datafication process is beneficent and nonmaleficent.
The principle of privacy guarantees respect for the data sources’ autonomy, since it assigns 
them control over their own data (Moore 2010, p. 27). Again, a lack of privacy is something 
that can be identified with the help of the PBE, since a lack of privacy is something that would 
make the PBE detect a lack of respect for autonomy as well as a lack of nonmaleficence. As 
soon as the data sources lose control over their data, their privacy is not protected. If this loss 
of control is intentionally created in order to gather as much data as possible, the process is 
maleficent. When we call for privacy, we do not ask for anything the PBE does not ask for 
already. Instead, we ask that the autonomy of the persons whose data is created and pro-
cessed is respected and we ask that this process of creating and processing the data is nonma-
leficent, beneficent, and just.
In order for the PBE to be implemented, i.e., for the autonomy of the data sources to be 
respected and the process to be just, beneficient, and nonmaleficent, privacy of the data 
sources and the same transparency for all stakeholders are prerequisites.
Despite differences from the field of medicine and application problems, the PBE approach 
is still important in digital ethics. For through the four biomedical principles all three predom-
inantly used moral theories find common ground. Thus, the principles’ implementation 
would provide protection from harmful interventions and preserve the possibility of self-­
development at the same time. Therefore, Beauchamp and Childress’ four principles are a 
necessary condition for an ethical approach to datafication. That is why, in the following, 
I suggest how to use the four principles in the context of datafication.
16.5  Use of the Principles
In order to find out whether the design of datafication is ethical, I will check whether the four 
biomedical principles are realized in the current design of datafication. Rather than identi-
fying more principles with the help of the PBE, I want the issues raised by this ethical approach 
to be more descriptive. So, by means of the PBE, I identify two ethical issues that datafication 
raises: the threat to the data source’s autonomy and the threat to the justice of the data 
collection.
The PBE draw our attention to the fact that datafication endangers the principle of jus-
tice for the data sources by a lack of knowledge over what happens with their data. 
Moreover, datafication might not be nonmaleficent for the data sources, when data sources 
suffer from the opaque circumstances of datafication. I argue that those conflicts with the 
principles could be solved by informing the data sources of the processes of datafication. 
Especially when one stakeholder has more control over the process than the other, an 
inequality of knowledge is unjust. In the context of datafication, once they have collected 
the data, the data processors are able to analyze data for any purpose. However, data 

--- Page 241 ---

Antonia Kempkens
234
sources have limited ­opportunities to keep their data to themselves, while not even ­knowing 
why that might be important  –­ not knowing what data processors intend to do with 
their data.
The information about the datafication process is important, because only if the process 
is known by and understandable for all stakeholders can unjust and maleficent procedures 
be identified. If, on the other hand, information about what happens to one’s data is not 
accessible and comprehensible, the data can be used without the data sources’ knowledge 
or consent and the analysis result could even be used for manipulative purposes. For 
example, Cambridge Analytica used data from Facebook to analyze the political positions of 
US citizens and subtly influence those who had not yet decided who to vote for in the 2016 
presidential election (Hu 2020, p. 2; Persily 2017, pp. 65–­66). The Facebook users affected 
did not know that their personal information had been used to determine how they could 
best be influenced and so they did not even realize that they were being influenced. In short, 
this example shows that datafication and the analysis it enables can be misused. When a 
lack of information does not allow for monitoring of the other stakeholders, this misuse is 
difficult to detect.
I claim that in the context of datafication, realization of the principles of justice and 
nonmaleficence is dependent on informing the data sources. When the process of datafication 
is opaque, harm and injustice can occur. Without information about the process, the other 
stakeholders may not be able to notice and point out such occurrences. Data sources have to 
know and understand what happens with their data, in order to be able to judge whether the 
datafication process is just and nonmaleficent.
The PBE also draw our attention to the fact that datafication endangers respect for the data 
sources’ autonomy by a lack of control over what happens with their data. Moreover, 
datafication might not be beneficent for data sources, if they do not want their data to be 
included in analyses. I argue that those conflicts with the principles could be solved by 
empowering the data sources. For example, in the context of health data, the effectiveness of 
treatments as well as possibilities for future prevention of disease can be analyzed. But on the 
grounds of health data, patients with chronic or psychological illnesses might be discriminated 
against. That is why health data is sensitive personal data that yields powerful information 
about patients. In order to avoid discrimination, patients have an interest in controlling who 
has access to their health data.
The data sources’ protection from discrimination is important, because it is essential for human 
well-­being (Moore 2010, pp. 33–­34). By enabling control over their own information, individuals 
can decide when and how to express their opinions –­ in the form of speech acts, written state-
ments, or assemblies. Thus, the individual may also be deliberately withholding information that, 
in the wrong hands, could lead to discrimination. For example, an employer or a health insurance 
provider may be suspected of discriminating against the chronically ill. That is why a person with 
a chronic illness should be free to keep their health information to themselves.
I suggest that in the process of datafication, realization of the respect for autonomy and 
beneficence is dependent on the empowerment of data sources. In the context of digitization, 
personal information is accessible from anywhere so datafication design has to adapt to 
technological developments by shifting its focus to the protection of that personal information. 
Empowered control over their own sensitive data constitutes the individual’s autonomy in a 
world where their data is analyzed without their consent or knowledge.
In summary, data sources must have knowledge of the datafication process on the one 
hand and control over the use of their data on the other. Control over their personal 
information constitutes the individual’s autonomy. In order to exercise control, data 

--- Page 242 ---

Ethical Design of Datafication by Principles of Biomedical Ethics
235
sources need to understand what happens with their data. This enables them to judge 
whether the datafication process is just, beneficent, and nonmaleficent. However, it is not 
the data sources who are responsible for the feasibility of their control, but the data 
processors. They should empower the data sources’ ability to control the use of their own 
data. By informing and empowering data sources, data processors can implement an 
ethical design of datafication.
16.6  Conclusion
In summary, datafication must meet certain conditions to be ethical according to the PBE. An 
ethical design of datafication would respect data sources’ autonomy and ensure the benefi-
cence, nonmaleficence, and justice of the datafication process. It has become clear that 
empowerment and informing of the data sources are necessary for the realization of these 
four principles in the context of datafication. For when the data source is informed, the prin-
ciples of justice and nonmaleficence can be realized and when the data source is empowered, 
the principles of autonomy and beneficence can be realized. Informed data sources can detect 
misuse and empowered data sources can autonomously control their own data in order to 
protect themselves from risks such as discrimination.
Clouser and Gert are still not happy with the PBE as an ethical approach: “It is clearly not 
a guide to action, but rather a checklist of considerations that should be kept in mind when 
reflecting on moral problems” (Clouser and Gert 1990, p. 227). I agree that the principles are 
a helpful checklist –­ they are first and foremost a pragmatic minimum standard on which 
consequentialism and deontology can agree. But in addition, the PBE helped us raise concrete 
ethical issues: for datafication to respect the autonomy of data sources, for information and 
control to be justly distributed and for the whole process to be both beneficent and nonmalefi-
cent, data sources need to be informed and empowered. I believe this can be construed as a 
guide to action.
Informing and empowering data sources are no longer principles with application 
­problems –­ they are clear requirements for an ethical design of datafication. Nevertheless, 
implementing these information and empowerment requirements is difficult. For example, 
the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (European Union 2016) stipulates that data 
sources must be asked for their informed consent before their data can be processed. 
However, in many situations it is difficult to inform each individual data source about the 
purposes of the processing and then ask for their consent, for example if a hospital wants to 
process the data of its patients for the purpose of a medical study. As soon as data is shared 
with different recipients and used for multiple purposes, it is not possible to inform the data 
sources in advance in a way that allows them to give informed consent (Barocas and 
Nissenbaum  2014, pp.  56–­61). In future research, it should be determined how data 
sources can be informed and empowered, so that an ethical design of datafication can be 
implemented.
Furthermore, only referring to the PBE in the digital context cannot be sufficient to make 
datafication and the use of AI ethical. As Mittelstadt would say, common goals are needed in 
the development of digital services, such as promoting data sources’ autonomy in order for 
ethical decision making in the digital context to become a cooperative process (Mittelstadt 2019, 
p. 3). Moreover, following Whittlestone et al., there should be a distinction between contexts 
in which datafication may be used and contexts in which it should not be used (Whittlestone 
et al. 2019, p. 199). This way, it might be possible to ethically design datafication.

17.1  Doing Medicine Means Making Value Judgments
Artificial intelligence is being employed in an increasing number of sectors of our lives. One 
of these is the domain of healthcare. Excelling especially at tasks whose execution benefits 
from taking into account large amounts of data, the advent of medical AI is hoped to 
contribute to improving the length and quality of our lives. Doctors already use algorithms 
to analyze electronic health records, to classify genes, to assess histopathological data, to 
evaluate risk factors, or to predict patients’ likely trajectories. In circumscribed areas of 
healthcare –­ like the detection of lymph node metastases (Ehteshami Bejnordi et al. 2017), 
interpretation of mammograms (McKinney et  al.  2020), analysis of electrocardiograms 
(Hannun et al. 2019), and identification of melanoma (Haenssle et al. 2018) –­ algorithms 
have even been claimed to outperform human experts in certain settings.
The ultimate goal of AI in healthcare, it therefore seems, is carrying out classic medical 
tasks. Used in diagnostic procedures, algorithms’ discriminative abilities are intended 
eventually to match those of human counterparts, becoming both as specific and as sensitive 
as the average doctor. Employed for prognostic tasks, AI is getting increasingly better at 
predicting the likely development of diseases, potential complications, or patients’ expected 
quality of life on the basis of symptoms, individual health data, and available treatments.
The healthcare sector is special, however, in that many seemingly purely medical questions 
also have important ethical components. Value judgments occur on the part of all stakeholders; 
when two treatment options are available, one of great efficacy but also coming with a high 
risk of severe side-­effects, the other safer but with little chance for improvement, the patient 
must investigate their preferences. Clinical data helps to lay out the options and associated 
probabilities, but the decision is ultimately a normative one; when a doctor tells her patient 
that “chemotherapy is medically indicated,” she is not solely expressing her clinical expertise 
but also implicitly making the judgment that prolonging life is good (Savulescu 1995); and 
when ICUs were overwhelmed during the first wave of the COVID-­19 pandemic, healthcare 
providers had to formulate rules specifying whom to admit first. Prioritization, of course, 
proceeded on the basis of medical parameters; but whether, for example, projected short-­term 
Embedding Ethics into Medical AI
LUKAS J. MEIER
17

--- Page 246 ---

Embedding Ethics into Medical AI
239
survival or estimated quality of life should be the guiding criterion in ranking patients is an 
inherently normative question (Meier 2022). Medical knowledge tells us what we can do, but 
it remains silent regarding what we should do (Marckmann 2000).
The situation is akin to that of autonomous vehicles. Self-­driving cars are not designed 
primarily to make morally relevant judgments but operating them sometimes creates 
situations in which making such judgments is inevitable. Their software must therefore be 
equipped with ethical decision principles that guide the cars’ behavior in situations of 
unavoidable harm. The same is true of autonomous weapons systems, which are developed to 
engage a certain class of target, yet their algorithmically enhanced selection of the latter on 
the battlefield comprises ethically highly relevant elements.
In medicine, value-­laden elements tend to occur to a greater extent where doctors are to 
perform overarching tasks –­ like suggesting treatment courses –­ and to a lesser extent in 
conjunction with very narrow diagnostic assignments –­ like melanoma recognition. So far, 
AI has been entrusted mainly with the latter class of activities. With rapid progress being 
made in machine learning, however, it appears likely that the percentage of applications of 
the former kind is going to increase significantly in the coming years.
Algorithms can be trained to make value judgments but there is an important difference to 
classifying genes or analyzing histopathological data: values are not facts.1 While diagnoses 
and prognoses can be validated empirically –­ a tissue section does or does not contain cancer 
cells; a patient develops or does not develop diabetes –­ values are neither externally verifiable 
nor falsifiable in the same way. They are, many people believe, time relative, culture specific, 
and differ considerably between individuals (Olson 2014; Mackie 1978). Unlike, for example, 
in tumor recognition, where larger datasets usually translate into greater discriminative 
ability and thus increase diagnostic accuracy, accumulating empirical information does not 
therefore by itself lead to improved algorithmic performance on tasks that require moral 
decision making.
It would, consequently, be best to leave value judgments exclusively to the stakeholders 
involved. However, as the example of autonomous driving shows, a strict separation of 
descriptive and normative tasks is not always going to be feasible. And it goes without saying 
that value-­laden dilemmas occur far more frequently in the domain of medicine, where 
questions of benefiting and avoiding harm, of patient autonomy and of distributive justice 
arise with nearly every single treatment option (Beauchamp and Childress 2013). Medical 
decision making is thus imbued with value judgments to an extent that some have wondered 
whether there are any purely descriptive contexts in healthcare (Kelly et al. 2015). For this 
reason, we will likely not be able categorically to exclude AI from interfering with questions of 
value without foregoing the medical benefits that this novel technology is undoubtedly going 
to bring.
If we cannot bar algorithms from (also) engaging in ethically relevant aspects of healthcare, 
and if we are not willing to put ourselves at the mercy of automated value-­insensitive medical 
decision making, then we will need to integrate ethics into medical AI. Two steps are especially 
crucial for this endeavor: implementing a moral theory that forms the frame of the ethical 
calculations, and equipping algorithms with input variables adequate for conveying to the 
machine context-­specific value judgments and preferences. I shall begin by exploring the 
former task. I will briefly introduce the main moral theories before discussing how well each 
of them could be integrated into healthcare algorithms. Considering their respective 
advantages and disadvantages, I shall ultimately suggest a compromise solution based on 
principlism. Finally, I will describe how medical AI could be designed so as to take into account 
individual and context-­specific preferences.

17.2  Three Main Moral Theories
Philosophers distinguish between three main types of moral theories: consequentialist, 
deontological, and virtue-­ethical. Proponents of consequentialist approaches hold that 
whether an act is morally right depends on the outcomes of that act. The action that produces 
the best overall result is the one to prefer. Consequentialism admits of various subtypes that 
differ in many of their properties –­ most notably in what this overall good is taken to consist 
in and in the way it is calculated. The most influential type of consequentialist ethics  –­ 
utilitarianism –­ focuses on the value of well-­being, which is often regarded as a function of 
happiness, pleasure, or desire satisfaction. Classic utilitarian doctrines were expounded by 
Jeremy Bentham (1789), John Stuart Mill (1863), and Henry Sidgwick (1877).
Critics have pointed out that consequentialism appears to permit that in certain 
circumstances, people are harmed or killed if doing so generates greater benefits for a larger 
number of individuals (Arneson 2019). To take a simple example from the realm of medicine, 
a single organ donor can save the lives of up to eight people and improve the quality of life for 
dozens of patients through tissue donation. Some versions of consequentialism can therefore 
entail that doctors would act morally if they sacrificed a patient to obtain his organs for 
transplantation. However, that the consequences of an action can justify any kind of act is in 
stark contrast with most people’s moral intuitions. What seems to be required is the categorical 
prohibition of certain actions irrespective of their good or bad overall consequences.
Deontological theories promise exactly this. Deontologists hold that actions are morally 
right when they conform with a particular norm or a set of such norms. Actions are therefore 
regarded as innately moral or innately immoral independent of their respective consequences. 
Many variants of deontological moral systems have been proposed, of which the most 
influential one is the Kantian (Kant  1993).2 Other well-­known examples are the Ten 
Commandments and –­ featuring prominently in the debate on AI –­ Isaac Asimov’s Three 
Laws of Robotics (Asimov 1942).
Deontological ethics are often criticized for a weakness that can be regarded as the mirror 
image of the difficulty identified in teleological ethics like consequentialism: in some situations, 
complying with an absolute deontological norm would lead to catastrophic global 
consequences (Alexander and Moore 2021). A physician may, for example, have the moral 
duty to refrain from testing a chemical substance on a single patient against that patient’s will 
even though her failure to do so would mean certain death for thousands of innocent people 
waiting for an antidote following a mass poisoning incident.
The third major type of normative ethical theory is virtue ethics. Virtues are morally 
desirable dispositions of character. Originating in ancient Greek philosophy,3 virtue ethics 
was especially influential in the Scholastic period.4 Unlike consequentialist ethics, virtue 
ethics is not primarily concerned with generating the best possible outcome for the largest 
number of individuals and unlike deontological ethics, it is not founded on fixed moral 
principles or duties to which actors ought to adhere. Rather, it is based on the conviction that 
morally praiseworthy actions are the result of an individual’s acquiring certain character 
dispositions (Aristotle 1995; Hume 1826).
Virtue ethics has faced objections for not generating codifiable principles that explicitly 
specify the right course of action in any particular situation and for thereby promoting 
cultural relativity of ethical values (Hursthouse and Pettigrove 2023). It would seem that on 
a virtue-­ethical basis, healthcare personnel could not be equipped with hard-­and-­fast 
guidance as to how to treat their patients. Instead, solving healthcare dilemmas would have 
to build on observation and subsequent imitation of moral exemplars. Moreover, the moral 

--- Page 248 ---

Embedding Ethics into Medical AI
241
habits so obtained may not be generalizable and thus not be applicable across clinical cultures. 
Which course of action is deemed the right one could consequently depend on factors that 
some people might regard as morally arbitrary.
17.3  Implementing Ethical Theories into Medical AI
Having recapitulated the major contenders and some of their respective strengths and 
weaknesses, I shall now examine how each of them would fare if implemented into healthcare 
algorithms. Prima facie, consequentialist ethics seems to be ideally suited for computerization. 
Jeremy Bentham (1840, p. 14) himself wrote of a “process of a moral arithmetic.” However, 
if this hedonic calculus is to be carried out correctly, the effects of every possible action on 
every single member of the moral community must be taken into account, including any 
long-­term consequences that may arise, which are potentially infinite. Specifying a horizon –­ 
temporal, spatial, social, or otherwise –­ beyond which consequences are to be ignored is a 
trickier task than it may initially appear. Should the algorithm’s scope be limited to influences 
exerted on an individual patient’s health? Should consequences for the whole healthcare 
system be taken into account –­ for instance, those affecting other patients who could, or could 
not, be treated with scarce medical resources that the original patient receives? Or should 
factors be incorporated even beyond healthcare, such as consequences for the patient’s 
relatives or for her workplace?
Consequentialist computation also entails the difficulty of reliably predicting the future 
effects of all possible actions that need to be taken into consideration (Allen et al. 2000). 
Especially in healthcare, the success or failure of a particular treatment in a particular patient, 
including the various side-­effects that come with the different treatment options, is often very 
hard to foresee. Moreover, as just mentioned, any therapy chosen will also exert influences on 
other individuals that often lie beyond the medical domain. These, too, are not always straight-
forwardly predictable.
Finally, how exactly should the calculation be done? This difficulty relates to the respective 
weights to be attached to the actions in question vis-­à-­vis the greater good. Should, for 
example, a certain increase in the quality of life or an extension of the length of a patient’s life 
be regarded as the greater contribution to the overall good? How are individual health benefits 
valued against economic costs to the healthcare system as a whole and, by extension, against 
treatments available to, or withheld from, other patients? Many of these questions arise in 
healthcare also without attempting to construct medical AI. However, the quest for algorithmic 
implementation forces us to give them a final form, and this is exceptionally difficult when not 
even the philosophical debates have been resolved.
In contrast, a major problem with the computational implementation of deontological 
moral systems is the resolution of conflicts that arise either between the principles –­ in the 
case of multi-­rule systems (Gips  1995)  –­ or, in single-­rule systems like the Kantian, 
between different duties that flow from the same guiding principle (Beauchamp and 
Childress 2013; Ross 2007).5 If, for example, a physician has promised to attend to her 
severely ill patient but suddenly an emergency comes in and the same doctor must operate 
immediately, Kantian ethics demands that both duties be fulfilled, as they are categorical. 
Even though this may not be humanly possible, no mechanism is offered for solving the 
dilemma. Since the algorithmic implementation of ethics cannot be more encompassing 
than the implemented theory itself (Anderson and Anderson 2007), the result would be a 
state of indecision.

--- Page 249 ---

Lukas J. Meier
242
Artificial intelligence that operates in a virtue-­ethical framework faces an analogous 
difficulty in cases of conflicts between competing virtues (Allen et al. 2000). Furthermore, 
virtue-­ethical approaches would bring with them the problem that understanding why the 
algorithm prioritizes a particular action over another is difficult when this decision is the 
result of certain “traits” that the algorithm has acquired rather than the consequence of 
following explicit ethical principles  –­ as in the case of deontology  –­ or of the impartial 
calculation of goods and bads  –­ as in the case of consequentialism (Berberich and 
Diepold 2018). Concerns about algorithmic opacity are ubiquitous in the literature on AI 
(Braun et al. 2021; Watson et al. 2019). Especially in an area as sensitive as healthcare, 
transparency and explainability are paramount.
Hence, it is not only decisive that medical algorithms reach reliable conclusions but also 
how they achieve this goal. The patient herself, her relatives, clinical personnel, and –­ in cases 
of appeal –­ the courts will want to understand the deliberative process behind the recommen-
dation. As I have already established, this usually includes empirical facts about the respective 
disease and available therapeutic options as well as value judgments that may underlie the 
doctor’s or the algorithm’s suggestion. Both should be made explicit. That a healthcare 
algorithm has come to take a decision in the way it did, rather than in another, as a consequence 
of having encountered certain sets of training data, rather than others, cannot be regarded 
as a satisfactory response in medical settings.
17.4  A Compromise Solution for Medical AI
Until very recently, the problem of being forced to act despite relying on imperfect ethical 
theories that seem inherently incommensurable pertained only to human action. With the 
acquisition of the ability to construct AI, we are now forced to take a definite decision: which 
moral system to implement? Humans are flexible enough to somewhat mitigate the theories’ 
respective deficits by negotiating ethics also across moral systems, that is, chiefly by considering 
motives and consequences at the same time. In principle, algorithms may be able to do the 
same but there is still a long way to go until we reach this point. At least for the time being, AI 
would likely benefit from a more monolithic implementation to avoid the additional difficulty 
of requiring a way of adjudicating between two or more ethical theories, which would be 
extremely challenging –­ both from a conceptual standpoint (Parfit 2011) as well as concerning 
practical realization.
The domain of healthcare is in a unique and advantageous position in this regard. Even 
half a century ago, medical ethicists realized that bedside decision making does not leave 
much room for attempting to resolve the profound conceptual disagreements arising with 
each of the many ethical dilemmas that occur in healthcare institutions on a daily basis. In 
1979 Tom Beauchamp and James Childress published the first edition of their Principles of 
Biomedical Ethics, in which they suggested that instead of trying to settle the controversy over 
the main moral theories, one should rely on a set of prima facie principles that is derived from, 
and thus in accordance with, our everyday moral convictions. These principles would thus 
offer a foundation for the structured analysis of medical cases in spite of the as yet unresolved –­ 
and potentially unsolvable –­ fundamental moral disputes.
Famously, the proposed principles are beneficence (attend to the patient’s welfare), 
nonmaleficence (do not inflict evil or harm), respect for autonomy (take actions on the basis of 
the patient’s choices and values), and justice (distribute healthcare resources fairly). This ­mid-­
level approach has its roots in both teleological and deontological moral systems: two of the 

--- Page 250 ---

Embedding Ethics into Medical AI
243
four principles –­ beneficence and nonmaleficence –­ originate in utilitarian considerations 
(Beauchamp and Childress 2013); the principle of autonomy is Kantian in spirit. Although 
not free from criticism (Meier et al. 2022a; Gillon 2015), Beauchamp and Childress’ approach 
is currently the dominant methodology for doing bioethics in the Western world (Veatch 2020). 
It offers a set of moral commitments “to which all doctors can subscribe, whatever their 
culture, religion (or lack of religion), philosophy or life stance” (Gillon 2015, p. 115). Not 
only for clinical ethics committees, of which many structure their discussions along the lines 
of this approach, but also with regard to the algorithmic implementation of moral principles, 
this de facto consensus creates a favorable situation for the field of bioethics.
In clinical reality, at least two of the four principles are usually in conflict; for example, 
when a doctor weighs the benefits that a planned intervention is hoped to bring against its 
side-­effects, beneficence and nonmaleficence collide. When a patient demands that an entirely 
healthy part of her body be amputated, there is a clash between nonmaleficence and the 
respect for autonomy. And when several patients compete for the last available ventilator, 
considerations of justice interfere with questions of beneficence.
Historically, many authors held that avoiding harm is weightier than the duty to benefit 
the patient, which is expressed in the ancient formula primum non nocere (Ross  2007). 
Following W. D. Ross’s major insight to refrain from regarding ethical principles as absolute 
obligations but to conceive of them as merely prima facie duties, Beauchamp and Childress 
deny this supposition.6 Their principles therefore do not come with a meta-­rule that would 
specify which action to select when the principles collide (Clouser and Gert  1990; 
Rhodes 2015). Instead, one must balance them on a case-­by-­case basis. While doing so incurs 
some of the difficulties that I have identified for the algorithmic implementation of deontolog-
ical systems, this openness ensures that the approach is adaptable to different jurisdictions, 
healthcare systems, and cultural values (Gillon 2015, 2003).
That principlism can be integrated well into medical AI was shown in a recent pilot study 
(Meier et al. 2022b). The algorithm, designed to aid in medical decision making, combines 
empirical and normative parameters to advise on a range of moral dilemma situations that 
occur in medical institutions. It thus relies on the expected postoperative quality of life or on 
the likelihood of a planned intervention to succeed just as much as, for example, on the 
patient’s respective risk tolerance. Beauchamp and Childress’ principles form the algorithm’s 
ethical basis (Hein et al. 2022). Taking into account the empirical and normative parameters 
of each individual case, the algorithm has learned to balance the principles accordingly in 
order to reach a recommendation as to whether a particular medical intervention should be 
undertaken or not (Meier et al. 2022b).
To be clear, principlism does not solve the ethical incommensurability sketched above. 
Rather, it offers a way of temporarily sidestepping fundamental philosophical disputes in 
order to render ethics applicable at the bedside. For decades, this mid-­level approach has per-
mitted healthcare personnel to take clinical decisions without having to engage in lengthy 
foundational debates. Now, however, this characteristic is equally valuable for algorithmic 
design: where one would otherwise be forced to settle on a single one of the three main moral 
theories for implementation –­ consequentialism, deontology, or virtue ethics –­ principlism 
offers a compromise. In combining elements of teleological and deontological theories, mid-­
level approaches bridge a serious conceptual gap –­ if, in exchange, one is willing to accept that 
any moral justifications so derived do not reach the most profound layer of philosophical 
justification.
Principlism is, of course, not the only mid-­level approach in use today. Rather than 
proceeding deductively from a fixed set of rules, proponents of casuistry favor a bottom-­up 

--- Page 251 ---

Lukas J. Meier
244
approach that derives moral judgments mainly from the analysis and comparison of 
individual cases (Jonsen 1991). Advocates of narrative ethics hold that only the particular 
circumstances of a situation confer moral significance, which is why this approach relies 
on storytelling, emphasizes the importance of the patient’s perspective, and pays attention 
especially to social roles and circumstances (Charon and Montello 2002; Montello 2014). 
Feminist ethics, finally, highlights the difficulties of conceiving of bioethical reasoning as a 
domain open only to certain experts, criticizes the dominance of androcentric structures, 
and aims to strengthen participation for traditionally excluded groups (Sherwin  1992; 
Wolf 1996).
To the best of my knowledge, none of these approaches to medical ethics has so far been 
integrated into healthcare AI, so that a faithful assessment of algorithmic performance on 
their basis cannot yet be given. However, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, a chatbot based on large lan-
guage models, was shown to be able to take into account feminist ethics when explicitly 
prompted to do so (Rahimzadeh et al. 2023). While ChatGPT offers comments on cases in 
medical ethics, it does not normally specify concrete solutions to moral dilemma situations. 
And while the bot’s analytic capabilities are quite impressive, they are also still seriously 
flawed (Meier 2023).
17.5  Realizing Normative User Input
Ethical theories provide the background against which healthcare algorithms would issue 
normatively relevant outputs. This does not mean, however, that they would also thereby 
automatically incorporate individual normative preferences. Healthcare is a sector in which 
values and personal preferences can vary substantially. While one patient may wish to stay in 
hospital to receive the best available care, another may opt to return home as soon as possible 
even if this would decrease their chances of recovery. And while one doctor may advise her 
patient to undergo the most radical intervention available to increase their likelihood of 
survival, another may suggest following a more conservative approach so as to preserve as 
much residual quality of life as possible.
Professional consultations ideally take into account such value judgments just as much as 
they rely on empirical medical facts. Especially in the Western world, the second half of the 
previous century saw a shift from a predominantly paternalistic medical culture toward an 
increasingly autonomy-­based model in which patient preferences were gaining more and 
more weight in the process of decision making vis-­à-­vis supposedly objective criteria regarding 
which interventions are generally most successful at restoring health (Emanuel and 
Emanuel 1992).
Although we will likely not entrust the whole process of medical decision making to AI, 
algorithms are still going to control significant elements of it. Unless we manage to endow 
them with the capacity to ingest individual preferences, there is consequently a danger of a 
second age of medical paternalism coming on: algorithmic paternalism –­ a state in which AI 
gives healthcare advice on the basis of what seems most beneficial overall to patients with the 
same assortment of statistically relevant medical and social parameters, rather than aiming 
for the course of action that would emerge when additionally taking into account the patient’s 
personal values. The more complex and overarching the tasks outsourced to AI are becoming, 
the more pressing this issue is going to be. While, for instance, algorithms for the mere 
detection of eye diseases may not normally require intricate normative input, providing the 
latter will be crucial as soon as they are supposed to also issue treatment recommendations. 

--- Page 252 ---

Embedding Ethics into Medical AI
245
Automation bias –­ the tendency of users to trust machine-­generated results over human 
judgment (Goddard et al. 2012) –­ may exacerbate this problem even further.
One cannot know how to benefit a particular patient (principle of beneficence) and how to 
avert harm from them (principle of nonmaleficence) without, in line with the principle of 
autonomy, also taking into account individual preferences and values. Benefiting is therefore 
not exclusively medically benefiting, just as harming need not be harming in an exclusively 
medical sense. The normative dimension plays a significant role in defining and understanding 
what may initially appear to be wholly empirical categories.
Value judgments do not only arise at the level of the individual patient, however. Questions 
that are of relevance for the distribution of medical resources among individuals also neces-
sitate the making of morally relevant judgments. Represented by Beauchamp and Childress’ 
principle of justice, their scope can be global, pertaining to allocation procedures within the 
whole healthcare system, or local, taking into account only the availability of treatment 
resources in the medical institution in question. Since healthcare systems differ widely in 
both the resources available to them (Meier et al. 2022b) and in what is regarded as an ethical 
distribution of these resources (Meier 2022), the ability to convey normative preferences to 
medical algorithms is essential for purposes of fair allocation, too.
To ensure that individual and global preferences and value judgments are considered in 
medical algorithms, one therefore requires suitable variables for normative input. In addition 
to, say, the statistical likelihood of a particular curative option succeeding, there should be 
input parameters that enable patients to specify their individual risk tolerance or the 
maximum therapy-­induced reduction in the quality of life that they would be willing to tol-
erate. And apart from empirical variables that doctors may enter into an algorithm to describe 
a disease, medical AI must also permit them to express whether they favor, for instance, a 
more radical or a more conservative approach. Finally, when the whole healthcare system is 
faced with an emergency, such as a pandemic, there ought to be an option to specify modifi-
cations in what is regarded as a just distribution of medical resources in the given 
circumstances.
Realizing this goal requires both algorithms that can handle inputs of the described kind 
and user interfaces that permit their specification in an adequate form and to a sufficiently 
detailed degree. This is by no means a trivial undertaking: while one can always address any 
kind of normative preference in human-­to-­human conversations, values cannot be conveyed 
to algorithms unless the design of the latter explicitly permits the very type of input in 
question. It is therefore mandatory that AI employed for healthcare purposes be equipped 
with a broad spectrum of normative input abilities if the task that it is meant to perform 
would also (partly) rely on nonempirical input if carried out by a human. Finally, just as new 
empirical information that may improve, for instance, automated melanoma detection is 
incorporated into the database of recognition algorithms, value datasets should also be regu-
larly updated to account for possible diachronic shifts in personal and global values and 
preferences.
17.6  Conclusion
Recently, the German Medical Association emphasized that algorithms ought not to have any 
business in the making of ethical decisions in medical contexts (Bundesärztekammer 2020). 
As I have argued, however, disentangling purely empirical tasks from normative ones may not 
always be feasible. Normative questions permeate medicine. Unless medical AI will only ever 

--- Page 253 ---

Lukas J. Meier
246
be employed for rather narrow tasks, it will therefore also inevitably come into contact with 
value-­laden and preference-­based aspects. With algorithmic performance increasing, there 
will be greater economic incentive to outsource to AI ever more complex tasks, thereby also 
predictably expanding the scope of the normative aspects that need to be handled by machines. 
Hence, finding ways of embedding ethics into medical algorithms is going to be paramount.
On the basis of this projection, I argued that if we want to reap the full benefits of the 
advent of medical AI, we would do well to concentrate our efforts on two factors in particular: 
implementing a moral theory and designing algorithms in ways that permit the input of values 
and preferences on the part of patients, doctors, relatives, and other stakeholders. I examined 
the three main moral theories and detailed their respective strengths and weaknesses, both 
conceptual and with regard to algorithmic implementation. Principlism I presented as a fea-
sible compromise to facilitate the timely completion of the endeavor despite unresolved 
fundamental disputes. Finally, I sketched how personalized value input could be realized: fine-­
grained mechanisms suitable for obtaining value-­related parameters should be encoded to 
rein in and normatively shape the automated processing of medical data. In this way, the 
autonomy of patients and healthcare personnel can be protected and the risk of algorithmic 
paternalism minimized.
The introduction of AI is going to transform medicine in profound ways. Increasing diag-
nostic and prognostic accuracy, and following patients’ every move in the form of apps, wear-
ables, and intelligent prostheses, there is great potential for AI to expand diagnostic surveillance, 
increase cost-­effectiveness, and reach heretofore underserved populations. But with great tech-
nological potential also comes great potential for failure. As has often been the case in human 
history, what we can hope for when a new technology becomes available does not only depend on 
the nature of the innovation itself but also on our ability and our willingness to use it prudently.
