18.1  Introduction
In this chapter I will argue that it is possible to raise an ethical machine in much the same way 
that human children are raised and educated. In particular, I maintain that it is possible to 
create virtuous machines insofar as they are able to first imitate moral exemplars before 
applying what was learned to exhibit virtuous behavior in novel scenarios. To argue for this 
successfully, there are two strands of thought that I aim to bring together. The first is that 
virtue ethics, and in particular aretaic-­exemplarism, is a normative theory that can feasibly 
be implemented in machines. The second strand is that training machines to play games 
using virtual environments can reveal the value in utilizing a similar approach to train a 
machine to exhibit virtuous behavior. For this reason, I will be discussing how machines learn 
to play board games like chess but especially the video game StarCraft II. It is therefore my aim 
in section 18.2 to briefly outline different approaches to implementing machine ethics before 
exploring the possibility of raising virtuous machines in section  18.3. In section  18.4  I 
examine how machines can learn to do incredibly complex things, e.g., mastering the game 
of StarCraft II, before suggesting in section 18.5 that there are relevant similarities between 
learning to play StarCraft II and learning to exhibit virtuous behavior.
18.2  Implementing Machine Ethics
Though it is a clichéd (and not entirely helpful) example, autonomous vehicles (AVs) have, in 
a sense, brought the classic Trolley Dilemma to life.1 In its updated form, an AV replaces the 
trolley and the people on the tracks are replaced with the AV’s occupants and pedestrians. 
And instead of having a third onlooker decide to “pull the lever,” the question revolves around 
how the AV itself ought to decide what to do in this contrived, unavoidable accident scenario.2 
In short, the question of interest is how can the AV resolve this dilemma? How does the AV 
decide whether, in an unavoidable accident scenario, to veer off the road and harm the 
­occupants or continue on its path and harm the pedestrians?
Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility 
of Virtuous Machines
MARTEN H.L. KAAS
18

--- Page 257 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
250
These questions are not merely rhetorical. AI-­enabled systems are increasingly autono-
mous and capable of performing tasks that, were a human to perform them, we would say 
require some amount of intelligence. This change was noted over a decade ago by machine 
ethics pioneers who argued that because of the increasing complexity of engineered systems, 
we may soon be required to expand the circle of moral agents to include machines since “the 
systems themselves [will have] to make moral decisions –­ to be programmed with ‘ethical sub-
routines’” (Wallach and Allen 2008). Surveys of the field of machine ethics have revealed 
multiple dimensions and taxonomies with which one might classify different approaches to 
implementing machine ethics, i.e., different approaches to programming a machine with 
“ethical subroutines.”
Certain approaches to implementing machine ethics focus on replicating normative 
ethical theories including versions of consequentialism, deontology or some combination 
thereof (Tolmeijer et al. 2021). An AV in an unavoidable accident scenario might therefore 
just behave in whatever way is prescribed by the normative theory that was chosen for 
implementation. Other approaches to implementing machine ethics are better understood 
in terms of the way in which ethical knowledge is acquired by a machine, i.e., in a top-­
down, bottom-­up, or hybrid fashion. Still others are better classified in terms of their output 
or what they do. Ethical machines can engage in action selection/execution, can act as 
decision support systems (DSS) by recommending certain courses of action, can attempt to 
appropriately represent aspects of ethical decision making and can engage in a kind of 
principal component analysis to select the most fitting elements, given a set of alternative 
options to implement an ethical machine, to include in the final system (Tolmeijer 
et al. 2021).
For simplicity and conceptual clarity, our focus will be on the acquisition of ethical 
knowledge and the decision making/behavior that follows (hence my use of the phrase “eth-
ical decision making and behavior”) and so I will primarily distinguish between machines in 
which ethics is implemented in a top-­down, bottom-­up, or hybrid fashion.
18.2.1  Top-­down Approaches
An intuitive approach to implementing machine ethics might be to simply specify those 
actions or behaviors that are morally impermissible and those that are morally obligatory. 
Theoretically, a machine with this sort of knowledge would behave perfectly morally as it 
would both avoid all immoral actions whilst performing all morally required actions. This 
kind of approach is paradigmatically top-­down, and a fictional exemplar would be Asimov’s 
Four Laws of Robotics.
The essential feature of top-­down approaches to implementing machine ethics is that they 
involve the specification of rules, instantiated in algorithms, that promise solutions to ethical 
problems. Such approaches to implementing machine ethics are popular, and for good reason. 
If ethical rules or principles can be explicitly stated, then acting ethically would just be a 
simple matter of following the rules, and “following the rules” is something that machines are 
exceptionally good at (Kaas 2021; Wallach and Allen 2008). Ethical knowledge is simply 
hard-­coded into the machine at the start and it merely abides by those rules or principles, 
thereby behaving morally. Such approaches have been used in simplistic proof-­of-­concept sce-
narios, e.g., where a robot has to bump into a “human” to prevent them from falling into a 
“hole” in the ground (Winfield et al. 2014),3 and in more convincing demonstrations, e.g., for 
use in an elder care robot to ensure that a patient is cared for and their autonomy respected 
(Anderson et al. 2017; Townsend et al. 2022).

--- Page 258 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
251
But top-­down approaches to implementing ethics are beset by certain fundamental 
limitations. The first limitation stems from the explication problem, i.e., the need to explicitly 
define the ethical concept(s) of interest (Kaas 2021). Even in the proof-­of-­concept scenario 
mentioned above, the notion of “harm” requires unambiguous explication. In this very 
simple scenario where a robot is supposed to bump into a human to prevent them from 
falling into a hole, the potential consequences must be assigned a numerical value between 
0 and 10 to denote their harmfulness. On this scale, a collision between a robot and human 
rates as a 4 (for both robot and human) whereas falling into the hole rates as a 10 (for both 
robot and human) (Winfield et al. 2014). The ethical concept(s), harm in this example, not 
only stand in need of explicit definition, but also ideally require widespread agreement on 
that definition. And while a consensus might emerge for definitions in simple well-­defined 
scenarios, such a consensus becomes impossible as the complexity of the scenario and 
action space grows.4
Setting aside this explication problem, top-­down methods for implementing machine 
ethics are also limited precisely because the ethical concept(s) of interest are fixed. In 
short, top-­down approaches are fundamentally rigid given the explicit fixing of a particular 
ethical concept. Moreover, this rigidity does not dissipate if the ethical concept(s) or 
principle(s) are spelled out in excruciating detail (i.e., the rules are fine-­grained). 
Philosophically, a detailed general principle is contradictory at worst and self-­defeating at 
best. After all, a general principle is supposed to apply to a wide set of contexts, contexts 
which do not need to be spelled out in detail beforehand (e.g., consider the difference bet-
ween general relativity and special relativity).5 Practically, a detailed general principle is 
computationally unfeasible, especially as the domain of decision making and behavior 
becomes more general.
But even assuming that rigidity can be minimized or is a nonissue, successful top-­down 
approaches to implementing machine ethics will be limited by their domain specificity 
(Kaas 2021). That is, the machine will only be able to act appropriately in certain prespecified 
contexts. Importantly, this does not mean that it is not worthwhile to pursue top-­down 
approaches to implementing machine ethics, nor am I arguing that all such attempts are 
doomed to failure. My point is only that top-­down approaches to implementing machine 
ethics, if they are to be successful, necessarily involve specifying a well-­defined use context. 
And indeed, this is more or less recognized by those taking this approach to implementing 
machine ethics, for example by specifying the ethical principles (among others) that might 
apply to a machine intended to help users dress (Townsend et al. 2022).
18.2.2  Bottom-­up Approaches
A less intuitive approach to implementing machine ethics would be to allow the machine to 
learn for itself those actions or behaviors that are morally impermissible and those that are 
morally obligatory. This is, in a nutshell, the idea behind bottom-­up approaches to implement-
ing machine ethics. Instead of specifying the rules/heuristics that the machine ought to abide 
by and hard-­coding knowledge and decision procedures, it is only necessary to specify at the 
outset the goal(s) to be achieved, such as via some performance metric, and the rewards6 the 
machine will receive as it works toward the goal. While these are certainly not trivial tasks, 
bottom-­up approaches are not beset by the fundamental limitations of top-­down approaches, 
and it is worth briefly drawing out why that is the case.
The first limitation, the explication problem, is a nonissue for bottom-­up approaches to 
implementing machine ethics because there is simply no need to define the ethical concept(s) 

--- Page 259 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
252
of interest beforehand, or indeed define any concept of interest beforehand. The notion of an 
“excellent” or “creative” chess player does not need to be explicitly defined when using bottom-
­up approaches because the feedback used to cultivate such behavior in a machine is purely 
instrumental and need not require fixed standards of positive evaluation. Is the machine 
exhibiting harmful behavior or playing chess poorly? Then simply adjust the feedback and 
begin the training anew. There is no need to explicitly define “harm” for example at the outset 
as we saw above.
Bottom-­up approaches are also not fundamentally rigid in part because there is no explicit 
fixing of the ethical concept(s) of interest. With top-­down approaches, the ethical knowledge 
is embedded in the machine from the outset and there is no process of learning or discovery 
required for the machine to engage in ethical decision making and behavior. With bottom-­up 
approaches, the ethical knowledge is acquired through a process of learning and discovery as 
a result of the machine receiving feedback as it works toward achieving a prespecified goal. It 
is this learning process that confers flexibility, albeit at the cost of requiring appropriate 
training time. This is another reason why top-­down approaches are often preferred in practice 
despite their rigidity.
Embedding ethics in a machine at the outset obviates the need for training data (which can 
be costly and time-­consuming to obtain), for selecting a learning regime (e.g., setting and 
fine-­tuning an appropriate goal and rewards in addition to other technical features), and for 
actually training the machine (which can be costly computationally, financially, and environ-
mentally). Nevertheless, in principle, bottom-­up approaches are flexible in two senses. First, 
machines could be trained to behave ethically in increasingly complex environments within 
the same domain and, second, they could be retrained to behave ethically in wholly different 
domains (Kaas 2021).
Naturally, given their flexibility, bottom-­up approaches to implementing ethics are not 
necessarily limited by the domain specificity that restricts successful top-­down approaches. 
DeepMind’s AlphaZero nicely illustrates this flexibility, especially in contrast to IBM’s Deep 
Blue (Silver et al. 2018). The former required no input from expert human chess players, 
utilized a deep neural network for perception and evaluation of board states, and utilized a 
general-­purpose reinforcement learning algorithm. Deep Blue in contrast required input 
from expert human chess players, utilized handcrafted features for perception and 
evaluation of the board states, and utilized domain-­specific augmentations to choose a next 
best move.
In short, top-­down approaches to implementing ethics, or chess-­playing abilities for 
example, amount to a static brute-­force approach that has little or no applicability outside the 
original domain of interest. This is because the success of top-­down approaches depends 
entirely on a machine’s adherence to the prespecified and explicitly defined rules that could be 
rendered impotent and unable to generate the desired behavior if there is even a modest 
change in domain. Deep Blue would not function properly, i.e., play chess at grandmaster 
level, if one of the rules of chess was changed, nor would it be capable of playing any other 
relatively similar board game. In contrast, bottom-­up approaches to implementing ethics, or 
chess-­playing ability, amount to a dynamic learning approach that can have applicability 
outside the original domain of interest. This flexibility of bottom-­up approaches has been 
demonstrated time and again, first by DeepMind’s AlphaZero which learned to play three dif-
ferent board games (chess, Go, and shogi) using the same deep reinforcement learning 
architecture and later by the transformer architecture (that utilizes bottom-­up approaches to 
learning) which underlies large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI’s ChatGPT (Bommasani 
et al. 2022; Silver et al. 2018; Vaswani et al. 2017).

--- Page 260 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
253
18.3  Capturing Normative Knowledge
While related to normative ethical theories, top-­down and bottom-­up approaches to 
implementing machine ethics are agnostic with regard to ethical theory. That is, one need not 
commit to a particular ethical theory to participate in the project of implementing machine 
ethics. Nevertheless, certain ethical theories are more or less amenable to implementation in 
machines via top-­down or bottom-­up approaches. Consequentialist and deontological theories, 
for example, are more amenable to top-­down implementations because for the former, ethical 
dilemmas are resolved by choosing the action that results in the best consequences whereas for 
the latter, ethical dilemmas are resolved by consulting and abiding by some set of principles or 
duties. For the consequentialist or deontologist, things flow downward, i.e., from the general 
theory to specific circumstances, instances or cases. Particularist or casuist theories, on the 
other hand, are more amenable to bottom-­up implementations because the emphasis in these 
theories is on the examination of specific cases first, from which one might begin to extract 
moral principles (if such principles can be extracted at all). For the particularist or casuist, 
things flow upward, i.e., from specific circumstances, instances or cases to a general theory.
For certain ethical theories, however, it is not entirely clear whether they are more ame-
nable to top-­down or bottom-­up implementation. Virtue ethics, for example, can be thought 
of as a hybrid approach combining elements of both top-­down and bottom-­up approaches.7 
For our purposes, a virtue can be understood as an acquired character trait that disposes the 
possessor of that virtue to reliably behave in an excellent/exemplary manner. So the virtues, 
such as courage, empathy, and honesty, might dispose one to engage in heroic actions 
informed by intelligent fear and hope, to be moved by the emotions of others to alleviate 
suffering, and to demonstrate exemplary respect for truth alongside the practical expertise to 
express that respect, respectively (Vallor 2016; Zagzebski 2017).8
Virtue ethics is top-­down in the sense that the virtues just mentioned of courage, empathy, 
and honesty, among others, are often specified at the outset and are supposed to inform decision 
making and behavior at the lower level of specific cases. On the other hand, a core component 
of virtue ethics is the notion of moral habituation or emulation (Vallor 2016; Zagzebski 2017). 
Briefly, this is the idea that, even in spite of knowing what the virtues are, one must learn how 
to appropriately apply these virtues. That is, “we first become moral not by studying moral 
philosophy or listening to moral arguments, but by repeatedly doing moral things until they 
become habitual” (Vallor 2016, p. 67). And this kind of moral development, i.e., the cultivation 
of a moral character, is a bottom-­up process that begins, in the earliest stages, with the imitation 
of exemplars of moral excellence. In other words, a first step to becoming good and cultivating 
a moral character is to “study what is done by truly good people, and consistently try to do the 
same” (Vallor 2016, p. 68). Furthermore, machines excel at this kind of imitation via the use 
of certain bottom-­up machine learning methods. The basic idea is that one can have a dataset 
of, say, exemplary chess games and, through the use of machine learning, train a machine to 
imitate that exemplary game play. Analogously, one could have a dataset of exemplars of moral 
excellence and similarly train a machine to imitate those exemplars and their morally excellent 
character. So let us examine this idea in more detail.
18.3.1  Aretaic-­exemplarism
Before proceeding, it is important to note that we must not confuse the appearance of a morally 
excellent or virtuous character with the actual possession of a morally excellent or virtuous 
character.9 To actually possess a virtuous character requires, among other capacities, 

--- Page 261 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
254
reflective self-­examination, intentionality, prudential judgment, affective sensitivity, and 
moral imagination (Gibert  2023; Smith  2019; Vallor  2016; Wallach and Vallor  2020). 
Whether machines possess any of these capabilities is unlikely, and an in-­depth examination 
of this issue is outside the scope of this chapter. In any case, one does not need to commit to a 
view on this issue to seriously consider the possibility of a machine imitating a virtuous 
person and thereby behaving virtuously itself.10
This is the basic idea behind the aretaic-­exemplarist approach to implementing machine 
ethics: a machine can learn to behave in a morally excellent way, i.e., virtuously, by imitating 
exemplars of moral excellence (Gibert 2023). This approach is grounded in the normative 
theory of exemplarism which is an agent-­based version of virtue ethics that has features that 
nicely align with the advantages of bottom-­up approaches to implementing ethics outlined 
above (Zagzebski 2010, 2017). One of the most important is the idea that one can pick out 
exemplars of moral excellence using direct reference by simply pointing, as it were, to a person 
like that, i.e., a person with a virtuous character. Importantly for our purposes, picking out a 
person with a virtuous character does not require us to explicitly define “virtuous character,” 
thus avoiding the explication problem, as Zagzebski explains.
Picking out exemplars fixes the reference of the term “good person” without the need for descrip-
tive concepts. It is not necessary for ordinary people engaged in moral practice to know the nature 
of good persons –­ what makes them good. . . We need not associate a descriptive meaning with 
“good persons” that is sufficient to identify them, and users of our language can successfully refer 
to good persons even when they associate the wrong descriptions with the term “good person.” 
(Zagzebski 2017, p. 15)
And the way that Zagzebski believes we can pick out exemplars of moral excellence is through 
the emotion of admiration: “exemplars are those persons, the persons who are most imitable 
or most deserving of emulation. They are most imitable because they are most admirable” 
(Zagzebski 2017, p. 15).
But crucially, there is a difference between mere imitation and emulation. As we shall see 
in the concrete examples below, and as Zagzebski highlights, mere imitation is insufficient for 
moral development. Emulation, as a form of imitation, is different because the person being 
emulated is seen as a model and we imitate that person because we want to be like that person 
in a certain respect. For human moral development, inculcating the right sort of motivations 
is (almost always) imperative, and for Zagzebski emulation that arises from the feeling of 
admiration can explain how the imitator develops virtuous motives. She succinctly summa-
rizes her position thus: “The model I [Zagzebski] am proposing starts with admiration of an 
exemplar, which leads to an imaginative ideal of oneself, which in turn produces emulation of 
the exemplar’s motives and acts” (Zagzebski 2017, p. 138).
As mentioned at the beginning of this section, it is highly unlikely that machines can 
engage in the kind of moral imagining necessary for the kind of emulation Zagzebski has in 
mind. Nevertheless, it is not entirely accurate to say that machines are engaged in mere 
imitation. This is because what the machines are imitating can be carefully selected by human 
designers, e.g., morally relevant data from human exemplars, which I discuss in the next 
section. In any case, and as mentioned above, the mere imitation of a virtuous exemplar may 
suffice to produce the appearance of a morally excellent character in a machine even if that 
machine cannot actually possess such a character.
It must also be noted that feelings of admiration do not guarantee that we have identified an 
exemplar of moral excellence, which again nicely aligns with another advantage of bottom-­up 

--- Page 262 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
255
approaches to implementing ethics, namely their flexibility. Zagzebski’s exemplarism is 
therefore “compatible with the view that our identification of exemplars is revisable” given 
that we can be “mistaken in our judgment that some person we call paradigmatically ‘good’ 
is really good” (my emphasis) (Zagzebski 2017, p. 16). In the same way that one can, using 
bottom-­up approaches, retrain a machine to exhibit desired behaviors, so too can we revise 
and “retrain” our feeling of admiration after careful reflection and in light of critiques raised 
by others (Zagzebski 2010, 2017).11
The point is that one can use moral exemplarism as a basis for implementing machine 
ethics in a bottom-­up way, and this is precisely what some scholars have already suggested 
(Gibert 2023; Mabaso 2021). In particular, I want to focus on Gibert’s proposal for creating a 
generalist virtuous machine, so let us examine his argument.
18.3.2  The Possibility of Virtuous Machines
Building on the ideas of Zagzebski’s exemplarism and Mabaso’s proposal for creating a 
specialist virtuous machine, to wit, an ethical robot teacher, Gibert identifies three key steps 
for building a generalist virtuous machine (Gibert 2023; Mabaso 2021; Zagzebski 2017). The 
first step is to build a base of people with a virtuous character by identifying those who will 
serve as the moral exemplars (Gibert 2023). In the specialist case of an ethical robot teacher 
that Mabaso considers, this step amounts to “identify[ing] morally praiseworthy teachers in 
the school, district or even nationally” (Mabaso 2021). But for Gibert, whose interest, like 
mine, is in a generalist virtuous machine, one need not restrict themselves to moral exemplars 
from a single type of background or profession. The challenge, as Gibert points out, is that it 
is not a simple matter to identify moral exemplars. Asking moral exemplars to self-­identify is 
unlikely to produce any genuine moral exemplars and much more likely to produce many 
who are not exemplars of moral excellence, and using a standardized test to identify moral 
exemplars is fraught with complications, the most serious of which is that such a test would 
be circular, i.e., because in order to test for a virtuous character, one must know how to 
describe that beforehand (and so the explication problems rears its head again) (Gibert 2023).
To establish the base of moral exemplars, Gibert appears to largely endorse something like 
Zagzebski’s suggestion that we follow our feeling of admiration. Specifically, he mentions that 
moral exemplars can be chosen through our collective intelligence, so people nominate two or 
three others in their life that they trust to make morally sensitive decisions and who they con-
sider to be more virtuous than the average person (Gibert 2023). Indeed, as Gibert notes, “the 
group of virtuous people does not have to be flawless to make the aretaic-­exemplarist approach 
effective” since an above-­average base of virtuous people could still serve as the basis for 
training a machine that will behave better than the average person (Gibert 2023).
The second step involves collecting morally relevant data from the base of moral exem-
plars. Because Gibert focuses on the example of an AV, he suggests that you could, for example, 
“ask your virtuous people, or some of them, randomly chosen, to answer questionnaires 
about their moral beliefs and intuitions on many topics,” such as how they might respond to 
Trolley Dilemma-­like scenarios when driving a car (Gibert  2023). Gibert argues that the 
difference between asking a group of moral exemplars about their beliefs and intuitions 
versus an average group of people is that the former indicate what one ought to do whereas 
the latter only indicate what it is socially acceptable to do (Gibert 2023). In short, the former 
is normative and the latter descriptive. So if one is able to collect enough morally relevant 
information from the moral exemplars, then the hope is that, after training a machine to imi-
tate the moral exemplars, such machines would be able to exhibit morally excellent behavior 

--- Page 263 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
256
themselves, even when faced with novel situations. As with the first step, though machine 
learning techniques generalize imperfectly to novel ­situations, Gibert maintains that even 
imperfect virtuous machines could be desirable (Gibert 2023).
The third and final step involves implementing a decision algorithm. Again, because Gibert 
focuses on implementing an aretaic-­exemplarist approach for AVs, he outlines different ways 
in which one might actually encode the data gathered from the moral exemplars. If, for 
example, in an unavoidable accident scenario involving a child and a senior, where the AV 
will hit one or the other, the data collected from the moral exemplars is such that 20% would 
save the senior, 50% would save the child, and 30% would choose randomly, how might this 
data be encoded into the AV (Gibert 2023)? One option is to encode the majority voice so the 
AVs always save children. Another option is to encode all views proportionally via 
manufacturing so that the AVs have a “preference” as to which option they “choose.” Gibert, 
however, defends a third option called proportional draw wherein the diversity of views on 
what to do is integrated into each AV (Gibert 2023). Though this introduces some amount of 
unpredictability, Gibert argues that this is tolerable given the grounding in virtue ethics.
It is well known that, according to this [virtue ethics] approach, opposite actions may both be 
morally right, to the extent that this corresponds to what distinct virtuous people would have 
done. Socrates might favor the senior while Jesus would save the child, and both actions would be 
therefore morally right. The proportional draw option echoes a certain flexibility and imprevisi-
bility that can be associated with virtue ethics. (Gibert 2023)
Although Gibert relies on the example of an AV to illustrate his view, he maintains that the 
three steps just outlined could serve as a model to build other kinds of virtuous machines, and I 
largely agree with this assessment. But I believe that Gibert limits his approach in the very first 
step. Gibert’s approach is mostly, if not entirely, predicated on finding a suitable base of moral 
exemplars and then extracting the morally relevant data from those exemplars, an enormously 
time-­consuming and difficult task. In what follows, I will argue that this aretaic-­exemplarist 
approach can be enhanced using virtual moral exemplars acting in simulated environments. 
And to argue for this effectively, I need to discuss how machines learn to play games.
18.4  Machine Learning and Games
To sum up the preceding sections, bottom-­up approaches to implementing machine ethics are 
better suited for creating ethical machines compared to top-­down approaches, especially if 
one is interested in a generalist machine not limited by domain. The aretaic-­exemplarist 
approach to ethics, grounded as it is in the imitation of moral exemplars, is particularly ame-
nable to implementation in machines because bottom-­up approaches to machine learning 
involve elements of imitation. In short, creating machines that behave ethically because they 
have learned to imitate moral exemplars is feasible.
From a machine ethics point of view, exemplarism is a pragmatic approach to building AMAs 
[artificial moral agents] because the goal is at least conceptually and practically clear –­ teach 
AMAs to learn from moral exemplars and to improve themselves over time. (Mabaso 2021)
As I have argued elsewhere, reinforcement learning (RL), a distinct paradigm of machine 
learning methods, is particularly well suited for the raising12 of ethical machines because it 
involves goal-­directed learning from interaction with an environment guided by the use of 

--- Page 264 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
257
reward signals that the machine attempts to maximize (Kaas 2021). There are two things to 
note here. First is that the goal can vary and include the imitation of behavior. For example, 
one could have data about how moral exemplars drive or data about how moral exemplars 
work toward any arbitrary goal (e.g., shopping in any commercial district) and use this data 
to stimulate imitative behavior in machines trained on this data (Wu and Lin 2018). But the 
second thing to note is that though RL involves goal-­directed learning from interaction with 
an environment, this environment need not be the real world. In contrast to Gibert, I maintain 
that data collected from humans acting in the real world is not necessary to raise machines 
that behave virtuously according to the aretaic-­exemplarist approach. All that one needs is a 
simulated moral exemplar, a digital Jesus, identifiable by us through our feelings of admiration, 
whose behavior can be emulated and perhaps even improved upon by machines trained using 
bottom-­up machine learning. Zagzebski even acknowledges as much, writing that “it does 
not matter if the person who elicits our admiration is accurately described or even if he or she 
is fictional” because “insofar as exemplars reveal the admirable to us, fictional exemplars can 
serve that purpose as well as the exemplars who actually lived” (Zagzebski 2017, p. 87). 
Though Zagzebski was probably not thinking about a digital Jesus or a virtual Confucius as 
fictional exemplars, they are certainly compatible with the aretaic-­exemplarist approach and 
perhaps even desirable in the context of implementing machine ethics.
18.4.1  Learning from Simulations
The use of simulated13 environments and even simulated humans has a long history in 
computer science and AI research. In the early 1990s, Tesauro developed one of the first 
machines to successfully play the board game backgammon using RL (Tesauro  1994). 
Importantly, the way the machine learned to play backgammon was from simulated games of 
self-­play, i.e., it played against itself, not on an actual board but in simulation, and learned 
from the versions that won and lost (Tesauro  1994). More recently, Google’s DeepMind 
division developed a general reinforcement learning machine, AlphaZero, which learned and 
mastered the games of Go, chess, and shogi using the same basic process; beginning with 
naïve strategies, AlphaZero learned how to play these board games through simulated self-­
play (Silver et al. 2018). Even the use of simulated humans is not without precedent. IBM’s 
Watson, the machine that appeared on the game show Jeopardy!, learned how to make 
strategic wagers by playing against carefully crafted virtual models of human contestants 
rather than simply through games of self-­play (Sutton and Barto 2018).
The point is that just as one can teach a machine to play a board game and even discover 
and improve upon human strategies and tactics using simulated experience generated via 
self-­play, so too could one teach a machine to behave virtuously using simulated experience 
generated via interaction with simulated moral exemplars. To better consider this possibility, 
and its limitations, let us take a brief journey through the world of StarCraft II.
18.4.1.1  StarCraft II: Features Unique to Real-­time Strategy Games
Like chess, each game of StarCraft II begins with a known initial state, but that is where the 
similarities with chess, and almost all other board games, end. First, as “real-­time” suggests, 
player actions (which are performed using a point-­and-­click interface with a mouse and 
keyboard) in StarCraft II are not limited by whose turn it is but rather their ability to play the 
game in real time, i.e., in parallel. Players who are able to execute more actions (e.g., clicks or 
button presses) per minute (APM) may therefore have an advantage over players with a lower 
APM, but obviously this is not always the case. Moreover, players are responsible for both the 

--- Page 265 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
258
high-­level planning and execution of macroactions as well as the fast-­paced microactions of 
individual units.
Second, players in StarCraft II compete for resources and positioning on the map by 
controlling their units. StarCraft II is therefore a multiagent problem on two different levels: 
two players compete for victory at the higher level while also controlling units which need to 
collaborate to achieve a common goal at the lower level (Vinyals et al. 2017).
Third, StarCraft II is a game of imperfect information. In contrast to board games like chess 
in which both players can fully observe the entire board and have complete access to 
information regarding the position of the opponent’s pieces, maps (i.e., the board) in StarCraft 
II are only partially observable via a local camera which must be actively moved by the player. 
There is also a “fog of war” obscuring the entire map. Unless a player’s unit or structure is 
nearby to reveal a portion of the map, including revealing enemy structures and units in that 
area, that portion of the map will remain hidden from the player.
Fourth, the action space is vast and diverse, so much so that any top-­down approach to 
playing the game at an expert human level would utterly and spectacularly fail. Consider that 
in a game of chess, there may be an average of 31 potential moves that a player might make 
which would result in, after a typical 40-­move game, a mind-­boggling 10120 board configura-
tions (Haugeland 1981). Yet IBM’s Deep Blue could reach human expert levels of play in 
chess through the use of hard-­coded chess-­playing heuristics and brute-­force searches for the 
next best move; in short, using a top-­down approach to playing the game (Campbell 
et al. 2002). In a game of StarCraft II, on the other hand, there may be as many as 1026 poten-
tial moves that a player might make at any given moment which would result in, after a typical 
game, a conservative estimate of 101685 possible game states (Ontanon et al. 2013; Vinyals 
et al. 2019). It must be noted, however, that while there are certainly very many possible 
strategies and game states, professional human gameplay revolves around a slowly shifting 
“meta,” i.e., a set of popular strategies.
Fifth, the high branching factor and especially the depth of the game, i.e., the time between 
the first action and final action, mean that there is a rich set of challenges in temporal reward 
assignments and exploration that must be addressed before machines can successfully learn 
to play a game of StarCraft II at expert human levels (Vinyals et al. 2017). StarCraft II games 
can last for many thousands of frames and actions which means that the consequences of 
decisions made in the early or mid-­game may not be seen until much later in the game. 
Complicating things even further is the fact that different units and buildings can engage in 
local unique actions which may vary as a player unlocks different technology trees (Vinyals 
et al. 2017). There are, in short, a varying set of legal actions that a player might make 
depending on decisions made earlier in the game.
Taken together, these unique properties of StarCraft II means that it is practically impos-
sible for top-­down approaches and/or classical AI techniques (i.e., symbol manipulating 
systems in which knowledge, facts, and rules are explicitly represented,14 as was the case 
with Deep Blue) to achieve expert human levels of play. Indeed, the Elite AI native to 
StarCraft II can be set to play certain popular strategies, which suggests that it was created, 
in part, using top-­down approaches which means that ultimately it is not a very good 
StarCraft II player.
18.4.1.2  Mastering StarCraft II through Imitation and Learning
StarCraft II is an incredibly complex game, but one that DeepMind’s AlphaStar machine was 
able to master, i.e., achieve human expert levels of play by reaching the Grandmaster league 
on the official online matchmaking system Battle.net playing against human opponents 

--- Page 266 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
259
(Vinyals et  al.  2019). This feat was made possible by using bottom-­up machine learning 
methods, and RL in particular, so let us examine in more detail how AlphaStar was trained 
since this can help us understand how it may be possible to train a machine to behave 
virtuously.
Like chess, StarCraft II features a vast and cyclic state space of nontransitive strategies and 
counterstrategies in which no one strategy is optimal; although strategy A may be preferred 
over strategy B, and B might be preferred over C, there is no guarantee that A will be preferred 
over C (Vinyals et al. 2019). Unlike chess, however, the state space of StarCraft II is so vast that 
discovering novel strategies, or rediscovering well-­known strategies, is intractable using the 
same naïve self-­play RL methods used to train AlphaZero (Vinyals et al. 2019). To circumvent 
this early exploration problem, AlphaStar was initially trained to imitate human StarCraft II 
players using supervised learning, another paradigm of bottom-­up machine learning. But 
simply imitating humans is not enough to master StarCraft II and so AlphaStar was subse-
quently trained by a RL algorithm that was designed to maximize the win rate (one of the 
reward signals employed throughout training) against a mixture of opponents (Vinyals 
et al. 2019). AlphaStar is therefore better thought of not as one machine but as many differ-
ent ones, each of which plays a different strategy. RL methods that utilize this type of 
population-­based fictitious self-­play (FSP) avoid cycling through strategies “by computing a 
best response against a uniform mixture of all previous policies,”15 i.e., a uniform mixture of 
all previous decisions/behaviors (Vinyals et al. 2019).
Such a training regime, however, is not viable when the state space is as vast as it is in 
StarCraft II. Given the immense range of strategies possible in a game like StarCraft II, there 
is a danger that FSP alone might lead to a convergence on local maxima, i.e., FSP might 
lead AlphaStar to prefer a specific strategy but only because it is an effective strategy when 
playing against similar opponents. To ensure that the main AlphaStar would be as robust 
as possible, i.e., capable of responding appropriately to a variety of opponent strategies, 
researchers at DeepMind extended this approach in order to compute a best response 
against a nonuniform mixture of opponent strategies (Vinyals et  al.  2019). Two novel 
strategies were therefore implemented in order to train AlphaStar, strategies that could be 
used when training a machine to better explore the space of ethical decision making and 
behavior.
The first strategy was the utilization of a prioritized fictitious self-­play (PFSP) mechanism 
that adapts the mixture of opponents such that versions of AlphaStar with the highest win 
rates are pitted against each other; this provides the main versions of AlphaStar “more oppor-
tunities to overcome the most problematic opponents” in a kind of self-­play competition 
bracket (Vinyals et al. 2019). Prioritizing gameplay against opponents with high win rates 
therefore ensures that the main versions of AlphaStar are exposed to and able to appropri-
ately respond to specialized but effective strategies.
The second training strategy was the use of a league system consisting of three different 
types, or versions, of AlphaStar that primarily differed in their mechanism for selecting the 
opponent mixture. The main versions of AlphaStar, the ones that will eventually be pitted 
against human players, must become as robust as possible. So in addition to the main versions 
of AlphaStar, there are also so-­called “main exploiter” versions that play only against the 
main versions and whose purpose it is to identify potential exploits in the main versions 
(Vinyals et al. 2019). The third version of AlphaStar, the “league exploiters,” also utilize a 
PFSP mechanism and their purpose is to find systemic weaknesses of the entire league and so 
are not targeted by the main exploiters; the exploiters only play against the main versions 
(Vinyals et al. 2019).

18.5  From Excellence in StarCraft II to Moral Excellence?
A detailed discussion of StarCraft II and AlphaStar in the preceding sections was necessary to 
make the following claims apparent. First, StarCraft II is an incredibly complex game. Second, 
it is possible for machines to reach expert human levels of play using bottom-­up machine 
learning techniques. Not only could AlphaStar play StarCraft II at expert human levels, but 
the use of RL techniques allowed it to innovate and develop novel strategies and play styles. 
Despite the complexity of StarCraft II, many expert human players consider the very early 
stages of the game to be well mapped out, i.e., there is a standard of play considered most 
optimal. Yet AlphaStar often deviates from this standard and also displays its own novel 
strategies.16 Third, and most important, StarCraft II and ethics are relevantly similar; that is, 
ethics is more like StarCraft II than like chess, at least in the following respects: ethical decision 
making and behavior occurs in real time and with imperfect information. The researchers 
working on AlphaStar note this significance of their achievement, writing:
Like StarCraft, real-­world domains such as personal assistants, self-­driving cars, or robotics 
require real-­time decisions, over combinatorial or structured action spaces, given imperfectly 
observed information. Furthermore, similar to StarCraft, many applications have complex 
strategy spaces that contain cycles or hard exploration landscapes, and agents may encounter 
unexpected strategies or complex edge cases when deployed in the real world. The success of 
AlphaStar in StarCraft II suggests that general-­purpose machine learning algorithms may have a 
substantial effect on complex real-­world problems. (Vinyals et al. 2019)
In contrast to chess, and indeed in contrast to many contrived ethical thought experiments 
that are meant to pump philosophy students’ intuitions,17 real-­world ethical decision making 
and behavior is not accomplished with perfect information. Behaving ethically would, 
presumably, be easier if one had access to all of the relevant nonnormative and/or normative 
information prior to making a decision; making ethical decisions is difficult precisely because 
one often possesses only a fraction of the relevant information. Consider that someone 
responsible for hiring a new employee might find themselves having to choose between two 
candidates whose qualifications are identical. How ought the new hire be chosen, i.e., on 
what basis should one be preferred over the other if they are both equally qualified? Such a 
decision is made difficult because of a lack of access to all the relevant information (e.g., the 
candidate’s character, how well they might fit within the organization and broader community, 
which normative ethical theory is true, etc.) that might make the decision easier and, more 
importantly, the ethically preferable decision, i.e., the decision that a virtuous person would make.
Just as people need to make ethical decisions using imperfect information, so too must 
players in a game of StarCraft II make decisions based on the information at hand. Whether 
decisions made in the moment will result in a winning outcome for the player is often not 
known. Similarly, whether decisions made in the moment are ethical or not is also often not 
known until some point in the future although, importantly, this is where the analogy begins 
to break down, especially in the context of virtue ethics.18 Insofar as we are concerned with 
machine ethics, bottom-­up machine learning methods are clearly capable of teaching a 
machine how to guide itself through a state space via a sequence of sensible actions when 
given imperfect information.
Ethical decision making and behavior, like StarCraft II, features hard exploration landscapes 
(i.e., a vast action space that would be fruitless to explore naïvely). This is quite obvious if we 
imagine how a “blank slate” human (analogous to the randomly weighted neural network 

--- Page 268 ---

Simulating Moral Exemplars: On the Possibility of Virtuous Machines
261
present in a machine prior to any training) might approach trying to drive a car ethically, i.e., 
as a moral exemplar would. If we place this human inside the vehicle in the driver seat, it is 
clear that there is a vast sequence of potential actions, both in terms of breadth (i.e., there are 
many branches) and depth (i.e., each branch terminates after many steps), they would need 
to explore before stumbling upon a sequence that results in them driving a car ethically.
Ethical decision making and behavior also contains cycles (e.g., related “strategies,” as it 
were) in two important senses. Consider again an AV in an unavoidable accident scenario. It 
may be that (A) sparing more lives is preferred over sparing fewer lives, (B) sparing human 
lives may be preferred over sparing animals’ lives, and (C) sparing young lives may be preferred 
over sparing old lives (as in Gibert’s example above). But even though (A) is preferred over 
(B) and (B) is preferred over (C), (A) is not necessarily preferred over (C), as might be the case 
where an AV collides with either two children or three adults. Just as there is no one optimal 
strategy in StarCraft II, so too is there no one “optimal strategy” when it comes to ethical 
decision making and behavior.
Ethical decision making is also cyclic in a second broader sense akin to episodicity. While 
ethical decision making and behavior is not, in theory, an episodic task, many activities that 
involve ethical decision making and behavior are practically episodic in nature. Consider again 
the example of driving ethically. It may be practical, and potentially even advantageous in the 
field of machine ethics, to think of driving ethically as an episodic task, i.e., as a task with an 
“end” and “reset” to some initial state, that end being the reaching of a destination and the 
reset being the setting of a new destination.
Finally, while there is a clear global goal in StarCraft II, the use of bottom-­up RL techniques 
in machines like AlphaZero and AlphaStar demonstrates how vague concepts like intuition, 
creativity, optimal strategy, and excellence can be operationalized. There is, in principle, no 
reason why a concept like moral excellence could not be operationalized given the right kind 
of training regime and an appropriate reward signal. There is, in short, no need to define a 
notion of “moral excellence” because such training would amount to an operationalization of 
the concept of moral excellence. Moreover, we would be able to recognize such moral excel-
lence in a machine through our feeling of admiration. AlphaStar’s training, and in particular 
the use of population-­based PFSP, suggests that the idea of using a virtual community of 
moral agents to raise an ethical machine is practically feasible and even desirable given the 
fact that machines trained in such a fashion could rediscover and improve upon ethical 
norms; we might learn from machines what moral excellence looks like (or could look like) in 
certain situations.19
Research in the domain of game playing is illuminating how bottom-­up machine learning 
methods can be applied to raise robust ethical machines capable of responding appropriately 
in real time to complex environments given imperfect information, as a person with a vir-
tuous character would. Indeed, this research highlights something worth emphasizing, 
namely that machines might be raised to exhibit a certain character or personality and that it 
may be possible to cultivate a virtuous character in machines, an approach that is not often 
taken seriously in machine ethics (i.e., taking an aretaic-­exemplarist approach as opposed to 
a consequentialist or deontological approach). Implementing machine ethics will therefore 
amount to raising machines as one might raise a child to live an ethical life; first by imitating 
moral exemplars and second by applying what was learned via imitation to novel scenarios. It 
is certainly true that ethical decision making and behavior involves global goals or outcomes 
that are difficult, if not impossible, to explicitly define and translate into appropriate reward 
signals. But for practical purposes, local goals and outcomes can be explicitly defined and even 
translated into formal reward signals that capture a morally excellent character in certain 

--- Page 269 ---

Marten H.L. Kaas
262
circumstances. Similarly, it is not necessary to define what exactly a virtuous character looks 
like before one is able to proceed with the business of implementing machine ethics. Just as 
explicit definitions of creativity and excellent chess play are not needed to say that what 
AlphaZero is doing is playing excellent and creative chess, so too are explicit definitions of 
morally excellent behavior not needed to say that what a given machine is doing is exhibiting 
morally excellent behavior.
18.6  Conclusion
Although there are myriad ways to implement ethics in machines, I have argued that 
bottom-­up approaches to implementing ethics are to be preferred over top-­down approaches. 
Not only is it conceptually and practically possible for machines to learn from experience to 
exhibit morally excellent behavior, such an approach is grounded in the normative theory of 
aretaic-­exemplarism and virtue ethics, an oft overlooked ethical theory in discussions on 
machine ethics. Furthermore, impressive strategies utilized to train machines to play complex 
games can be repurposed for implementing ethics in machines given the similarities between 
the two activities. By definition, moral exemplars, when acting in character, do what is right 
in the circumstances in which they find themselves, despite lacking perfect information and 
despite real-­time constraints. Machines can similarly cope with a lack of perfect information 
and real-­time constraints. This ability, when coupled with the imitation of a moral exemplar, 
allows for the possibility of machines that exhibit virtuous behavior. Such a route to 
implementing machine ethics may not be easy, but it is worth pursuing considering the 
benefits they may offer. Ultimately, raising admirable machines that exhibit virtuous 
behavior is in everyone’s interest.
