19.1  Introduction
Philosophy has a long-­standing tradition in thinking about the notion of trust.1 While today 
interpersonal trust is often considered the paradigm case of trust, different historical periods 
have emphasized various forms of trust practices and different actors within trust relation-
ships. In the Middle Ages, for instance, trust in human beings was frequently seen as mis-
placed, with trust in God regarded as the paradigmatic form of trust. In the early modern 
period, trust emerged as a topic in the political philosophy of international relations. Theorists 
of international law examined the possibility of trust between states, delving into the condi-
tions under which such trust could flourish.2 In the eighteenth and early nineteenth cen-
turies, philosophical debates on trust revolved around the concept of interpersonal trust, 
with a particular focus on the trust that exists between friends (Frevert 2013).
Since the 1980s, the debate on trust in philosophy has significantly intensified 
(Hartmann 2001, 7). Prompted by the diagnosis of a crisis of trust (cf. O’Neill 2002), this 
relatively new interest in trust in the late twentieth century focused on social and political 
trust. The social sciences, in particular, took a keen interest in understanding the origins of 
societal trust, exploring its sources and seeking to analyze its implications for societal cohe-
sion and stability.3 In the latter half of the twentieth century, philosophical discussions about 
trust increasingly began to address technological contexts, gaining significant prominence in 
recent decades. Notably, the development of civilian nuclear power and the evolution of 
­genetic engineering have played pivotal roles in this shift. These technologies have raised 
­complex questions about trust in science and scientific institutions, as well as their respon-
sibility (Jonas 1979).
In recent years, the philosophical exploration of trust has gained new momentum, driven 
by the advances in computer science and information technology. Artificial intelligence (AI) 
in particular raises numerous trust-­related questions in both practical applications and 
philosophical debates. Central issues include whether AI is an appropriate subject of trust, 
whether trust in AI production processes is well placed, whether AI-­based decision-­making 
Trust in AI
KAROLINE REINHARDT
19

--- Page 273 ---

Karoline Reinhardt
266
procedures are trustworthy, and what criteria for trustworthiness could be discerned with 
regard to AI.
This chapter explores the multifaceted nature of trust in AI. It aims to outline emerging 
trust issues in applied philosophy of AI, providing an introduction to the concept of trust and 
offering an overview of key debates in the field. The central question of this chapter is whether 
AI can be considered an appropriate object of trust and, if so, under what conditions such 
trust is warranted. Addressing this question requires engaging with the philosophical debate 
on trust, which revolves around two main issues: the nature of trust and the identification of 
suitable objects of trust. In the context of AI, this discourse traditionally examines trust in 
individuals, institutions, and technologies. How can we make sense of concepts like trust with 
regard to AI? Can we apply or modify traditional concepts of trust, such as interpersonal 
trust, social trust, or trust in institutions and technologies, so as to understand the kind of 
relation people have toward this novel technology?
I will provide a concise overview of the debates surrounding these questions and argue 
that trust in AI does not align neatly with any one of these paradigms. Instead, it incorporates 
elements from all three dimensions. This complexity arises from the fact that AI is an often 
highly interactive, adaptive socio-­technical system –­ a hybrid entity that encompasses not 
only technological components but also social, institutional, and cultural dimensions –­ with 
probabilistic components.
However, in this chapter, I do not aim to develop a comprehensive theory of trust in AI but 
rather to emphasize the importance of taking diverse conceptualizations seriously. At the 
same time, there is a clear need for a robust theory of trust in AI that does justice to the com-
plexity of the phenomenon. Despite more than two decades of empirical research on trust in 
AI, the task of formulating an adequate conceptual framework remains unresolved.4 This 
theoretical endeavor is further complicated by the fact that AI itself is a “moving target,” con-
stantly evolving in its capabilities and applications. Thus, all considerations presented here 
must therefore be understood as being somewhat provisional.
19.2  The Philosophy of Trust and AI
Many philosophical theories of trust converge on the recognition of two essential elements: 
epistemic uncertainty and vulnerability. Trust requires a situation in which the outcome is 
not fully predictable. It entails a lack of complete knowledge about what will happen. At the 
same time, trust involves vulnerability, as it entails taking a risk –­ often one that exceeds what 
might be considered prudent. By placing trust, we expose ourselves to potential harm or loss 
(e.g., Luhmann 1968; Baier 1986). Baier, thus, argues: “Trust [. . .] is accepted vulnerability 
to another’s possible but not expected ill will (or lack of good will) toward one” (Baier 1986, 
235). These dual aspects of uncertainty and vulnerability are fundamental to understanding 
the nature of trust, including trust in AI.
AI systems are opaque, as users typically lack secure knowledge about the accuracy or 
reliability of individual outcomes. This opaqueness contributes to uncertainty, particularly 
when decisions depend on complex, probabilistic processes that are not fully transparent or 
explainable. At the same time, AI systems frequently outperform alternative methods, mak-
ing them attractive and increasingly integrated into critical decision-­making processes 
across various domains. They are entrusted with significant decisions and functions in our 
daily lives, from healthcare and finance to transportation and governance. However, this 
growing deployment of AI systems also amplifies our vulnerability: the more we delegate to 

--- Page 274 ---

Trust in AI
267
these technologies, the more we expose ourselves to risks associated with errors, biases, and 
failures inherent to these systems.
While there is a broad consensus in philosophical debates that epistemic uncertainty and 
vulnerability are essential components of trust relationships, opinions diverge when addres­
sing other aspects. Is trust a mental or psychological attitude? Does it rest on certain beliefs or 
experiences? Is it an emotion or does it have affective components? Is trust volitional, meaning 
that we can choose to trust? How does trust differ from reliance? This last question is particu-
larly relevant in the context of AI, where much debate revolves around whether the appro-
priate stance toward this technology is not trust, but rather reliance, if anything at all.
In the first part of this section, I will outline the philosophical debate on trust and how it 
relates to the conceptualization of trust in AI. I will show that in conceptualizing trust in AI, 
we must take into account various aspects and dimensions of trust, as this has profound 
implications for how AI should be appropriately regulated and for determining what forms of 
trust management are both feasible and ethically warranted. In the second part of this sec-
tion, I will turn to three forms of trust –­ interpersonal trust, trust in institutions, and trust in 
technology  –­ and trace how the current debate on trust in AI positions itself regarding 
whether trust in AI should be understood primarily through the lens of interpersonal trust, 
institutional trust, or technological trust. I will argue that trust in AI cannot be fully reduced 
to any one of these forms. Instead, it encompasses elements of all three.
19.3  What is Trust?
19.3.1  Trust and Belief
According to so-­called doxastic accounts of trust, on the one hand, trust entails a belief 
regarding the object of trust (Adler 1994; Hardin 2002; Fricker 2006; Hieronomy 2008; 
McMyler 2011; Keren 2014). This belief may concern the trustworthiness of the entity in a 
generalized sense, for instance “I believe that you are trustworthy”, or may be focused on a 
specific expected behavior, such as “I believe that you will do what I entrust you to do.” Some 
approaches argue that the statements “I believe that you are trustworthy” and “I trust you” 
are indeed equivalent (Hardin 2002; Hieronomy 2008; McMyler 2011), suggesting that trust 
is fundamentally a matter of holding a belief about someone’s trustworthiness. Others argue 
that such a belief about the object of trust is a necessary but not a sufficient condition of trust 
(Keren 2014).5 Nondoxastic accounts, on the other hand, contend that while a belief in the 
trustworthiness of the object of trust is often present in trust relations, it is not a necessary 
component of trust (Holton  1994; Becker  1996; Jones  1996; Faulkner  2007; Frost-­
Arnold 2014). According to these views, trust can exist independently of explicit beliefs about 
trustworthiness. Instead, trust may be characterized by a certain attitude, disposition, or 
practice of relying on another, even in the absence of specific beliefs. This approach ­emphasizes 
that trust is not solely a cognitive state but may involve emotional, volitional, or relational 
aspects that are not reducible to mere belief. Consequently, trust can manifest in actions and 
relationships without requiring a conscious or articulated belief in the other’s 
trustworthiness.
The implications for AI are profound, particularly concerning the certification and regula-
tion of AI systems, as well as the question of whether trustworthiness truly plays a decisive 
role in the adoption of AI-­based services, as is often assumed. If the doxastic account is correct 
and trust is primarily belief based, then efforts to establish criteria for trustworthiness and 

--- Page 275 ---

Karoline Reinhardt
268
potentially certify systems as trustworthy make sense. Such approaches align with the idea 
that users’ trust in AI is contingent upon their beliefs about its reliability, competence, or 
moral alignment. However, if trust is not, or not solely, belief based, and the relationship bet-
ween trustworthiness and trust is more obscure, then these approaches may lose their effi-
cacy. In this case, certification might fail to address the more complex, affective, or relational 
dimensions of trust that influence whether users actually engage with AI systems. This raises 
critical questions about how best to foster genuine trust in AI beyond mere regulatory 
compliance.
19.3.2  Trust and Volition
Trust is often considered not merely a passive state but an active, volitional commitment, 
where an individual consciously decides to place trust in another person, institution, or 
system. This volitional aspect becomes particularly evident in situations where the evidence 
for trustworthiness is unclear or absent, yet trust is extended nonetheless. Unlike beliefs, 
which are typically seen as involuntary responses to perceived evidence, trust can involve a 
deliberate choice to rely on someone or something, even in the face of uncertainty. This 
decision to trust, despite potential risks or lack of full assurance, underscores that trust is not 
solely about assessing and responding to evidence but also about exercising a form of judg-
ment that goes beyond mere cognitive evaluation (Holton 1994, with regard to self-­trust: 
Hinchman 2018). This aspect of trust has, again, implications in the context of AI: if trust 
involves a decision, then it may be possible to decide to trust certain AI applications based on 
certifications or regulatory assurances, even without holding a belief in the technology’s 
inherent trustworthiness –­ perhaps due to a lack of knowledge or understanding required to 
form such a belief.
From this perspective, certification efforts would indeed make more sense, but the resulting 
trust relationship would have a structure distinct from what purely doxastic accounts assume. 
In this model, I hold a belief about certification standards or similar assurances and derive 
from this primary trust in the certification a secondary trust in the technology. However, this 
secondary trust requires a conscious decision, as it does not stem from a belief in the tech-
nology itself. This distinction underscores that trusting AI often involves a layered and medi-
ated process, combining volitional commitment with indirect forms of assurance.
19.3.3  Trust and Attitude
Some philosophers conceptualize trust not as belief but rather as an attitude. This perspective 
highlights that trust is not just about believing that someone is trustworthy, but also involves 
a readiness or willingness to rely on them, a predisposition to interpret their actions favorably, 
and an openness to being vulnerable in the relationship. Karen Jones, for instance, discusses 
trust as an affective attitude (Jones 1996): “to trust someone is to have an attitude of opti-
mism about her goodwill and to have a confident expectation that, when the need arises, the 
one trusted will be directly and favorably moved by the thought that you are counting on her” 
(Jones 1996, 5 f.). This view departs from traditional belief-­centric theories of trust by empha-
sizing the affective and attitudinal components of trust, which allows it to be understood as 
more than just a cognitive assessment of trustworthiness.
This reconceptualization broadens our understanding of trust and is also relevant when 
applied to AI, where the relational and affective dimensions of trust may shape user interactions 
as much as –­ or even more than –­ rational assessments of technical reliability. When trust is 

--- Page 276 ---

Trust in AI
269
understood as an attitude, it implies that users approach AI not just as a tool but as something 
they feel a certain openness towards. This openness may manifest in several ways, for instance in 
their willingness to use AI applications, driven by an optimistic expectation that the system will 
act in their best interest, even if they do not fully understand its mechanisms. It might also shape 
how users interpret the results produced by AI systems. Those with a trusting attitude are more 
likely to view outcomes favorably, attributing errors to anomalies rather than fundamental flaws. 
Additionally, trust as an attitude might influence users’ readiness to make themselves vulnerable, 
e.g., by sharing private information with AI systems. This approach thus helps to better under-
stand user interactions with AI that we could not explain on a purely doxastic basis.
19.3.4  Trust and Emotion
In the philosophical discourse on trust, the relationship between trust and emotion has gar-
nered significant attention. As highlighted, for instance, again by Jones (1996), it seems evi-
dent that trust is not merely a matter of experience, evidence, or calculation, but also involves 
significant affective components. She argues that trust is not merely a cognitive assessment 
but fundamentally involves an emotional attitude. It also encompasses an affective orienta-
tion toward another person, characterized by optimism and a positive expectation. Similarly, 
Richard Holton (1994) supports the view that trust involves emotional dimensions, empha-
sizing that it often encompasses feelings of hope and anticipation beyond mere cognitive eval-
uations. These positions emphasize that trust is not solely a rational or belief-­based construct 
but is deeply intertwined with affective experiences.
This has led to debates about whether trust itself might be classified as an emotion. However, 
there is considerable disagreement on what exactly an emotion is. Thus, defining trust as an 
emotion is challenging, given the considerable disparities in philosophical understandings of 
what constitutes an emotion. Bernd Lahno argues, for instance, for a more modest thesis that 
trust at least exhibits elements typically associated with emotions, such as its affective inten-
sity, its role in shaping interpersonal relationships, and its capacity to influence how we per-
ceive and respond to others (Lahno 2001a, 2018). Thus, while trust may not fit neatly into the 
category of emotion, it undeniably shares characteristics with emotional states.
This affective understanding of trust has profound implications for how we conceptualize 
trust in AI. While much of the current philosophical literature focuses on questions of what 
trust is and when it is justified to trust, emotional aspects of trust often remain overlooked. Yet, 
these aspects are critical for understanding both our relationship with AI and how this rela-
tionship can be managed. For example, affective trust can foster a sense of connection with AI, 
particularly in systems designed for social interaction, such as virtual assistants or care-­giving 
robots. This raises ethical concerns about manipulation and overreliance on systems that sim-
ulate emotional understanding. Eva Weber-­Guskar further warns of the danger of emotional 
alienation that arises when humans project authentic emotions onto machines that lack gen-
uine feelings (Weber-­Guskar 2021). She emphasizes that such projection can blur the bound-
aries between human and machine interactions, raising significant ethical and social concerns 
(Weber-­Guskar 2024). This blurring challenges our understanding of emotional authenticity 
and the nature of human relationships, as individuals may begin to form connections with 
entities incapable of reciprocating or genuinely engaging in emotional exchanges.
These concerns highlight the need for careful reflection on the design and implementation 
of emotionally responsive AI, as well as on the ethical implications of fostering human–­
machine relationships that might compromise the integrity of human emotional experiences. 
The emotional dimension of trust relationships must be taken seriously. Emotional responses 

--- Page 277 ---

Karoline Reinhardt
270
to AI systems –­ whether projection or connection –­ are not merely side-­effects, but integral to 
how trust (in AI) develops and functions. Addressing these emotional dimensions is crucial 
for ethical considerations on how users engage with AI systems and how they should be 
designed so as to respect human emotional experiences.
19.3.5  Trust and Reliance
Some philosophers argue that trust may not be the appropriate framework for understanding 
our relationship with AI. They contend that what we often describe as “trust in AI” might be 
more accurately framed as reliance. The distinction between trust and reliance is a central 
issue in the philosophical analysis of trust. Some philosophers argue that while reliance can 
exist without trust, trust cannot exist without some form of reliance, since trust inherently 
involves a reliance on the trustee to fulfill expectations of the trustor. They argue that trust is, 
thus, essentially a species of reliance (Goldberg 2018, 97). However, while both concepts 
involve a form of dependence on others or things, they differ in other respects. Reliance refers 
to a practical dependence on someone’s actions or on a system to function as expected, often 
grounded in rational calculation or evidence of reliability. Trust, however, seems to go beyond 
mere reliance. Some argue that it goes beyond mere reliance by incorporating an expectation 
of goodwill and a personal commitment from the trusted party (Hawley 2019). According to 
Baier and others, trust often seems to imply a deeper, affective connection, where the trustor 
believes that the trustee will act with a sense of responsibility and care, even in the absence of 
strict oversight or guarantees.
If trust truly requires an expectation of the other party’s goodwill, the concept cannot be 
meaningfully applied to AI systems, as these lack will, let alone goodwill, in the relevant sense. 
In human–­AI interactions, this distinction becomes particularly important, since humans 
often attribute goodwill to agents they trust, assuming those agents are intentionally acting 
in their favor. However, AI lacks true intentionality because it does not have consciousness or 
moral agency. Even if an AI system reliably achieves outcomes that seem aligned with good-
will (e.g., a healthcare AI saving lives), these outcomes result from design and programming, 
not from an intentional desire to help. Thus, if trust inherently involves relying on the moral 
intentions and goodwill of another, it cannot be properly extended to nonhuman entities 
such as machines, whose actions are driven by algorithms and programming rather than by 
any moral or conscious intent.
This distinction raises important questions about how we should understand our relation-
ships with technology and whether the language of trust is appropriate in these contexts 
(Weckert 2011). Some philosophers thus argue that trust may not be the appropriate frame-
work for understanding our relationship with AI as it is a technology, suggesting instead that 
reliance is a better conceptual fit. From this perspective, they maintain that we should not 
“trust” AI at all (e.g., Ryan 2020). However, this approach faces several challenges.
First, it must be acknowledged that people frequently describe their relationship with tech-
nology, including AI, in terms of trust and genuinely experience trust in AI systems. Ignoring 
this experiential dimension risks overlooking an important aspect of how humans interact 
with these systems. Second, the concept of reliance might fail to capture some unique char-
acteristics of AI systems; the probabilistic nature of many AI systems, combined with their 
capacity to operate in complex and adaptive ways, makes their outputs less straightforward 
compared to traditional technologies. Unlike the results of a calculator, which are determin-
istic, AI systems’ outputs entail probabilistic results and are often opaque in nature. While 
reliance implies a functional dependency on a system’s consistent performance, trust encompasses 

--- Page 278 ---

Trust in AI
271
an acceptance of uncertainty and a willingness to engage with the system despite the potential 
for error or opacity. These factors suggest that trust, rather than mere reliance, remains 
­crucial for understanding human–­AI interactions, although it may need to be redefined.6
19.4  Whom to Trust? Three Paradigms –­ and Trust in AI
As we have seen, depending on which dimension of the nature of trust –­ belief, volition, atti-
tude, emotion, or reliance –­ is emphasized, different aspects of human–­AI interactions come 
to the forefront, revealing different needs for regulation. Trust in AI cannot, however, be 
meaningfully reduced to any single one of these dimensions. Rather, all aspects likely play a 
role –­ maybe to varying degrees, depending on the specific context and perhaps even on 
individual personal characteristics. To adequately capture the phenomenon of trust in AI, all 
these dimensions must be taken seriously. Only then can we derive appropriate conclusions 
for the ethical development of this relationship  –­ whether on legal-­political, societal, or 
personal levels.
The same applies when considering another way of distinguishing trust: interpersonal 
trust, trust in institutions, and trust in technologies. For some time, the philosophical debate 
has focused on determining which of these three forms of trust most accurately corresponds 
to trust in AI. As we will see, trust in AI cannot be reduced to any one of these paradigmatic 
forms either. Instead, it encompasses aspects of all three. This is partly because AI constitutes 
an adaptive socio-­technical system with probabilistic and, in many cases, highly interactive 
components. These features blur traditional boundaries between the three forms of trust, as 
AI systems exhibit elements of personal interaction, institutional frameworks, and techno-
logical infrastructure simultaneously. Understanding trust in AI therefore requires an inte-
grative approach that accounts for this unique and hybrid nature.
19.4.1  Interpersonal Trust
In contemporary philosophical discussions, interpersonal trust is often seen as the paradigmatic 
form of trust, manifesting across a wide range of relationships: “Interpersonal trust seems to be 
a pre-­condition to many of our most valued and closest relationships, yet there is no one formula 
or set of characteristics that constitute interpersonal trust” (Potter 2020, 24, cf; Jones 1996, 6). 
This type of trust can be found in intimate relationships, such as friendships or romantic partner-
ships, where one might trust a friend to provide emotional support or a partner to be honest and 
open about their feelings. Trust in strangers, however, such as relying on someone for directions 
or help in a moment of need, also exemplifies interpersonal trust but in a different context. These 
diverse trust practices highlight the variety of human relationships and the different expecta-
tions involved. For instance, in a friendship, trust might revolve around confidentiality and loy-
alty, while between lovers, it could center more on emotional vulnerability and mutual 
dependence. A further example is the trust inherent in the doctor–­patient relationship, where a 
patient trusts the doctor to act in their best interest, providing accurate diagnoses and appro-
priate treatments based on their expertise. When it comes to strangers, trust might involve a cal-
culated risk, often grounded in social norms or the hope of mutual benefit.
Interpersonal trust, especially in intimate relationships, is frequently accompanied by emo-
tions such as affection, love, or a sense of security, and can itself be experienced as a generalized 
emotional attitude toward the person. Trust in strangers, however, is more prone to epistemic 
limitations and biases, as it often requires making decisions based on limited information. 

--- Page 279 ---

Karoline Reinhardt
272
Additionally, there are scenarios where trust serves a pedagogical function, such as entrusting 
children with responsibilities to foster their growth and competence (Horsburgh  1960; 
Pettit 1995; McGeer 2008, 241). This diversity in interpersonal trust practices underscores the 
complexity and multifaceted nature of trust in human interactions.
Though interpersonal trust is nowadays often regarded as the paradigm case of trust, his-
torically other subjects of trust have been more prevalent. As noted by Frevert, in earlier dis-
courses on trust, trust in people was initially viewed with skepticism (Frevert 2013). Instead, 
trust was considered more appropriately placed in entities such as God, where it was seen as a 
more stable and reliable form of trust. It was only later that trust in humans became a 
significant part of the debate, particularly in contexts involving experts, such as doctors, and 
in close personal relationships, like those between friends.
The definition of trust significantly influences which relationships are deemed suitable for 
it. For instance, as previously mentioned, certain types of trust relationships, such as those 
involving expectations of goodwill or moral intent, cannot be meaningfully established with 
technologies, which lack consciousness and intentionality. Some authors emphasize that a 
unique feature of trust, especially interpersonal trust, is the possibility of feeling betrayed 
(Baier 1986, 235). This feeling of betrayal is not only possible but is considered an appro-
priate response to a breach of trust, underscoring the deeply personal and relational nature 
of trust between individuals –­ distinguishing it from mere reliance or trust in technology.
Human–­AI interactions thus challenge interpersonal understandings of trust in many 
ways. One reason is that AI systems, unlike human agents, do not experience or respond to 
vulnerability. They operate based on algorithms and data without personal stakes or emo-
tional engagement. Thus, while users may be and feel vulnerable when relying on AI sys-
tems, this vulnerability is not reciprocated in the same way as it would be in human–­human 
relationships. This asymmetry challenges us to reconsider how we conceptualize and man-
age trust in these interactions. One issue the philosophical debate on trust discusses inten-
sively is whether traditional understandings of trust, like interpersonal trust, can be 
meaningfully extended to nonhuman entities like AI systems, which lack the intentionality, 
consciousness, emotionality, or moral agency that many theories of trust presuppose.
At the same time, as said above, humans form emotional bonds with AI and experience 
trust in these systems, or the betrayal thereof. For instance, users may become frustrated with 
incorrect directions and scold these technologies when errors occur. In part, this can be 
attributed to the high interactivity and adaptivity of certain AI systems. Their interactivity 
becomes particularly apparent in systems that engage dynamically with users, mirroring 
aspects of interpersonal exchange and thereby inviting trust. Furthermore, their adaptivity –­ 
such as the ability to learn from inputs and adjust results –­ can foster perceptions of respon-
siveness. Moreover, as previously noted, the probabilistic nature of AI systems complicates 
the idea of a purely reliance-­based relationship, in a traditional understanding, since out-
comes are not always deterministic. This complexity underscores the need for a nuanced 
understanding of trust in AI, which accounts for its unique interactive, adaptive, and proba-
bilistic features: human–­AI interactions exhibit aspects of interpersonal trust.
19.4.2  Trust in Technology
In contemporary society, reliance on technological artifacts has become nearly unavoidable, yet 
these technologies are growing ever more complex and quite often, we are unable to grasp their 
inner workings –­ yet we continue to use them. For example, many car drivers would struggle to 
explain the mechanics of an internal combustion engine, despite relying on cars for daily 

--- Page 280 ---

Trust in AI
273
transportation. This gap in understanding is even more pronounced with digital innovations 
such as AI. AI systems, particularly those employing advanced techniques like deep learning, 
operate through processes that are opaque not only to lay users, but often even to experts in the 
field. The comprehension of such intricate technologies remains elusive for many of us, espe-
cially for those without specialized knowledge in computer science, statistics, or stochastic 
processes. For most users, grasping such complexity is simply out of reach: “Yet, as technology 
becomes increasingly complex, users may lack a deep understanding of its intricacies. As a resort 
they turn to trusting the technology to function as expected, allowing them to engage with 
­technology without fully comprehending its underlying mechanisms. Trust then simplifies 
­complexity” (Pöll 2024). Users rely on technology to perform as expected, sidestepping the need 
for exhaustive understanding. Trust, in this sense, functions as a simplification tool 
(cf. Luhmann 1968), enabling interaction with technologies whose inner workings remain opaque.
Many technologies thus in general fulfill the condition of epistemic uncertainty, and AI 
appears to do so to an even greater extent. At the same time, the increasingly pervasive 
integration of technology like AI into everyday life, combined with the sensitivity of tasks del-
egated to AI such as decision making in healthcare, finance, or criminal justice, ensures that 
the vulnerability condition of trust is also met: users often depend on these systems in high-­
stakes contexts where errors could have profound consequences.
Trust in technologies, however, appears to operate differently from interpersonal trust. What 
does it mean to say that we trust technologies? For instance, we likely trust that an airplane will 
stay in the air when we board it, but do we actually trust the airplane itself? Some philosophers 
hold that trust in technologies ultimately refers not to the artifact itself but to those who design, 
manufacture, and maintain these technologies. From this perspective, trust in technologies could 
be seen as reducible to interpersonal trust. Another view focuses on the technological infrastruc-
ture: instead of reducing trust in technology, according to this view, we actually place trust in the 
artifact itself. What we trust, then, is the functionality of the technology, not just the person who 
made the artifact (Nickel 2013). As Pöll has pointed out, “some suggest that proper coding can 
generate trust as it manifests and reinforces contractual agreements in the form of algorithms. In 
code expectations, rights and responsibilities are made explicit, guiding and limiting user interac-
tions, but also providing some clarity, simplifying the use of ever more complex technology” 
(Pöll 2024). Yet another view suggests that trust in technologies, especially as socio-­technical 
systems, extends beyond the artifact and the individuals involved, encompassing elements of 
political and legal regulation and control. We trust that the airplane will stay in the air not only 
because we trust the engineers’ expertise but also because we have faith in the certification 
processes and maintenance regulations. Therefore, trust in technologies would involve interper-
sonal, technological, and institutional elements.
19.4.3  Trust in Institutions
The debate surrounding trust in institutions centers on whether this form of trust can be 
reduced to interpersonal trust or whether it constitutes a distinct and genuine form of trust in 
its own right. Reductionist accounts of institutional trust argue, much like reductionist accounts 
of trust in technology, that ultimately, trust in institutions can be reduced to trust in the individ-
uals who work within them. According to this view, trusting an institution is essentially about 
trusting the people who represent and execute its functions. In contrast, nonreductionist 
accounts maintain that trust in institutions extends beyond the individuals within them, 
encompassing trust in the structures and processes of these institutions, that is, nonhuman 
entities that define the institution. This perspective suggests that institutional trust is rooted in 

--- Page 281 ---

Karoline Reinhardt
274
the reliability and integrity of the institution as a whole, rather than being merely a sum of the 
trust placed in its members (Lahno 2001b; Teng 2021; Townley and Garfield 2013).
This understanding of trust proves particularly relevant for the philosophy of AI in at least 
two significant respects. First, from a nonreductionist perspective on trust in institutions, 
trust is not limited solely to interpersonal relationships but extends to nonpersonal entities as 
well. This broader conception allows for the inclusion of AI systems within the domain of 
trust. Second, trust also pertains to structures and processes, which is especially compelling 
when considering AI as a socio-­technical system. When AI is described as a socio-­technical 
system, it refers to the idea that AI is not just a technical artifact but is embedded within and 
interacts with broader social, cultural, economic, and institutional contexts. This concept 
emphasizes that the development, deployment, and impact of AI cannot be fully understood 
or managed purely from a technical standpoint. Instead, AI systems are shaped by and, in 
turn, shape social norms, practices, power dynamics, and organizational structures. A nonre-
ductionist perspective on trust in institutions thus underscores the importance of recognizing 
that trust in AI systems is not merely about the reliability or functionality of the technology 
itself, but also about how these systems are integrated into and interact with the social and 
institutional landscapes in which they operate.
19.5  Conclusion
The examination of trust in the context of human–­AI interactions has reignited 
fundamental questions about the nature of trust itself. AI systems inherently present 
unique challenges to theories of trust, particularly as they become more pervasive and are 
entrusted with increasingly significant decisions and functions in our daily lives. The more 
we delegate to these technologies, the greater our vulnerability to them becomes. In certain 
respects, AI creates even more reason to trust it, given that we rely on it to perform tasks for 
which we often lack secure knowledge about the accuracy of individual outcomes, yet it 
frequently outperforms alternative methods. Therefore, not trusting AI could be suboptimal 
in the broader context. However, many philosophical theories struggle with the concept of 
trust in AI. Classical paradigms seem ill suited to capture the nature of this trust, as it does 
not fit neatly into categories like interpersonal trust, since AI is not a person, or institu-
tional trust, even though institutions play a crucial role in its development, regulation, and 
deployment. Nor does trust in AI seem to align entirely with trust in technology. Some even 
argue that technologies cannot truly be trusted and that reliance is a more appropriate 
concept –­ this applies to AI as well.
Whether the question “Can we trust AI?” is meaningful depends significantly on the under-
lying concept of trust. If we adhere to the view that trust is only applicable to persons, then 
trusting AI would only be conceivable in the context of so-­called strong AI, which possesses 
human-­like consciousness or autonomy. However, if we adopt a broader understanding of 
trust –­ one that extends beyond human agents to include nonhuman entities –­ then it becomes 
plausible to consider if we can indeed trust AI.
Furthermore, it is important to note that due to the technical specifics of AI, we cannot 
rely on these technologies in the same way we rely on the functioning of a calculator. Unlike 
a calculator, which only makes errors when it is malfunctioning, AI operates as a probabilistic 
learning model where “errors” are inherent to the technology itself. While AI models may 
outperform many alternatives in general, they can still make incorrect decisions in individual 
cases, and these errors are not necessarily a sign of malfunction. In AI, errors are an expected 

--- Page 282 ---

Trust in AI
275
aspect of the system’s operation, which fundamentally distinguishes it from ­simpler, deter-
ministic technologies like calculators.
In this respect, we cannot simply rely on AI in the same straightforward manner we rely on a 
calculator; rather, if we are to engage with AI meaningfully, it requires a form of trust. Unlike a 
calculator, which offers predictable and error-­free results under normal functioning, AI sys-
tems operate within a probabilistic framework, where uncertainty and potential errors are 
inherent. Therefore, reliance on AI alone is insufficient because it overlooks the nuanced and 
often unpredictable nature of AI’s decision-­making processes. It is also worth ­noting that many 
AI applications are designed with user interfaces that actively invite trust.
Despite philosophical theories that might argue that this trust is misplaced or inappropriate, 
the reality is that many people do, in fact, experience trust in AI. Instead of merely dismissing 
this trust as inappropriate, we have to consider creating frameworks that appropriately 
address and respond to the way people interact with and trust AI systems.

absent or insignificant, she proposes the term “reliance” as a more appropriate descriptor.

20.1  Introduction
The increasing presence of nonbiological entities, such as robots and embodied ­conversational 
agents (ECAs), challenges our traditional understanding of “the other,” the category of 
entities we perceive as minded creatures. They put under pressure our standard view of “the 
other,” which has been centered on humans. To address this challenge, some researchers 
have proposed the concept of “other-­ware” as a framework for studying our interactions with 
these newcomers (Hassenzahl et al. 2021; Saßmannshausen et al. 2023). Others have argued 
that any firm and clear distinction between human persons and robots could not be found 
and thus we have to recognize other forms of otherness (Gunkel  2012,  2018,  2023). In 
agreement with this line of thought and based on a phenomenologically inspired enactive 
approach to social cognition, Safdari (2021, 2023) has put some flesh on these bones. This 
approach emphasizes the embodied and situated nature of human cognition, suggesting that 
our interactions with others, including robots and ECAs, are shaped by our embodied experi-
ences and the context in which they occur.
More specifically, from a phenomenological1 point of view, experiencing a certain entity as 
an other takes place on three different levels: the that level –­ experiencing an entity as a minded 
one; the what level  –­ determining the other’s specific state of mind; and the why level  –­ 
reasoning about the other’s past and future mental states (Zahavi 2014, pp. 167–­168). The 
first level is entirely experiential and direct, while the other two levels are cognitive and infer-
ential. This means that when we encounter another human being, as an instance of “the 
other,” we don’t initially grasp their mindedness through inferential procedures; instead, we 
directly experience their mindedness. However, we need some sort of cognitive reasoning and 
inferences to understand what specific mental state they are in at the moment (e.g., thirsti-
ness) and why they are in this state (e.g., because they just have finished running).
When it comes to the first level, also known as basic empathy, two mechanisms can be 
identified as being responsible, one perceptual and the other interactive-­pragmatic. The first 
mechanism implies that perception is smart enough to immediately pick up the entities that 
manifest expressiveness2 (Gallagher 2001, 2008). And the interactive-­pragmatic mechanism 
Are Large Language Models Embodied?: Basic

implies that the ability to establish a harmonious embodied interaction (more about this in 
the sections that follow) results in our ability to experience the other as the other. Here, we 
need to tread carefully as these two mechanisms, while conceptually distinct, are fully 
integrated in the lived experience. In other words, both mechanisms are simultaneously at 
play in the concrete experience of encountering the other.
Numerous empirical studies provide compelling evidence that people often interact with 
robots and ECAs not as mere technological objects but as the others (Breazeal  2002; 
Rosenthal-­von der Pütten et al. 2013). As I have argued, both these mechanisms operate in 
human–­robot interactions, leading to our perception of robots as “others.” However, when 
people engage in cognitive reflection on their interactions with robots, they often conclude 
that robots lack internal states and are merely inanimate technological artifacts. This is why 
Breazeal, in her experiments with Kismet, a very well-­known social robot, contends that:
If asked before the respective experiment if they could imagine treating a computer like a person, 
they strongly deny it. Even after the experiment, they insist that they treated the computer as a 
machine. They do not realize that they treated it as a peer (2002, p. 15).
Therefore, this experiential relationship occurs solely at the “that” level, devoid of the other 
two levels. Due to the absence of the “what” and “why” levels in this experiential relation, it is 
more accurate to describe robots as “pseudo-­others” rather than “perfect others.”
Now we are seeing the emergence of another group of newcomers, namely large language 
models (LLM), which appear at first glance to challenge this framework. The challenge is 
rooted in the fact that on one hand, LLMs like ChatGPT evoke the same experiential relation 
with the users. For example, in a recent study by Jacobs et al. (2023), it was observed that 
exposing individuals to ChatGPT significantly enhanced their perception of the AI system as 
a minded entity. In this experiment, 148 participants from diverse backgrounds were shown 
three separate conversations with GPT-­4. Following these exposures, participants were asked 
to rate the degree to which they perceived ChatGPT as a minded entity. The authors of the 
study draw the following conclusion:
Our findings indicate that participants significantly increased their mind perception of ChatGPT –­ 
both in terms of what it can do (its agency) and what it can feel (its experience) after being given 
short examples of its capabilities. These changes in mind perception are remarkable for … the 
changes in mind perception occurred after only a very brief exposure (i.e., the presentation of 3 
examples) (Jacobs et al. 2023, p. 12).
However, while people regard these LLMs as the other, at first glance it seems that the previously 
mentioned two mechanisms responsible for the experiential constitution of the other could 
not be found in this relationship. LLMs, such as ChatGPT, lack a face to display facial expres-
sions, so their interaction with people lacks the perceptual component; they also lack a body 
to interact with people in the same way that a robot or another human can. Thus, it appears 
that the phenomenological-­enactive framework, which was developed to explain our interac-
tion with robots, cannot account for our interaction with LLMs.
In the rest of this chapter, I will look closely at these two mechanisms and how they play a 
part in our interactions with LLMs. First, I will explore the perceptual component, followed by 
an analysis of the interactive-­pragmatic component. This thorough examination will pave 
the way to evaluation of the underlying processes that contribute to our sense of otherness in 
human–­LLM interaction.

20.2  The Perceptual Component
When it comes to interacting with LLMs, it could be acknowledged that there is no perceptual 
component involved. They exist purely in the digital realm. They cannot display facial expres-
sions that convey emotions or intentions. Instead, we typically interact with them through 
text-­based interfaces. This might be a simple chat window, a more elaborate virtual environ-
ment, or even voice-­activated interaction. Regardless of the format, the core experience lacks 
the rich sensory information that shapes our perception of “otherness” in face-­to-­face inter-
actions. However, recently some scholars have argued that these interfaces might be consid-
ered as real faces.
Galit Wellner (2014), for example, makes the argument that screens can be thought of as 
quasi-­faces. She contends, drawing on a Levinasian line of thought, that while screens and 
faces are different on the ethical level –­ that is, screens do not demand an ethical response, in 
contrast to genuine human faces –­ they have essential similarities on an ontological level. 
First, both conceal their inner workings. The face hides emotions and thoughts, while the 
screen masks the algorithms. Second, both facilitate communication. Humans use facial 
expressions to communicate with each other, while they use the screen to communicate with 
their technological artifacts. Third, both of them operate based on language. In case of 
human–­human interaction they dialogue with each other to exchange ideas and emotion 
while they dialogue with screens, through touching, typing, etc., to operate applications and 
perfume various actions on their devices. Fourth, both have extensions beyond their immediate 
form; hands complement facial expressions while keyboards act as extensions of the screen. 
Finally, neither is truly neutral. A face can lie through expressions, just as a screen can pre-
sent misleading information and disappoint us.
This similarity list approach, in my opinion, has a number of issues that prevent me find-
ing it persuasive. First, it is based on a false assumption that is obviously at odds with phenom-
enological findings. From a phenomenological standpoint  –­ which Wellner likewise is 
committed to –­ the face hides inner states such as feelings and ideas. There isn’t enough space 
here to delve into the details but suffice it to note that the body, including the face, isn’t just an 
object among the objects. It is the center of intentionality, allowing direct perception of the 
subject’s mental states. In other words, the face doesn’t conceal internal states but rather 
reveals them. This perspective, known as direct perception theory, has garnered significant 
support from both philosophical and scientific viewpoints (Cavallo et  al.  2016; 
Gallagher 2001, 2008; Helton,2018; Meltzoff 1995; Zahavi 2001, 2011). Therefore, without 
any intermediary or inference, the subject’s face discloses  –­ or perhaps more accurately, 
­constitutes  –­ their inner life, whereas the screen does not directly convey any meaning. 
Furthermore, if we accept the first proposed similarity, we also have to admit that numerous 
types of artifacts, like printers and cars, have faces. Because their internal mechanisms are 
hidden by their external cover, this challenge also applies to the fourth similarity she pro-
poses. Keyboards and hands are not the same thing because the hand, as an expressive 
extension of the face, is not an object among other objects. Her second and third suggested 
similarities are overly inclusive. Both of these features are present in other technological 
objects, such as elevators and printers, because it is through their external covers that we 
communicate with them.
Ultimately, the face is more than just an interface; it is a central aspect of human embodi-
ment. Facial expressions, along with hands as expressive extensions, contribute significantly 
to the complexity of human–­human interaction. Keyboards, on the other hand, represent a 

--- Page 288 ---

ARE LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS EMBODIED?
281
specific tool for interacting with the screen, not an extension of self-­expression in the same 
way. While the face and the screen share some superficial similarities in function, a deeper 
analysis reveals significant differences on the ontological level.3 The face plays a unique role 
in direct perception and embodies human intentionality, while screens are a technological 
interface lacking the nuanced expressiveness of the human body.
20.3  The Interactive-­pragmatic Component
Therefore, it seems more fruitful to set aside this perceptual aspect and instead focus on the 
second interactive-­pragmatic component. Upon reflecting on this second component, we 
realize that it necessitates a body as a vehicle for interactions. This raises the question: What 
does “body” mean in this context? Is it necessarily a tangible, physical body? If so, then it 
seems that our enactive framework fails to explain our empathic relationship with LLMs. 
However, if the answer is no, then we need to clarify in what sense LLMs’ interactions with 
people are embodied. In the sections that follow, I will examine different influential accounts 
of embodiment in the fields of robotics, AI, and cognitive science. I demonstrate briefly why 
they are phenomenologically insufficient. Then, drawing mainly on the literature on phe-
nomenologically inspired enactivism, I propose three distinct ways of understanding embodi-
ment: Being embodied as being located; being embodied as being situated; and being embodied 
as being able to establish a dynamic history of interaction. I will delve into these three mean-
ings of embodiment in more detail in the sections that follow.
20.4  What is Embodiment: Lessons from Robotics and Cognitive Science
Margaret Wilson, in arguably the most frequently cited account, identifies six distinct views 
of cognition as an embodied phenomenon (2002).
(1)	 Cognition is situated: which implies that cognition is situated within the context of task-­
specific sensory information (input) and actions (output). Wilson equates situation with 
immediate environmental stimuli. Therefore, under this definition, thinking about a 
future trip to Isfahan wouldn’t be considered situated cognition because it lacks direct 
sensory input.
(2)	 Cognition is time pressured: Beyond immediate environmental stimuli, Wilson argues that 
being situated also involves real-­time constraints. This comes into play when the agent 
doesn’t have enough time to construct the necessary representations, forcing them to 
deal with the situation directly without the cognitive mediation of those representa-
tions. Conversely, in cases where the agent isn’t rushed and has the time to contemplate 
a situation in an offline manner –­ decoupled from the immediate context –­ cognition can 
be considered nonsituated in this second sense.
(3)	 We offload cognitive work onto the environment: the agent uses her immediate surround-
ings to reduce cognitive workload when faced with situations where offline cognition is 
not feasible. For example, using fingers for calculations utilizes the environment to 
lessen the mental burden.
(4)	 The environment is part of the cognitive system: this is a stronger version of the previous 
idea. Here, the agent doesn’t merely use the environment for cognitive purposes; instead, 
the environment itself becomes part of the cognitive procedure. This means that 

--- Page 289 ---

ABOOTALEB SAFDARI
282
­cognition isn’t solely a mental activity but a distributed event involving the mind, body, 
and environment. Wilson, however, disagrees with this notion. While acknowledging 
the environment’s significant influence on cognition, she argues that it shouldn’t be 
considered part of the cognitive system itself.
(5)	 Cognition is for action: this perspective posits that cognitive processes are inherently 
action oriented, serving to facilitate adaptive behavior. Empirical evidence supports this 
notion, as particular visual stimuli can unconsciously prime motor activity. For example, 
the presentation of a rectangular object with a specific orientation can unconsciously 
prepare the observer for a subsequent grasping task, provided the target object shares 
that same orientation. However, Wilson challenges this view as representing a limited 
account of cognition. Many cognitive acts, such as appreciating a sunset, go beyond 
simply guiding motor behavior.
(6)	 Offline cognition is body based: this is probably the most encompassing view of embodied 
cognition in Wilson’s account, suggesting that even offline cognition can be considered 
embodied. This is exemplified by mental imagery, where performing a mathematical 
operation can be imagined through simulating finger movements without any actual 
physical manipulation. In this way, cognition can be embodied while remaining 
independent of the immediate environment.
As can be understood from the above summary, this account leaves the concept of the body 
largely unexplored. Consequently, in regard to the context of this chapter, several ambiguities 
arise. While a comprehensive analysis is beyond the scope of this chapter, let’s examine a few 
key issues.
The first definition of embodiment, situatedness, raises the question of whether a physical-­
biological body is necessary. Could a physical, nonbiological body suffice? For instance, are 
virtual bodies (avatars) situated within their virtual environments considered embodied 
under this definition? Even seemingly disembodied entities like algorithms could be argued to 
be situated (and thus embodied) in this sense, as they operate within a specific context 
performing input–­output tasks. By extension, virtually any object could be modeled as 
performing an input–­output task. For example, a pencil receives pressure from a hand (input) 
and produces written marks (output). This notion requires further elaboration to be suffi-
ciently restrictive and informative. Furthermore, Wilson’s understanding of time’s role in 
cognition is overly simplistic. Time plays a fundamental and inherent role in our cognitive 
processes and conscious experiences. While a detailed exploration falls outside the chapter’s 
scope, it’s crucial to note that reducing time’s role to situations where an animal is rushed is 
misleading. This paradoxically implies that an animal is embodied only when in a hurry, but 
disembodied otherwise.
Finally, the notion of “offloading cognition” onto the environment presents an overly com-
putational view of embodiment. Within this framework, the environment is reduced to a 
mere tool or a massive calculator, facilitating the execution of our computational processes. 
These limitations highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of embodiment in 
which the nature of the body has been considered.
This motivates Tom Ziemke’s alternative approach, which prioritizes the nature of the 
body itself (2001, 2003, 2004, 2022). Being embodied, in his opinion, can have six distinct 
meanings depending on the nature of the body.
(1)	 Structural coupling: this notion suggests that a system is embodied if there is a bidirec-
tional channel between it and its external environment. However, Ziemke argues that 

--- Page 290 ---

ARE LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS EMBODIED?
283
this definition is not restrictive enough. He points out that, in a broad sense, every 
system, even a static one like a granite outcrop, exhibits some form of structural cou-
pling with its environment.
(2)	 Historical embodiment: which suggests that the history of agent–­environment interac-
tion is what constitutes embodiment.This notion is also overly inclusive and encom-
passes noncognitive systems like granite outcrops, which simply exhibit a history of 
structural coupling with their environment.
(3)	 Physical embodiment: which implies that an entity needs a physical body in order to be 
embodied. This idea is problematic as well because it includes seemingly noncognitive 
entities like desks and chairs.
(4)	 Organismoid embodiment: this notion aligns with physical embodiment but imposes an 
additional constraint: the physical body must resemble a living organism in terms of its 
form and sensorimotor capabilities. Humanoid robots, for example, would be considered 
embodied under this definition.
(5)	 Organismic embodiment: this notion presents a stronger version of the previous one, 
restricting embodiment not only to physical, organism-­like bodies but specifically to 
living organisms. Consequently, cognition, under this definition, is confined to biological 
entities with living bodies.
(6)	 Social embodiment: this notion emphasis the role of embodiment in social interactions. 
Ziemke leaves open for future study the question of whether embodiment in this sense 
necessitates a living, biological body.
This account, by explicitly considering the nature of the body, offers a more nuanced and 
fruitful framework compared to Wilson’s proposal. Under this framework, we can con-
clude that LLMs are not embodied according to the third, fourth, and fifth definitions and 
the sixth definition is left open for future research. However, under the broader definitions 
that focus solely on coupling with the environment (first and second), LLMs could be con-
sidered minimally embodied. Nevertheless, one could reasonably object that this level of 
embodiment is too rudimentary and lacks the depth typically associated with the concept. 
Thus, the definitions suggested by this account are whether too strong to include LLMs or 
too naïve and include nearly everything. Therefore, the challenge lies in finding a middle 
ground between overly restrictive definitions that exclude LLMs altogether and overly 
broad definitions that encompass nearly every system with any form of environmental 
interaction.
Beyond the aforementioned limitations, I think Ziemke’s account suffers from a more 
fundamental issue: its phenomenological inadequacy (further explored in the next 
­section). While he bases his definitions on the nature of the body, his understanding 
appears restricted to physical bodies. By “body,” he seemingly refers only to different 
forms of physicality –­ biological/living bodies or mechanical/robotic ones. This restricted 
view leads to a number of problems. First, his definition of structural coupling or histor-
ical embodiment focuses solely on how an animal/agent physically connects to the envi-
ronment. The lack of a phenomenological lens prevents him from acknowledging more 
nuanced forms of coupling. Second, this inadequacy also prevents him from offering a 
sufficiently comprehensive account of social embodiment. He either reduces this concept 
to organismoid embodiment or leaves it unexamined for future exploration. In what 
follows, I propose a phenomenologically adequate understanding of embodiment and 
show how it provides insight into both the embodied and disembodied aspects of our 
interactions with LLMs.
