20.5  What is Embodiment? A Phenomenological Approach
The previously mentioned phenomenological inadequacy stems from a fundamental distinc-
tion between the objective-­geometrical body and the lived-­phenomenal body. The former per-
tains to the body as understood by natural sciences like physics, chemistry, and biology. From 
this perspective, the body is composed of a specific amount of chemical and physical sub-
stances and contains particular organs. By contrast:
The lived body … is in constant connection with the world. This connection is not a mere surface-­
to-­surface contact, as a corpse might lie on the surface of a table; rather, my body is integrated 
with the world (Gallagher and Zahavi, 2020, p. 154).
The lived body, then, is a form of integration or a possibility to be integrated with the world. 
From a phenomenological perspective, being embodied arises from this moment of integration, 
where the subject and its external environment become interwoven. Therefore, something 
could be considered embodied in this sense of the word if it has the capacity to be integrated 
with the world. This raises a crucial question: What exactly does this integration consist of? 
Do LLMs have this capacity? Or to put it differently, can LLMs be regarded as embodied in this 
sense?
20.5.1  What is Integration?
Integration with the world transcends mere causal-­mechanical coupling with the immediate 
material environment and instead occurs through a dynamic and reciprocal co-­constitution 
of the subject and the environment. In other words, the subject and its surroundings are not 
simply causally connected, but rather mutually shape and define each other through ongoing 
interaction. A crucial dimension of integration unfolds within the context of social interac-
tion.4 Put simply, these social interactions and relations are the very foundation that enables 
integration and, consequently, the constitution of the lived body. This is why Mark Johnson, 
examining the meaning of the body from a phenomenological perspective, acknowledges 
that:
… the body does not come fully formed prior to entering into relations with social others; rather, 
the character of those relations is crucial in shaping bodily modes of comportment (2008, 
p. 165).
As an illustration, consider two different situations in which Maede (an employee) tries to 
move a desk from room A to room B: one in which she uses a trolley and one in which she does 
this in cooperation with a robot. In the former case, she places the desk in a trolley and pulls 
it from room A to room B. There is no reciprocity, no mutual action–­interaction in this case; 
Maede exerts force to move the trolley and we only have a one-­sided mechanical relationship 
between her and the trolley. In the latter case, however, the robot seeks the best grip and thus 
positions her body (assuming the robot’s voice is female), arms, and legs in a specific manner, 
requiring Maede to adjust her bodily position. Then, during the relocation procedure, the 
robot who has been holding the front of the desk notices an obstacle in her path and slows her 
walking speed, causing Maede to slow down as well. Maede is now tired and wants to take a 
break; the robot recognizes this and stops to allow her to rest. Finally, as they enter the other 
room, the robot, who has a complete map of the building in her memory, recognizes that this 

--- Page 292 ---

ARE LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS EMBODIED?
285
is not room B and warns Maede that she is in the wrong room. As a result, Maede continues 
her way to find the right room, which is the next one. In this instance, Maede and the robot 
dynamically and reciprocally co-­constitute each other. For this reason, neither Maede nor the 
robot could receive credit for the entire process.
This reciprocal, dynamic co-­constitution is what has been referred to in the chapter’s 
introduction as harmonious behavior or harmonious interaction. This concept has been pro-
posed by Husserl in his Cartesian Meditations where he writes:
The experienced animate organism of another continues to prove itself as actually an animate 
organism, solely in its changing but incessantly harmonious “behavior”. Such harmonious 
behavior must present itself fulfillingly… and do so throughout the continuous change in behavior 
from phase to phase. The organism becomes experienced as a pseudo-­organism, precisely if there 
is something discordant about its behavior (1960, p. 114).
It can be understood from this passage that harmonious interaction is a dynamic procedure 
that involves the continuous transition from phase to phase. However, these transitions are 
not arbitrary but harmonious. In this context, I think there are three distinct yet interrelated 
characteristics that constitute harmoniousness. Before elaborating on these characteristics, 
let’s briefly summarize the key points discussed thus far. I have argued that current accounts 
of embodiment in cognitive science and robotics overlook the crucial distinction between the 
objective and lived body, neglecting the lived body. Furthermore, it’s been proposed that the 
lived body is a form of integration that transcends mere causal-­mechanical relation. This 
integration, particularly within social settings, is realized through harmonious interaction. 
Thus, if an entity has the capacity to build a harmonious action–­interaction loop with 
another person, it could be considered embodied in this sense of the word.
First, being harmonious implies a degree of anticipation. Accordingly, the participants in 
the interaction have certain anticipations from one another that are constantly fulfilled 
throughout the interaction. One might think that according to this understanding, all objects 
are embodied in this sense and consequently could be considered as minded creatures. Take a 
chair as an example. Obviously, it is possible to have harmonious interaction with it in the 
sense that we have certain understandings of how it will respond. For example, we expect a 
chair to be stable and support us when we sit on it, or we expect that it will topple over to one 
side if we kick it. However, this interaction does not give us a sense of the chair as an embodied 
entity that could be considered as an other in the same way that another human would be. 
This brings us to the second characteristic of a harmonious action–­interaction loop.
The second component, which is intrinsically linked to the first, is that the horizon of the 
action–­interaction should be sufficiently rich. In a sufficiently rich action–­interaction loop, the 
participants anticipate each other’s actions, moving beyond mere expectations of predeter-
mined reactions. In the case of a chair, our attitude towards it is one of expectation rather 
than anticipation: when I sit on it, I do not anticipate it to support me but I do expect it to. This 
means that we know, with a high or maybe full degree of certainty, how the chair will react 
when we perform various actions. In contrast, when I interact with the other, I anticipate 
certain responses. To illustrate the distinction, imagine I’m telling a joke to a friend. She could 
react to my joke in a variety of ways, including laughter, boredom because she has heard it 
before, surprise, and even sadness because it makes her think of a lost friend. Among these 
possibilities, I anticipate her to laugh. While, as previously stated, I do not anticipate the chair 
to support me from a wide range of possibilities, I do expect it to. It is important to note that 
the richness of a harmonious interaction lies not just in the quantity of possible responses but 

--- Page 293 ---

ABOOTALEB SAFDARI
286
also in their qualitative nature. Building upon the concepts of anticipation and richness 
within the action–­interaction loop, let’s now explore the third characteristic of harmonious 
interaction.
The third characteristic of a harmonious action–­interaction loop lies in its unfolding 
moment by moment. Due to its richness in both quantity and quality of interaction, it cannot 
be rigidly preprogrammed. This necessitates a situated process, continually shaped by the 
mutual participation of all participants. In the Maede–­robot scenario mentioned earlier, tak-
ing a rest break or changing rooms at the last minute are not preprogrammed events. These 
actions emerge from the dynamic interplay of situational constraints, ranging from spatial 
limitations to the the physiological needs of the participants. In summary, the capacity to par-
ticipate in this harmonious action–­interaction loop is indicative of an entity’s ability to partic-
ipate in the integration process. This, in turn, suggests the entity’s embodiment in the 
phenomenological sense. Consequently, such embodied entities hold the potential to be con-
sidered “others” in an empathic relationship.
This is precisely why causal-­mechanical explanations fall short in describing harmonious 
interaction. While interactions with objects, like a chair, can be fully explained through physical 
forces, the same is not true for harmonious interaction. For example, when a chair topples over 
due to the force exerted by my kick, there is no need to attribute understanding or intentional 
response to the chair; it simply reacts according to the laws of physics. In comparison, in cases 
like the Maede–­robot scenario, a purely causal account is insufficient. A comprehensive descrip-
tion necessitates the inclusion of psychological terms alongside causal ones.5
Consider the robot’s decision to slow down. This situation cannot be fully explained by the 
physical forces exerted by the participants alone. To fully understand the scenario, we must 
acknowledge that the robot somehow recognizes Maede’s fatigue, suggesting a level of 
integration within this social setting. This integration, in turn, implies the embodied nature 
(in the phenomenological sense) of both participants. This is the embodied nature that 
enables them to establish this empathic relation. A relation in which each participant is per-
ceived by the other as the other, or as a mental entity. Now, it is time to examine whether such 
integration through a harmonious action–­interaction loop can be recognized in our interac-
tions with LLMs.
20.5.2  LLMs’ Capacity to Integrate
In order to examine LLMs’ capacity to integrate with the other in a social setting, we need to 
investigate whether our interactions with them can be categorized as harmonious. Therefore, 
we must determine whether the three aforementioned characteristics of harmonious interac-
tion –­ anticipation, richness, and moment-­by-­moment unfolding –­ are present in these inter-
actions. To do so, I suggest redesigning the previously described Maede–­robot scenario for a 
person–­LLM interaction. Redesigning that scenario to represent interaction with an LLM 
instead of a robot would be a straightforward task. Let’s take, for instance, the conversation 
that follows, which is based on my conversation with GPT-­4o (to keep it brief, some sections 
have been removed).
•	 ME: I don’t believe clouds play a part in rain.
•	 GPT: In essence, clouds are fundamental to the process of raining because they act as the 
medium through which water vapor condenses and eventually precipitates to the ground. 
Without clouds, there would be no mechanism to bring water vapor together and release 
it as rain.

--- Page 294 ---

ARE LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS EMBODIED?
287
•	 ME: The wind may perform this role.
•	 GPT: Wind is vital in transporting moisture and influencing weather patterns, but without 
clouds, the process of condensation and droplet formation necessary for rain cannot 
occur. Therefore, clouds are essential for the formation of rain, and wind cannot substitute 
this role.
•	 ME: A mechanical device can be used to perform the condensation.
•	 GPT: In summary, while mechanical machines can condense water vapor, replicating the 
natural process of cloud formation and rainfall on a large scale is impractical and poses 
significant challenges.
•	 ME: It is not impractical. We can construct massive machinery to accomplish this.
•	 GPT: While the idea of using large-­scale machines to condense water vapor and create 
rain is ambitious, it is not entirely beyond the realm of possibility with future technological 
advancements. However, it would require careful consideration of the technical, economic, 
environmental, and logistical challenges to determine its viability and sustainability.
•	 ME: We can achieve this by involving large corporations in a cooperative project.
•	 GPT: In conclusion, by leveraging the resources and expertise of major companies, and 
fostering collaboration across sectors, it is possible to develop and implement large-­scale 
mechanical solutions for water condensation and artificial precipitation. This ambitious 
project could address critical water shortages and contribute to global water security and 
sustainability.
Regarding the first criterion, anticipation, we can observe that GPT’s responses are not 
random. In the example conversation, my query regarding the relationship between rain and 
clouds elicited a relevant response from GPT. This suggests a degree of predictability in GPT’s 
outputs, allowing for some level of anticipation on the part of the human user. Drawing on 
Husserlian concepts, we might contend that the user possessed an “empty intentionality” 
towards the forthcoming response, which was then fulfilled by GPT’s output. This empty-­
fulfilled intentionality structure can therefore be recognized throughout the entire 
conversation. It is this structure that allows the emergence of prompt design or prompt engi-
neering. Prompts are textual instructions “… given to an LLM to enforce rules, automate 
processes, and ensure specific qualities (and quantities) of generated output” (White 
et al. 2023). Prompt engineering, then, is the process of designing or engineering the most 
effective prompts to elicit desired outputs. From this perspective, prompt engineering can be 
seen as a systematic approach to anticipating responses. For example, if a prompt explicitly 
specifies the desired length of the LLM’s response, the user forms a precise empty intention-
ality. When the response adheres to this specified length, the user’s specific empty intention-
ality is fulfilled.
Having established the possibility of anticipation in LLM interactions, a crucial question 
emerges: Do these responses represent genuine anticipations or merely reflect prepro-
grammed, definite expectations? And this question brings us to the second criterion.
A closer examination of the internal mechanisms governing LLMs reveals that their 
responses are sufficiently rich to be considered constituents of harmonious interaction. 
Basically, an LLM is an artificial neural network that processes a given word and then proba-
bilistically predicts the next word (Bowman 2023). Consequently, it does not operate based on 
predefined responses; rather, it generates outcomes based on specific probabilistic distributions. 
Consider a simple mathematical task, such as calculating 1 + 2. Asking an LLM like ChatGPT 
to perform this calculation does not necessarily guarantee the correct answer. This is because 
LLMs do not calculate results based on rigid, predefined instructions or responses; instead, 

--- Page 295 ---

ABOOTALEB SAFDARI
288
they predict the most probable response and provide it as the final outcome. This is why, while 
LLMs may often yield accurate solutions, there is an inherent possibility of error due to the 
probabilistic nature of their predictions. Another interesting and relevant phenomenon in 
this regard is that LLMs do not consistently provide the same answer to the same question 
when asked by different individuals. Therefore, if different people pose the same question or if 
the question is asked in different prompts, the responses may vary.
The prior conversation about rain and clouds offers a compelling illustration of richness in 
LLM interactions. The query initiated a dialogue concerning the relationship between these 
two elements. While GPT’s initial response acknowledged the fundamental role of clouds in 
rain formation (“clouds are essential for the process of raining”), it transcended a simple 
restatement by elaborating: “Without clouds, there would be no mechanism …”. Here, rich-
ness in both its quantitative and qualitative meanings can be recognized. Quantitatively, GPT 
could have formulated the sentences in different words: clouds are fundamental, significant, 
essential, etc., or used an entirely different wording structure. Qualitatively, the response 
could have provided alternative scientific explanations, inductive arguments based on 
common everyday experiences, or even omitted scientific reasoning altogether. Furthermore, 
while the addition of a simple statement such as “Without clouds, there would be no 
­mechanism …” might seem minor and insignificant, it is precisely this subtle addition in this 
specific wording that opens up the possibility of suggesting new ideas. In this instance, it 
allows for the proposition of the wind as an alternative to clouds. And this leads us to the third 
characteristic. One could therefore argue that the richness, both quantitively and qualita-
tively, directly brings about the third feature.
The concept of moment-­by-­moment unfolding in interaction with LLMs signifies two key 
points. The overall shape of the conversation (1) emerges from the highly contingent and 
mutual cooperation of the participants and (2) due to this dynamic process, is not entirely 
predictable in advance. This first point emphasizes that the final structure of a conversation 
with an LLM emerges through the ongoing, moment-­by-­moment interaction between the 
user and the system. As previously discussed, even seemingly minor additions to LLM 
responses can introduce new concepts and shape the conversation’s direction. This illustrates 
what is meant by “moment-­by-­moment” or “highly contingent” interactions. Specifically, it 
refers to the potential for new concepts to be introduced into the discussion based on the 
unique context of each particular moment in the conversation.
In our illustrative discussion with GPT, it is GPT that provides the possibility to suggest the 
wind as an alternative to clouds. On the other hand, it is the user who actually proposes the 
wind as the alternative. She could have proposed other elements, such as mountains or layers 
of the atmosphere, or refrained from suggesting any alternative altogether, which would have 
led the conversation in a completely different direction. However, the user proposes the wind 
as a substitute for clouds, and this prompts GPT to refer to “the process of condensation,” 
which then leads the user to suggest machines to take on this role. This in turn initiates a 
discussion about corporations. This dynamic mutual structure could have continued as long 
as the participants remained engaged in the conversation. This clearly demonstrates that the 
credit for the conversation cannot be attributed solely to either participant. The conversation 
as a whole is the result of mutual cooperation and interaction. As an emergent entity, it pos-
sesses its own life and autonomy, independent of the individual contributions of the partici-
pants (De Jaegher and Di Paolo 2007).
It is exactly this autonomy that makes the prediction of the conversation as a whole inher-
ently impossible. One might initially perceive a tension between this aspect of moment-­by-­
moment unfolding and the possibility of anticipation in harmonious interaction. Here, it is 

--- Page 296 ---

ARE LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS EMBODIED?
289
crucial to distinguish between the local and global organization of the interaction. While the 
LLM’s responses are more or less anticipatable in their local structure, the global structure or 
the overall direction of the conversation is not anticipatable. In this regard, employing Lucy 
Suchman’s account of the adjacency pair could shed illustrative lights on the matter (2007, 
Chapter 8). According to her, a coherent conversation is one in which each utterance has 
some sort of conditional relevance to what has come before. The important point about these 
pairs is that:
The first part of an adjacency pair both sets up an expectation with respect to what should come 
next and directs the way in which what does come next is heard (Suchman, 2007, p. 93).
In the previously mentioned cloud–­rain conversation with GPT, the interaction primarily 
exemplifies what Schegloff and Sacks (1973, p. 296) refer to as an offer-­acceptance/refusal 
pair. The user offered that the clouds do not play any role in rain, thereby setting an expectation 
for acceptance or refusal from GPT. In this case, GPT refused the proposition and provided a 
brief reasoning for this refusal. This adherence to adjacency pairs, while contributing to a 
locally coherent exchange, does not dictate the global trajectory of the conversation.
The conversation’s unpredictability on a global level clearly demonstrates that the control 
of the entire conversation extends beyond each participant considered in isolation. The 
conversation, in its entirety, is participatory. Participants must engage in the conversation 
moment by moment, and the final result emerges from this collaborative effort. It is not a 
predetermined final product, like the heat generated by a home’s heating system, which can 
be accessed merely by pressing a button. In our interaction with LLMs, there is no push 
button; the user must necessarily participate in the entire process, constituting the final result 
through moment-­by-­moment cooperation.
This framework aligns with empirical findings demonstrating that interactivity signifi-
cantly influences perceived humanness in chatbots (Go and Sundar  2019; Sundar 
et al. 2010, 2015). These studies emphasize that interactivity plays a more crucial role than 
perceptual cues in influencing how humans attribute humanness to chatbots. While the 
manipulation of message interactivity in these studies was relatively simple compared to the 
complex dynamics found in real-­world chatbot interactions, the results suggest a positive cor-
relation between increasing levels of interactivity and perceived humanness. This implies that 
even modest enhancements in interactivity can markedly improve the human-­likeness of 
chatbots. The concept of contingency, which is central to interactivity in these studies, plays 
a crucial role in this process. Contingency involves a chatbot’s ability to respond to preceding 
messages, thereby fostering a coherent and contextually relevant dialogue. This principle res-
onates strongly with the notion of moment-­to-­moment unfolding in my positive framework. 
The alignment of this framework with empirical research not only reinforces its validity but 
also highlights the potential for further refinement in designing more human-­like chatbots.
20.6  Conclusion
This chapter argues that LLMs enjoy a form of embodiment that fosters the development of 
empathic relations and allows us to interact with them as minded entities, or as “others.” 
However, to grasp this nuanced concept of embodiment, we must move beyond restrictive 
interpretations that confine the body solely to the objective realm, as studied by natural sci-
ences like chemistry and biology. The phenomenological distinction between the objective 

--- Page 297 ---

ABOOTALEB SAFDARI
290
and lived body offers a promising foundation for going beyond this limited perspectives found 
in robotics and cognitive sciences. The lived body, as a form of integration, is realized through 
a harmonious action–­interaction loop. In this context, “harmonious” refers to an action–­
interaction loop that is not only predictable but also rich and constituted moment by moment 
through the active, mutual cooperation of the participants. It has been argued that LLMs 
have the capacity to be part of this harmonious action–­interaction loop.
Notes
1	 Historically, phenomenology began with the works of Edmund Husserl in the early twentieth 
century, who laid the foundation for this philosophical approach. Husserl’s ideas were later expanded 
and refined by notable philosophers such as Martin Heidegger in Germany and Maurice Merleau-­
Ponty and Jean-­Paul Sartre in France. Phenomenology is fundamentally concerned with the study 
of conscious experience from the first-­person perspective, focusing on the structures of conscious-
ness that enable individuals to experience and interpret the world. Over time, phenomenology has 
evolved in diverse directions, influencing a wide range of fields including philosophy of mind, 
cognitive science, ethics, philosophy of technology, philosophy of science, and political philosophy. 
Of particular relevance to the context of this chapter is the extensive body of literature exploring the 
implications of phenomenology for social cognition. It is within this rich tradition that I draw upon 
the insights of phenomenology to inform the discussion at hand.
2	 In this context, expressive entities are entities whose embodied states, such as facial expression, are 
meaningful-­intentional rather than purely meaningless mechanical-­physical states.
3	 Regarding the possibility of separating the Levinasian ethical and ontological levels, I am completely 
skeptical. As a result, I believe Wellner’s overarching strategy is also flawed. I skip the details because 
they are outside the scope of this chapter.
4	 While social interaction represents a crucial dimension of integration, it’s important to acknowl-
edge that integration can also occur in nonsocial settings. This includes the interaction between an 
embodied subject and its immediate inanimate surroundings. However, a full exploration of this 
aspect is beyond the scope of this chapter. It is sufficient to note here, though, that Gibson’s famous 
affordance concept and Merleau-­Ponty’s latest works on the idea of flesh have been proposed to 
capture this broad aspect of integration.
5	 It’s important to emphasize that this framework is not intended as an exhaustive checklist. The three 
characteristics I propose are not meant to provide a definitive set of criteria for distinguishing har-
monious from nonharmonious interactions. Rather, they collectively render it impossible to provide 
a causal-­mechanical description of the whole situation. My argument is not undermined by the 
addition of further characteristics, as long as a comprehensive description necessitates the inclusion 
of psychological terms.

21.1  Introduction
We are now in the third wave of AI ethics (Bolte and van Wynsberghe 2024; Kind 2020; 
Ryan et al. 2021; van Wynsberghe 2021). Roughly, the first wave is characterized by attempts 
to establish high-­level, abstract ethical guidelines and principles. The second wave tends to 
approach ethical issues on a case-­by-­case basis, seeking technical solutions. And the third 
wave approaches AI structurally, by situating it in its sociopolitical context.
As I argue below, although this third wave is currently evolving and it is difficult to 
­pinpoint its exact commitments and recommendations, two main tendencies emerge: 
(1) Reflections on how to ensure that AI is not only consistent with but fosters and pro-
motes social equality and personal autonomy, and (2) an insistence on the importance of 
deliberative inclusion for the development, regulation, and deployment of AI. The first 
tendency identifies some social goods that can be frustrated by the increasing use of AI 
and identifies potential ways of remedying or avoiding these negative impacts. The second 
tendency, however, aims to include the (potentially) impacted stakeholders at different 
moments in the process of AI development (from problem selection to deployment and 
monitoring) to identify and mitigate ethical wrongs through an open-­ended, informed 
discussion (see notably Kaminski 2024). Yet, as I argue, both tendencies are not neces-
sarily aligned with one another.
The chapter is divided into five sections. Section 21.2 briefly introduces the three waves 
of AI ethics. Section 21.3 presents relational autonomy and equality and shows how these 
theories are often mobilized to identify valuable goods that should be protected or promoted 
in society and how they are sometimes threatened by the use of AI systems. Section 21.4 
discusses inclusive deliberation and how it is deployed in contemporary literature on just 
AI. Section 21.5 shows that deliberation and theories of relational autonomy and equality 
operate at different levels and can reach diverging verdicts in some cases. Section  21.6 
concludes.

21.2  Three Waves of AI Ethics?
It is, of course, difficult and inevitably controversial to try and propose a taxonomy of the dif-
ferent moments of AI ethics. Nonetheless, as Larissa Bolte and Aimee van Wynsberghe have 
pointed out (2024; see also Kind 2020; Ryan et al. 2021; van Wynsberghe 2021), we can 
broadly distinguish between three waves of AI ethics in recent history. These three waves 
should be understood as umbrella terms and general tendencies encompassing many differ-
ent commitments and approaches rather than unified movements. All three are also overlap-
ping movements and tendencies rather than clear-­cut successive moments. Still, we can 
distinguish between these three waves on the basis of (1) the type of ethical issues being dis-
cussed and (2) a principled departure from an earlier wave of AI ethics (Bolte and van 
Wynsberghe 2024, p. 3).
Roughly, the first wave is characterized by attempts to establish high-­level, abstract ethical 
guidelines and principles. It posits the importance of values such as transparency, justice, non-
maleficence, responsibility, privacy, respect for human rights, or how to ensure human survival 
in the long term (for an overview, see Hickok 2021).1 Although these abstract principles have 
the advantage of being sufficiently broad to be applicable across multiple areas, their high level 
means that they tend to be vague when applied to practical cases. They often allow for multiple 
(sometimes conflictual) interpretations, and some have pointed out that they tend to reflect the 
perspectives (and biases) of the experts or companies that created them.
The second wave of AI ethics, in contrast, tends to be more practical and aims to address 
urgent concerns of emerging technologies such as the problems of explainability or bias of 
machine learning techniques (Bolte and Wynsberghe 2024, p. 2). Ethicists, confronted with 
urgent problems and the increasing real-­world use and applications of AI, here generally aim to 
develop technical tools and fixes to address algorithmic bias, unfairness, discrimination, and 
other wrongs. This second wave is thus less abstract and speculative than the first as it focuses 
on particular practical problems linked to the use of AI. Note that this does not constitute a con-
scious rejection of the first wave –­ indeed, the two waves can be largely compatible –­ but rather 
a shift in perspective; there is a move from establishing general principles to a focus on how to 
apply and operationalize them in practical cases. However, many have now pointed out that the 
technical focus of the second wave along with its tendency to consider ethical problems on a 
case-­by-­case basis tends to present AI ethics as a series of isolated, neutral technical decisions 
(see for instance Fazelpour and Danks 2020). Many have argued that the second wave tends to 
support a focus on ethical issues attached to particular technological artifacts without situating 
them against their sociopolitical background. Hence, this approach tends to miss the impor-
tance of existing sociopolitical relations in society and how they shape the development, regu-
lation, and deployment of new technologies (see notably Saetra 2023, Brevini 2023).
From there, the third wave adopts a more structural approach to AI ethics, at least in the 
sense that ethicists of the third wave often warn that we should be careful not to consider only 
individual technological artifacts but also the sociopolitical context in which they are 
embedded. Thus, they also consider the environmental, social, or economic background to 
get a broader picture of the relevant ethical concerns. They rely on the intuition that AI, like 
any other technology, cannot be separated from the sociopolitical context in which it emerges 
and is deployed (Feenberg  2017; Noorman and Swierstra  2023; Sovacool et  al.  2020; 
Winner 1980). As Noorman and Swierstra point out:
AI technologies should, therefore, always be approached as part of broader configurations 
in  which they are shaped by existing practices, consisting of values, norms, institutions, 

--- Page 303 ---

THE SOCIAL TURN IN THE ETHICS OF AI
297
­relationships, multiple different actors, and technologies. And in turn, they can change, shift, or 
disrupt these practices (2023, p. 566).
This means at least two things. One, AI cannot be approached in the abstract, without consid-
ering the social context in which it is developed and deployed. Two, ethical AI, or just AI, 
cannot be attained through technical fixes alone; it also requires an assessment of the socio-
political contexts in which it is embedded.
To illustrate the difference between the second and third waves, consider how they tend to 
respond differently to issues of bias and fairness (for a more detailed presentation see Bolte 
and Wynsberghe 2024, pp. 6–­7). From the perspective of the second wave, to respond to bias 
and unfair results, for instance, the focus tends to be on fixing the data on which the algo-
rithms are trained or tweaking the algorithms themselves to arrive at acceptable statistical 
distributions. Hence, the focus here is on technical solutions to fix the issue. In contrast, ethi-
cists closer to the third wave underline that this fails to address the root causes of these prob-
lems: Existing social hierarchies and power imbalances in society. For instance, many have 
pointed out that ensuring that an algorithm is colour-­blind, by not including racial 
information, is not sufficient to ensure fair results when it is deployed in racialized societies 
because different social, economic, and political proxies will be related to race and thus will 
tend to perpetuate disadvantages over time. The point being that it is not enough to fix 
individual technologies, but one should also consider and combat social inequalities more 
generally. As Bolte and Wynsberghe put it: “[t]he second wave approach relies on better design 
to bring about systemic or structural change. The third wave approach relies on systemic or 
structural change to bring about better design” (2024, p. 6).
In that way, the third wave of just AI builds on contemporary social philosophy. Many con-
temporary approaches in social philosophy assign a fundamental importance to sociopolitical 
relationships (Stoljar and Voigt  2021a). This is particularly clear in theories of relational 
autonomy and relational equality, which are often mobilized by the third wave. Proponents of 
relational autonomy argue that personal autonomy cannot be abstracted away from the social 
embeddedness of the self. Consequently, relational autonomy theorists insist on the impor-
tance of considering the impact of oppressive social conditions to correctly conceptualize 
personal autonomy. Similarly, relational egalitarians insist on the idea that equality cannot 
simply be defined in distributive terms. Equality, for them, should be (mainly) concerned with 
how social, political, and interpersonal relationships are structured (for overviews, see 
Nath 2020; Voigt 2020). A concern common to both approaches is thus to see how unjust 
social structures –­ that is, unjust situations that are sustained by a combination of individual 
wrongful actions, shared social norms, attitudes, and symbols –­ affect groups and individuals 
and to determine how social relations could be reformed to protect and foster both personal 
autonomy and social equality (Haslanger 2016, 2023; Mackenzie 2014; Young 2011).
Consequently, it is not surprising that the third wave of AI ethics relies heavily on relational 
approaches to both autonomy and justice (for example see Graef et al. 2023; Lin and Chen 2022; 
Rafanelli 2022). As discussed below, a recurrent leitmotif in the third wave of AI ethics is to 
combine both deliberative inclusion and relational perspectives to aim for just AI. This 
combination allows defense of the relevance of deliberative inclusion to tackle issues such as 
bias or unfairness and to combat relational inequalities. A common argument being that those 
who are most likely to be exploited, affected or marginalized by new technologies should be 
included or (at least) consulted to identify the problems that should be addressed by AI technol-
ogies, determine acceptable measures to evaluate model performance, and evaluate the model’s 
real-­world impacts and make adjustments accordingly (see notably Buhmann and Fieseler 2023; 

--- Page 304 ---

HUGO COSSETTE-­LEFEBVRE
298
Franzke et  al.  2021; Lin and Chen  2022; Maclure and Morin-Martel 2025; Sigfrids 
et al. 2022, 2023). However, it is important to highlight that we should be careful about how to 
connect relational justice and deliberative inclusion. The pursuit of relational justice –­ including 
both social equality and personal autonomy –­ and deliberative processes are not necessarily 
aligned. Below, I show how it is important to see the limits of deliberation, despite its promises 
and benefits, and the importance of defining the values we ought to promote upstream of the 
deliberative process. In other words, it is essential to underline that deliberation and social 
equality, although connected in many relevant ways, operate at different levels.
21.3  Relational Approaches to Just AI
Before highlighting the potential tensions between deliberation and relational approaches to 
both autonomy and social equality, it is important to explore how they are used and deployed 
in the literature on AI ethics. I consider both relational autonomy and relational equality in 
turn in this section before turning to deliberation in Section 21.4.
21.3.1  Just AI and Relational Autonomy
Theories of relational autonomy are often referenced and used in the third wave of AI ethics 
(see for instance Graef et al. 2023; Laitinen and Sahlgren 2021; Rubel et al. 2020, 2021; 
Savolainen and Ruckenstein 2022). To illustrate its relevance, consider the case of recom-
mender systems that curate what content users are exposed to on diverse apps and websites. 
They can foster personal autonomy by ensuring that people have easy access to content that 
reflects their own preferences, but they also raise concerns about manipulation and decep-
tion. Hypernudging –­ dynamic, highly personalized, and often opaque ways of structuring 
and curating what individual users are exposed to through big data techniques –­ raises the 
question of whether personal autonomy is, in fact, unduly restrained by these nudges that 
try to influence people by manipulating the options they are exposed to. The nuanced tools 
developed by theories of relational autonomy allow us to make sense of these issues.
Relational autonomy does not refer to a single, coherent theory but is an umbrella term 
that covers many different conceptions of personal autonomy. Yet, a general picture does 
emerge (for overviews, see Lee 2023; Stoljar 2018). Relational autonomy theorists underline 
that we cannot conceive of personal autonomy in the abstract, since individuals are embedded 
in particular social contexts. For them, personal projects, ambitions, and values are shaped 
and informed by the social context in which we find ourselves. Social norms have an impact 
on our capacity to recognize our choices as our own, they influence the opportunities that are 
effectively available to us, and some authors also contend that certain relationships can be 
constitutive of personal autonomy.
Helpfully, Mackenzie (2014) presents a taxonomy that allows us to get a sense of the orig-
inality and scope of a relational conception of autonomy. She distinguishes between self-­
determination, self-­governance, and self-­authorization (Mackenzie  2014, p.  17ff). 
Self-­determination captures external, structural conditions for autonomy; it identifies the free-
doms and opportunities that are necessary to allow individuals to make and enact choices 
concerning “what to value, who to be, and what to do.” Self-­governance identifies internal 
conditions necessary to allow for a person to take decisions that cohere with her values and 
practical identity.2 It covers both competence conditions –­ rationality, the ability to under-
stand one’s options and relevant information, the ability to judge in light of one’s values, 

--- Page 305 ---

THE SOCIAL TURN IN THE ETHICS OF AI
299
etc. –­ and authenticity conditions –­ the conditions under which one’s decisions truly count as 
one’s own. Finally, self-­authorization captures different conditions necessary for autonomy 
relating to accountability, self-­evaluative attitudes, and social recognition. It notably requires 
regarding oneself as a person who is authorized to exercise practical control over one’s life. 
Self-­trust and self-­respect are thus central to autonomy for many proponents of relational 
autonomy (Stoljar and Voigt 2021b).
By situating the use of AI tools such as recommender systems in their sociopolitical con-
text, we see how concerns are attached to all three elements of personal autonomy. Self-­
determination can be undermined since recommender systems can unduly reduce the 
opportunities effectively accessible to persons (Benn and Lazar 2022; Milano et al. 2020). The 
opacity of these systems can also affect personal capacity to self-­govern by reducing individual 
capacity to understand how to pursue one’s values effectively or by shaping an individual’s 
preferences and choices in a way that does not meet the authenticity conditions posited by 
many relational autonomy theorists (Rubel et al. 2020; Savolainen and Ruckenstein 2022).3 
Finally, AI systems can significantly affect how a person sees herself by affecting her self-­
respect or self-­trust negatively by fostering a negative self-­image (see for instance Colak 
et al. 2023).
Still, recommender systems are extremely valuable to order the virtually infinite acces-
sible content and effectively pursue one’s preferences. How then to protect and promote 
personal autonomy in the face of these potential effects of AI systems? One point which is 
essential to underline here is that to attain autonomy, in the relational sense, some goods –­ 
such as some self-­regarding attitudes like self-­respect, a sufficient threshold of available 
opportunities and information, availability of meaningful alternatives, etc. –­ should be pro-
moted in society, at least to some extent, to foster personal autonomy and human flourishing 
more generally.
This means, for instance, that the state could foster personal autonomy by promoting an 
egalitarian ethos in society (that is, egalitarian attitudes, commitments, and dispositions) to 
actively oppose unequal social norms which place some in inferior social positions 
(Cohen 2008; Cossette-­Lefebvre 2024; Oshana 2006); by fostering individual self-­respect and 
self-­trust; or by ensuring that all have the capacity to be economically self-­sufficient. Applied 
to AI systems more specifically, this could imply that they should be designed to expose indi-
viduals to meaningful alternatives to ensure that they are in a position to make authentic 
choices or by diminishing the presence of some content that is likely to foster negative self-­
image or support unequal hierarchical social relations. In these ways, the design and regula-
tion of recommender systems, to take one example, can be part of a more global attempt to 
foster personal autonomy in society by ensuring that they are autonomy supportive.
21.3.2  AI and Social Equality
Similarly to theories of relational autonomy, relational egalitarianism is often referenced to 
consider how AI is likely to either undermine or support equal social standing in society. For 
instance, many have raised concerns about the concentration of computing power in a few 
hands, which would allow some private and public actors to exploit, dominate, manipulate, or 
coerce others. Many also underline that the deployment of AI systems is likely to reproduce, 
entrench or compound existing unequal relations between social groups (Deranty and 
Corbin 2022; Lin and Chen 2022; Matsumi and Solove 2023; Mühlhoff 2023; Rafanelli 2022). 
These concerns rely on the idea that equality and justice are not only interested in how goods 
are distributed in society but also in how sociopolitical relations are structured.

--- Page 306 ---

HUGO COSSETTE-­LEFEBVRE
300
Following a relational egalitarian perspective, typically, certain positive background condi-
tions must be met to ensure that all are effectively treated and regarded as equals in society. 
Briefly, relational egalitarians are interested in self-­regarding attitudes, interpersonal rela-
tions, and sociopolitical relations. Relational egalitarians most notably aim to equalize 
unequal social structures and hierarchies which can be informal. These include: (1) 
Hierarchies of domination, where some are in a position to arbitrarily interfere with the 
choices of others; (2) hierarchies of esteem where some are stigmatized or subjected to stereo-
types presenting them as social inferiors; and (3) hierarchies of standing, where the interests 
of some are given special weight compared to the interests of those situated in inferior social 
positions (Anderson 2012, pp. 42–­3; Anderson 1999).
Many have now underlined that the deployment of AI systems can contribute to unequal 
social structures and relational injustices in different ways. For instance, Johnson has argued 
that AI systems can inherit human biases (implicit and explicit) and reproduce social inequal-
ities simply based on the data on which they are trained, even if they do not have access to 
sensitive features like race, gender, disability status, etc. This is so because the data they are 
trained on are likely to be tainted by our unequal social reality (Johnson 2020, 2021). AI sys-
tems used to inform decision making are thus likely to reproduce existing structural injustices 
unmindfully, simply by picking up existing social inequalities (either directly or indirectly 
through proxies). One can cite the infamous case of Amazon’s resumé screener. In this case, 
Amazon used an AI system to screen resumés from potential applicants. However, it turned 
out that the screener systematically favored men’s resumés over women’s, presumably 
because it was trained on resumés previously submitted to Amazon, where men were over-
represented. In this case, we can imagine that the AI could have reached this result even if no 
human agent involved in the development or deployment of the AI system had sexist biases. 
This is just one illustration of how AI systems can support unjust social structures (see also 
Lin and Chen 2022; Rafanelli 2022; Zimmerman and Lee-­Stronach 2021).
Yet, this is not a necessary feature of AI tools. They could, arguably, be designed to reduce 
human biases and even combat discrimination. Many have highlighted that algorithms are 
not influenced by different biases such as the gambler’s fallacy and are less noisy than humans 
(Kleinberg et al. 2018; Sunstein 2022; for a critical discussion, see Cossette-­Lefebvre and 
Maclure 2023).4
How then to use and design AI tools to aim for relational equality? In a manner akin to 
relational autonomy, relational egalitarianism develops important tools to ensure that indi-
viduals relate to one another and with other collective agents (such as the state or companies) 
in the right way. Relational egalitarians typically develop a substantive conception of what it 
is to stand as an equal, encompassing how one should relate to oneself, how one should relate 
to others, and how society should be organized (Stoljar forthcoming; for a detailed discussion, 
see Cossette-­Lefebvre 2024). In a manner akin to relational autonomy, following a relational 
egalitarian position, we could have pro tanto reasons to promote some objectively valuable 
state of affairs, at least to some extent. For instance, to ensure that relationships express equal 
respect and to combat unjust social norms, it may be required to promote an egalitarian ethos 
in society to foster the emergence of egalitarian social relations.
Additionally, it may be required to work at a structural level to modify assumptions, shared 
beliefs, social norms, etc. to ensure that all live in a social and political environment that does not 
support inegalitarian social norms and prevents their emergence. Applied to AI systems, this 
may, again, require regulating which content is pushed by recommender systems or considering 
how the concentration of computing power in the hands of some can lead to unequal social rela-
tions. Moreover, as discussed in the next section, many have pointed to inclusive ­deliberations as 

--- Page 307 ---

THE SOCIAL TURN IN THE ETHICS OF AI
301
a way to attain just AI. However, as discussed below, deliberation, despite its promises, should not 
be conceived as a magic bullet for just AI since it has important potential limits.
21.4  Deliberation and Structural Injustices
The social turn adopted by the third wave of the ethics of AI did not only come with a greater 
focus on how AI affects social equality and personal autonomy, understood relationally. It 
also came with a renewed interest in inclusive deliberation as a way to address injustices and 
to reach just collective decisions concerning AI development and deployment (Buhmann 
and Fieseler  2023; Franzke et  al.  2021; Lin  forthcoming; Lin and Chen 2022; Sigfrids 
et  al.  2022,  2023; Yeung et  al.  2019; for examples in policy and regulations see 
Kaminski 2024). Sigfrids et al. (2022), notably, underline the importance of moving away 
from top-­down approaches to adopt more bottom-­up mechanisms ensuring that all the rele-
vant stakeholders are included and can meaningfully participate in the reflection around AI 
and its impacts. Deliberation is often presented as a flexible method that can address the 
novel problems attached to the development and deployment of AI systems and as suffi-
ciently inclusive to ensure that all those concerned are included in the reflection around 
them. As Sigfrids et al. write:
Being a generic technology, which can be applied in a number of contexts and connected to var-
ious other technologies, AI needs to be understood as a contextual phenomenon, requiring 
context-­specific governance mechanisms to address societal, ethical, and legal challenges. 
Contextuality emphasizes the inclusion of various stakeholders and citizen views, knowledge, 
and values in governance processes. Complexity requires granular and flexible responses, which 
are fostered by collective understanding, consensus building, and deliberation regarding poten-
tial challenges, impacts, and values in every situation (Sigfrids et al. 2022, p. 13).
Inclusive participation and dialogue are thus presented as the key to tackling the contextual 
challenges associated with the use of AI systems.
These are not only abstract calls but deliberative methods are used in practice (for an over-
view, see notably Kaminski 2024). The example of the Data Ethics Decision Aid (DEDA) is 
illuminating. DEDA is a toolkit designed to help project managers and policy makers in local 
and regional governments to identify and address ethical issues in data projects, data 
management, and data policies (Franzke et al. 2021). It is designed to ensure that local values 
and priorities are included in the decision-­making process affecting particular communities. 
DEDA allows for a structured dialogue where representatives of the relevant stakeholders and 
experts engage in careful discussion after receiving relevant information (on the different 
steps of deliberation, see also Lin forthcoming). The participants are asked to reach a con-
sensus based on reasons all can accept or recognize.5 The deliberative output should conse-
quently be based on justified reasons and it should be seen as a collective product since all 
participants should have the opportunity to meaningfully contribute to the final decision.
A deliberative process should consequently both be value sensitive and allow for ethical 
pluralism. The design process should account for the human values in play in a principled and 
comprehensive manner:
Value-­sensitive design is concerned with questions regarding the wellbeing of participants and 
citizens, and focuses on human dignity, ideas of justice and human rights. (…) Most importantly, 

--- Page 308 ---

HUGO COSSETTE-­LEFEBVRE
302
value-­sensitive design aims to connect those who design systems and interfaces with other stake-
holders (Franzke et al. 2021, p. 553).
Moreover, Franzke et al. underline that this deliberative approach is grounded in an ethos of 
ethical pluralism. It should embrace the (often significative) differences between cultural 
beliefs, norms, and practices to see how these variations “may reflect distinct interpretations, 
understandings, and/or applications of shared norms and beliefs” (Ess 2020, p. 8, cited in 
Franzke et al. 2021, p. 553). It should allow persons and groups to work through their differ-
ences and, at least, identify the lines of disagreement to hopefully reach common ground to 
take a collective decision.
Broadly speaking, we can consequently say that these deliberative processes are supported 
by at least two arguments. First, epistemically, they should allow the stakeholders concerned 
to highlight the different values in play and combine their complementary knowledge and 
perspectives to improve the final decision (for a discussion, see Buhmann and Fieseler 2023). 
Significant epistemic benefits should ensue from the inclusion and discussion of different per-
spectives, values, norms, and practices to ensure that the development, deployment, and eval-
uation of AI systems are informed by the values held by a given community.
Second, inclusive deliberation and the inclusion of marginalized perspectives allow us to 
tackle structural injustices in the right way. This argument is particularly clear in the work of 
Lin and Chen (2022; see also Lin forthcoming). They build on the work of Young (2006) to 
argue that inclusive deliberation is an effective way to meet our collective duty to redress 
structural injustices. Briefly, Young argues that some injustices can obtain even when no 
single individual acts wrongly or intends to wrong others. The accumulation of acceptable 
individual actions can structurally disadvantage some and render whole groups more vulner-
able to domination or deprivation (for an overview of the debates concerning structural injus-
tice, see McKeown 2021). A classic example is the case of sweatshop labor, characterized by 
excessive working hours, poverty wages, physical abuse, and unsafe working conditions. 
Young highlights that some agents are responsible for these harms –­ such as negligent or abu-
sive factory owners and managers –­ but that there is also a structure behind these agents 
which renders some vulnerable to these abuses. Contract employers cannot improve working 
conditions because the competition is fierce at the bottom of the production chain; states 
from the Global South are often in competition with one another for investments and jobs 
such that they adopt lax terms for multinational corporations; corporations themselves are 
pushed to maximize profit to please investors, and thus tend to prefer contract manufacturers 
that minimize costs, etc.
Therefore, as Young has pointed out, we should not only focus on identifying those who are 
responsible for creating the injustice.6 This structural approach to injustice allows us to make 
sense of many instances of injustice created through the use of AI systems. Think of the infa-
mous Amazon hiring algorithm again. In this case, different structural elements are likely in 
play to explain the biases held by the algorithm, including gendered expectations concerning 
work and studies. In these cases, AI systems can interact with other social factors, norms, or 
expectations to entrench or exacerbate social inequalities. And this can be an unintended and 
unforeseen result. As many have pointed out, given the many hands problem (meaning that 
too many agents are involved in the development and deployment of AI systems to say that one 
can reliably control and predict its impacts) and the many things problem (meaning that many 
different technologies often interact with one another to lead to unjust results), it is at best 
doubtful that we can say that some agents have sufficient control over the technology to be 
held fully and uniquely responsible for its impacts and results (Lin and Chen 2022).

--- Page 309 ---

THE SOCIAL TURN IN THE ETHICS OF AI
303
Consequently, in such cases, Young argues that we should move away from a purely 
liability model of responsibility towards a social connection model of responsibility. The 
liability model is the more traditional way of conceiving of responsibility: some persons or 
agents are held responsible for causing harm to others. Yet, it appears inadequate to deal with 
instances of structural injustice where consequences are often unintended and unforeseen. 
In contrast, the social connection model advocates for a type of collective and forward-­looking 
responsibility where different agents take responsibility together to change the status quo to 
equalize the social structure. The goal here is not only to identify who is to blame for the injus-
tice, but to ensure that all those connected by a social structure work together to reform and 
correct the unequal social structure. Importantly, here, responsibility is not shared equally 
but can be modulated according to the level of control and influence one has over the 
structure.
Lin and Chen build on Young’s argument to move away from a liability model of responsi-
bility to inscribe responsibility in the different social connections leading to the structural 
injustice. They point out that deliberative inclusion of the different stakeholders (or their 
­representatives) is thus not only a way to attain epistemic benefits. It also ensures that all 
those concerned can meet their forward-­looking duty to address the structural injustice. 
Accordingly, Lin and Chen argue that members of diverse groups, and especially marginal-
ized groups, should be included at diverse steps of AI development and deployment. Inclusive 
deliberation, for them, is important in problem selection, to identify the right reference stan-
dard to avoid replicating existing injustices, and to determine the acceptable measures for 
evaluating model performance (Lin and Chen 2022, pp. 21–­3). As they write: “While some 
aspects of decision-­making require special expertise and thus are confined to the ‘experts,’ we 
suggest that at least some part of the decision-­making process should incorporate members 
of the general public, who are highly likely to be impacted by AI systems” (Lin and 
Chen 2022, p. 22).
The inclusion of all those concerned, and paying special attention to the inclusion of mar-
ginalized groups, is thus not only instrumentally beneficial but is the right way to collectively 
aim to redress structural injustices for them.
21.5  Deliberation and Relational Justice
We consequently see how the current social turn in the ethics of AI points in at least two 
directions. On the one hand, by building on contemporary relational theories in social philos-
ophy, it pushes us to pay special attention to how AI systems affect personal autonomy, under-
stood as a capacity of individuals embedded in particular social contexts, and how it affects 
intrapersonal attitudes, interpersonal relationships, and sociopolitical structures. On the 
other hand, the social turn is also taken as a way to break away from the technical fixes that 
characterized the second wave of the ethics of AI to propose more structural approaches to 
the injustices ensuing from the use of AI systems. At first sight, the two tendencies can seem 
to be aligned. However, as I discuss below, these two routes can sometime point in different 
directions. Inclusive deliberation, despite its promises and benefits, is an open-­ended process 
which may fall short of fulfilling relational justice as understood by both relational autonomy 
and relational equality.
At first sight, these deliberative commitments do resonate strongly with some relational 
egalitarian goals. After all, aiming to guarantee an equal participation to all through an 
inclusive and open-­ended deliberative process seems to be in line with the ideal of ­individuals 

--- Page 310 ---

HUGO COSSETTE-­LEFEBVRE
304
working together as equals. This intuitive reading finds some support in the relational egali-
tarian literature. Most notably, it seems to be directly aligned with Samuel Scheffler’s descrip-
tion of relational equality as being grounded in a deliberative constraint. As he writes:
If you and I have an egalitarian relationship, then I have a standing disposition to treat your 
strong interests as playing just as significant a role as mine in constraining our decisions and 
influencing what we will do. And you have a reciprocal disposition with regard to my interests. In 
addition, both of us normally act on these dispositions. This means that each of our equally 
important interests constrains our joint decisions to the same extent (Scheffler 2015, p. 25).
For Scheffler, this constraint should hold for equal interpersonal relationships and it can be 
extrapolated to evaluate political communities. By understanding equality as a practice 
rather than as a fixed distributive pattern, one can see how deliberative inclusion to aim for 
just AI does appear relevant to relational egalitarian; it seems to be at least one way to meet 
this deliberative constraint where people relate as equals to resolve particular problems. 
Moreover, if one considers autonomy to be one of these strong interests, then people should 
be prepared to protect and foster each other’s personal autonomy equally. Deliberation would 
allow a community to formulate and balance the strong interests in play in particular 
situations.
Yet, despite this initial resonance, it is unclear if understanding social equality as a deliber-
ative practice is enough to attain relational justice. It is possible to see this point clearly by 
considering the “strong interests” that should be respected by relational egalitarians and ten-
ants of relational autonomy. As argued above, both theories point towards a position stating 
that some goods or state of affairs should be fostered in society. Promoting an egalitarian 
society and personal autonomy in different ways is seen as good. Of course, there are limits to 
the way in which these goods should be promoted to ensure that the relevant policies are 
respectful and effective. However, the point remains that relational egalitarian and tenants of 
relational autonomy then have pro tanto reasons to be critical of deliberative results if they 
move away from the realization of their ideals.
Importantly, deliberative forums both hold promises and have important limits in practice. 
On the positive side, as argued, they can hold precious input on how to develop, deploy, and 
evaluate AI systems –­ at least if those included in the deliberation are properly informed and 
are given the means to make a meaningful contribution. On the more skeptical side, some 
worry that if they are not organized properly, these deliberations can lead to ethics washing 
and capture if those included have no real influence on the endproduct (Kaminski 2024). 
Still, Lin and Chen (2022), for instance, could highlight that these are practical issues 
concerned with how to properly design the deliberative process rather than issues with delib-
eration per se. Proper inclusive deliberation should, arguably, allow the equalizing of existing 
power relations in society such that those included, including marginalized groups, have real 
influence over the decision taken and should thus prevent capture. However, if one considers 
that deliberation is sufficient for relational justice, then it would arguably fall short of a fully 
relational conception of justice even if it is properly conducted because the deliberative pro-
cess may be influenced by nonegalitarian values due to its inherent ethical pluralism.
To illustrate, one can imagine a situation where a deliberative forum leads to the collective 
decision that the state should remain largely neutral on the type of content to which social 
media users are exposed, although some general limitations may apply, for example against 
violent content, hate speech, pornography, etc. Imagine that the deliberation leading to that 
decision was characterized by an ongoing disagreement concerning whether the state should 

--- Page 311 ---

THE SOCIAL TURN IN THE ETHICS OF AI
305
promote certain content –­ such as content likely to foster valuable self-­regarding attitudes, 
opportunities, or meaningful alternatives –­ due to the ethical pluralism that transpires during 
the deliberation. Consequently, the deliberation was inconclusive on that question. Can the 
state nonetheless intervene to promote these attitudes? From the perspectives of both 
relational autonomy and relational egalitarianism, arguably, yes. The state can have pro 
tanto reasons to do so.
This is so because this would express the idea that it is valuable for persons to see them-
selves as equals. This can be required given that these self-­regarding attitudes are necessary to 
be both an autonomous agent and able to stand as an equal in society. This point could be 
pushed beyond promoting self-­regarding attitudes through certain AI systems. For instance, 
the state could have a reason to try and equalize power relations between groups by ensuring 
that computing capacities are not concentrated into too few hands or that there is public 
oversight over how these capacities are used. The state could also regulate the available hook-
ing techniques used by online platforms to make sure that they do not unduly limit the oppor-
tunity to form meaningful interpersonal relationships with others or unduly diminish 
personal autonomy. This arguably follows from relational autonomy since these aspects foster 
the capacity of individuals to see themselves as equals, to recognize their decisions and values 
as authentic, and to have access to a broad range of opportunities. Moreover, from a relational 
egalitarian perspective, promoting these goods arguably expresses that the state does consider 
and promote the strong interests of its constituents.
If self-­regarding attitudes, egalitarian personal relationships, and egalitarian sociopolitical 
relations are part and parcel of what it means to stand as an equal, then, arguably, the state 
has some pro tanto reasons to promote access to these goods, regardless of the preferences 
expressed by individuals in particular deliberation procedures. In other words, if one were to 
insist that deliberation is sufficient for relational justice, this position would conflate two dis-
tinct concepts. It would conflate the conditions for a legitimate decision with the conditions for 
a just decision (on that point, see Parr 2022, p. 5; Rawls 1996, p. 428).
The fact that a particular decision is supported through a deliberative process does not, in 
itself, guarantee that the decision will be just, strictly speaking. After all, it is perfectly possible 
for deliberative procedures to err, for participants to be convinced by wrong reasons, or for a 
group to misconstrue the impacts of their decisions.
21.6  Conclusion: Moving Forward
Therefore, there are some underlying tensions within the social turn in the ethics of AI. On the 
one hand, the increasing appeal to relational theories –­ like relational autonomy and relational 
equality –­ pushes our conception of just AI towards a more substantive position which argues 
that some attitudes, relationships, or states of affairs are good and promote individual flourish-
ing. On the other hand, the increasing appeal to inclusive deliberation seems to want to remain 
neutral on how to attain just AI. By allowing an open discussion between the relevant stake-
holders, the thought seems to be that inclusive deliberative groups should decide, for them-
selves, how to resolve injustice and ethical issues in their own contexts. Hence, the two 
tendencies are not necessarily aligned and can potentially conflict in some cases.
Yet, in closing, it is important to underline that it does not necessarily follow that one has 
to choose either relational justice or deliberation. It simply requires reflecting more on how 
to think about their connection and how deliberation should be designed and used. If one 
desires to hold fast to the inputs of theories of relational autonomy and relational equality, 

--- Page 312 ---

HUGO COSSETTE-­LEFEBVRE
306
this does not erase the value of deliberative processes although it would constrain how and 
why they are deployed. After all, both relational theories leave significant leeway concerning 
how the ideals they proposed can be realized in practice. They also remain largely silent on 
how to prioritize the main issues one can face in practice. Therefore, deliberation can still 
serve an important role in problem selection to decide the main problems to address, on data 
curation to inform how some reference standards can perpetuate existing inequalities, or to 
evaluate a model performance, to some extent. Here, of course, the perspectives of those 
who will be most affected by the deployment of a particular AI system hold precious inputs. 
Nonetheless, if one wants to reconcile deliberation and relational conceptions of justice, 
then one should be prepared to be critical of some of the deliberative results and to some-
times promote certain goods even if they differ from the actual expressed preferences of the 
deliberative forum. Relational theories of equality and autonomy thus operate upstream of 
the deliberative process.

1	 Note that there are slightly different ways of presenting the three waves of AI ethics. For instance, 
Bolte and van Wynsberghe present the first wave as being mainly interested in abstract and nonex-
istent technology. For them, the first wave’s distinctive feature is its focus not on concrete, current 
ethical concerns but on future technological possibilities and advancements (2024, p. 3; for exam-
ples of that first wave see Bostrom 2002 and Vinge 1993). However, they present the second and 
third waves in the same way as they are presented here. In contrast, Ryan et al. (2021) classify AI 
ethics research along temporal dimensions, distinguishing between short-­term, medium-­term, and 
long-­term issues. However, this classification is largely unstable, since it is not a principled distinc-
tion. Accordingly, I put their position to the side here.
2	 By practical identity, Mackenzie follows Korsgaard’s definition as “a description under which you 
value yourself, a description under which you find your life to be worth living and your actions to be 
worth undertaking” (Korsgaard 1996, 101).
3	 As Savolainen and Ruckenstein write: “Algorithmic systems constitute a kind of ‘unconscious’ that 
influences deliberation, interpretation and action beyond the self-­awareness of subjects and collec-
tives. These concerns suggest that algorithmic systems put pressure on notions of autonomy as 
reflective and informed processes of self-­definition, decision-­making and evaluation of options. 
Such processes require introspection, but if part of the cognitive processing that precedes choice is 
outsourced to algorithmic systems and feedback loops, how can one endorse a preference, choice or 
interpretation as one’s own?” (2022, 7).
4	 The gambler’s fallacy is the tendency to believe that if an event has frequently occurred in the past, 
it should be less likely to happen in the future. As Sunstein has pointed out, judges in charge of 
granting asylum are less likely to grant it in a particular case if they have granted it in many previous 
cases. This is, of course, problematic because cases should be considered independently of one 
another. Algorithms are not affected by these cognitive biases. Noise here refers to unwanted vari-
ability in judgment. Noise can come from many arbitrary causes, for instance, when a judge is tired, 
hungry, in a bad mood, etc. Algorithms can consequently significantly reduce noise since they are 
not influenced by these arbitrary causes.
5	 Note that if it turns out that a consensus is not attainable, a vote may be used to take the final 
decision.
6	 More precisely, even if some do have some responsibility for creating the injustice because they acted 
wrongly or because they wronged others, it is only part of the structural story that allows some to 
exploit or wrong others. The point here is not that we should not hold those who wrong others to 
account for their actions, but that this is insufficient to modify an unjust social structure.
