22.1  Critical Theory and the Topic of Technology
Critical theory, in the narrow sense of the term, refers to a philosophical and sociological 
school of thought that originated at the Institut für Sozialforschung (Institute for Social 
Research) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, which was founded in the 1920s.1 Critical theory 
is strongly influenced by the work of Immanuel Kant, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Karl 
Marx, Friedrich Nietzsche, and Sigmund Freud, and characterized by its concern for relations 
of oppression and exploitation, its method of immanent-­transcendence, and its emancipa-
tory aim.
First-­generation critical theorists, like Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, Walter Benjamin, 
and Herbert Marcuse, showed a clear interest in the topic of technology and questioned the 
meaning of progress in the context of certain technological developments. Benjamin, for in-
stance, worried about the impact of the camera on the arts (Benjamin 1931, 1969) and wrote 
elsewhere that the illusion of technological progress had corrupted the German working class 
more than anything (Benjamin 1968). Technology also played a major part in Marcuse’s cri-
tique of capitalism; he connected capitalism’s characteristic industrial production processes to 
the arrival of a “one-­dimensional man,” i.e., the shaping of all aspects of human social life by 
technical, instrumental reason (Marcuse 1964). However, despite these and other influential 
contributions to the field, the topic of technology eventually disappeared from critical theory’s 
research agenda.
The most important attempt at reconnecting critical theory and technology is arguably 
that of Canadian philosopher Andrew Feenberg. Feenberg, a student and disciple of Herbert 
Marcuse, is best known for his work on “critical constructivism,” a technophilosophical posi-
tion which he developed over a number of years and publications (Feenberg 1999, 2017, 2022). 
In addition to Frankfurt School critical theory, Feenberg draws heavily on Heideggerian phe-
nomenology and Science and Technology Studies (STS) to show the socially constructed 
nature of technology design. He argues that, if technology is socially constructed, i.e., if tech-
nologies are designed to align with particular social contexts and demands, technology can 
be said to reify the social context of its creation (Feenberg 1999, p. 87; 2022 p. 33). The 
AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
ROSALIE WAELEN AND LARISSA BOLTE
22

--- Page 317 ---

AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
311
question concerning technology then becomes a political one (Feenberg 1999, pp. 82–­83). 
Here, Feenberg’s argument takes its cue from Frankfurt School critiques of ideology and 
instrumental reason. The assumption of technological neutrality, he argues, betrays a one-­
dimensionality of thought which posits instrumental reason as the only valid form of 
rationality and thus the current, contingent technical code as the only technically viable one 
(Feenberg 2022 pp. 16 and 25). Critical constructivism, on the other hand, uses moments of 
social resistance to technological design, such as workers’ demands for safer machinery 
(Feenberg 2022, p. 24) or the environmental movement’s impacts on industry (Feenberg 2022, 
pp.  29 and 37), to show the underdetermination of technological design by purely 
­instrumental reason. Feenberg calls for the democratization of technology through the 
inclusion and participation of a wider range of social actors in the design of technology 
(Feenberg 1999, 2022).
More recently, several other authors have pointed to the potential of critical theory to illu-
minate debates about the ethical and societal impact of emerging technologies, among which 
is artificial intelligence (AI).2 Stahl et al. (2014), first of all, argue in the context of information 
security that common concepts in critical theory are helpful in pinpointing ethical concerns 
that would otherwise be overlooked. Delanty and Harris (2021), secondly, analyze the role of 
technology in the critical theory tradition and share considerations for a contemporary criti-
cal theory of technology. These considerations include understanding the impact of tech-
nology on subjects’ cognitive capacities, engaging with the impact of technology on social 
rationalities, and identifying contradictions that hold back emancipation. Fuchs (2022), 
thirdly, builds on the work of first-­generation critical theorists and (post-­)Marxism to analyze 
modern communication technologies. Waelen (2022, 2023) argues for a critical approach to 
AI ethics, which entails analyzing AI’s ethical and societal implications in terms of power and 
in function of emancipation. This critical approach is presented as an alternative to the cur-
rently dominant approach of using checklists with ethical principles. Finally, in a recent book 
entitled Critical Theory of AI, Swedish sociologist Simon Lindgren (2023b) gives an elaborate 
yet comprehensive overview of the types of topics and issues that a critical theory of AI could 
cover. Lindgren also edited a book on the topic (2023a), covering a wide range of critical dis-
cussions of AI (in the broadest sense). Not covered by Lindgren (2023b) is the topic of 
progress, which is also central in the critical theory tradition and relevant to a critical theory 
of AI.
Despite these efforts, we must conclude that the topic of technology never fully reappeared 
on critical theorists’ research agenda. As Delanty and Harris put it, technology has been 
“curiously absent” in contemporary critical theory (Delanty and Harris  2021, p.  94). 
Confirming this observation is the fact that, during the Institute for Social Research’s 100th 
anniversary celebration in 2023, with a conference entitled “Futuring Critical Theory,” the 
topic of technology was barely mentioned. This absence of conversations about technology is 
especially surprising given that the topic of AI has become hard to ignore nowadays. Moreover, 
the aim of the conference on “Futuring Critical Theory,” and of critical theory in general, was 
to address contemporary challenges. Dealing with the influence of AI on our lives and with 
the powerful industry behind it certainly is one of the great challenges of our time.3
The purpose of this chapter is not only to convince the reader that the topic of AI, and tech-
nology more generally, should be addressed by contemporary critical theory, but also to show 
that critical theory can add something new and important to ethical, philosophical, and socio-
logical debates about AI. To achieve this second goal, we present the notion of progress as a topic 
that is both central to social critique and relevant in the context of a critique of AI. In sec-
tion 22.2, the next section, we describe the role that the notion of progress plays in the ­critical 

--- Page 318 ---

ROSALIE WAELEN and LARISSA BOLTE
312
theory tradition and how progress has been conceived by different critical theorists. The focus of 
this discussion lies on recent work by Amy Allen, Rainer Forst, and Rahel Jaeggi. In section 22.3, 
we critique AI by discussing various ways in which both backward-­ and forward-­looking narra-
tives about progress in the field of AI can be deemed ideological. In section 22.4, we criticize 
Frankfurt School critical theory for not treating narratives about technological progress as mor-
ally and politically laden. We argue that putting the topic of technology back on critical theory’s 
agenda involves reconsidering the conception of technological progress within critical theory. 
The chapter ends with a brief summary and conclusion.
22.2  The Notion of Progress in Critical Theory
As mentioned in the introduction, critical theory is characterized by its unique method of 
immanent-­transcendence and its emancipatory aim. Immanent-­transcendence means cri-
tiquing and transforming society by taking the current situation as a starting point and going 
from there, rather than trying to move towards some preconceived ideal. Critical theory’s 
emancipatory aim is both a normative and practical goal; critical theory seeks not only to 
identify but also to overcome social domination (Forst 2019).
Because of these central characteristics, critical theory is intimately related to the notion 
of progress. Even if critical theory’s method does not predefine what progress entails, the aim 
of overcoming or transcending social domination necessarily assumes a form of progress. At 
the same time, however, narratives of progress are often also the subject of critique. Moreover, 
narratives of progress ought to be the subject of critique. It is important to always maintain a 
critical attitude with regard to who is excluded or disadvantaged by certain conceptions of 
progress. In this section, we sketch this dual role of the notion of progress in critical theory, 
through a description of recent discussions on the topic by contemporary critical theorists 
Amy Allen, Rainer Forst, and Rahel Jaeggi.
First-­generation critical theorists questioned historical narratives about progress. 
Following industrialization and two world wars, there was widespread skepticism about the 
idea that historical processes are inherently progressive and especially regarding the idea that 
technological progress equals social progress. For instance, in their book Dialectic of 
Enlightenment, Horkheimer and Adorno (1947) argue that the Enlightenment’s promise of 
liberation has failed and deceived people. They contend that the opposite has happened 
because the masses, shaped by the culture industry, uncritically accepted capitalist ideology 
and adopted an instrumental way of thinking. Horkheimer and Adorno paint the picture of 
the myth of the Enlightenment, in which the formerly liberating ideals of science and reason 
turned oppressive in the hands of the new bourgeois elite who administer the domination not 
only of nature but also of humanity. Their analysis of the Enlightenment can be understood 
as a criticism of the typical Western understanding of modern (Western) history as a process 
of progress, from the dark into the light.4
However, the first generation’s critical attitude towards histories of progress disappeared 
with Habermas and Honneth, second-­ and third-­generation Frankfurt School critical theo-
rists. In her book The End of Progress, Allen argues that the critical theories of Habermas and 
Honneth are founded upon a “backward looking conception of progress as a ‘fact’” 
(Allen 2016, p. 13). She points out that Habermas and Honneth both tried to defend the 
method of immanent critique against accusations of foundationalism, by understanding nor-
mative principles as the result of, and justified by, processes of “progressive social evolution or 
sociocultural learning” (p. 14). Because of the centrality of historical notions of progress in 

--- Page 319 ---

AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
313
the work of Habermas and Honneth, Allen defends that critical theory must be decolonized in 
order to be truly critical. In line with post-­ and decolonial theory, Allen argues that modernity 
and the Enlightenment are characterized by a specific reading of history as a progressive pro-
cess. These histories of progress are problematic for two main reasons. First, European his-
tories of progressive processes are connected to colonialism, imperialism, racism, and also 
present-­day political and economic power imbalances. These histories of progress also rely 
“on a highly selective reading of Europe’s own history,” which denies the cultural and intel-
lectual influences of the outside world and Europe’s dependency on the resources of non-­
European land and labor power of non-­European people (Allen 2016, p. 17). The second 
problem that Allen raises is of an epistemological nature. She argues that judgments about 
historical progress are necessarily normative, meaning that histories of progress are never 
true facts but always reflect a certain point of view. In other words, “they remain judgments 
of progress for us” (p. 22).
Allen identifies her own notion of progress with a Foucauldian approach, i.e., with a 
notion inspired by a genealogical reading of history. Allen’s aim is to free thought from its his-
torical a priori. Critique has to proceed by critiquing the historical contingency of certain 
forms of domination, but has to refrain from a unified story of history progressing towards 
autonomy. Instead, history is always a story of progress and regress at the same time, in 
which the norms and practices we inherit both hold promise and act as a form of domination. 
Therefore, Allen suggests, history should deliberately be read as a series of unrelated events to 
achieve critical distance to current norms (Allen et al. 2016). The only guiding concern for 
Allen (and here she admits that the Foucauldian account contains a Kantian element) is with 
freedom and autonomy (Allen et al. 2016, p. 232).
For Jaeggi, Allen’s proposal to read history as a series of unrelated events negates the 
idea of social dynamics and makes way for relativism (Allen et al. 2016, p. 229), or, as 
Allen prefers to call the charge, conventionalism (p. 242). Like Allen, Jaeggi rejects all 
notions of freestanding normativity, but she reasons that out of the rejection of universal 
normative ideals on the one hand, and the need to remain critical of current conditions on 
the other, arises the need to ground normative judgments historically. In Jaeggi’s view, 
being able to speak about progress and regress means being able to speak about historical 
change and especially the dynamics that bring this change about (Allen et  al.  2016, 
p. 229).
Jaeggi’s views are strongly influenced by a Hegelian-­Marxist account of immanent cri-
tique (Jaeggi 2015). Jaeggi believes that critical theory cannot do without a notion of his-
torical normativity, and thus a notion of progress and regress in the face of moments of 
crisis. Moments of crisis reveal practical contradictions, i.e., limits to the prevailing system 
of thought, which open up opportunities for transcending the present social order. Thus, 
the shortcomings of the present social order give rise to new norms immanently by nega-
tion of what is not working. In Jaeggi’s conception, this corresponds to a “problem-­solving” 
activity, in which obstinate problems with social practices call for alternative forms of social 
organization. History can thus be described as a learning process in which problematic 
forms of social organization are procedurally replaced by others, which are, however, not 
without their own respective problems and solutions (Allen et  al.  2016, pp.  225–­227). 
Social crises thus derive a notion not of the “best” but of the “better.” This very idea, of 
course, implies a notion of progress, albeit a nonteleological and fallibilistic one (Allen 
et al. 2016, p. 227).
Another contemporary critical theorist discussing progress is Rainer Forst. Forst’s distinct 
critical approach is based on the notion of justification (Forst 2017). He argues that power 

--- Page 320 ---

ROSALIE WAELEN and LARISSA BOLTE
314
relations and normativity are closely related to one another, since social power relations con-
stitute normative orders that determine whether justifications are acceptable or not. This 
relation between power and normativity can prohibit emancipation. That is why critical 
theory, according to Forst, should involve analysis of the normative orders that determine the 
space of justifications for others. He argues that the relation between the notion of progress 
and the notion of justification is important, because “[t]he justification of progress lies in the 
progress of justification as a social practice among equals” (Forst 2019, p. 22). True progress 
can be realized, Forst argues, only when the members of a normative order are able to deter-
mine themselves what counts as progress and in which direction their society should develop 
(Forst 2017, 2019).5
Forst agrees with Allen (2016) that dominant stories about progress can promote forms of 
domination and are often entangled with Europe’s problematic history of colonialism and 
imperialism. Dominant stories about progress therefore need to be the object of critique. 
However, as Allen, Jaeggi, and Forst all agree, critical theory is nevertheless necessarily 
connected to the notion of progress, because critical theory’s imperative of emancipation is 
an imperative for progress. What Forst disagrees with (among other things) is Allen’s idea 
that critical theory could (or should) do without the historical, backward-­looking conception 
of progress. He writes:
I don’t see how we, who understand ourselves as participants and not merely distant observers of 
history, could (as Allen suggests) say that we should not be committed to any backward-­looking 
claim to progress and yet still hold on to a contextual, forward-­looking imperative of progress. 
That strikes me as a contradictory and ahistorical view that refuses to learn from history, a his-
tory containing regress as well as (we hope) progress, whatever criteria of emancipation we use 
(Forst 2019, p. 18).
In summary, progress has always been an important concept within critical theory, and it 
recently became a central topic of debate between contemporary critical theorists Allen, 
Jaeggi, and Forst. Progress is a multifaceted concept. It can be the subject of critique but at the 
same time some notion of progress is also intimately and inevitably related to the normative 
goal of critical theory. After all, the ideal of transcending the status quo as well as the goal of 
emancipatory social change imply a certain conception of progress. This conception is, on all 
accounts, necessarily nonteleological, historicized and nonuniversalizing.
22.3  Critiquing Narratives of Progress in AI
Allen (2016) makes a distinction between backward-­ and forward-­looking progress. Backward-­
looking progress, which can also be referred to as “historical progress” or “progress as a fact,” 
is historical in the sense that it explains historical events as unified, teleological processes of 
improvement. Through backward-­looking references to progress, dominant social or political 
powers tend to present historical events and developments as facts or unavoidable matters, 
while, in reality, these references to progress are necessarily normative interpretations of con-
tingent events and developments. Histories of progress (by which we mean backward-­looking 
narratives of progress) are therefore often ideological. Forward-­looking progress refers to con-
ceptions about how the present, the status quo, can be improved. In this section, we critique 
narratives about the history of AI as well as narratives about AI’s promises for the future, by 
showing that these narratives are ideological.

--- Page 321 ---

AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
315
Writing about the history of AI in 1977, McCorduck describes human-­made intelligence 
as an ancient human dream that was turned from fiction into science in the 1950s. According 
to McCorduck, the scientific pursuit of AI was bound to happen.
[T]he intelligent machine was an idea whose time had come, and it was not only that the com-
puter presented a medium with which such a dream could be realized. There was a constellation 
of events, most notably the shift from one dominant paradigm, the physicist’s notion of energy, to 
a new paradigm, the cyberneticist’s notion of information, and there were the continuing efforts 
to describe psychological and biological phenomena in mathematical terms. Because of these 
convergences, a young assistant professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College named John 
McCarthy, who himself had been fascinated by these issues for quite a while, suggested to his 
friends that some real progress could be made if only all of the people at work on these prob-
lems –­ all ten of them –­ spent the summer of 1956 together, helping each other (McCorduck 
et al. 1977, p. 953).
Bruce Buchanan (2006) describes AI’s history in a similar way, tracing the history of AI back 
to the ancient Greek mythology of Homer, René Descartes’ thought experiments, Gottfried 
Leibniz’s and Blaise Pascal’s interest in calculators, Jules Verne’s and Isaac Asimov’s works of 
fiction, the character called Tiktok in Frank Baum’s The Wizard of Oz, the Jewish story of the 
Golem of Prague, and so on. Like McCorduck (1977), Buchanan (2006) aims to show that 
scientific developments in AI are a realization of a long-­held human dream.
After the famous Dartmouth conference in 1956, which established the term “Artificial 
Intelligence,” research on AI took off. In these early years, the field benefitted greatly from 
increased government funding as well as improvements in computer speed and storage 
capacity. But in the 1970s, developments in the field stagnated and funding dried out. 
Eventually, in the 1980s, researchers received new funding and developed new algorithms 
(namely, neural networks). However, despite these theoretical developments, many of the 
initial aims of these projects were not achieved, and funding initiatives stopped once again by 
the end of the 1980s. Nevertheless, AI had some major breakthroughs in the 1990s and early 
2000s –­ such as IBM’s Deep Blue beating the world chess champion in 1997 and the intro-
duction of various speech recognition systems by Dragon Dictate, Apple, Microsoft, and IBM.
What served these successes was the fact that computing power had improved, which 
meant that computers could process more information and do so faster than before. While the 
algorithms behind many successful AI systems today were already developed in the 1980s, 
the breakthrough in deep learning-­based AI did not come until 2012 (when the AlexNet 
computer vision model won the ImageNet competition with astounding accuracy levels), 
because it was then that sufficient computing power and big amounts of training data became 
available (Mitchell 2019).
What we find in these histories of AI is a common tendency to describe the technology in 
a linear and deterministic manner. The history of AI is usually portrayed in a linear way, first 
of all, because it explains developments in the field as steps forward in a single direction, with 
artificial general intelligence (AGI) as the ultimate goal. It is often pointed out that there have 
been so-­called “AI winters” when funding and research initiatives were low, but these AI win-
ters do not negate the story told about AI’s road to success and the inevitability of AGI. The 
common narrative about AI’s history is deterministic, secondly, because it presents man-­made 
intelligence as a bound-­to-­happen realization of something that humans have dreamed of 
throughout history and across cultures. This narrative is presented as factual while in reality 
it depends on a highly contingent interpretation of historical myths, philosophies, and works 
of art.

--- Page 322 ---

ROSALIE WAELEN and LARISSA BOLTE
316
The contingency of developments in AI can be shown through various examples of the 
decisive role played by institutions and the visions of individuals in steering AI in a certain 
direction. One such example is the influence of research funding on the directions that 
research takes. Rockwell Anyoha describes how a lot of AI development in the 1980s was 
funded by the Japanese government, which pushed Edward Feigenbaum’s idea of expert sys-
tems. Anyoha explains that the Japanese funding initiative was eventually dropped because 
the expert systems that were developed during the funding period did not meet the expecta-
tions of the funder. Nevertheless, Anyoha notes, “it could be argued that the indirect effects of 
the [funding initiative] inspired a talented young generation of engineers and scientists”. 
Indeed, in the decades that followed, the focus on expert systems rather than AGI remained 
central in AI research and development.
Another example of the contingency of AI’s development has to do with the field’s long-­
held obsession with automizing the game of chess. Nathan Ensmenger (2011) describes how 
some of the “founding fathers of AI” –­ such as Alan Turing, John McCarthy, Herbert Simon, 
and Claude Shannon –­ actively pushed for the development of computer chess and for mak-
ing chess the measure for intelligence in AI research. They chose chess as the benchmark not 
because it is an objective measurement of human intelligence but because they were them-
selves fans of the game and because using chess as a measurement had strategic benefits. 
Chess was popular and esteemed in Western culture (more than the Chinese game of Go, for 
instance), it was relatively easy to automize, and there was already an elaborate system in 
place for measuring performance in chess.
Ensmenger argues that the focus on chess helped AI research gain publicity and created 
excitement about the concept of AI, but harmed progress in the field as well. First, the impor-
tance of computer chess to AI research made the field heavily dependent on cash prizes and 
the gamification of research. Second, computer chess was based on the relatively simple 
minimax algorithm, which was well suited for automizing chess but not for further devel-
oping and theorizing machine intelligence. Choosing a different game as a benchmark, 
Ensmenger writes, “might have shaped the research agenda of the discipline in a very differ-
ent direction” (Ensmenger 2011, p. 17).
A third example is provided by Marc Anderson (2024), who argues that McCarthy’s visions 
for and work on AI constituted an ideological program that shapes the field to this day. As one 
of the founding fathers of AI and the main organizer for the Darthmouth conference, 
McCarthy had a major impact on the field. Anderson describes how AI, from the start, was 
based on a very specific understanding of human intelligence. Anderson refers to various 
assumptions that underly this understanding of human intelligence –­ such as the mechanical 
function of language and the value of efficiency. Philosophical positions that McCarthy con-
sidered to fit his vision of AI are “scientism, scientific materialism, and a ‘real’ common-­sense 
world of objects which can be manipulated, subject to causal relations” (Anderson 2024, 
p. 7). According to Anderson, McCarthy’s view of human intelligence and endorsement of a 
highly rational worldview are ideological and the influence of this can still be seen in AI 
research and development today. This also means that McCarthy’s program endorsed a 
specific view on progress in AI –­ namely a move towards the realization of a machine that can 
simulate this highly rationalized conception of intelligence.
Finally, not just histories of progress in AI but also forward-­looking narratives about 
progress are ideological. Claims that big tech companies like Google and OpenAI make about 
where the field of AI is headed are both deterministic and normative. In a recent interview, 
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, describes the prospect of AGI in a linear and deterministic 
matter, i.e., in the same way as the history of AI is usually told. Altman says: “It’s going to be 

--- Page 323 ---

AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
317
different for sure, but I think the only way out is through. We just have to go do this thing. It’s 
going to happen. This is like now an unstoppable technological course. The value is too 
great.”6 Similarly, the website of OpenAI states that “our research will eventually lead to 
artificial general intelligence, a system that can solve human-­level problems” and its mission 
statement is described as ensuring that AGI “benefits all of humanity.”7
Claims like these are ideological because they present technological developments, in this 
case the arrival of AGI, as an unavoidable necessity, which keeps society from questioning it. 
Moreover, Altman insinuates that this “unstoppable technological course” implies progress in 
a moral-­political sense, by adding that “the value is too great” and claiming that OpenAI’s 
products will be able to “benefit all of humanity.” Paul Schütze (2024) describes how Google 
makes similar ideological statements about AI. These promises about the progress that AI will 
bring are presented as undisputable facts, while in reality they represent specific interests and 
a particular worldview.
Although much more could be said on the topic, the examples in this section show that the 
visions and interests of a select group of people play a huge role in shaping the field of AI. 
Through their dominance, AI researchers, funding agencies, and entrepreneurs have pre-
vented emancipation in a variety of ways –­ for example by fostering a masculine work culture 
and stereotype that excludes women (Ensmenger 2015) or by excluding other disciplines 
from the development of a new form of intelligence (we’d like to think, of course, that things 
would have turned out differently had philosophers and ethicists been part of AI research 
from the start).
As explained in the previous section, histories of progress can be ideological and serve to 
keep problematic power imbalances in place. Such false narratives of progress need to be over-
come in order to achieve true progress. As we demonstrated in this section, a critique of AI 
should reveal the ideology hidden behind narratives of progress in AI. Critical theorists should 
analyze the ways in which the development and goals of the field of AI rest on contingent, 
nonteleological processes. The need for such critique of AI does not reject a historical under-
standing of AI altogether. We can learn from AI’s history about the hidden normativity in AI 
and about forward-­looking conceptions of progress associated with it.
22.4  Reconsidering Technological Progress
Forst (2017, 2019) makes a distinction between moral-­political progress and progress in life 
conditions. Moral-­political progress is related to emancipation and forms the goal of critical 
theory. Progress in life conditions refers to quantifiable improvements of people’s life conditions 
(e.g., access to food, healthcare, and education). Forst, like other critical theorists before him, 
understands technological progress merely in the latter sense, as the improvement of people’s 
lives through technical means. Although he acknowledges that evaluative questions about 
the social costs of such technological progress can be asked (Forst 2019, p. 19), he does not 
relate technological progress to moral-­political conceptions of progress and the critique 
thereof. In this section, we argue that Forst and other contemporary critical theorists are 
wrong in leaving technological progress out of their discussions of moral-­political progress. 
Current developments in the field of AI urge critical theory to reconsider its conception of 
technological progress.
As pointed out in the introduction, work on the role of technology in modern societies 
has not always been absent from critical theory. The first-­generation Frankfurt School, 
and especially Herbert Marcuse’s one-­dimensional man, famously critique the role of 

--- Page 324 ---

ROSALIE WAELEN and LARISSA BOLTE
318
instrumental –­ i.e., technical –­ rationality in upholding industrial capitalism. These first-­
generation Frankfurt School analyses of technology still hold some sway today. Critiques 
of the operationalization and rationalization of labor processes and culture are certainly 
not unheard of today, in the age of AI, and the power over technology and technological 
development continues to lie in the hands of a small elite. At first glance, it is thus all the 
more surprising that critical theory’s initial interest in technology seems to have fallen by 
the wayside.
At a second glance, however, this development becomes more understandable and it has all 
to do with the characterization of technology in these early accounts. While early Frankfurt 
School thinkers do recognize the ideological function of technology and its employment in 
industrial capitalism, they do not overcome the identification of technology with instrumental 
rationality. As Delanty and Harris (2021, p. 92) argue, the early Frankfurt School leans heavily 
towards the notion of Technik, i.e., the technical control of nature and the mastery of material 
conditions, as opposed to the more cultural notion of Technologia, as in the practical knowledge 
of the arts and crafts. With technology being restricted to the notion of Technik, critique of tech-
nology must remain at the level of critiquing the application of instrumental rationality towards 
unworthy ends or in domains where it does not belong (cf. also Feenberg 1999, p. 157).
The same characterization of technology as Technik results in a particular conception of 
technological progress. The restriction of the nature of technology to instrumental reason 
leaves little room for anything but the characterization of technological progress as progress 
in life conditions embraced by Forst and others before him. If technology cannot be criticized 
but for its application, there is no such thing as moral-­political progress in or of technology.
Hence, the rigid distinction between the social and the technological realm goes back to the 
very foundations of Frankfurt School critical theory. However, this does not mean that the 
distinction cannot or should not be scrutinized. Important work in this direction has been 
done by Feenberg, whom we have introduced in section 22.1 as one of the few contemporary 
critical theorists engaging with technology at length. In his 1999 book Questioning Technology, 
Feenberg argues that the modern story of technological progress is one of technological 
determinism. Feenberg critiques the narrative that technologies have an autonomous 
functional logic, which makes it possible to trace the trajectory of their development without 
any reference to society, as well as the idea that societies need to adapt to technological 
progress unidirectionally (p. 77). Feenberg argues: “These two theses of technological deter-
minism [unilinearity and unidirectionality] present decontextualized, self-­generating tech-
nology as the foundation of modern life. (. . .) Determinism thus implies that our technology 
and its corresponding institutional structures are universal, indeed, planetary in scope” 
(Feenberg 1999, p. 78). Feenberg argues that, instead, technology should be understood as 
socially constructed.
Two points are remarkable about Feenberg’s argument. For one, we readily recognize a 
characterization of technology-­as-­Technik in Feenberg’s description of technological deter-
minism. Indeed, the two notions of technology are complementary. If technology is nothing 
but the mastery of nature, value neutral in itself and merely following a logic of efficiency, 
progress becomes a matter of more or less mastery. Moral and political questions are excluded 
from this story of progress, at least until technological progress unilaterally interferes with 
society. Second, this story of progress is exactly the kind that has been rejected by critical the-
orists of the Foucauldian and Hegelian-­Marxist variety by way of methodological choice, 
namely one that is teleological, dehistoricized, and universalizing. If technological progress 
can be read nondeterministically, critical theory thus has every interest in performing that 
reading.

--- Page 325 ---

AI, Critical Theory, and the Concept of Progress
319
Such nondeterministic readings of technological progress are already available. As has 
been indicated above, Feenberg argues against this form of technological determinism by 
arguing for the underdetermination of technological design by instrumental reason and thus 
the embeddedness of technology with sociopolitical value judgments. Assuming underdeter-
mination, public contention against the design of the technosystem becomes possible 
(Feenberg 2017, p. 199). A different, more critical approach to technology is therefore pos-
sible. Indeed, Feenberg argues, there can be no notion of progress in the sense embraced by 
critical theorists without a concrete basis in the social world –­ a basis which the study of 
technical arrangements provides (Feenberg 2017, p.198).
We also see glimpses of this possibility outside critical theory. In recent years, scholarship 
on the ethics and politics of AI has grown exponentially. At first, this debate focused mainly 
on the impact of specific AI applications on ethical principles like privacy, nondiscrimination, 
and transparency. Eventually, many scholars in the field recognized that AI not only has a 
strictly ethical impact but also a broader social and political impact (Coeckelbergh 2022). 
Now, a shift is taking place from a focus on individual AI applications and their implications 
towards a broader analysis of the AI industry and its role in political, social, and economic 
structures (Bolte and van Wynsberghe 2024). Recent debates on the ethics and politics of AI 
go far beyond evaluative questions about the ways in which AI can improve life conditions; 
these debates confirm that AI technology and its development most certainly have a moral-­
political dimension. There is thus work to be done for critical theory to reconsider its own 
conception of technological progress and to construe technology, including AI, as a proper 
object of critique.
22.5  Conclusion
In this chapter, we have shown by means of a discussion of the concept of progress that the 
topic of technology ought to be addressed by critical theory. This is necessary, both because 
addressing technology’s role in society aligns with critical theory’s emancipatory ambitions 
and also because critical theory can add new and valuable perspectives to ongoing debates 
about the ethics and social impact of AI. If critical theory wants to remain relevant to con-
temporary philosophy and social theory, and continue its ambition of challenging present-­
day struggles for emancipation, it needs to start to take seriously (again) the important role of 
technology, and particularly AI, in today’s society and the power dynamics within it. Given 
AI’s growing importance in nearly all aspects of society, we urgently need to overcome false 
narratives about progress in AI and align society’s conception of technological progress with 
a notion of social progress that is determined democratically by the members of society them-
selves. A major challenge for achieving true progress in the context of AI is the fact that the 
society that is affected by AI, is a global one. Moreover, the moral demand for self-­determination 
regarding technological progress implies having to struggle against the social, political, and 
economic power of big tech companies.
