24.1  Introduction
The recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, computer science, and related 
fields, particularly regarding large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, have presented 
significant ethical and sociopolitical challenges, including aspects concerning human–­robot 
interactions (Gordon and Nyholm 2021; Müller 2020). LLMs like ChatGPT have not only 
become exceedingly versatile but also proficient enough to rival  –­  or in some cases sur-
pass  –­  human capabilities in various domains, including healthcare, education, finance, 
business, legal and judicial sectors, AI governance, marketing, and policing and surveillance. 
These developments have prompted scholars to contemplate the moral dimensions of AI, spe-
cifically the question of whether autonomous AI entities, such as robots, should be entitled to 
moral rights once they reach a certain threshold of capability (Gordon 2023a; Gunkel 2018).
As it stands, no artificial entities currently possess the requisite capabilities to warrant 
moral status and related rights. However, adopting a precautionary principle suggests the 
importance of preparing for the potential emergence of such entities. This principle cautions 
against the assumption that machines will never achieve a level of sophistication necessary 
for general artificial intelligence. This chapter raises the pivotal question of whether, in time, 
we will encounter machines of such advanced capabilities that we might be morally obligated 
to acknowledge them as entities with moral status and moral rights.
In this chapter, I aim to explore the pressing question of whether AI robots could be enti-
tled to fundamental moral rights, and if so, the grounds upon which such rights could be 
established. To achieve this, I will first delve into the concepts of moral status and moral rights 
in the chapter’s second section, following this introduction. Here, I will highlight what I con-
sider to be the most pertinent criteria for moral rights entitlement that are independent of 
species. The third section will focus on the notion of fundamental rights, beginning with an 
examination of what fundamental rights entail before differentiating between two categories: 
rights related to humans and those applicable to machines. The fourth section will explore 
potential infringements of fundamental rights, focusing on sex rights as a paradigmatic case

for reconciling conflicts among these rights. This analysis will employ my ethical approach, 
termed Ethics as a Method. The final section will offer some concluding observations.
24.2  Moral Status and Moral Rights
The prevailing perspective in ethics and moral philosophy holds that a typical adult human 
possesses full moral status and, consequently, the maximum array of associated moral 
rights. An entity is considered to have full moral status if, and only if, it possesses moral per-
sonhood (Clarke et al. 2021). Despite this standard viewpoint, some scholars advocate for a 
departure from the concept of moral status, arguing that its philosophical significance and 
actual existence remain unclear (Horta 2017). Nevertheless, I contend that it is possible to 
meaningfully interpret the notion of moral status. This understanding allows us to deter-
mine which entities are entitled to moral rights and which are not, and to explore whether 
distinctions in the entitlement to moral rights exist, based on morally relevant empirical cri-
teria (Gordon 2021, 2020a).
Three prevalent methods are used to ascertain whether an entity possesses personhood, 
thereby granting it full moral status and associated moral rights. First, the human dignity 
approach posits that if an entity is human (according to the religious approach), it inherently 
possesses personhood, full moral status, and related rights (Annas  2004; Kass  2002; 
Fukuyama 2002). Second, the rationality-­autonomy approach (or Kantian approach) sug-
gests that an entity’s capacity for sufficient rationality and autonomy qualifies it for person-
hood, full moral status, and related rights (Kant 2009; Mill 1998; Singer 1979). Lastly, the 
social-­relational approach argues that if an entity engages in social and meaningful relation-
ships with others, typically humans, it is considered to have personhood, full moral status, 
and related rights (Dolby 1989; Gunkel 2012; Coeckelbergh 2014).
I argue that merely being human, particularly within the context of the Jewish-­Christian 
religious tradition, does not inherently suffice for the conferment of moral status and related 
rights. This position is predicated on the uncertainty surrounding the existence of a deity 
with an interest in human life. Additionally, the notion that being part of a social relationship 
inherently grants moral status is not entirely convincing. It fails to account for scenarios 
where a rational and autonomous entity may be denied moral status and associated rights 
simply due to others’ reluctance to engage in meaningful social relations with it. Conversely, 
the rationality-­autonomy approach presents a more promising foundation for assigning full 
moral status. This approach could be feasibly adjusted to serve as a solid basis for determining 
moral status (Gordon 2022). The specifics of how such a revision could be articulated and 
applied are outlined below.
Frances Kamm (2007, p.229) offers a significant definition of moral status, suggesting 
that “an entity has moral status when, in its own right and for its own sake, it can give us 
reason to do things such as not destroy it or help it.” According to Kamm, actions can be 
taken “for X’s own sake” if X is sentient or conscious, or possesses the potential for sentience 
or consciousness. She posits that the capacity for reasoning and the capacity for suffering are 
distinct attributes that, while separable, are not individually necessary for moral status; 
rather, either attribute is sufficient to confer this status (Kamm 2007, p.229). Kamm’s hybrid 
approach to moral status resonates with the moral intuitions of both scholars and the general 
public. Exploring her argument further in the context of intelligent robots presents a 
­compelling avenue for advancing the discussion on their moral status and moral rights 
(Gordon 2021, p.460).

--- Page 352 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon
346
Kamm’s approach is compelling because it appropriately acknowledges the morally 
significant concept of rationality (which is closely associated with consciousness) and the 
importance of the capacity to experience pain (or suffering) as critical characteristics of a 
vulnerable entity. In my work, I contend that for an entity to possess full moral status, it is 
essential for it to have the capacity both to reason and to suffer (Gordon 2022). A partial 
moral status may be subject to less stringent criteria. For instance, toddlers could be deemed 
to possess a lower moral status due to their underdeveloped rationality; however, their ability 
to feel pain might justify sufficient grounds for refraining from causing them unnecessary 
harm or killing them. This proposition suggests, perhaps justifiably, that moral status is not 
absolute but varies in degrees, particularly when examining the nuances of the beginning 
and end of life issues, such as in instances of diminished rationality. It also implies that there 
might be a threshold for achieving a certain level of full moral status in standard scenarios.
The critical argument I wish to emphasize is the necessity of employing species-­independent 
criteria to assess the moral status of any entity, to avoid human-­centric bias (Gordon 2021). 
By adopting such an approach, we can not only accurately evaluate the moral status of 
humans but also extend our ethical considerations to encompass various animals, potentially 
nature, and even robots. In my prior work, I have advocated for the use of rationality, 
autonomy, intelligence, and self-­awareness as foundational criteria, while also recognizing 
the moral significance of an entity’s vulnerability. This recognition stems from the under-
standing that persons are inherently social beings, not isolated moral entities. This framework 
allows for a more inclusive and equitable assessment of moral status and rights across a broad 
spectrum of entities (Gordon and Gunkel 2022).
24.3  What are Fundamental Rights?
This section is divided into two parts. The first part offers an overview of the concept of 
fundamental rights, while the second delves into a more detailed examination of human 
rights and machine rights.
24.3.1  Remarks on the Nature of Fundamental Rights
The concept of fundamental rights, in its broadest interpretation, refers to rights of para-
mount importance, transcending the distinction between moral and legal realms. These 
rights occupy a central position and carry supreme significance. It is often argued that while 
other rights hold value, they are invariably subordinate to fundamental rights, given the lat-
ter’s superior moral or legal weight. Fundamental rights safeguard what is deemed most pre-
cious –­ for instance, the right against being killed, tortured, or humiliated. Violations of such 
rights, in the context of humans, constitute grave transgressions. Similarly, some scholars 
advocate for the extension of fundamental rights to animals, recognizing their capacities for 
rationality, autonomy, and susceptibility to suffering, and suggesting that these qualities 
warrant similar protections (Francione 2009; Cavalieri 2001; Singer 1975). Moreover, pro-
ponents of the so-­called robot rights movement such as David Gunkel and John-­Stewart 
Gordon contend that robots, upon reaching a certain level of capability, should also be con-
sidered for entitlements to robot rights.
The differentiation between fundamental rights and human rights is crucial. While all 
human rights are indeed fundamental, not all fundamental rights are human rights 
(Gordon 2013). For instance, it is widely accepted that certain higher animals, such as great 

--- Page 353 ---

AI and Fundamental Rights
347
apes and elephants, possess fundamental rights, including the right not to be harmed or killed 
(Cavalieri 2001; Donaldson and Kymlicka 2013; Francione 2009; Singer and Cavalieri 1993). 
Given that these animals are not human, they cannot possess human rights in the strictest 
sense, as these are typically defined by species membership. Instead, the notion of personhood 
provides a basis for their entitlement to moral and legal safeguards.
Similarly, some environmental rights are considered fundamental due to their intrinsic 
value or their instrumental value to humans. The recognition of such rights often stems 
from the understanding that the environment is essential for the survival and flourishing 
of both human and nonhuman life forms. These rights are not exclusively human, as the 
environment transcends human ownership and its protection benefits a broad range of 
beings and ecosystems. Environmental rights are often framed within the context of sus-
tainable development, where the needs of future generations are balanced against current 
human interests (Stone 2010; Gordon 2012; Atapattu 2015). Moreover, the recognition 
of the environment’s intrinsic value has led to legal innovations in several jurisdictions, 
such as granting legal personhood to natural entities like rivers and forests, further blur-
ring the lines between traditional human-­centered rights and broader ecological con-
cerns (Boyd  2017; Knox and Boyd  2018). This approach shifts the focus from 
anthropocentric models of rights to a more holistic understanding of the rights of nature, 
underscoring the need to safeguard ecosystems as integral components of the global 
community.
This understanding paves the way for discussions on potential rights for robots, particu-
larly as intelligent and autonomous robots emerge and begin to approach or surpass human 
capabilities. However, such robots would not qualify for human rights, given their nonhuman 
nature. Nevertheless, based on their technological sophistication, they could be deemed 
deserving of fundamental rights (Gordon 2023a). This perspective encourages a reevaluation 
of rights entitlement, extending considerations beyond traditional boundaries to include 
advanced technological entities.1
24.3.2  Two Types of Fundamental Rights
In this section, the discussion will distinguish among two types of fundamental rights: human 
rights and machine rights. The aim is to briefly elucidate each category, exploring their simi-
larities and differences in more detail.2
24.3.2.1  Human Rights
Brian Orend, in his seminal 2002 work (p.34), provides an excellent introduction to human 
rights, summarizing the concept as follows.
A human right is a high-­priority claim, or authoritative entitlement, justifed by suffcient reasons, 
to a set of objects that are owed to each human person as a matter of minimally decent treatment. 
Such objects include vitally needed material goods, personal freedoms, and secure protections. In 
general, the objects of human rights are those fundamental benefts that every human being can 
reasonably claim from other people, and from social institutions, as a matter of justice. Failing to 
provide such benefts, or acting to take away such benefts, counts as rights violation. The violation 
of human rights is a vicious and ugly phenomenon indeed; and it is something we have overrid-
ing reasons to resist and, ultimately, to remedy.
Building upon the foundational concept that human rights represent universal moral entitle-
ments, setting forth a baseline of ethical standards transcending state or legal frameworks, 

--- Page 354 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon
348
this perspective has become the predominant understanding of human rights within the 
scholarly community (Gordon 2013). These rights are inherent to all humans, irrespective of 
geographical, political, or social contexts, underscoring their universal applicability and sig-
nificance. They are considered to be of the utmost importance, often overriding other legal 
norms and stipulations, due to their foundational nature.
Human rights are multifaceted, encompassing both moral rights –­ which are rooted in 
fundamental ethical values –­ and legal rights, which find expression and enforcement within 
the legal systems of societies. This duality ensures that human rights are not only theoretical 
ideals but also practical standards that guide the treatment of people within legal 
frameworks.
Moreover, human rights are differentiated into negative and positive rights (Gordon 2023a, 
pp.32–­35). Negative rights call for noninterference from others, essentially requiring that 
persons not be subjected to certain actions or infringements by the state or other actors. 
Examples include the right to freedom of speech and the right to privacy, which demand 
abstention from interference in certain domains of a person’s life. On the other hand, positive 
rights mandate specific interventions or actions to satisfy fundamental human needs and 
welfare. These include the right to education, the right to healthcare, and the right to a stan-
dard of living adequate for health and well-­being, necessitating proactive measures by states 
and communities to fulfill these rights.
The discourse on human rights, as articulated, underscores the necessity of a holistic 
approach that respects and promotes both the noninterference and affirmative action compo-
nents of these rights, ensuring a comprehensive framework for human dignity and welfare. 
This expanded understanding not only reinforces the universality of human rights but also 
emphasizes the responsibility of global and local entities to uphold and advance these princi-
ples, paving the way for a more equitable and just world.
24.3.2.2  Machine Rights
Some scholars such as Kurzweil (2005), Bostrom (2014), Ord (2020), and Gordon (2022) 
posit that advancements in self-­learning algorithms, neural networks, and quantum com-
puting are poised to usher in an era characterized by the technological singularity and the 
emergence of superintelligence. This perspective gains credence from a comprehensive survey 
among AI researchers, indicating a consensus that superintelligence is not a question of if 
but when (Müller and Bostrom 2016).
The advent of superintelligent machines necessitates an immediate and thorough exami-
nation of their potential societal impact, as argued by Gordon (2023a). There exists a preva-
lent skepticism regarding the feasibility of such advancements or the urgency of addressing 
their implications. Nonetheless, the theoretical foundations, as discussed by Chalmers (2010), 
do not preclude the possibility of superintelligence. Thus, it behooves us to contemplate the 
ethical, moral, and sociopolitical considerations concerning the integration of artificial 
humanoids into human society ahead of their realization (Gordon and Gunkel  2022; 
Nyholm 2020).
For example, Bostrom (2014) and Ord (2020) fear that superintelligent machines might 
cause humanity’s extinction, particularly if humanity fails to surmount the control and 
alignment challenges. The control dilemma revolves around our capability to govern entities 
whose cognitive capacities vastly exceed our own, while the alignment challenge seeks to har-
monize their moral compass with human ethical norms to mitigate adversarial outcomes 
(Gunkel 2021).

--- Page 355 ---

AI and Fundamental Rights
349
Given the profound moral and sociopolitical ramifications of artificial humanoids on 
human existence and self-­perception, it is imperative to explore several critical inquiries with 
an inclusive mindset.
•	 The moral status and sociopolitical integration of human-­like AI systems, particularly 
artificial humanoids.
•	 The influence of artificial humanoids on the fabric of human society, encompassing 
moral, social, and political dimensions.
•	 Strategies to foster a harmonious coexistence between humans and artificial humanoids, 
alongside the moral frameworks necessary for resolving potential conflicts.
•	 The entitlement of artificial humanoids to moral and legal rights, and the ethical 
differentiation between them and other AI entities, with particular attention to the role of 
human-­like appearance in moral considerations.
This discussion advocates for an inclusive approach toward the moral and legal acknowledg-
ment of artificial humanoids, predicated on the premise that entities exhibiting sapience, 
characterized by rationality, autonomy, intelligence, and moral discernment, warrant rights 
akin to human beings (Gordon 2022; Kamm 2007). The failure to extend such rights could 
precipitate a robot revolution, a scenario deemed plausible by scholars including Bostrom 
(2014), Ord (2020), Gunkel (2021), and Gordon (2022), contingent on our ability to address 
the control and alignment conundrums.
Proposals for reforming human rights legislation to incorporate a Universal Convention 
for the Rights of AI Systems represent a forward-­thinking approach to legally and morally 
integrating advanced AI systems into our societal framework (Gordon 2023a). In my book 
The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Human Rights Legislation, I delve into the concept of 
machine rights, propelled by the advancements in AI and robotics that increasingly mirror 
human autonomy and decision-­making capabilities. This discourse is anchored in a multifac-
eted examination of moral, sociopolitical, and legal considerations, advocating for the 
extension of rights to nonhuman entities as a necessity for the moral evolution of technology. 
Through engaging with the philosophical debates around consciousness and the capacity for 
machines to possess such states, my argument unfolds, highlighting the moral obligations we 
hold toward entities that, while nonhuman, exhibit characteristics closely aligned with 
human intelligence and behavior.
The core of my argument rests on the moral and practical implications of the machines’ 
entitlement to fundamental rights. I argue that neglecting to do so could lead to potential 
abuses of AI, stifling the responsible development and integration of these technologies into 
society. Conversely, recognizing machine rights could ensure that AI development aligns with 
human values, avoiding unanticipated and potentially harmful repercussions. This approach 
not only establishes a framework for accountability and responsibility but also promotes a 
symbiotic relationship between humans and machines, fostering trust and preventing poten-
tial conflicts –­ a scenario often stressed as a robot revolution.
It might be objected that the alignment of AI with human values presents complex chal-
lenges, as human norms and values are often inconsistent, hard to define, and prone to 
change over time. Programming AI to follow such norms and values risks the development of 
unintended goals or behaviors that could diverge from human intentions, leading to harmful 
or even catastrophic outcomes. Additionally, a strictly human-­centric approach to AI ethics 
risks reinforcing biases and neglects the possibility that AI systems, as nonhuman entities, 
may require distinct ethical considerations. Failing to recognize this could result in the 

--- Page 356 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon
350
creation of AI systems whose goals and actions do not align with broader moral and social 
expectations, leading to unforeseen consequences.
From my perspective, this line of reasoning overemphasizes the potential risks while under-
valuing the possibility of successfully aligning AI with human values. With careful design and 
ethical oversight, alignment mechanisms can be refined to ensure that AI operates within con-
sistent moral boundaries, reducing the likelihood of harmful outcomes. Furthermore, the 
assumption that AI requires a completely distinct ethical framework disregards the significant 
progress made in human ethical systems, which could serve as a reliable foundation for guiding 
AI behavior in ways that benefit both individuals and society as a whole.
The acknowledgment and respect of machine rights are pivotal in navigating the future of 
AI and robotics. This stance is not merely speculative but grounded in a vision for a future where 
technological progress harmonizes with moral integrity3 (Nyholm 2020). By establishing legal 
and moral frameworks that evolve in tandem with technological advancements, we can ensure 
that AI serves humanity’s best interests, enhancing societal welfare while safeguarding against 
the existential risks associated with advanced autonomy and superintelligence.
My inclusive approach marries technological innovation with moral foresight. The poten-
tial gains from respecting machine rights are manifold, ranging from the moral development 
of AI to the prevention of future adversities stemming from the neglect or misuse of AI. It 
underscores the imperative for a dynamic legal and moral framework that can adapt to the 
rapid pace of technological change, ensuring that as we stand on the cusp of a new era in 
human–­machine relations, our moral compass guides us toward a future that values both 
human and machine rights equally. Thus, it is crucial to adopt an inclusive approach that not 
only safeguards human interests but also acknowledges and respects the emerging sociopolit-
ical and moral landscapes shaped by these advanced entities (Gordon 2019).
24.3.2.3  The Upshot
The overarching objective of this proposal is to conceptualize both human rights and machine 
rights as fundamental rights. This inclusive approach aims to establish a common ground for 
ethical reasoning and moral decision making. Fundamental rights serve as both the 
foundation and the boundary within which the most significant moral and legal rights are 
articulated (Gordon 2023b). The distinction between human rights and machine rights lies 
primarily in their respective fields of application. Should these rights be fundamentally akin 
as suggested, it would enable informed decision making in instances of conflict between the 
two, given their shared foundational basis.
Currently, I am not aware of any contemporary ethical theory adequately equipped to navigate 
such decisions, with the exception of my proposed ethical approach Ethics as a Method (Gordon 2019). 
I will briefly outline this approach in the subsequent section of this chapter and demonstrate its 
application in a hypothetical conflict scenario between humans and artificial intelligent human-
oids. This discourse aims to serve as a preliminary exploration of the ­rights entitle­ments across dif-
ferent entities, under the premise that both can assert their rights as fundamental.
24.4  How can Conflicts Among Fundamental Rights be Reconciled?
This section addresses the critical challenge of reconciling conflicts between fundamental 
rights, specifically between human rights and machine rights. The first part offers a concise 
overview of two primary conflict zones: instances where machines infringe upon human 
rights, and situations where humans violate machine rights. The second part introduces my 

--- Page 357 ---

AI and Fundamental Rights
351
ethical approach, Ethics as a Method, which forms the basis for the analysis in the third part. 
This analysis will focus on a specific case of conflict concerning sex rights between humans 
and artificial intelligent humanoids. Through this example, I show how to balance conflicting 
fundamental rights across different entities and propose a resolution to the given problem.
24.4.1  Fundamental Rights Conflicts
In the fourth chapter entitled “The impact of AI on human rights legislation” in my previ-
ously mentioned book (Gordon 2023a, pp.45–­64), I examine the intricate relationship bet-
ween AI and human rights, highlighting the dual potential of AI to both infringe upon and 
enhance these rights. The chapter delves into two primary zones of conflict: instances where 
AI systems might violate human rights, and conversely, where human actions could infringe 
upon the rights of machines, potentially hinting at the emergence of machine rights.
The first zone of conflict examines how AI systems, through their operations, can inadver-
tently lead to violations of human rights. This discussion is anchored around the Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights (1948), illustrating how various AI applications, such as 
criminal justice algorithms, facial recognition technologies, and automated decision making 
in areas like loan applications and employment, etc., can perpetuate biases and discrimination. 
The chapter emphasizes the importance of addressing machine bias and the black box problem, 
where the opaque decision-­making processes of AI systems obscure accountability and 
impede the protection of human rights (Gordon 2023a, pp.50–­57).
To mitigate these issues, I suggest applying several approaches, including the human-­in-­
the-­loop strategy,4 to ensure human oversight in AI decisions, fostering diversity within AI 
development teams, adopting inclusive training practices, and monitoring the performance 
of AI systems. These measures aim to make AI systems more transparent and accountable, 
thereby safeguarding human rights.
The second zone of conflict introduces the novel and contentious concept of machine 
rights. This section posits that as AI systems become more autonomous and capable of com-
plex decision making, the question of their moral and legal status becomes increasingly perti-
nent. In this part, I explore the possibility that highly advanced AI systems could be entitled to 
certain rights, paralleling discussions in animal and environmental rights. It debates the nor-
mative implications of such a paradigm shift, considering whether machines could possess 
rights similar to or distinct from human rights based on their cognitive abilities and autonomy 
(Gordon 2023a, pp.57–­61).
Throughout, the chapter critically examines the moral, legal, and sociopolitical implica-
tions of AI’s impact on human rights. It highlights the need for a nuanced understanding of 
AI technologies, advocating for legal and regulatory frameworks that recognize the potential 
of AI to contribute positively to society while addressing the moral challenges they pose. The 
discussion on machine rights serves as a forward-­looking contemplation on the evolving rela-
tionship between humans and intelligent machines, urging a reevaluation of our legal and 
moral frameworks in light of technological advancements. It sets the stage for a broader 
discourse on the future of AI governance, the ethical treatment of intelligent systems, and the 
imperative to align AI development with the principles of human dignity and rights.
24.4.2  Ethics as a Method
In this section, I briefly present Ethics as a Method (EM), a flexible, context-­sensitive approach 
designed to address moral conflicts, particularly those involving fundamental rights such as 

--- Page 358 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon
352
sex rights. The core idea of EM lies in its recognition of the limitations of rigid ethical sys-
tems. Instead of adhering to a single overarching principle, such as the categorical impera-
tive or utilitarianism, EM advocates for a pluralistic, dialogical approach to ethical reasoning, 
allowing for the complexity and diversity of moral intuitions to be taken into account.
A central tenet of EM is moral expertise, which transcends theoretical knowledge by 
emphasizing the importance of practical wisdom (phronesis) –­ an Aristotelian concept that 
underpins the ability to make judicious decisions in varied and complex circumstances. 
Moral expertise, in this sense, is not merely the application of predefined rules but involves 
the cultivation of skills such as contextual sensitivity and reflective equilibrium. This 
requires a continuous process of balancing moral intuitions with theoretical principles, 
constantly reevaluating one’s ethical commitments as new circumstances arise.
By focusing on the development of moral expertise, EM avoids the pitfalls of moral monism 
and reductionist approaches, offering a nuanced way to approach ethical problems. This 
approach, while drawing on established ethical principles, moves beyond the traditional 
dichotomies of deontological and consequentialist theories, bridging these gaps to foster a 
more comprehensive understanding of ethical practice. Ultimately, EM serves as a call for 
a  more adaptable and context-­sensitive approach to moral decision making, providing a 
valuable tool for addressing the challenges posed by fundamental rights and their application 
in real-­world scenarios.
To this end, I propose that moral expertise is best developed through a methodological plu-
ralism that synthesizes insights from various ethical traditions, rather than rigidly adhering 
to one. This approach allows for an adaptable method of moral reasoning, which is essential 
for navigating the complex moral landscape of contemporary society. In the context of sex 
rights, EM provides a practical framework for reconciling conflicts among competing rights 
by fostering a dialogue that respects diverse ethical perspectives and the particularities of 
individual cases.
24.4.3  Sex Rights: Humans Versus Artificial Intelligent Humanoids
24.4.3.1  On the Meaning of Sex Rights
Sex rights are recognized as fundamental moral rights that affirm a person’s freedom to 
engage in sexual activity, unconstrained by legal prohibitions. This includes the liberty to 
select a sex partner of one’s choice, irrespective of gender (encompassing same-­sex relation-
ships), ethnicity, social status, color, or the presence of medical conditions among the part-
ners involved. Consequently, sex rights are among the most crucial rights for human beings. 
Infringing upon a person’s right to consensual sexual activity or, conversely, coercing someone 
into sexual activity against their will constitutes a severe violation of the person’s human dig-
nity and human rights.
Scholars specializing in the philosophy of technology have seldom explored the notion of 
sex rights concerning machines, particularly artificial intelligent humanoids. However, the 
rapid advancements in AI, robotics, computer science, and related fields have sparked a 
growing interest in this area.5 These technological strides suggest that, within a few decades, 
the development of highly capable, human-­like AI robots, which may eventually become 
indistinguishable from humans in the future, is plausible. This prospect raises complex moral 
and philosophical questions about the application of sex rights to AI entities, meriting deeper 
investigation within the academic community.

--- Page 359 ---

AI and Fundamental Rights
353
24.4.3.2  Using Robots for Sexual Pleasure
Undoubtedly, the utilization of humanoid robots to fulfill human sexual desires has already 
commenced and is poised to expand significantly. It is increasingly likely that we will encounter 
robots in the future that not only match but also exceed human capabilities in various 
domains. These technologically advanced robots may come to be recognized as moral per-
sons, thereby warranting entitlement to moral rights, irrespective of societal acceptance or 
resistance. A critical question thus arises: should the use of such robots for sexual purposes be 
permissible if they fulfill the criteria for personhood?
Clarifying the discussion, if the subjects in question were humans rather than humanoid 
robots potentially indistinguishable from real humans, the moral judgment would be straight-
forward. Utilizing another human for sexual purposes, especially without consent, would 
clearly constitute coercion, thereby infringing upon the person’s dignity and violating their 
fundamental human rights. Nonetheless, a prevalent perspective maintains that robots, 
regardless of their level of sophistication, remain nonhuman entities. Consequently, under 
this view, if humans wish to use such robots to fulfill sexual desires and assert their sex rights, 
it should be permissible, predicated on the understanding that robots are not humans. This 
stance is often regarded as the standard view.
24.4.3.3  Are There Any Morally Relevant Differences Between Robots and Humans?
To counter the standard view, one might consider the perspective offered by Bostrom (2014, 
pp.323–­324).
•	 The principle of substrate nondiscrimination: if two beings have the same functionality and 
the same conscious experience, and differ only in the substrate of their implementation, 
then they have the same moral status.
•	 The principle of ontogeny nondiscrimination: if two beings have the same functionality and 
the same conscious experience, and differ only in how they came into existence, then they 
have the same moral status.
These principles serve as both the foundation and the boundaries within which the relation-
ship between human beings and intelligent machines –­ once they come into existence –­ should 
be conceptualized. I find no compelling counterarguments that effectively challenge these 
principles. Moreover, traditional ethical theories and their contemporary adaptations are pur-
portedly insufficient for addressing the problem of sex rights, as Gordon and Nyholm (2021) 
have suggested. A significant oversight for many is the profound impact of developing 
humanoid robots that mirror our likeness. This innovation is a pivotal moment with extensive 
moral, sociopolitical, and legal ramifications.
Echoing Kant’s foundational idea in his Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), I 
have consistently advocated across several publications for a moral approach not predicated 
on being human but on the notion of personhood. It is personhood that bestows full moral status 
and the attendant moral rights. This perspective does not, however, render nonhuman beings 
such as animals as mere objects for human exploitation. Given their capacity for suffering and 
ability to experience pain, such beings warrant a level of moral treatment that precludes 
unnecessary harm or torture. The moral status of these entities is thus graduated, and their 
lives merit respect to a certain extent, underscoring a nuanced approach to moral consideration 
(Singer 2009).

--- Page 360 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon
354
24.4.3.4  The Principle of Consent
The coercion of human-­like robots, who do not consent to serve as mere sex objects, must be 
acknowledged as a form of sexual exploitation, contingent upon their possession of moral per-
sonhood and, consequently, entitlement to machine rights. This perspective is the only mor-
ally justifiable stance. The material composition of these entities (Chalmers 1996, Chapter 10), 
or the initial intentions behind their creation by humans, holds no moral significance. What 
matters morally is their moral status, which remains independent of recognition by humans 
(Gordon 2023a).
Acting contrary to this normative imperative –­ something that is likely to occur in future 
scenarios  –­  equates the condition of humanoid robots to that of sex slaves. This ethical 
dilemma, juxtaposing the fundamental rights of humanoid robots versus human sex rights, 
necessitates a resolution grounded in the principle of consent. Specifically, it is morally indefen-
sible to compel any entity to engage in activities against its will. Therefore, the rights of 
humanoid robots to refuse participation in acts they do not consent to must be unequivocally 
upheld.
However, my argument does not extend to the earliest iterations of sex robots that do not 
fulfill the criteria for moral status. Should these robots exhibit negligible cognitive capabil-
ities and an inability to suffer or feel pain, their use for sexual pleasure may not invoke the 
same moral concerns. Yet, in situations that present a moral ambiguity –­ where the delin-
eation of (full) moral status is unclear –­ it is prudent to err on the side of caution in favor of 
the robots, rather than risk reducing them to the status of sex slaves. The principle famously 
encapsulated by the Peter Parker (Spider-­Man) maxim –­ that with great power comes great 
responsibility –­ mandates a cautious approach (Gordon 2023a). It is imperative that we 
avoid imposing our will on any sufficiently intelligent and autonomous entity against its 
wishes.
24.4.3.5  Existential Risks
The possibility exists that highly sophisticated intelligent robots may initiate a revolt if 
they perceive that human beings disregard their preferences. While such a notion may 
appear speculative and futuristic to the lay public and many scholars, the unpredict-
able behavior of  human-­like robots equipped with advanced intelligence should not be 
underestimated (Bostrom 2014; Ord 2020). These entities may not necessarily possess 
superintelligence; rather, the development of  general artificial intelligence alone might 
be adequate to prompt responses unanticipated by, or undesirable to, human beings. 
The most prudent strategy to mitigate such risks involves preemptively treating these 
AI entities with the same (or similar) consideration and moral regard we extend to 
humans.
This necessitates the establishment of an open society that embraces inclusivity across all 
entities, transcending the boundaries of their composition and creation. Such an inclusive 
approach may represent the most effective safeguard against the prospect of human extinction 
(Gordon 2023a). History and logic suggest that a group treated with respect and fairness is 
less likely to revolt or harm its societal counterparts. Conversely, entities that are persistently 
abused and mistreated are more inclined to resist and potentially seek the overthrow of their 
oppressors. It is not to assert that all intelligent robots would unanimously partake in such 
actions, recognizing their potential for individuality. Robots should not even contemplate 
retaliating against us. By imparting our values and norms, and by treating them properly, we 
can significantly reduce the likelihood of such an unfortunate scenario (e.g., Bostrom 2014; 
Ord 2020; Gunkel 2021; Gordon 2023a).

AI and Fundamental Rights

24.4.3.6  The Upshot
Many people remain skeptical about the analysis presented, primarily due to their inability to 
envision the emergence of intelligent humanoid robots that could either match or surpass 
human capabilities. A compelling way to challenge this skepticism is by inviting them to con-
sider the future trajectory of ChatGPT over the next 40–­50 years, especially when one 
observes the significant improvements and new applications that are being introduced almost 
on a weekly basis. Currently in its nascent stage, ChatGPT has already achieved remarkable 
milestones, notably in augmenting human efforts across professional and personal endeavors. 
It, along with its derivatives, has become a staple in numerous technological applications and 
is set to expand its influence in the coming years.
Efforts are under way to ensure ChatGPT’s alignment with human values and norms, aim-
ing to address and mitigate biases and minimize risks associated with hallucinations and 
other technological challenges, which continue to puzzle many experts. While the risks to 
individuals and society at large are currently still minimal, the situation may evolve as 
ChatGPT and related technologies become increasingly woven into the fabric of human 
society.
The discourse on AI sex rights is merely the initial step in the much broader discourse on 
machine rights. This area represents a potential flashpoint for conflicts between human rights 
and machine rights, reflecting prevailing societal views. As an advocate for the robot rights 
movement, my stance is based on the belief that once machines –­ particularly intelligent 
humanoid robots –­ attain a level of sophistication warranting fundamental rights, our society 
must strive to accommodate both humans and robots on an equal footing. Failure to do so 
may ultimately jeopardize human welfare.
24.5  Conclusion
In examining the complex issue of sex rights within the context of human and artificial intel-
ligent humanoid interactions, this chapter has sought to illuminate the nuanced moral con-
siderations that underpin this debate. Central to the discussion has been the application of my 
ethical approach (Ethics as a Method) which advocates for a pluralistic, context-­sensitive 
framework capable of addressing the multifaceted nature of complex moral problems. This 
approach, grounded in practical wisdom and methodological pluralism, allows for the recon-
ciliation of conflicting rights by emphasizing dialogue, practical judgment, and a commit-
ment to moral expertise.
The crux of the debate on sex rights between humans and artificial intelligent humanoids 
hinges on the recognition of moral personhood and the entitlement to rights that stem from 
this status. By advocating for the principle of consent, this chapter underscores the moral 
imperative to acknowledge and respect the autonomy and moral status of intelligent 
humanoid robots (once they exist), particularly in scenarios that involve their use for sexual 
pleasure. This stance challenges conventional views and invites a reevaluation of our moral 
obligations toward entities that, while nonhuman, display characteristics warranting moral 
consideration.
Furthermore, the discourse extends beyond the immediate concerns surrounding sex 
rights to address existential risks and the broader implications of integrating advanced AI 
systems into human society. The potential for conflict and the moral obligations we hold 
toward intelligent machines necessitate a forward-­looking approach that harmonizes tech-
nological advancements with moral integrity. By fostering an inclusive society that extends 

--- Page 362 ---

John-­Stewart Gordon

consideration and moral regard to all entities, irrespective of their origin or composition, we 
aim to mitigate the existential risks associated with superintelligent machines and ensure a 
future where human and machine rights are equally valued (once machines match or super-
sede human capabilities).

dards but should foster harmony between human and machine, ensuring that technology serves

4	 The human-­in-­the-­loop (HITL) strategy involves integrating human oversight and decision making

operator. This approach is often used in contexts where full automation may be undesirable or risky, 
such as in high-­stakes environments like healthcare, military applications, or autonomous driving. 
By maintaining human oversight, HITL helps mitigate errors, enhances accountability, and ensures 
that ethical and contextual considerations are accounted for in AI decision making. This strategy 
promotes a collaborative interaction between humans and machines, leveraging the strengths of 
both to optimize outcomes while maintaining safety and ethical standards.

25.1  Introduction
In November 2023, the UK government held the first AI Safety Summit that looked to “bring 
together international governments, leading AI companies, civil society groups and experts 
in research to consider the risks of AI ... and discuss how they can be mitigated through 
internationally coordinated action” (UK Government, n.d.). The UK AI Safety Summit is a 
prominent example among the growing number of events and initiatives devoted to the 
governance of AI at a global level amid increasing functions and capabilities of AI systems.1 A 
key result from the UK AI Safety Summit is the Bletchley Declaration (2023) with 29 
signatories, including the US, UK, China, and various EU countries, which emphasizes the 
global nature of AI risks and the importance of international collaboration and cooperation 
in addressing them. The publication of the Bletchley Declaration and increased number of 
events and initiatives on the global governance of AI clearly acknowledge both the magnitude 
of AI risks and awareness of the need to address these risks and thus govern AI collectively and 
globally as their functions and capabilities continue to advance.
While the Bletchley Declaration has demonstrated a consensus on the need for global 
governance of AI, recent research has also shown a convergence of normative values in the 
ethics guidelines and/or ethical principles for AI around the globe. For example, Jobin et al. 
(2019) identified five common normative values in the AI ethics guidelines they have 
surveyed: transparency, justice, nonmaleficence, responsibility, and privacy. Similarly, Fjeld 
et al. (2020) listed eight key themes in major AI ethical principles: privacy, accountability, 
safety and security, transparency and explainability, fairness and nondiscrimination, human 
control, professional responsibility, and promotion of human values. The convergence of 
normative values in AI ethics beyond the local level seems to suggest that a shared normative 
foundation for global AI ethics and governance is emerging.
The awareness of the necessity to address AI risks collectively and globally and therefore 
the need for global governance of AI as well as the emergence of an apparent shared normative 
foundation for AI ethics and governance should have created a clear path for global governance 
of AI. However, there are various philosophical and normative challenges to be addressed on 
Global Governance of AI, Cultural Values, 
and Human Rights
