--- Page 366 ---

Pak-­Hang Wong
360
the path to a satisfactory global governance of AI. Here, I shall focus on two philosophical and 
normative challenges owing to cultural values. First, even if there is indeed a convergence of 
normative values in AI ethics and governance, this convergence may not be sufficiently 
informative and efficacious when the normative values are constructed at a very abstract 
level and devoid of local, cultural inputs. Once the local, cultural inputs are taken into 
account, however, we can observe a substantial divergence in the interpretation and 
implementation of these normative values (Jobin et  al.  2019). Second, when there are 
substantial differences in how normative values are interpreted and implemented, imposing 
a specific interpretation and implementation of these normative values on countries without 
respecting their cultural values can lead to the charge of technological imperialism 
(Wong 2016). I will then propose human rights as an appropriate normative basis for global 
governance of AI and discuss whether and how the human rights approaches (HRAs) to AI 
governance can overcome the two challenges.
25.2  Cultural Values and the Two Challenges to Global Governance of AI
Governing AI amounts to the establishment and enforcement of rules, practices, and processes 
for guiding and/or regulating the development and deployment of AI systems to ensure their 
alignment with some predefined normative values and/or with specific social, ethical, and 
political objectives (cf. Mäntymäki et al. 2022).2 Accordingly, global governance of AI is the 
establishment and enforcement of the rules, practices, and processes at the global level. So 
construed, any attempts at global governance of AI must be built on a normative foundation 
that is shared  –­ or at least shareable  –­ across different cultures around the globe, which 
provides the normative ground for the rules, practices, and processes. There must also be 
some means to enforce the shared normative values behind the rules, practices, and processes, 
without which any attempts to govern AI will be ineffective. When we take seriously the 
possible differences in understanding and/or interpreting of normative values by different 
cultures, the requirements for a shared normative foundation and its enforcement generate 
two philosophical and normative challenges.
In his provocatively titled article “The uselessness of AI ethics,” Luke Munn (2023) argues 
that existing AI ethical principles are meaningless3 because they are “highly abstract and 
ambiguous, becoming incoherent” (Munn 2023, p. 870). Recall also Jobin et al.’s (2019) 
observation that there is a substantial divergence in the interpretation and implementation of 
normative values in AI ethics, particularly when the normative values are no longer 
considered at an abstract level. More specifically, they point out that the differences can be 
found in “(1) how ethical principles are interpreted; (2) why they are deemed important; 
(3) what issue, domain or actors they pertain to; and (4) how they should be implemented” 
(Jobin et al. 2019). I contend that one source of the differences in their interpretation and 
implementation, and likewise their ambiguity and thus incoherence, is the differences in 
local culture.
For example, the Indian government attempted to argue that privacy is not a value in the 
Indian value system (Marda and Acharya 2014), and a number of Chinese scholars have 
defended the justifiability and value of state interference in private affairs against the liberal 
view of state interference, where state interference in private affairs is rarely justifiable 
(Song 2018). In effect, earlier research in intercultural information ethics and intercultural 
digital ethics has convincingly demonstrated the interplay among information and digital 
technologies, cultures, and ethical values (Capurro  2005; Nakada and Tamura  2005; 

--- Page 367 ---

Global Governance of AI, Cultural Values, and Human Rights
361
Ess 2020). Researchers in this field have also cautioned against ethical universalism due to its 
propensity for dogmatism and intolerance, and have defended pluralistic approaches for 
assessing the ethical issues of information and digital technologies that account for reasonable 
moralities from different cultures (Ess  2006,  2020; Capurro  2007). The discussion in AI 
ethics and governance should not overlook the insights from intercultural information ethics 
and intercultural digital ethics. In short, normative values in AI ethics and governance should 
be viewed as culturally sensitive, and cultural sensitivity may offer room for “cultural excuses” 
in their interpretation and (non-­)implementation (Wong 2020).4
A key challenge to global governance of AI via the lens of cultural values is to establish a 
normative standard that is both universally respected and culturally adaptable. Minimally, a 
shared normative language is needed in the discussion and resolution of normative issues in 
AI across different cultures. The shared normative language will allow different cultures to 
interpret and implement normative values in AI ethics and governance in ways that are 
culturally grounded and globally coherent.
When differences in the interpretation and implementation of values in AI ethics and 
governance are indeed warranted by cultural differences, for example the different interpretation 
and (non-­)implementation by a state does not violate a minimal set of rights of its community 
members, the imposition of a specific set of normative values (or a specific understanding and/
or way of implementation of those normative values) over the local values (or the local 
understanding of the values) raises imperialistic concerns. The imposition of values on other 
cultures in the context of global governance of AI can be achieved through direct intervention 
or indirect intervention. For instance, more powerful states can use economic and/or political 
sanctions to threaten and penalize states that do not adopt the normative values for AI ethics 
and governance favored by them. It is, however, unclear how direct intervention of this kind can 
be morally justified insofar as it fails to respect –­ or, at least, tolerate –­ diversity in values of 
different cultures, which are of equal worth (Taylor 1992; Rawls 1999).
The imposition of normative values can also be achieved indirectly through 
institutionalization, such as the introduction of global standards (Cihon  2019; Auld 
et al. 2022; cf. Waldby and Slater 2008). Imagine another scenario where access to software, 
hardware, and/or computing resources is only available if the development and deployment 
of an AI system can be shown to align with international standards based on a particular 
view of normative values in AI ethics and governance. In this scenario, developers and 
deployers of AI systems cannot but accept the particular view of normative values if they are 
to develop and/or release their AI systems at a global scale. In other words, those who do not 
accept the international standards, and the related understanding of normative values for AI 
ethics and governance, are excluded from the global network of development and global 
market. I contend that the introduction of standards is an inherently value-­laden project, as 
it designates the normative criteria for inclusion to the global network and market.
A major adverse implication of the introduction of value-­laden international standards for 
AI ethics and governance is the potential delegitimization of AI ethics and governance based 
on local values, especially when the local values are in conflict with dominant accounts of AI 
ethics and governance, as the local values do not enable developers and deployers of AI 
systems to enter the global network and market. Of course, international standards do not 
always have to raise imperialistic concerns. Introduction of international standards does not 
raise imperialistic concerns when the standards and values they are based on are accepted by 
the local developers and deployers, as the standards and related values can no longer be 
viewed as being imposed on them. To do so, however, the creation of the standards must 
include the local values or, at least, sufficiently acknowledge their importance.

--- Page 368 ---

Pak-­Hang Wong
362
The discussion of international standards points to the significance of inclusion of 
local values and the local acceptance of a specific understanding of normative values to 
address the imperialistic concerns. Another key challenge to global governance of AI via 
the lens of cultural values, therefore, can be formulated as the question of legitimacy of 
normative values of AI ethics and governance, i.e., whether and how a specific under-
standing of normative values can be accepted by various cultures that are part of the 
global governance of AI.
25.3  Human Rights Approaches to Global Governance of AI
It is far from obvious that there are clear, conclusive answers to the two challenges regarding 
cultural values outlined in the previous section. In this section, I shall propose the HRAs to AI 
governance as a good candidate for global governance of AI that can respond to the two 
challenges. The HRAs (Access Now 2018; IEEE 2018; Raso et al. 2018; Latonero 2018; AI 
HLEG  2019; ARTICLE 19  2019; McGregor et  al.  2019; Kriebitz and Lütge  2020; Yeung 
et  al.  2020; Prabhakaran et  al.  2022) intend to be a universal and globally enforceable 
framework, and they have made explicit reference to major European and international 
human rights documents, including, for example, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights 
(UDHR), the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the International 
Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) (Access Now  2018; Raso 
et al. 2018; Latonero 2018), the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (GPs) 
(Raso et al. 2018; ARTICLE 19 2019; McGregor et al. 2019), and the European Convention 
on Human Rights (ECHR) (Yeung et al. 2020).
The wide acceptance of the UDHR and related documents and their international 
legitimacy offer an immediate response to the question of legitimacy of normative values of 
AI ethics and governance. Human rights also provide a global normative standard and a 
shared, comprehensible normative language to assess and deliberate on various social, 
ethical, and political implications of AI systems. At the same time, the legal implementation 
of international human rights has “the margin of appreciation,” which allows local 
governments room for discretion, and thus can be viewed as culturally sensitive. So construed, 
the HRAs also have a readily available response to the need for a normative standard that is 
both universally respected and culturally adaptable. Moreover, there are international human 
rights instruments that supply enforceable mechanisms of accountability and redress 
required by genuine governance of AI. Researchers have pointed out that there are well-­
established institutions and organizations at the international and national level to promote 
human rights and to monitor, prevent, and respond to human rights violations which the 
HRAs can utilize in practice (McGregor et al. 2019; Yeung et al. 2020; Jones 2023).
The appeal to human rights in global governance of AI serves three purposes: (1) it offers 
a prima facie shared normative standard to identify, anticipate, and evaluate the harmful (or 
beneficial) impacts of AI, (2) it confers legitimacy on the global governance of AI given the 
wide and international acceptance of human rights documents, and (3) it provides a set of 
legal and institutional measures to prevent, mitigate, and rectify the harm caused by them 
based on existing legal and institutional frameworks. In this way, compared to approaches 
that aim to develop global AI governance through AI ethical principles and/or their 
underlining values, the UDHR and related documents may serve as a more robust universal 
normative standard in the HRAs, which is supposedly applicable and enforceable across 
nations and cultures.

--- Page 369 ---

Global Governance of AI, Cultural Values, and Human Rights
363
25.4  Where are Cultural Values in the Human Rights Approaches 
to AI Governance?
The HRAs purportedly have overcome the two challenges from cultural values through 
universality and (global) legitimacy of the UDHR and related documents, but they have been 
questioned from different fronts. For instance, the idea of human rights has been criticized for 
being inherently “Western” and so it may not be straightforwardly applicable to “non-­
Western” cultures (Panikkar 1982; Bell 1996; Metz 2012). Relatedly, there is a long-­standing 
philosophical debate over the role of culture in the normative justification of human rights 
(Bauer and Bell  1999; Cohen  2004; Angle  2013; Renteln  2013; cf. Chan  2019) and if 
cultures and cultural values are indeed essential to the normative justification of human 
rights, then the HRAs will need to accommodate cultural differences explicitly. There are also 
worries about global power asymmetry in shaping the human rights agenda and practices, 
thereby turning human rights into a tool to serve the interests of power (Gilabert 2018). 
There are also issues with conflicting interpretations of specific human rights and their 
implementation as well as the criteria used to evaluate and settle conflicts between different 
interpretations (Macioce 2016, 2018).
The questions raised above are not decisive against the HRAs as the basis of global 
governance of AI, but they do call for the inclusion of cultural values in their conceptualization 
and application. To resolve disputes over conflicting interpretations of human rights in 
practice, Macioce (2016, 2018) calls for a reference to local values. To counter undue power 
and the misuses of human rights by the power in the global context, Gilabert (2018) defends 
the significance of attentiveness to local differences, human interpretative fallibility as well as 
humility and multiplicity in the interpretation of human rights. Yet it is an open question as 
to how exactly cultural values can be included in the HRAs, and the answer to this question 
depends on the nature of human rights presupposed by the HRAs.
There are two major conceptions of human rights: moral conceptions and political 
conceptions. As Cruft et  al. succinctly summarize, the key disagreement between the two 
conceptions is that, according to moral conceptions of human rights, “[human rights] are 
(1) moral rights that (2) all human beings possess (3) at all times and in all places (4) simply in 
virtue of being human and (5) the corresponding duty bearers are all able people in appropriate 
circumstances” (Cruft et al. 2015, p. 4), whereas the “political conceptions [of human rights] 
argue that human rights are not based on certain features of humanity; rather, the distinctive 
nature of human rights is to be understood in light of their role or function in modern 
international political practice” (Cruft et al. 2015, p. 6). In the following, I shall refer to the 
accounts of human rights by Tasioulas and Rawls to illustrate the differences between the two 
concepts for the HRAs.
25.4.1  Moral Conceptions of Human Rights and Human Rights Approaches 
to AI Governance
John Tasioulas (2012, 2013, 2015) offers one of the most comprehensive moral conceptions of 
human rights. In his pluralist approach to the grounds of human rights, Tasioulas holds that 
“human dignity and universal human interests are equally fundamental grounds of human 
rights, characteristically bound together in their operation” (Tasioulas  2015, pp.  53–­54).5 
Tasioulas defends “the human nature conception of human dignity,” in which the normative 
value of human dignity derives from a variety of capacities and features that constitute the 
species of human beings, and argues that this view of human dignity guarantees an equality of 

--- Page 370 ---

Pak-­Hang Wong
364
basic moral status and a fundamental level of respect among individuals qua human beings 
(2015, pp. 54–­55). Human interests are the things required for or that contribute to human 
well-­being, and, by universal human interests, Tasioulas means human interests that are:
objective, standardized, pluralistic, open-­ended, and holistic in character. By objective, I mean that the 
interests are interests of human beings whether or not they are believed by them to be interests of 
theirs and whether or not they actually desire their fulfilment or would do so were they fully 
informed of certain non-­evaluative facts. Describing them as standardized indicates that in their 
specification one may abstract from some variations among individuals by focusing on the 
standard case of an ordinary human being living in a modern society. [...] There is a plurality of 
interests in play [...]. This means that our basic interests cannot be reduced to some single 
overarching value [...]. What is envisaged is a flexible, many-­faceted approach to the grounding 
of human rights, whereby more than one interest, or combination of interests, grounds the 
existence of any given right. The list of interests is open-­ended rather than definitively established 
once-­and-­for-­all [...]. In coming to understand the nature of universal human interests, we need 
to grasp their holistic character, the way they bear important noninstrumental relations to each 
other, so that an interest’s nature and significance is partly determined by its location within a 
broader web of prudential values. (Tasioulas 2015, pp. 50–­51)
The HRAs based on the moral conceptions will therefore invoke human dignity or universal 
human interests as normative justifications (Latonero  2018; AI HLEG  2019; Yeung 
et al. 2020).
There are various critiques being made against the moral conceptions of human rights, in 
particular a lack of cross-­cultural legitimacy from human dignity and universal human 
interests. For example, Peimin Ni (2014) argues that early Confucians regard the potential to 
become morally excellent as the defining feature of human beings, and thus our inner moral 
potentiality can serve as the foundation of human dignity in Confucianism. He also points 
out that early Confucians believe individuals can lose their moral potentiality through a 
sustained failure to fulfill their moral responsibility. Accordingly, “human dignity [is] an 
achievement, a demand one develops from the world of concrete feelings within, a 
­self-­realization obtained through one’s efforts in ‘establishing’ and ‘promoting’ others” 
(Ni 2014, p. 195).
The Confucian account of human dignity is markedly different from the common account 
of human dignity at work in the moral conceptions, in which being human in itself guarantees 
individuals an equality of basic moral status and a fundamental level of respect. When the 
HRAs are based on the moral conceptions of human rights supported by the common account 
of human dignity, and when this common account of human dignity is not shared by other 
cultural traditions, e.g., Ni’s Confucian account of human dignity, then the HRAs would 
either lack normative justification in cross-­cultural settings, or proponents of the HRAs 
would have to reject alternative understandings of human dignity as untenable. Neither of 
these two options is desirable, however. The first option rejects the HRAs as a genuinely 
universal and globally enforceable framework, whereas the second option, an outright 
dismissal of other moralities without first engaging with them, can only be, as Caney notes, 
“a form of philosophical arrogance” and would leave us “epistemically handicapped” 
(Caney 2000, p. 60).
Similar arguments can be made about universal human interests as well. Recall the Indian 
government’s claim that privacy is not a value in the Indian value system, or the claim that 
Chinese citizens have little expectation and interest in state noninterference in their private 
affairs. Both these claims aim to deny that some human interests are universal and thus they 

--- Page 371 ---

Global Governance of AI, Cultural Values, and Human Rights
365
are not a proper source of normativity for India and China respectively. Here, possible cultural 
variations in human interests call into question universal human interests as the normative 
ground for human rights and thus for HRAs. Indeed, if certain human interests are not shared 
by other cultural traditions, it seems that the HRAs based on those human interests would 
become inapplicable in the cross-­cultural context, or these human interests would have to be 
imposed on other cultures. It is certainly true that Tasioulas’ interpretation of universal 
human interests as being objective, standardized, pluralistic, open-­ended, and holistic is 
useful to mitigate this concern, as his notion does not restrict universal human interests to a 
single set of human interests, nor does it confine them to the actual interests of the people. 
Given the plurality of ideals of well-­being, however, what constitutes universal human interests 
will always remain deeply contested, and therefore universal human interests may fail to offer 
a universal normative basis for the HRAs.
This discussion demonstrates the need to engage with cultural values in constructing the 
normative foundation of the HRAs. Caney (2000) has rightly noted that successful inclusion 
of the values in other cultural traditions can strengthen the legitimacy of human rights by 
ensuring that people who espouse different cultural values assent to human rights through 
their own values. It is also helpful to be reminded that most, if not all, cultural traditions in 
the world are internally diverse and so have within themselves rich normative resources. The 
cross-­cultural applicability of HRAs can therefore be much strengthened by drawing upon 
those normative resources.
For instance, pace Ni, proponents of the HRAs can draw from Irene Bloom’s (1998) 
Confucian account of human dignity, which stresses instead the potentiality to become mor-
ally excellent as shared by all individuals, to defend the normative significance of human 
dignity for human rights and for the HRAs. Or, to return to the two cases mentioned above, 
the Indian government’s claim that privacy is not an interest of people has also been forcefully 
countered by efforts to demonstrate privacy as a fundamental value in classical Hindu law 
(Ashesh and Acharya 2014) and Islamic law (Marda and Acharya 2014). Similarly, recent 
works in Confucian political philosophy have demonstrated the need for a virtuous (Confucian) 
government to restrict itself in interfering with the lives of people in order to allow the people 
to genuinely acquire Confucian virtues through their own acts (Angle 2015; Ying 2021), 
which can be used in defending noninterference of the state as an interest for Chinese citi-
zens. Accordingly, proponents of the HRAs can critique the violation of privacy in the Indian 
context through the Hindu and/or Islamic understanding of the value of privacy, and they 
can also remain critical of state interference in the Chinese context through the view that a 
virtuous (Confucian) government ought to leave enough room for individuals to decide and 
act for themselves. In short, there are rich philosophical and normative resources from other 
cultural traditions, and proponents of the HRAs can improve their normative foundation and 
allow it to be applied legitimately in a cross-­cultural context by engaging with them.
25.4.2  Political Conceptions of Human Rights and Human Rights 
Approaches to AI Governance
There are, however, justified concerns about the moral conceptions of human rights given the 
diversity in cultural values and their incommensurability. The political conceptions of human 
rights are formulated in part as a response to this concern. Instead of grounding human rights 
in some metaphysical or theological views of human nature or human well-­being, political 
conceptions aim to ground human rights by their functions.6 For instance, John Rawls (1999) 
has developed a version of the political conceptions of human rights, and writes that

--- Page 372 ---

Pak-­Hang Wong
366
Human rights are a class of rights that play a special role in a reasonable Law of Peoples: they 
restrict the justifying reasons for war and its conduct, and they specify limits to a regime’s internal 
autonomy. [...]
[...] Human rights set a necessary, though not sufficient, standard for the decency of domestic 
political and social institutions. In doing so they limit admissible domestic law of societies in good 
standing in a reasonably just Society of Peoples (Rawls 1999, pp. 79–­80).7
So construed, human rights serve as a standard for sanction and intervention and for 
membership in good standing in the international community, both of which are essential to 
a well-­functioning international order. The proponents of the HRAs assume the political 
conceptions of human rights when they emphasize the importance of the human rights as 
legally binding commitments to the international community (Raso et al. 2018).
The political conceptions of human rights overcome the justified concerns about the 
diversity of cultural values and their incommensurability by grounding human rights on 
their functions that are independent of specific cultures and would be acceptable to those 
who share the need for a well-­functioning international order, e.g., limiting sovereignty 
and inhibiting the indecent domestic political and social institutions. However, the content 
of human rights that could be derived from the functions of human rights is foreseeably 
minimal, given the disagreements between sovereigns in the international community. 
For example, Rawls’ own list of human rights includes only “freedom from slavery and 
serfdom, liberty (but not equal liberty) of conscience, and security of ethnic groups from 
mass murder and genocide” (1999, p. 79). Accordingly, it seems doubtful whether the 
political conceptions can support the human rights the proponents of the HRAs hope 
to include.
It is, however, where engaging with cultural values becomes essential to the proponents of 
the HRAs based on the political conceptions. As Joshua Cohen (2004) argues, the resulting 
content of human rights can be more than minimal if we identify human rights at the 
juncture of convergence among cultures. He distinguishes between substantive minimalism, 
that requires human rights to be grounded on a set of de facto overlapping values in various 
cultural traditions, and justificatory minimalism that maintains human rights should “be 
independent of particular philosophical or religious theories that might be used to explain 
and justify its content” (2004, p. 193) such that they can be justified and accepted by various 
cultural traditions. Cohen’s justificatory minimalism entails that the proponents of the HRAs 
need to look into the different cultural values if they are to justify a broad(er) range of human 
rights that matches the human rights in UDHR and other human rights documents for the 
HRAs in a cross-­cultural context.
In fact, Cohen’s justificatory minimalism allows proponents of the HRAs to shift the 
burden of defending the global legitimacy of human rights and thus HRAs from themselves 
to those who want to invoke cultural differences to disregard or violate the existing set of 
human rights, in that accepting the existing set of human rights is a condition for member-
ship in good standing in the international community, and so it is the task of local cultures to 
see how their cultural values may align to global human rights, and it is the deviation from 
them that must be justified. Here, justificatory minimalism does not entail that the existing set 
of human rights always trumps cultural values. Instead, it entails that the existing set of 
human rights is the normative default but nonetheless open for reflection and deliberation 
from various cultural perspectives. In other words, the HRAs based on political conceptions 
also need to be open and responsive to justifications for divergence from the existing set of 
human rights and their interpretations in and by other cultures.

--- Page 373 ---

Global Governance of AI, Cultural Values, and Human Rights
367
Alternatively, Chan (2019) has proposed justifying human rights by looking at the positive 
consequences they produce in practice qua international human rights. He illustrates this 
with the example of the right to privacy. According to Chan, privacy is, and should be, 
included as a human right because of its importance to the society and globally and also because 
of the good consequences it provides to individuals with and through privacy-­as-­a-­human-­
right. In other words, insofar as the proponents of the HRAs based on political conceptions 
can demonstrate the positive consequences of human rights –­ both locally and globally –­ in 
question, the HRAs can use them as a part of the global normative standard to govern AI.
Chan’s proposal is particularly useful to the proponents of the HRAs in that consequential 
evaluation allows them to decide and defend what human rights can and should be included in the 
HRAs on the basis of positive consequences, which in turn is important in countering an 
unnecessary proliferation of human rights for global governance of AI. As Chan acknowledges 
that what constitutes good consequence in the consequential evaluation remains open to 
debate, I shall add to his view that cultural values ought to be included in the evaluation. 
Recall the claim made by Caney (2000) that assent from local cultures will strengthen the 
legitimacy and stability of international human rights and therefore facilitate their 
implementation. I contend that the actualization of the good consequences of human rights, 
in whatever way one formulates them, depends significantly on local support. Accordingly, 
engaging with cultural values is important, even if only instrumentally so, to the HRAs 
supported by consequential evaluation.
25.5  Conclusion
Global governance of AI is inherently challenging because of the need to balance universal 
normative standards with the diversity of cultural values. The discussion here has identified 
two challenges via the lens of cultural values: the requirement of a normative standard that 
is both universally respected and culturally adaptable and the question of legitimacy of the 
normative standard (and/or the normative values) for AI ethics and governance at the global 
level. Responding to the two challenges, I have defended the view that the HRAs are uniquely 
positioned to offer a robust basis for global governance of AI when their proponents take 
cultural values seriously and engage with them. More specifically, I have outlined two concep-
tions of human rights which the HRAs can build on, i.e., moral conceptions and political 
conceptions of human rights, and described how they can genuinely include cultural values 
in their approaches.
My arguments for the HRAs as the basis of global governance of AI, of course, are far from 
conclusive, but I contend that human rights do offer a promising path to a shared, globally 
legitimate, and enforceable normative standard. More importantly, the two conceptions of 
human rights do suggest two possible ways to incorporate cultural values into the global 
governance of AI, i.e., through aligning and reinterpreting local values through human 
rights, or through demonstrating the positive consequences of upholding the human rights 
in question to the locals, which is essential to a genuine global governance of AI.
Before ending the discussion, it is useful to recall a radical critique against human rights, 
i.e., that human rights’ alleged universalism and absolutism endow moral superiority to the 
human rights language in its present and dominant form, thereby making human rights 
apolitical and closing off the space of discussion about human rights, and therefore human 
rights can be viewed as a form of political exploitation and an obstacle against oppression and 
reactionary politics (cf. Marneros  2023). Regardless of how this radical critique is to be 

--- Page 374 ---

Pak-­Hang Wong
368
addressed, the critique helpfully foregrounds the importance of reminding ourselves to see 
human rights, including their (re)interpretation and implementation, as open to continuous 
negotiation, which requires us to maintain an open attitude toward the meaning of human 
rights and be attentive to cultural peculiarities when applying human rights across cultures 
(Smuha 2020). It is precisely the openness to interpretation and reinterpretation that allows 
the HRAs to take seriously and engage with other cultural values. To wit, the radical critique 
serves as a crucial reminder that human rights are not the endpoint of discussion and/or an 
absolute normative standard. In short, human rights, as the normative standard for the 
HRAs in the global context, should be viewed as an ongoing process of negotiation and 
(re)construction that is responsive to cultural values.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is considered to be one of the most significant technological 
­breakthroughs in several decades. Looking back at pivotal moments in the history of tech-
nology, like the shift from steam to electricity as the power source in industry, observers ­predict 
that AI technologies are set to boost productivity and create large profits. At the same time, 
there is a worry that AI-­driven automation will displace a large share of the workforce. In the 
medium to long run, this would not only reinforce the ongoing global trend of labor capturing 
a smaller share of total production and undermine the income-­tax centered models for fund-
ing welfare state institutions, but also concentrate economic and political power to a few 
major AI developers (Abbott and Bogenschneider  2018; Acemoglu and Johnson  2023; 
Karabarbounis 2024). Over and above these economic effects, there is an additional concern 
that AI systems may achieve abilities that would threaten the continued dominance –­ or even 
existence –­ of humans.
With stakes like these, it is crucial to ask who controls how AI is developed and deployed, 
and who owns the value it potentially creates. Currently, most powerful AI models, as well as 
the consumer-­facing applications relying on those models, are controlled by a relatively small 
number of companies. Major decisions about what kind of AI to develop are made primarily 
by the boards of these companies, the managers and teams of engineers working in them 
and, in a formal sense, their shareholders. The revenues generated with AI technology go 
back into the companies, and their often wealthy founders and leaders. Call this the private 
ownership model.
Today, it is often assumed that the private ownership model can be sufficiently fair and 
democratic, as long as there is sufficient regulation of –­ and ethical considerations within –­ the 
AI industry. The recently passed European AI Act is designed to protect consumers and citi-
zens from particularly risky applications of AI technology. Surprisingly, many of Silicon 
Valley’s business leaders claim to support efforts for redistributing some of the value the tech-
nology stands to create, including the idea of a Universal Basic Income or even unconditional 
access to computing power (Streitfeld 2024). Still, as long as AI technology remains privately 
owned, citizens can only react to or try to circumscribe significant decisions made in AI com-
panies. Concerns like these reinvigorate long-­standing issues around ownership and control 
Collective Ownership of AI
MARKUS FURENDAL
26

--- Page 379 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
373
over the economic sphere that go back at least to the century-­old debate around markets and 
centralized planning (Adaman and Devine 1996). Given that we are still early in the trajec-
tory of the commercial AI industry, and the economic effects have yet to materialize, we are 
currently at a unique point in time from which we can evaluate the benefits of different ways 
of organizing AI technology, and use governance to promote certain ideals.
This chapter hence explores the prospect of collective ownership of AI. The term is intended 
to capture different ways of changing the ownership structures of AI technology and com-
panies, with the aim of increasing the degree of social control over the technology and the 
value it creates. The aim is, first, to sketch some of the ways in which private ownership and 
control over AI could be complemented by different forms of collective alternatives, and sec-
ond, to explore two sets of arguments for pursuing policies to promote forms of collective 
ownership, having to do with economic equality and justice, and political equality and 
democracy, respectively. The format of the chapter does not allow for a detailed discussion of 
economic theory or philosophical theories of property, and I can only briefly discuss some of 
the many objections that could be made to the positions sketched here. I do not claim that 
collective ownership would solve all the problems associated with the private model, nor that 
it lacks problems of its own. Rather, the goal is simply to provide the first systematic discussion 
of the notion of collective ownership of AI, and prepare the ground for continued debate.
The upshot of the analysis is that, while there are several rationales for criticizing the way 
the private ownership confers profits and power to the owners of AI technology, the solution 
does not necessarily involve abandoning the private model. The case for going further than 
mere regulation of the AI industry and encouraging some form of collective ownership seems 
more compelling, however, if we also consider that AI technology may come to concentrate 
economic and political power to such a degree that it threatens institutions designed to pro-
mote justice and democracy.
The next section introduces the notions of private and collective ownership, discusses who 
controls AI technology today, and presents the analytical framework that guides the rest of 
the chapter. The following two sections discuss justice-­based and democracy-­based rationales 
with the aim of reconstructing the strongest version of each. Section 26.4 discusses some 
objections to the analysis I have presented, and a brief section 26.5 concludes.
26.1  Private and Collective Ownership of AI
In order to explore the notion of collective ownership of AI, we must consider, first, what dis-
tinguishes private and collective ownership models of productive assets, and second, in what 
ways it makes sense to think of AI as something that can be owned to begin with. In a basic 
sense, private ownership means that property rights are held by agents outside the state. 
Conversely, collective ownership could be described as giving these rights to the state or some 
other publicly controlled collective entity. There is a common assumption that ownership 
matters because of the ways in which it confers control; in the traditional Marxist picture, for 
instance, the point of making the means of production collectively owned is to increase public 
control over the economy. Contrast this with a liberal ideal which rather seeks to maintain a 
distinction between the public and private spheres. Appealing to this ideal, liberals could 
oppose collective ownership because they want to prevent political power from exerting too 
much influence over what individuals do in the market.
In practice, however, it is difficult to describe productive assets as fully private or collective, 
since ownership rights are already circumscribed by regulation. For instance, tax laws give 

--- Page 380 ---

MARKUS FURENDAL
374
the state a right to some of the profits generated by property, and health and safety measures 
prevent factory owners from employing workers to use machines in particularly dangerous 
ways. Moreover, the relation between ownership and control is made more complex by the 
fact that ownership can be more or less dispersed. If the state is not democratically controlled, 
then “collective” ownership of the means of production could be abused by a small political 
elite. Similarly, although the ownership over publicly traded business corporations is widely 
dispersed and, in a sense, collective, real control is arguably held not by the shareholders but 
rather the managers and executives who are employed by the firm and act on behalf of the 
owners (Wright 2010, pp.114–­116; Brouwer et al. 2022).
In the broadest sense, AI is clearly not the kind of property about which it makes sense 
to talk of ownership and the associated rights such as use, exclusion, and transfer 
(Becker  1980). It is rather a set of mathematical and statistical methods or ideas, the 
fundamental character of which makes them unsuitable candidates even for intellectual 
property rights. For talk of owning or controlling AI to make sense, it should hence be con-
sidered as having to do with the concrete applications of these methods, or the constructed 
artefacts that rely on them. Although no one can own machine learning, for instance, pat-
ents could be awarded to an individual who develops a particular neural network-­based 
system, or to the agency DARPA when it develops autonomous weapons systems using AI 
technology. Similarly, the large language model GPT-­4 could arguably be considered the 
property of OpenAI and under the current legal framework, they can license the use of the 
model in any way they see fit.1
Consider, next, the current ecosystem of AI. When it comes to the development of so-­called 
foundation AI models and the consumer-­facing applications that they power, there is an over-
whelming dominance from the private sector. In 2023, 108 models were released by industry 
and only 28 by academia. Granted, a majority of foundation models are open-­sourced and 
thus freely available in their entirety. Still, access to the most prominent models –­ including 
models from OpenAI, Google, Amazon, and Anthropic –­ is typically licensed and the under-
lying details of their design are proprietary information owned by the firms that developed 
them (Maslej et al. 2024, p.58).
This degree of dominance from industry has not always been the case, however. Before the 
breakthroughs in the machine learning approach in the mid 2010s, most notable AI models 
were developed in academic institutions (Maslej et al. 2024, p.46). The reason industry has 
pulled ahead is generally attributed to the discovery that scaling up the models in terms of the 
amount of data they are trained on produces ground-­breaking results, albeit in a highly 
resource-­intensive process. This has made training cutting-­edge models incredibly costly and 
necessitated massive capital investments. While Google’s pioneering Transformer model 
released in 2017 is approximated to have cost around 900 dollars to train, the estimated 
training cost of their 2023 flagship model Gemini Ultra is around 190 million dollars. (Maslej 
et al. 2024, p.64) It is not entirely clear just why developing AI technology is so expensive, but 
the standard explanation refers to the price of cloud computing services, which in turn are 
expensive in part because of bottlenecks in the production of the necessary hardware, 
including the chips called GPUs (Clark 2023). One could speculate that there is also significant 
rent-­seeking from the top AI talent, who are in short supply as more and more companies 
compete to hire AI engineers. Since the term “training costs” lacks a precise definition, how-
ever, and since companies keep most of the details around training runs secret, most esti-
mates build on several levels of educated guesses.2
Even if we cannot neatly divide the economy into mutually exclusive categories of private 
and public ownership, it is nevertheless clear that ownership in the current AI ecosystem is 

--- Page 381 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
375
best described as primarily private, since the right to decide how to develop and deploy AI –­ as 
well as the potential profits created by the use of the technology –­ are held primarily by non-
state entities and individuals, largely excluding nonowners from direct control. AI development 
and deployment are primarily financed by private capital, and aim to provide private com-
panies with AI models protected by existing property law.3
A few concrete examples of what a move toward collective forms of ownership could 
entail will help us when evaluating the rationales below. With regard to AI research, 
endeavours like the Manhattan project, the Apollo project and, more recently, Operation 
Warp Speed illustrate that it is not necessarily impossible for publicly funded research efforts 
to overcome the massive training costs described above, if there is political will and align-
ment with other policy goals. The 2023 executive order signed by the Biden administration 
in the US, for instance, created multiple national AI research institutes, and there is growing 
interest in Europe in creating a so-­called “CERN for AI” (Hoos and Irgens 2023; The White 
House  2023). Policies around research funding and economic incentives can also steer 
private research in particular directions. The current patent-­based system for innovation 
could, for instance, be complemented by a collectively funded and democratically controlled 
system of prizes for specific innovations. In such a system, collective decisions would stake 
out the preferred direction of AI development, AI companies would be able to recover their 
investments, but the resulting AI models would be freely available (Erman and 
Furendal 2022, pp.286 f).
With regard to consumer-­facing AI products and the value they create, we could rely on 
schemes like those above to create so-­called public option complements to private AI com-
panies’ products, i.e., AI models that are “government-­provided, quality-­assured and uni-
versally available at a reasonable and fixed price” (Mazzucato and Li 2020, p.1). Going a 
step further, strategies for moving toward collective ownership include setting up economic 
incentives for start-­ups to be organized as worker cooperatives, or to shift the ownership of 
companies to employees through employee stock ownership plans and similar schemes. 
Another method involves collective capital institutions such as sovereign wealth funds or 
pension schemes buying stocks in publicly traded AI companies, or having companies 
offset some of their profits as shares in democratically controlled citizens’ funds. A third 
and much more radical method is to simply nationalize AI-­developing companies, 
much like states have nationalized valuable industries and providers of public goods in 
previous eras.
Note that these are examples meant to illustrate the principled discussion below. It goes 
without saying that all such policies should be carefully evaluated, in terms of their benefits 
and problems, and their legitimacy and political feasibility, before they are possibly pursued. 
Still, the first step in this process involves analyzing the philosophical and political values 
associated with each model. Hence, instead of focusing exclusively on particular proposals 
and their merits, this chapter will engage with the prior task of evaluating the rationales that 
speak in favor of shaping the ownership of AI in one way or the other through political 
decisions.
The rest of this chapter is devoted to discussing four rationales that have to do with either 
the value of justice or the value of democracy. They should not be considered as four steps in 
an argument for collective ownership, but rather as four building blocks that can be modified 
and combined, and further developed into comprehensive arguments. The first rationale is 
primarily backward-­looking, since it has to do with how AI technology is being developed. 
The other three are forward-­looking, since they have to do with the effects AI technology can 
have on society.

--- Page 382 ---

MARKUS FURENDAL
376
26.2  Justice-­based Rationales
A commonly voiced critical observation in the age of generative AI is that, if it were not for the 
data that the models have been trained on, AI models would be nowhere near as powerful as 
they are. These data have, in turn, been generated through an unprecedented monitoring of 
individual behavior through wearable hardware, software apps, and social media. In addition, 
every last nook of the internet has been surveyed by automatic crawlers, who harvest vast 
collections of text, video, audio, images, and music (Metz et  al.  2024; Zuboff  2019). A 
prominent justice-­based argument for some form of collective ownership of AI departs from 
this observation, and says that changes to the private model are necessary to ensure the cre-
ators of these data are fairly compensated.
The first step in evaluating this argument is to distinguish between different forms of data 
production. The claim above seems relatively straightforward in cases where the works of 
particular artists have been used to train AI models without permission or compensation. 
When AI image generators became popular in 2022, for instance, users noticed that they 
often imitated the style of digital artist Greg Rutkowski, who for a long time had uploaded 
high-­quality fantasy images, including extensive descriptions of each work, to the internet. 
This practice made his images particularly suited for scraping and collecting into databases, 
and gave his style an outsized influence over the way certain AI models generated images 
(Heikkilä 2022). Even though AI companies have, in fact, treated everything that is publicly 
available on the internet as if it fell in the domain of “fair use” –­ and several of them are cur-
rently being sued by copyright holders who disagree (Brittain 2024) –­ it seems relatively easy 
to create a licensing scheme where the latter are compensated if their creations are in the 
training set of AI models. The company Adobe, for instance, recently solicited individuals to 
sell short annotated videos of people doing everyday things, such as walking or opening a 
door, to be used when training a text-­to-­video generator (Ford 2024). With a sufficiently 
robust licensing model in place, the problem of fair compensation for intentionally created 
data like these does not seem to require changes in the ownership of AI technology itself, 
although it would most likely change the economic viability of the companies developing 
these models.
It seems much more difficult, however, to design a system that compensates individuals for 
the use of what Shoshana Zuboff has called behavioral surplus data, that is, the by-­products 
from living our lives in digital societies (Zuboff 2019, p.69). Two fundamental problems pre-
vent the licensing solution from being generalized to this case. The first is that data about any 
particular individual are, in fact, practically worthless. Unlike artists who can point to the 
influence their intellectual property has on particular AI models, the value of most of our 
individual data is negligible. Texts, images, and data about your behavior become valuable 
only when they are aggregated into collections of data about large groups of individuals, or a 
sufficiently large corpus for AI models to train on.4 This does not make a licensing scheme 
impossible, but it demonstrates that conceptualizing the value of data as derivative of the 
labor expended in producing them is likely to leave beneficiaries of such a scheme 
disappointed.
The second, and more fundamental, problem is that it seems difficult to set up the necessary 
contracts between individuals and AI developers that a licensing scheme requires. There are 
multiple reasons to question whether end-­user license agreements, for instance, constitute 
complete contracts in the technical sense in which economists use the term (Wong et al. 2024, 
p.6). Most obviously, the data powering current AI models are regulated by contracts signed 
long before either users or companies were familiar with the concept of training data. The 

--- Page 383 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
377
internet forum Stack Overflow, for instance, has collected high-­quality discussions around 
computer programming since 2008, and even profiled itself by banning the use of AI-­
generated text in the answers that users provide to each other’s questions. This made it all the 
more surprising when the company recently struck a deal with major AI developers, selling 
access to their unique corpus of high-­quality text produced by human users. When contribu-
tors complained, Stack Overflow pointed to a clause in its terms of service which declares 
content produced by users to be the property of the company (Dave 2023; Grimm 2024). In 
response, users could reasonably insist that the agreement fails to live up to the clause about 
contractors having complete and perfect information given that many of them agreed to sign-
ing over rights to their answers without knowing that, in the future, this resource could be 
used in this way.
In light of these problems, I suggest that the most reasonable version of the rationale we 
are currently considering does not conceptualize data as individual property, but rather as a 
form of collective resource or “digital commons” (Dulong de Rosnay and Stalder 2020). A 
further benefit of this is that it allows us to recognize that the recent boom in AI capabilities is 
not just a result of training sets building on the work of living artists, but rather the fact that 
AI models consume and repeat all hitherto existing human culture, or at least that which is 
digitized and standardized in datasets. This is true beyond the domain of AI: every current 
generation builds on the intellectual, cultural, and material assets that previous generations 
have passed on. Not even the significant innovations in algorithmic processing which were 
necessary to unlock the value of the digital commons would have been possible without the 
common intellectual inheritance from previous generations. If data are digital commons, 
then the current boom in AI development is in fact a form of primitive accumulation, and the 
value AI creates is due to the fact that private companies are enclosing what was originally 
owned collectively.
Theorists have long argued that, when such enclosing happens, compensatory schemes 
are needed to ensure fairness. At the end of the eighteenth century, for instance, Thomas 
Paine suggested that, since the Earth is a form of common property owned by all humans, the 
privatization of natural resources creates an obligation to compensate those who can no 
longer access them. Specifically, he suggested this should take the form of a capital grant 
awarded to everyone when they turn 21 (Paine 2004; Vallentyne et al. 2005). The preemi-
nent proponent of Universal Basic Income in our age, Philippe van Parijs, has similarly argued 
that the distribution of the opportunity to engage in value-­creating activities such as well-­
remunerated work or the invention of new technologies is neither natural nor necessarily 
fair. In his view, then, “. . . the taxes that fund a basic income are not levies on what was cre-
ated out of nothing by today’s producers, but rather fees to be paid by these producers for the 
privilege of using their personal benefit for what we have collectively received” (Van Parijs and 
Vanderborght 2017, p.107). Proponents of data-­owning democracy and digital socialism 
similarly argue that, because data are valuable and inherently collective in nature, it is not 
enough to simply regulate their use. The most promising way forward is rather to make citi-
zens formal owners of data, in cooperatives, data trusts, or other institutions (Chan et al. 2023; 
Loi et al. 2023; Muldoon 2022).
In summary, the most convincing version of this backward-­looking, justice-­based ratio-
nale for collective ownership says that, since the data on which AI models are trained are a 
form of commons, and since the value created by enclosing the commons should be distrib-
uted fairly, AI-­developing companies should share the benefits created by their technology 
more widely. Compared with the individual-­level licensing scheme considered above, the 
collective approach is more inclusive when it comes to who should be compensated: one’s 

--- Page 384 ---

MARKUS FURENDAL
378
right to compensation is not based on one’s authorship of data that have gone into training 
sets, but rather on the collective ownership of the digital commons. On the other hand, the 
argument only demonstrates why fair compensation is necessary, and not that this requires 
changes to the private ownership model. As we just saw, it might be the case that redistribu-
tive schemes such as a universal capital grant or basic income are enough to satisfy this.
26.2.1  AI as a Threat to Justice-­promoting Institutions
A related but distinct justice-­based rationale is forward-­looking and holds that collective own-
ership is necessary since private ownership either threatens to undermine existing institu-
tions that serve the interest of distributive justice, or prevents the creation of new institutions 
for fair compensation.
Consider, first, in what ways AI technology challenges existing institutions designed to pro-
mote a fair distribution. Today, many countries can be characterized as having more or less 
extensive welfare states, with some degree of taxation, redistribution, and provision of basic 
healthcare, education, public goods, and other resources, supported by the broadly liberal 
egalitarian view that individuals should be able to cooperate as equals under fair terms. One 
worry about AI technology is that automation threatens the viability of the welfare state not 
only by displacing workers –­ creating costs in terms of unemployment benefits –­ but also by 
undermining its funding model in a more fundamental way. Automation can indeed be 
defined as a shift from labor to capital as the factor of production (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2018, 
p.5 f), and neither unemployed workers nor the machines that replace them pay income tax. 
In the long run, economists suggest, automation may hence destabilize taxation schemes and 
macroeconomic models –­ which typically assume that the labor share of income is stable –­ and 
threaten a key source of government revenue needed for existing institutions (Korinek 2020).
The second issue becomes apparent when we ask how we should raise the resources needed 
to fund new redistributive institutions, like a Universal Basic Income. One strategy would be to 
conceptualize the willingness to give up parts of company revenue as a laudable corporate 
social responsibility effort which would not only do good but might also translate into good-
will for the companies, as recently suggested by proponents of the so-­called ‘windfall clause’. 
This proposal would have companies pledge that they will give away a share of their AI-­
boosted profits in the future, which could then be used to fund redistributive efforts (O’Keefe 
et al. 2020). Another strategy is to move away from taxing labor and ramp up taxes on differ-
ent forms of capital, including the physical infrastructure on which AI technology depends, 
and the rents extracted from those who own the data on which AI models are trained. A 
related idea which has received some attention recently is to tax fixed resources, including 
land, much more heavily (Korinek 2020).
How does collective ownership compare to these alternative solutions to AI-­driven auto-
mation’s impact on the welfare state? With regard to nonmandatory strategies like the former, 
I suspect most people are less optimistic about the intentions of key industry actors today 
compared with just a few years ago, in light of the backtracking of the more idealistic visions 
expressed by entities like OpenAI. A windfall clause thus seems bound to remain an empty 
promise. A change in the tax regime seems more promising, however, and could potentially be 
a politically feasible solution to the disruptive effects of automation.
There is nevertheless one important reason to consider forms of collective ownership as 
important complementary strategies, and it has to do with the normative justification of the 
redistributive scheme. Political interventions to redistribute resources often trigger strong 
intuitions that they are a form of expropriation. Many people feel that the income they 

--- Page 385 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
379
­perceive to be theirs should not be given to someone else unless they are presented with a con-
vincing justification, or that the capital they have accumulated should be theirs to invest 
without the disincentive of taxation (Korinek 2020; cf. Murphy and Nagel 2002, who respond 
by questioning that all of our income is ours to begin with). The strategy of funding the wel-
fare state through changes in ownership structures rather than taxation is a possible way to 
circumvent, as opposed to reject, this objection. For instance, instead of having the state tax 
AI companies’ profits, it could create democratically controlled collective capital institutions 
like sovereign wealth funds, pension funds or a citizens’ fund, in which companies are required 
to offset some of their profits as shares (Furendal and O’Neill 2024). A Universal Basic Income 
funded by such a fund would involve seeing citizens not as parasites on the productive AI 
developers, but rather as collecting their dividends as legitimate owners of parts of the 
companies.
Now, which of these strategies is most feasible is clearly an empirical question which 
cannot be settled here. The point, however, is that we should not overlook the potential 
political force of the collective ownership strategy. A new land tax may be an attractive way 
of raising funds efficiently, but there is no logical connection between land value and the 
hardships suffered by displaced workers. A political story that begins with the digital com-
mons analysis reviewed above, however, and then describes those displaced by automation as 
rightful owners who should take part of the value created by the technology that displaced 
them, seems rather attractive. It makes sense to fund redistribution by tapping the produc-
tivity achieved through automation, and it is politically expedient to describe it as legitimate 
profit sharing rather than remedial taxation.
26.3  Democracy-­based Rationales
Let us turn, finally, to discussing two democracy-­based rationales. The first says that collective 
ownership is necessary for the governance of AI to be democratic. The second says that 
collective ownership is a safeguard against private owners of AI technology undermining the 
preconditions for democratic governance more generally.
A key implication of the private ownership model is that most decisions concerning the 
future of AI are restricted to the small group of people working in tech companies, leaving 
nonowners without direct decision-­making authority over the way AI is being built and 
used. Is this a problem? Voters can, after all, influence the shape of AI development 
­indirectly –­ by electing politicians who make laws, supervise and set the boundaries for what 
these companies may do –­ as demonstrated by the recent US executive order on AI and the 
EU AI Act. Voters’ interests are also represented if elected governments publicly fund AI 
research and steer the general direction of AI development. It might also be reassuring that 
many private companies have developed internal ethics guidelines regulating their work on 
AI, and that both employees and managers are concerned about the potential risks of the 
technology (Erman and Furendal 2022; Selling and Strimling 2023). Still, decision makers 
in companies are not authorized by the general electorate, and have not been mandated to 
make significant decisions by the wider public who experience their consequences. On a rea-
sonable understanding of democratic legitimacy, then, it is not sufficient that the interests of 
private AI decision makers and the population align. A more robust process is needed to 
ensure key democratic values like representation and accountability (Erman and 
Furendal 2024). Democratizing AI, then, might very well require changes to the private 
model of ownership.5

--- Page 386 ---

MARKUS FURENDAL
380
This line of reasoning can find additional support from a classic argument for extending 
democratic principles from the political to the economic sphere, which appeals to the two 
being analogous. Robert Dahl, for instance, has argued that “if democracy is justified in gov-
erning the state, then it must also be justified in governing economic enterprises” (Dahl 1985, 
p.111; Frega et al. 2019). The basic democratic intuition that people should have a say about 
decisions that apply to them could be interpreted to mean that indirect control over the 
economic sphere is not enough. The most radical interpretation rather says that, since own-
ership confers control, the full realization of this ideal requires that the wider public become 
actual owners (Buller and Lawrence 2022). Although this is a general point about ownership 
of productive assets, it seems particularly important when it comes to AI development and 
deployment. In a well-­functioning democracy, it could perhaps be realized by creating state-­
run AI enterprises with the mandate of voters to act in their interests. In a country with 
strong civil society actors or democratically run collective capital institutions, granting them 
formal influence by providing a seat on the boards of AI companies could help to promote the 
interest of citizens (Wright 2010, pp.116 f). None of these solutions is perfect but they could 
potentially alleviate some of the democratic concerns around the private ownership model of 
today.
The second democracy-­related argument centers not on how to increase the democratic 
control over AI-­developing companies, but how the decisions of those companies could 
threaten existing democratic institutions. The last few years have seen extensive debate 
around the way AI can be used as a tool to more effectively interfere with elections and under-
mine trust and other key values of well-­functioning democracies (Coeckelbergh 2024). A dis-
tinct concern, however, is that the concentration of economic power in top AI-­developing 
companies like Microsoft, Google, and Meta makes them politically influential actors in their 
own right, which limits the ability of citizens to make collective decisions about how to orga-
nize society. This is a specific instance of a more general problem in democracies, where high 
degrees of wealth concentration enable capital owners to extend their economic power into 
the political sphere (Brouwer et al. 2022).
In some cases, it is relatively easy to recognize the exercise of such power, as when econom-
ically powerful AI companies lobby lawmakers to tailor legislation to suit their interests, 
which typically involves less strict regulation than what other civil society actors prefer, on 
the basis of promoting “innovation” (Perrigo 2023; Tallberg et al. 2024). Other times, how-
ever, less visible kinds of structural constraints created by economically powerful private 
actors make certain collective decisions so difficult or costly that they are pushed off the table. 
The global mobility of capital, for instance, creates a regulatory race to the bottom which 
restricts countries’ ability to set the tax rates citizens prefer. Politicians in economically chal-
lenged areas often go to great lengths to accommodate requests for tax breaks and public 
subsidies from companies promising to create jobs. The economic potential of AI technology 
could very well reinforce the concentration of such structural power, granting whoever owns 
the technology significant sway over decisions that are formally made by democratic institu-
tions (Cohen 1989; Wright 2010, p.83).
Importantly, unlike the problems we have discussed so far, this appears to be a distinct 
challenge which cannot be addressed through simple redistributive mechanisms but rather 
requires changes in ownership structures. That is, to counteract the kind of structural con-
straint on democratic decision making that economically strong AI-­developing companies 
constitute, it is not enough to simply redistribute the value created by AI technology. Neither 
is legislating around the kinds of AI they can develop, since there is a risk that all the regulatory 
efforts discussed as alternatives to changes in ownership structures could be undermined if 

--- Page 387 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
381
AI companies become too powerful. Hence, to institute forms of collective ownership of those 
companies would not only give democratically selected representatives a seat at the table 
where the structurally consequential decisions are made. It could also help approximate the 
democratic ideal, by ensuring that a wider set of goals endorsed by the community would go 
into strategic decisions (Furendal and O’Neill 2024, pp.316–­320).
26.4  Objections and Replies
There is undoubtedly a lot to react to in the discussion above, but two objections seem espe-
cially important to address here. The first rejects the account of property presented in the 
discussion on digital commons. The second argues that any move toward collective owner-
ship is likely to come at a cost in terms of stifling innovation and economic growth.
First, a sceptic could point out that the analogy between the commonly owned Earth and 
the digital commons fails because unlike natural resources, data are nonrival goods; the fact 
that an AI company scrapes the internet does not, in fact, prevent anyone else from doing the 
same. Moreover, on a standard Lockean understanding, the transformation of the digital 
commons to private property is justified by the fact that AI developers mix what they collect 
with their labor (Nozick  1974). Raw data not only have to be cleaned and labeled, but 
significant resources are typically spent on having human workers finetune the way AI 
models treat the data, in a process known as reinforcement learning from human feedback. A 
better metaphor, the sceptic could conclude, would be that data are like a stream of water in 
which AI companies build hydroelectric plants and thereby gain property rights over the 
electricity produced, all the while allowing the water to flow freely for whoever else wants to 
build another power plant.
In response, we could nuance the initial claim to say that the enclosure of the digital com-
mons is happening at a unique point in history, such that it will never again be as easy or 
cheap to extract the value contained in them. The main reason for this is that, as the Stack 
Overflow example illustrates, there is currently an abundance of high-­quality human-­
produced data online. Reports suggest, however, that leading AI companies have already 
incorporated most of these data and indeed reached the end of the data’s potential, forcing 
them to scramble for additional resources. The main alternative is to train AI models on the 
output of other AI models but research indicates that this may lead to “model collapse,” with 
quickly cascading errors (Maslej et al. 2024, pp.52–­55).6
A second reason for believing that the last few years have seen a uniquely cheap and easy 
process of enclosure is that the ecosystem of the internet, in which most of this valuable data 
has been produced, is disrupted by the introduction of generative AI. First, there is a rapid 
increase in the absolute number of AI-­generated websites, synthetic media, and news ser-
vices. If model collapse is a real threat, this part of the internet cannot be used to train new AI 
models. Second, as this undermines existing funding models for news sites and content crea-
tors, the relative share of AI-­generated media increases even further. One reason why LLMs 
can produce excellent text is that they are trained on articles produced by journalists who are 
employed to write excellent texts. If generative AI disrupts the news industry, however, this 
kills the goose that lays the golden eggs. In this sense, even though the digital commons will 
always include high-­quality data from the period up until around 2022, we cannot expect 
them to continue to be enriched by human contributions in the future.
The second objection worth discussing here says that, even though collective ownership 
might be attractive from the point of view of justice and democracy described above, any 

--- Page 388 ---

MARKUS FURENDAL
382
move away from the private ownership model will be costly in terms of other values. Free and 
private enterprise could be said to be a requisite for scientific and economic progress, and 
given the value-­creating potential of AI technology, it is not obvious that we should slow 
down progress (Andreessen 2023).
A first response rejects the key assumption behind the objection, by emphasizing the ways 
in which private research depends on public goods provided through collective effort and 
basic research in publicly funded academic settings (Mazzucato 2014). In addition, even if 
private enterprise is currently pushing the research frontier, and academia struggles to attract 
top AI talent, we can easily imagine scenarios where the roles are the opposite. An interna-
tional AI project of CERN or Apollo project size would arguably be able to compete both in 
money and prestige, not least because we could assume that many AI engineers are motivated 
not merely by receiving the highest possible salary but also by curiosity and the chance to 
push the limits of knowledge. It arguably matters less whether this happens in a private 
company or in a publicly funded and controlled project (Wright 2010, p.63).
A second response would say that the objection relies on the implicit assumption that 
progress and development are good. We need not deny this but could simply note that 
what the optimal pace of technological and economic progress is should arguably be up 
for democratic decisions. It might very well be the case that democratic decision makers 
agree that AI progress should proceed at a rapid pace. A move toward collective ownership 
would ensure, however, that voices that are currently mostly overlooked also have a say in 
these deliberations. Some have raised concerns, for instance, about whether it is wise to 
devote resources and energy to developing AI models in light of other global challenges 
such as climate change. A more nuanced version of this concern says that it is a waste of 
resources to develop multiple cutting-­edge AI models which are roughly as competent, as 
Silicon Valley companies currently do in fierce competition and at great economic and 
ecological costs. In a democratic deliberation, proponents of these views would have a say 
and a chance to influence AI development, just as much as the progress-­friendly voices 
which currently dominate.
26.5  Conclusion
This chapter has explored the somewhat radical proposal that the largely private ownership 
model that characterizes contemporary AI development and deployment creates challenges 
for the ideals of distributive justice and democracy, and that this might lead us to consider 
moving toward forms of collective ownership of AI. There are undoubtedly more reasons that 
are worth considering, but which I have been forced to leave out.7 A more extensive discussion 
would also weigh the goal of promoting democracy and justice against additional values, and 
address a number of well-­rehearsed arguments in favor of the liberal model of maintaining a 
distinction between the public sector and the private economic sphere. The aim has neverthe-
less been to offer a first step in the careful evaluation needed to assess whether we should, 
indeed, move toward more collective ownership of AI.
The next step in such an evaluation also needs to engage in the difficult process of spelling 
out in more detail how collective ownership could work. Depending on which of the ratio-
nales discussed here we think is most convincing and important, different institutional efforts 
to create collective ownership of AI will have different benefits and drawbacks. Consider, for 

--- Page 389 ---

Collective Ownership of AI
383
instance, that although worker cooperatives might promote the interests of employees in the 
AI industry, it would not help those who are displaced by automation. Relatedly, nationalizing 
Silicon Valley’s giants might perhaps empower Americans but would still leave a vast majority 
of the world’s population without any influence, even though the economic ramifications of 
AI automation are likely to be global. Great care and additional thought are thus needed 
when moving from the principled level on which I have focused to the more applied level of 
designing institutional solutions.

27.1  Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a curious sort of thing. On the one hand, these systems are 
designed and manufactured technological artifacts. They are things. And like any of the other 
things that we encounter and use each and every day, they are objects with instrumental 
value. On the other hand, these things are not quite like other things. They seem to have social 
presence, they are able to talk and interact with us, and many are designed to mimic or 
simulate the capabilities and behaviors that are commonly associated with human or animal 
intelligence. AI therefore invites and encourages zoomorphism, anthropomorphism, and 
even personification.
So should AI be classified as a thing, a technological object that we can use and dispose of 
as we decide and see fit? Or is it the case that AI and other seemingly intelligent systems can 
or even should be something like a person, i.e., another subject who would need to be 
recognized as a kind of socially significant other with some claim on us? These questions, 
which have been a staple in science fiction, are no longer a matter of fictional speculation. 
They are science fact and a very real legal and philosophical dilemma.
This chapter investigates the opportunities and challenges of extending to AI the moral 
and legal status of person, and it proceeds in three steps or movements. The first defines the 
concept of person as developed and deployed in both the philosophical and legal literature on 
the subject. The second performs a cost/benefit analysis of extending this concept to AI and 
other seemingly intelligent and/or socially interactive technologies. And the existing literature 
on the subject presents good reasons for, on the one hand, resisting personification of AI, and, 
on the other hand, for applying the category of person to cover these technological innovations. 
The third and final part reviews a number of alternatives that have been proposed to respond 
to and redress this apparent impasse, providing the framework for an alternative classificatory 
scheme that can scale to the opportunities and challenges of the twenty-­first century 
and beyond.
AI Personhood
