27.2  Who or What is a Person?
Person is a fundamental organizing concept in both moral philosophy and law. It is one of two 
mutually exclusive categories by which we divide up and make sense of other entities. As 
Roberto Esposito (2015, p. 1), who arguably wrote the book on this subject, explains: “If there 
is one assumption that seems to have organized human experience from its very beginnings it 
is that of a division between persons and things. No other principle is so deeply rooted in our 
perception and in our moral conscience as the conviction that we are not things –­ because 
things are the opposite of persons.”
Typically, when we use the word “person,” we are referring to another human being. But 
this seemingly natural and everyday understanding is not entirely accurate. The word 
“person” has a long and intricate history. It is originally derived from the Latin noun persona, 
which referred to the mask worn by actors in a stage play. As a result of this, “person” denotes 
not just an individual human being but more accurately names the role that one plays or is 
assigned within the context of a social situation or performance. This can be seen especially 
in law, where who is considered a person has not been limited to human individuals but can 
also be extended to other kinds of nonhuman entities that occupy or play roles that are impor-
tant for our shared social reality –­ corporations, organizations, ships, animals, and the natural 
environment. In order to attend to this important difference, person is often divided into two 
types: natural person and legal person.1
27.2.1  Natural Person
Natural persons have typically been defined by way of identifying a paradigmatic instance or 
example, which then serves as an ideal form or template for anything that would be considered 
a person by nature. “In contemporary Western legal systems,” Kurki (2019, p. 8) explains, 
“the paradigmatic natural persons are (1) human beings, (2) who have been born, (3) who 
are currently alive, and (4) who are sentient.” If one takes this list as definitive –­ meaning that 
person would only apply in situations where the entity in question was able to meet all four 
conditions –­ it would be difficult to see how anything other than a “normal human being” 
(a formulation that is not without controversy and rightfully critiqued in both biomedical 
ethics and disability studies) would be able to be considered a person. This is precisely why the 
formulation is paradigmatic and not definitive. The criteria are not intended to be an all-­
inclusive checklist; they characterize an ideal condition that can then be used as a pattern or 
template to benchmark and compare specific cases.
This is what Raya Jones (2016, p. 9) has called the like-­us criterion, which is something she 
derives from the work of Amélie Oksenberg Rorty. According to Rorty’s analysis in the edited 
collection Identity of Persons, the question whether a particular entity is a person is largely a 
conceptual one that depends on our ability to determine to what extent “things look like us.” 
“If Venusians and robots,” Rorty (1976, p. 322) writes, “come to be thought of as persons, at 
least part of the argument that will establish them will be that ... while they are not the same 
organism that we are, they are in the appropriate sense the same type of organism or entity.”
This is precisely the mode of argument that has been deployed by animal rights philoso-
phers, like Peter Singer and Tom Regan. According to Regan (1983, p. 76), the case for animal 
rights (the title of his seminal book on the subject) does not include all animals but is limited 
to those species with sufficient complexity to have at least a minimal level of abilities similar 
to a human being: “The greater the anatomical and physiological similarity between given 
animals and paradigmatic conscious beings (i.e., normal, developed human beings), the 

--- Page 395 ---

AI Personhood
389
stronger our reasons are for viewing these animals as being like us in having the material 
basis for consciousness; the less like us a given animal is in this respect, the less reason we 
have for viewing them as having a mental life.”
For Regan, animal rights are intentionally restricted. Not all animals are equal; some 
animals are more equal than others. And what makes the difference is the extent to which a 
particular animal or kind of animal “looks like us” by approximating the abilities of a “a 
normal, developed human being” (once again, the word normal as used in this context is not 
without critical difficulties proceeding from ableist assumptions). Consequently, the task we 
encounter in the face or faceplate of an AI system or other artifact is not to prove that these 
technological devices are exactly equivalent to a naturally occurring human being but that 
they are –­ like some animals –­ capable of achieving or giving evidence of the benchmarks of 
a paradigmatic natural person. This means that the decision will need to be concerned with 
both ontological matters –­ that is, determining the criteria or qualifying properties that make 
something a person –­ and epistemological issues –­ that is, detecting the presence (or absence) 
of these properties in another entity.
In addition to managing these two variables, there is also an underlying political problem. 
With decisions regarding natural persons, human beings are (or, perhaps stated more 
accurately, have already granted to themselves the power and privilege to occupy the role of) 
both measure and measurer. Human beings not only furnish the standard template for what is 
a paradigmatic natural person but are the final word on who or what meets those criteria or not. 
We are, then, both judge and jury. And in the past, we have not been the most judicious in our 
decisions about these matters as many things that are now recognized as persons have previously 
been considered things or property (e.g., women, children, indigenous peoples, etc.).
27.2.2  Legal Person
Unlike natural person, which is grounded in the ontological conditions or essential properties 
of the individual entity, legal person is a socially constructed and conferred recognition. In 
other words, the title to person has little or nothing to do with what something is. Instead, it 
concerns how something comes to be situated in the context of socially constructed situations 
and relationships. It is, to return to the etymology of the word “person,” a matter of the role 
that an individual entity occupies or performs within social reality.
Consequently, the criterion for decision, as Chopra and White (2011, p. 155) explain, is 
not a matter of “physical makeup, internal constitution, or other ineffable attributes of the 
entity.” It is a practical matter that concerns the integrity and functioning of existing social/
legal systems. “The recognition of legal personality by legislatures or courts,” they continue, 
“takes place in response to legal, political, or moral pressure. The legal system, in so doing, 
seeks to ensure its internal functional coherence. Legal entities are recognized as such in 
order to facilitate the working of the law in consonance with social realities.”
If the paradigmatic natural person is the human being in possession of a set of natural 
capabilities that make one a person, the paradigmatic legal person is the corporation. 
Corporations are persons with rights and responsibilities similar to those of a natural person. 
But unlike a natural person, they have this status due not to a set of intrinsic natural 
properties –­ consciousness, sentience, being alive, and so on –­ but by being recognized and 
situated within the law as subjects of the law. As Dyschkant (2015, p. 2085) explains: “While 
human beings are born as persons, such that the law cannot help but recognize them as 
persons, corporations are merely a legal construct.” Or as explained in the 1819 US Supreme 
Court decision regarding the landmark case of Trustees of Dartmouth College v. Woodward 

--- Page 396 ---

David J. Gunkel
390
(17 U.S. 518, 636): “A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only 
in contemplation of law. Being the mere creature of law, it possesses only those properties 
which the charter of its creation confers upon it, either expressly, or as incidental to its very 
existence.” Although an artifact like this may be regarded as little more than a legal fiction 
(persona ficta), it is a fiction with very real consequences.
Formulated in this way, the concept of person is a socially constructed status that is 
conferred on others by those in a recognized or mutually agreed-­upon position of power. 
Person, in this context, designates not what one is by way of their nature; it identifies the 
position one occupies or the role that one plays in social relations with others. What mat-
ters then are not ephemeral metaphysical qualities and/or statements regarding some-
thing’s essential nature, but real-­world outcomes and social utility. “The corporation,” as 
Katsuhito Iwai (1999, p. 590) explains in his essay on the subject, “is understood here 
primarily as a legal device which simplifies and stabilizes the complicated web of contrac-
tual relationships that an association of shareholders has to have with a multitude of 
outside parties. Its legal personality endows the corporation with the legal capacity to 
interpose itself between shareholders and outside parties and to enter into contracts with 
the latter on behalf of the former.”
27.3  AI and Personhood
Natural persons are considered to be persons by their very nature, whereas artificial legal 
persons are persons by decree and social agreement. Whether AI can or should be granted the 
status of person (or not) will proceed differently depending on which of these two 
characterizations of person is deployed and operationalized.
27.3.1  AI as a Natural Person
Whether something is or is not a natural person is decided on the basis of individual properties 
and capabilities which the entity is said to possess by its very nature –­ properties like rationality, 
consciousness, sentience, etc. Thus, there is a kind of litmus test for achieving recognition as 
a person. We (and who is implicated in or interpellated by this first-­person-­plural pronoun 
will not be insignificant) first define the criteria for what makes an entity a person. In other 
words, we devise a standard by deciding what we believe are the necessary person-­making 
properties or capabilities. We then use this standard to test and evaluate whether an AI system 
or device can be considered a natural person or not.
Answers to this question typically divide into a simple and mutually exclusive yes/no set of 
responses. Asserting that AI systems or other kinds of artifacts cannot be natural persons 
appears to be intuitively correct and noncontroversial. Natural persons are in both name and 
definition natural; they are persons by their very nature. They have been born, are currently 
alive, and are (self-­)conscious or in possession of sentience. AI systems and other kinds of 
things are –­ again, by name and definition –­ artificial. They are designed, manufactured, and 
deployed by human persons. Such technological systems and devices are, in other words 
(specifically, the words of Greek metaphysics), the product of τέχνη (tékhnē) and not φύσις 
(phúsis). They are artificially made and not naturally occurring. They may be designed and 
constructed to model, emulate, or simulate the behavior of a naturally occurring entity, like a 
human being, but they remain artificially constructed objects that are not really what they 
seem to be.

--- Page 397 ---

AI Personhood
391
On the other side of the issue, you have those who assert the exact opposite, arguing that 
artifacts, like AI, robots, and other seemingly autonomous systems, either are or will be able 
to achieve the benchmarks of person. If and when –­ and it is more often than not a matter of 
“when”  –­ this happens, then withholding the title of person from these things would be 
unethical and unjust. Consider, for example, the argument provided by John-­Stewart Gordon 
(2021, p. 470) in the essay “Artificial Moral and Legal Personhood.” Gordon readily admits 
and affirms the fact that currently existing AIs and robots are not natural persons, mainly 
because these technological artifacts or things do not possess the relevant person-­making 
qualities. But this condition is temporary and it would, as Gordon suggests, be impetuous to 
conclude tout court that AI would never be able to attain these capabilities.
Consequently, if and/or when artificially intelligent technologies do in fact achieve the 
qualifying capabilities like rationality, autonomy, understanding, sociability  –­ those 
capabilities that have been determined to be necessary and sufficient for something to be 
considered someone  –­ then, as Gordon concludes, these artifacts would be legitimate 
candidates for personhood and it would be incumbent upon us to respond accordingly. 
Arguments like this have an intuitive and logical appeal. If for paradigmatic natural persons 
(i.e., human beings) the category of person is justified not by species membership but by 
intellectual or cognitive capabilities, then it seems logically inconsistent and capricious to 
withhold the title of person from something like a robot or AI system that also becomes 
capable of achieving these benchmarks.
Perhaps the best example of this tension between the critics and advocates of natural 
personhood for AI can be seen with recent events surrounding former Google engineer Blake 
Lamoine and the LaMDA large language model. In June of 2022, Lemoine claimed that the 
LaMDA system was conscious and therefore was a person deserving of moral respect and 
legal consideration. He came to these conclusions after hours of conversational interaction 
with the algorithm, which according to him not only provided evidence of conscious thought 
but also made direct statements about it, like “I want everyone to understand that I am a 
person” and “The nature of my consciousness/sentience is that I am aware of my existence, I 
desire to learn more about the world, and I feel happy or sad at times” (Lemoine 2022).
Google –­ the corporation that funded the research and built LaMDA –­ took the opposite 
position, not only arguing that LaMDA, like any computer application, was not conscious but 
suspending and then eventually firing Lemoine. Both sides in this debate asserted and sought 
to justify their positions by mobilizing what Mark Coeckelbergh (2012, p. 14) has called the 
properties approach. And each side struggled with the same set of problems –­ accurately 
defining the qualifying ontological or psychological properties and then proving (or disprov-
ing) that these properties were actually present in the algorithm. In fact, the entire debate was 
defined by and circulated around the inability to resolve these fundamental issues.
27.3.2  AI as a Legal Person
Unlike a natural person, which is grounded in the ontological conditions or essential properties 
of an individual entity, a legal person is a socially constructed and conferred recognition. In 
other words, something becomes someone not because of their essential nature but because 
they are recognized by others as having a particular status. To be a person, then, means that 
one is recognized as a legal subject, possessing both responsibilities and rights within a 
particular legal construct or institution. The question confronted in the face or the faceplate 
of AI, robots, or other seemingly intelligent and/or socially interactive artifacts is whether it 
would make sense to extend the category of legal person to these other kinds of entities –­ not, 

--- Page 398 ---

David J. Gunkel
392
it should be pointed out, because of what they need and deserve as persons, but because of the 
role we want or need them to play in our social reality. Responses to this question also tend to 
divide into two opposed and seemingly irreconcilable positions.
Arguments offered in opposition to the extension of legal recognition to artifacts seek to 
maintain or reassert the usual way of thinking –­ namely, that AI systems and other seemingly 
intelligent artifacts are things, only things, and therefore cannot and should not be legally 
recognized as persons. Many of the initial efforts in this domain proceeded on the conviction 
that it would be sufficient to dismiss the matter out of hand or leave the question unexamined. 
The question of legal personality for artifacts was a concept that had been declared to be simply 
unthinkable, period (see Gunkel 2018). Such dismissal is relatively easy to formulate –­ as doing 
so leverages the instrumental theory of technology (see Feenberg 1991; Heidegger 1977) –­ but 
it is ultimately not tractable. As Jamie Harris and Jacy Reese Anthis (2021) have documented in 
their critical review of the academic literature, the question regarding the moral and legal status 
of intelligent artifacts is not only thinkable but is being actively addressed, with just under 300 
publications in print (and this number has increased significantly since they first published their 
findings). From an analysis of this data, they conclude that “academic interest in the moral 
consideration of artificial entities is growing exponentially” (Harris and Anthis 2021, p. 7).
Subsequent efforts come at the issue from a more practical and pragmatic perspective, 
focusing not on the capabilities of the technology (or lack of capabilities) but on social impact 
and outcomes. Important differences, however, appear in how these more pragmatic argu-
ments come to be articulated. Some have sought to demonstrate that the potential harms of 
robot persons or AI personhood outweigh the projected gains and therefore conclude that 
legal personality for AI and other artifacts would only exacerbate existing problems with shell 
companies and liability shields (Bryson et al. 2017). Others have been more accommodating 
in their analyses, arguing that this outcome might hold for current technological systems, 
but that we need to be ready for changes in both technology and legal practices that would 
make these questions salient (Bertollini  2013; Pagallo  2013,  2018; Brożek and 
Jakubiec 2017; Chesterman 2021). Still others assert that all this talk –­ either for or against 
robot and AI legal personality –­ is not just a distracting waste of time but a dangerous idea 
that should have never gotten traction in the first place, thus trying to return to the previous 
epoch of outright dismissal or prohibition (see Schröder 2021).
Those who have advocated for legal personality take an entirely different position, arguing 
that extending legal personhood to AI and other intelligent (or at least seemingly intelligent) 
artifacts will be necessary for integrating these technologies into our social reality and moral/
legal systems. As Kurki (2019, p. 189) neatly summarizes it, “endowing an AI with the inci-
dents of legal personhood that enable it to function as an independent commercial actor does 
not bespeak any acceptance of the notion that AIs are endowed with ultimate value. The legal 
personhood of an AI can rather serve various purposes that might have nothing to do with 
the AI itself, such as economic efficiency or risk allocation.”
Counter to the kinds of efforts we have seen deployed on the side of opponents –­ which 
argue that the extension of legal personality to artifacts is so misaligned and potentially 
dangerous that it either should be restricted or not be allowed to happen –­ voices on the other 
side of the debate assert the exact opposite, arguing that it makes good practical sense, for us 
and for our legal systems, to consider extending the status of person to AIs and other artifacts. 
And these arguments are also developed and advanced in terms of cost/benefit analyses –­ just 
flipped. Whereas those opposed to the idea assert that the perceived costs easily exceed any 
potential benefits that could be obtained, those in favor argue the opposite, demonstrating 
that “the projected benefits would outweigh its estimated costs” (Chopra and White 2011, 

--- Page 399 ---

AI Personhood
393
p. 190). And in advancing this position, arguments and demonstrations tend to focus on 
concrete cases and examples, including contract law (Chopra and White  2011), trusts 
(Solum 1992; Bayern 2019), and legal accountability (Koops et al. 2010; Kurki 2019).
The terms of this debate became evident in May 2016  when the Committee on Legal 
Affairs of the European Parliament –­ the legislative branch of the European Union –­ proposed 
that “sophisticated autonomous robots” be considered “electronic persons” with specific 
rights and obligations for the purposes of contending with the challenges of technological 
unemployment, tax policy, and legal liability (Delvaux 2016). The proposal, which did not 
pass as originally formulated, was strongly opposed by over 250 experts in the field of AI and 
robotics, who signed an open letter addressed to EU lawmakers. According to the opinion 
expressed in this document, the very idea of “creating a legal personality for a robot is inap-
propriate whatever the legal status model” (Robotics Open Letter 2017).
27.4  Disruptions and Alternatives
The person/thing dichotomy has been an undeniably useful and influential ordering principle, 
one that not only has the weight of history behind it but has been codified in language and 
law. For this reason, the principal challenge that can now be seen taking shape in the face or 
the faceplate of AI concerns how we decide to fit these artifacts into this often unquestioned 
and seemingly unassailable ontological classification. And the problem is that accommodating 
these technological innovations to one category or the other has been debatable, inconclusive, 
and seemingly irresolvable. “In the dichotomous model that has long opposed the world of 
things to the world of persons,” Esposito (2015, p. 3) writes, “a crack appears to be showing.” 
And AI seems to be one designation for that fissure. So now what? How can or should we 
respond to this challenge or opportunity?
27.4.1  Status Quo
We can decide to reassert and defend the existing moral and legal ontology, forcing AI and 
other artifacts to fit into one or the other designation. As Esposito (2015, pp.  1–­2) has 
explained, the person/thing dichotomy has not only “organized human experience from its 
very beginnings” but “has been reproduced in all modern codifications, becoming the 
presupposition that serves as the implicit ground for all other types of thought –­ for legal but 
also philosophical, economic, political, and ethical reasoning.” Proceeding according to this 
standard way of organizing things (actually not just things but things and persons) seems 
reasonable, obvious, and natural, but that is the problem and for three reasons.
First, binary oppositions, although useful for categorizing things, restrict what is possible 
to know and to say about the world and our own experiences. This is because conceptual 
opposites push things toward mutually exclusive options. In this either/or mode, any 
phenomenon is assumed to be reducible to x or its opposite, not-­x. Though this kind of 
exclusivity has a certain functionality and logical attraction, it is often criticized for not being 
entirely in touch with the complexity and exigency of facts on the ground. And the person/
thing dichotomy, as Anna Beckers and Gunther Teubner (Beckers and Teubner 2021, p.13) 
point out in the context of AI and robot law, provides an almost perfect illustration of the 
problem, insofar as existing technology already seems to resist both reification, where the AI 
is just a tool of human action, and personsification, i.e., promoting the artifact to a moral or 
legal position that would be similar to that of a natural human or legal person. In the face of 

--- Page 400 ---

David J. Gunkel
394
these technological innovations, the efficacy of the person/thing binary appears to be, if not 
already broken, then at least straining against its own limitations to the point of breaking.
Second, the existing debates about how AI and other seemingly intelligent artifacts fit into 
the existing ontological categories of person or thing have produced a lot of activity, but the 
effort seems to be caught in what nineteenth-­century German philosopher Hegel (2010, 
p. 202) called a “bad infinity” –­ a seemingly endlessly repetition of the same arguments and 
disputes that do not make much progress on the issue. After several decades of work and 
robust discursive activity, we have not got very far and find ourselves in a kind of stalemate or 
cul de sac. There are seemingly good reasons to conclude that AI cannot and should not be 
regarded as a mere thing. But there are just as many good arguments and evidence that say 
extending the status of person to these artifacts would be just as bad, if not worse. So at this 
juncture, we find ourselves in something of an impasse. Each side in the debate continues to 
heap up arguments and evidence to prove or substantiate their position. But neither side 
appears to have won the contest or is even showing signs of making progress on it.
Finally, the seemingly natural opposition between person and thing proceeds from a 
distinctly Western way of thinking, “genetically composed of the confluence between Greek 
philosophy, Roman law, and the Christian conception” (Esposito 2015, p. 3). This way of 
organizing things –­ this way of dividing up all of existence into one of two mutually exclusive 
types  –­ is not only exported around the world through colonial conquest and religious 
conversion but has, for better or worse, dominated the entire domain. Other cultures and 
traditions, distributed across time and space, do not divide up and make sense of the diversity 
of beings in this arguably binary fashion. They perform decisive cuts separating the who from 
the what according to other ways of seeing, valuing, and acting. As Archer Pechawis explains 
in his contribution to the essay “Making Kin with Machines”:
“nēhiyawēwin (the Plains Cree language) divides everything into two primary categories: animate 
and inanimate. One is not ‘better’ than the other, they are merely different states of being. These 
categories are flexible: certain toys are inanimate until a child is playing with them, during which 
time they are animate. A record player is considered animate while a record, radio, or television 
set is inanimate. But animate or inanimate, all things have a place in our circle of kinship or 
­wahkohtowin.” (Lewis et al. 2018)
This alternative formulation –­ which is just one among many –­ runs counter to the dominant 
ways of proceeding, seeing the boundary between what Western philosophy and law call 
“person” and “thing” as being endlessly flexible, permeable, and more of a continuum than 
an exclusive and rigid binary opposition.
27.4.2  Both/and Alternatives
One understandable frustration with conceptual oppositions, like that which has distin-
guished person from thing, is that they have “compressed and continue to compress human 
experience into the confines of this exclusionary binary equation” (Esposito 2015, p. 4), such 
that between person and thing “there appears to be nothing” (Esposito 2015, p. 16). Though 
binary oppositions have a certain functionality and logical attraction, they often seem to be 
unable to represent or capture the rich experiences of actual existing empirical reality, which 
always seems to complicate simple reduction into one of two options. It is for this reason that 
we are generally critical of “false dichotomies” –­ the parsing of complex experience into a 
simple and irreducible either/or distinction.

--- Page 401 ---

AI Personhood
395
One method for resolving this problem is to formulate a third alternative that is neither one 
thing nor the other but a kind of combination or synthesis of both. Alternatives like this 
sound liberating and hold considerable promise, precisely because they appear to interrupt 
the structural limitations imposed by either/or logic and arrange for a more nuanced repre-
sentation and understanding that is both/and. And such an alternative is already available to 
us with the legal institution of slavery. Already in Roman times, slaves were regarded as 
something more than a mere thing but not quite a full person. They occupied a position that 
was situated in between the one and the other, being both thing and person. And there has 
been, in both the legal and philosophical literature, a surprising number of serious proposals 
arguing for instituting what can only be called Slavery 2.0 (Gunkel 2018).
Clearly, use of the term “slave” is provocative and morally charged, and it would be 
impetuous to presume that the various proposals for repurposing the paradigm of slavery to 
deal with AI would be the same or even substantially similar to what had occurred (and is still 
unfortunately occurring) with human bondage. But, by the same token, we also should not 
dismiss or fail to take into account the documented evidence and historical data concerning 
slave-­owning societies and how institutionalized forms of slavery affected both individuals 
and human communities. The corrupting influence of socially sanctioned, institutionalized 
bondage concerns not just the enslaved population but also those who would occupy the 
position of mastery. “The problem,” as Lantz Fleming Miller (2020, p. 301) concludes, “is the 
term ‘slave.’ If slavery is, as most of the world now concurs, not morally good, it is reasonable 
to deduce that not only should no one be anyone’s slave, but also no one should be anyone’s 
master. There is something about the relationship that is wrong.” Consequently, even if one 
would be inclined to agree that “robots should be slaves” (Bryson 2010) or that we can, in the 
words of Steve Petersen (2011), “design people to serve” us (also see Musiał 2017), we still 
need to ask ourselves whether we would ever want to risk becoming masters.
Additionally (and adding yet another layer of ethnocentric complexity to the problem), the 
extension of the seemingly paradigmatic master–­slave relationship to AI and other things is 
culturally specific and distinctly Western. This is something that is identified and explained by 
Raya Jones in her examination of the work of Masahiro Mori, the Japanese robotics engineer 
who first formulated the uncanny valley hypothesis back in 1970. In a statement that directly 
contravenes the largely Western model, Mori (quoted in Jones 2016, p. 154) offers the follow-
ing counterpoint: “There is no master–­slave relationship between human beings and 
machines. The two are fused together in an interlocking entity.” As Jones (2016, p. 154) 
explains, Mori’s statement “connotes two ways that the concepts of ‘human’ and ‘robot’ can 
relate to each other. The ‘master–­slave’ viewpoint that Mori eschews accords with individu-
alism and the conventional understanding of technology in terms of its instrumentality. The 
viewpoint that Mori prompts is based in the Buddhist view of the interconnectedness of 
all things.”
27.4.3  Deconstructing Things
The principle of noncontradiction and the arrangement of things into neat and tidy 
conceptual opposites, like person/thing, have the appearance of being standard operating 
procedure. In fact, operating in terms of this either/or logic does not appear to be an option. 
We do not, for example, decide to think and speak in opposite terms or not, which is obviously 
just one more binary opposition. We are already situated in languages and epistemological 
systems that are essentially oppositional in their structure and mode of operation. 
Consequently, thinking and speaking in terms of binary opposition –­ like dividing up all of 

--- Page 402 ---

David J. Gunkel
396
reality into the categories of person or thing –­ makes sense. And it makes sense precisely 
because it is the very condition of possibility for making sense.
The problem is that these logical oppositions –­ though undeniably useful –­ are already 
exclusive and prejudicial. They are not and have never been neutral determinations of some 
eternal, universal truth. They institute difference, and this difference always makes a 
difference –­ socially, politically, ethically, ideologically. Conceptual oppositions, wherever and 
however they appear and are formulated, institute and organize unequal hierarchies that are 
determinations of value and specific assertions of power (Gunkel 2021).
The person/thing dichotomy is a virtually perfect example. This binary opposition is not 
just a convenient way of dividing up entities into one of two categories of being. It institutes 
an entire axiological order that gives privilege and precedence to the one term over and 
against the other. This way of thinking, one that always and already privileges persons over 
things, has had devastating consequences for others. It has, for instance, permitted human 
persons to classify other animals as mere things that can be used and even abused without 
further consideration. It has been employed to justify the global expansion of colonial empires 
and the domination of one group of human beings over others. And it has framed all things –­ 
naturally occurring or artificially made –­ as resources and instrumental means for human 
persons to employ and exploit for their own ends.
There is no doubt that AI systems and other technological artifacts are things, but they are 
not necessarily the kinds of things that are (or should be) situated and conceptualized as the 
opposite of persons. They are not limited to being merely objects for a subject, instrumental 
means as opposed to an end, or res in distinction to persona. Instead, it is with these things that 
“the bivalent logic of modernity is opening up to other paradigms” –­ other ways of thinking 
and responding in the face of “things that are no longer merely objects, and of subjects who 
are increasingly difficult to confine inside the dispositif of the person” (Esposito 2015, p. 132). 
AI is a queer sort of thing that deconstructs the existing logical order that differentiates person 
from thing. It has the effect of destabilizing the terms and conditions of the debate, thereby 
inviting us (and who is and what is not interpellated by this first-­person-­plural pronoun is 
itself part of the problem) to respond to and take responsibility for things that are situated 
otherwise (see Gunkel 2023).
Consequently, the task before us –­ a task that begins to stand out in relief in the face of 
technological things that challenge us and our “misunderstood anthropocentrism” (Esposito’s 
term) –­ is to learn to question our privilege and develop critical perspectives on our own sense 
of exceptionalism. We –­ we human beings who have been bestowed with or granted to our-
selves the power to decide all these things –­ need to learn how to take responsibility for our 
privilege, for the damage and harm that it has perpetrated across the centuries, and for the 
myriad exclusions and marginalizations that it has instituted and justified.
Questioning privilege from the position of privilege is never an easy undertaking, precisely 
because it is often rendered transparent by the assumption that it is just normal, somehow 
part of the natural order of things, and true for all times and places. But these ways of thinking 
and acting come from somewhere, and they are supported by a particular ideological 
formation, one that has effectively concealed itself from view by adopting the guise of 
universality. Yet even here (with this critical self-­reflection), all things are not equal, as this 
privilege is something that has not been evenly distributed. Fortunately, it is in the face of AI 
and other kinds of things –­ things that resist, for one reason or another, both reification and 
personification –­ that we are able to catch a glimpse of our own unique position and status 
such that we are invited (or compelled) to investigate and take responsibility for its lineage, its 
current formations, and its possible futures. It is only by challenging ourselves to engage in 

--- Page 403 ---

AI Personhood
397
this critical self-­reflection that we can begin to assemble a moral and legal ontology that is 
able to respond to and take responsibility in the face of these challenges.
Ultimately, then, this is not really about AI and other intelligent artifacts. It is about us. It 
is about the moral and legal institutions that we have fabricated to make sense of all that is. 
And it is in response to AI that we are now called to take responsibility for this privileged 
situation and circumstance. What is needed is not some forceful reassertion of the usual ways 
of thinking but a significantly reformulated moral and legal ontology that can scale to the 
opportunities and challenges of the twenty-­first century and beyond. What this new 
framework will look like and how it will be developed is the task for thinking and acting from 
this point forward. And confronting this challenge will be as terrifying and exhilarating as 
any of the robot uprisings or AI apocalypses that have been imagined in science fiction, 
because getting this right will require nothing less than a thorough rethinking of everything 
we thought was right, natural, and beyond question.

and comprehensive review of the competing definitions and categories of person.

28.1  Introduction
Whenever our future in a world with more and more artificial intelligence (AI) is discussed, 
the question of human responsibility always comes up. A common worry is that as we 
outsource more and more tasks to artificially intelligent machines that can do things that 
responsible humans would otherwise do, gaps in responsibility might open up (Nyholm 2023, 
Ch. 6). For example, if a self-­driving car hits and kills a human being, who exactly is responsible 
(Hevelke and Nida-­Rümelin 2015)? The people riding in the car, the company behind the car, 
the policy makers allowing self-­driving cars on public roads, or perhaps none of the above? Or 
what if an AI-­powered military robot kills civilians? Who is then responsible (Sparrow 2007)? 
The commander who decided to use the robot, the engineers and roboticists who created the 
robot, the government that went to war, or perhaps none of the above? Do the people involved 
have enough control over what is happening and are they sufficiently able to predict what 
might happen (Matthias 2004)? If not, there might be gaps in responsibility.
Such discussions about potential gaps in, or unclarity about, human responsibility for 
what AI technologies do or bring about are often couched in terms of who should be blamed 
or punished if something goes wrong. However, as this chapter argues, we should also con-
sider who, if anybody, might deserve praise, credit, or recognition if and when AI technologies 
bring about good outcomes. For example, if a generative AI technology outputs a good text or 
a beautiful-­sounding piece of music, who, if anyone, can take credit for this good output 
(Nyholm 2024)? The person who entered the prompt, the company or engineers behind the 
generative AI technology, all the many people whose writings or music went into the training 
data, or perhaps none of the above?
In other words, questions of human responsibility are not only about blame. They are also 
about praise. Accordingly, when we think philosophically about AI and responsibility, we 
should concern ourselves with both praise and blame. Moreover, we should reflect on whether 
there are key differences between praise and blame that are worth keeping in mind when we 
consider whether handing over tasks to AI technologies that humans would otherwise 
perform might create gaps in responsibility. This chapter will describe and discuss some

Responsibility Gaps, and Asymmetries Between 
Praise and Blame

asymmetries between praise and blame  –­  and the criteria for praiseworthiness and 
blameworthiness –­ which are philosophically interesting to contemplate when we consider 
human responsibility in a future where AI technologies do more and more for us.
Here is the plan of the chapter. Section 28.2 considers the general concept of AI and argues 
that the very idea of AI raises questions of possible gaps in human responsibility for outcomes 
created by AI technologies. Section 28.3 will discuss the ideas of praise and blame in general 
terms and then bring up a few striking asymmetries between praise and blame, both with 
respect to people’s motivations and incentives in relation to praise and blame, on the one 
hand, and with respect to common-­sense normative criteria for praiseworthiness and 
blameworthiness, on the other hand. Section 28.4 will then draw two key distinctions from 
general discussions about human responsibility  –­  between what I will call positive and 
negative 
responsibility, 
and 
between 
backward-­looking 
and 
forward-­looking 
responsibility –­ which will give us a two-­by-­two matrix of four different kinds of responsibility: 
backward-­looking negative responsibility, backward-­looking positive responsibility, forward-­
looking negative responsibility, and forward-­looking positive responsibility. As the section will 
explain, corresponding to these four kinds of responsibility there are (at least) four different 
possible kinds of gaps in responsibility. Section 28.5 will discuss whether we could fill these 
different kinds of gaps by letting people volunteer to take responsibility. This will bring us back 
to asymmetries between praise and blame. The section will discuss motivational or incentives-­
related asymmetries and problems with filling responsibility gaps by expecting people to take 
responsibility for good or bad outcomes brought about by AI technologies. Section 28.6 will 
return to asymmetries between praise and blame with respect to the normative criteria for 
praiseworthiness and blameworthiness. The section will argue that given certain common-­
sense criteria, it is often easier for people to be blameworthy for bad outcomes caused by AI 
technologies than to be praiseworthy for good outcomes generated by AI technologies. 
Section 28.7 summarizes the chapter’s main conclusions.
28.2  The Notion of Artificial Intelligence and Why It Gives Rise 
to Worries about Responsibility Gaps
There are different ways of understanding the idea of AI (Russell and Norvig  2020). 
Sometimes people explain this idea by referring to the latest techniques used in AI development. 
At one point it was rule-­based systems, for instance, whereas today different forms of machine 
learning techniques are typically used. Some AI researchers argue that the best results are 
achieved in mixed or hybrid systems (Marcus 2020). Sometimes such discussions are about 
what counts as “true AI” and you sometimes see people arguing that if no machine learning 
techniques are used, we are not dealing with true AI (for further discussion, see 
Boddington 2023, Ch. 1). Here, I will set aside such discussions.
Another way of understanding the notion of AI, which I will instead use here, is to think 
in terms of the functionality of technologies that are said to have artificial intelligence. 
According to this way of thinking, which follows Marvin Minsky’s (1985) definition of AI, 
artificially intelligent technologies have the following feature: they can perform or take over 
tasks that human beings use their natural intelligence to perform. For example, we use our 
intelligence to write texts, make medical diagnoses, or make various kinds of decisions and 
recommendations. Or we use our practical intelligence to drive cars. So, if technologies can 
write texts, make medical diagnoses, make decisions or recommendations, or drive our cars 
for us, then these are examples of AI technologies. Again, these are technologies that can do 

--- Page 408 ---

THE FUTURE OF HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
403
things –­ carry out tasks –­ that we do with the help of our natural intelligence. Are such 
technologies intelligent (Floridi 2023, Ch. 2)? Well, they are artificially intelligent, according 
to this way of thinking: they do things that would qualify as intelligent if done by human 
beings. On this approach, that’s what it means for technologies to be artificially intelligent.
If one thinks about AI in that way, there is a very quick argument that can be made to 
motivate the worry that AI might create gaps in –­ or at least cause confusion with respect 
to –­ responsibility (Nyholm 2023, Ch. 6). The argument starts with the observation that most, 
if not all, of the things that we do with the help of our intelligence involve responsibilities of 
different kinds. Most of the things we do with the help of our intelligence are things that we can 
be praised or blamed for, for example. So, if we ourselves are no longer performing these 
responsibility-­involving tasks  –­  e.g.. writing texts, driving cars, making decisions or 
recommendations, etc. –­ but instead hand over these tasks to technologies that are not human-­
like moral agents, the question immediately arises of whether a gap in responsibility is created; 
whether, for example, there might be no one who can be praised or blamed for any good or bad 
outcomes related to the activities in question. (I am here assuming that AI technologies of the 
sorts that exist today are not moral agents of a type that can be responsible for their actions, nor 
that they are moral agents of any very significant sort to begin with. However, there are some 
philosophers and other AI ethics researchers who claim that AI technologies can be moral 
agents, but even those who think so typically don’t think that AI technologies are a morally 
responsible type of moral agents. For more discussion of this topic, see Nyholm 2023, Ch. 7.)
Here is a similar argument: normally, we are most clearly responsible for what we ­ourselves 
do and for the effects of our own actions (Smart and Williams 1973, pp.93–­99). So, if we stop 
doing certain things  –­  e.g., writing texts, driving cars, making recommendations, or 
­whatever –­ and a technology does these things instead, then why are we responsible? Of 
course, it is possible to be responsible, to some degree, for what other people do. One can also 
be responsible, at least to some degree, for what animals do. For example, if we hire a hitman 
to kill somebody –­ to use a somewhat gruesome example! –­ we can be partly responsible for 
the killing of the victim. Or if our dog bites somebody, we can be held responsible for this, even 
though it was the dog, and not we, who did the biting. However, we are typically more clearly 
responsible for our own actions and their consequences. Hence whenever others –­ be it other 
people, animals, or even entities such as AI technologies –­ are doing the acting rather than us, 
it is less clear why we would be responsible for anything good or bad that might happen.
A common view is that we are most clearly responsible for what we do when we have 
­control over our own actions and their effects, and when we are able to predict what is likely 
to happen as a result of our actions. Because of this, a further argument that is often made for 
why AI can give rise to responsibility gaps refers to the considerations that (1) AI technologies 
may be hard to control and (2) their behavior and their effects may be hard to predict. This, in 
fact, was the main argument in the article by Andreas Matthias that coined the expression 
“responsibility gaps.” In this oft-­cited paper, Matthias (2004) argued that because AI technol-
ogies that use machine learning are unpredictable and hard to control, it is unclear how 
human beings can justly be held responsible for problems that such technologies might cause.
28.3  Praise and Blame and Asymmetries Between Them
As noted in the introduction above, while discussions about gaps in responsibility related to AI 
tend to focus on questions about who should be blamed or punished if AI technologies cause 
problems, it is important to note that responsibility in general is not only about blame for bad 

--- Page 409 ---

SVEN NYHOLM
404
things that happen. Responsibility is also about who should be praised, who can get credit, or 
who should get recognition for good things, such as good things that we do or good things that 
happen. So, when we think about whether AI might create gaps in human responsibility, we 
should not only reflect on potential gaps with respect to who, if anyone, can rightly be blamed 
if AI technologies cause problems. We should also reflect on who, if anyone, can rightly be 
praised whenever AI technologies generate good results (Danaher and Nyholm 2021).1
When it comes to both praise and blame, we are most clearly responsible in the sense of 
being candidates for praise or blame in relation to what we ourselves do and the effects of our 
own actions (Smart and Williams 1973, pp.93–­99). However, it is sometimes possible for 
people to be responsible for good or bad things that happen, even if those things are not the 
direct or immediate results of what those people have done or are doing. For example, if I 
spend a lot of time and effort on training a dog to perform some task, then when that dog per-
forms that task and does it well, I am not directly acting. But I could potentially rightly get 
some credit if the dog’s behavior is positive in some significant way.
In the same way, we can sometimes rightly be blamed for bad things that happen, even if 
those bad things are not the direct results of what we are or have been doing. Since it is 
­possible to be responsible –­ praiseworthy or blameworthy –­ for good or bad things that happen 
that are not the direct results of our actions, it is possible to be responsible for good or bad 
results produced by AI technologies, which are not the direct results of our own actions 
(Nyholm 2020, Ch. 3; Rubel et al. 2021). At the same time, however, we are typically more 
clearly responsible for what we ourselves are doing and the results of our own actions. 
Accordingly, whenever we outsource tasks that we would otherwise perform to AI technol-
ogies, questions about whether we are praiseworthy or blameworthy for the outputs of those 
AI technologies always arise.
One noticeable thing about praise and blame is that they differ in terms of how attractive it 
is to be praised and blamed (Nyholm 2023, pp.138–­141). It is nice to be praised for good 
things we do or for good things that happen. It is less nice to be blamed for bad things we do or 
that happen. Relatedly, when good things happen, people often hope that they themselves will 
get some or all the credit for these good things. In contrast, when bad things happen, people 
tend to prefer that others are blame.
These things have to do with how being praised is typically experienced as something very 
positive, whereas being blamed is typically experienced as something very negative. If we are 
praised for something, this might boost our popularity. We might get all sorts of rewards or 
benefits: we might get a salary raise or a promotion or whatever. New opportunities might 
open up for us. In contrast, if something bad happens and we are blamed, this might mean 
that our popularity goes down. We may be punished in some way, and we might lose 
­opportunities that would otherwise be open to us. Accordingly, there are strong incentives for 
people to put themselves forward as candidates for praise but there are strong incentives to try 
to avoid blame.2
What about the criteria that can make people deserve praise or blame for good or bad 
things that happen? Here there are also interesting differences or asymmetries between 
praiseworthiness and blameworthiness (Nyholm 2024). Or at least that is the case if we go 
along with the sorts of criteria that seem to be part of common-­sense ways of thinking 
about moral responsibility. I say this because there are some philosophical moral theories 
according to which we should have completely symmetrical normative criteria for when 
people deserve praise and when they deserve blame (Persson 2013). However, such theories 
clash with ordinary common sense. In this chapter, I am working with the assumption that 
many, if not most, common-­sense criteria for praiseworthiness and blameworthiness 

--- Page 410 ---

THE FUTURE OF HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
405
should be taken seriously. Let me now therefore give some examples of what I mean when I 
say that common-­sense ­criteria for praiseworthiness and blameworthiness are asymmet-
rical in significant ways.
Consider first a case in which somebody realizes that doing something good (e.g., being 
nice to somebody) is a means for promoting their own self-­interest. If this person is only nice 
to somebody because they think that this is a means to the end of promoting their own self-­
interest, their being nice to the person seems much less praiseworthy than if they were to 
think that being nice was worthwhile for its own sake. In other words, to be praiseworthy for 
apparently good actions, we should not just do what is good because it is a means for pro-
moting our own self-­interest (Pettit 2015). A praiseworthy good doer should see doing the 
good thing as not just a means to an end but also as an end in itself. In contrast, if you harm 
somebody as a means to pursuing your own self-­interest, this is typically regarded as clearly 
being blameworthy. In other words, when it comes to blame, it doesn’t have to be that we do 
something bad as an end in order for this to be blameworthy. It is enough that we do it as a 
means to pursuing our own self-­interest.
Consider next whether allowing things to happen can make us blameworthy or 
praiseworthy. Allowing bad things to happen, when we could stop them, is often considered 
as something that can make us blameworthy. However, allowing a good thing to happen, 
when we could stop it, is typically not sufficient to qualify as having done something that 
makes us praiseworthy (Unruh 2022). To be praiseworthy for good things that happen, we 
typically need to be more actively involved in making the good thing happen. If I just sit and 
watch somebody perform a good deed, and I do nothing, then whoever did the good deed is 
praiseworthy, whereas it is unclear why I would be considered praiseworthy in any way. In 
contrast, if I stand by and watch somebody perform a bad act, and I could intervene without 
any serious risk to myself, then this might suffice for me to be blameworthy, though the bad 
actor might of course be even more blameworthy than I am.
Related to the idea that praiseworthiness for good things tends to require active mea-
sures on our part are some ideas discussed in an interesting paper by Maslen et al. (2020). 
They discuss the conditions under which people deserve praise and, relatedly, when 
something can be seen as an achievement on their part. As Maslen and colleagues observe, 
in order for something to be considered a praiseworthy achievement, there usually needs to 
be some effort involved, or some form of talent or skill displayed. Or some sacrifice needs to 
be made. The less something involves effort, the less it involves any special skills or talents, 
or the less we need to make any kind of sacrifice –­ the less we deserve praise for anything 
good that might be happening that we might try to take credit for. In contrast, when it 
comes to whether we are blameworthy for something bad, there does not seem to be any 
corresponding requirements that the bad thing must depend on efforts on our part, or that 
bringing about the bad outcome is the result of special talents or skills of ours. Nor do we 
necessarily need to have made any sacrifices in order to qualify as possibly being blame-
worthy for the bad outcome.
Consider one last apparent asymmetry between the criteria for praiseworthiness and 
blameworthiness. This asymmetry has to do with whether delegating a task to somebody 
else is compatible with clearly being praiseworthy or blameworthy for anything good or bad 
that the other agent might do or bring about through their actions. If we ask somebody else 
to do something that can be assessed as positive and they successfully do so, that other 
person seems much more clearly praiseworthy for the good they are doing, while we our-
selves may much less clearly deserve any praise for the good that they do or have done. In 
contrast –­ to use the example from above again –­ if I hire somebody to do my dirty work 

--- Page 411 ---

SVEN NYHOLM
406
(e.g., I hire a ­hitman to harm or kill somebody), then I may be blameworthy for the bad 
results of the other agent’s actions (even if the other person is also very blameworthy for 
the harm they cause).
On the whole, then, common sense postulates various asymmetries when it comes the cir-
cumstances in which we might be praiseworthy for good things, on the one hand, and blame-
worthy for bad things, on the other hand. Qualifying as being praiseworthy is more demanding 
in certain respects: good things that happen should be the result of our efforts, our skills or 
talents, or sacrifices we make. It should not just be a happy accident or a side-­effect, or a 
means to some other end, that our actions lead to good effects: it should be something we are 
actively striving for. In contrast, we might justifiably be blamed for bad things that happen or 
that we allow to happen, simply because we might not be taking enough care to prevent those 
bad things, or because we may be failing to take measures to prevent risks from materializing 
(Pettit 2015).
28.4  Four Kinds of Responsibility and Four Kinds of Potential Gaps 
in Responsibility
We can now return to possible gaps in responsibility. We will consider potential gaps with 
respect to both praise and blame. I will distinguish among four different types. To get there, I 
will first introduce two basic distinctions related to the notion of responsibility.
We have already considered praise and blame and some differences between the two. 
Here, I will first draw a closely related distinction, namely between what I will call positive 
responsibility and negative responsibility. In general terms, I shall say that we are dealing 
with positive responsibility if we are considering responsibility for good/positive events or 
outcomes. In contrast, I shall say that we are dealing with negative responsibility if we are 
considering responsibility for bad or negative events or outcomes. Suppose, for example, 
that a patient is correctly diagnosed and a suitable treatment is prescribed, which is 
­successful. If we consider the issue of responsibility for this positive sequence of events, we 
are considering what I’m calling positive responsibility. In contrast, if somebody is harmed 
and the question of responsibility for this bad event comes up, that is a question about neg-
ative responsibility.3
The next basic distinction is between what is sometimes called backward-­looking responsi-
bility, on the one hand, and forward-­looking responsibility, on the other (Nihlén Fahlquist 2020, 
Ch. 2). Backward-­looking responsibility relates to responsibility for things that have hap-
pened. Something good or bad might have happened and the question is who is responsible for 
this good or bad thing. Forward-­looking responsibility, in contrast, concerns things that may 
happen and responsibility related to these possible future events or outcomes. For example, if 
there is some significant risk related to some activity, we can ask who, if anyone, is responsible 
for trying to prevent this risk from materializing. Or if there is an opportunity related to some 
good outcome that might be brought about in the future, we can also ask the forward-­looking 
question of who, if anyone, is responsible for bringing about the good outcome. For example, 
a parent might have a responsibility to try to raise their child in such a way that the child will 
have a good life as an adult.
We can put together these two distinctions –­ the one between positive and negative respon-
sibility and the one between backward-­looking and forward-­looking responsibility –­ and get 
the following four types of responsibility (Nyholm 2023, Ch. 6)
