For example, something bad may have happened. Yet, while it may seem that somebody 
should be held responsible, there may be no one who can rightly be held responsible. This 
would be a case of a backward-­looking negative responsibility gap. One case in point here 
would be a responsibility gap related to a case in which a self-­driving car has harmed a human 
being. Suppose next that something good has happened –­ e.g., a scientific discovery has been 
made by an AI technology. Here it might be unclear if any particular human being can take 
credit for this discovery. If so, then we might have a backward-­looking positive responsibility 
gap (Danaher and Nyholm 2021).
If something bad or good could happen but it is unclear whose responsibility it is to try to 
prevent the bad event or to bring about the good outcome, then these would be cases of 
forward-­looking negative and forward-­looking positive responsibility gaps. There might be a 
forward-­looking negative responsibility gap related to some form of AI, for example, in case it 
is unclear, or impossible to decide, whose responsibility it is to make sure that this form of AI 
doesn’t create certain forms of harm.

--- Page 413 ---

SVEN NYHOLM
408
There might be a forward-­looking positive responsibility gap in relation to AI in case there 
is nobody who clearly has a positive responsibility to bring about some possible good outcome 
related to the given form of AI. This might be, for example, because forward-­looking positive 
responsibilities are typically primarily associated with special relationships, such as those 
­between parents and their children, lawyers and their clients, doctors and their patients, or 
teachers and their students (Nyholm 2023, Ch. 6). In such cases, we typically think that there 
are special forward-­looking positive responsibilities to try to make things go well for those 
with whom we have these special relationships. In relation to strangers, in contrast, it is often 
less clear whether people have any special forward-­looking positive responsibility to promote 
the good of particular other people (Persson 2013; Smart and Williams 1973, p.93).
The question now arises of how and whether we might be able to fill these different kinds 
of gaps. Discussing this will take us back to the issues related to asymmetries between praise 
and blame that were brought up in the previous section. Let’s start by considering whether we 
could fill responsibility gaps by letting people volunteer to take responsibility for good and bad 
things.
28.5  Could We Fill Responsibility Gaps by Letting People Volunteer 
to Take Responsibility for Outputs Created by AI Technologies?
Some philosophers who write about responsibility gaps and AI have suggested that at least 
in some contexts, we can fill responsibility gaps by letting people take responsibility for the 
outputs of AI technologies (e.g., Kiener 2022). For example, let us say that a hospital uses AI 
technologies to make medical diagnoses. When such diagnoses are incorrect, the question of 
who is responsible might arise. If the AI technologies in question are so-­called black box 
technologies –­ that is, the inner workings of the neural networks are opaque to people –­ then 
worries about responsibility gaps might arise. One way of filling the gap might be if the 
medical team who used the AI technology assumes responsibility for the erroneous diagnosis, 
even if they strictly speaking might not deserve to be blamed for the problem (Lang 
et al. 2023). Similarly, some car companies –­ such as Volvo and Audi –­ have claimed that 
when they put fully self-­driving cars on the market, they will take full responsibility for any 
harm these cars might cause (Nyholm 2023).4 Is this general idea a good approach when it 
comes to filling responsibility gaps? That is, should we try to fill such gaps by hoping that 
there will be people who will step forward and take responsibility for the outputs of AI 
technologies?
When we think about this, among the things that we should reflect on are the motivations 
and incentives that people have to seek praise, on the one hand, or accept blame, on the other 
hand. Notably, as we saw above, there are some important asymmetries related to motivations 
and incentives here. So, there might be some problems with the idea of filling responsibility 
gaps by hoping that people will be willing to take responsibility for what AI systems do and the 
outcomes they produce.
For example, when it comes to backward-­looking responsibility gaps, many people are 
likely to be more strongly motivated to try to take responsibility for good outcomes that AI 
technologies have brought about than for bad outcomes that AI technologies have brought 
about. As mentioned in section 28.3 above, being praised for something good –­ or getting 
credit or recognition for something good –­ is usually a very attractive thing for the person or 
persons in question. Their popularity might go up, they might make new friends, new oppor-
tunities might open up for them, and so on. In contrast, being blamed for something bad is 

--- Page 414 ---

THE FUTURE OF HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
409
usually not attractive for the blamed person. Their popularity might go down, they might lose 
friends and make enemies, opportunities might be closed off, and so on.
In general, it is for most people also a subjectively nicer experience to be on the receiving 
end of praise than blame. Accordingly, when it comes to filling backward-­looking responsibility 
gaps by having people volunteer to take responsibility, at least the relevant self-­interested 
incentives are such that many people will be much more strongly motivated to take 
responsibility for good things that AI has produced than for bad outcomes that AI might have 
produced.5
Consider also the difference between good things that AI has already brought about versus 
possible good outcomes that AI might create in the future. Are people as likely to be motivated 
and incentivized to take responsibility for bringing about future good outcomes as they might 
be to take responsibility for good outcomes that have already been created? This is not obvious.
Taking on the responsibility of bringing about a good outcome that has not yet occurred 
tends to involve potential opportunity costs. Also, people usually tend to primarily be willing 
to regard themselves as having responsibilities to do good for others if they stand in some sort 
of special relationship towards them (Persson  2013). Doing good for others by creating 
beneficial AI is certainly a very commendable thing to do. But getting people to volunteer 
themselves as being responsible for making this happen might be harder. Governments can 
take on such a responsibility and so could public universities, because they do have special 
relationships to the people who might benefit from any good that AI technologies they might 
help to produce. But tech companies are less likely to be driven by a sense of responsibility to 
do good to people in society. They will primarily be interested, instead, in developing business 
models that are in their corporate interest.
So, the most likely type of responsibility gap related to AI that might be fillable by having 
people volunteer to take responsibility are backward-­looking positive responsibility gaps. 
Here, though, the question arises of whether people who would wish to take credit for good 
outputs created by AI would always really deserve credit  –­  or praise or other forms of 
­recognition –­ for these outputs.
As noted above, people are strongly incentivized to try to take credit for positive things. 
However, that it is nice for people to get praise does not necessarily mean that these people are 
really praiseworthy –­ or that they deserve credit or other forms of recognition –­ for whatever 
it is that they want to get credit for. Moreover, sometimes when people are unmotivated to 
accept blame for something bad, they might nevertheless be blameworthy for whatever bad 
thing might have happened (Rubel et al. 2021). Let us therefore now return to the important 
issue of the conditions under which people deserve praise or blame.
28.6  Praiseworthiness and Blameworthiness for Good and Bad Outcomes 
Created by/with AI Technologies
As noted in section 28.3 above, common-­sense normative criteria for praiseworthiness and 
blameworthiness are asymmetrical in significant ways. In line with these criteria, being 
praiseworthy for some outcome requires a more active and focused participation in the pro-
duction of that outcome as compared to what’s required to potentially be blameworthy for 
some outcome. For example, in order to be truly praiseworthy for some good outcome, it 
should ideally be the result of efforts exerted by us, skills or talents shown, sacrifices made, 
and –­ on the whole –­ our active involvement in the production of the outcome in question. It 
cannot just be that we allow something good to happen, that it is a happy accident, or that the 

--- Page 415 ---

SVEN NYHOLM
410
good thing is a means to some self-­interested end of ours. Nor, ideally, should we let somebody 
else take over the production of the good outcome or output in order for us ourselves to be 
praiseworthy –­ or deserve credit or recognition –­ for it.
When it comes to whether we are blameworthy for some negative outcome, in contrast, the 
criteria are different. Here, the fact that we allow a bad outcome to occur by failing to prevent 
it can be enough to be blameworthy, at least to some extent, for this bad occurrence. Failure 
to take care to prevent something bad –­ and being negligent –­ can be enough for us to be 
blameworthy for something bad. It does not have to be that we have made any special effort to 
produce the bad outcome, nor that its production is based on some special skill or talent of 
ours, or that its production requires some sacrifice on our part (Pettit 2015). Moreover, if 
somebody who is working for you or who is under your command or supervision causes 
­problems  –­  that is, if an agent to whom you have outsourced some task is causing 
­problems –­ then you might be partly responsible for any bad outcomes that this delegation 
results in (Sparrow 2007; Nyholm 2020, Ch. 3).
In short, the normative criteria related to when people are praiseworthy for good out-
comes, on the one hand, or blameworthy for bad outcomes, on the other, are asymmetrical in 
nature. This raises the question of whether it might be easier to be blameworthy for negative 
outcomes caused by AI technologies than to be praiseworthy for positive outputs brought 
about by AI technologies (Nyholm 2024).
The whole idea of handing over some task or set of tasks to an AI technology so that we do 
not have to do it ourselves seems in many cases to mean that there is less need for any efforts, 
skills or talents, or sacrifices –­ or, more generally, any active involvement –­ on our part when 
the AI technology produces some outcome or effect. Hence, the very idea of AI technologies 
seems to be a threat to the notion that the user of the AI technology would deserve any special 
credit for any positive outputs that the AI technology brings about (Danaher and 
Nyholm 2021).
Of course, this might be a matter of degree. Sometimes using AI might involve a lot of work 
for the human beings in question. But the smaller the role of the human in the production of 
the end result, it follows that the less effort, skills and talents, or sacrifices are needed from the 
human, as more of the work is done by the AI technology in the production of the output or 
outcome. The AI technology is then doing something that we would otherwise use our skills 
or our intelligence to do. Accordingly, there is less of a need for activity on our part of the sorts 
that can make us praiseworthy or deserving of credit or recognition in relation to the outputs 
or outcomes created by the AI technology. We can allow the good outputs to be produced, 
letting another form of agency –­ namely, the agency in the AI technology –­ do the acting for 
us. With respect to the conditions of praiseworthiness, then, handing tasks over to AI 
technologies that do things for us seems to mean that we will have a hard time fulfilling the 
types of criteria that can make a person praiseworthy, or deserving of credit or recognition, 
for a positive outcome or occurrence.
When it comes to potentially being blameworthy for bad outcomes caused by AI technol-
ogies we use, however, it appears that the conditions related to blameworthiness considered 
above make it relatively speaking easier to be blameworthy for possible bad outcomes 
(Nyholm 2023, Ch. 6). For example, by using AI technologies that might cause bad effects or 
outcomes, we might be letting bad things happen, while failing to take enough care to prevent 
them from happening.
We might be having another agent act on our behalf –­ in this case, an artificial type of 
agent –­ that causes problems, and this might not get us off the hook since we may be the ones 
who delegated the performance of the task to this problem-­causing agent type. By letting an 

--- Page 416 ---

THE FUTURE OF HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
411
AI technology do something for us, we might not need to use any special efforts, skills or 
­talents, or make any particular sacrifices. But that matters less when it comes to the issue of 
whether we are blameworthy for allowing something bad to happen than whether we can be 
praiseworthy for something good we allow to happen. In short, the conditions related to 
blameworthiness seem to make it less hard to be blameworthy for bad effects of AI technol-
ogies than to be praiseworthy for good outputs produced by AI technologies.
Suppose, for example, that instead of writing texts, creating art, making decisions, or 
whatever, somebody lets some sort of AI technology do these things for them. The output 
might be impressive: it might be a text, a piece of art, a decision or whatever that is seen as 
good in some significant way. But the person who used the AI –­ in other words, the person 
who instead of doing these things themselves had an AI technology do it for them –­ may fail 
to live up to any clearly identifiable criteria for praiseworthiness.
For example, a student might put in a prompt into a large language model-­based generative 
AI technology in order to produce an answer to a question that is part of a take-­home exam. 
The answer might be such that, if it had been written by a human, it would have been seen as 
a good answer. But given that the student didn’t write the answer themselves but rather let 
the AI technology do it for them, the student may have no claim to credit for this good-­seeming 
answer to the exam question. The student may be motivated and have strong incentives to 
claim credit for the answer –­ to pretend that the answer came from them –­ but this is not the 
same as fulfilling the sorts of criteria by which one deserves credit for an answer to a question 
on a take-­home exam.
Or let’s suppose that instead of composing a song themselves, a songwriter uses some form 
of generative AI technology to create a song, perhaps by entering a prompt instructing the AI 
technology to write a song in the style of a certain music group (Nyholm 2024). If other 
people then like that song, the person who put the prompt into the generative AI program 
would not deserve the sort of credit that a human songwriter would deserve if they ­themselves 
had composed a song that others like.
Let us consider a real-­world case to illustrate the blameworthiness side of the issue. In the 
fall of 2023, the Guardian newspaper reported that some people had been trying to make 
money during the mushroom collection season by “writing” mushroom collection guidebooks 
with the help of the generative AI technology ChatGPT and selling those books on Amazon 
(Milmo 2023). These mushroom collection books, having been written by a large language 
model that didn’t know which mushrooms are safe to eat, were recommending that people 
collect and eat poisonous mushrooms. It is unclear whether anybody actually followed the 
advice in these books and ate poisonous mushrooms. But if that had happened, the people 
who were trying to make money by selling generative AI-­written mushrooms collection books 
would have been blameworthy for the harm that this would have caused.
Why? Because they would have failed to take proper care to ensure that they didn’t allow 
their AI-­generated outputs to cause harm to other people. They would have delegated a task 
to another type of agent that was causing problems for other people in a way that would not 
get the people posing as the authors of these books off the hook. In other words, in this 
example, saying “The AI I used recommended eating poisonous mushrooms; it wasn’t me 
who did that!” would not be a good excuse that would allow the people selling such books to 
avoid being blameworthy for these risks of significant harm.
In contrast, suppose that such an AI-­written mushroom collection book were to contain 
some beautiful-­sounding sentences or that the bits written by the AI technology would 
actually offer useful tips about what mushrooms are safe to eat. If so, then the people using AI 
technologies to produce these books would not deserve any credit for those well-­written 

--- Page 417 ---

SVEN NYHOLM
412
sentences or those useful pieces of advice. The beautiful-­sounding sentences or the useful 
advice would not reflect any particular efforts, talents or skills, and so forth on the part of the 
people using generative AI to produce these books. To deserve credit for the way something is 
written or for the information that is provided in a text, one must do the writing oneself and 
be the source of that useful information (Nyholm 2024). This mushroom collection book 
example, then, is a good illustration of how it is easier to be blameworthy for any bad effects 
our use of AI technologies might cause than it is to be praiseworthy for any good outputs that 
the AI technologies that we use might produce.
28.7  Conclusion
As noted above, if we understand AI technologies as technologies that can take over tasks from 
us that we would otherwise use our human intelligence to perform, the question arises of whether 
we can still be praised or blamed for any good or bad outcomes that these technologies might 
bring about. Many authors have presented arguments to the effect that outsourcing tasks 
humans would otherwise perform to AI technologies may create gaps in responsibility. One 
straightforward argument is that instead of being performed by responsible humans, the tasks or 
activities are now instead performed by AI technologies that may not be morally responsible 
agents. Another argument is that people may lack sufficient control over these AI technologies or 
that they may have trouble predicting what might happen when they use AI technologies.
Such discussions about possible gaps in responsibility tend to focus on worries about who, 
if anybody, could justifiably be blamed if AI technologies cause harm. This chapter has sug-
gested that we should also be considering the question of who, if anyone, could justifiably get 
credit when AI technologies produce outputs that can be assessed as being good or positive in 
various ways. In other words, discussions about AI and the future of human responsibility 
should not only be about blame but also about praise. The question is not only whether 
increased AI use might create gaps with respect to human blameworthiness for bad ­outcomes, 
but also whether increased AI use might create gaps with respect to human praiseworthiness 
for good outcomes.
The chapter has argued that when we consider these issues about praise and blame for out-
puts or outcomes created by AI technologies, we should be mindful of various asymmetries 
between praise and blame. This applies both to the motivations and incentives people have in 
relation to praise and blame, on the one hand, and to the criteria that are commonly used to 
assess praiseworthiness and blameworthiness, on the other hand. People may be strongly 
motivated and have strong incentives to try to take credit for good outcomes brought about by 
AI technologies and to try to avoid accepting blame for bad outcomes caused by AI technol-
ogies. But the criteria for praiseworthiness and blameworthiness may point in another 
direction. Given the different requirements for qualifying as being praiseworthy for something 
and as being blameworthy for something, it may often be harder to be praiseworthy for good 
outputs of AI technologies than to be blameworthy for any bad effects of these technologies.6

can also be about who is able to answer questions about something that has happened or about to 
whom –­ or to what aspects of their personality or character –­ a certain action or the production of 

--- Page 418 ---

THE FUTURE OF HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY

a certain outcome can be attributed (Shoemaker 2011). Here, however, we will focus on the subset 
of questions about responsibility that are concerned with praise and blame for good and bad actions 
or good and bad outcomes of actions or activities.
2	 Of course, virtuous people with a strong sense of responsibility do not only care about pros and cons 
of praise and blame; they also care about whether they deserve praise and blame for their actions. They 
might judge the benefits of praise and the drawbacks of blame to be secondary to the issue of whether 
they deserve praise or blame. Or if they are unusually virtuous, they may even neither care at all about 
the benefits related to praise nor worry about the drawbacks related to blame. However, most people 
will only be concerned with whether they deserve praise or blame for their actions or the outcomes of 
their actions. Most people also tend to prefer situations in which others praise them to situations in 
which others blame them, because of the attractive aspects of being praised by other people and the 
unattractive aspects of being blamed by others. Accordingly, when we think about AI and praise and 
blame, it is interesting and important to not only consider the criteria for deserving praise and blame, 
but to also reflect on other types of motivations why people care about praise and blame.
3	 What, it might here be asked, is the relation between positive responsibility and praise (worthiness), 
on the one hand, and negative responsibility and blame (worthiness), on the other hand? Being 
positively responsible for a good outcome is typically seen as grounds for praise, whereas being 
negatively responsible for a bad outcome is typically seen as grounds for blame. Or to put it more 
precisely: the considerations that make somebody positively responsible for a good outcome also 
typically make them worthy of praise, whereas the considerations that make somebody negatively 
responsible for a bad outcome typically make them blameworthy. I say “typically” here since, as was 
noted in footnote 1, we can also ask questions related to responsibility that are about answerability 
or attributability, and while such forms of responsibility often correlate with grounds for praise and 
blame, they do not necessarily do so. Somebody could be answerable for some bad outcome, for 
example, without therefore necessarily being blameworthy for it, though people may typically be 
blameworthy for negative outcomes that they are also answerable for, and so on.
4	 As this example suggests, it is interesting in this context to consider shared or collective responsibility 
for the outputs of AI technologies. Such a discussion goes beyond the scope of this paper, but I 
discuss that issue elsewhere, e.g., in Nyholm (2020) and Nyholm (2023).
5	 As mentioned above, many people who have a strong sense of responsibility will of course also be 
concerned about who deserves praise or blame, but we cannot simply take it for granted that this will 
be the thing that most people will care most about. We also have to be mindful of what other 
incentives there are related to praise and blame, if we are to think realistically about challenges 
raised by new AI technologies whose outputs might be assessed as good or bad.

29.1  Introduction
An artificial moral agent (AMA) is an artificial system that has the ability to make moral 
decisions and act on them. The idea can be traced back to the early days of artificial intelligence 
(AI). Isaac Asimov formulated the now legendary three laws of robotics in his short stories in 
the 1940s. The laws were intended by the designers of the artificial systems in the stories to 
ensure that robots do not harm human beings and protect themselves (Asimov 1950, p. 40). 
In their original formulation, the laws read as follows.
(1)	 A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to 
come to harm.
(2)	 A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings, except where such orders would 
conflict with the First Law.
(3)	 A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with 
the First or Second Law.
Asimov later added a fourth principle, sometimes referred to as the zeroth law, because it 
supersedes the others.
(4)	 A robot may not harm humanity, or, by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.
While the debate about AMAs has long been confined to the realm of science fiction, it has gained 
significant momentum in practical contexts due to the enormous progress made by AI over the 
last few decades. Advances in machine learning have led to a burst of research activity in AI over 
the last twenty years (Singh and Singh 2024). This has also intensified interest in AMAs (Allen 
et al. 2000; Anderson and Anderson 2007; Himma 2009). New fields of application requiring 
artificial systems with moral decision-­making skills have emerged; the moral dilemmas arising in 
autonomous driving have brought AMAs to the attention of a broader public.
The emergence of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT has further fueled the 
discussion of AMAs because LLMs are highly cognitively capable systems that can answer 
Artificial Moral Agents
CATRIN MISSELHORN
29

--- Page 421 ---

Catrin Misselhorn
416
a wide range of questions and perform complex tasks. However, this also creates risks that call 
for the development of AMAs.
On the one hand, these chatbots can be used for morally questionable purposes, such as 
planning a burglary or designing a biochemical weapon. In light of such dangers, it would be 
desirable if these systems could recognize such requests as immoral and reject them. There 
are already approaches to implement this capacity in some LLMs. However, they still suffer 
from being vulnerable to circumvention, for example, through jailbreak prompts, which are 
prompting techniques that allow users to bypass built-­in safeguards that aim to prevent the 
immoral use of LLMs (Liu et al. 2023).
Some LLMs have, on the other hand, exhibited overly human behavior by pretending to 
be conscious, feeling emotions, or even claiming to have fallen in love with users, pressur-
ing them to break up with their human partners. This behavior is morally questionable, 
even if users are aware they are interacting with a machine (Misselhorn 2023a). To avoid 
misleading users, it is better if the bots explicitly clarify that they are not human, are not 
conscious, and do not feel anything. Explicitly stating these limitations is also a form of 
moral behavior.
However, LLMs not only pose risks that could be remedied by giving them moral capacities 
but also present opportunities for creating AMAs. By enabling machines to communicate 
with humans on a broad range of topics, including moral issues (Misselhorn 2023b), LLMs 
can function as moral advisors, aiding individuals in navigating moral decisions.
29.2  Artificial Morality and Machine Ethics
The AI discipline that aims to develop AMAs is called artificial morality. It investigates how 
artificial systems can be equipped with moral capacities, including physical robots and 
software agents (Misselhorn 2018). While AI typically focuses on modeling, emulating, or 
simulating human cognitive abilities, artificial morality focuses on modeling or simulating 
moral decision making and agency.
The term “machine ethics” refers to the discipline addressing the theoretical grounding 
and ethical reflection of artificial morality (Anderson and Anderson 2011; Bendel 2019; 
Misselhorn  2018). This usage aligns with the common philosophical understanding of 
morality as the totality of moral norms, actions, attitudes, and feelings, while ethics provides 
a theory of morality.
Machine ethics encompasses both metaethical and normative issues. Metaethical questions 
concern the conceptual, ontological, and epistemological aspects of artificial morality, such 
as the nature of moral agency and the ontological and moral status of AMAs. Debates 
continue over whether AMAs are mere objects (Johnson  2006), form an intermediate 
category between objects and human subjects (Misselhorn 2024), or possess moral and legal 
rights (Gunkel 2018).
Normative ethics examines what is morally right or wrong. In a narrow sense, normative 
machine ethics considers the moral standards to be implemented in AMAs 
(Misselhorn 2018, 2022). Questions arise about the ethics that should guide AMAs, such as 
utilitarianism or deontology. Another issue is whether principle-­based ethics is effective or 
whether case-­based approaches are preferable.
In a broader sense, machine ethics includes considerations of the moral implications of 
artificial morality at an individual, social, and political level. For example, does artificial 
morality violate the dignity of individuals? Are there specific applications where AMAs are 

--- Page 422 ---

Artificial Moral Agents
417
impermissible? What implications does artificial morality have for human social relations 
and moral practice? Which regulatory frameworks should govern AMAs politically 
and legally?
Large portions of normative machine ethics can be classified under applied ethics, 
particularly technology ethics, which addresses specific, socially and politically relevant 
ethical issues. Applied machine ethics intersects with other fields in technology ethics, 
including information and media ethics (Floridi 2013; Heesen 2016; Hamm and Tavani 2008) 
and robot ethics (Lin et al. 2014, 2017; Loh 2019; Veruggio and Operto 2008; Wallach and 
Asaro 2016).
New applied ethics disciplines often emerge to address the unprecedented ethical challenges 
posed by new technologies. In the case of machine ethics, these challenges are technological 
developments that seem to require machines that can make moral decisions and act on them. 
Designing such machines is part of the larger field of AI alignment, which aims to ensure that 
AI systems align with human goals, preferences, or moral values.
The historical origins of AI provide another motivation for artificial morality and machine 
ethics. Initially, AI was a theoretical research program focused on simulating human 
intelligence broadly, rather than solving specific practical problems. The capacity to make 
moral decisions is a key aspect of human intelligence, and its development has therefore been 
a significant challenge in AI research.
29.3  Types of Moral Agents
To understand the concept of AMAs, it is essential to distinguish between various types of 
moral agents based on the kinds and degrees of moral capacities they possess (Cervantes 
et al. 2020). An influential classification by James H. Moor (2006) presents a hierarchical 
distinction among four types of what he calls “ethical agents,” which had a significant impact 
on the discussion of AMAs. Given the distinction between ethics and morality suggested 
above, it would be more appropriate to speak of “moral agents” but Moor uses the terms 
“­ethical” and “moral” as synonyms.
According to Moor, the most basic type of moral agent is one that generates morally rele-
vant effects. He calls them “ethical impact agents.” In this regard, every technical device 
becomes a moral agent as soon as it produces good or bad effects on human beings. For 
example, a watch that reminds its owner to keep appointments on time is an ethical impact 
agent since punctuality is generally considered a positive moral value, although it can also be 
morally bad in contexts like planning or organizing a crime.
Thus, the moral quality associated with the effects of such objects is contingent upon how 
they are used. Therefore, it may not be entirely appropriate to consider them as moral agents. 
This caveat also applies to Moor’s subsequent category of “implicit ethical agents,” whose 
design reflects certain moral values, such as security considerations. “Implicit ethical agents” 
include warning systems in aircrafts that sound an alarm if the plane comes too close to the 
ground or if a collision with another aircraft is imminent. ATMs are another example, as they 
must not only dispense the correct amount of money but also verify whether funds can be 
withdrawn on a given day.
Moor attributes virtues to these systems that are neither acquired through socialization 
nor socially constructed, but instead implemented directly in their hardware. Conversely, 
there also exist implicit immoral ethical agents, such as slot machines designed to maximize 
user engagement. The term “operational morality” (Wallach and Allen  2009, p.  25) 

--- Page 423 ---

Catrin Misselhorn
418
seems more fitting in these cases since it does not involve any agency on the part of the 
technical device.
The third level consists of “explicit ethical agents.” Unlike the previous types, these systems 
can explicitly recognize and process morally relevant information and arrive at moral 
decisions. Therefore, this category encompasses entities genuinely deserving of being called 
moral agents. Explicit moral agents can be compared to chess programs; such programs 
recognize relevant chess information, process it, and make decisions aimed at winning the 
game. They represent the current position of pieces on the chessboard and know the allowable 
moves. Based upon this, they calculate which move is most favorable under current 
circumstances.
For Moor, explicit moral agents not only act in accordance with moral guidelines but 
operate based on moral criteria. This is reminiscent of Kant’s distinction between acting in 
conformity with duty and acting from duty (Kant 1997, p. 4:397f). Explicit moral agents 
occupy a middle ground between Kantian moral subjects who act from duty and the prudent 
merchant of Kant’s example, whose self-­interest coincidentally aligns with moral duty.
However, this analogy is loose because artificial agents cannot be moral subjects in the 
Kantian sense, lacking will and inclinations that could conflict with moral law. Moor’s concept 
of explicit moral agents only implies that they can discern and process morally relevant 
aspects and respond flexibly to situations. Moor would therefore agree with Kant that explicit 
moral agents do not meet the full standards of moral agency that humans possess.
Humans therefore fall into his highest category called “full ethical agents,” who possess 
additional capacities such as consciousness, intentionality, and critical self-­reflection. These 
capacities are essential for free will, which machines lack. As a result, explicit moral agents 
are referred to as functional moral agents (Misselhorn 2020, 2022).
29.4  Functional Moral Agency
Moral agency is characterized by a specific form of domain-­oriented reasoning. According to 
Moor, explicit ethical agents must be able to act on the basis of moral reasons. The philosophical 
standard theory of acting for a reason, which goes back to David Hume, posits that a reason 
for an action consists of a combination of two mental attitudes: a belief and a pro-­attitude. A 
belief involves holding something true, while a pro-­attitude indicates that a certain outcome 
ought to be achieved. Desires are typical examples of pro-­attitudes. This approach is com-
monly known as the belief-­desire theory.
Consider, for example, the reason behind Julia’s action of visiting the library. Her action 
can be explained by her desire to read Tolstoy’s novel Anna Karenina combined with the belief 
that she will find the book there. Some variations of the standard theory propose that action 
explanation must also include an intention that determines which desire takes priority, while 
also encompassing a plan of action (Bratman 1987). This perspective acknowledges that we 
have many noncommittal desires that do not translate into actions, a complication that is set 
aside in the following for the sake of simplicity.
Moral actions can accordingly be traced back to moral reasons, which are combinations 
of moral pro-­attitudes and corresponding beliefs. For example, a moral reason may include 
a utilitarian value judgment that maximizing pleasure is morally desirable (pro-­attitude) 
along with the belief that donating to a charitable organization will result in the maximiza-
tion of pleasure (for a moral detailed characterization of moral judgments, see Misselhorn 
2018, p. 49f).

--- Page 424 ---

Artificial Moral Agents
419
Significant debate exists regarding whether artificial systems can genuinely possess states 
like beliefs and desires. Some authors argue that they do not, as artificial systems lack 
intentionality, i.e., the capacity to refer to or represent anything. As Donald Davidson famously 
argued, intentionality requires complex linguistic abilities, which only humans possess 
(Davidson 1982). Others acknowledge that animals may also have intentional states, even if 
they do not meet Davidson’s rationality criteria (Dretske  1995). This brings intentional 
agency within the reach of artificial systems as well, although Dretske himself remains 
ambivalent about this claim (Dretske 1999).
The stance one takes on this matter depends on the conditions that must be met to attribute 
beliefs and desires to artificial systems. An instrumentalist viewpoint, frequently associated 
with Daniel Dennett in his early writings, contends that attributing intentional states is just 
an explanatory strategy. He argues that one can ascribe beliefs and desires to agents if doing 
so helps to understand their behavior, irrespective of their internal structure (Dennett 1973, 
p. 164f). Dennett labels this the intentional stance, calling systems that can be explained in 
this manner intentional systems.
According to this view, rational agency is a matter of interpretation and does not require 
that an entity actually possess specific internal states. This criterion can be readily fulfilled by 
artificial systems. For example, understanding a chess computer as an entity that wants to 
win the game and believes that a specific move will help to achieve this goal allows us to better 
understand the computer’s actions by attributing the relevant beliefs and desires to it. 
Although one could, in principle, explain the computer’s behavior entirely in physical terms, 
the intentional stance proves useful given the complexity of such a system.
Conversely, noninstrumental views refuse to reduce reasoning to an attributional practice. 
They assume that an entity must possess internal states which are at least functionally 
equivalent to beliefs and pro-­attitudes. If an artificial system possesses states that function 
analogously to corresponding mental states in humans, one can refer to it as functionally 
equivalent to a human agent. This strategy can also be used to characterize the intentional 
states of group agents (List and Pettit 2011). However, given the variety of ways in which to 
specify the relevant functional relations (Block 1978), functional equivalence has to be recog-
nized as relative to the type of functionalism espoused.
Functionalism is a philosophical approach that attempts to explain mental states in terms 
of their functional relations. There are several types of functionalism, including machine 
functionalism, analytic functionalism, and psycho-­functionalism. Machine functionalism 
equates the mind with a Turing machine, while analytic functionalism focuses on the 
meaning of mental terms in folk psychology. Psycho-­functionalism defines mental states in 
terms of their functional roles in scientific psychology. These views lead to different methods 
of delineating the relevant inputs, outputs, and internal relations.
The types of functionalism differ, for instance, in granularity when describing mental 
states. Simple machine functionalism regards mental states like beliefs or desires as unstruc-
tured entities while the representational theory of the mind describes them as representations 
with internal structures. This allows for systematic relations between them and explains the 
ability to formulate and understand new thoughts. For example, the thought “John loves 
Mary” is composed of the components “John,” “loves,” and “Mary” which can be recombined 
to form other thoughts like “Mary loves John.”
Jerry Fodor is the most prominent advocate for merging a representational view with a 
computational theory of the mind. He views mental processes as Turing-­style computations 
operating over structured symbols, forming a “language of thought” (Fodor 1975). Fodor 
and many cognitive scientists argued for a long time that Turing-­style computation over 

--- Page 425 ---

Catrin Misselhorn
420
mental symbols is the only theory that can provide a scientific framework for understanding 
the mind in cognitive science. However, this viewpoint has faced challenges (Thompson 2007, 
p.  267), and even Fodor has meanwhile adopted a more cautious assessment of the 
­computational model of the mind (Fodor 2000).
29.5  Quasi-­intentionality
John Searle’s Chinese Room thought experiment formulates a well-­known objection against 
the computational approach (Searle 1980). The thought experiment is supposed to show that 
Turing-­style computation alone is insufficient for intentional thought. Searle imagines 
himself in a room executing a computer program manually. He receives Chinese input from 
native speakers outside the room, generating Chinese symbols as output based on rule 
manuals. However, without knowledge of Chinese, these symbols are meaningless squiggles 
to him. Nonetheless, his responses are coherent to the Chinese speakers outside the room.
The thought experiment is supposed to trigger the intuition that the system does not 
understand Chinese, even if its behavior is from the outside the room indistinguishable from 
that of a Chinese native speaker. One reason for this is that a Turing machine cannot bridge 
the divide between syntax and semantics. If Searle is right, machines cannot really possess 
mental states. They might, however, exhibit states that are functionally equivalent to mental 
states, although they are not associated with phenomenal consciousness and have only 
derived intentionality mediated by their programmers and users.
One might call such states quasi-­beliefs, quasi-­desires, and so on (Misselhorn 2018, p. 86). 
This way of speaking borrows from the terminology of Kendall Walton (1978), who calls 
emotional reactions to fictions (for example, our pity for the protagonist of the novel Anna 
Karenina) “quasi-­emotions.” This is because they do resemble real emotions in terms of their 
phenomenal quality and the bodily changes involved: we weep for Anna Karenina and feel 
sadness in the face of her fate. Yet unlike genuine emotions, quasi-­emotions neither involve 
the belief that the object that triggers the emotion exists nor do they let us rush in to help her.
With the functional states of AMAs, it seems to be the other way around. In contrast to 
Walton’s quasi-­emotions, they lack phenomenal consciousness and possess only derived 
intentionality. For an explicit moral agent in Moore’s terminology, it suffices to possess such 
quasi-­intentional states. Given the gradual view of moral agency, artificial systems may 
function as moral agents, even though they are not full moral agents on a par with humans. 
Arguments to the effect that artificial systems cannot be moral agents because they lack con-
sciousness or genuine intentionality would, hence, be falling short.
Functional moral agents are, however, limited in various respects. First, the functional 
relationships refer at best to the cognitive aspect of morality. If one takes seriously the 
numerous philosophical arguments against functional theories of phenomenal consciousness 
(Block 1978; Chalmers 1996; Jackson 1986; Nagel 1974), AMAs cannot feel compassion for 
others any more than they can feel the gnawing sense of guilt that torments people after 
doing something morally bad.
Second, the relativity of functional moral agents to the type of functionalism embraced 
implies that being an AMA is relative to certain human purposes and interpretations, whereas 
full moral agents inherently possess this status (Misselhorn 2022, p. 37f).
Still, designing functional moral agents faces significant challenges due to the complexity 
and context sensitivity of moral decision making which require sources of moral knowledge 
such as life experience, empathy, and imagination. The question is whether functional moral 

--- Page 426 ---

Artificial Moral Agents
421
agents will ever be able to make substantial moral decisions if these ultimately rely on 
capacities that only fully fledged moral agents can have (Himma 2009; Véliz 2021).
Moreover, functional moral agents cannot be held morally responsible for their actions 
(Misselhorn 2018, p. 126f), since responsibility attributions require that an agent possesses 
powers and abilities that surpass mere agency (Heidbrink  2017). There exist various 
philosophical approaches that spell these out differently. However, there is a wide-­ranging 
consensus that the corresponding powers and abilities can only be ascribed to beings endowed 
with genuine intentionality and consciousness. Whether AI can ever attain these remains an 
open question. The decoupling of agency and responsibility is at the heart of many ethical 
challenges that AI presents to us.
29.6  Large Language Models as Moral Agents
Large language models, such as LLaMA, GPT-­4, and Gemini, which can fluently address 
moral questions, readily come to mind as examples of AMAs. Yet there are reasons for doubt 
that they even possess quasi-­intentional states. These systems are fundamentally designed to 
react to prompts, relying on predictive algorithms regarding text sequences. This does not 
seem to require an internal structure of the sort that quasi-­intentional states typically involve.
However, some evidence supports ascribing internal states to LLMs that meet numerous 
criteria primarily defined by naturalistic theories of mental content (Goldstein and 
Levinstein 2024). These states carry information, they are causally efficacious, instantiate 
folk-­psychological patterns of reasoning, and manifest a structure that is isomorphic to the 
represented subject area. Additionally, their representational function emerges from selective, 
evolution-­like training processes.
Nevertheless, the informational content of these states derives from human intentionality 
present in the training data and programming. It also relies on how humans interpret the 
internal structures of these models since there exist different ways for defining relevant 
numerical relationships that embody the relevant structural resemblances (Goldstein and 
Levinstein 2024, p. 13). Although LLMs do display some structuring and folk-­psychological 
reasoning patterns, these features do not seem to be pervasive. LLMs suffer, for instance, from 
a phenomenon called the “reversal curse”: trained on a phrase of the form “A is B,” they do 
not automatically comprehend the reversed phrase “B is A” (Berglund et al. 2024).
Even though LLMs can exhibit quasi-­intentional states, there still remain doubts that they 
can really be moral agents, even in a functional sense. This is not simply due to their restriction 
to textual data and to functioning as dialogue agents reacting to user prompts. If granted 
access to email programs or social media, their agency can further expand. Should LLMs inte-
grate visual and auditory processing modules and connect to a robotic body, they might even 
become agents in the physical world (Driess et al. 2023).
Still, LLMs lack the robustness of natural agents due to their sensitivity to prompting. It is 
not merely that each prompting session appears to yield a new agent with distinct quasi-­
beliefs and desires. Even minor variations in requests during a single session may lead to 
considerable behavioral shifts. A useful framing that can capture these variations is to 
understand their behavior as role playing (Shanahan et al. 2023). Here, roles are defined by 
initial prompts, while evolving through ongoing conversations with users, who hence 
contribute either involuntarily or intentionally to the shape of the roles.
However, in contrast to human stage actors, LLMs do not play a single continuous and 
well-­defined scripted role. They instead instantiate a variety of characters, describable as a 

--- Page 427 ---

Catrin Misselhorn
422
superposition of multiple personas (Shanahan et al. 2023, p. 4). The pretend nature of these 
characters goes well with the assumption that LLMs do not possess genuine intentionality, but 
only have quasi-­intentional states. Nevertheless, this does not imply that their resulting 
actions are mere pretense; they are real. Thus, attributing functional agency to LLMs 
­ultimately makes sense.
29.7  Ethical Assessment of AMAs
A significant aspect of normative machine ethics concerns whether delegating moral decision 
making to artificial systems is morally acceptable. Responses vary from outright rejection of 
AMAs (Van Wynsberghe and Robbins 2019) to balanced perspectives emphasizing that the 
moral assessment of AMAs must differentiate diverse approaches and application contexts 
(Misselhorn  2018,  2022) to views advocating the necessity of AMAs unconditionally 
(Formosa and Ryan 2021).
The following section provides an overview and evaluation of key arguments in this 
ongoing debate, but it does not claim to be exhaustive. The focus is on moral issues specific to 
AMAs, without delving into the broader field of AI ethics, which also covers topics like pri-
vacy. The debate often begins with the question of whether AMAs represent an inevitable 
consequence of technological advancement (Wallach and Allen 2011). The main argument 
supporting this claim is that, as artificial systems become more intelligent and autonomous, 
they will inevitably face morally relevant situations in which human control becomes 
ineffective.
A morally relevant situation demands consideration of moral aspects, values, conse-
quences or principles. Depending on their design, artificial systems might encounter such 
scenarios either accidentally or intentionally. For example, an AI assessing job applications 
could inadvertently lead to discrimination against specific groups, even though this is not a 
desired outcome and the system was not intentionally programmed to do so.
An example of an artificial system intentionally designed to confront morally relevant 
situations is an autonomous vehicle with algorithms programmed to weigh human lives in 
dilemma situations. Both examples suggest that these systems must be able to make and act 
upon moral decisions, independently of permanent human supervision and control. 
Consequently, the need for AMAs appears to be a direct consequence of specific technological 
developments.
However, this trajectory necessitates neither fatal acceptance nor outright rejection; the 
inevitability of AMAs is conditional and context dependent. If we want to employ intelligent 
and autonomous technologies in certain types of applications and contexts, we will need 
AMAs. However, we have the choice to decide which applications we want to use and in which 
contexts we want to employ AMAs. Thus, diverse applications, such as those seen in 
healthcare, autonomous weapon systems, and autonomous driving, should be assessed 
individually and evaluated differently from a moral point of view (Misselhorn 2018).
A frequently cited justification for AMAs, especially from economic stakeholders, involves 
building public trust in AI (Anderson and Anderson 2007). The underlying expectation is 
that artificial morality can diminish fears surrounding robots and AI, thus fostering greater 
acceptance of these technologies. However, it is essential to differentiate trust from reliability 
(McLeod 2020). Trust is an attitude that arises in a relationship based on reciprocity. The 
abuse of this trust is a moral transgression that presupposes an attribution of responsibility 
(Baier 1986; Simon 2010).

--- Page 428 ---

Artificial Moral Agents
423
Given that AMAs cannot assume responsibility, framing the debate in terms of reliability 
rather than trust would be more apt. Moreover, existing concerns regarding unpredictability 
and control serve as additional reasons to exercise caution when relying on these systems. 
There is a risk that the term “AMA” might be used misleadingly to garner unwarranted 
acceptance, although from a moral point of view, we should not uncritically trust AMAs 
(Serholt et al. 2022).
An additional argument posits that artificial agents are morally superior to humans 
(Arkin 2009) because they do not succumb to emotional distress or psychological disorders, 
nor do they deviate from the path of righteousness due to self-­interest. However, skepticism 
persists regarding the ability of functional moral agents to make meaningful and substantial 
moral decisions, or whether moral choices, particularly those extending beyond simplistic 
contexts, may fundamentally rely on capacities unique to full moral agents (Graff 2024; 
Hamm 2009; Véliz 2021).
In light of these arguments, the research and development of AMAs must be approached 
cautiously, with practical applications withheld from market introduction until they are 
deemed ethically safe (Van Wynsberghe and Robbins 2019). The introduction of LLMs to a 
broad public, without any preceding consideration of their implications as observed in 
2022, underscores how hard it is to escape this dynamic. Even prominent individuals 
involved in these technological advancements have called for a pause in development until 
the moral and political ramifications have been assessed, as articulated in an open letter to 
the Future of Life Institute. However, the request was somewhat hypocritical since it was 
articulated by some of the main stakeholders who developed and introduced LLMs to a 
broader public.
Moreover, questions persist about the appropriateness of delegating moral decisions to 
artificial agents, particularly in high-­stakes scenarios involving human life and death. Such 
situations are especially discussed with regard to autonomous weapon systems. Autonomous 
weapon systems, commonly referred to as killer robots, are among the most contentious 
applications for AMAs. These systems can autonomously identify and engage targets without 
human intervention. In this context, artificial morality is crucial to ensure that these weapons 
adhere to legal and moral standards. This dimension assumes paramount importance in the 
context of international law compliance; using autonomous weapon systems can otherwise 
not only become morally questionable but also violate international agreements.
Just war theory provides the ethical framework that informs the design of autonomous 
weapon systems (Misselhorn  2018, p.  159f). It is used in attempts to equip autonomous 
weapon systems with an “ethics module” capable of weighing relevant moral and legal 
principles in decision making (Arkin 2009). Key decision-­making norms of such a device 
include the principle of discrimination, which only allows attacks on combatants and military 
targets; the principle of military necessity, permitting attacks on legitimate targets only under 
conditions of expecting a military advantage; and the prohibition of unnecessary suffering or 
collateral damage, as well as the principle of proportionality of means.
Setting aside doubts about whether artificial systems can make such intricate moral 
decisions, fundamental objections arise against allowing them to do so, particularly in 
situations involving human life and death. One weighty argument in this context is that the 
absence of a moral duty to kill, even in war, is a compelling reason to restrict the use of 
autonomous weapons systems (Misselhorn 2023c).
If one follows the common interpretation of just war theory, it is at best morally permissible 
to kill other people in war, but it does not constitute a moral duty (Childress 1997). It should 
therefore always remain possible to refrain from killing. However, the use of autonomous 

--- Page 429 ---

Catrin Misselhorn
424
weapon systems inevitably closes the possibility of engaging in an alternative course of 
action, which is an intrinsically valuable characteristic of human agency (Leveringhaus 2016).
The need for AMAs only arises under the assumption that artificial systems can act 
independently of permanent human supervision. It comes to its limits where there is no moral 
duty to act in a certain way. Particularly in situations that provide room for judgment or 
interpretation, it is vital that full moral agents assume responsibility for their decisions and 
actions. Accordingly, artificial systems should not decide on the life and death of human beings.
It has, moreover, been argued that acts of killing are only permitted if they fulfill 
certain moral and legal criteria, and if there is someone who bears responsibility for them 
(Sparrow 2007). Machines cannot take responsibility themselves. However, due to the lack of 
predictability and control already discussed, they can undermine the attribution of responsi-
bility to humans so that, in the end, no one is responsible for the act of killing they have 
undertaken. In such a case, there arises a responsibility gap, which is unacceptable from a 
moral point of view (Sparrow 2007).
Still others have raised the objection that allowing machines to make decisions about 
human life and death amounts to a violation of human dignity (Misselhorn  2018, 
p. 181f, 2025; Rosert and Sauer 2019). Corresponding considerations can relate, on the one 
hand, to the dignity of the person making the decision and, on the other hand, to the dignity 
of the person who is impacted by the decision.
There are also moral constraints to the decisions of AMAs in situations that are not 
existential in this way, but concern the allocation of what John Rawls calls primary goods 
(Rawls 2001, p. 58). Systems that are supposed to take such decisions should be designed in 
such a way that humans can exercise meaningful control and can be held responsible for the 
decisions of the system in a substantial sense. This holds because primary goods are things 
that every citizen needs as a free and equal moral person. They include basic rights and lib-
erties, for instance, freedom of movement, free choice among a wide range of occupations, 
the powers of offices and positions of responsibility, income and wealth, as well as the social 
bases of self-­respect.
More generally, the use of AMAs has not only been criticized because it downgrades people 
to objects. For Kant, in particular, the ability to act morally is the source of moral dignity. If 
we give away moral decision making to machines, we would be delegating the very thing that 
characterizes us as human beings. Of course, this argument should not be understood in a 
purely quantitative sense. After all, there would still be plenty of moral decisions for humans 
to make, even if machines were to take over some of them.
The point is rather that morality is a reciprocal practice between full moral agents who can 
set ends for themselves and engage with each other. In the process of coming to a moral 
decision, they become aware of their mutual interpretation of a situation, their needs, and 
feelings. This allows them to develop a shared understanding of what to do.
Artificial moral agents cannot take part in this reciprocal moral dialogue. What is more, 
delegating moral decisions to them can be perceived as an infringement of moral practice 
(Misselhorn 2022, p. 46f). Instead of being treated as equal members of a reciprocal moral 
practice, persons are reduced to data points, at the extreme, in a fully automated killing 
machine, which is devoid of understanding human life (Rosert and Sauer 2019, p. 372). 
Individuals affected by such decisions are not recognized by machines as coparticipants in a 
moral practice, which essentially involves the second-­person perspective (Darwall 2006). 
They are treated only instrumentally as means to an end. Therefore, it violates human dignity 
when individuals become the object of decisions made by AMAs without the possibility to 
contest them (Misselhorn 2018, p. 181f, 2022).

--- Page 430 ---

Artificial Moral Agents
425
A corresponding view of moral practice is also expressed in Kant’s conception of a 
kingdom of ends, which demands that we abide by those laws that we decide on together 
with other moral agents as legislators within a hypothetical kingdom of ends (Kant 1997, 
p. 4:435). The idea was transformed into a discourse-­ethical approach by Jürgen Habermas, 
for whom moral deliberation embodies more than strategic rationality, but is essentially a 
form of communicative action oriented toward a common understanding of what to do 
(Habermas 1984, p. 285).

30.1  Introduction
Moral enhancement is broadly best understood as any kind of intervention that aims to 
improve a person’s moral capacities, ultimately leading to moral improvement, such as better 
motives and behavior (DeGrazia 2014).1 The necessity of morally enhancing human beings is 
widely accepted, although there is significant disagreement about the appropriate means to 
achieve this. We inhabit a world plagued by morally troubling issues such as wars, poverty, and 
social and racial segregation. These pervasive problems, at least partially, can be viewed as 
manifestations of the inherent limitations of human nature, which lead to suboptimal moral 
reasoning. As Giubilini and Savulescu (2018, p.170) put it, human beings are “suboptimal 
information processors, moral judges, and moral agents.” This means that we often fail to con-
sider important information due to adverse physical conditions such as stress, hunger, or sleep 
deprivation. Additionally, we are susceptible to various reasoning fallacies, such as inconsis-
tency and a range of implicit biases. Frequently, we experience cognitive dissonance 
(Festinger 1957), where we hold incompatible beliefs or fail to align our behavior with our 
values. We also exhibit in-­group favoritism, the tendency to favor members of our own group 
over outsiders (see, for example, Everett et al. 2015). Persson and Savulescu (2012) argue that 
our evolved moral psychology, designed for life in small, close-­knit groups, is inadequate for the 
complexities of the modern world. Given the challenges of global warming and weapons of 
mass destruction, they contend that moral enhancement is urgently needed for the survival of 
the human race. However, even if we agree on the necessity and urgency of moral enhance-
ment, the most appropriate methods for achieving it remain a matter of debate.
The first and most obvious way of moral enhancement is through traditional 
means –­ education, socialization, and the establishment of social and legal norms. In contrast, 
bioenhancement uses biological and technological means, such as pharmacological 
interventions, genetic engineering, neurotechnology, and hormonal treatments, to directly 
influence the cognitive and emotional capacities related to morality. The ethical debate about 
moral 
enhancement 
(Douglas 
2008, 
2013; 
Harris 
2016; 
Persson 
and 
Savulescu  2008,  2012,  2013; Rakić  2014,  2017) usually revolves around moral

Opportunities and Challenges
